content:
Several  polls of US voters taken around the recent midterm elections show that an overriding concern about the Trump administration is corruption.
Just days after the midterms, senior figures in the Democratic Party were quick to proclaim that they will be investigating corruption accusations when they take their seats in January.
It's highly likely that many of those investigations will center on the Trump administration's and the Trump family's links to wealthy Middle Eastern countries.
"The incoming Democratic majority in Congress will no doubt aggressively use their powers to investigate the administration's alleged wrongdoings," Amy Hawthorne, a non-resident fellow at the Washington-based think tank, the Arab Center, wrote in a commentary after the midterms. "Cases involving the Middle East will be their top targets."
Financial disclosures made by President Trump in the middle of this year showed that during 2025, his businesses made about $2 billion in income. This was triple the income he reported the previous year, observers noted.
"According to the information available … Middle Eastern countries and businesses have directly contributed to the bottom line of Trump's family businesses — more so than any other region of the world," Brian Katulis, a senior fellow and expert in US foreign policy at the Middle East Institute in Washington, wrote in a July text after the presidential disclosure. "Gulf entities paid around $300 million to the president's businesses in 2025."
Billions in cryptocurrency
A lot of the money Trump made in 2025 came from the sale of a stake in a cryptocurrency company, World Liberty Financial, Katulis noted.
The company was founded by the Trump and Witkoff families in 2024 — Steve Witkoff is Trump's special envoy to the Middle East — and in 2025, a large portion of it was sold to an investment firm backed by a senior United Arab Emirates official, Sheikh Tahnoon bin Zayed Al Nahyan. The latter serves as the UAE's national security advisor and is also the brother of the UAE's president.
The deal was done in January 2026 behind closed doors, shortly before Trump's inauguration as president. In May 2026, the US agreed to allow the UAE access to advanced artificial intelligence chips, despite objections from some national security advisers.
Trump's critics allege a connection, the Trump administration denies it.
There are also other alleged instances of Trump administration corruption with links to the Middle East.
Trump Towers in the Middle East
Various Trump deals with Saudi and Emirati real estate developers are also being questioned because of possible conflicts of interest.
The Gulf real estate developers, which have close ties to their governments and respective royal families, have agreed to build Trump-branded golf resorts, hotels, mansions, skyscrapers and towers in Saudi Arabia, the UAE, Qatar and the Maldives.
In 2025, Trump reported $59.5 million in foreign real estate licensing income, ten times more than he made in 2023, business media outlet CNBC reported in August. Nearly two-thirds of that money came from projects in the Gulf, CNBC said.
Ethics watchdogs argue that, "the deals create conflicts between Trump's political leadership role and private interests" because some of those Gulf states and their developers were also "pursuing major US investments, seeking government permits or pressing for favorable economic and diplomatic relations."
Qatar's flying gift
When the Qatari royal family gifted Trump a luxury jet , worth around $400 million, in May 2025, politicians and ethics experts asked about the propriety of taking such a pricey present from a foreign government.
After his presidency ends, Trump was apparently planning to donate the plane to his Florida-based project, the Donald J. Trump Presidential Library Foundation. Currently, it is unclear whether the Qatari plane will end up there and there's been speculation Trump will try to keep it for personal use.
The library is a non-profit and has received tens of millions in funding — an investigation by the CBS network traced over $100 million in donations — from lawsuits and via corporate donors.
Democratic Senator Elizabeth Warren has already said the library project would be investigated. "Giant corporations and foreign governments should not be able to buy influence in Washington with donations to the president's library," she told CBS.
Gaza's 'Board of Peace'
Plans for the so-called Board of Peace were created in September 2025 and the body was to facilitate a ceasefire and reconstruction in Gaza.
It was set up to be a kind of multilateral international organization, similar to the United Nations, except that Trump would serve as its chairman indefinitely and member countries donating $1 billion if they want to sit on the board permanently.
The Board of Peace has not achieved much in Gaza, experts say, and there have been several worrying developments.
Four months after its establishment, the World Bank account set up to manage Board of Peace funds was empty, the Financial Times newspaper reported in May . Instead, money had been deposited into a private JP Morgan bank account, over which there was no oversight.
There have apparently been contributions of around $3 million from Morocco and $20 million from the UAE, as well as pledges of $7 billion from board members and $10 billion from Trump.
The board's legal status was also changed to make it into an international non-governmental organization. This change in legal status may aim "to avoid US congressional oversight and keep much of its activity opaque," Zaha Hassan, an attorney and senior fellow at the Carnegie Endowment for International Peace, warned in a June commentary . It also "gives Trump ultimate decision-making authority, including over financial matters," she noted.
'Trump crime family'
"The Trump crime family is the top of our investigative priorities," the most senior Democrat on the House Oversight Committee, Robert Garcia, said after the midterms .
And he has already expressed concerns about the behavior of Trump's son-in-law Jared Kushner in the Middle East.
Most of the issues around Kushner involve potential conflicts of interest. Kushner is acting as a volunteer envoy in the Middle East and has been deeply involved in negotiations to end the Gaza conflict and the Iran war.
In early October, CNN published an investigation that detailed links between Kushner's private equity company, Affinity Partners, and investments into leading Israeli military manufacturers.
It's also been reported that while he was travelling in the region, Kushner was trying to raise billions for his equity firm.
In March, Democratic politicians, including Garcia, wrote letters to the president's office, saying they had "serious concerns about whether the White House is letting Mr. Kushner use his influence for personal financial gain."
The potentially most damaging claims against Kushner come from a recent book, "Prince and Thieves," published late October by American investigative journalist Matthew Cole.
Cole alleges, "Kushner worked with the UAE to shape US policy across the Middle East and that, in the course of this work, he was given access to bank accounts containing roughly $2 billion," the New York Times wrote in its review .
Kushner denies the allegations about any such slush fund held by an Israeli bank and has threatened to sue Vanity Fair  magazine, which published excerpts from the book.
But, as the New York Times concluded, "Cole's work is sufficiently calm, detailed and forensic to necessitate a large-scale and urgent congressional inquiry."

content:
US President Donald Trump announced on Friday that his deputy chief of staff and architect of his administration's strict immigration policy, Stephen Miller, will become his new chief of staff.
Miller replaces Susie Wiles, who had been in the post since Trump's second inauguration in January 2025. With the nod, Miller becomes the top aide to the president.
Trump announced the move by saying Miller was "one of my most trusted advisers," adding that Wiles has done an outstanding job and would be "moving over" to the "Trump political operation."
"He gets it" and is "very good politically. And he's a very good man. He'll do a great job, great manager," Trump said.
Wiles also commented on her exit from the White House, saying that her work there was "the honor of a lifetime."
The move comes after Trump's Republican Party lost control of the House and Senate after a midterm election rout at the hands of Democrats .
One of Trump's longest-serving aides
The 41-year-old Miller is one of Trump's longest-serving advisers , having joined Trump's long-shot 2016 presidential campaign as a speechwriter.
Although his portfolio as deputy chief of staff was wide-ranging, Miller is most responsible for Trump's policies and rhetoric on immigration.
Miller's appointment is a signal that Trump intends to continue on with his hard-line immigration policies, despite voters rejecting Republicans around the country.
Miller is known for taking controversial positions and is one of the Trump administration's most vocal advocates, frequently making media appearances to defend extreme positions.
A controversial figure
On immigration, Miller's ideas have included calling for federal agents to make 3,000 arrests every day, while allowing the agency to target migrants who have lived in the US for decades. He is widely created with helping expand the remit of Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) .
When ICE comes knocking: the fight against Trump's deportations

On foreign policy, Miller has defended extrajudicial strikes on boats in Caribbean Sea allegedly used by drugs smugglers, and defended the administration's military operation to snatch Venezuelan leader Nicolas Maduro in January.
Also in January, Miller went on broadcaster CNN and claimed that the US had the right the seize Greenland , after Trump said controlling the Danish territory was a strategic necessity.
"We live in the real world, Jake, that is governed by strength, that is governed by force, that is governed by power. These are the iron laws of the world since the beginning of time," Miller told CNN host Jake Tapper.
Miller also has not held back on attacking the administration's opponents.
During the midterm campaign, Miller called Democrats "extremists, freaks and America-hating lunatics" on social media.
He also promoted claims about election fraud in California and Alaska, which were not substantiated.
As Trump has lost control of both chambers of Congress, Miller has been credited with working in the background to create an obstructionist strategy for the White House to block Democratic legislation. Trump has taken to the strategy and has said, "I guess I'll become Mr. Veto."
Democrats vow to 'fight' Miller's agenda
After Trump's announcement, New York Democratic Congressman Hakeem Jeffries, who could become the next speaker of the House, posted on social media that Miller was a "dangerous xenophobe and reckless extremist who has American blood on his hands," referring to the deaths of US citizens protesting ICE raids.
Senator Chuck Schumer issued a statement saying the Trump had "learned nothing" after the Republican's election drubbing.
"Stephen Miller is the architect of the most barbaric, inhumane policies of this administration," said Schumer, who is positioned to become the next Senate majority leader in January.
"Trump couldn't have made a worse choice. Our Democratic majorities will fight him every step of the way," he said.

content:
Could Trump's veto stop the Democratic majority?
United States President Donald Trump has announced that Stephen Miller is replacing Susie Wiles as White House chief of staff.
In a post on his Truth Social account on Friday, Trump said Miller would start his new job on Monday, calling him “one of my most trusted advisors”.
“Susie Wiles, who has done an outstanding job, will be moving over to the Trump Political Operation. I want to thank her for her service as Chief of Staff — She has done a great job!”
Wiles, the most high-profile departure yet from the White House after Republicans’ overwhelming midterm losses, said Friday would be her last day.
“Serving President Trump in the White House has been the honour of a lifetime”, she wrote in a social media post. “I’m so proud to have been a part of what we’ve accomplished together, from securing our border and cutting taxes to strengthening our economy and putting America First”.
Al Jazeera learned that Wiles, who oversaw Trump’s return to the presidency in 2024, handed her resignation to Trump in the White House’s Oval Office on Thursday. A Republican Party official confirmed it was accepted by the president, who has since said he wanted to make a change.
Miller has been one of Trump’s closest confidants throughout both presidential terms, after joining the president’s first election campaign as an adviser in 2016.
Democrats are widely expected to launch investigations into Miller upon taking control of the US House of Representatives and Senate in January.
“Just days after the American people rejected his corrupt and lawless presidency, Donald Trump is doubling down,” Democratic Congressman Robert Garcia, the likely incoming chairman of the US House’s Oversight Committee, said in a statement to Al Jazeera. “Oversight Democrats will continue to investigate Miller for his misconduct, and we will fight against his hateful policies in Congress and the courts.”
He added, “Stephen Miller should lawyer up”.
Trump was widely expected to shake up his staff after the midterm drubbing, which saw Democrats net seven US Senate seats, with two states, Alaska and Mississippi, still counting their results. Democrats, as of Friday, have also won 253 seats in the 435-member US House, with 27 races still set to be counted.
Despite the vote, which was widely viewed as a referendum on Trump, Miller’s appointment largely represents a doubling down on his most controversial policies, offering a potential view of the course the president plans to chart for his final two years in office.
Miller, a domestic adviser to the president, has been the driving force behind some of the Trump administration’s most controversial policies, including its far-reaching immigration crackdown in the US.
Garcia called Miller “the architect of the unconstitutional ICE raids that have terrorised our communities and kidnapped and killed American citizens and immigrant families”.
Some White House staff members immediately praised the announcement soon after it was announced.
“Stephen Miller is a Trump OG, someone who has been with the President since the very beginning”, White House communications director Steven Cheung posted on X. “There is no bigger advocate for the Trump agenda than Stephen, and he will help the Administration deliver on monumental victories for the rest of this historic second term”.
Miller has not yet commented on the election results, but on election day, he urged Trump supporters to vote in a post on X.
“Send a message to the corrupt media, corrupt Democrats and corrupt left-wing politicians who want to steal your future and destroy the inheritance of your children,” he wrote. “Get to the polls and protect the ones you love.”

En Haïti, "depuis l’arrivée des forces salvadoriennes, les gangs semblent paniqués"
Le déploiement de troupes salvadoriennes contre les gangs suscite un espoir chez une partie de la population haïtienne, comme le rapportent nos Observateurs. Dans les territoires qu'ils contrôlent, les gangs chercheraient à empêcher toute expression de soutien à l'opération menée par le président Nayib Bukele.
Publié le : Modifié le :
Environ 2 000 militaires salvadoriens ont été déployés en Haïti depuis la fin du mois d’octobre. Le président salvadorien Nayib Bukele justifie cette opération par la recherche de quatre ressortissants de son pays, portés disparus depuis le 18 octobre, après l’attaque de leur véhicule blindé à Croix-des-Bouquets, au nord-est de Port-au-Prince, la capitale du pays.
Les quatre hommes, des techniciens militaires affectés à la Force de répression des gangs (FRG), une mission internationale autorisée par le Conseil de sécurité de l’ONU en 2025, auraient été attaqués dans une zone contrôlée par plusieurs groupes armés, dont les gangs Chèn Méchan et 400 Mawozo.
Pour afficher ce contenu YouTube, il est nécessaire d'autoriser les cookies de mesure d'audience et de publicité.
Une extension de votre navigateur semble bloquer le chargement du lecteur vidéo. Pour pouvoir regarder ce contenu, vous devez la désactiver ou la désinstaller.
Depuis le début de l’intervention militaire salvadorienne, de violents affrontements ont lieu entre les soldats salvadoriens et les gangs dans la zone où les techniciens militaires ont disparu. Pourtant, les habitants dont la rédaction des Observateurs a recueilli les témoignages accueillent favorablement l’arrivée des troupes de Bukele. Un soutien qu’ils n’osent toutefois pas exprimer publiquement, par crainte des représailles.
"Il est presque interdit de prononcer le nom du président salvadorien à haute voix"
Daniel* habite à la Croix-des-Bouquets, le quartier de la capitale où les techniciens salvadoriens ont été attaqués. Il témoigne du climat de tension qui y règne :
“Il est presque interdit de prononcer le nom du président salvadorien à haute voix dans la zone. Il y a des gens qui sont très contents de cette intervention mais qui ne peuvent pas l’exprimer.”
Malgré l’intensification des affrontements à proximité de son domicile, notre Observateur se dit favorable à l’intervention salvadorienne :
“ Je suis très content de cette opération. J’ai hâte que nous retrouvions notre liberté. Les gangs sont en très grande difficulté, ils ont perdu beaucoup de gens [il n’est pas possible d’établir de façon indépendante combien de membres de gangs seraient morts depuis le début de l’intervention salvadorienne, NDLR]. Ils craignent davantage les Salvadoriens que la FRG et les forces haïtiennes. Les Salvadoriens sont mieux équipés : ils disposent notamment d’hélicoptères de combat et d’un plus grand nombre de véhicules blindés.”
Pour afficher ce contenu X (Twitter), il est nécessaire d'autoriser les cookies de mesure d'audience et de publicité.
Il explique que les habitants sont pris en otage par les gangs :
“Les bandits armés surveillent tout le monde. S'ils te surprennent avec un téléphone, ce sera l’exécution directe. S'enfuir n’est pas facile. S'ils te surprennent avec une mallette par exemple, les gangs te posent des questions. Les jeunes se cachent pour ne pas être obligés de combattre.”
Selon lui, comme plusieurs habitants contactés par notre rédaction, les gangs contraindraient les habitants à participer à des manifestations contre l’intervention salvadorienne, comme celle qui a eu lieu le 2 novembre à Canaan, au nord de Port-au-Prince.
Pour afficher ce contenu X (Twitter), il est nécessaire d'autoriser les cookies de mesure d'audience et de publicité.
"Les gangs sont inquiets face à cette intervention"
Marie Yolène Gilles, fondatrice de la Fondasyon Je Klere (FJKL), un organisation de défense des droits humains, est du même avis :
“Ce sont les gangs qui ont organisé cette manifestation et forcé les gens à y prendre part. Cela montre à quel point ils sont inquiets face à cette intervention.”
Pour elle, un signe de cette panique est l'initiative prise par Wilson Joseph, alias Lanmo Sanjou, chef du gang 400 Mawozo, qui contrôle le secteur de Croix-des-Bouquets, d’envoyer une lettre au secrétaire général de l’ONU. Datée du 1er novembre, celle-ci demande l’envoi d’une délégation chargée de faciliter un dialogue et une médiation en Haïti.
Lanmo Sanjou figure sur la liste des personnes sanctionnées par le Conseil de sécurité des Nations Unies pour son implication dans de graves violations des droits humains en Haïti. Son groupe est associé à la coalition Viv Ansanm, une alliance de plusieurs gangs armés haïtiens, désignée comme organisations terroristes étrangères (FTO) par les Etats-Unis.
Marie Yolène Gilles dénonce la manœuvre de Lanmo Sanjou :
“C’est un groupe terroriste qui essaie de se faire passer pour un groupe armé non étatique respectueux du droit international humanitaire (DIH). Il dit vouloir la paix, ils ont oublié les crimes qu’ils ont commis, ce sont des choses qu’il faut juger au nom de la loi. Les gangs veulent négocier pour bénéficier de l'amnistie, mais comment peut-on amnistier des criminels comme ceux de Viv Ansanm?”
Marie Yolène Gilles explique que son association n'a, pour l'heure, pas été en mesure de confirmer l'existence de victimes civiles collatérales dans les affrontements entre les gangs et les forces salvadoriennes. Les difficultés à communiquer avec les habitants, liées notamment aux coupures de réseau et à la surveillance exercée par les groupes armés, compliquent la collecte d'informations et la vérification des faits.
Elle rappelle l’urgence de créer un couloir humanitaire et appelle le gouvernement Haïtien à prendre en charge les déplacements de personnes vivant dans la zone concernée par les affrontements.
Elle aussi espère que la présence des militaires salvadoriens va amener un changement dans le pays:
“Haïti est plongé depuis plusieurs années dans un conflit armé interne et une grave crise sécuritaire. L’État a fait appel à des mercenaires étrangers, sans obtenir de résultats. Les différentes missions internationales n’ont pas non plus réussi à rétablir la sécurité. Le président Bukele a réussi à démanteler les gangs dans son pays. Nous espérons que son intervention en Haïti produira des résultats. Depuis l’arrivée des forces salvadoriennes, les gangs semblent paniqués.”
Dans un communiqué du 4 novembre 2026, la Fondasyon Je Klere (FJKL) demande au gouvernement de rompre le contrat avec les mercenaires étrangers et d’utiliser les fonds alloués dans un programme de formation de jeunes soldats haïtiens avec l’appui des soldats salvadoriens.
La stratégie de Nayib Bukele et la durée de son engagement militaire en Haïti restent incertaines. Initialement déployées pour retrouver les quatre techniciens salvadoriens disparus le 18 octobre à Croix-des-Bouquets, les forces salvadoriennes semblent avoir élargi leurs opérations à la lutte contre les gangs. Le véhicule des techniciens a été retrouvé calciné, mais il n’y a aucune trace des quatre hommes.
Pour afficher ce contenu X (Twitter), il est nécessaire d'autoriser les cookies de mesure d'audience et de publicité.
Wilson Joseph, alias Lanmo Sanjou, ainsi que certains habitants de Croix-des-Bouquets, affirment qu'ils seraient morts. Les autorités haïtiennes et salvadoriennes estiment toutefois qu'ils pourraient être retenus en otage. Le président Bukele a menacé d'intensifier les opérations si les techniciens ne sont pas libérés vivants et indemnes.
*Son nom a été modifié à sa demande, pour préserver son anonymat.

content:
Armed men thought to be linked to an ISIL (ISIS)-affiliated group have raided villages in eastern Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC), killing dozens of people, according to authorities and civil society groups.
The attackers also set fire to a health post during their overnight assault on Cantine, about 50km west of Beni in North Kivu province, forcing patients with confirmed and suspected Ebola infections to flee.
Fighters with the Allied Democratic Forces (ADF) armed group set fire to several houses and killed civilians, Beni territorial administrator Colonel Charles Omeonga told the Reuters news agency on Friday.
Justin Paluku, head of a local civil society group, also blamed the ADF for the attack.
“So far, we have counted 33 bodies and more than 50 houses set on fire, along with various other forms of material destruction,” he told the AP news agency.
Tchetche Aliamini, another local civil society leader, confirmed the death toll to Reuters and said that most of the victims suffered gunshot wounds, while others had been burned or hacked with machetes.
The violence forced many villagers to flee to other parts of the province, where the fastest-spreading Ebola outbreak in history is raging.
Among those who fled were 180 patients from the local hospital, including suspected Ebola cases and one confirmed Ebola case, said Christian Kakule, medical director of the Kelekele Hospital Centre in Cantine.
“High-risk contacts and other individuals under monitoring have all fled,” he said. “Our concern is that when probable cases end up out in the open like this, they can become a source of transmission and trigger an outbreak of the disease.”
He said there was gunfire and homes were set ablaze as close as 50 metres from the hospital.
North Kivu currently accounts for almost half of all new infections in the DRC’s Bundibugyo outbreak and is the second most affected province after the epicentre, Ituri.
North Kivu was the epicentre of three previous Ebola outbreaks, including one in 2018-2020, which until this year was the DRC’s largest and deadliest.
The Africa Centres for Disease Control and Prevention (Africa CDC) has recorded more than 10,000 cases and 5,300 Ebola deaths across the DRC.
The ADF, which has roots in Uganda and pledged allegiance to ISIL in 2019, has long operated in the border region and routinely attacks civilians. In July 2025, it killed 66 people in eastern DRC in what the United Nations called a “bloodbath”.
About 100 other armed groups operate in the DRC, most prominently the Rwanda-backed M23, which has seized key cities in the east of the country while Ebola cases increase.
“This represents a major security failure,” Paluku, of the civil society group, told AP. “Given the number of loyalist and security forces deployed in this area, it is incomprehensible how the enemy managed to bypass their defences to kill civilians and inflict such significant material and human casualties.”
summary: Locals blame ADF armed group, which pledged allegiance to ISIL in 2019, for the deadly raids on North Kivu villages.

content:
Stephen Miller, Donald Trump’s most controversial aide and the architect of his sweeping immigration crackdown, will become his new White House chief of staff days after Republicans lost control of the US Congress in US midterm elections.
The president announced the extraordinary appointment on Friday, confirming that Susie Wiles – his current chief of staff, and the first woman to serve in the role – had been ousted.
In a social media post, Trump called Miller, 41, “one of my most trusted advisors” and praised Wiles for doing “an outstanding job”. Miller will begin on Monday.
Wiles, 69, reportedly handed in her resignation on Thursday night and said in a social media post that serving Trump “has been the honor of a lifetime”.
Holding an umbrella, Trump emerged from the White House South Portico on Friday for a trip to Florida. “I wanted to make a change,” he said. “I think Susie’s done a very good job ... Stephen’s been great, and we’ve got to make moves.”
“Stephen’s been with me from the beginning. He gets it,” the president said. “Very good politically and he’s a very good man. He’ll do a great job. Great manager.”
Trump then boarded the Marine One helicopter, followed by Miller, secretary of state Marco Rubio and close aide Natalie Harp.
In a statement, Wiles added: “I’m so proud to have been a part of what we’ve accomplished together from securing our border and cutting taxes to strengthening our economy and putting America First.”
She said her commitment to “the President and the mission” will not change.
Miller posted on X that he was “honored beyond words” to serve as Trump’s chief of staff. He added: “The mission now is more clear than ever: Fight with all of our soul to support our President and defend this magnificent Republic.”
But a growing chorus of Democrats condemned the appointment.
Hakeem Jeffries, who is poised to become the first Black speaker of the House, posted: “Stephen Miller is a dangerous xenophobe and reckless extremist who has American blood on his hands. His presence in government should be eradicated like a malignant tumor. Fire him today.”
Chuck Schumer, likely to be the next majority leader of the Senate, wrote: “Donald Trump learned nothing from his historic defeat. Stephen Miller is the architect of the most barbaric, inhumane policies of this administration. Trump couldn’t have made a worse choice. Our Democratic majorities will fight him every step of the way.”
Miller’s appointment is the first sign of a shake-up at the White House following Republicans’ catastrophic defeat in the midterms. His record as a far-right firebrand implies that Trump is preparing for an aggressive fight against congressional Democrats’ oversight and investigations.
Chris Whipple, author of The Gatekeepers: How the White House Chiefs of Staff Define Every Presidency, told CNN: “It’s almost a declaration of war by Trump … He [Miller] only knows one gear and that’s full-throttle, full steam ahead over the cliff.”
David Axelrod, a veteran Democratic strategist, added on X: “For those who hoped the @POTUS might pivot to work with the incoming Congress, the appointment of Miller is a bucket of ICE cold water.”
Miller is one of the most polarising figures in the administration and one of Trump’s closest and longest-serving advisers, having joined his 2016 presidential campaign as a speechwriter. He is a former aide to the former senator Jeff Sessions of Alabama, who would go on to serve as Trump’s first attorney general.
In Trump’s first term, Miller was the driving force behind policies such as family separation and a travel ban on Muslim-majority countries. More than a hundred Democrats in Congress signed a letter to Trump calling Miller a “documented white nationalist” and demanding his removal.
A biography of Miller, written by journalist Jean Guerrero in 2020, was entitled Hatemonger.
after newsletter promotion
Miller has served as deputy chief of staff since Trump’s return to the presidency in January 2025. He had been hugely influential in hardline immigration policies and demanding an end to birthright citizenship. He is also one Trump’s most ardent, outspoken and pugnacious defenders.
Appearing on Sean Hannity’s Fox News show on Monday, just before the midterms, Miller said of the president: “He saved America from a corrupt political class. He saved America from open borders. He saved America from countries that want the American way of life to end, from foreign adversaries, from domestic adversaries.”
Miller added: “President Trump took a bullet for you, he bled for you, he faced life in prison for you. And what he needs from you tomorrow is your vote.”
Wiles is the longest-serving White House chief of staff for Trump, who cycled through four of them during his first four-year term.
Wiles led Trump’s 2024 presidential campaign to victory and was credited with bringing discipline to a chaotic effort and clamping down on leaks from his second administration.
The Florida operative generally shunned the limelight. At Trump’s 2024 election night victory party, she repeatedly shook her head and avoided the microphone as Trump tried to coax her to speak to the crowd.
But Wiles made headlines last year when Vanity Fair magazine published a series of interviews with her and other top Trump administration officials. Her comments stood out for their candour, including her observation that Trump has an “alcoholic’s personality”.
Her departure came months after she indicated she no longer showed evidence of breast cancer after she underwent months of treatment for the disease. She went public with the diagnosis in March.
Critics said Miller’s appointment showed that Trump had learned the wrong lessons from Tuesday’s electoral reckoning.
Becca Balint, a Democratic congresswoman from Vermont, posted on X: “On Tuesday, the American people rose up and overwhelmingly voted in opposition to the disgusting and inhumane policies of this second Trump administration. What does Trump do? He promotes Stephen Miller – the architect of some of this administration’s worst decisions. Sickening.”
Anthony Scaramucci, who had a brief spell as White House communications director during Trump’s first term, tweeted: “Trump saw the midterm results and decided elevating Stephen Miller is the answer. 🤣 He is even more delusional than I thought. Or maybe he actually wants to finish destroying the @GOP? 🤔”
summary: US president confirms Susie Wiles, current chief of staff and first woman to serve in the role, will step down Stephen Miller, Donald Trump’s most controversial aide, and the architect of his sweeping immigration crackdown, will become his new White House chief of staff. The US president announced the extraordinary appointment on Friday, confirming that Susie Wiles – his current chief of staff, and the first woman to serve in the role – would be stepping down on Monday. content:
Stephen Miller, one of Donald Trump’s fiercest allies and architect of the administration’s hardline deportation agenda, will now be the White House chief of staff. The role is a promotion for Miller, who currently serves as an adviser. Trump said that Miller will start the job on Monday 9 November, less than a week after Republicans’ crushing defeat in the midterm elections.
Wiles will now take a role in Trump’s political operation, which includes his Super Pac Maga Inc. On social media, she said that serving the president has been “the honor of a lifetime”. Wiles has been in the president’s orbit for over a decade, and prior to her role at the White House, she managed, alongside Chris LaCivita, Trump’s winning 2024 presidential campaign.
Trump later told reporters that he decided to promote Miller because he“wanted to make a change”. He praised Wiles, and said that Miller had been by his side “from the beginning”. “Sometimes in life you have to make moves,” the president said.
Meanwhile, Democrats blasted Trump’s decision, after Republicans faced a drubbing in the midterm elections. Chuck Schumer, the Senate minority leader, said that the president “learned nothing from his historic defeat”, and Congressman Robert Garcia – poised to be the chair of the House oversight committee – advised Miller to “lawyer up”. Garcia said that in the majority, Democrats on his panel will “continue to investigate [Stephen] Miller for his misconduct, and we will fight against his hateful policies in Congress and the courts”.
This concludes our live coverage of the second and final Trump administration at the end of a momentous week. We leave you with the news:
The elevation of Stephen Miller, the architect of Donald Trump’s brutal and unpopular mass deportation agenda, to White House chief of staff suggests that the president has no intention of rolling back the crackdown, even after voters delivered a sweeping rebuke by electing Democrats to every House seat along the US border with Mexico.
While Trump’s hardline supporters were thrilled, there was bipartisan dismay at the news. “Stephen Miller belongs nowhere near the Oval Office,”the NAACP president said. “He belongs before a judge. He’s a thug who will be remembered as the architect of Trump’s vile and authoritarian regime.”
Republican congressman Marlin Stutzman, who said on Wednesday, “I think Stephen Miller should be fired this morning”, told Semafor appointing Miller was a “horrible decision.”
Senator Chris Murphy was released from a hospital on Friday following treatment for a stroke and plans to spend several weeks at a rehabilitation center as he works to recover, the Connecticut Democrat said in a statement.
Multiple reporters said that the phrase “wartime consigliere” had been used by the White House to describe Miller, which is a reference to what a close adviser to mafia boss is called in The Godfather. The phrase has been used repeatedly in recent years by people close to Trump to describe what he is looking for in a right-hand man, who will use slash-and-burn tactics to defend him at all costs.
White House produces taxpayer-funded ad promoting Stephen Miller
As social networks continue to fill with anger at the selection of Stephen Miller as White House chief of staff, the White House released a taxpayer-funded ad to promote the Trump aide, in the form of a hype video starring the man himself posted on official government social media accounts.
The Associated Press reports that the US secret service said a suspect has been taken into custody and charged after officers found him in a vehicle near the White House with multiple guns, claiming he heard voices in his head telling him to kill Donald Trump.
The arrest Thursday night happened after secret service officers approached a man “acting suspicious” in a parked car, according to a Homeland Security statement. US officials said the suspect – identified as Ronny Yordrix Guanipa Chrinos – went on to describe voices in his head that were telling him to come to the nation’s capital and kill the Republican president.
Progressive Democrat Aisha Wahab wins a full term to represent California’s 14th congressional district
Progressive Democrat Aisha Wahab has been re-elected to Congress to represent California’s 14th congressional district, defeating fellow Democrat Melissa Hernandez, for a House seat formerly held by Eric Swalwell, who resigned in April over sexual misconduct allegations he has denied.
Wahab, a former California state senator, previously won a special election to serve out the rest of Swalwell’s term in August, when she also beat Hernandez, the president of the board of directors for the Bay Area Rapid Transit agency.
The White House says Miller's is Trump's 'wartime consigliere'
After his speech in Florida on Friday, a reporter asked Donald Trump about a phrase White House officials are using to explain his choice of Stephen Miller as his new chief of staff.
“Mr President, there’s people describing Stephen Miller as your ‘wartime consigliere’ – do you agree with that characterization?” the reporter asked.
“Well, he’s a great fighter,” Trump replied. “He’s been with me right from the beginning, 2015, he was with me from before 2016, 2015, and he’s very loyal, smart, does a great job. He’s been an MVP every year. He’s been just great. So we’re very happy with him – and he’s gotten great reviews.”
Stephen Miller struck a typical pose while lecturing reporters in the Oval Office in October. Photograph: Kevin Lamarque/Reuters
That final remark was perhaps an indication of just how cloistered the president is, given that there has been widespread anger at dismay at his choice of Miller from Democrats and some Republicans, but the White House issued a press release on the appointment which claimed “The news was met with widespread praise”, followed by quotes lauding Miller from five dozen current and former administration officials, Republican lawmakers and pundits.
Multiple reporters said that the phrase “wartime consigliere” had been used to describe Miller by White House sources on Friday, which is a reference to what a close adviser to mafia boss is called in The Godfather.
The phrase has been used repeatedly in recent years by people close to Trump to describe what he is looking for in a right-hand man, who will use slash-and-burn tactics to defend him at all costs.
In 2020, Matt Gaetz, a Republican congressman from Florida at the time who was later Trump’s first choice to be attorney general in his second term, told the New York Times that Trump’s choice of Mark Meadows as his fourth White House chief of staff was “a great move” since “he’s a great wartime consigliere and we’re heading into election season.”
In 2023, as Trump faced multiple criminal investigations, Steve Bannon described his legal adviser Boris Epshteyn as “a wartime consigliere.”
The role Trump seems to be looking to fill is one that was first played in his life by Roy Cohn, his former personal lawyer and fixer, who had been a top aide to senator Joseph McCarthy during investigations into supposed communist infiltration of the US government in the 1950s.
It was Cohn who had first advised Trump in 1973 to respond to the federal government’s allegation that Trump and his father had violated laws against racial discrimination in housing by refusing to rent to Black tenants, by going on the offensive and countersuing the government for $100bn.
In 2017, when the support for Trump’s campaign from the Russian government was under investigation, Trump was enraged that his first attorney general, Jeff Sessions, decided to recuse himself instead of undermining the probe. “Where’s my Roy Cohn?” the president reportedly asked aides.
On Tuesday, voters resoundingly rebuked Donald Trump and his brutal mass deportation campaign that sent military tanks and masked agents though residential streets.
But on Friday, the president doubled down. He named Stephen Miller – the architect of the administration’s most aggressive immigration policies – as his chief of staff.
It was never likely that Trump – who rose to political prominence on the promise that he would expel immigrants en masse from the US – would dampen his agenda, even after voters rejected Republican candidates up and down the ballot, near and far from the southern border, in blue and deep-red states.
But the elevation of Miller – a zealous, anti-immigrant crusader who has been by Trump’s side since the president’s first term – is an ominous signal that the deportation machine that Trump has built up over the past two years will be driving ahead at full speed.
Miller more than any single other person is responsible for unleashing a series of violent immigration raids across US cities this year and last, for sending hordes of masked agents in military gear through residential streets to round up undocumented immigrants. He has pushed the administration to all but shut down legal immigration as well. In his previous roles – as a deputy chief of staff and policy adviser – he has stuck close to Trump’s side and stoked the president’s most extreme instincts.
“The elevation of Stephen Miller to White House chief of staff signals a doubling down on the administration’s cruelest impulses,” said Faisal Al-Juburi, the co-chief executive of Raíces, a Texas-based humanitarian aid and immigration services non-profit. “Miller’s promotion guarantees an acceleration of mass deportations and of brute force unleashed within our neighborhoods.”
After immigration agents shot and killed Alex Pretti, a nurse, amid immigration raids in Minneapolis, it was Miller, according to the Wall Street Journal, who raised the idea that Trump could invoke the Insurrection Act to send in military troops.
The US Department of Justice moved on Friday to dismiss the lawsuit it brought against the state of California, in which it sought to keep roughly 20,000 ballots it alleged went to noncitizens from being counted.
The supreme court ruled against the Trump administration on Monday, after several lower courts sided with California officials, who argued the federal government was seeking to interfere in state-run elections.
The request to dismiss the case comes three days after the final votes were cast in the midterm elections and about a week before a scheduled hearing where a special master would have been asked to evaluate the accuracy of the list provided by the federal government.
California officials argued that the list is out of date and includes legitimate voters — a sentiment that the federal judge presiding over the case echoed in his blistering order denying the federal government’s request.
South Carolina Democrat Nancy Lacore wins former congresswoman Nancy Mace's House seat
Democrat Nancy Lacore won her party’s 254th seat in the House, defeating Republican Jenny Costa Honeycutt in the race to replace Republican Nancy Mace in representing South Carolina’s first congressional district.
Lacore is a former Navy vice admiral who served as chief of the Navy Reserve before she was fired last year without explanation by the former Fox News weekend host Donald Trump chose as defense secretary, Pete Hegseth.
In 2024, US Navy rear admiral Nancy Lacore saluted after placing a wreath at the statue of the Lone Sailor during a ceremony in honor of the Battle of Midway in Washington DC. Photograph: Shawn Thew/EPA
Lacore’s victory ensures that the Democrats will have at least 254 seats in the next Congress, with 19 races still to be called, nine of which are led by Democrats. Republican have currently won 162 seats.
Mace chose to run for governor instead of re-election to the House, but finished a distant fifth in the Republican primary in June before starting a podcast, Get Maced, that she recently used to promote the racist conspiracy theory that “Radical Islam Is CONQUERING America From Within”.
Reading aloud from prepared remarks to NASA officials at Cape Canaveral in Florida on Friday, Donald Trump ran through a list of what he called evidence that Americans were “the greatest pioneers explorers, inventors and innovators who ever lived.”
“America is the nation that dreamed and created the modern world,” Trump said, peering at a teleprompter from beneath a USA cap. “We laid the railroads, harnessed electricity and invented the lightbulb, the telephone, the airplane, the assembly line, the television, the microchip, the personal computer, the internet, GPS, the smartphone, and almost every other thing- think of it – almost every other thing that’s worth mentioning.”
He then looked out at the audience and veered off-script to comment: “That’s a cool list, though, when you think, huh? How about a little piece of each of them? Wouldn’t that be nice? You wouldn’t be sitting here right now. You’d be someplace else.”
The president then returned to his prepared remarks, looking back at the teleprompter and saying: “We charted the human genome to cure diseases,” but stumbled badly over the word “genome” which he pronounced “guh-nome”.
Despite Trump’s attempt to claim that the US deserves credit for sequencing all the DNA in human chromosomes, the Human Genome Project was, in fact, the work of an international network of geneticists.
The president made the flub minutes after boasting about the fact that his uncle, John Trump, had been a long-tenured professor at MIT. Trump has repeatedly claimed that his uncle’s intelligence and scientific knowledge was passed on to him through his genes, giving him an innate understanding of complex scientific questions, from the novel coronavirus that caused a global pandemic in 2020 to nuclear weapons.
Trump expresses satisfaction at stock market plunge after Republican losses in midterms, deflects blame from himself
Donald Trump, remarkably, gave yet another speech on Friday, delivering remarks at the John F. Kennedy Space Center in Cape Canaveral, Florida in his official capacity as president, which were, nonetheless, threaded through with partisan political talking points.
The president emerged to the theme tune from his rallies, God Bless the USA, and mimed dancing, before starting his speech by celebrating the victories of two Florida Republicans, Byron Donalds, the governor-elect, and senator Ashley Moody.
The pair were the only two candidates Trump rallied for in the past month who won competitive races.
He then praised members of his administration who were present, singling out the US ambassador to the United Nations, Mike Waltz, for “the way you took on, the Cubans”. Waltz was recently engaged in a spat with a Cuban official at the UN which played on heavy rotation on Fox News, the president’s window on the world.
Trump then suggested that he was glad that the US stock market plunged after the Republican wipeout at the ballot box, on fears that companies building AI data centers might not be as free to push ahead with regulation by a Democratic Congress.
“Yesterday, you know, our country lost $3 trillion, all because of an election,” Trump said. “If we were to gain $3 trillion, I probably would have been more unhappy. But you know what that means; that means that they thought somebody else did well in an election.”
“By the way, I was not on the ballot, just in case you had any question,” he added. “Because if we were on the ballot, we would’ve won but we weren’t.”
Senator Chris Murphy discharged from hospital after stroke as doctor says he expects full recovery
Senator Chris Murphy was released from a hospital on Friday following treatment for a stroke and plans to spend several weeks at a rehabilitation center as he works to recover, the Connecticut Democrat said in a statement.
“Thank you for the outpouring of support my family and I have received over the last few days,” Murphy said. “I want to be direct with you, so here is my diagnosis. Last Saturday afternoon, I felt something was not right with my body and called 9-1-1 out of an abundance of caution, and I’m glad I did. I was diagnosed with a small bleed in the thalamus region of my brain.”
“The doctors are very encouraged by the progress I’ve made so far. In order to take my recovery seriously and get back to work on the quickest timeline possible, I will be spending several weeks at a rehabilitation center after being discharged from the hospital today,” he continued.
The senator also released a statement from Dr Jose Suarez, the chief of neurosciences critical care at the Johns Hopkins Hospital. “Senator Murphy experienced a small hemorrhagic stroke. He has shown tremendous progress, and at the current rate of improvement, we expect that he will make a full recovery following rehabilitation,” the doctor said.
Indiana Republican congressman reportedly calls Trump's promotion of Stephen Miller to chief of staff 'a horrible decision'
The morning after the midterm wave that swept away dozens of his colleagues, congressman Marlin Stutzman, an Indiana Republican who held his seat, told voters that Donald Trump’s mass deportation agenda was a major factor, and called on the president to fire its architect, Stephen Miller.
“The press ran with it, the Democrats ran with it, and it looked bad on us – the deportation effort,” Stutzman said on Wednesday. “President Obama deported more illegals than what President Trump has. But you know what? he didn’t he didn’t go out and talk about it the way that, you know, we did. I mean, frankly, I think Stephen Miller should be fired this morning. I mean, there needs to be some changs at hte White House.”
Asked by Semafor on Friday what he made of Trump’s decision to not fire but promote Miller, Stutzman told the outlet it was a “horrible decision.”
Several newly elected Democrats and Senator Bernie Sanders have renewed calls for datacenter moratoriums in the days after the US midterm elections. The sweeping Democratic victory, which was buoyed in part by backlash to the tech industry, has added momentum to efforts to slow down the multi-trillion-dollar buildout of the controversial facilities.
On the social media platform X, Sanders posted a call for an immediate national datacenter moratorium this week. “Americans don’t want Big Tech oligarchs wrecking the environment, gutting jobs and threatening humanity’s future,” Sanders said on Wednesday.
Sanders was joined by several Democrats, including Representative Yassamin Ansari of Arizona – a state where Elon Musk’s SpaceX has proposed a datacenter project that would span more than 700 acres.
“Top of the Democratic agenda on day 1 needs to be a pause on advanced AI development, regulation of this out of control industry, and a ban on artificial superintelligence,” Ansari posted Wednesday on X. Musk mocked her post in a retweet, and the two sparred, with Ansari forecasting congressional hearings, telling the centi-billionaire: “See you soon.”
The pushback to the buildout of datacenters, which tech companies need to power the AI products that have become central to their businesses, was one of the most visible issues of the midterms. Opposition to datacenters figured heavily in campaigns across the US, while voters passed dozens of local ballot measures aimed at restricting datacenter projects in their states.

content:
As an early stab at rules for conversation, Cicero did a fine job: watch your tone, never look bored, never lose your temper and never ramble on, particularly about yourself, he advised.
Now scientists have followed in the great orator’s footsteps and discovered a telltale signature of an enjoyable chinwag. The secret of a mutually satisfying exchange is a healthy dose of pink noise, they say.
The colour of noise tends to animate physicists more than linguists, but researchers at Dartmouth College in New Hampshire in the US found the concept provided fresh insights into what makes a good conversation.
Kathryn O’Nell, the first author on the study, said: “In physics, people talk about pink noise as existing on the edge of chaos, where you can stay at a stable point, but you’re not stuck there for ever.
“It’s particularly cool for conversation, because you can stay somewhere long enough to really get to know each other, to understand the topic, but you’re not stuck there while it gets stale.”
The researchers analysed more than 1,000 conversations between strangers, who answered questions on the chats afterwards. People enjoyed conversations more, wanted to continue chatting, and felt a stronger sense of connection when the tête-à-têtes exhibited more pink noise, they found.
To see whether the effect applied beyond strangers, the researchers ran a similar analysis on conversations between friends about their formative experiences. Again, more pink noise meant more enjoyment.
The effect had real-world consequences, too. When the scientists turned to speed-dating conversations, they found that more pink noise predicted which pairs met up for a second date. Details have been published in Science Advances.
Nailing down what makes a great chat is notoriously tricky, the researchers said. In a bold opening statement to their paper, the authors write: “Good conversation is like pornography – it is difficult to define, but we know it when we see it.”
Colloquially, people talk about being in sync, but the metaphor misses something, said Dr Emily Finn, a neuroscientist and senior author on the paper. “In sync can be incredibly dull,” she said. People can be in sync when they repeat each other’s words and circle a single subject. They might well be immensely bored.
In the study, the scientists took conversations and fed each side into an AI called MPNet. The program scored every turn of the chat on 768 different criteria, covering aspects such as meaning, tone and context. This allowed the scientists to quantify how conversations ebbed and flowed over time.
Conversations exhibit white noise when people fail to follow what has just been said: the chat might jump all over the place, or be dominated by a person who seems oblivious to the other person’s responses. Other conversations can have red noise, which arises when people mirror each other’s language and fall into a conversational rut.
Pink noise lies somewhere in between: a conversational Goldilocks zone that balances stability and flexibility. People will synchronise as they explore a topic, then drift apart as they pull in fresh ideas before converging again to explore those.
The pinkiness of a conversation depends on the people involved, but O’Nell said she suspected the skill could be learned and developed. As part of the study, the team analysed podcasts fronted by two hosts and found that the pinkiness of their conversations increased over the first 50 episodes.
Prof Elizabeth Stokoe, a conversation analyst at the London School of Economics, praised the researchers for moving beyond the idea that “more similarity is better”. But asking whether a conversation is enjoyable risks missing the point, she added.
“There’s a lovely study of a phone call in which a father and his daughter, a young woman with learning disabilities living in residential care, take a long time to say goodbye, and the ending is painful and poignant,” she said. “Reducing conversations to whether they are ‘enjoyable’ can feel bloodless, since many of the conversations that matter most in our lives are like this.”

content:
Prince Harry and five other prominent figures have launched a legal challenge against a judge’s verdict in their unsuccessful claims against the Daily Mail’s publisher, Associated Newspapers.
Harry, Doreen Lawrence, the mother of the murdered black teenager Stephen Lawrence, the singer Elton John and his husband, David Furnish, and the actors Elizabeth Hurley and Sadie Frost faced a legal bill of more than £50m after losing their case claiming that Mail journalists used unlawful methods to source stories.
In an unequivocal ruling in July, Mr Justice Nicklin dismissed their case, stating that the claimants had not proved any information had been obtained unlawfully.
His 436-page written verdict, after an 11-week trial, said it could not be inferred that a story had been obtained unlawfully if there remained a legitimate and realistic legal way in which it could have been sourced.
In a statement issued on Friday, a spokesperson for Harry and his five fellow claimants said: “We confirm that the claimants have today filed applications with the court of appeal for permission to appeal the judgments of Mr Justice Nicklin in respect of his dismissal of their claims and the indemnity costs order.
“The claimants respectfully disagree with those unprecedented decisions, which they consider to be legally and factually flawed.”
Court staff confirmed on Friday that an application to appeal against the rulings had been filed at the court of appeal.
Barristers for the claimants had alleged during the trial that private investigators, freelance journalists and staff at Associated Newspapers had carried out acts including voicemail interception, landline tapping and obtaining information by deception, also known as “blagging”.
But lawyers for the publisher said Daily Mail and Mail on Sunday journalists had provided a “compelling account of a pattern of legitimate sourcing of articles”, including friends and “leaky” social circles, press officers and spokespeople, as well as previous reporting, freelance journalists and stories from other newspapers and news agencies.
Associated’s legal team described the claims as “lurid” and “preposterous”.
after newsletter promotion
After the verdict the former Mail editor Paul Dacre said the case was a “conspiracy” orchestrated by press regulation campaigners to “destroy a paper”.
Harry and Lawrence said the verdict was a “complete and obvious whitewash”. They added: “When the court says there is not sufficient evidence of wrongdoing … then one does wonder how justice was ever going to be achieved.”
In August, Nicklin ruled that the claimants had to pay £9,544,355 within seven days as an initial contribution to the publisher’s costs before further hearings to determine the total sum.

content:
Ueno collapse raises questions about state influence and accountability.
Paraguay is engulfed in political turmoil after a banking scandal put its president and major institutions under scrutiny.
At the centre is Ueno, a fast-growing digital lender, whose collapse has left millions of people unable to access their savings. But the fallout goes beyond the banking sector.
Congress has rejected President Santiago Pena’s resignation and is pressing ahead with impeachment proceedings. He’s accused of negligence and being complicit in an alleged cover-up of the bank’s insolvency.
So, what went wrong? Were regulators compromised by political influence? And who should be held accountable?
Presenter: Dareen Abughaida
Guests:
Daniel Duarte Braga – Journalist and contributing editor to The Paraguay Post
Mariano Machado – Principal Americas analyst at global risk intelligence firm, Verisk Maplecroft
Javier Farje – Historian specialising in Latin American affairs
summary: Ueno collapse raises questions about state influence and accountability.

content:
Democrat Scott Colom is on the verge of winning a Senate seat in Mississippi in a stunning upset, but ballots are still being counted in a close race where Colom holds a lead of just under 2,000 votes over Republican incumbent Cindy Hyde-Smith. Losing ruby-red Mississippi would be the final straw for Republicans after a midterm sweep by Democrats that turned Texas blue and saw a Democrat elected to the seat once held by the late South Carolina Republican senator Lindsey Graham.
A possible legal fight is also brewing, as both sides trade sharp legal letters about the procedures for counting remaining ballots. National voting groups and attorneys have descended upon the magnolia state, joining the local groups that worked to mobilize voters. Democratic and Republican groups, including Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee (DSCC) and Democratic election attorneys from the Elias Law Group, have deployed hundreds of volunteers and lawyers to all the state’s 82 counties to oversee the final rounds of counting.
In Mississippi, voters who cast affidavit ballots on election day because they don’t have photo IDs have five business days to visit their local circuit clerk’s office to present an acceptable photo ID, or sign a religious objection affidavit. They have until 10 November to do so, which is also the last day for mail-in ballots to arrive and be counted.
Mississippi has no automatic recount law. A recount can only happen if ordered by a court in response to a lawsuit against a county or county election commission from a political party or campaign. Mississippi law does not establish a system for challenging ballots on a statewide scale, so the process would have to be county-by-county basis.
“Mississippians did their part. Now election officials must do theirs,” Nsombi Lambright-Haynes, executive director of One Voice, a local civic organization said in a statement. “Voters who followed the rules and were still turned away, moved to an affidavit ballot, or left off the rolls through no fault of their own deserve answers and action. We will not let administrative failures erase the voices of the people.”
On Thursday, the National Republican Senatorial Committee (NRSC), which represents Hyde-Smith, sent a letter to county election commissioners and circuit clerks in the state, demanding that they separate and preserve all affidavit ballots cast in the 3 November general election.
“As the democratic process continues to play out, we are committed to ensuring that every single lawful ballot is accurately counted and the voices of all Mississippians are heard,” NRSC’s ergional press secretary, Samantha Cantrell, said in a statement.
Colom’s campaign manager, Gerard Henderson, called the NRSC’s letter a “desperate stunt” in a statement.
“We’re confident that when every lawful ballot is counted, Scott Colom will be Mississippi’s next US senator,” he said.
Colom’s legal counsel sent a letter to the 82 counties, their election commissioners and their circuit clerks on Thursday, too. That letter said that the demands “have no basis in Mississippi law, and if you depart from ordinary election procedures as you have been asked to do, you will violate Mississippi voters’ rights and Mississippi election law”.
“Notwithstanding Hyde-Smith’s letter, you should therefore do as you are legally obligated to do: continue conducting this election using ordinary, lawful procedures,” the letter reads. “Do not segregate accepted affidavit ballots from other paper ballots. And certainly do not do anything that would allow a particular ballot to be traced to a particular voter, in violation of the “fundamental principle of the right to cast a secret ballot.”
On Friday, the NAACP sent its own letter to county election commissions in the state, calling on election officials to “strictly adhere to state law during the post-election ballot counting and certification process”.
“Every voter in Mississippi deserves to have their vote counted strictly according to the law,” Derrick Johnson, the NAACP’s president and CEO, said in a statement. “The NAACP is on the ground monitoring every stage of this post-election process in every corner of the State. We will be watching closely to ensure election commissioners are permitted to follow every legal procedure and every ballot is accounted for free from intimidation and threats.”
Mike Hurst, the chair of the Mississippi Republican party and general counsel of the Republican National Committee, addressed reporters in a press conference outside the Hinds county courthouse in Jackson on Thursday afternoon. He said that there could be approximately 20,000 outstanding ballots left to be counted.
While many have suggested that those ballots would likely only further boost Colom’s lead over Hyde-Smith, Hurst said: “A significant number of these, we believe, are in and remain in Republican leaning districts, precincts and counties.
“We are firm in our conviction that if the law is and was followed, that Mississippians will have spoken clearly and unequivocally and that Senator Hyde-Smith will be re-elected to another term to represent the great state of Mississippi,” Hurst said.

content:
Activists have stormed the site of a Microsoft datacentre being built in Amsterdam, as the backlash to the social and environmental harms of the AI boom spreads across Europe.
Protesters from Geef Tegengas, a Dutch direct action group, clashed with police while breaking into a construction site at Westpoort, Amsterdam, where some members climbed a crane, lit flares and tied helium balloons to equipment.
The action comes amid Europe-wide resistance to the rapid expansion of energy-hungry AI, with more than 100 groups involved in a two-day series of protests to demand moratoria on the construction of new datacentres.
The break-in at the Dutch site, where protesters hung banners objecting to Microsoft’s services to the Israeli military and US Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE), was separate from the pan-European “Stop Dirty Data Centres” campaign, which targeted the same site but whose affiliated members stayed outside the perimeter fence.
Police said in a statement to NOS, a Dutch public broadcaster: “The police attempted to prevent [the occupation] and arrest protesters, but were unable to prevent it and force was used.
“An officer was slightly injured during the protest.”
Protesters from both groups said police used force and teargas to dispel the activists trying to enter the construction site. Organisers and local media reported hundreds of protesters on each side of the fence.
Smaller protests took place in the centre of Bristol, in the UK, at a datacentre in Berlin, Germany, outside the Polish parliament in Warsaw and at the main square in Zagreb, Croatia. Further protests are expected on Saturday.
Stop Dirty Data Centres, a coalition of independent groups that include national branches of Greenpeace and Friends of the Earth, said it had not coordinated or promoted the direct action that took place in the Netherlands, but that is was “understandable” communities would turn to a range of tactics when they were unable to meaningfully participate in decision-making.
“Big tech and government are racing ahead with large-scale datacentre development despite significant public concern about the impacts on local communities, natural resources and other industries,” said Owen Espley, campaign coordinator. “Many datacentre developments are planned with limited transparency or scrutiny, while communities across Europe are being shut out of decisions that will shape their local environments and futures.”
The ecological fallout of the datacentre boom has alarmed some climate scientists, while growing frustration with AI’s societal impact – from energy bills and job losses to the role of tech companies in undermining democracy – has increased public anger. In the US midterm elections this week, nearly every proposed moratorium on datacentres on the ballot was approved.
after newsletter promotion
Roos Molenaar, an activist from Geef Tegengas, said the struggle against big tech was inseparable from the fight against oppression and fascism. “We won’t accept Amsterdam being used for the creation of AI slop and the facilitation of genocide,” said Molenaar. “This datacentre is gulping up our drinking water to make the rich even richer.”
A spokesperson for Microsoft said it was aware of the demonstration and that its first concern was the wellbeing of everyone at and around the site. “We understand that people feel strongly about the project, and we respect their right to express those views peacefully. However, we do not condone any actions that are unlawful or that put people’s safety at risk.”
A spokesperson for Pure Data Centres, the site owner, said it respected the right to peaceful protest but that entering a live construction site was unlawful and dangerous.
“Our immediate priority is everyone’s safety, and we respectfully ask those on site to leave safely and engage with us in dialogue about the development and any concerns they may have,” a Pure DC spokesperson said.
Governments across Europe have supported the building of AI datacentres to boost tax revenues and catch up with the breakneck deployment of computing power in the US and China, with some framing the AI race as a matter of national security.
But datacentres have emerged as a flashpoint for public anger over issues from environment and energy to human rights and democracy. Last week, an investigation by the Guardian and Investigate Europe found evidence of dangerous conditions for some of the workers building them.

Josep Borrell : "Quelle voix européenne s'est élevée contre Trump et la guerre en Iran ?"

Cette semaine, Caroline de Camaret reçoit Josep Borrell, ancien Haut représentant de l'Union européenne (UE) pour les Affaires étrangères jusqu'en 2024. Également président du Parlement européen entre 2004 et 2007, il a aussi été l'ancien ministre socialiste des Affaires étrangères du gouvernement de Pedro Sanchez et préside désormais le Cidob (Barcelona Centre for International Affairs). Il décrypte avec nous la colère des jeunesses européennes, les élections américaines de mi-mandat ou encore les élections anticipées en Espagne. Il dresse aussi un constat amer de la politique étrangère de l'UE dans les dernières années.
"Les problèmes sociaux de chaque pays, c'est d'abord la responsabilité de ces pays-là"
Depuis plus d'un mois, le tumulte des colères sociales résonne en Europe. Italie, Espagne, France… Si les revendications sont multiples, les Européens battent notamment le pavé contre le coût de la vie et la précarisation. Quelle est la responsabilité de l'Union européenne dans ce mécontentement ? Pour Josep Borrell, "il ne faut pas demander des pommes aux merisiers. Les problèmes sociaux de chaque pays, c'est d'abord la responsabilité de ces pays-là." Il analyse : "S'il y a une grogne, s'il y a un malaise partout en Europe, c'est pour des raisons communes à l'Europe. Mais prétendre que l'Union européenne va résoudre ça, non. En France, les problèmes que vous avez, ce sont des problèmes français. En Espagne, ce sont des problèmes espagnols. Ils ont un dénominateur commun, c'est le manque de perspective de la jeunesse. C'est le problème du logement, du coût de la vie, de la précarité. Mais ça, ce n'est pas l'Union européenne qui va les résoudre."
"Il y a un refus d'une partie des forces politiques à faire fonctionner l'État de droit"
L'Europe a également été le théâtre de plusieurs transitions politiques dans l'année écoulée, notamment en Hongrie ou en Pologne. Dans la première, le Premier ministre libéral, Péter Magyar, a organisé la destitution du président ultra-conservateur Tamas Sulyok. Mais à Varsovie, le Premier ministre ne parvient pas à faire entrer des juges indépendants au Tribunal constitutionnel, contré par un Président issu du parti ultraconservateur Droit et Justice (PiS). L'ancien chef de la diplomatie européenne observe : "Ce qu'il se passe, c'est clairement un refus d'une partie des forces politiques à faire fonctionner l'État de droit, l'État de droit tel que nous le comprenons, qui veut dire la séparation des pouvoirs, l'indépendance des juges. Partout, l'indépendance des juges devient une question."
"On retarde artificiellement l'élargissement de l'UE"
En parallèle, la question de l'élargissement de l'Union européenne continue à se poser, avec des pays comme l'Ukraine, la Moldavie ou le Monténégro qui progressent sur le chemin de l'adhésion. Mais en France, par exemple, les partis en tête pour l'élection présidentielle s'opposent à tout élargissement. Josep Borrell remarque : "Il y a très longtemps que l'élargissement bat doucement, parce qu'on sait bien qu'à la fin du chemin, il faut passer par une procédure nationale dans les États membres qui risque d'échouer (...) On ne peut pas avoir les États candidats tout le temps dans le frigidaire, retarder artificiellement la fin du processus parce qu'on a peur que les États membres ne veulent pas." En Serbie, où la Liste des Étudiants vient de renverser le président pro-russe Aleksandar Vučić, le processus d'adhésion à l'UE peut, lui aussi, reprendre. L'ancien diplomate européen tempère : "La Serbie va passer par une situation difficile parce que le parti des étudiants devra gouverner. (...) Eux, ils sont pressés, ils veulent devenir membre de l'Union européenne. (...) Il va y avoir un tournant, ou au moins, ils veulent qu'il y ait un tournant. Est-ce qu'ils vont en être capables ?"
"Que fait la Commission européenne pour empêcher que Trump se comporte ainsi ?"
Les élections américaines de mi-mandat ont été, pour Josep Borrell, "un véritable tremblement de terre". Alors que la vague bleue déferle sur la Chambre des représentants et le Sénat, les Européens espèrent que les démocrates formeront une digue face à un Donald Trump instable et de plus en plus favorable à la Russie. Josep Borrell, s'il salue cette victoire, interpelle l'Europe : "C'est bien que les électeurs américains aient voté contre Trump, clairement. Mais nous, de notre côté, il faudrait aussi faire notre partie du travail. Tout le monde se plaint de la guerre en Iran. Mais quelle voix européenne, hormis l'Espagne, s'est levée contre la guerre en Iran ?". Il déplore ainsi l'hypocrisie de certains dirigeants européens comme Giorgia Meloni qui se distancient soudainement de leur allié et note que les autorités européennes ont trop ménagé le président américain : "Je rappelle que le chancelier allemand, quand les États-Unis ont commencé à bombarder l'Iran, a dit qu'il ne voulait pas embêter ses amis américains avec des considérations mineures sur le droit international. Maintenant, on dit que (le résultat des élections, NDLR), c'est très bien. Mais vous, qu'est-ce que vous avez fait pour empêcher que Trump fasse ce qu'il fait ? Que fait la Commission européenne pour empêcher que Trump se comporte ainsi ?"
Citant également l'inaction de l'Europe sur le volet commercial et les droits de douane, il regrette le comportement de la Commission qui investit, selon lui, toujours plus aux États-Unis : "Ce n'est pas seulement les droits de douane. Les engagements qu'on a pris d'acheter plus d'armes américaines, d'investir plus dans l'économie américaine... On a le rapport Draghi qui dit que le problème, c'est que l'Europe exporte trop de capitaux vers les États-Unis. Et la présidente de la Commission européenne dit 'on va faire encore plus, on va investir plus aux États-Unis, on va acheter plus d'armes, plus de gaz.'"
Si les élections peuvent avoir des conséquences positives sur le soutien à l'Ukraine, Josep Borrell reste prudent : "Il va continuer à aimer Poutine, mais il sera un peu plus contraint. Mais il y a un droit de veto présidentiel. Et le droit de veto, il y a besoin de deux tiers des voix pour le surmonter."
"Pedro Sanchez a clamé dans le désert pour que l'Union européenne agisse"
Le 29 novembre, les Espagnols se rendront aux urnes pour une élection anticipée qui pourrait bien provoquer la chute du gouvernement Sanchez. Le Premier ministre espagnol s'est démarqué, ces dernières années, par des positions fortes sur le plan international, alors qu'il était empêtré dans divers scandales sur le plan national. Pour l'ancien ministre espagnol des Affaires étrangères, "Pedro Sanchez ne se présente pas comme l'anti-Trump. Pedro Sanchez se présente comme (le chef d') un gouvernement qui rend des comptes aux citoyens. (...) Si vous voulez juger le gouvernement espagnol du point de vue de la politique étrangère, elle est aux antipodes de celle de Vox. Le gouvernement espagnol a mené une politique étrangère un peu isolée dans l'ensemble de l'Union européenne, mais ferme et, de mon point de vue, correcte. Il a clairement dit 'ce que Netanyahu est en train de faire à Gaza, c'est un génocide'. Et il a clamé dans le désert pour que l'Union européenne agisse. La présidente de la Commission n'a rien voulu faire et la majorité des États membres non plus. C'est le seul pays qui ait dit non aux 5 % des dépenses militaires. Et il mène une politique du point de vue migration, qui est aussi très différente de celle que la droite veut imposer partout en Europe."
Avant de préciser : "Nous sommes dans une démocratie parlementaire. En Espagne, celui qui gagne, ce n'est pas celui qui reçoit le plus de voix, c'est celui qui est capable d'avoir une majorité parlementaire en faisant des coalitions avec d'autres groupes." La droite devra donc faire alliance avec le parti d'extrême-droite Vox pour gouverner.
Emission préparée par Oihana Almandoz, Perrine Desplats, Florine Hausfater, Charlotte Prudhomme et Isabelle Romero

What Trump’s midterms debacle could mean for US support for Ukraine
The Republican Party's crushing defeat in midterm elections has left Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky optimistic about future support for Kyiv and stronger transatlantic relations. But with US President Donald Trump retaining broad foreign policy powers, the Democratic majority in Congress may have limited scope to bring about substantial change.
The Democrats’ sweeping victory in US midterm elections this week is already reshaping the political map, both domestically and abroad. In Kyiv, the mood is cautiously optimistic, shared FRANCE 24’s correspondent Emmanuelle Chaze, who said Ukrainians understand that US foreign policy still runs through the White House. Few of them expect an immediate shift in how the US approaches the war with Russia, especially given US President Donald Trump’s tense relationship with Ukraine as of late.
