Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky told German public broadcaster ZDF on Thursday that Democrats were “speaking very clearly about supporting Ukraine” and “renewing the connection between the US and Europe”. He added he was hopeful to be able to push for more funding and aid with defence. While the Democrats’ control of Congress could indeed lead to financial relief for Ukraine and more sanctions on Russia, their room for manoeuvre remains limited.
Trump said Friday that a “big, beautiful agreement” to end the war is close – one he claims could involve “all of Europe” – and US-mediated talks between Russia and Ukraine are due in Abu Dhabi next week. But the European Union (EU) said “a lot of work” was still needed and EU spokeswoman Paula Pinho noted it would “obviously be up to the EU to decide on matters which affect its security”.
FRANCE 24 spoke with James M. Lindsay, a senior fellow in US foreign policy at the Council on Foreign Relations, about what the results could mean for the war in Ukraine and US-Europe relations.
FRANCE 24: Now that the Democrats have gained control of Congress, how much room will they have to push for greater support for Ukraine? And how likely is it that they will make it a priority?
James M. Lindsay: The incoming Democratic Congress will be more supportive of Ukraine than the Trump administration has been. Congressional Democrats, however, are going to find it difficult to translate their policy preferences on Ukraine into actual policy change. The reason for that is because the president of the US – despite seeing his party lose in historic fashion on election day – retains significant authority over US foreign policy.
But I would anticipate that the Democrats will put ending the war with Iran, reaffirming US support for Ukraine, and reining in President Trump's use of tariffs high on their to-do list.
Read moreTrump’s stillborn diesel deal: Why Russian oil tankers are not heading to the US
How much power does Trump hold over foreign policy and how might he leverage it following the midterms defeat?
First and foremost, the president alone decides who the United States negotiates with and what to negotiate over. Congress can have views on these issues. It can criticise the president in the hope it can persuade him to change his mind. But it cannot dictate the terms of the negotiations. So the big unknown that remains after election day – now that we know what Congress will look like in January – is how President Trump will respond.
Donald Trump prides himself as a dealmaker. Perhaps he will view the results as an opportunity to show how he can negotiate with the Democratic Congress. If so, the desire of many Democrats and many Republicans: to take a tougher line with Russia and to do more to help Ukraine, could have great success.
But if you look at President Trump, he is someone who historically when challenged, doubles down rather than backs down. So perhaps he will continue to push ahead with his policy towards Russia and hostility towards Ukraine.
What other challenges will the Democrats face trying to set their foreign policy agenda in Congress?
For Democrats, the victory on Tuesday has sent expectations soaring both inside the United States and abroad about how much a Democratic Congress will be able to redirect US foreign policy. They will find it very hard to satisfy these expectations, which could lead to very big disappointment down the road, both at home and overseas.
One challenge congressional Democrats are going to have – on Ukraine, as well as on the Iran War – is that they won the election in November, but they don't take office until the beginning of January.
Congress is going to have a hard time putting its stamp on policy – no matter how many speeches senators and representatives give, affirming their faith in things like the transatlantic relationship. So in essence, if the president decides that he is going to persist with the disruptive foreign policies he has championed during the first two years of his second term, Congress will find it difficult to rein him in.
This interview has been edited for clarity and brevity.

Chancellor Friedrich Merz's Christian Democrats (the CDU) and their Bavarian sister party, the CSU , want to nominate a joint candidate to be the next president of Germany when the special "Bundesversammlung" committee that elects one votes at the end of January.
It's long been clear that the CSU favor the current speaker of Bavaria 's parliament, Ilse Aigner, for the role.
But on Friday, multiple German news outlets like Spiegel , the Süddeutsche Zeitung and the DPA news agency cited sources in the CDU as saying that party's leadership had also decided on putting Aigner forward.
DPA reported that Merz would officially recommend Aigner as a candidate at a meeting of the CDU's leadership that will convene in Berlin on Sunday and Monday.
On the record, however, party officials would neither confirm nor deny the reports, pointing only to the upcoming meetings on Monday.
Germany's first woman as president?
If chosen, Aigner would be the 13th person and the first woman to take up the role as post-war Germany's head of state, which is a more ceremonial one with primarily symbolic power, while the bulk of the political and legislative power resides with the chancellor.
She would also be the first CSU politician to hold the office.
Aigner, 61, is currently the speaker of the state parliament in Bavaria.
The youngest of four sisters and the daughter of an electrician, she worked in the family business in her early adult life before going into politics. She's a Roman Catholic, single and has no children.
Aigner began her parliamentary career in the Bavarian legislature in 1994, then moved to the Bundestag federal parliament in 1998, before returning to the Bavarian chamber in 2013.
She spent five years as federal agriculture minister under then-Chancellor Angela Merkel.
She would also be the first CSU politician to hold the office.
Current President Frank-Walter Steinmeier , a heavy hitter for years for the Social Democrats before becoming head of state, is nearing the end of his second five-year term in the role, having assumed the office in March 2017.
What steps remain on the path to Germany picking a new president?
The CDU/CSU's junior coalition partners, the Social Democrats ( SPD ), have also made it clear they would back a presidential bid from Aigner.
"If the CDU steering committee does indeed officially assert itself on Monday and put forward Ilse Aigner, then on behalf of the SPD I can only say that we would welcome this and support it," SPD chairman Lars Klingbeil said at an event in Berlin.
A large committee known as the Bundesversammlung chooses the German president. It will vote on January 30, 2027.
It's made up of all 630 Bundestag parliament members, and another 630 people assigned to represent the various German states — weighted according to each state's share of the national population.
Most of these are regional lawmakers, but municipal politicians and people from other walks of public life are also sometimes given a vote.
The CDU/CSU and SPD combined have a majority of roughly 50 seats in the special committee.
Beyond this, Merz is expected to try to rope in support for Aigner from the Greens, a party that has long championed more female representation at the top of politics and that would not seem to have a realistic chance of propelling a candidate of its own into the role.
This suggests that if Aigner's nomination were to materialize and solidify, she should have fairly good chances of succeeding Steinmeier.

Meghan Markle's father, Thomas Markle Sr., was arrested Friday morning by federal agents in Florida on charges related to child abuse, including sexually explicit photographs of himself with prepubescent girls, US federal prosecutors said .
Thomas Markle Sr. was charged with one count of possession of child sex abuse imagery, prosecutors said in a statement.
The 82-year-old was arrested outside the city of Tampa on Florida's west coast.
The director of Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI), Kash Patel, said that "Mr. Markle allegedly targeted innocent children and sought to steal their innocence through his criminal actions."
Patel said their agents "moved quickly" to identify and locate the explicit material, and then arrested Markle Sr. in Florida.
Sex abuse images discovered in storage units
First Assistant US Attorney for central California Bill Essayli said federal agents searched two storage units in the Los Angeles area and "seized approximately 78 items, including slides, film negatives, and books" that contained suspected child sexual abuse images.
"Mr. Markle is accused of possessing child sexual abuse material, including photographs depicting himself with minor girls," said Essayli in a statement. "These allegations are extremely serious, and we will prosecute Mr. Markle to the fullest extent of federal law."
If convicted, Thomas Markle Sr. would face a statutory maximum sentence of 20 years in federal prison.
Markle Sr. was first reported to the police in the Philippines and to the FBI last month by his son, Thomas Markle Jr, after he claimed to have found child sex abuse material at his father's home in the Philippines, according to reports by the UK newspaper The Sun.
Meghan Markle , the wife of Prince Harry, recently said she was "deeply distressed" by allegations that a collection of child sexual abuse images had been found at her father's home.
She revealed that a letter containing "troubling allegations" about him had been sent to London police in 2018.
The FBI said last month that it would assist Philippine authorities with the case where possible.
Meghan's father famously didn't attend her wedding at Windsor Castle
Meghan, an American citizen who starred in the US television drama "Suits," married Harry at Windsor Castle in 2018 .
Her father did not attend their wedding, prompting extensive coverage in the British media of Meghan's estrangement from her father.
Thomas Markle Sr., a retried television lighting and photography director, was living in the Philippines earlier this year when he suffered a stroke and had his left leg amputated.
That forced him to return to the US.
"I have supported, cared for him and helped him for years — but that stops now," Markle Jr. told The Sun. " I won't speak to my father ever again unless I’m called to give evidence against him."

content:
Is the artificial intelligence (AI) gold rush coming to an end, or is this simply a reality check?
That's the question which is hanging over investors, and which has prompted steep falls on the world's stock markets.
The sell-off in the US on Thursday was most dramatic on the Nasdaq, home to tech industry titans such as Alphabet, Nvidia, Meta and Apple.
It followed sweeping gains by the Democrats in this week's midterm elections in the US, which have given the party full control of Congress.
A number of leading Democrats campaigned against the unhindered expansion of data centres, which have underpinned the growth of artificial intelligence.
Fears this will lead to more regulation of AI appear to have concerned investors. But worries about the industry's prospects have been growing for some time.
AI boom
The release of Chat GPT by Open AI in late 2022 is widely seen as having generated massive public and corporate interest in the practical uses of AI. It also sparked a modern-day gold rush.
Investors flocked to put their money into companies producing computer chips and networking infrastructure, building data centres and providing the energy to power them, as well as developing the AI itself. The value of tech companies soared.
The boom continued into this year. Investments in AI are expected to reach $1trillion in 2026 alone according to research by Goldman Sachs. The sector has scooped up so much available cash that other industries have seen their own borrowing costs increase as a result.
But investors want returns, and in recent months concerns have been growing about whether the AI boom can produce the expected riches.
Those worries have emerged at a time when public comments from AI researchers casting doubt over the safety of artificial intelligence - even suggesting it could represent an existential threat to humanity - have been grabbing headlines and fuelling speculation that a clampdown could lie ahead.
Democrat opposition
While the Trump administration has been all-in on AI, or "super intelligence" as the president likes to call it, many leading Democrats tapped into grassroots concerns about the expansion of data centres and their impact on local communities.
These were largely focused on the facilities' high consumption of water and electricity, which many feared would push up their household bills – as well as the noise, use of land, and general disruption associated with them.
A Gallup poll published in May showed 71% of Americans would oppose the building of a data centre in their community. The figure for a nuclear power station was 53%.
James Talarico, who won the Senate race in once staunchly Republican Texas, was one of those to respond to this scepticism.
"While we want to protect America's leadership in artificial intelligence, we are still grappling with how it will affect everything from how we work to how our children learn," he said.
"We must protect Americans and establish clear, consistent laws for businesses."
With control of both houses of Congress, Democrats are now expected to challenge the president's technology agenda more vigorously, while introducing legislation which could curb the expansion of the industry.
Texas' Democratic governor-elect Gina Hinojosa campaigned against data centres, pledging a moratorium on the construction of new facilities.
Hinojosa's win could present opposition to tech multi-billionaire Elon Musk, who has moved large parts of SpaceX and Tesla's operations to the state, for years a Republican stronghold.
The Tesla boss had spent nearly $450m to back Republican campaigns in the midterms.
Where next for stocks?
As the co-founder of the British-based technology firm Arm Holdings, Tudor Brown, points out, "stock values are based on future earnings not present earnings". If the rewards are not likely to be as great as expected, some investors will choose to sell up.
The falls seen on stock markets over the past 24 hours would appear to have been triggered by the midterm results. But concerns that tech firms have become overvalued were being expressed long before the elections.
The question now is whether this is simply the removal of froth from an over-exuberant market, or a sign that the AI rush is a bubble about to burst, with much wider consequences.
Nandini Roy Choudhury of Future Market Insights thinks investors will assess whether the political shift could result in restrictions on data centre construction, energy consumption and the deployment of AI technology.
She adds there is unlikely to be an immediate widespread recovery in tech stocks as traders are likely to be more selective, favouring firms with stronger balance sheets.
Brown thinks the impact will be limited. Share valuations, he thinks, were inflated by expectations of "almost infinite AI growth", which have been followed by "a bit of a panic".
"There is a natural floor to this", he says. "After that it will reflect I think that actually there's still a lot of money being made in these companies".
summary: Fears of more AI regulation appear to have sparked fear among investors, but concerns about the industry have been growing for some time.

content:
En ambos lados de la frontera que separaba las dos Alemanias se celebró la caída del Muro de Berlín el 9 de noviembre de 1989. 37 años después, parece persistir una profunda desconfianza mutua.
Tres creadores alemanes que han abordado la historia de la división del país  desde perspectivas muy distintas explican cómo perciben esa realidad.
¿Botas de invierno? ¡Mejor golosinas!
La escritora Lea Streisand, nacida en 1979, vivió de primera mano la caída del Muro cuando era niña en Berlín Este. Su biografía como ciudadana de la antigua República Democrática Alemana ( RDA ) ha sido un tema recurrente en sus libros y textos. Es el caso, por ejemplo, de su novela Hufeland Ecke Bötzow (Ullstein, 2019), donde narra el periodo de la reunificación desde la mirada infantil.
"El 9 de noviembre de 1989 fue sencillamente maravilloso ", comenta a DW. Todos los ciudadanos de Alemania Oriental recibieron 100 marcos de bienvenida que su madre gastó en unas prácticas botas de invierno. Un amigo de sus padres la compensó después permitiéndole comprar tantas golosinas en el supermercado, que estas le duraron hasta Navidad.
"El regusto amargo llegó después, con todo lo que ocurrió a lo largo del año siguiente", rememora Streisand. "De repente, a una velocidad increíble, desapareció todo un sistema y se construyó otro nuevo, como diciendo: 'Ahí lo tienen'. Creo que para la gente fue demasiado rápido".
La población de la RDA había impulsado el cambio mediante un movimiento por los derechos civiles y numerosas manifestaciones. Pero había mucha gente que no necesariamente deseaba que el Estado desapareciera.
Una de esas personas fue Anke Feuchtenberger, nacida en 1963. Llegó al mundo en Berlín Este, creció allí y en Pomerania Occidental, donde hoy vuelve a residir y donde dice sentirse "muy en casa". Feuchtenberger está considerada la dibujante de cómics más influyente del país y también ha alcanzado reconocimiento internacional.
"Nosotras, como artistas, intentamos entonces impulsar un cambio de rumbo con carteles y panfletos. Queríamos más libertad, pero no necesariamente abolir el socialismo", explica. La caída del Muro despertó en ella sentimientos encontrados. "Comprendí muy pronto que el impulso creativo y revolucionario de nuestro movimiento quedó rápidamente sepultado por el consumo. También afloraron con fuerza tendencias nacionalistas que ya se percibían antes", recuerda. "Eso me dio miedo".
Por su parte, el fotógrafo y artista visual Simon Menner, nacido en 1978 en Emmendingen, Baden-Wurtemberg, vivió la caída del Muro de manera mucho más distante. Era un niño y, según cuenta, todo aquello le resultaba "más bien abstracto". Berlín quedaba muy lejos, aunque hoy reside allí. La imagen de la Alemania Oriental transmitida por las películas y documentales sobre la reunificación le parecía excesivamente sombría. "Y eso que el oeste en los años ochenta también era gris y bastante conservador".
El tesoro fotográfico de la Stasi
Buena parte del trabajo de Menner gira en torno a la vigilancia y sus mecanismos. En los archivos del Ministerio para la Seguridad del Estado, hoy integrados en el Archivo Federal y accesibles al público, encontró una inmensa colección fotográfica que le fascinó tanto como le inquietó.
Su libro fotográfico Top Secret (Hatje Cantz, 2012) reúne una selección de imágenes que ofrecen una visión única del funcionamiento interno de la Stasi . Algunas resultan inquietantes; otras, extrañas e incluso absurdas. Menner también quiso acceder al archivo fotográfico del servicio secreto de Alemania Occidental. No lo consiguió.
La literatura como puente
Para Lea Streisand, la literatura puede desempeñar un papel importante en la comprensión mutua. "La literatura transmite experiencias que otros no han vivido", afirma. "Permite sumergirse en el universo mental de alguien que ha tenido vivencias diferentes y entender mejor qué ocurrió".
En 2023, Anke Feuchtenberger publicó la novela gráfica Genossin Kuckuck ("Camarada Cuco"), un volumen de casi 500 páginas editado por Reprodukt. La obra recorre varias décadas, desde la infancia de su protagonista en el ficticio pueblo oriental de Pritchitanov, durante los años sesenta de la RDA, hasta el periodo posterior a la reunificación.
Durante las presentaciones públicas suele surgir con frecuencia un tema concreto: la protagonista, Kerstin, apenas ve a sus padres porque ambos trabajan a tiempo completo. En la RDA el empleo era un derecho garantizado para todos, pero también una obligación cívica. Quizá, reflexiona Feuchtenberger, el interés que esto suscita en Alemania Occidental tenga que ver con que durante mucho tiempo allí fue menos habitual que ambos progenitores trabajaran a jornada completa.
¿Cómo será el futuro?
Al mirar hacia el futuro común, las dos mujeres procedentes del este se muestran más optimistas que el alemán occidental. "En Berlín muchas veces ya ni siquiera noto si estoy en el este o en el oeste", dice Simon Menner. Aun así, cree que los responsables políticos deberían escuchar mucho más tanto a los mayores como a los jóvenes. De lo contrario, advierte, el panorama podría complicarse en los próximos años, en alusión a los recientes éxitos electorales del partido político de ultraderecha AfD .
"Es muy importante mirar más allá de nuestras propias fronteras mentales, porque la gente tiene problemas en todas partes del mundo", sostiene Anke Feuchtenberger. "Seguir fijándose únicamente en el abismo que se ha abierto entre alemanes del este y del oeste no ayuda a avanzar".
Para ella, la noción misma de frontera ha perdido gran parte de su significado personal. Lo atribuye en parte a los numerosos viajes que ha realizado por distintos lugares del mundo. También hace hincapié en que observa, desde su localidad cercana a la frontera polaca, cómo los animales, ignorando por completo esas divisiones, van y vienen como quieren.
"Todo este asunto de este y oeste ya no interesará en absoluto a nuestros hijos", asegura Lea Streisand. "A los jóvenes les da igual de dónde procedan sus padres. Lo que les preocupa es si podrán conseguir un trabajo con el que mantener a una familia o si tendrán que ir a la guerra. Ahora mismo hay otras cosas mucho más importantes".
(ms/cp)

content:
Russia’s battlefield gains in Ukraine have fallen to almost nothing this year, according to the latest figures from independent observers and Kyiv’s military.
Territory seized by Russian forces in the first 10 months of 2026 amounts to 117.38 sq km (45.32 sq miles), according to the Institute for the Study of War (ISW), a Washington-based think tank that uses open-source geolocated footage.
By comparison, gains in 2025 were 5,304 sq km (2,047.95 sq miles), including 473 sq km (182.63 sq miles) of Russian territory recaptured in the Kursk region, while in 2024 they were 3,604 sq km (1,391.31 sq miles).
That means Russia advanced at a rate of 0.38 sq km (0.15 sq miles) a day this year, compared with 13.25 sq km (5.12 sq miles) a day in 2025 and 9.9 sq km (3.82 sq miles) a day in 2024.
In addition, Russia is suffering higher casualties this year.
Ukraine’s General Staff put the estimated number of Russian personnel killed or seriously wounded from January 1 to October 31 at 381,300.
Al Jazeera cannot independently verify casualty claims by either side.
Estimated Russian losses have repeatedly broken new monthly records for the entire war since the summer – 42,860 in July, 46,230 in September and 54,400 in October – as Ukraine’s military sought to reach a monthly target of 50,000 casualties set by President Volodymyr Zelenskyy in January.
The losses are far beyond Russia’s estimated recruitment capacity of 24,000-30,000 a month.
While Russia lost firm control of Ukrainian territory in April and May, it increased its areas of infiltration, where control is contested.
In September and October, however, Russia lost both firmly controlled and infiltrated territory, ISW assessments show.
Zelenskyy and his prime minister have cited these worsening trends as the reasons why Russia is intensifying long-range strikes targeting energy infrastructure. Civilians have been killed in those attacks, leading Ukrainians to believe that Moscow is opting for psychological warfare.
Russia unleashed an unusually heavy barrage during the week ending on November 6, including 2,346 drones and more than 80 missiles across Ukraine.
The strikes reached a crescendo on November 3, with 370 drones and 76 missiles.
Hundreds of thousands of families are struggling with blackouts at the beginning of winter.
In one of Russia’s deadliest attacks this year, in the village of Komyshuvakha in the Zaporizhzhia region, at least 50 people were killed.
“The invaders knew that on Mondays, humanitarian aid was distributed at the Komyshuvakha resilience centre. Residents of the community come here for food, medicine, essential items,” Ukraine’s military intelligence service (GUR) said.
The attack came on the day a six-day ceasefire ended in Oleshky, 250km (155.34 miles) southwest of Komyshuvakha in the Kherson region.
Brokered by US First Lady Melania Trump, the localised ceasefire was the longest ever observed and enabled the warring sides to evacuate 800 residents of the besieged town, which is in Russian-occupied Ukrainian territory.
Russian military reporter Vladimir Romanov was arrested by authorities in his country after reporting that Oleshky residents who had opted to go to Ukraine had filled 17 buses, while those who opted to go to Russia filled four.
Moscow has cited the alleged abuse of its Russian-speaking minority in Ukraine as one of the main reasons for its full-scale invasion in 2022, and has claimed that it would be welcomed as a liberating force.
The oil war
Ukraine resumed almost daily targeting of Russian refineries during the past week, hitting eight in seven days.
Russian Deputy Prime Minister Alexander Novak said three refineries were hit on October 30.
Ukraine hit two more refineries in the Ufa complex in the Bashkortostan Republic on October 31. The following day it struck Lukoil’s Nizhegorodnefteorgsintez refinery in Nizhny Novgorod, and a production and dispatch station in the Samara region the day after that. It hit the Yaroslavl oil refinery on November 3, and the Ryazan oil refinery on November 5.
The strikes were designed to deprive Russia of energy and export revenue and scupper a deal reached by Russian President Vladimir Putin and Donald Trump on October 9, when the US leader invited Russia to sell 1.8 million tonnes of diesel to the global market by the end of the year to help bring down transport prices.
Trump’s invitation flew in the face of US oil sanctions and the Lindsey Graham Act the president had signed into law 11 days earlier, which gave him the power to impose sanctions on other countries buying Russian oil.
The Kremlin has since pumped four tankers full of diesel fuel, reported the Financial Times (FT), in hopes of selling it to the US and effectively ending oil sanctions against it. But those tankers have reportedly failed to find buyers willing to risk the legal consequences of purchasing Russian oil. The Kremlin dismissed the FT’s report as fake news.
On October 27, US Senator Richard Blumenthal, who co-authored the Lindsey Graham Act, warned a Greek shipping company operating one of the four diesel-laden ships not to attempt to offload its cargo in the US.
“The President may have given a licence to facilitate this transaction, but only Congress can make it legally valid,” Blumenthal had written, effectively warning all shippers they would face a legal tangle between statutory law and presidential executive orders.
US courts have struck down many of Trump’s executive orders in his first two years in office.

content:
Yemen’s government forces and the Houthi rebel group are trading blame for an attack on the al-Hadara market in the Taiz governorate, that both sides say killed and injured dozens of people.
The spokesperson for the Yemeni government forces, Colonel Majed al-Nazili, said the “terrorist” Houthis struck the market on Friday with ballistic missiles, causing dozens of civilian casualties. He accused the Iran-backed group of committing a “war crime” and called for accountability.
The Houthis, however, accused Saudi Arabia, which backs Yemen’s internationally recognised government, of having launched three air strikes on the market, killing at least 30 civilians and injuring eight others.
Its Ministry of Health and Environment in the Yemeni Houthi-controlled capital Sanaa said Riyadh committed a “horrific crime” and called for an independent international investigation into Saudi Arabia’s “systematic targeting” of civilians.
Al Jazeera could not independently verify the reports,and there has been no response so far from the Saudi-led coalition forces.
Al Jazeera’s Yousef Mawry, reporting from Sanaa, said fighting has been ongoing in the al-Waziiya district where the market is located. The area is controlled by the Houthis, who are also known as Ansar Allah (Arabic for Supporters of God).
The Saudi-led coalition has been carrying out attacks on a daily basis to gain control of the district and its strategic mountain range, Mawry said.
“Whoever controls the al-Waziiya district controls the majority of the western Red Sea coastal line,” he added.
The Yemeni army said it recaptured several areas in the Taiz governorate on Friday, including the al-Nidani village, Shaab al-Sarari, large parts of the Sanamat area and the Ribat al-Qarn area in Dhi al-Barh.
Government forces also imposed a siege on entrances to the al-Sarari area, according to the military.
While the Houthis control much of the governorate, the city of Taiz is government-held. An ongoing Houthi siege on the city has lasted for 30 days and affected hundreds of thousands of people in the area.
The United Nations has repeatedly warned of a catastrophe inside Taiz city, where supplies of food and medicine are becoming increasingly scarce.
Yemen’s internationally recognised government launched Operation Dawn of Yemen on October 5 to take control of territories held by Houthi fighters.
Since the start of the military operation, neither Yemen’s government-controlled territories nor Saudi Arabia has been safe from Houthi missile attacks.
The Houthis have been firing missiles and drones daily into Saudi Arabia, hitting oil facilities and disrupting air traffic over the kingdom.
summary: The attack on al-Hadara market in Taiz governorate's al-Waziiya district killed at least 30 people, Houthi rebels say.

content:
Russell Brand’s barrister has reported himself to his professional regulator after being accused of launching a tirade at a journalist shortly after his client had been found guilty of rape.
Ian Winter KC “confronted” the Sunday Times journalist Rosamund Urwin, whose investigation led to Brand’s victims coming forward, telling her: “I hope you are pleased with yourself.”
Urwin responded: “I’m pleased justice has been done,” to which Winter replied: “Well, it wasn’t. You fucked it.”
“Congratulations,” he added, in an incident that happened outside the courtroom door at Southwark crown court on Thursday afternoon, with a group of journalists watching.
In a statement issued on Friday lunchtime, Winter said he had referred himself to the Bar Standards Board, his professional regulator.
He said: “Having seen the ways matters have been characterised in today’s press, I consider my professional duty requires me to self-report those allegations to the Bar Standards Board so the matter can be subject to proper scrutiny.
“I have made such a report.”
The incident happened moments after a jury had found Brand guilty of rape and three counts of sexual assault at the conclusion of a four-week trial. He was cleared of two further charges of rape and one of attempted indecent assault.
Brand, 51, had denied all the charges against him, and argued through his lawyer that he had been wrongly accused and was the victim of a media conspiracy.
After the trial, experts added to calls for a change in the law to ensure juries are warned against “rape myths”.
In his closing speech, Winter said none of the complainants had “resisted or screamed or even tried to leave” during their encounters with Brand.
Claire Waxman, the victims’ commissioner for England and Wales, is seeking to update the law to ensure juries are warned against “rape myths”. She criticised “outdated and harmful assumptions” that victims must have to have screamed or tried to fight off their attacker or immediately reported an offence.
Judges routinely issue directions cautioning juries against relying on such stereotypes. But Waxman’s office said it needed to be stated plainly in legislation to ensure consistency.
Mr Justice Bennathan, the judge in Brand’s trial, told the jury in his legal directions not to assume the delay in making complaints to the police meant the allegations were untrue.
Deniz Ugur, the deputy director of the End Violence Against Women (EVAW) coalition, said: “It is really appalling to see defence lawyers intentionally lean into a whole range of tired tropes and myths about rape. “Rape myths like the ones we’ve seen in this case have no place in the courtroom.”
The head of Scotland Yard, Sir Mark Rowley, told BBC Radio 4’s Today programme he supported Waxman’s call. “I think what I’ve heard reported heads towards, it’s getting very close to victim-blaming, which is something we’ve thought very hard about in policing and make sure we don’t do.
“People fall into myths about [how] a rape victim must behave in a certain way, must react in a certain way. The evidence is really clear. Some people will fight. Some people will freeze. Some people will tell people straight away. Some people bottle it up for years. There isn’t one way of reacting.”
On Friday a No 10 source said the prime minister, Andy Burnham, believed that Waxman’s calls should be examined.
Speaking after the trial, Urwin told a Times podcast she approached Winter after the verdict because her name had been mentioned during the trial. “I thought he’s talked about me a lot, I’ll go and introduce myself and that is a legitimate thing to do,” she said. “I was surprised to be confronted and spoken to in that way.”
It is understood that several complaints have been submitted to the Bar Standards Board but the regulator said it would not “comment as to whether or not it has received any information about potential misconduct by a barrister regardless of how any information comes to our attention”.
A spokesperson said complaints were usually handled confidentially unless they resulted in a disciplinary tribunal hearing.
The comedian Katherine Ryan criticised the barrister on her podcast, Telling Everybody Everything, saying: “That was so unprofessional, so inappropriate, so aggressive. Really sickening.”
Ben Taylor, the editor of the Sunday Times, defended Urwin, his newspaper’s chief news correspondent. He said: “I found what Mr Winter did quite extraordinary. I have never seen or heard of a barrister behaving in this way.
“There’s a really serious point here, which is that it was not Ros who found Russell Brand guilty at Southwark crown court.
“It was a jury of eight men and four women who have sat through this case. They’ve listened to the evidence, they’ve listened to the defence, and they have gone away and they’ve come back with some very considered verdicts.
“By impugning Ros’s integrity, what Mr Winter is doing, and he should really be called to account for this, he’s impugning the integrity of the entire case.
“He’s impugning the integrity of a jury … who have sat there solemnly and done their duty, and the judge who oversaw the case and everybody else involved. I think what he did was reprehensible.”
During the trial, Winter had argued that reporting of allegations against Brand by the Times, the Sunday Times and a Channel 4 Dispatches documentary had “poisoned the well”, and rendered it impossible for his client to have a fair trial.
The trial judge, Mr Justice Bennathan, dismissed an attempt by Brand to block his trial from taking place because of negative media coverage.
In a pre-trial argument, Brand, through Winter, had accused the journalists who first exposed him as a sexual predator of being “criminals”, suggesting their reporting in 2023 had made a fair trial impossible and venturing that they may have committed the crime of perverting the course of justice.
But the judge rejected that attempt to stop the trial, ruling that Brand could simply be tried by people who had not seen the previous media reporting.
A Ministry of Justice spokesperson said: “Rape myths have absolutely no place in our courts and victims should never feel as though they are the ones on trial.
“Judges are already able to give directions to counter rape myths but we are going further by changing the law to stop irrelevant sexual history and previous allegations being weaponised against rape victims.
“We will also carefully consider the victims’ commissioner’s proposals as we continue to strengthen protections for victims.”
Brand was convicted of raping a 21-year-old fan in 2009 and sexually assaulting three women in separate incidents between 2004 and 2009.
He is in custody and due to be sentenced on Monday.

Dans un entretien accordé à France 24, John Bolton, ancien conseiller à la sécurité nationale de Donald Trump lors de son premier mandat, réagit aux élections de mi-mandat, qui ont vu une large victoire du Parti démocrate. Il estime que "c'est le début de la fin" du rôle du président américain au sein du Parti républicain.
John Bolton estime que les résultats des élections de mi-mandat marquent "la fin" de l'ère Trump au sein du Parti républicain.
Il explique notamment que "dans sa dernière allocution publique avant le scrutin de mardi, le président n'a pas parlé de sujets tels que le coût de la vie et le pouvoir d'achat, mais de ses projets de construction et de rénovation".
Les démocrates ont repris le contrôle de la Chambre des représentants et du Sénat, signant ainsi la pire performance des républicains depuis les élections de 1974, dans le sillage du scandale du Watergate.
Donald Trump a affirmé que les républicains avaient perdu parce que son nom ne figurait pas sur les bulletins de vote. John Bolton n'est pas de cet avis. Selon lui, "pendant la campagne, Trump a tout fait pour que les électeurs votent aussi pour lui. Il leur a répété à plusieurs reprises : 'Faites comme si mon nom figurait sur le bulletin de vote'".
Interrogé sur le tweet de J.D. Vance – qui attribuait la défaite des républicains aux élections de mi-mandat à la guerre en Iran –, John Bolton estime que le vice-président américain cherche à faire passer le message suivant : "Je suis encore plus MAGA que le président".
summary: Dans un entretien accordé à France 24, John Bolton, ancien conseiller à la sécurité nationale de Donald Trump lors de son premier mandat, réagit aux élections de mi-mandat, qui ont vu une large victoire du Parti démocrate. Il estime que "c'est le début de la fin" du rôle du président américain au sein du Parti républicain.

content:
The colour purple has links to royalty, the Catholic church, Prince, Gordon Brown’s ties and Barney the dinosaur and it now has a new association – autumn 2026.
It has been deemed fashion’s favourite colour having been spotted on autumn/winter catwalks, with Balenciaga, Celine and Valentino showcasing all-purple designs.
Jennifer Lawrence and Zoë Kravitz have also been spotted wearing purple, while Naomi Ackie and Nicola Peltz have worn it on the red carpet. The high street is in on the trend too, with Cos, H&M and Asos selling purple knitwear and accessories.
This season’s shade has been called “royal purple” – a vivid take on the colour, rather than a darker plum or muted lilac. This is a contrast to the neutrals that have dominated fashion in recent years.
In fact, fashion insiders are leaning into the bright theme by often pairing purple with red. Vogue recently declared that autumn’s “coolest colour clash” had arrived.
In 2024, the trend forecasting agency WGSN predicted that the colour – a shade it called “fresh purple” – would be fashionable this autumn. Sara Maggioni, WGSN’s head of womenswear, sees its popularity as part of a wider shift. “[We are seeing] a growing appetite for brighter, more expressive shades,” she says. “This reflects a gradual move away from the restraint of quiet luxury as consumers become more confident in using colour to express their personal style.”
Purple is sometimes seen as a “tricky” colour by designers because it’s hard to ignore. This now may be part of its selling point. “A couple of months ago I loathed it,” says Daisy Murray, the fashion commerce editor at Grazia. “It was a lightbulb moment for me – I’m a big fan of a bold red, particularly in summer, so a punchy purple suddenly made sense.”
after newsletter promotion
Kassia St Clair, the author of The Secret Lives of Colour, says purple has long been linked to the wealthy and powerful. Tyrian purple is associated with the Romans – when dye was made from the secretions of molluscs near the ancient city of Tyre. However, with the mollusc population declining and the collapse of the Byzantine empire in 1453, the method for making the dye was lost. “But the reputation of purple lingers,” St Clair says.
The problem was solved in 1856 when the chemist William Henry Perkin accidentally created a bright purple liquid while attempting to find a treatment for malaria. The first chemical dye, which Perkin called mauve, began to be produced, and Queen Victoria and her granddaughter Princess Eugenie began to wear it. St Clair says purple became so popular that the satirical magazine Punch said everyone in London had “caught the mauve measles”.
Purple’s associations with the elite remain today. “We do still have a simmering cultural awareness of the associations between purple and power,” says St Clair. “These things persist for an extraordinarily long time despite the fact people don’t know the history.”
Maggioni argues that purple’s popularity is bolstered by a more modern context, too. “[Fresh purple] has a ‘phygital’ quality – it can work across physical settings and virtual worlds,” she says. “Its vivid, slightly otherworldly character suits digital imagery and immersive environments, where colour can be intensified [and] transformed.”
Of course, purple clothing is worn in the real world – with something as prosaic as the weather a factor. “[Red and purple are the] colours of autumn and winter – think heather and rosehips,” says Murray. “There’s something about purple that really suits dark evenings,” adds St Clair. “It’s hard to imagine it in beautiful spring light.”

Who: Valencia vs Real Madrid What: La Liga Where: Mestalla Stadium, Valencia, Spain When: Saturday, November 7, at 9pm (20:00 GMT). How to follow: Al Jazeera Sport will bring you all the build-up from 17:00 GMT ahead of our live text commentary stream
Jose Mourinho’s Madrid visit Valencia knowing that a win will provisionally draw them level with league leaders Barcelona.
Madrid have had some wobbles so far this season, but have won their last seven games in all competitions – including four in the league and an El Clasico win over Barca since a 2-1 defeat to Atletico Madrid in September.
Mourinho’s side are currently third in the La Liga table, three points behind the leaders Barcelona, with the Catalan side set to play second placed Atletico on Sunday.
Valencia will be hoping to inject some life into their season as they go into the weekend second bottom of the table, having taken just nine points from 11 games.
Mourinho hails ‘extraordinary’ Bellingham
Madrid’s coach lavished praise on Jude Bellingham after the midfielder scored a brilliant back-heeled goal against AEK Athens in the Champions League on Wednesday.
On a night when Bellingham became the youngest player to make 60 appearances in European club football’s top competition, the England midfielder scored and was named player of the match as Madrid rallied to a 3-2 win.
“He is a unique player. Today, there is no midfielder in world football like Jude, who is complete on all levels,” Mourinho said.
“I don’t have many words because, for me, he is an absolutely extraordinary player. Even on a day when he doesn’t have a great match, one of those jaw-dropping performances, he still brings work, leadership, ambition, quality, and goal-scoring ability. He is an extraordinary player.”
Bellingham, who was also the youngest player to make 50 appearances, reached his latest landmark at the age of 23 years, 128 days, overtaking iconic former Madrid goalkeeper Iker Casillas.
He struck in the 32nd minute by connecting with Marc Cucurella’s cross and flicking a first-time shot past goalkeeper Alberto Brignoli.
“It was just instinct really,” he said. “I found myself in a good position and managed to do the only thing that came naturally in that position. It was a nice one.”
Valencia get ‘very important’ win at Elche
Coach Javier Aguirre said his Valencia side needed the win over Elche last weekend, which came courtesy of a second half goal by substitute Nigerian striker Sadik.
“It’s a very important win for us, because we’d come off three matches without a victory, and now we have Real Madrid CF coming up. We couldn’t afford to get cut adrift,” he said.
“Getafe CF and RCD Espanyol both won, so if we hadn’t done likewise, a rather large gap would have opened up.”
“It’s a very significant win, both in terms of the result and the performance.”
What have the coaches said about the match?
Mourinho, Real Madrid: “This match is one of the toughest matches in the entire Spanish league. Valencia’s coach is extremely difficult, he has great experience, he knows what he wants, and he has a clear philosophy in working with teams, so it will be a very difficult match.”
Aguirre, Valencia: “You don’t need extra motivation for that game. We’ll be playing against one of the best sides in the world, and I hope that we have a good game.”
Prediction
The Opta supercomputer has made Real Madrid the clear favourites, with a win probability of 70.4 percent. Valencia were given a 12.7 percent chance of winning, while a draw was estimated at a 16.9 percent likelihood.
Head-to-head
Previous matches: 216
Real Madrid wins: 114
Valencia wins: 59
Draws: 43
Last five encounters:
February 8, 2026: Valencia 0-2 Real Madrid (La Liga)
November 1, 2025: Real Madrid 4-0 Valencia (La Liga)
April 5, 2025: Real Madrid 1-2 Valencia (La Liga)
January 3, 2025: Valencia 1-2 Real Madrid (La Liga)
March 2, 2024: Valencia 2-2 Real Madrid (La Liga)
What happened in their last encounter?
Real Madrid won 2-0 at Valencia in February as second-half goals by Alvaro Carreras and Kylian Mbappe settled a largely uneventful contest.
Real dominated possession but found chances hard to come by, with Valencia keeper Stole Dimitrievski rarely called into action as the visitors struggled to turn control into threat.
It took them until the 65th minute to break the deadlock through Carreras before Mbappe wrapped up the points in stoppage time.
Valencia’s team news
Sergi Canos, Diego Lopez and David Otorbi will all be unavailable due to injuries, while Jose Manuel Copete is a doubt as he continues to struggle with a knee issue.
Loanee Harvey Elliott returns from suspension, and striker Sadiq looks to have regained full fitness after a hamstring injury and is likely to start.
Predicted starting XI:
Dimitrievski (goalkeeper); Martinez, Tarrega, Pepelu, Gaya; Rodriguez; Maffeo, Mayol, Guerra, Rioja; Sadiq
Real Madrid’s team news
Rodrygo, Raul Asencio, and Ferland Mendy remain unavailable due to injuries, while Vinicius Junior will miss out as he serves the final game of a domestic suspension.
Predicted starting XI:
Courtois (goalkeeper); Valverde, Konate, Huijsen, Cucurella; Tchouameni, Bernardo; Guler, Bellingham, Diomande; Mbappe

An explosion believed to have been caused by a missile attack on an oil tanker in the Persian Gulf has left one seafarer dead, the vessel's operating company said on Friday.
Greek management firm Velos Tankers said the Marshall Islands-flagged tanker MT Velos Sapphire was sailing toward Bahrain when it was attacked.
"The company is greatly saddened to report the death of one of its seafarers, who was found fatally injured on board after having initially been reported missing in the aftermath of the explosion," the firm said.
The explosion caused a fire to break out in the ship. The crew were able to extinguish the fire without reporting any other injured.
Bahrain's Khalifa Bin Salman Port ultimately took in the ship, and an investigation into the incident will be launched to assess the extent of the damage to the vessel's hull.

Iran using 'everything it can' to stop oil flows
The incident is the latest in a string of attacks on ships in the Persian Gulf by Iran.
US newspaper The Wall Street Journal  cited regional officials, security firms and analysts in a report detailing how Iran is using everything it can to stop the flow of oil leaving the Strait of Hormuz.
The report said Tehran has launched bomb-laden undersea drones, fired rocket-propelled grenades and deployed crews to attach limpet mines to ships over recent weeks.
According to data from the UK Maritime Trade Operations Center (UKMTO), October saw the highest monthly number of attacks in the Strait of Hormuz since the war began, with more than 35 incidents.
At least five vessels have been attacked so far in November, UKMTO added.
The increasing attacks coincides with signs of recovery in shipping through Hormuz . US Central Command said last month it had helped Gulf countries export 1.5 billion barrels of oil via Hormuz since the summer.
On Thursday, Iranian media reported that five oil tankers and a tugboat caught fire after hitting mines in the Strait of Hormuz.
On Friday, Iran's Revolutionary Guards said two more oil tankers were on fire in the strait, state media reported.
Iran destroys missile over Qeshm Island
Meanwhile, Iranian media said Friday that Iranian air defenses had destroyed a US MQ-1 drone over Qeshm Island in the Strait of Hormuz.
Washington did not confirm the incident.
It all comes in the wake of the US launching strikes on Qeshm Island on Tuesday, with Iranian state media reporting five explosions in rapid succession.
A statement attributed to Iran's Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei warned that the Middle East war would widen if the US resumes its attacks.
Khamenei   has rejected the notion that Washington will change course after midterm elections dealt a blow to President Donald Trump .

content:
Paraguay’s president impeached amid bank collapse crisis
Paraguay’s President Santiago Pena is facing impeachment following the collapse of Ueno Bank, a major digital bank, which has plunged the South American country into its deepest political crisis in more than a decade.
Pena announced his resignation on Thursday, but politicians formally filed impeachment charges against the president. Pena, a former International Monetary Fund (IMF) economist, then requested a 72-hour extension to present his defence at an impeachment hearing, because he had been given less than 12 hours to answer “an accusatory writ and about 300 pages of attachments”, adding: “That is not due process.”
However, the Senate convened a rare session on Friday to consider Pena’s political future, opting to move forward with efforts to remove him from office.
Until March 2025, Pena held a stake in Grupo Vazquez, the parent company that owns Ueno Bank.
What is Ueno Bank?
Ueno Bank was established in 1976 and remained a small financial operation for decades.
After being granted a full banking licence in 2023, it rebranded and grew to become a household name in Paraguay within five years. Customers were incentivised with cashback offers on groceries and it built a network of more than 70 branches. The bank sponsored Paraguay’s national football team and its name was plastered across the country’s main stadium.
Ueno bank reported that it had 3 million customers, roughly 60 percent of Paraguay’s adult population.
The digital bank managed $800m of public funds, including about $380m invested by Paraguay’s state pension and health fund, according to data from the Central Bank of Paraguay.
What has happened to the bank?
On Monday, Paraguay’s central bank decided to put Ueno bank into resolution – the strongest action it can take short of placing the bank into liquidation – after finding that its solvency ratio, a measure of its capital against its risk-weighted assets, had dropped to less than half of the legal requirement.
Resolution allows regulators to transfer a failing bank’s deposits to other institutions before liquidating remaining assets.
Customer accounts were frozen, leaving millions of depositors, retirees and workers scrambling to recoup their savings and unpaid wages.
Ueno Bank’s nearly 3 million customers still cannot withdraw cash, make digital payments or use their bank cards.
“Santiago Pena and the Colorado Party have stolen all our savings,” said Luis Pineda, one of the protesters marching to Congress on Wednesday. “We are fed up with 70 years of plunder,” he added, an apparent reference to the right-wing Colorado Party which has ruled Paraguay almost uninterrupted for more than seven decades.
What caused the Ueno Bank collapse?
Regulators at Paraguay’s central bank found a pattern of risky lending to “insiders”, reported ABC Color, a leading Paraguayan newspaper. This means that executives or major investors of a bank have approved questionable, low-security loans for themselves, their families or their own businesses. In this case, Ueno had loaned $146m to companies tied to its owner, Grupo Vasquez, which has links to Paraguay’s president.
Investigators found loaned amounts went beyond legal limits and were not backed up by enough collateral to cover the debts if they went bad.
Central Bank regulators found Ueno’s loans to companies linked to its owners were poorly documented while the bank had wrongly counted some expenses as assets.
Once the books were corrected, Ueno’s capital, the cushion banks must keep to absorb losses, was revealed to be less than half the legal minimum.
How is President Pena involved?
Protesters blame President Pena personally for the crisis because of his ties to the failed bank. Until recently, he held a financial stake in Ueno Bank’s parent holding company. After taking office in 2023, Pena appointed the former head of Ueno’s predecessor company, Carlos Carvallo, to head the country’s central bank, giving an insider the role of overseeing the institution. Carvallo has resigned from his position.
Pena denies any improper ties to the bank.
Protesters also say they are unhappy that so much public pension money was invested with the bank under Pena despite warnings about its high-risk insider lending practices.
What happens to people with savings in the bank now?
Paraguay’s Congress rushed through a law on Wednesday, providing a state-guaranteed fund for repaying depositors within five business days, starting on Thursday with small accounts holding up to $1,600.
The fund insures up to about $36,000 per customer, which the central bank says will cover the full balances of an estimated 97 percent of customers.
What other action is being taken?
Paraguay’s Public Prosector’s office has ordered multiple criminal investigations. On Thursday, a judge ordered six Ueno executives, including founder Miguel Vazquez and bank President Juan Manuel Gustale, to be detained pending trial, while two others were placed under house arrest. In all, prosecutors have charged 27 bank officials and associates with breach of trust and attempted fraud.
Paraguay’s President Santiago Pena has tried to step down and wants Congress to approve his resignation. However, opposition politicians want him to be formally removed from office rather than merely allowing him to resign. They argue that allowing Pena to step down would preserve his eligibility to become a senator for life and shield him from possible prosecution.
Paraguay’s Attorney General Emiliano Rolon Fernandez has ordered three criminal investigations into the Ueno Bank crisis, including allegations involving Pena and other current and former government officials, the prosecutor’s office said on Thursday.
The investigations will examine authorities’ oversight of the bank, their handling of its failure and the placement of public funds in the lender.
Is this the first banking crisis in Paraguay?
No. Paraguay has a long history of bank failures and went through a prolonged banking crisis from the mid-1990s to the early 2000s.
In 1995, the central bank was forced to close Bancopar, which had severe liquidity problems and had also practised insider lending to companies linked to the bank’s owners. Three more banks also failed because of risky practices and poor oversight. The government was forced to cover the deposits of customers of all four banks, causing lasting damage to public confidence in Paraguay’s banking system.
Other banks including Banco General, and Banco Aleman were closed in this era. Banco Union and the state-linked Banco Nacional de Trabajadores and Banco Plus also failed.
Have there been other bank collapses?
Banco Espirito Santo in Portugal collapsed in 2014 with losses of $4.8bn when it was revealed that the family-controlled banking group had hidden losses. The Bank of Portugal had to split and rescue what was the country’s second largest private bank. That happened as Portugal was recovering from a deep recession, austerity cuts and bail-out obligations to the International Monetary Fund (IMF), the European Central Bank (ECB) and the European Commission.
In 2008, the three major commercial banks in Iceland – Glitnir, Kaupthing and Landsbanki – all collapsed within days following the bankruptcy of Lehman Brothers. The three banks were heavily exposed because they had borrowed from foreign capital markets far too aggressively. Iceland did not shore up the banks, instead seeking help from the IMF and launching criminal investigations.
The collapse of Lehman Brothers triggered banking crises in other countries, including the United Kingdom, but banks there were mostly propped up or rescued by governments.
Fraud and insider lending caused the collapse of Banco Intercontinental Baninter in the Dominican Republic in 2003 with losses of $2.2bn.
And in 1991, Bank of Credit and Commerce International, a globally active bank, collapsed with losses of $10bn. Extensive fraud, hidden bad loans, and illicit operations masked the true scale of the deficit until the intervention of regulators. It was shut it down simultaneously in more than 70 countries.

content:
Thomas Markle, the father of Meghan, the Duchess of Sussex, was arrested by US federal agents in Florida on Friday and charged in connection with possession of child sexual abuse material, according to the Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI).
Markle, 82, was taken into custody at a senior care facility in Polk county early on Friday, and made a brief initial appearance in federal court in Tampa on Friday afternoon, the Associated Press reported. He was later released with the condition that he be electronically monitored.
A 14-page federal criminal complaint says that agents seized approximately 78 items and alleges that Markle kept child sexual abuse material, including sexually explicit photographs of himself with prepubescent girls, in two Los Angeles-area storage units that he rented for nearly two decades.
An affidavit filed with the complaint that led to the arrest stated that two of the images inside the units showed a man identified by a witness as Markle with a nude underage girl.
The document, filed in federal court in California, said the recovered material included dozens of slides, photographs, film negatives and books containing the illegal material. It said the FBI was still reviewing the material.
The director of the FBI, Kash Patel, said: “Mr Markle allegedly targeted innocent children and sought to steal their innocence through his criminal actions. This FBI will use every single resource at our disposal to protect innocent kids – any predator who targets children will have zero safe haven in this country or anywhere they try to hide.”
Patel thanked FBI agents in Los Angeles and Tampa, and authorities in Mexico, the Philippines, and Marshall Islands that he said were involved in the investigation.
Some details in the criminal complaint are redacted, such as the name of the federal agent who signed the complaint, who states that they are assigned to the violent crimes against children unit in the LA office of the FBI. The case is presented as United States of America v Thomas Wayne Markle.
“Mr Markle is accused of possessing child sexual abuse material, including photographs depicting himself with minor girls,” Bill Essayli, first assistant US attorney for the central district of California, said in a statement released by the US department of justice.
“These allegations are extremely serious, and we will prosecute Mr Markle to the fullest extent of federal law.”
Essayli told the Associated Press that there was no evidence of victims in the US, based on the seized material, but that the investigation was ongoing. He said his office was aware of public reporting that Markle might have dementia.
Markle is charged with one count of possession of child sexual abuse material, and faces up to 20 years in federal prison if convicted.
Efforts by the AP to reach Markle’s court-appointed lawyer for comment were unsuccessful, the news agency said.
Meghan, the wife of Prince Harry, said last month that she was “deeply distressed” about allegations that a collection of child sexual abuse images was found at her father’s former home in the Philippines.
The duchess also revealed that a letter containing “troubling allegations” about her father was sent to police in London in 2018.
She had issued a statement after the Sun newspaper published claims that her half-brother, Thomas Markle Jr, alleged he had found a stash of images belonging to their father at his Philippines residence. He was named as a person of interest in the case earlier this week.
According to the justice department statement, FBI agents interviewed a person last month who was aware that Markle was renting the two storage units in California after the bureau became aware of developments in the Philippines.
Markle rented the units since 2008, it said, with his most recent payments on both made last month by auto-pay.
Photographs produced by the Daily Mail showed Thomas Markle Sr being taken away in a wheelchair, in handcuffs, wearing a black T-shirt and surrounded by agents wearing jackets marked “FBI”. The UK tabloid asked Markle if he was a pedophile and he replied: “No.” Markle did not answer when the newspaper asked if he had ever collected child sexual abuse material.
A spokesperson for the duchess did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
Authorities in the Philippines, where Markle had previously lived for some time, began investigating him last month over allegations he possessed child sexual abuse images. British police last month said they would refer allegations about him to overseas law enforcement agencies after finding that claims had not been passed to other authorities when they were first received.
He has denied the accusations, telling the Daily Mail they were untrue and “sick lies”.
Markle is a retired television lighting and photography director and he did not attend the 2018 wedding of Harry and Meghan, amid acrimony and estrangement between father and daughter. Meghan has since said she decided to distance herself from him to protect her children.
The duke and duchess returned to live in Britain in the summer after six years in the US.
The Associated Press and Reuters contributed reporting

La déroute du camp Trump aux États-Unis est-elle d’abord celle de sa politique économique ? Au début de son second mandat, le président américain Donald Trump promettait un nouvel âge d'or et se posait en champion du pouvoir d'achat.
Deux ans plus tard, le bilan est loin des promesses. La guerre en Iran et les droits de douane pèsent sur le portefeuille des Américains. Et quelle politique économique Donald Trump pourra-t-il mener au cours des deux prochaines années, désormais en minorité au Congrès ?

Nouvelle liste des Bleus : Mbappé et Tchouaméni de retour, première convocation pour Pablo Pagis
Zinédine Zidane a dévoilé, vendredi, la nouvelle liste de joueurs de l'Équipe de France qui disputeront les matchs pour accéder aux quarts de final de la Ligue des nations, face à la Turquie et l'Italie. On y retrouve notamment Kylian Mbappé et Aurélien Tchouaméni, remis de leurs blessures. Pablo Pagis, attaquant du Paris FC, a été convoqué pour la première fois.
Ils font leur grand retour. Le capitaine Kylian Mbappé, le milieu Aurélien Tchouaméni et le défenseur Ibrahima Konaté, remis de leurs blessures, ainsi que l'attaquant Marcus Thuram, effectuent leur retour en équipe de France, selon la liste divulguée vendredi 6 novembre par le sélectionneur Zinédine Zidane. L'attaquant Pablo Pagis, lui, est convoqué pour la première fois.
Pablo Pagis, le fils de l'ancien attaquant de Ligue 1 Mickaël Pagis, va découvrir l'équipe de France à 23 ans. Il a notamment profité des absences sur blessure d'Ousmane Dembélé, de Maghnes Akliouche ou encore d'Esteban Lepaul.
"Pablo Pagis est sélectionné ce soir parce qu'on a eu un petit souci avec Akliouche, qui est un petit peu touché", a reconnu Zinédine Zidane en conférence de presse. "Pablo était dans la liste élargie, c'est un joueur que je veux voir, un joueur intéressant, différent", a-t-il ajouté.
Des retours attendus
Mbappé, meilleur buteur de l'histoire des Bleus (107 sélections, 67 buts), revient après avoir été touché au genou le 25 septembre en Turquie (1-0). Depuis son retour sur les pelouses, il a inscrit huit buts en sept rencontres avec le Real Madrid.
Le milieu de terrain Aurélien Tchouaméni effectue son retour chez les Bleus alors qu'il n'avait pas été convoqué par "Zizou" à l'occasion de sa première liste. Appelé lors du précédent rassemblement avant de devoir quitter le groupe sur blessure, Ibrahima Konaté fait lui aussi son retour pour la première fois depuis la Coupe du monde, comme le latéral droit Malo Gusto, le milieu de terrain Warren Zaïre-Emery et l'attaquant Marcus Thuram.
Le milieu Warren Zaïre-Emery, le défenseur Malo Gusto et le gardien Robin Risser sont également rappelés après avoir manqué le premier rassemblement de l'ère Zidane, le Parisien et le portier de Lens ayant déclaré forfait pour cause de pépins physiques alors que l'arrière droit de Chelsea, présent au Mondial-2026, n'avait pas été retenu.
En revanche, le sélectionneur doit se passer des services de plusieurs cadres (Ousmane Dembélé, William Saliba, Manu Koné, Jules Koundé, Maxence Lacroix) et des attaquants Maghnes Akliouche et Estéban Lepaul, blessés.
La France affrontera l'Italie à Milan et la Turquie à Bordeaux, les 12 et 15 novembre dans le cadre de la Ligue des nations. Il ne manque plus qu'un point aux Tricolores, en tête de leur groupe avec trois victoires et un nul, pour se qualifier pour les quarts de finale. "On a deux matches à gagner et on va essayer de les gagner", a prévenu Zinédine Zidane.
La liste complète communiquée par Zinédine Zidane
Gardiens : Mike Maignan (AC Milan), Guillaume Restes (Toulouse), Robin Risser (Lens)
Défenseurs : Andy Diouf (Inter Milan), Malo Gusto (Chelsea), Jérémy Jacquet (Liverpool), Pierre Kalulu (Juventus), Ibrahima Konaté (Real Madrid), Adrien Truffert (Bournemouth), Dayot Upamecano(Bayern Munich), Lenny Yoro (Manchester United).
Milieux : Eduardo Camavinga (Real Madrid), Rayan Cherki (Manchester City), Lucas Da Cunha (Côme), Adrien Rabiot (AC Milan), Aurélien Tchouaméni (Real Madrid), Warren Zaïre-Emery (Paris Saint-Germain).
Attaquants : Bradley Barcola (Liverpool), Désiré Doué (Paris Saint-Germain), Kylian Mbappé (Real Madrid), Michael Olise (Bayern Munich), Pablo Pagis (Paris FC), Marcus Thuram (Inter Milan).
Avec AFP

On y retrouve notamment Kylian Mbappé et Aurélien Tchouaméni, remis de leurs blessures. Pablo Pagis, attaquant du Paris FC, a été convoqué pour la première fois.

content:
Donald Trump will be blocked from putting a “rightwinger” on the US supreme court, according to Chuck Schumer, the soon-to-be Senate majority leader, in remarks that were a preview of how Democrats intend to wield their power come January.
In an interview with the Associated Press, Schumer said Democrats would not confirm “any crappy nominees” to the supreme court, lower courts or Trump’s cabinet.
“The bottom line is we’re not going to allow a rightwinger on the court,” Schumer said. Four supreme court justices are in their 70s, and its two most conservative justices, Clarence Thomas and Samuel Alito, are the oldest on the court at 78 and 76 years old, respectively.
After scoring massive midterm-election wins and taking back both chambers of Congress, Democratic leaders are planning their comeback for when the new Congress is sworn in. That includes major pushback against the US president and his policies.
Some Democrats are planning to launch investigations into Trump and members of his administration. On Tuesday evening, Robert Garcia, the soon-to-be chair of the House oversight committee, warned Republicans to “lawyer up”.
Others are preparing to push forward legislation they promised to voters, and Democratic leaders will enjoy wide margins in both the House and Senate to pass key priorities like restoring Medicaid cuts from Trump’s “One Big Beautiful Bill” and halting funding for the war in Iran. Trump has indicated he plans to veto bills he doesn’t agree with.
Democrats have secured 54 Senate seats for the next Congress, and that number would increase to 56 if Democratic candidates in Mississippi and Alaska triumph. Neither race has been called, but the Democrats lead in both. Democrats also will have at least 253 House seats after flipping more than 40 seats, as of Friday morning.
Schumer told the Associated Press he anticipates Democrats will have enough power to reject Trump’s nominees and halt other policies.
The supreme court is one area where Democrats plan to push back heavily.
During his first term, Trump nominated three justices to the supreme court, Neil Gorsuch, Brett Kavanaugh and Amy Coney Barrett, which solidified a 6-3 conservative majority that has batted away many – though not all – of the challenges to Trump’s second term policies.
Thomas or Alito still have six weeks left of a Republican Senate that could in theory confirm a Trump appointee to the high court, but Thomashas not indicated he plans to retire.
Alito denied rumors he was retiring and reiterated his plan to Fox News on Thursday, telling the news organization he plans to stay on the court for the remainder of the term, regardless of Democrats’ sweeping win.
As Democrats prepare for their return, Republicans are reflecting on how and why they lost so badly.
Over the last few days, top Republicans have played the blame game, pointing fingers at Trump’s war with Iran and tariffs for raising everyday costs.
JD Vance, the vice-president, acknowledged how the Iran war caused widespread frustrations. Ted Cruz, a senator from Texas, said Trump’s tariffs drove up costs. Ron DeSantis, the governor of Florida, admitted Republicans’ vote on the Epstein files reflected poorly on the party.
Trump, meanwhile, has directed his attention to personal issues – largely related to construction projects in Washington DC.
But he suffered another blow on Friday when a federal judge blocked construction work from beginning on his planned triumphal arch for 14 days, after it was given the go ahead on Thursday by a commission packed with Trump loyalists.
On Monday, the day before the consequential elections, the US president held a press conference to unveil his administration’s latest upgrades to the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool. The costly and controversial project has been in and out of headlines over the last year because administration officials sought to blame “vandals” for the project’s failures. A Trump-appointed US attorney later determined those failures were the result of poor work.
On Wednesday, the day after Republicans lost the majority in Congress, Trump held another press conference to show off the latest renovation to the White House ballroom, another costly and controversial project.
The US president spent more than 20 minutes discussing the details of his ballroom and only addressed his party’s massive failures when reporters asked him directly about it.
On Thursday, after suffering even more losses in Congress, Trump held a press conference in the Oval Office to sign a proclamation preventing future presidents from changing the design of his gilded Oval Office and Cabinet Room.
“I just thought it was very important that nobody be allowed to come and take it down and try and do something with it,” Trump said on Thursday.

content:
This is Atiku Abubakar's seventh attempt to become Nigeria's president
Published
Nigeria's Federal High Court has sacked the leadership of the opposition African Democratic Congress (ADC) party - and also ruled that the nomination of its presidential candidate, former Vice-President Atiku Abubakar, is invalid.
A statement from the ADC said the ruling was another desperate attempt to cripple the opposition.
Presidential elections are scheduled to take place on 16 January when President Bola Tinubu's main challengers are again expected to be Abubakar and former Anambra State Governor Peter Obi.
What is the row about?
Several high-profile politicians joined the ADC in 2025 - disillusioned by the factional infighting in the once powerful Peoples Democratic Party (PDP).
Among them were Abubakar - who had served as vice-president between 1999 and 2007 when the PDP was in power - and former Senate president David Mark.
As accommodations were made for the line-up of political heavyweights, Mark took over as its interim chairman.
But Nafiu Bala Gombe, a former ADC national deputy chairman, argued before the court that this was not lawful as Mark and others had not been elected at a national convention.
Instead, he said, he himself should have taken over the party's leadership following the resignation of the ADC's former chairman in 2025.
This is not first time the Federal High Court in the capital, Abuja, has ruled on the leadership of the party.
In July, judge Musa Liman said Mark had been chosen in accordance with the country's laws and the party's constitution - in a case brought by another former ADC member.
Abubakar said the latest case raised serious legal concerns: "Why, after that judgment, was another case filed to reopen the same dispute?"
In a statement, the ADC added that Thursday's judgement by Justice Peter Lifu was aimed at stifling the opposition momentum and "was a calculated attempt to weaken the ADC and frustrate" Abubakar's candidacy.
What happens next?
The ADC says it will challenge the ruling at the Court of Appeal.
In a statement on Facebook, Abubakar, 79, said he would contest the election despite the ruling, external.
"Let me be clear to every Nigerian who has stood with us: I am in this race. I am not going anywhere. We will be on the ballot. No threat, blackmail or court manoeuvre will make me abandon you or the cause we share," he wrote on Friday.
He had previously questioned the timing of the judgment, coming "barely a day after a mammoth crowd turned out in Sokoto [northern Nigeria] to welcome him" as he launched his campaign.
Political parties in Nigeria have increasingly been taking internal issues to court.
But as it stands, the electoral commission has issued its final list of candidates, external - and Abubakar is on the ticket for the ADC with former Rivers State Governor Rotimi Amaechi as his running mate.
Will the latest ruling affect the opposition?
The ADC is seen as the most powerful opposition to President Tinubu. Many influential politicians opposed to the ruling All Progressives Congress (APC) have already defected to the party.
The legal saga could complicate things - it may cause uncertainty for hundreds of ADC candidates as well as raise questions over who has the authority to represent them.
Peter Obi - the other main presidential candidate, who is on the ballot for a second time - said he was shocked by Thursday's high court ruling.
He released a statement on X with the heading, external: "Do not undermine democracy".
The 65-year-old went on to say: "My concern is that three months before a general election, it is in the public interest to have certainty.
Obi had briefly joined the ADC before leaving earlier this year to join the Nigeria Democratic Congress (NDC) - in part because of the legal challenges within the ADC.
"The sustenance of democracy in Nigeria, in the midst of encroaching military rule in West Africa, should strengthen our resolve to protect opposition politics and not stamp out opposition parties," he said.
The NDC's candidate said that, as president, he would ensure that the existence of opposition parties would be respected.
"This is a time to strengthen our democracy by allowing the opposition to thrive."
Additional reporting by Chris Ewokor in Abuja

content:
Un total de 854 migrantes que viajaban en siete embarcaciones precarias llegaron durante la madrugada y la mañana de este viernes (06.11.2026) a la isla de El Hierro, en las islas canarias españolas, según Salvamento Marítimo español.
Los ocupantes de los siete cayucos son personas de origen subsahariano, según los servicios sanitarios, que alcanzaron estas islas españolas situadas en el océano Atlántico procedentes de África a través de la llamada ruta atlántica, uno de los recorridos migratorios más peligrosos y mortíferos del mundo.
La primera embarcación fue localizada a cuatro millas del puerto de La Restinga en la isla del Hierro y escoltada por la Salvamento Marítimo hasta el muelle, donde llegó de madrugada con 134 personas a bordo.
La segunda llegó también de madrugada con 174 personas, mientras que la tercera lo hizo poco después con otras 166.
El cuarto cayuco, el que transportaba más personas de los siete, arribó ya de día con 235 ocupantes.
A continuación desembarcaron las 54 personas del quinto cayuco, las 39 del sexto y las 52 del último.
Según la información recabada de los servicios sanitarios y de emergencia, los ocupantes de los siete cayucos son de origen subsahariano y en su mayoría varones, aunque en todas las embarcaciones viajaban también mujeres y menores.
Por el momento se desconocen los lugares de salida de los cayucos y la procedencia concreta de sus ocupantes.
Todos recibieron una primera atención sanitaria en la isla de El Hierro, mientras que 350 personas fueron derivadas a la vecina Tenerife, la más grandes de las islas Canarias, por la Administración del Estado, y otras 350 iban a ser trasladadas por la tarde.
Esas llegadas se suman a otras decenas registradas esta semana en las vecinas islas de Lanzarote y Gran Canaria, y tan solo en el pasado mes de octubre un total de 6.194 inmigrantes han llegado a ese archipiélago en embarcaciones precarias, más que durante todo el primer semestre de 2026, cuando fueron rescatadas 3.708 personas, según el Ministerio del Interior español.
Y en noviembre continúan las constantes llegadas de barcazas: sin contar los rescates de este viernes, durante los cinco primeros días de noviembre habían llegado más de 3.200 migrantes a las islas Canarias.
La cifra ha encendido las alarmas en varios de los servicios de asistencia, porque se acerca a unos ritmos que no se veían en la ruta canaria desde los meses récord de 2023 y 2024.
ct (efe, reuters)
summary: Un total de 854 personas, entre ellas mujeres y menores, llegaron en siete cayucos a El Hierro. Las llegadas a Canarias se aceleran: más de 3.200 migrantes arribaron al archipiélago en los primeros cinco días del mes.
