content:
Climate change is increasing the frequency and intensity of extreme heat events
Published
Human activities are causing world temperatures to rise, posing serious threats to people and nature.
Things are likely to worsen in the coming decades, but scientists argue urgent action can still limit the worst effects of climate change.
What is climate change?
Climate change is the long-term shift in the Earth's average temperatures and weather conditions.
The world has been rapidly warming for around a century, causing weather patterns to change.
Since the 1980s, each decade has been warmer than the previous one, the Met Office says.
2024 was Earth's hottest year on record, with climate change mainly responsible for the high temperatures.
It was also the first calendar year to surpass 1.5C of warming compared to "pre-industrial" levels of the late 1800s, according to the Copernicus climate service, external.
Temperatures remained high in 2025, despite a slight cooling from a natural weather pattern called La Niña.
The opposite El Niño pattern, combined with climate change, makes it likely that 2026 will also rank among the hottest years ever recorded.
How are humans causing climate change?
The climate has changed naturally throughout the Earth's history.
But natural causes cannot explain the particularly rapid warming seen over the last century, according to the UN's climate body, the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC).
This has been without doubt caused by human activities, especially the widespread use of fossil fuels - coal, oil and gas - in homes, factories and transport systems.
When fossil fuels burn, they release greenhouse gases - mostly carbon dioxide (CO2). This CO2 acts like a blanket, trapping extra energy in the atmosphere near the Earth's surface. This causes the planet to heat up.
Since the start of the Industrial Revolution - when humans began burning large amounts of fossil fuels - the level of CO2 in the atmosphere has risen by more than 50%.
The CO2 released from burning fossil fuels, external has a distinctive chemical fingerprint. This matches the type of CO2 increasingly found in the atmosphere.
What effects of climate change have already been seen?
Climate change has already had a huge effect, including:
more frequent and intense extreme weather, such as heatwaves and heavy rainfall
rapid melting of glaciers and ice sheets, contributing to sea-level rises
the shrinking of Arctic sea-ice
warmer oceans, which can fuel more intense storms and harm sea life
These changes are already having serious consequences for people and economies around the world.
In August 2026, the partial collapse of a glacier caused an avalanche of ice and rock to descend on Nepal and Tibet
Flash floods in Nepal killed more than 1,400 people in August 2026. Nepal's Finance Minister, Swarnim Wagle, said it could cost up to a tenth of the economy to rebuild.
Climate change increased the chances of the glacier collapse which triggered the flood, World Weather Attribution group scientists said.
Why does 1.5C matter and how will future climate change affect the world?
The more the world warms, the worse the impacts of climate change become.
Nearly 200 countries pledged to try to limit global warming to 1.5C above pre-industrial levels in the 2015 Paris agreement.
That target is generally understood to mean an average annual increase of 1.5C over 20 years rather than a one-off rise in a single year.
Long-term warming of 1.5C would bring serious consequences for many populations.
But an increase of 2C or more would bring even greater impacts, the IPCC says.
These include:
more people exposed to extreme heat
increased risks to food security in some regions due to more extreme weather
greater chances of some climate-sensitive diseases spreading, such as dengue
more species being threatened with extinction
The call to restrict temperature rise to 1.5C was partly designed to avoid crossing so-called "tipping points".
It is not clear exactly where they sit, but once these thresholds are passed, changes could accelerate and become irreversible.
These could include the collapse of the Greenland Ice Sheet, warm Atlantic Ocean currents or further loss of the Amazon rainforest.
The Earth's poles are especially vulnerable to rising temperatures
About 3.3 to 3.6 billion people are highly vulnerable to climate change, the IPCC says.
People living in poorer countries are expected to suffer most as they have fewer resources to adapt.
This has led to questions about fairness, external, because these places have typically only been responsible for a small percentage of greenhouse gas emissions.
However, knock-on impacts could be felt over wide areas. For example, crop failures linked to extreme weather could raise food prices globally.
What are governments doing about climate change?
Reaching net zero CO2 emissions is essential to limit global warming, the IPCC says.
This means reducing emissions as much as possible and actively removing any remaining emissions from the atmosphere.
Most countries have, or are considering, net zero targets, external.
There has been encouraging progress in some areas, such as renewable energy and electric vehicles.
But humanity's CO2 emissions are still at record highs, causing long-term warming to reach 1.4C in 2025.
The latest UN Emissions Gap Report, external said the 1.5C limit was likely to be breached in the coming years.
A return to 1.5C by 2100 was possible, but it would require "urgent and stringent cuts to greenhouse emissions", the report added.
Otherwise, global warming could reach nearly 3C by the end of the century, the UN said.
World leaders meet every year to discuss their climate commitments.
In 2025, the COP30 climate conference ended without any new agreements on fossil fuels or deforestation in the final deal.
Countries had previously agreed on the need to "transition away from fossil fuels in energy systems" at the COP28 talks in 2023.
At COP29 in 2024, richer countries committed to giving developing nations at least $300bn (£223bn) a year by 2035 to help them tackle climate change. But this is far less than poorer countries say they need.
Governments are gathering in Turkey for the next round of talks, COP31, in November 2026.
What can individuals do about climate change?
Major changes need to come from governments and businesses, but individuals can help through actions like:
taking fewer flights
using less energy
improving their home's insulation and energy efficiency
switching to electric vehicles or living car-free
replacing gas boilers with electric systems like heat pumps
eating less red meat

content:
Taiwan says it is closing its representative office in Papua New Guinea and will stop buying liquefied natural gas (LNG) from the country, blaming Chinese political pressure on the South Pacific nation.
Taiwan’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs said on Friday that Papua New Guinea had repeated previous demands that staff leave its office in the capital, Port Moresby, within a set deadline and had pushed for its closure.
These actions “reflect China’s continued use of political pressure and economic influence to interfere in other countries’ diplomatic decisions and suppress Taiwan’s international space”, it said in a statement.
China, which claims Taiwan as part of its territory, had welcomed Papua New Guinea’s decision in July to shutter Taiwan’s office in Port Moresby. Taipei rejected the move, and the office remained open in the interim.
The Pacific has long been an area for diplomatic competition between China and Taiwan. Papua New Guinea has formal diplomatic relations with China, but it had allowed Taiwan to have a representative office in Port Moresby.
Taiwan has formal diplomatic ties with only three Pacific Islands nations: Palau, Tuvalu and the Marshall Islands. It also has a representative office in Fiji. Just 12 countries maintain formal diplomatic ties with Taiwan.
Taiwan previously announced that it had stopped spot purchases of LNG from the South Pacific nation, but on Friday the ministry said it also would no longer sign new spot purchase contracts with the country.
Taiwanese LNG purchases accounted for one-third of Papua New Guinea’s exports.
Last year, Taiwan imported about 8 percent of its natural gas from Port Moresby.
Taipei will also end technical cooperation and assistance programmes, “including medical missions, related scholarship and talent development programmes”, the ministry said.
summary: Amid the fallout, Taiwan says it will stop purchases of liquefied natural gas from Port Moresby.

content:
Nepal became the first country approved to receive money from a fund for damages linked to climate change after flash floods in August 2026
Published
In Paris in 2015, almost 200 countries signed a landmark agreement designed to limit global warming to 1.5C and avoid its worst impacts.
But despite some progress in areas like renewable energy, the world has continued to warm at a rapid pace.
A recent UN report said the target was likely to be breached in the next few years and that "urgent and stringent" action would be needed to return the world to 1.5C.
What is the Paris climate agreement?
The Paris Agreement is at the heart of the international commitment to tackle rising global temperatures.
It came into force on 4 November 2016 and saw almost all the nations of the world agree to cut the greenhouse gas emissions which cause global warming.
However, the United States - the world's second biggest greenhouse gas emitter - withdrew from the deal in January 2026 under President Donald Trump.
The US also withdrew during Trump's first presidency, but it rejoined in 2021 under his successor President Joe Biden.
The only other UN member states outside the Paris agreement are Iran, Libya and Yemen.
What does the Paris Agreement say?
The Paris Agreement lists a series of commitments:
to "pursue efforts" to limit global temperature rises to 1.5C, and to keep them "well below" 2.0C above those recorded in pre-industrial times, generally considered to mean the late 19th Century
to achieve a balance - known as net zero - between the greenhouse gases that humans put into the atmosphere and the gases that they actively remove, in the second half of this century
each country to set its own emission-reduction targets, reviewed every five years to raise ambitions
richer countries to help poorer nations by providing funding, known as climate finance, to adapt to climate change and switch to renewable energy
The 1.5C target is generally accepted to refer to a 20-year average rather than a single year.
So, while 2024 was more than 1.5C warmer than pre-industrial times, it did not mean the Paris Agreement threshold has been breached
Why does keeping global warming to 1.5C matter?
Every 0.1C of warming brings with it greater risks for the planet, such as longer heatwaves, more intense storms and wildfires, according to climate scientists.
But a very large body of scientific evidence shows that warming of 2C or more would bring far greater impacts, on top of those felt at 1.5C, UN scientists say.
These include:
more people being exposed to extreme heat
higher sea levels as glaciers and ice sheets melt
increased risks to food security in some regions due to more extreme weather
greater chances of some climate-sensitive diseases spreading, such as dengue
more species being threatened with extinction
the loss of virtually all coral reefs
Some changes could become irreversible if so-called "tipping points" are crossed.
It is not clear exactly where these sit, but once these thresholds are passed, changes could accelerate and become irreversible.
These could include the collapse of the Greenland Ice Sheet, warm Atlantic Ocean currents or further loss of the Amazon rainforest.
What does The Paris Agreement promise for poorer countries?
The Paris deal restated a 2009 commitment that richer countries should provide $100bn (£73bn) annually by 2020 to help developing nations deal with the effects of climate change and build greener economies.
Although only $83.3bn was raised in 2020, data from the OECD, external shows the goal was reached in each of the three years after 2022.
Almost two-thirds of the money in recent years has gone towards efforts to limit global warming, while around a quarter has been used to help nations adapt to climate change.
In 2023, countries agreed for the first time that a fund should be established exclusively for loss and damage. This is money to help countries recover from the impacts of climate change.
Nepal became the first country approved to receive money from the fund after a flash flood in August 2026 killed more than 1,400 people.
At COP29 in 2024, richer nations committed to providing $300bn (£219bn) a year to developing nations by 2035. Developing countries - which had hoped for more - criticised the "paltry sum".
What has happened since the Paris Agreement?
World leaders meet every year to discuss their climate commitments at international summits known as COPs (Conference of the Parties).
All COPs since 2015 have tracked how countries are building on what they promised in Paris.
At COP28 in 2023, countries agreed for the first time to "contribute" to "transitioning away from fossil fuels", although they were not forced to take any specific action.
Countries also agreed to treble the global capacity of renewables - such as wind and solar - by 2030.
But the final deal at COP30 in 2025 failed to directly mention fossil fuels. Instead, the host of the conference, Brazil, published a voluntary roadmap for moving away from fossil fuels, which will be discussed at COP31.
That COP is taking place from 9 to 20 November 2026 in Antalya, Turkey and is co-hosted by Australia.
A "coalition of the willing" composed of 57 countries has also organised its own conferences separate from the COP process to discuss phasing out fossil fuels.
The first meeting was held in Santa Marta, Colombia in April 2026, and another conference is scheduled for July 2027 in Tuvalu.
Is the world on track to meet the 1.5C target?
The long-term 1.5C global warming target has not yet been breached.
But the latest UN Emissions Gap Report, external said the limit was likely to be exceeded in the next few years after "decades of insufficient climate action".
In the "lowest possible" scenario, warming would still reach 1.7 to 1.8C by the mid-century, the report said.
A return to 1.5C by 2100 is possible, but it will require "urgent and stringent cuts to greenhouse emissions", the UN added.
Specifically, emissions would need to be cut by 18% between 2025 and 2030.
The report found that the pledges governments have made so far would only cover half of these cuts.
Without further action, global warming could reach nearly 3C by the end of the century, the research said.

content:
Protesters broke into the construction site of a Microsoft   data center in Amsterdam on Friday, climbing cranes and hanging balloons while police stood by.
The action opened two days of planned protests in 16 countries, with campaigners demanding a pause in major artificial intelligence data center construction over concerns about electricity, water and environmental damage.
What happened in Amsterdam?
More than 100 activists gathered at the site, marching arm in arm before entering. Some danced or carried placards reading: "Screw your data center."
"These data centers are destroying our world. It's becoming uninhabitable because of all the resources they consume. That's why we're here today," protester Sam van der Beek said.
Site owner Pure Data Centres, which plans to invest more than $1 billion (€890 million) in the project, urged protesters to leave safely and discuss their concerns.
Microsoft said it respected people's right to express their views peacefully but did not condone unlawful actions.
The Stop Dirty Data Centres coalition said other planned actions included a march in Dublin, a protest outside Poland's parliament and a demonstration against another Microsoft data center in Denmark.
Why are campaigners opposing data centers?
The protest group said more demonstrations are planned in several European countries on Saturday, including Ireland, Poland, Denmark, Finland, Spain, Italy, the Netherlands, France and the UK.
Campaigners say the facilities strain electricity and water supplies, compete with housing and other businesses for resources and threaten climate goals.
They also raise concerns about job losses and the concentration of power in technology companies.
The coalition said it was not calling for existing data centers to close. It wants governments to establish clearer rules before further large-scale construction proceeds.
Technology companies argue that data centers provide essential infrastructure for AI and cloud services used by businesses, governments and consumers.
The dispute comes amid growing scrutiny of the industry's expansion. A Google project in Finland faces a criminal investigation over land clearances, while Italy and Portugal are tightening environmental rules for data centers.
The Netherlands has about 200 data centers planned, under construction or operating.

content:
La Bolsa de Nueva York intenta recuperarse este viernes tras su desplome del jueves ligado a las preocupaciones sobre el sector de la inteligencia artificial (IA).
Hacia las 15H15 GMT, el índice tecnológico Nasdaq avanzaba un 1,83% y el índice amplio S&P 500 ganaba un 1,09%, lejos, sin embargo, de compensar las pérdidas de la víspera. El Dow Jones subía un 0,14%.
"El mercado espera poder presionar hoy el botón de reinicio, pero el camino a seguir dista mucho de estar claro, dado todo el tumulto que siguió a las elecciones" legislativas de medio mandato en Estados Unidos el martes, señaló Patrick O'Hare, analista de Briefing.com.
Alza que no compensa el desplome
El Nasdaq sufrió el jueves su peor caída desde abril de 2025, lastrado por el desplome de los valores ligados a la IA.
Los fabricantes de chips recuperan algo de terreno en esta última sesión de la semana. Nvidia (+5,53%), Broadcom (+3,09%) o AMD (+10,38%) subían aunque sin lograr borrar por completo las pérdidas del jueves.
Con la amplia victoria de los demócratas en Estados Unidos los mercados temen normas más estrictas para los centros de datos, inmensos almacenes de servidores indispensables para la IA, especialmente intensivos en consumo energético.
Y es precisamente el desarrollo masivo de las infraestructuras vinculadas a la IA lo que ha impulsado los valores tecnológicos a máximos en los últimos años.
summary: Temor por posibles regulaciones y freno a infraestructura hicieron caer las acciones este jueves en Wall Street, pero la semana terminó al alza.

content:
A government spokesman has said that, despite talks with the German Ice Hockey Federation (DEB), the International Ice Hockey Federation (DEB) and others, the impasse caused by last week's Court of Arbitration for Sport (CAS) ruling remains.
Since the October 30 decision, several leading ice hockey nations — including Finland , Sweden and Czechia  — have said they would refrain from playing against Russia in any tournament in which it is allowed to take part. Several key sponsors have also threatened to pull out, should the Russians be allowed to play.
The first tournament to be affected would be the Men's World Juniors, which opens in Canada  in late December, followed by the IIHF's premier event, the Men's World Ice Championship, to be hosted by Germany in May.
Hosting Worlds 'practically impossible'
Stefan Kornelius, the spokesman for  Germany's government , told reporters in Berlin on Friday that talks held with various stakeholders had made clear that Russia's participation would render the hosting of the championship "practically impossible — both from a sporting and an economic perspective."
Kornelius said talks would continue and the government still hoped for a diplomatic solution that would allow Germany to host the championship — as planned — in Gelsenkirchen, Mannheim and Düsseldorf in May.
"Our goal must be to hold the tournaments as scheduled," he said. "However, given the boycotts that would follow Russia's readmission, that would effectively be impossible. For this reason, we intend to explore — through dialogue — how we can still ensure the tournament takes place."
Following the CAS ruling that the IIHF must allow Russia to return to international play, DEB chairman Frank Lutz had conceded that Germany may be forced to consider withdrawing as championship host.
German visa restrictions on Russians in place
Asked at Friday's press conference whether Germany could issue visas to a Russian team for the tournament, a Foreign Ministry spokesman declined to answer categorically, but did indicate that this would be difficult under restrictions currently in place.
"At a time when Russia is waging a war of aggression against Ukraine , there can be no 'normalcy' — and we will certainly not pretend that there is," said spokesperson Martin Giese.
Earlier this week, Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney categorically ruled out Russian players taking part in the World Juniors in Alberta.
"While Russia and Belarus are supporting this illegal, unjustified war in Ukraine, as long as that's going on, there will be none of those athletes competing for their countries in Canada," he said.
"So, if you're asking specifically about the World Juniors," he said, "the Russians will not be there."
Consensus remains elusive
Russian President Vladimir Putin has also weighed in on the issue, accusing countries opposing Russia's return to international sport of violating the rights of his country's athletes.
The IIHF Council had originally called two days of meetings, on Monday and Tuesday, to try to reach a consensus on how to respond to the CAS decision — before extending discussions for a third day, on Thursday. By Friday, its members had evidently still not reached a consensus.
This comes as the Women's Ice Hockey World Championship , which is not affected by the CAS decision, opened in Denmark — and with the clock ticking toward the start of the World Juniors in Alberta on December 26.
summary: A week after a court ruled that Russia must be allowed to return to international ice hockey, the way forward remains unclear. Berlin is seeking a solution that will allow Germany to host next year's Word Championship.

content:
Ireland says bomb threats 'likely ... a coordinated campaign of disruption'
The Irish government has warned against a “likely coordinated campaign of disruption” in a statement responding to the latest bomb threats against European flights after similar threats were issued against some Irish media organisations (11:22).
“The threats made this morning against media organisations here are very serious.
Hoax threats such as these cause fear, distress and disruption to people going about their daily lives and activities; they achieve no positive purpose whatsoever. It is not known yet who is responsible for these threats, whether it is individuals or a centralised or coordinated effort.
However, these threats come on the heels of the ongoing disruption to aviation around Europe caused by similar threats, and it seems likely that this is a coordinated campaign of disruption.”
It continued:
“The Gardaí, working in cooperation with the Defence Forces, and our cyber and aviation authorities, are working to establish who is responsible. The Gardaí and the Defence Forces are in ongoing liaison with their European security counterparts. Every effort will be made to identify those responsible and to hold them to account.
The main priority, however, is to ensure that people are kept safe, despite the unavoidable and unwelcome disruption that this may cause.
The Gardaí have been alive to the risk of disruptive threats such as these in the context of planning for EU Presidency events and are exercising the relevant protocols in response.”
And, on that note, we will be closing the blog for today.
At least 18 flights have been disrupted by another round of false bomb threats across Europe, bringing this week’s total to more than 50, amid growing concern about a potentially “coordinated campaign of disruption” (14:15, 16:53).
Prague has seen the largest number of alerts, nine (13:14), with issues reported also on flights to and from Brussels (13:26), Paris (12:03), Rome (11:35) and Sofia (12:58).
The number of bomb threats represents only a tiny fraction of all flights across Europe, with almost 27,000 flights scheduled today (13:31).
Separately, bomb threats were also issued against Bulgarian, Irish, and UK news organisations, disrupting broadcasts and prompting staff evacuations in Ireland (11:22).
Further threats were distributed to media organisations this afternoon, but could not be immediately verified as genuine (17:16).
Ireland has warned against a “likely … coordinated campaign of disruption,” as it condemned attacks causing “fear, distress and disruption to people going about their daily lives” (14:15).
'This is only the beginning,' group claiming responsibility for hoax threats says
A number of European media outlets – including news organisations in Bulgaria, Ireland, and the UK – have reported that a group claiming responsibility for this week’s threats sent an email to several outlets warning of further attacks on transport across Europe.
“This is only the beginning,” it reportedly said.
We have chosen not to reproduce the email in full, given its unsubstantiated claims.
Meloni warns civilian infrastructure appears to be 'under attack' after recent incidents
Italian prime minister Giorgia Meloni has warned that “what’s being attacked is civilian infrastructure,” as she highlighted the evolving nature of threats and how they change people’s thinking about defence and security which is “not just talking about weapons, but safeguarding citizens’ daily lives.”
Italian prime minister Giorgia Meloni pictured in Rome earlier this week. Photograph: Stefano Carofei/Sintesi/SIPA/Shutterstock
Meloni said that it wasn’t clear if the attacks on French blood banks, refrigerators and planes were connected, but they all highlighted the newly emerging threats and were “a cause for concern.”
“When hackers attempted to alter the temperature of the refrigerators that store blood for transfusions, that blood was secured by a system that costs money; when you pay to buy that system, do we consider it defence spending or healthcare spending? When they tell us that the resources committed to defence and security are money taken away from healthcare or hospitals, that’s nonsense, because … we need both,” she said.
Belgian government to have another go at finding compromise on budget
I promised you an update on the situation in Belgium, and it looks like King Philippe has successfully pushed the government to resume talks on the next year’s budget.
Prime minister Bart De Wever pictured during a plenary session of the Chamber at the Federal Parliament in Brussels yesterday. Photograph: Nicolas Maeterlinck/Belga/Shutterstock
Prime minister Bart De Wever offered to resign on Monday following months of talks that failed to yield an agreement on €10bn in spending cuts and tax increases that he says are needed to stabilise Belgium’s finances.
After their second meeting today, the king’s office said talks would resume immediately as coalition partners seek to bridge remaining differences and reach an agreement to avert the prospect of early elections, Reuters reported.
The Royal Palace said that in conversations with the king this week all five parties in the government coalition had shown a willingness to compromise.
The king therefore tasked the prime minister with starting a new round of negotiations and with reporting back to the king on 16 November.
De Wever did not speak to the press waiting outside the palace before and after his meeting with the king.
Belgian prime minister Bart De Wever leaves the Royal Palace after a meeting with King Philippe in Brussels, Belgium. Photograph: Olivier Matthys/EPA
I keep monitoring the situation on European airports for you.
During an earlier disruption at Venice airport (11:33), a number of planes had to be diverted elsewhere: Brussels Airlines’s flight from Brussels and KLM from Amsterdam went to Trieste, whereas Air France’s service from Paris, Iberia’s service from Madrid, and Aegean’s from Athens went to Bologna.
Some of them have since completed their journeys flying back to Venice.
Ireland says bomb threats 'likely ... a coordinated campaign of disruption'
The Irish government has warned against a “likely coordinated campaign of disruption” in a statement responding to the latest bomb threats against European flights after similar threats were issued against some Irish media organisations (11:22).
“The threats made this morning against media organisations here are very serious.
Hoax threats such as these cause fear, distress and disruption to people going about their daily lives and activities; they achieve no positive purpose whatsoever. It is not known yet who is responsible for these threats, whether it is individuals or a centralised or coordinated effort.
However, these threats come on the heels of the ongoing disruption to aviation around Europe caused by similar threats, and it seems likely that this is a coordinated campaign of disruption.”
It continued:
“The Gardaí, working in cooperation with the Defence Forces, and our cyber and aviation authorities, are working to establish who is responsible. The Gardaí and the Defence Forces are in ongoing liaison with their European security counterparts. Every effort will be made to identify those responsible and to hold them to account.
The main priority, however, is to ensure that people are kept safe, despite the unavoidable and unwelcome disruption that this may cause.
The Gardaí have been alive to the risk of disruptive threats such as these in the context of planning for EU Presidency events and are exercising the relevant protocols in response.”
Dutch military police clears KLM flight from Prague
The Dutch military police has confirmed that it has checked a KLM flight to Amsterdam faced with a bomb threat and confirmed that no explosives were on board.
The statement did not identify the exact flight, but we know that a flight from Prague to the Netherlands was among the nine that saw bomb threats in Czech Republic, and local Dutch media said the affected flight was coming from the Czech capital, which means it was the flight KL1350.
While the number of bomb threats issued against European planes can sure be unsettling, it’s worth remembering it’s still a tiny, tiny, fraction of all flights taking place in Europe today.
Eurocontrol’s daily counter says there will be 26,709 flights in Europe today.
Hungary scrambles fighter jets to monitor three civilian flights, minister says
Hungary’s fighter jets have been scrambled three times this morning to escort civilian flights in Hungarian airspace after reported bomb threats, defence minister Romulusz Ruszin-Szendi said on Facebook.
He said the first alert came in response to a threat issued against a WizzAir flight from Brussels to Sofia (that’s the W64328 we reported on earlier at 12:58), and two more for flights from Prague to Cyprus and Bucharest (the latter one is the Tarom we reported on earlier at 12:16).
Looking at Prague’s departures board, the Cyprus flight will be Wizz Air’s W64600 to Larnaca.
The Prague airport has confirmed to the Guardian that nine flights have been affected by bomb threats so far today, one up from the latest update (12:26).
“The Police have taken the necessary security measures in response. Operations at Prague Airport remain unaffected,” a spokesperson said.
Some other planes appeared to be disrupted too, with AJet’s service from Istanbul eventually diverting to Vienna after making several circles around Prague – although there is no suggestion that it was affected by this morning’s threats.
At least 17 flights have been reportedly disrupted today, but we are getting less detail from airports and national authorities about false alerts today, making it more difficult to keep track of all planes affected.
It’s also interesting to see civil aviation authorities’ planes or helicopters flying near some of the affected airports today, including Prague and Bucharest, keeping a watchful eye on what’s going on.
Two planes land safely after alerts en route to Sofia
A Bulgarian transport ministry spokesperson told AFP alerts were also received for two flights to Sofia on Friday, and that both flights coming in from London Stansted Airport in Britain and from Brussels landed safely.
Looking at the airport’s arrivals board, that’d be W64328 from Brussels and FR1730 from London Stansted.
Tell us: have you been affected by the bomb threats to flights in Europe?
Multiple flights across Europe have been diverted or forced to make emergency landings following a series of bomb threats this week, prompting security checks and widespread disruption.
Are you on one of the affected flights or has your journey disrupted? What happened, and how did you feel? What information were you given by the airline or authorities, and how was the situation handled?
“We have been present solely as a security measure. It is therefore our assessment that there is no or has been any danger to passengers or others using the airport. We are investigating the new threats in line with the threats that arrived yesterday, and therefore have no further information.”
FlightRadar24 tracking service shows that some of these searches are making other planes circle near Prague Airport, with at least four planes currently holding near the airport.
At least eight flights to and from Prague affected by bomb threats this morning
We are also getting a bit more detail from the Prague airport authorities on disruptions that once again affected its operations this morning.
At least eight flights to and from Prague were hit by bomb threats, its spokesperson confirmed to AFP.
It concerned incoming flights from Denmark, Spain, and the UK, and outgoing flights to the Netherlands, Cyprus, Romania, Italy, and the UK, Denisa Hejtmánková said.
Passengers walk towards Vaclav Havel Airport Prague after multiple flights bound for Prague received bomb threats. Photograph: Gabriel Kuchta/Getty Images

content:
Власти Финляндии готовятся вновь ужесточить условия въезда в страну граждан РФ. Премьер-министр Петтери Орпо в пятницу, 6 ноября, допустил введение полного запрета на въезд россиян. Это стало бы "последовательным решением", заявил он журналистам после заседания правительственного комитета по внешней политике и политике безопасности.
Российским спортсменам могут отказать во въезде в Финляндию
Орпо напомнил, что Финляндия ограничивает въезд в страну граждан РФ с 2022 года, после начала полномасштабного российского вторжения в Украину. Среди прочего власти в Хельсинки отказались от выдачи россиянам туристических виз. "Сейчас мы хотим получить возможность отказывать во въезде в том числе профессиональным спортсменам ", - цитирует его заявление финская общественно-правовая медиакомпания Yle .
В свою очередь министр иностранных дел Элина Валтонен написала в соцсети X, что ее ведомство в сжатые сроки подготовит поправки к более раннему решению правительства, касающегося въезда россиян . "Россия должна прекратить свою захватническую войну в Украине", - добавила она.
Yle напоминает, что в середине ноября в Хельсинки пройдут два матча НХЛ, в которых должны участвовать в том числе российские хоккеисты. После этого в финской столице состоится турнир по фигурному катанию Finlandia Trophy, в котором также планируют участвовать россияне. В конце ноября на горнолыжном курорте Рука на севере Финляндии состоится этап Кубка мира по лыжным гонкам, на который намерены приехать российские спортсмены.
Суд в Лозанне обязал допустить хоккеистов из РФ к международным турнирам
Дискуссии о въезде в европейские страны россиян , продолжающих полномасштабную войну против Украины , вновь обострились после решения Спортивного арбитражного суда ( CAS ) в Лозанне, который в конце октября обязал Международную федерацию хоккея на льду (IIHF) допустить российские сборные на международные турниры. После этого IIHF выразила несогласие с этим решением, указав на проблемы получения виз, обеспечения безопасности, логистики и изменения в формате соревнований в короткие сроки.
Кроме того, сборные шести стран Европы - Дании, Латвии, Норвегии, Финляндии, Чехии и Швеции - отказались на предстоящем чемпионате мира играть со сборной России. Недовольство решением CAS выразили и в Немецком хоккейном союзе (DEB). "Это решение кардинально меняет исходную ситуацию в отношении чемпионата мира по хоккею 2027 года в Германии. Допуск России к участию влечет за собой для нас, как для принимающей стороны, значительные последствия в сфере безопасности, политики и экономики", - заявили в DEB.

content:
Achieving "net zero" is the world's key strategy to fight climate change, which is already having serious consequences for people and nature around the globe.
But the political consensus around the UK's net zero policies has collapsed, with the Conservative and Reform parties now branding them too difficult and expensive.
What does 'net zero' mean?
Net zero means balancing the amount of planet-warming "greenhouse" gases produced by human activities with the amount being actively removed from the atmosphere.
Effectively this means no longer adding to the total amount of these gases in the atmosphere to limit climate change.
Greenhouse gases include carbon dioxide (CO2) and methane. Their levels in the atmosphere are increasing rapidly due to human activities, including burning fossil fuels, chopping down forests and farming.
In practice, reducing these emissions means switching from coal, oil and gas to cleaner energy sources like wind and solar power.
It also involves adopting green technologies like electric vehicles and heat pumps to replace petrol or diesel cars and gas boilers.
But not all emissions can be eliminated.
So remaining emissions must be matched by things like planting trees, restoring peatlands or using machines to remove CO2 from the air.
But there are limits to these "carbon removal" techniques in scale and cost. That is why most of the focus is on drastically reducing emissions in the first place.
Why are net zero targets needed?
The world is warming because of humanity's greenhouse gas emissions, which increase global temperatures by trapping extra energy in the atmosphere near the Earth's surface.
This is bringing more heatwaves and extreme weather as well as melting ice sheets and raising sea levels.
In 2026, the UK experienced its hottest summer on record, which the Met Office said was made 130 times more likely by climate change.
Aiming to avoid the worst of these impacts, nearly 200 countries signed the landmark 2015 Paris Agreement. A target was set to reach net zero globally in the second half of the century.
Around 140 countries, external have their own net zero targets, covering roughly three-quarters of global emissions and 80% of the world's population.
It's widely accepted that richer nations will need to get to net zero before poorer ones, which often have fewer resources to switch to cleaner technologies and have contributed less to climate change historically.
Sea-level rises increase the chances of coastal flooding during storms
What is the UK doing to reach net zero?
The UK's greenhouse gas emissions have fallen sharply: in 2025 they were 54% lower than in 1990, according to provisional data, external.
This figure only includes emissions generated within the UK and not from products manufactured abroad and imported.
Successive UK governments have pledged to reach net zero by 2050 and the target was written into law in 2019.
To help achieve this, the current Labour government has committed to:
rapidly increase wind and solar generation to achieve "clean power" by 2030
end the sale of new fully petrol and diesel cars by 2030
subsidise electric heat pumps to replace gas boilers
invest in technology to capture and store CO2
These policies began to be implemented under Sir Keir Starmer's government and have continued to be pursued by Prime Minister Andy Burnham.
However, recent decisions have led some environmentalists to question whether the government can still meet its targets:
Approving the Jackdaw gas field in the North Sea
Reducing planned investment in heat pumps and carbon capture, external to pay for defence
Holding a consultation on whether to weaken electric car targets
The chancellor's support for a third runway at Heathrow
In June, the government's independent adviser, the Climate Change Committee (CCC), warned that the UK was "not moving fast enough", external towards net zero.
However, the Chancellor, John Healey, said in his autumn budget speech, external that the government remained "unshakably committed" to the goal.
Heat pump installations are rising but remain below targets
Where do UK parties stand on net zero?
When former Conservative Prime Minister Theresa May signed the UK's 2050 net zero target into law in 2019, it passed through parliament with the support of all major parties.
But that political consensus has since fragmented. The term "net zero" is often used by critics to attack environmental targets, which they claim are being put ahead of economic goals.
Labour Prime Minister Andy Burnham has said he is "determined" to meet the 2050 deadline, a policy also backed by the Liberal Democrats.
Meanwhile, the Green Party wants net zero "as soon as possible, and more than a decade ahead of 2050".
These parties argue that it's in the UK's economic interest to move away from fossil fuels, which can be volatile in price. Supplies can also be interrupted by international events like the US-Israel war on Iran.
But the Conservatives and Reform UK want to scrap the UK's net zero target, calling the current plans costly and unachievable.
They argue that, in isolation, the UK's efforts make little difference to climate change, not least because UK emissions are much smaller than those of countries like China and the US.
The SNP has targeted net zero by 2045 for Scotland, while Plaid Cymru has introduced a 2040 deadline in Wales.
What will net zero cost the UK?
There is no single path to net zero, which means there is no fixed price.
But the Climate Change Committee says the policy will require tens of billions of pounds a year by the end of the 2020s, most of which it expects to come from the private sector rather than government spending.
By the early 2040s, the CCC calculates that the savings from moving away from fossil fuels to cleaner, more efficient technologies should outweigh the costs, external.
Multiple studies have found that, globally, the economic cost of tackling climate change is much smaller than letting warming continue unchecked, which would result in widespread and increasing climate hazards.
However, as with any transition, the costs and benefits can be unequally felt. For example, while there is huge potential for new clean energy jobs, those employed in the oil and gas industry are likely to be negatively affected.

The support will be available to residents struggling with the cost of living
Published
Plans have been announced to help more people access affordable food, financial advice and help with heating costs this winter.
New community shops are due to open in Pendeford and Graiseley and a shop in Bilston is set to reopen. About 17,000 people have used Wolverhampton's network of community shops over the past six months, said City of Wolverhampton Council.
But council leader Stephen Simkins said many residents still faced difficult choices over household bills. "We know times are still tough for many residents," he added.
The council said more than 135,000 people have received support through its cost-of-living programmes, while more than £18.5m has been distributed to residents.
Simkins said: "Our ambition is simple, we want Wolverhampton to be a city where everyone has the opportunity to live a safe, secure and happy life.
"This winter, we will protect the most vulnerable and ensure nobody is left behind."
The new measures have been announced alongside the launch of a new three-year financial wellbeing strategy to support residents struggling with living costs.
About three tonnes of food are redistributed each month through weekly community markets, with plans to expand the scheme during the winter.
The authority is also extending its Community Chefs programme into schools.
More than 1,000 people have taken part in the initiative in the past six months, producing about 6,000 meals, said the council.
The Boost financial wellbeing service, launched in January to help residents reduce costs and manage household budgets, will also be expanded through the winter.
The council said winter warm packs have already been distributed through the city's family hubs, while adult social care teams are working with health services to help reduce seasonal pressures on the NHS.
summary: The plans aim to help more people access food, financial advice and help with heating costs.

Wounded French protesters to sue interior minister over police brutality
Around ten demonstrators wounded at recent protests in France on Friday said they will sue Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez over police brutality. Student and cost-of-living protests in recent weeks have been marred by violence, including reports of police inflicting serious and lifechanging injuries on protesters – many of whom are minors.
Lawyers representing people wounded during protests in France said on Friday they would sue the interior minister over alleged police brutality.
France has been rocked by high school student blockades and mass cost-of-living protests in recent weeks – less than six months ahead of elections to replace centrist President Emmanuel Macron – with the far right leading in the opinion polls.
Rights activists have accused law enforcement officers of disproportionately using force during the rallies, leading to serious injuries including a 15-year-old losing a hand to a crowd-control grenade.
"We now believe it is imperative to target the person responsible for these mutilations and massive damage, namely Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez," attorney Arie Alimi said at a press conference of lawyers representing at least 18 victims.
He said the lawyers would lodge a complaint with the Court of Justice of the Republic (CJR) – the only court able to deal with cases against sitting members of government.
"We are collectively bringing a case before the CJR against Mr. Laurent Nuñez for the orders he gave to use weapons which he knows to be mutilating," Alimi said.
Around ten of their clients have given consent to sign this collective complaint before the CJR, the lawyers said.
Alimi said the chances were slim it would lead to the opening of an investigation.
But "we have to do something to prevent more people from being mutilated, especially children," he said.
Read moreSevere injuries at French student protests draw scrutiny to police tactics
'Greatest proportionality'
Nuñez has said that since the beginning of the high school protest movement police had acted with "the greatest proportionality".
On Friday evening, he said he sincerely regretted the injuries but every time police officers used force, it was "within a legal and reglementary framework".
He said "intermediate" crowd-control means, such as grenades and tear gas, were essential for police to carry out their job.

Police's rubber-coated projectile balls or grenades have caused at least 20 people – including teenagers – to be seriously injured during protests since mid-September, according to an AFP count.
As of October 30, police had opened 105 internal investigations into allegations of police brutality, according to a source close to the case.
Of those, 52 were linked to the high school student movement, 48 to violence during mass protests on October 17 and 18, and five to incidents on October 24.
Earlier cases included a 14-year-old who in September lost most of his teeth when a police officer appeared to fire a grenade at him at very close range.
A 15-year-old in October lost his hand at a protest when a ball grenade exploded. A police union source said he picked it up, but a witness said the grenade landed on him.
Read moreFrance faces reckoning with public order policing after violent protest weekend
'Horrifying'
Alimi said more cases were still being discovered, with a particularly "horrifying" toll for October 17 – a day when arson and looting broke out in several cities on the sidelines of peaceful protests.
"It feels like being in a wartime infirmary," he said.
Among those wounded on October 17 was his client Ahmed Benmezroua, a 27-year-old independent photographer who had been attending his first protest in Paris. He almost died after a grenade ruptured an artery in his leg, he said.
A young engineer was "on the verge of losing his foot" after a grenade exploded underneath it in the same area on the same day, the lawyer said.
A 19-year-old nursing student was hit in the eye with a sting-ball grenade, resulting in a fractured nose and possible loss of the use of an eye, Alimi added.
In the city of Strasbourg near the German border, a 27-year-old lost an eye after police fired a sting-ball grenade on October 17, the lawyer said.
At a protest the same day in the eastern city of Mulhouse, a student called Maissa lost the use of an eye just before her 18th birthday, her attorney Pierre Brunisso said.
Several demonstrators were wounded in the eye during the Yellow Vest protest movement that shook Macron's first term.
(FRANCE 24 with AFP)

La COP31 en Turquie s'ouvrira avec peu d'attentes de la part de l'Union européenne
La COP31, qui s'ouvrira lundi 9 novembre à Antalya en Turquie, suscite peu d'attentes chez les Européens. La Commission européenne a expliqué vendredi ne pas s'attendre à une "révolution" en matière de climat, mais espère néanmoins des progrès concrets en matière d'énergies propres.
Un rendez-vous climatique qui s'ouvrira sans grand enthousiasme côté européen. Pour Bruxelles, la COP31 n'apportera pas de "révolution" tant le contexte international est difficile, mais l'Union européenne garde encore l'espoir d'obtenir des progrès concrets en matière d'énergies propres, a expliqué la Commission vendredi 6 novembre à Bruxelles.
À voir aussiCOP31 : le déficit de financement est "ahurissant", alerte l'ONU
La conférence de l'ONU sur le climat s'ouvre lundi 9 novembre à Antalya, en Turquie, et doit s'achever le 20 novembre. Elle sera centrée sur le thème de l'électrification.
"Ce n'est un secret pour personne que le contexte géopolitique est très difficile actuellement", a souligné un fonctionnaire européen, notamment en raison du retrait des États-Unis de l'Accord de Paris sur le climat. À la COP31, "nous devons ajuster nos attentes. Nous ne pouvons pas espérer une révolution en matière d'action climatique. Mais ce que nous voulons, c'est réellement montrer et consolider des progrès constants", a expliqué ce responsable.
"Aucune volonté politique"
En matière de financements climatiques, l'Union européenne, premier contributeur mondial, "respectera ses engagements", mais "il n'y a aucune marge de manœuvre et aucune volonté politique" pour des engagements financiers supplémentaires, a aussi rappelé ce fonctionnaire.
"Il n'est pas question de prendre un nouvel engagement financier", a-t-on abondé de source française, lors d'un échange distinct avec des journalistes.
La France s'est toutefois dite ouverte à une discussion sur la part de la finance pour l'adaptation au changement climatique, réclamée par des pays en développement. "Ce sera l'un des enjeux de la COP" et "il faudra qu'on apporte une réponse", a-t-on jugé dans l'entourage de la ministre française de la Transition écologique, Monique Barbut.
À la COP31, l'Union européenne soutiendra notamment l'initiative de la présidence turque en faveur de "l'électrification" de l'économie, pour remplacer des combustibles fossiles, a aussi indiqué la Commission.
La Turquie vise un objectif non-contraignant de 35 % d'électricité dans la consommation finale d'énergie d'ici 2035, contre environ 20 % actuellement.
Vers plus d'électricité "propre" ?
L'Europe plaide pour que la mesure concerne bien l'électricité "propre", issue des renouvelables ou du nucléaire, afin de décourager la production d'électricité dans les centrales à charbon, particulièrement polluantes.
Mais Bruxelles sait que le terme "propre" sera difficile à faire figurer dans la déclaration finale de la COP, face aux résistances des producteurs de combustibles fossiles.
"Le terme 'propre' peut poser problème à certains acteurs. Il pourrait exister d'autres façons de formuler cet objectif", a estimé un fonctionnaire européen.
À voir aussiL'Australie, une future présidente de la COP toujours très dépendante du charbon
L'UE veut une électrification "aussi propre que possible. Il reste à voir comment cela sera finalement formulé", a-t-il dit.
La France insiste de son côté pour que l'objectif d'électrification soit inclus dans une décision formelle de la COP, donc contraignante, "adoptée par toutes les parties, et pas seulement par un petit groupe d'États". "Ça enverra un message beaucoup plus fort si c'est le cas", a-t-on jugé.

content:
Democratic Senator Jon Ossoff and Republican Vice-President JD Vance
Published
Ballots are still being counted in the US midterm elections but the political landscape is already pivoting to the 2028 White House race.
Buoyed by major gains in Congress, Democrats will have momentum as they prepare for the contest to succeed President Donald Trump.
But a good showing in the midterms does not guarantee a White House win two years later. Barack Obama was re-elected in 2012 despite huge Republican gains in 2010.
No one has yet entered the presidential race but potential candidates will be preparing behind the scenes.
Vice-President's JD Vance's reflection on where the midterms went wrong for Republicans has been interpreted as him paving the way for a 2028 run.
The results of Tuesday's election and the historic size of Democratic gains could shape the White House race in several ways. Here are four takeaways.
1. Big winners in the midterms now have momentum
Several prominent potential presidential candidates were running in the 2026 midterms - and some emerged looking strong.
Georgia Democratic Senator Jon Ossoff won by a sizeable margin in the politically competitive state that Trump won in 2024.
While he has previously said he has no plans to run for president, his successful campaign, with several viral moments, helped boost his national profile.
Another potential Democratic nominee, Pennsylvania Governor Josh Shapiro, swept aside his Republican challenger.
Shapiro has not committed to a 2028 run but analysts point to his broad appeal in swing-state Pennsylvania as a sign that he could be competitive on the national stage.
Illinois Governor JB Pritzker also won after a campaign pundits in his state described as a "tune-up" for a presidential run.
California Governor Gavin Newsom could not run for re-election in the midterms but he is invested in the outcome of a ballot initiative to tax the state's wealthy residents which he campaigned against.
On the Republican side, there were two potential 2028 names running in Arkansas.
Republican Senator Tom Cotton and Governor Sarah Huckabee Sanders - a one-time Trump administration press secretary - were able to stay in office by a narrower margin than before, both earning just above half of the votes in the conservative state.
2. JD Vance and Trump's allies under pressure
Exit polls suggest the swing against Republicans was partly due to anger felt by voters at the actions of the Trump administration.
That could present a challenge to his potential successors who come from the ranks of the current leadership, including Vice-President JD Vance and Secretary of State Marco Rubio.
"The one person who has been hurt badly by this election campaign is Vance," said Karen Beckwith, a professor of political science at Case Western Reserve University in Ohio.
Vance has already sought to distance himself from defeat - and from a foreign policy adventure in Iran that was politically disastrous for his party.
"The reason we lost is the war," he wrote on X.
Rubio has denied reports he is considering leaving his post ahead of a 2028 presidential run.
Other possible Republican candidates may benefit from not being part of the administration. Some have been staking out a position on what went wrong and what next.
In a lengthy post on X, Senator Ted Cruz, who was not running this year, said that too many Republican politicians seem like "they didn't care" about the economic issues faced by voters.
"It is dark right now, but it is always darkest before the dawn, and morning is coming," he wrote. "That is my fervent prayer, and that is my commitment to you."
Florida Governor Ron DeSantis, who abandoned his 2024 presidential run after being trounced by Trump early on, was similarly critical and pointed to Republican victories in Florida as a sign of what can be accomplished.
Former New Jersey Governor Chris Christie was blunt in his assessment: "The Trump era is over."
3. Left and centre Democrats in fight for future
Both the centrist and left wings of the Democratic Party have claimed victory from the results as each side sifts through possible 2028 contenders.
Dozens are already making moves, Obama's former adviser Jim Messina has told the BBC.
El-Sayed's win in Michigan was a breakthrough moment for left-wing Democrats because he triumphed in a swing state.
His supporters now claim his win could supercharge left-wing candidates in the 2028 election.
"The old notions of electability are out the door, and bold economist populist outsiders proved they can win in battleground states," said Adam Green, the co-founder of the Progressive Change Campaign Committee.
Green added that the "water is now warm" for candidates such as New York Democratic representative Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez to run in presidential primaries and "know that they can win."
Moderate Democrats, however, claimed victories across the country, with the "Blue Dog Caucus" of moderate and conservative Democrats gaining at least 14 seats in Congress, nearly doubling its current size.
This has led many within that wing of the party to conclude that centrist candidates that bill themselves as pragmatic and willing to work with conservatives could woo Republican voters.
Given the success of Democratic candidates who focused on cost of living issues, an economy-first approach will likely be a focus again in two years.
Amirah Siquierah, the director of federal affairs at the Working Families Party, said successful candidates in 2028 will combine economic populism with newer concerns such as data centres.
4. Support of Hispanic voters must be earned
Both parties must contend with a changing political map and a shifting coalition of support for 2028.
Once "safe" Republican parts of the country can no longer be considered conservative strongholds.
Texas is left with only one Republican at a statewide level, which means its 40 electoral college votes could be up for grabs in 2028.
Christina Pascucci, a political commentator and one-time Senate candidate in California, said the midterms "challenge long-held political assumptions" and show that "neither party can afford to take its traditional strongholds for granted".
That is true of both Democrats and Republicans who will need to win over swing voters, added Pascucci, now the CEO of Atlas Global, a global communications and advisory firm.
"Neither party owns these voters," she said.
Texas has a new Democratic governor, Gina Hinojosa
The Trump coalition of working class and Latino voters faltered, reversing many of the gains he had made with those electorates in his successful 2024 campaign.
Driena Sixto, a former spokesperson for Turning Point USA and a conservative political commentator, told the BBC that she believed that Republicans will have to change their messaging to Latino voters ahead of 2028 for any future candidate to be able to reverse the trend.
"Last time, the campaign message was one of safe communities and fighting back against trafficking," she said.
"After the president was sworn in, I think a lot of messaging from the White House did too much to highlight deportations. That was the divide."

Millions of people in Sudan who have been displaced by the country’s civil war risk being left without emergency shelter due to funding shortages and depleting aid stocks, according to the United Nations refugee agency and the International Organization for Migration.
An estimated 15.4 million people across Sudan urgently need emergency shelter and basic household items, but funding shortages mean humanitarian agencies can prioritise assistance for only approximately 10 percent of those in need, the two UN agencies said in a joint statement on Friday.
“IOM and UNHCR remain committed to working with local humanitarian organisations and other partners to maintain shared supply pipelines, pre-position emergency stocks in priority areas and deliver assistance where needs are greatest,” the statement said. “But these efforts cannot be sustained without predictable and flexible funding.”
So far, only 936,000 people have received assistance, leaving a large gap between needs and available resources, according to the statement.
Since war broke out in 2023 between the Sudanese army and the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces (RSF), about 8.6 million people have been displaced within the country, making Sudan the world’s largest displacement crisis.
Meanwhile, more than 4.6 million people have fled across the country’s borders.
More than 5.2 million people have also returned to their areas of origin, often finding homes, infrastructure and basic services destroyed, the UN says.
“For families repeatedly displaced by conflict, a safe place to sleep and basic household supplies are far more than everyday necessities,” the joint statement said.
“They offer a measure of safety and dignity, particularly for women, children and other people at heightened risk. For those returning home, shelter assistance is often the first step towards rebuilding their lives.”
Speaking from Khartoum, IOM Sudan chief Mohamed Refaat said the agency was struggling to maintain operations as resources dwindled.
“Just this year, IOM was able to distribute more than 40,000 tonnes, but our warehouses are completely empty now,” he said.
Refaat said the number of internally displaced people could rise again despite recent returns. He said agencies had already scaled back ambitions because of limited funding.
They called for urgent funding to replenish emergency stocks and prevent worsening conditions for displaced Sudanese.
summary: Fewer than 1 million of the 15.4 million people in need emergency shelter in Sudan have received assistance.

Партии "Мирная Россия" Ильи Яшина и "Рассвет" Екатерины Дунцовой внесли в России в реестр  "иностранных агентов" . В список также включили медиапроект "Разоблачено", журналиста Бориса Грозовского и других общественных деятелей . Соответствующее заявление появилось на сайте министерства юстиции страны в пятницу, 6 ноября.
Добавление в реестр партии "Рассвет", которую  признанная "иноагентом" Дунцова основала в январе 2024 года в России, в ведомстве объяснили распространением "недостоверной информации" о решениях и политике российских властей, а также об избирательной системе страны. Отмечается также, что партия распространяла материалы других "иноагентов".
К обоснованию включения в реестр "Мирной России", учредительный съезд которой прошел в июне в Берлине , прибавились выступления против войны РФ в Украине , и распространение материалов организаций, которые признаны "нежелательными" в России .
А решение по медиапроекту "Разоблачено", который называет себя объединением "независимых журналистов и блогеров", объяснили в том числе и "призывами к участию в несанкционированных митингах".
В список добавили еще 5 человек
Помимо организаций, реестр "иноагентов" пополнили пять человек: фем-активистка Леда Гарина, публицист Борис Грозовский, правозащитник Николай Родькин, поэт Галина Рымба и журналист Мурат Темиров. Все они, как указывает Минюст России, среди прочего выступали против войны в Украине. Родькина и Рымбу, в частности, обвинили в "пропаганде ЛГБТ-отношений ", Грозовского - в фейках о Русской православной церкви ( РПЦ ), а Гарину - в сборе средств для Вооруженных сил Украины ( ВСУ ).
Минюст расширил список осужденных релокантов
Кроме того, Минюст России пополнил запущенный в конце октября  список граждан страны, к которым применяются так называемые "временные ограничительные меры". 6 ноября в него включили сразу 10 человек - журналист Юрий Дудь, писатели Борис Акунин (настоящее имя - Григорий Чхартишвили) и Дмитрий Быков , блогер Александр Невзоров, оппозиционер Дмитрий Гудков и руководитель проекта "Мемориал. Поддержка политзаключенных" Сергей Давидис.
В список попали сразу несколько человек, связанных с Алексеем Навальным и основанным им Фондом борьбы с коррупцией ( ФБК ). В из числе: Сергей Ухов и Ксения Фадеева - бывшие главы пермского и томского штабов Навального соответственно, руководитель политических проектов ФБК  Леонид Волков , а также журналист-расследователь ФБК Сергей Ежов.
На данный момент в реестре 22 человека.

Police in the eastern German state of Saxony-Anhalt said two people were killed on Friday when a small plane crashed onto the A2 highway northeast of Magdeburg, police said.
The crash closed all Hannover-bound lanes on one of Germany's main east-west routes. Police in Magdeburg said initial findings indicated that no road vehicles were involved.
What do we know about the plane crash?
The aircraft came down at around 2:48 p.m. local time (1348 GMT/UTC) between the town of Burg and the Krahenberge highway rest area.
It caught fire, and emergency crews recovered both occupants dead. The cause of the crash was not immediately known.
Photographs showed firefighters extinguishing the remains of a red-and-white aircraft. Its tail lay on the roadway, with burned wreckage on an embankment.
How was traffic affected?
Police and emergency crews remained at the scene. It was unclear how long the closure would last.
The A2 connects the greater Berlin area with Germany's most populous state,  North Rhine-Westphalia , and is a major route for traffic crossing Germany.
summary: Two people have died after a small plane crashed onto Germany's A2 highway near Magdeburg. The crash closed the Hannover-bound lanes on a major east-west route, with no road vehicles reported to be involved.

content:
European and Asian stock markets fell sharply on Friday after the Democrats’ decisive victory in the midterms triggered a rout in US tech stocks a day earlier.
A sell-off on Wall Street on Thursday was followed by sharp falls in Asian stock markets on Friday. The investor sentiment then reached London, where the market was, at one stage, poised for its worst day since March.
The FTSE 100 index, which tracks blue-chip shares listed in London, was down as much as 254 points, or 2.35%, at 10,528 points during a wave of selling in morning trading. But by the close of the day it had clawed back some of its losses to be down 1%, helped by a rise in US stocks when Wall Street reopened.
Germany’s Dax index fell by 2%, France’s Cac 40 dropped by 0.8% and Spain’s Ibex lost 0.6%.
Susannah Streeter, the chief investment strategist at Wealth Club, said: “The tech sell-off has intensified, with the pain of the brutal sell-off on Wall Street carried straight through to Asia and knocking sentiment in Europe.
“Big worries are colliding – the build-out of datacentres looks set to slow, which risks shredding the spending spree underpinning the boom, right at the time that investors have become super nervous about returns on this massive investment.”
However, there were signs of easing jitters on Wall Street on Friday, where tech stocks rose, lifting the S&P 500 share index by 0.3% and the tech-heavy Nasdaq closed up 1% – which only recovered a portion of their previous day’s losses.
That followed a stronger-than-expected employment report that showed the US economy added 165,000 new jobs in October, pulling the unemployment rate down to 4.1%.
On Thursday, the Nasdaq share index had its worst day in 19 months after slumping 5.5%.
Chip stocks led the slump on Thursday, with the memory maker SanDisk tumbling by 22% and the hard drive maker Western Digital falling by 17%. Wall Street’s “fear index”, the Vix, jumped by more than 60% to its highest levels since the early weeks of the Iran war, in a sign of rising market volatility.
The heavy falls continued in Asia on Friday, with Japan’s Nikkei 225 index sinking 6% and South Korea’s Kospi index tumbling more than 6.5%.
“It’s actually a bit of a disaster,” said Christopher Forbes, the head of Asia and Middle East at CMC Markets.
“[Clients] were long index, long stocks, and they all got carried out. All night, all day – we had client margin calls, client complaints … because it’s a very emotional thing, right? People are wedded to their positions and views on a stock or outcome, and you’re telling them: ‘Look, you’ve just lost money.’”
Chris Beauchamp, the chief market analyst at the investing and trading platform IG, said: “Yesterday’s [Thursday’s] brutal session marked a dramatic turnaround from Wednesday, but with AI fears still prominent there is a risk that there is much more selling to come.
after newsletter promotion
“Investors remain on watch for a potential resumption of the Iran conflict, and are nervously watching the oil price after its slump earlier in the week. All in all it remains a very febrile atmosphere.”
However, despite the sharp losses suffered on global stock markets around the world, most indices are still up for the year. The Nasdaq Composite index remains up 6.35% since the start of January – even though it is more than 10% below its peak.
The FTSE 100 has gained almost 7.5% in 2026 – but it is now more than 300 points below the record high set in July.
Mohit Kumar, an economist at the investment bank Jefferies, said that while he did not expect a quick rebound from Thursday’s losses in the US, he also did not believe it marked the “start of the unwind of the AI trade”.
He said: “AI investment has been a key driver of US growth and we do not see the Democrats as giving up on this growth engine. Datacentres and AI infrastructure also create jobs and Democrats would be reluctant to let those jobs move on to other states or outside the country.”
Stock market tremors have also hit the London Metal Exchange, with copper poised for its biggest weekly fall since March.
Benchmark three-month copper, a key metal used in the semiconductor, electronics and automotive industry, has dropped 0.61%, leaving it positioned for a 2.79% fall this week.
Craig Lang, a principal analyst at the consultancy CRU, said the price of copper was increasingly influenced by the AI market and “sentiment towards datacentre expansion”.

The English amateur cricketer who went viral for finger-clicking trickery has been handed a two-year suspension, the North Yorkshire and South Durham Cricket League has said.
The fielder Brian Devine, dubbed “Clicky Ponting” on social media in a nod to former Australia captain Ricky Ponting, was accused of tricking umpires by clicking his fingers to make the sound of a ball nicking the bat as deliveries were missed and caught by the wicketkeeper.
The video footage went viral on social media and made international headlines earlier this year. A three-person disciplinary panel reviewed the footage and considered player interviews and written statements before imposing the ban.
“The player concerned is suspended from all cricket under the ECB’s [the England and Wales Cricket Board] jurisdiction for two years, from 30 September 2026 to 29 September 2028. This covers playing, coaching, umpiring, scoring and managing junior teams,” the NYSDL said in a statement on Friday.
Additionally, Saltburn Cricket Club have been fined 300 pounds ($402.87) and their second XI has been relegated to Division Three of the NYSDCL and will start the 2027 season with a 60-point deduction, the league added.
Devine and Saltburn admitted the charges, but the club appealed against their sanction.
Saltburn said in a statement reported on gazettelive.co.uk: “The club fully participated in the disciplinary proceedings and accept the decision of the appeal following the original decision from the league.”
In a statement to the Press Association, the league said, “The league recognises the strain this has placed on many people, especially those who were abused online and in person.
“We ask everyone to respect that the formal process is now complete. The league will make no further comment.”
Ricky Ponting, who led Australia to two 50-over World Cup titles, told the Reuters news agency that he found the controversy amusing, although he was less impressed that his name had become associated with the player.
“I had a bit of a chuckle to myself and pretty much forgot about it after that,” he said in an interview earlier this year.
“I guess it wasn’t a nice thing to have my name associated with someone who’s blatantly cheating but … honestly I had a laugh and a joke about it.”
