Une organisation de colons extrémistes israéliens a établi un avant-poste à quelques kilomètres de Gaza
Depuis trois semaines, le mouvement de colonisation extrémiste Nachala a installé un campement temporaire dans la forêt de Simhoni, à trois kilomètres de la bande de Gaza, avec pour objectif d’entrer dans l’enclave palestinienne. Leur sort pourrait dépendre du prochain gouvernement qui se formera à la suite des élections législatives du 27 octobre.
Dans la nuit du 15 au 16 octobre 2026, des militants de Nachala, une organisation de colons israéliens d’extrême droite, ont construit, en quelques heures, un avant-poste à quelques kilomètres de la bande de Gaza. En une nuit, les membres de l'organisation ont établi un campement rassemblant des mobil-homes et des tentes où se sont installées une vingtaine de familles.
Pour afficher ce contenu Instagram, il est nécessaire d'autoriser les cookies de mesure d'audience et de publicité.
"Le site provisoire des 'Pionniers de Gaza' a franchi une nouvelle étape importante vers la création d'une colonie à part entière à Gaza", déclare Reut Ben Kemoun, l’une des figures du mouvement Nachala, dans une vidéo republiée par Settlers from Within, un compte X qui recense les violences des colons à l’encontre des populations palestiniennes.
Avec ce campement temporaire, l’objectif pour ces militants est de rétablir des colonies dans la bande de Gaza. Ce n’est pas le premier avant-poste créé près de l’enclave. En septembre 2025, une cinquantaine de personnes issues de l'organisation Nachala avaient occupé un terrain vague à Shave Darom, près de la bande de Gaza, avec le même objectif.
Le Premier ministre, Benjamin Netanyahu, défend l’instauration d’un contrôle sécuritaire sans appeler à la recolonisation de l’enclave tandis que ses ministres, Itamar Ben Gvir et Bezalel Smotrich affichent clairement leur souhait de recoloniser Gaza.
Pour afficher ce contenu X (Twitter), il est nécessaire d'autoriser les cookies de mesure d'audience et de publicité.
Le campement est situé cœur de la forêt de Simhoni, située à seulement trois kilomètres de Gaza, non loin du kibboutz Kfar Aza dans la province du Néguev.
La rédaction des Observateurs a géolocalisé l’avant-poste et obtenu des images satellite datant du 22 octobre 2026, démontrant la présence d’installations avec une large tente bleue, symbole des campements du mouvement Nachala.
En attendant "l’installation au cœur de la bande de Gaza"
Pour attirer de potentiels visiteurs, l’organisation Nachala a lancé une opération de communication. L’invitation ci-dessous, mise en ligne par un habitant du campement sur X, liste différentes animations prévues sur le campement : des activités manuelles, des structures gonflables ou encore un atelier de préparation de barbes à papa… L’occasion ? Célébrer la création de ce lieu temporaire en attendant "l’installation au cœur de la bande de Gaza".
Sur les réseaux sociaux, les militants de Nachala publient régulièrement des images de leur vie sur le campement. On peut les voir notamment faire du jardinage.
Mais aussi préparer les repas.
Pour afficher ce contenu Instagram, il est nécessaire d'autoriser les cookies de mesure d'audience et de publicité.
Ou des festivités nocturnes.
Pour afficher ce contenu Instagram, il est nécessaire d'autoriser les cookies de mesure d'audience et de publicité.
Une organisation sanctionnée huit fois par l’Union européenne
L’organisation extrémiste Nachala n’est pas nouvelle et est bien connue des associations qui agissent contre la colonisation des terres palestiniennes.
"Nachala est une organisation active depuis une décennie. Leur activité principale est d’établir des colonies et des avant-postes en Cisjordanie et de mettre la pression sur le gouvernement. Depuis le 7 octobre 2023, [ses membres] se préparent et font des plaidoyers pour établir une colonie dans Gaza.", explique Hagit Ofran, qui travaille pour le projet "Settlement Watch", de l’ONG israélienne Peace Now.
Fondée par la militante d’extrême droite pro-colonies Daniella Weiss, Nachala avait fait parler d’elle lors de l’instauration d’un campement sauvage nommé "Evyatar" sur le territoire de la ville palestinienne de Beita, dans le nord de la Cisjordanie. Établie une première fois en 2013, l’avant-poste a été légalisé et établi comme une colonie par le gouvernement Netanyahu en juin 2024. Cette installation reste illégale au regard du droit international.
Soutenu par l’extrême droite israélienne, l’avant-poste a reçu la visite de représentants politiques tels que Limor Son Har-Melech, vice-présidente de la Knesset et députée du parti d’extrême droite Otzma Yehudit, dirigé par Ie ministre de la Sécurité nationale, Itamar Ben Gvir. Elle avait déjà participé à une opération réalisée par Nachala visant à franchir la frontière de la bande de Gaza, en février 2026.
Pour ses activités d’occupation illégale, l’organisation Nachala fait l'objet de huit sanctions européennes. Elle est notamment accusée de "jouer un rôle de facilitation et d'encouragement d'actes coercitifs menant au déplacement forcé des Palestiniens".
L'avant-poste situé dans la forêt de Simhoni n’a, pour le moment, pas reçu d’autorisation du gouvernement pour s’implanter durablement. En Israël, les espaces forestiers sont en grande partie gérés par le Fonds national juif (FNJ), un organisme lié au mouvement sioniste.
Interrogé par la rédaction des Observateurs, le FNJ assure avoir déposé plainte auprès de "la police et des autorités locales". Selon le site d'information israélien Ynet, la police prépare l’évacuation des militants de Nachala. Ces derniers auraient affirmé "ne pas s’opposer à l’évacuation" tout en annonçant leur intention de "se déplacer ailleurs jusqu'à atteindre Gaza".
Dans une vidéo diffusée le 4 novembre sur le compte Instagram dédié aux projets des "Pionniers de Gaza", Reut Ben Kemoun, toujours sur place, réaffirme son projet et annonce la tenue d’une conférence intitulée "Le Renversement de Gaza 2", le 19 novembre 2026.
Un avenir incertain, conditionné par le nouveau gouvernement
Pour Hagit Ofran de Peace Now, l’urgence ne réside pas dans l’évacuation du campement, mais dans la menace qu’il représente pour l’intégrité du territoire palestinien.
"Il existe une menace qu’Israël laisse établir une colonie dans Gaza, spécifiquement car le gouvernement a créé cette situation où Israël contrôle énormément la bande de Gaza (...) Ils ont tellement détruit ce territoire qu’il est désormais vide et prêt pour être colonisé. Il existe donc une menace sérieuse que Nachala établisse une colonie, mais elle ne peut pas le faire sans le soutien du gouvernement.", explique-t-elle.
Ainsi, les dernières élections législatives, qui se sont tenues le 27 octobre, pourraient avoir un impact considérable dans l'avenir des territoires palestiniens. Le camp de Benjamin Netanyahu, composé de la droite et de l’extrême droite pro-colonies, a obtenu 53 sièges contre 48 pour le bloc d’opposition centriste, mené par Gadi Eisenkot. Alors que le gouvernement sortant a perdu le soutien du parti ultra-orthodoxe, le camp centriste, soutenu par les partis arabes, ayant obtenu de manière inédite 19 sièges à la Knesset, se trouve dans une bonne position pour former le prochain gouvernement.
Bien qu'il soit contre la formation d'un État palestinien, Gadi Eizenkot a affiché son opposition au projet de recolonisation de la bande de Gaza. Ainsi, l’avenir de l'avant-poste établi par Nachala reste donc incertain. "Le prochain gouvernement peut avoir une politique bien différente. Peut-être qu’ils seront poussés à rester ou, au contraire, à abandonner”, précise Hagit Ofran. Avant de conclure : "C’est très difficile de savoir ce qu’ils vont faire".

Seven families from Helsingor, a coastal city north of Copenhagen, are facing their former landlord in Denmark’s Supreme Court.
In a two-day hearing that began on Friday, they are arguing they were forced from their homes because of where they, or their parents, come from.
Their leases were terminated in 2022 under a 2018 law, once known as the “ghetto law”, which targets social housing estates where more than half of residents are classed as “non-Western”. The government claims the law is aimed at integration. But rights groups have for years fought against the measures, saying they are discriminatory.
“It’s about whether the criteria regarding the tenants’ origin is neutral or not,” Eddie Khawaja, the families’ lawyer, told the news agency AFP.
So what does “non-Western” mean, and could the courts bring the law down? Here’s what you need to know:
What does ‘non-Western’ mean?
It is a statistical label that covers most of the world.
In 2020, the UN Human Rights Office said: “Statistics Denmark, under the Danish Ministry for Economic and Interior Affairs, defines ‘non-Western’ as any country outside the EU, with the exceptions of Andorra, Australia, Canada, Iceland, Liechtenstein, Monaco, New Zealand, Norway, San Marino, Switzerland, the USA, and the Vatican State.
“The effect is that ‘non-Western’ disproportionately means Denmark’s non-white, non-European ethnic populations,” it stated. The label also covers descendants: anyone born in Denmark if neither parent is a Danish citizen born in the country.
That means a Danish citizen born and raised in Copenhagen can still be “non-Western”.
How does the law work?
Through lists.
Every December 1, the government names “parallel societies”.
These are social housing areas of at least 1,000 people where more than 50 percent are “non-Western” immigrants and descendants.
An area must also meet two of four criteria on unemployment, crime, education, and income.
Areas on the list for five years become “transformation areas”, which the government used to call “hard ghettos”.
They must cut public family housing to 40 percent by 2030 through sales, demolition or conversion.
An estate with the same social problems but fewer “non-Western” residents faces no such obligation.
Why did Denmark bring it in?
The government says the goal is integration.
The law was part of a plan called “One Denmark without Parallel Societies: No Ghettos in 2030”.
In 2021, Kaare Dybvad Bek, then interior minister, said too many non-Western foreigners in one area “increases the risk of an emergence of religious and cultural parallel societies”.
Who has been affected?
Thousands of people.
About 11,000 people across Denmark will have to leave their homes by 2030, according to tenants’ associations.
In Helsingor, the landlord Boliggarden announced in early 2020 that it would renovate 96 apartments at the Nojsomhed estate. It then terminated the tenants’ leases. Most of those tenants were of foreign origin.
“They didn’t want the estate to be labelled ‘hard ghetto’ so they wanted to forcibly move us out when we advocated for other solutions,” Riad, a 33-year-old plaintiff who did not want his family name published, told AFP.
What has the EU court said?
The law may be discriminatory, but Danish judges ultimately make the final decision about whether it violated Danish laws prohibiting ethnic discrimination.
The Court of Justice of the European Union (CJEU) ruled in December 2025, in cases brought by tenants from Mjolnerparken in Copenhagen and Schackenborgvaenge in Slagelse. It said nationality or country of birth alone does not determine ethnic origin, but an allegedly neutral criterion covering many origins could be linked to ethnicity.
That runs contrary to the Danish government’s position and the reasoning of the lower Danish courts in the Helsingor case, which found that the “non-Western” does not describe an ethnic group and therefore did not result in discrimination that violated Denmark’s Equal Treatment Act.
Danish judges must decide whether the “non-Western” criterion really rests on residents’ ethnic origin, the court said, and consequently, if people included in the criterion are afforded less favourable treatment.
Less favourable treatment, it noted, could include “an increased risk of early termination of their leases”.
Has Denmark changed the law?
No.
In January, Sophie Haestorp Andersen, then minister for social affairs and housing, told a parliamentary hearing that authorities must keep applying the law until the Eastern High Court rules, the Danish outlet Danske Kommuner reported.
The four-party coalition in power since June includes the Green Left (SF), which voted for the law in 2018, according to the public broadcaster DR. The party’s Jacob Mark is now minister for children, elderly affairs and housing.
What happens next?
No date has been officially set for the verdict, but reports suggest it could be handed down later this month.
If the families win, they would probably be rehoused in homes similar to the ones they had to leave.
The Mjolnerparken case is still before the Eastern High Court.

Tourisme en Nouvelle-Calédonie : des tour-opérateurs sur place
Pour afficher ce contenu YouTube, il est nécessaire d'autoriser les cookies de mesure d'audience et de publicité.
Une extension de votre navigateur semble bloquer le chargement du lecteur vidéo. Pour pouvoir regarder ce contenu, vous devez la désactiver ou la désinstaller.
Publié le :
Des tour-opérateurs australiens, néo-zélandais et français sont actuellement dans le nord de la Nouvelle-Calédonie – à Hienghène et Poindimié –, deux destinations authentiques et culturelles. Leur objectif : découvrir les richesses du Caillou et promouvoir la destination dans leur catalogue. De quoi booster l'économie en berne depuis les émeutes de 2024 qui avaient secoué l'archipel.
Également au sommaire de cette émission : .
Mobilisation dans les Outre-mer contre la vie chère
La grève générale a rassemblé des milliers de manifestants partout en France, y compris dans les Outre-mer. Principale revendication : la lutte contre la vie chère.
Mayotte face aux incendies
Depuis le mois de juillet, plus de 350 hectares sont partis en fumée. Dernière zone touchée : le massif du Bénara, à Bandrélé. La culture sur brulis – le fait de défricher par le feu – est pointée du doigt.
Le Pacifique uni contre le narcotrafic
En Nouvelle-Calédonie, un séminaire a réuni, cette semaine, une douzaine de pays de la région pour tenter d'enrayer un phénomène qui prend de l'ampleur. L'objectif est de renforcer la sécurité et la coopération. Près de 17 tonnes de stupéfiants illicites, de la cocaïne pour l'essentiel, ont été saisies dans cette zone au cours des cinq premiers mois de l'année.
Des taureaux voyagent de la Nouvelle-Calédonie jsuqu'à Tahiti
Quatre taureaux reproducteurs ont parcouru 4 500 kilomètres en avion pour rejoindre les élevages polynésiens. Objectif : contribuer au renouvellement génétique du cheptel.
Mariage traditionnel à La Réunion
À La Réunion, les époux Picardo ont choisi de se dire "oui" une seconde fois lors d'un mariage traditionnel. Ils ont défilé dans les rues de Saint-Denis en tenue d'époque – un véritable voyage dans le temps.

Turkey to push for 'electrification' drive at COP31 as climate threats mount
COP31 host Turkey is set to push for a "electrification" drive to help meet global elergy demand as the UN climate conference kicks off in Antalya on Monday. The annual summit takes place this year under the shadow of a cost-of-living crisis fuelled by the war in the Middle East.
Nearly 200 nations gather for the COP31 summit in Turkey on Monday but tensions over geopolitics, finance and fossil fuels are tempering expectations of a major breakthrough in tackling the climate crisis.
More than 100,000 people are expected at the UN's two-week climate negotiations in the Mediterranean resort city of Antalya.
Tougher action on fossil fuels – the main driver of climate change – appears unlikely and budget-strapped developed countries are reluctant to commit more money to help developing nations cope with climate impact.
Read moreEl Nino set to intensify before peaking in December, UN warns
An energy crisis and cost-of-living pressures, fuelled by the war in the Middle East, are also looming over the gathering.
"This is not going to be the COP that changes the world," said Paul Watkinson, France's former chief negotiator at climate summits.
"It's an intermediate COP in many ways. But it is an important conference and it does need to make sure it makes progress," he said.
A senior EU official, who spoke on condition of anonymity, also tempered expectations, adding: "We cannot expect a revolution in terms of climate action from the Antalya COP."
The talks follow deadly floods in Nepal, searing heatwaves in Europe and major wildfires in Indonesia.
Read moreMore than half of Europe faced intense summer heat stress, EU monitor says
An exceptionally strong El Nino climate phenomenon is forecast to peak later this year, adding to extreme weather and possibly helping to make 2026 or 2027 the hottest year on record.
The outlook is increasingly bleak: the United Nations warned in September that global temperatures were on course to exceed 1.5C above preindustrial levels, breaching the most ambitious threshold set by the Paris Agreement.

'Implementation COP'
Turkey is presiding over COP31, with Australia leading negotiations under an unusual arrangement that settled a dispute over who would host the conference.
"COP31 comes at a difficult time for the world," said Australian climate minister Chris Bowen. "Reaching consensus among nearly 200 countries will not be easy but cooperation remains essential."
COP31 president Murat Kurum, Turkey's environment minister, said the conference would strive "to turn the commitments of past COPs into real results".
Turkey is promoting an "action agenda" alongside the formal negotiations that encourages countries to support non-binding pledges on issues from artificial intelligence to waste management.
Its centrepiece is an "electrification" drive to raise the share of global energy demand met by electricity from around 20 percent today to 35 percent by 2035.
"This year's energy crisis has shocked us out of our complacency," Kurum said. "Electrification is the answer. It protects communities from volatile global markets and cuts emissions."
Turkey and Australia also want electrification to appear in a "cover decision" – an overarching political statement negotiated by consensus.
The European Union has called for "clean" electrification – a term that could spark debate over the role of fossil fuels in the Turkish initiative.
The EU official suggested the bloc might be willing to find a compromise.
"The word 'clean' may be difficult for some. There may be other ways of formulating this without having it so explicit," the official said.
Cosima Cassel, a climate diplomacy expert at think tank E3G, said the Turkish COP31 presidency's proposal was "carefully worded".
It is "quite an open pledge that I think is going to enable quite a few countries to come on board", Cassel said.
Read moreThree-quarters of world's displaced people face severe climate risks, UN says
Money fight
Countries committed to transition away from fossil fuels in a landmark pact at COP28 in 2023, but have struggled to agree on how to turn that pledge into action.
COP30 ended with a deal that made no explicit mention of fossil fuels after oil-producing countries opposed the language.
Instead, Brazil produced a voluntary "roadmap" with proposals for phasing out fossil fuels that each country can tailor to their circumstances.
Observers say Turkey and Australia are keen to avoid a repeat of last year's fossil fuel fight.
But a feud looms over wealthy nations' unfulfilled financial commitments to help developing countries deal with climate change.
The group of African negotiators is demanding that a pledge to triple adaptation finance – money to cope with the worsening impacts of climate change – be added to the negotiation agenda.
Recent elections, meanwhile, have given climate campaigners a boost, with Democrats seizing control of the US Congress in a setback to US President Donald Trump, who calls global warming a hoax.
A US congressional delegation will attend COP31, but the Trump administration is not taking part in the negotiations.
Fresh from his re-election win over conservative challenger Flavio Bolsonaro, Brazilian President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva will travel to Antalya next week.
(FRANCE 24 with AFP)

content:
Tesla CEO Elon Musk has said the company will wind down production of Cybertrucks at its Texas facility amid poor sales.
Trillionaire Musk made the announcement in a post on X on Friday, saying the wind-down would enable the company to increase its production of the new Cybercab model, launched as part of a foray into the so-called robo-taxi industry.
“Tesla will be winding down production of the Cybertruck at Gigafactory Texas around the middle of next year to make room for increased Cybercab production,” Musk wrote.
Announced in 2019, the Cybertruck’s stark design, featuring an angular stainless steel exterior, proved immediately polarising.
At an unveiling ceremony that year, Musk sought to prove its windows were shatterproof. But the exhibition backfired, with metal balls launched at the car cracking two of the windows.
The vehicle quickly became a symbol of opposition to Musk as he became increasingly involved in United States politics, including briefly leading the Department of Government Efficiency (DOGE) panel tasked by the administration of US President Donald Trump with cleaving federal government agencies.
Musk most recently spent nearly half a billion dollars in the US midterm election campaign in support of Republican candidates, including more than $200 million in support of the failed Senate candidacy of Republican Ken Paxton in Texas. Beyond Tesla, Musk’s SpaceX company is also based in Texas.
But the spending did little to prevent a blue wave in US politics, which saw Democrats take commanding control of the US House of Representatives and Senate. The shift could spell investigations into Musk’s work with the federal government.
Musk had initially predicted the Cybertrucks, which became available to consumers at the end of 2023, would sell at a rate of about 250,000 a year.
The model fell far below that target. In 2024, about 38,965 units were sold. That figure declined by nearly half in 2025, with 20,237 sold.
In his announcement on Friday, Musk did not say whether Cybertruck manufacturing would shift to another factory. The plant in Texas is the only known production site.
In response to a user on X, Musk called the Cybertruck the “best vehicle Tesla has ever made”, hailing the “end of an era”.
summary: Released in 2023, the truck has become a symbol to some of opposition to Musk amid foray into US politics.

content:
French gendarmes and rescue workers at the scene of the crash in Lent, eastern France
Published
A young girl and an 18-year-old man have died after a bus crashed in eastern France, local authorities have said.
The bus was travelling between Lyon and Bourg-en-Bresse when it crashed at around 07:00 local time on Friday in the town of Lent.
The bus was carrying 43 passengers, including 15 children, the Bourg-en-Bresse prosecutor's office said. Three people are in a critical condition and at least 13 others have sustained minor injuries.
French President Emmanuel Macron said his thoughts were with the victims, the injured, and their families.
In a post on X, he said the nation stood by their side and thanked the rescue teams involved.
The town's mayor Yves Cristin told French media the bus "left the road and hit a tree in the ditch".
The two people killed have been identified by authorities. However, there have been differing reports as to the age of the girl.
The prosecutor's office said it was "opening an investigation into the incident, on charges of road homicide and aggravated road traffic injuries".
The driver has been taken to hospital after sustaining injuries and has not yet been questioned by police. French Transport Minister Philippe Tabarot said initial tests indicated there were no traces of alcohol or drugs in his blood.
Photos circulating in French media show a blue and white bus tilted in what appears to be a ditch on the roadside. Trees line the side of the road. The front of the bus appears to be heavily damaged.
Local mayor Cristin told BFM TV: "I arrived minutes after the accident and people were in shock.
"The side of the bus was torn off, and clearly, the people who were on that side must have been seriously injured."
Addressing weather conditions at the time of the crash, the mayor told Le Figaro "there was a bit of fog, the road was wet" but there were "no major difficulties".
Speaking to the same paper, Fabrice Pannekoucke, head of the Auvergne-Rhône-Alpes region, said: "At this stage, there are no particular explanations or interpretations that can be given."
Tabarot said the bus did not operate "exclusively on school routes" but that there were "many schoolchildren on board".
Transport Minister Philippe Tabarot (centre) arrived at the scene following the crash
French Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu said the accident was tragic, and thanked the firefighters, medical teams and police who attended the scene.
Earlier, French Education Minister Édouard Geffray said it was "always difficult when our children are victims of accidents of this nature".
Emergency services were at the scene and medical helicopters were deployed to take victims with serious injuries to a specialised hospital.
More than 100 firefighters and 50 gendarmes were also at the scene.
The local town hall was opened to provide shelter and coordinate with emergency services, the local mayor said.

content:
Все больше российских регионов снижают выплаты семьям погибших на войне в Украине. Эксперты говорят, что сокращение субсидий уже становится тенденцией. Власти вынуждены экономить на фоне нехватки средств в местных бюджетах. Несмотря на то, что в 2027 году Россия намерена потратить на военные нужды 17,1 трлн рублей , а это рекордные расходы со времен распада Советского Союза, пособия родственникам "участников СВО", а также выплаты по контрактам с Минобороны последовательно урезаются.
Интернет-издание "Важные истории" сообщает, что как минимум 12 регионов полностью или частично лишили так называемых "гробовых" семьи погибших. По подсчетам издания "ЧТД", речь идет о 15 регионах. При этом большинство таких решений было принято в 2026 году. Одновременно по меньшей мере в 17 регионах уменьшили выплаты за заключение контракта с военным ведомством. Например, в Петербурге отчисления снизили кратно - с 3,5 млн рублей до 1 млн, и это только по официальным данным. В то же время "Фонтанка" сообщает, что сумма единовременных выплат уменьшена до 400 тысяч.
"Федеральный центр финансирует войну, и из этого производят, в том числе, пушки и танки, которые сгорают на поле боя, - объясняет в беседе с DW экономический обозреватель Денис Морохин. - А регионы отвечают за вербовку, выплаты, бонусы при заключении контрактов".
Поскольку экономика не растет, а почти все гражданские отрасли уходят в минус, говорит Морохин, регионы получают все меньше денег от налогов на прибыль компаний. Собеседник ссылается на данные Банка Финляндии: рост российской экономики за прошлый год составил всего 1% и был обеспечен исключительно военными расходами. Без них экономика находилась бы в рецессии.
Москва эксплуатирует регионы
По словам экономиста Игоря Липсица, сокращение социальных выплат, в том числе напрямую связанных с войной, уже стало тенденцией. "Денег у регионов становится меньше. Во-первых, идет падение гражданской экономики , на которой кормятся регионы. Во-вторых, в РФ прошла налоговая реформа, в результате которой федеральному бюджету достается больше, а регионам меньше", - напомнил он в интервью DW.
Из-за нехватки средств, отмечает экономист, региональные власти вынуждены прибегать к коммерческим займам, ставки по которым достигают 15%. "Начинают отрезать все - начались увольнения муниципальных служащих, начинают увольнять людей из всякого рода социальных учреждений. И даже чиновников начинают увольнять".
По подсчетам DW, сокращения бюджетников на фоне недостатка денежных средств затронули больше 20 субъектов РФ из 89. По итогам прошлого года дефицит региональных бюджетов достиг рекордных 1,5 трлн рублей. По прогнозу Сбербанка, в этом году он может вырасти до 2 трлн рублей.
Экономия на военных в России
Необходимость бороться с дефицитом вынуждает власти экономить и на профессиональных военных. Впервые как минимум за последние 18 лет в России, очевидно, перенесут декабрьские выплаты военнослужащим на январь. "Вот это уже нехороший сигнал, - говорит Липсиц. - Даже на военных не хватает денег".
Правда, речь не идет о тех, кто находится на фронте. С другой стороны, деньги на войну у Путина начинают заканчиваться. С таким мнением выступает экономист и оппозиционный политик Владимир Милов . "Военным уже не первый год недоиндексируют денежное довольствие: его повышают всего на 4% в год. Но и эту индексацию в октябре не провели, - говорит он. - В реальном выражении денежные доходы военных заметно сокращаются".
Набор контрактников буксует
Немецкий экономист Янис Клюге (Janis Kluge) из берлинского Фонда науки и политики (SWP) указывает на то, что проблемы с выплатами по контракту и "гробовыми" могут затруднить привлечение новых добровольцев в армию. "Согласно данным о расходах региональных бюджетов России, в сентябре контракт с армией заключили 29,9 тысячи человек. Годом ранее за этот месяц набрали 31,9 тысячи. За первые девять месяцев 2026 года число новых контрактников составило 263 тысячи против 292 тысяч за тот же период прошлого года".
С другой стороны, пока набор контрактников, как говорит сам Клюге, "остается стабильным": "Около 1 000 человек в день, но все же темпы ниже, чем годом ранее".
Президент Киевской школы экономики Тимофей Милованов пишет о том, что в РФ растет преступность из-за действий вербовщиков. Мужчины, у которых есть долги и судимости, сталкиваются с давлением. В войну втягивают и срочников. "Путин обещает не отправлять срочников на войну. Однако офицеры давят на молодых призывников, заставляя их подписывать контракты. Россия использует указ 2022 года, чтобы удерживать таких военнослужащих на службе бессрочно".
Организация " Идите лесом ", помогающая мужчинам избежать призыва, в августе 2026-го получила втрое больше запросов, чем годом ранее. При этом вербовка часто носит насильственный характер , говорят правозащитники.
С другой стороны, возможность заработать деньги, воюя против украинцев, для многих россиян по-прежнему кажется привлекательной идеей, сказали в разговоре с DW аналитики берлинского Центра восточноевропейских и международных исследований (ZOiS) и Немецкого общества внешней политики. "Война в России нормализована, и в этом проблема. Она уже воспринимается обществом как данность", - говорит собеседник, пожелавший сохранить анонимность: "Если, например, посмотреть на уровень доходов и возможность заработка в регионах, то война по-прежнему остается значительным финансовым лифтом".
Медианная зарплата в России сейчас составляет около 60 тысяч рублей. "В надежде отсидеться в штабе, даже при условии сокращения бонусов и выплат при заключении контракта, люди готовы рискнуть, потому что выбора во многих регионах просто нет", - отмечает собеседник DW.

content:
Watch: Protesters demonstrate against Trump’s proposed arch
Published
A federal judge has temporarily blocked construction of US President Donald Trump's "triumphal arch" in the nation's capital.
US District Judge Tanya Chutkan ruled that there should be a 14-day pause before any work can start on the arch in Washington which the Trump administration had said could begin this week.
Earlier on Thursday the National Capital Planning Commission (NCPC) voted 8-4 to allow construction of the planned 250ft (72m) arch.
Trump appointees on the board said the arch would be a fitting tribute to US history and to veterans but opponents have argued it would block the view of Arlington National Cemetery, the resting place of thousands of US soldiers and service people.
The so-called Arc de Trump - a play on the name of the famous arch in Paris, the Arc de Triomphe - is one of the president's efforts to remake the capital city in his style and is meant to commemorate the country's 250th anniversary.
The approval on Thursday evening came after nearly nine hours of public comment.
"The White House commends the National Capital Planning Commission's decision to fully approve President Trump's historic vision to build a much needed Triumphal Arch in Washington, DC," a White House spokesperson told the BBC in a statement.
It is not yet clear when construction of the arch could begin, as several lawsuits seek to block the project.
The White House criticised the federal court that temporarily halted construction as an "activist district court."
"We are confident we will be fully vindicated as this litigation proceeds and look forward to seeing the completion of this magnificent Arch," the spokesperson said.
An artist's rendering of Trump's proposed arch near Arlington Cemetery
A rendering of the project's design from earlier this year includes a golden, winged Lady Liberty statue on the top of the arch, flanked by two gold eagles. The phrases "One Nation Under God" and "Liberty and Justice for All" are inscribed in gold on either side of the structure.
A website that the White House shared on social media on Friday also shows a video rendering of the arch that shows the structure emblazoned with the words "Golden Age of America" along one side.
It refers to the structure as "The Military Triumphal Arch".
The proposed structure is sprinkled with appliques that are visually similar to the golden embellishments Trump has added to the Oval Office.
The Trump administration has also said the arch would double as a complex to store military equipment - complete with the ability to deploy snipers and drones.
"There will be no facility like this anywhere in the World," Trump previously wrote on his Truth Social platform. He added that out of "the 59 top cities and Capitals", Washington is "the only one in the world that does not have a triumphal arch". He did not specify to which cities he was referring.
Mark Paoletta, the chairman of the NCPC and one of the Trump appointees, said at Thursday's meeting that the president understood "it's important to our national identity to display who we are through grand monuments".
He and other commissioners said the structure fulfils a 100-year plan to build a monumental work on Columbia Island, just as Congress and various commissions intended.
Paoletta added that the arch would honour the nation, its veterans and "provide the sacred ground of Arlington National Cemetery with the monumental gateway it deserves".
Anne Wright is among those who are opposed to the arch
Opponents have strongly disagreed.
Anne Wright, who spent 29 years in the US military and also worked in the diplomatic service, told the BBC she would try to stop the construction.
"We'll tie ourselves to the bulldozer, we've got veterans in wheelchairs and we'll chain the wheelchairs to these things," she said.
Wright referenced this week's midterm elections, in which Trump's Republican Party lost control of Congress, saying: "[Trump's] policy of war, of ego – they've been rejected."
Fellow veteran John Pomeroy - who served in the Air Force for six years, including during the Vietnam War, and whose parents are buried at Arlington - said the arch "would lessen the solemn nature of a visit to the cemetery".
He described Trump's suggestion that the arch could store military equipment as "silly" and a "half-baked idea", arguing it would be a target for terrorist attacks.
Like Wright, Pomeroy said he would "impede construction workers as much as I can" if they came to the site to begin work.
Democratic Congressman Jared Huffman argued in his statement to the commission that the arch would disrupt sightlines not just of Arlington but of the Lincoln Memorial, fracturing "a view meant to underscore the unity and sacrifice of the American people, and doing that with a structure we often associate with emperors or kings who built grand arches as tributes to themselves".
"This is a tribute to Donald Trump," Huffman added.
Lawsuits have been filed against the plans, raising concerns about the environment, traffic congestion and safety. There is also a disagreement over whether congressional approval is needed to build the arch.
It is one of several construction projects Trump has proposed for the US capital. That includes at the White House, where he is facing legal challenges over the construction of a ballroom, which is estimated to cost $400m (£300m).
His plans to renovate a 106-year-old golf course, which he has dubbed "trash island", is also being challenged in the courts.
Rebecka Pieder contributed reporting.

content:
"The reason we lost is the war," US Vice President JD Vance said , shortly after Republicans suffered a major defeat during the US midterm elections  in both the House and Senate. He was referring to the  US-Israel war against Iran .
On Monday, the day before the midterms, the US reportedly struck Iran's Qeshm Island, though US President Donald Trump had previously said there would be no new strikes before the elections .
Among fears of a renewed regional escalation, social media has been flooded with dramatic images and purported battlefield updates. Not all of them are genuine.
DW Fact check takes a closer look at three viral claims.
No Iranian missile drone attack on US aircraft carrier
Claim : In this post on X , a user claims that Iran launched a massive missile and drone attack on a US aircraft carrier, resulting in fatalities. It is accompanied by a video showing an explosion and its aftermath on what appears to be an aircraft carrier. The post has garnered over 643.000 views.
Verdict : Fake
The 15-second video is an AI-generated fake.
Although there have been reports of Iranian forces attempting to shoot down a US aircraft , there have been no credible reports of a successful attack on a US aircraft carrier that resulted in fatalities.
The AI video also predates the latest US strikes — it has circulated at least since May . At that time, it was shared alongside a different claim unrelated to the current situation.
Frame-by-frame analysis reveals several inconsistencies. At approximately three seconds in, the feet of a running person visually glitch. The sea in the background appears uniform and almost video game-like. At five seconds, several people appear to pass through one another, and their limbs also glitch.
The voices in the audio sound synthetic and appear closely synchronized with the visuals. Both AI Detection tools by Meta AI and Google Gemini identified strong indicators that the video was AI-generated. It is important to note, however, that such tools provide an assessment of likelihood, rather than definitive proof that something was created using AI.
The video is shaky and short — two characteristics that warrant closer scrutiny of possible AI use.
The visual nature of supposedly chaotically filmed videos  can cover up glitches that happen frequently in AI-generated content.

A burning building in South Korea, not US bases in Gulf
Claim : This user on X shares a video with the claim that "Iran attacks the US bases in the Gulf." A burning building is visible, with large dark plumes of smoke rising from it. It has been viewed over 55.000 times.
Verdict : Misleading
A reverse image search shows that the images are recycled and show a fire in South Korea in 2025 .
News reports indicated that a fire broke out at a Fashion Logistics Center in Cheonan. The same building is visible in the street-level view of South Korea’s Naver Maps street imagery , and its location matches the red building in a mountainous area which is shown on Google Maps satellite imagery .
Visual cues that match include the building itself, the white lettering "E-Land fashion" on the right side and the mountains in the background.
The reverse image search also reveals that the video has repeatedly circulated. It made rounds in July this year attached to Iran war posts in Tamil and English  with one post on X reaching 1.4 million views. Other posts linked it   to the war in Yemen and other conflicts, unrelated to the fire in South Korea.
Content farm's posts reach millions
Claim : "Iran has launched a major hypersonic missile attack targeting multiple Israeli military bases," an X account   writes . By the time of writing, the post had 2.5 million views.
Verdict : Misleading
Iran claims to have   hypersonic missiles  and has previously claimed to have fired Fattah-1 missiles at Israel — most recently in June 2025 .  There are no credible reports about Iranian hypersonic missile attacks during the latest escalation.
The account that has published the claim has more than 100,000 followers and posts with high frequency — often over 10 times a day. Most of the posts reach hundred thousands of views, often using urgent "Breaking" headlines and repeating similar posts. In one  post for example , it claims "the war has officially started" reaching more than 30 million views.  These are all hallmarks of a so-called " content farm ."
In a comment to DW, analyst Charlene Lin, from the internet watchdog NewsGuard, writes that this account is a South Asia-based content farm. The account has already been flagged in relation to other disinformation narratives.
Lin writes that such content farms in South Asia "seem to spread false claims about geopolitics by typically posing as pro-China/Russia/Iran users."
She adds that the account amplifies false claims alongside other accounts that appear to be part of the same network — typically within a short period of time.
Victoire Rio, an expert on social media monetization and information integrity, wrote to DW: "It's pretty common to see financially-motivated actors from South and Southeast Asia leverage prominent news issues to generate a financial profit off the engagement on platforms like X."

content:
Ministers say the withdrawal of the funding was "not a judgment on the quality of the work"
Published
The Welsh government will end funding for a tree-planting scheme in Uganda that was branded "woke" by opposition politicians.
Wales has given more than £4m to climate change charity Size of Wales since 2015, to work with Indigenous communities to plant trees in the African nation.
Ministers said budgetary pressures meant "difficult decisions" had to be made and the charity would lose its grant for the scheme at the end of March 2027.
Size of Wales has called on the government to reconsider.
Right-wing parties in the Senedd welcomed the decision, whilst left-wing politicians criticised it, with the Welsh Liberal Democrats accusing the Plaid Cymru-run government of "out-Reforming Reform".
Size of Wales, external works with Indigenous and local people worldwide to grow trees and protect at least two million hectares of tropical forests - an area the size of Wales.
The scheme, funded by previous Labour-run Welsh governments, has seen more than 25 million planted around Mbale in the Mount Elgon region of eastern Uganda.
Previous criticism by opponents of using taxpayers' money for the scheme led to Labour ministers last year pointing out that it amounted to about £270,000 a year, external - equivalent to 0.001% of the government's total annual budget in 2025.
The scheme is said to have led to more than 25 million trees being planted
A document published in August 2025 by the previous government stated Wales was "helping some of the very poorest people in the world adapt to climate change and improve their livelihoods" and protected local people in the Mount Elgon region from deadly landslides.
Plaid took over the Welsh government in May, with the decision to end the tree-planting scheme coming as it prepares to publish its draft budget for 2026-27 later this month.
A Welsh government spokesperson said it was developing "a new international strategy for Wales" and was "working to ensure that future investment demonstrates impact and value for money and delivers clear benefits for Wales as well as our international partners".
"We do not intend to renew grant funding for the Size of Wales Mbale tree-planting programme beyond its current end date of 31 March 2027," they said.
"That is not a judgement on the quality of the work. The programme has planted millions of trees and built important links between Wales and Uganda, and we look forward to continuing our dialogue with Size of Wales."
Planting trees is said to help protect locals from deadly landslides
The spokesperson said that recognising the success of a programme "is not the same as committing to fund the same delivery model indefinitely", and the government had to "make difficult choices about where limited resources can have the greatest impact".
They added: "We will never retreat from Wales being an outward-looking and globally responsible nation."
Responding to the decision, chairman of Size of Wales Tim Birch said: "At a time of deepening climate crisis, we need to strengthen, not retreat from, our commitment to global responsibility.
"As we prepare for COP31, Wales must continue to show global leadership.
"Taking action to protect tropical forests is in Wales' own national interests and working with international partners to restore ecosystems and build climate resilience is more important than ever.
"We urge the Welsh government to reconsider this decision and continue supporting the long-term partnerships that are so vital to our shared future."
The tree-planting scheme has long been criticised by Reform UK and Welsh Conservative politicians in the Senedd.
Reform UK's leader in Wales, Helen Jenner, welcomed the announcement and said her party had been calling "for an end to this ridiculous woke spending for years now".
"We have changed the conversation in Cardiff Bay and demanded that Welsh taxpayers' money be spent in Wales and not sent abroad for things like Ugandan trees," she said.
"Now, thanks to us, Welsh households will not be funding those trees."
The scheme has been active in the Mount Elgon region of eastern Uganda
The leader of the Welsh Conservatives in the Senedd Darren Millar said the decision was "long overdue but it is better late than never".
"It's outrageous that the Welsh government has been spending so much taxpayers' money on planting trees in Africa while our schools and hospitals have not been getting the cash they need," he said.
"It has no responsibility for foreign affairs or international development, so every pound spent on these things is a pound that is being taken away from our NHS, our education system and helping the Welsh economy.
"The Welsh government should put the people of Wales first, not vanity projects overseas."
But the leader of the Welsh Liberal Democrats Jane Dodds described it as a "short-sighted" decision.
"Tackling climate change and protecting nature isn't a luxury," she said.
"Size of Wales has planted millions of trees, built real links between Wales and Uganda, and helped communities protect forests that matter to all of us.
"Plaid are out-Reforming Reform by cutting international funding for work ministers admit has been a success.
"Wales' global responsibility shouldn't be the first thing to go."
Welsh Labour leader Ken Skates said: "In opposition, Plaid Cymru repeatedly championed international programmes.
"Yet again, it seems that what Plaid say is very different to what they actually do."
The Welsh government also provides a grant of £280,000 a year to the charity to deliver an education programme in Welsh schools, which runs until the end of March 2027, with a proposal for the future of the programme to be submitted and considered by the country's rural resilience and sustainability minister.

content:
Andy Burnham says it isn't fair if an employer 'holds all the cards'
Published
Businesses should publish salaries in job adverts now, Prime Minister Andy Burnham is telling firms, rather than wait for a new law to come in that will force them to do so.
The government is planning to make pay details compulsory in adverts, with legislation on the issue being brought forward "as soon as possible".
It argues the change will help jobseekers, particularly those applying for their first job, and could help prevent pay discrimination. However, one industry group said setting pay was a complex process and regulating adverts was not always suitable.
It comes a week after the UK's equality watchdog said employees should legally be able to find out what their colleagues are earning.
Burnham said the current system felt "weighted against the applicant" and the changes were aimed at "tilting the scales back".
"It can be quite soul destroying for young people these days, applying for jobs when the salary is not listed but sometimes they're not getting a reply," he told the BBC.
The prime minister added that publishing salaries in adverts was also important for closing the gender pay gap.
He was also challenged over whether MPs should be disclosing salaries when advertising for staff in their offices.
A number of politicians are currently advertising for roles without giving an expected salary., external
Burnham said: "It would apply completely to them too and the call I'm making today is, before the law changes do it voluntarily because it's the right thing to do."
Greater transparency
The Cabinet Office launched a consultation into pay and reducing discrimination in the summer, and the government said there had been "overwhelming support" for greater transparency, with 94% of respondents backing the move.
"Whether you're a young person starting out or a parent trying to support your family, you should know what a job pays before spending your time and effort applying for it," Burnham said.
The government said the move was part of attempts to reduce the nearly one million young people not in education, employment or training - or "Neet" - ahead of the final report of the Milburn Review into youth inactivity, which is due in the coming weeks.
Publishing salary details upfront could "expose unjustified differences in pay, give workers greater confidence to challenge discrimination and prevent disagreements over pay escalating into disputes".
The proposals are similar to measures being introduced in the European Union., external
Employers in Europe will have to disclose the initial pay or range for new roles, which must either be included in a published job advert or shared before an interview.
According to data from UK jobs website Adzuna, external, 51% of the adverts on its site in September had salary information, but the proportion has been falling in recent years.
Adzuna co-founder Andrew Hunter said being open about pay "should be the norm, not the exception".
He added that employers who put a salary on a job advert "attract more applicants, and better-suited ones".
'More complicated'
Previous research from the CIPD, external, an industry body for human resources managers, has indicated that the public sector and charities are more likely to reveal pay information that private firms, while pay ranges were more common than specific salaries.
But it found not all employers were "fully transparent", with pay ranges sometimes wider than £10,000.
CIPD chief executive Neil Carberry said that while, in principle, giving salary details was "a good thing", in practice it was "more complicated".
"There isn't always a single fixed figure, and employers will want to set pay based on a candidate's skills, experience and potential."
Carberry added the process was complex, saying that drafting job adverts is "best left to good employer practice rather than government regulation".
The government has said it will set out further details on what information will be required and how the legislation will be enforced "in due course".
Conservative shadow business secretary Julia Lopez said: "At a time when employers are finding it harder and harder to take on staff, Labour have decided to make their lives even more difficult.
"It should be up to businesses to decide what information they advertise about job openings, and to decide how to attract the best applicants.
"As long as they are not being dishonest, misleading or discriminatory, it should not be a matter for the government."
Last week, the Equality and Human Rights Commission (EHRC), said publishing salaries in job adverts would be a "positive step".
It also said bosses should be required to respond to questionnaires about colleagues' pay to cut pay discrimination.
At present, employers do not have to respond to employee requests for salary information about their co-workers.
The EHRC also said employers should be prevented from asking about current salary when offering a job to stop a history of discrimination from continuing.
Employers in the UK are currently allowed to ask you how much you get paid in your current role, but applicants are under no obligation to tell them.

summary: The government argues the change will help jobseekers and could help to prevent pay discrimination.

content:
European airlines have again been hit with a new wave of bomb threats - in the third such incident this week.
On Friday multiple flights to and from Lisbon, Rome, Prague and Sofia were targeted and the threats saw three planes escorted by Hungarian fighter jets, authorities said.
It also saw a number of high-profile media organisations, including Ireland's public broadcaster RTÉ, evacuated after threats were made against them - although there has been no concrete links between the messages against airlines and the broadcasters.
The disruption comes after nearly 30 aircraft and several airports across Europe were impacted by threats earlier this week, in what the UK called a "malicious hoax".
A Ryanair flight scheduled to leave Lisbon for Rome on Friday was targeted with a threat, the airline said, while at least 11 flights were targeted in the Czech Republic and Bulgaria, according to AFP.
France also reported at least four of its flights were targeted by threats, however they all landed safely.
No explosives have been found on any planes as of Friday.
As airlines were dealing with this latest wave of threats, several media outlets, including RTÉ, were evacuated after similar warnings were made against them.
Staff at the Irish Independent newspaper and the Dublin offices of radio stations NewstalkFM and TodayFM, were also advised to leave their buildings and UK broadcaster Sky said it also received a security threat.
In a statement, gardaí (Irish police) said they were "aware of a threat made against media organisations here and in Europe".
Armed gardaí were deployed to RTÉ'S Dublin headquarter after a bomb threat
While no link has been established between the threats against airlines and media outlets, the Irish government has warned it is a "likely coordinated campaign of disruption".
In a statement, it said: "Hoax threats such as these cause fear, distress and disruption to people going about their daily lives and activities; they achieve no positive purpose whatsoever. It is not known yet who is responsible for these threats, whether it is individuals or a centralised or co-ordinated effort.
Irish Prime Minister Micheál Martin described the situation as "worrying" and added his government's first priority was the safety of the Irish public.
"Yesterday, there appeared to be coordinated efforts to disrupt air travel," he said.
Martin told RTÉ it was not yet known if the threats had come from individuals or if it was a "coordinated attack" but said they were being taken seriously.
Ireland is scheduled to host two high-profile European Union meetings in Dublin next week.
Broadcaster Sky confirmed it had received a security threat, hours after RTÉ had evacuated its building.
The broadcaster, which is owned by Comcast, said in a statement read by a presenter on its news channel that the broadcaster had "carried out a security assessment and reported the matter to the relevant authorities".
"The safety and security of our colleagues is our primary concern, and we are working closely with authorities to ensure our people and operations remain secure."
Friday's disruption comes after the Russian extremist group "Male State", named in this week's hoax bomb threats to Italian airports, denied any link to the false warnings.
Replying to the BBC Russian Service, an account on Telegram - one of several linked to the so-called "Male State" and its founder Vladislav Pozdnyakov - mocked any suggestion the group was involved in emailing the threats.
"What Male State? Where have you seen it? It hasn't existed for many years," the message on the channel reads. "If tomorrow they sign a [threat] letter, say, from Putin, will you then try to reach our president to ask your stupid question?"

summary: No link has been established between the threats against the airlines and those against the media outlets.

content:
A new series of bomb threats caused more flight diversions across Europe on Friday, while also expanding to target a number of media organisations.
British broadcaster Sky said it was one of a number of newsrooms that received a bomb threat. “We have carried out a security assessment and reported the matter to the relevant authorities,” a spokesperson said.
Bulgaria’s Nova TV and the Irish public broadcaster RTE received emailed bomb threats from a purported “Mikhail Andropov”, headlined “Message to the West”, portraying the threats as a prelude to more disruptions across Europe.
RTE briefly evacuated staff, including radio and television presenters, in Dublin after an email was received on Friday morning. RTE Radio One presenter David McCullagh later told listeners that the threat warned that a bomb would explode within 45 minutes.
The Irish government said hoax bomb claims were also sent to Virgin Media, Newstalk radio and The Irish Independent newspaper and that it was unclear who was behind them.
“However, these threats come on the heels of the ongoing disruption to aviation around Europe caused by similar threats, and it seems likely that this is a coordinated campaign of disruption,” it said in a statement.
The incidents come a day after hoax bomb threats disrupted more than two dozen flights across Europe on Thursday, and days after other aircraft and a cruise ship received bomb alerts.
‘Hoax threats’ increasing
On Friday, jets escorted airliners flying from Brussels to Sofia and from Prague to Bucharest and Cyprus through Hungarian airspace due to bomb threats, Hungarian Defence Minister Romulusz Ruszin-Szendi said.
He also said NATO had ordered an air patrol near the Hungarian-Romanian border, the first report that the Western defence alliance had become involved.
Danish police said threats were directed at traffic at Copenhagen airport but that there appeared to be no danger to passengers. The airport said it was “operating normally”.
Czech police registered bomb threats to nine flights departing from or arriving in Prague. An airport spokesperson said no flights had been cancelled as a result.
France said four new bomb threats were made to aircraft flying over French territory, and that all landed safely.
A Ryanair flight from Rome landed as scheduled in Lisbon, CNN Portugal reported. A WizzAir flight from Prague to Rome was diverted to Venice.
About half a dozen flights were disrupted on Tuesday and more than two dozen on Thursday, some of them making unplanned landings or being escorted to their destinations by fighter jets.
European air traffic authority Eurocontrol on Friday said it was monitoring the situation and working closely with airlines, airports, navigation service providers and other groups across Europe “to mitigate any disruption to air traffic flows.”
Al Jazeera’s Frances Read, reporting from London on Friday, said that while the threats have not been credible so far, disruptions appear to be widening.
“The number of hoax threats this week is making governments sit up and take notice about where this might be coming from and also think of solutions for how to deal with it,” she said.
Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni said it was unclear whether the hoax threats were connected to cyberattacks that targeted supermarkets across Europe and France’s national blood service by raising the temperature of refrigerators and freezers connected to the internet.
“But they definitely all tell us the same thing: today, what is under attack are civilian infrastructures,” Meloni told reporters on Friday.
Spanish Foreign Minister Jos Manuel Albares said the bomb threats against aircraft constituted an “attempt at hybrid aggression and psychological warfare” and an attack on European democracy by autocratic forces.
“It is clear that this is no coincidence,” he told Spanish broadcaster RTVE.
summary: A string of hoax alerts causing flight diversions across Europe this week has broadened to include newsrooms.

content:
TikTok has been charged by the European Commission with failing to protect users’ mental health by exposing them to a relentless stream of content that risks worsening eating disorders and anxiety in a case that strikes at its business model.
Issuing a preliminary ruling on Friday, the EU regulator said TikTok’s algorithm “can be harmful” and was leading young and vulnerable users “down rabbit holes they cannot easily escape from”.
The Chinese-owned short-video platform, which has 189 million users in the EU, was found to have failed to prevent users from being served up repetitive content on themes such as body image or isolation, which can lead to anxiety, sadness, worsen existing eating disorders or mental health problems.
Officials said their investigation focused on legal content, where a single video might not be problematic, but the cumulative effect of watching scores of them on one theme could damage users’ mental health.
TikTok’s safeguards to mitigate the risks of “rabbit-hole effects” – where users are served narrow and repetitive content to keep them engaged – were found to be ineffective. For example, officials said, if a user checked a “not interested” button on a video about eating patterns, the algorithm would still offer them similar content on diet and body image. Similarly, refreshing a feed only provided a brief respite from a stream of content on one topic, it found.
“Every time a user scrolls or likes a video on TikTok, the algorithm serves more of the same leading users down rabbit holes they cannot easily escape from,” said the European Commission’s lead official on tech policy, Henna Virkkunen. “TikTok needs to step up its efforts to protect users’ wellbeing, including those of minors.”
In response, a TikTok spokesperson said: “The commission has made a series of statements that are fundamentally inaccurate and distort our platform’s architecture and our commitment to user safety.
“We have a strong record of protecting our community while giving users direct and intuitive control over their content experience.”
The company argues that its policies prohibit content that promotes disordered eating and risky weight-management behaviours. It also says that more than 79 million users in the EU used its “not interested” or keyword filters to screen out unwanted content in the first six months of 2026.
The Molly Rose Foundation, which was set up in memory of 14-year-old Molly Russell, who took her own life in 2017 after being exposed to a torrent of harmful online content, welcomed what it called the landmark findings “to seek to hold TikTok to account for the way their algorithm drives young people down rabbit holes of despair”.
A survey for the charity earlier this year found that nearly half of girls and a third of all UK teenagers saw suicide, self-harm and eating-disorder content on social media in a week.
The foundation called on the UK regulator, Ofcom, to open an investigation into TikTok’s “extremely damaging” algorithm.
The EU investigation strikes at TikTok’s business model, which is built on keeping users scrolling as long as possible.
EU officials want TikTok to change the design of its ForYou feed, to give users greater control over the content they see.
“We are addressing a business model,” a commission official told reporters, saying that a business model focused mainly on engagement “can potentially create a risk” especially for minors and vulnerable adults.
The findings are part of a broader investigation launched in February 2024 under the Digital Services Act, which obliges large internet companies to take action to prevent a wide range of harms, from disinformation to damage to mental health.
The commission has already found the company violated EU rules over its “addictive design” for features such as infinite scroll. The company said at the time “the commission’s preliminary findings present a categorically false and entirely meritless depiction of our platform” and that it would challenge the findings.
A complaint about lack of transparency over who paid for TikTok’s advertising was resolved when the company made binding commitments to change its policies last December.
TikTok, which now has a chance to examine the investigation file and mount a defence, could agree to change its recommender system to avoid a fine.
If EU officials uphold the finding, the company could be fined up to 6% of its global worldwide turnover.
summary: Regulator’s initial ruling says algorithm ‘can be harmful’ and led young and vulnerable viewers ‘down rabbit holes they can’t easily escape’ Business live – latest updates TikTok has been charged by the European Commission with failing to protect users’ mental health by exposing them to a relentless stream of content that risks worsening eating disorders and anxiety in a case that strikes at its business model. Issuing a preliminary ruling on Friday, the EU regulator said TikTok’s algorithm “can be harmful” and was leading young and vulnerable users “down rabbit holes they cannot easily escape from”. content:
Petropavlivska-Borshchagivka, Ukraine – A woman wearing a crisp new paramedic’s uniform and impeccable makeup kneels on the ground in front of several police officers guarding the rusty gates of a two-storey house.
She begs, yells and curses, claiming that forcibly conscripted men are being held in the building in the tranquil suburb of Petropavlivska-Borshchagivka, outside the Ukrainian capital, Kyiv.
One of the men has already died, claims the woman, who was later identified as Valentyna Moloda, a 49-year-old nurse who once worked at a plastic surgery clinic and has never been authorised to practise as a paramedic.
The ambulance she arrived in carries the logos of a private medical company that reportedly stopped operating in 2023. A woman from Moloda’s “ambulance team” livestreams the scene as a crowd swells, joining in her chants demanding access to what she calls a “torture chamber.”
“I’m on my knees, let me get to them,” Moloda screams, claiming that “armed people” allegedly “torture” 40 people inside who had evaded the draft.
Her claims resonate with people at the impromptu rally, in a country where conscription officers have become reviled public servants due to their sometimes brutal tactics.
Protesters lob eggs at police and throw tomatoes at the house. The crowd grows to 500 people, with many clashing with officers until midnight.
Clashes and counterclaims
Officials say that Moloda’s “rescue mission” on Monday afternoon – one of the most polarising scandals in Ukraine – was fake and required preparation.
But it had already gone viral online, with tens of thousands of people around the world lamenting Ukraine’s handling of conscription.
Glenn Diesen, a pro-Kremlin political analyst from Norway, shared a video and a photo on X of a teenager who fell while trying to film the house from the fence, claiming the boy was a victim of “great outrage and riots in Ukraine against the henchmen of [Ukrainian President Volodymyr] Zelenskyy and NATO.” His post has been widely shared.
Three days before Monday’s incident, Moloda and her driver “conducted a reconnaissance” of the house, Ukraine’s Chief of Staff Kyrylo Budanov said on Tuesday.
A former top military intelligence officer and one of Ukraine’s most popular and trusted public figures, Budanov interacted with Moloda at the time of the standoff.
Several young men clashed with police and tried to kick the doors of the house open until officers let Moloda and her team inside.
She came back minutes later to proclaim that she had just seen a man on the brink of death, another with a broken spine and one who was so badly beaten he was unable to talk.
“There’s blood on the mattresses,” she yelled, showing someone photos of the alleged victims on her phone, while the scene was livestreamed. “They [urinate] in a bottle.”
But careful observers would have noticed the videos were tagged as having been shot on Saturday. The crowd, however, kept growing, damaging police cars and clashing with officers.
Budanov arrived about six hours after Moloda started her livestream, and said that the besieged house on Solnichna Street had been used by the Azov Brigade, a former volunteer militia group of far-right nationalists and football fans that helped repel pro-Russian separatists in southeastern Ukraine in 2014.
Azov said apprehended deserters were kept in the house, while Azov’s commander Denys Prokopenko called the scandal a “sabotage behind the lines that discredits Ukrainian servicemen and creates a narrative that benefits Russia”.
The group has been accused of neo-Nazi sympathies and torturing war prisoners. The United States Department of State banned it from using US-supplied weaponry between 2014 and 2024, but it grew into a military force and became part of Ukraine’s National Guard. Its founder, Andriy Biletsky, led this year’s “Operation Vivaldi” to push Russian forces out of several strategic areas in eastern Ukraine.
After Budanov’s arrival, four men were allowed to walk out of the house into a bus, including the one Moloda claimed could not move because of a broken spine. The angry crowd did not allow the bus to leave.
‘Unfortunately, people believed that woman’
Al Jazeera visited Petropavlivska-Borshchagivka and talked to more than a dozen residents, who insisted on full or partial anonymity because Monday’s scandal has become so politicised.
“Both sides are wrong,” an elderly man who only gave his first name, Serhiy, told Al Jazeera, standing next to his wife outside a supermarket.
“Azov shouldn’t have kept their people there, and the fake doctor shouldn’t have started all this noise,” he said.
His wife signalled him to stop talking and ushered him away.
Locals laughed off comparisons some have made between Monday’s incident and the massive 2013-2014 protests on Maidan Square in central Kyiv that toppled pro-Russian Ukrainian President Viktor Yanykovych.
“This definitely wasn’t a mini-Maidan,” 17-year-old Mykola told Al Jazeera, a short distance from the house. “Unfortunately, people believed that woman and flocked here.”
Most of the locals called the incident a “provocation”.
Only one man in his 30s said that Moloda “tried to help” and should not have been apprehended on Tuesday.
Moloda was arrested and is being held in custody for 60 days without bail.
Prosecutors said they found evidence proving that she had at least once carried out “rescue services” as a fake paramedic for 107,000 hryvnia ($2,355).
The relatives of a deserter, Andriy Kuleshov, allegedly hired Moloda for about $7,000 to get him out of the Azov house, Pavlo Kurchenko, a senior Azov officer, told the media outlet Ukrainska Pravda.
Kuleshov is listed in Myrotvorets – Ukrainian for “peacemaker” – a controversial online database of alleged anti-Ukrainian figures, for crossing into separatist-controlled areas in southeastern Ukraine multiple times in 2015-2021, where his brother lives.
“[Moloda] wanted to create a political scandal,” Volodymyr Fesenko, head of the Kyiv-based Penta think tank, told Al Jazeera. “She is also suspected of ties to Russian intelligence. So far, there’s no confirmation of that, but Russia has used this scandal in its interests.”
It did – with the help of pro-Russia Ukrainians.
“People are being kidnapped and tortured. Some are sold to military units, others – to their relatives. The weaker ones simply die of torture and confinement conditions,” Artyom Dmitruk, a former Ukrainian lawmaker with a pro-Russian party who fled for Italy in 2024, said in televised remarks.
The scandal “answers the question about why Russia needs the special military operation, to uproot the resurgent neo-Nazism in Ukraine,” said Mikhail Sheremev, a “lawmaker” in Russia-annexed Crimea.
Violence and corruption
Russia’s 2022 full-scale invasion prompted a wave of volunteers to join Ukraine’s military, with tens of thousands enlisting across the country, often travelling to other regions because conscription offices near their homes were overwhelmed.
But after heavy losses and reports of poor planning, corruption and the cruelty of some officers, the number of volunteers fell dramatically.
Since 2023, conscription officers have been combing public places in search of people trying to avoid the draft. They have frequently forced them into their vans, often resorting to intimidation, beatings and torture, as Al Jazeera has reported, along with witnesses and human rights groups.
The officers claim there is no other way to mobilise the tens of thousands of men needed on the frontline to repel Russian forces.
The violence has led to corrupt practices.
As of August this year, 76 conscription officers had been arrested for accepting bribes of up to tens of thousands of dollars, stashing huge sums, and buying expensive properties in Ukraine and abroad.
Some draft-dodgers have secured fake exemptions from medical doctors, while others fled to neighbouring countries, either through bribes or by crossing the border without documentation.
Some forcibly drafted men secured the services of “fake ambulances”, according to prosecutors and police.
In 2025, border guards in the southwestern region of Zakarpattia detained a fake ambulance crew of three men who tried to take a person evading the draft to Romania for $10,000.

content:
The leader of a Kenyan doomsday sect has been sentenced to 200 years in prison for the murders of 190 children and one adult in one of the world’s worst cult disasters in recent history.
The sentence, comprising 100 years for murder by starvation and 100 years by direct homicide, came two weeks after the court in Kenya’s coastal city of Mombasa found the cult leader guilty of the crimes.
Prosecutors said Paul Mackenzie and his Good News International church ran a Christian doomsday sect whose members were ordered to starve themselves and their children to death to go to heaven before the world ended.
His accomplices threatened and beat victims to ensure they followed his orders. The emaciated bodies were found scattered in shallow graves and dumped in latrines. Some had been buried alive.
Mackenzie was arrested in 2023 after police received a tipoff, and weeks later authorities began uncovering bodies in shallow graves in the Shakahola forest near the coast in south-eastern Kenya.
In total, more than 400 bodies have been recovered. Many were severely decomposed and only 26 could be identified.
Mackenzie denied murder charges, saying he did not force the victims to starve, but the court rejected that argument.
The Shakahola tragedy has gripped Kenya since the discovery of mass graves in the forest more than three years ago.
It raised questions about how Mackenzie was able to continue operating despite being on the radar of the authorities since 2017, when police searched his premises.
In 2019, authorities shut down Mackenzie’s church and he relocated to the Shakahola forest, police said.
The case has also led to calls for tougher oversight of churches and other religious organisations in a country where religious faith plays a prominent role in public life.
Mackenzie, a former taxi driver, forbade cult members from sending their children to school and from going to hospital when they were ill, describing such institutions as satanic.
Cult members lived in makeshift homes of polythene sheeting and thatch that Mackenzie divided into areas with biblical names such as Jerusalem and Judea.
The plight of his followers began to emerge in March 2023, when a man told police his brother and wife had starved their children to death in the forest on Mackenzie’s orders.
Mackenzie was arrested but released on bail, after which relatives said he brought forward the date on which he told his followers the world would end. Police rearrested him and started combing through the forest more systematically and began exhuming mass graves.
Last month’s judgment covered 191 deaths while investigations into more than 200 other deaths are continuing.
Justice Diana Kavedza-Mochache said in a hearing lasting more than eight hours that in some cases children were isolated and denied food while their parents watched.
Mackenzie faces other charges over the forest deaths, including those of terrorism, which he has denied.
Prosecutors said that while he was in detention he also directed the deaths of 52 people in Kwa Binzaro village, about 18 miles from Shakahola. Mackenzie has pleaded not guilty in that case.
Reuters contributed reporting

China keeps a close eye on US midterm shake-up
To display this content from YouTube, you must enable advertisement tracking and audience measurement.
One of your browser extensions seems to be blocking the video player from loading. To watch this content, you may need to disable it on this site.
Issued on:
The US midterm elections have resulted in the Democratic Party taking control of both chambers of the US Congress, leaving Donald Trump as a lame duck president for the remainder of his term. Professor Steve Tsang of the SOAS China Institute tells FRANCE 24 that, while a weakened Trump could strengthen Beijing's negotiating position, the Chinese leadership is aware that Congress has relatively little sway over foreign policy and is keen to maintain warm personal ties between the two presidents.
Also on the show:
Joshua Wong, one of the best-known faces of Hong Kong's pro-democracy movement, has been sentenced to a further 10 years in prison under the Beijing-imposed National Security Law for "colluding with foreign forces". He is the only person to have been prosecuted twice under the controversial law, and the ruling has drawn criticism from human rights groups and Western governments.
Meanwhile, the Indian film "Ramayana" has hit cinemas worldwide. Based on a beloved ancient Hindu epic, it has been described as Bollywood's answer to "Star Wars". With a mega-budget of more than €400 million, the film is the biggest production in Indian cinema history and has been dubbed into nearly 40 languages.
Finally, Japan's Hiroshima Prefecture has appointed two cats as its tourism ambassadors. Siblings Yamato and Chidori have been serving as stationmasters at Shiwaguchi Station, one of many unmanned stations on a railway line facing possible partial closure due to declining passenger numbers.
