Watch: Is it the end of the road for Tesla's Cybertruck?
Tesla CEO Elon Musk has said production of the firm's Cybertruck is "winding down" in Texas, to focus on its self-driving Cybercab cars.
The model is only produced at Tesla's Austin base, and he did not clarify if manufacturing would be moved elsewhere or simply cease.
The Cybertruck has received a mixed response since its launch in 2023, with some praising its individuality and others simply labelling it ugly.
It has also suffered from disappointing sales, quality problems and recalls.
BBC technology reporter Shiona McCallum has this report.
summary: The car company's CEO Elon Musk has said production will halt in Texas, to focus on the firm's self-driving Cybercabs.

（德国之声中文网）此案的核心人物是网名 “李老师不是你老师” 的博主、自2015年起便居住在 意大利 的艺术家李颖。他在X平台帐号“李老师不是你老师”@whyyoutouzhele拥有220万粉丝。该账号因在2022年底中国爆发反对“清零政策”的“ 白纸运动 ”期间，转发海量来自中国民众的抗议实时图文与视频而备受关注。在这之后，该账号也经常发布由中国国内民众发送给他的视频、照片和文字叙述，内容多涉及抗议活动及其他在中国受到严格管控、或完全不予报道的政治敏感事件。
根据路透社看到的案卷，米兰检察官于10月23日通知10名嫌疑人（包括8名中国公民和2名意大利公民）调查已经结束，并给予他们在可能进入审判程序前做出回应的最后机会。该文件揭示了意大利检察官所称的这场“针对海外中国政府批评者进行监控和恐吓的协同行动”。
李颖对于此次调查表示欢迎。他在给路透社的一份声明中表示，由于他致力于分享关于中国普通民众的“真实故事”，他本人、家人以及关注者多年来一直遭受着“持续不断的骚扰和威胁”。 “因此，我很高兴看到此案取得进展，也非常感谢调查人员。”
2024年10月，在意大利都灵，李颖通过自家门上的猫眼，拍到一名男子在他住所旁的墙上喷涂了“stupro”（意大利语，意为“强奸”）一词。检察官随后据此展开了调查。
调查人员称，他们发现了一场有系统的监视行动：嫌疑人多次前往李颖被认为居住的地点，拍摄入口照片，在附近的咖啡馆监视相关建筑，翻找垃圾桶，向居民打探信息，并追踪李颖的行踪。
检察官表示，其中一名嫌疑人在秘密监视行动中收集了超过4000张照片和35段视频。案卷还显示，李颖通过社交媒体和电子邮件收到了死亡威胁，其中包括“我要砍下你的头”、“我们要惩罚你”等信息，并附有突击步枪、手枪和刺刀的图片。
两名为首的嫌犯被指控代表中国警方行事，同时与中国外交官及统战部成员保持联系。这两人连同另外两人，被指控参与了一个犯罪团伙，其目的是“阻挠“中国异见人士行使言论自由的权利”——根据意大利法律，这一罪名最高可判处七年监禁。
案卷显示，以上四名涉嫌组织者中的一人招募了中国公民去跟踪李颖，而另一名嫌疑人则出价每天100欧元，雇人协助锁定李颖的行踪。李颖的个人信息被发布在网上，其身在中国的亲友也受到了压力。李颖深感自身安全受到威胁，被迫不断更换住所，在米兰和都灵之间辗转，试图躲避追踪。
首次公开露面
10月31日，李颖出席了《纽约时报》记者袁莉在日本东京举办的“不明白节”，这是他首次公开露面。他在访谈中谈到自己选择站出来露面的原因、遭遇跨境镇压而逃亡的经历、以及通过运营账号所窥见的中国社会百态。
“李老师不是你老师”遭跨境镇压案反映出意大利正日益加强对“中国监控并施压批评者”行为的审查。意大利警方2月份表示，源自中国的网络攻击曾针对意大利内政部，旨在搜寻中国异见人士，并查明负责调查中国犯罪团伙的警务人员身份。中国外交部当时回应称，北京坚决反对黑客攻击，并驳斥了有关此事的“虚假信息”。
一个月后，意大利媒体报道称，罗马方面已下令驱逐八名中国公民，这些人被怀疑受中国政府指使，对异见人士进行监视。意大利内政部当时拒绝置评。
(路透社）

Pope Leo XIV is kicking off a three-nation tour of Latin America on Friday, November 6, with a visit to Uruguay, the region’s least Catholic and most secular country, three weeks after undergoing lung cancer surgery that had put the entire trip into question. After Uruguay, he will then go to Argentina and Peru. FRANCE 24's Hanna Roberts has more.

En Inde, un agriculteur sauve son île de l'érosion en plantant, seul, une forêt à main nues. Baptisé "Forest Man", Jadav Payeng a consacré plus de 40 ans de sa vie à mettre en terre des arbres un par un sur son île, menacée par l'érosion. Aujourd'hui, la forêt porte son nom et s'étend sur plus de 500 hectares.

content:
Tundu Lissu says the trial is politically motivated
Published
Tanzania's main opposition leader, Tundu Lissu, has been found guilty of inciting unrest and sentenced to four years in jail, in a case that has raised concerns about political freedom in the East African country.
A panel of three judges at the High Court in Dar es Salaam acquitted him of the more serious offence of treason, saying prosecutors had failed to prove a key element of that charge.
But they said the 58-year-old, who has been detained since April last year, had encouraged his supporters to disrupt the disputed 2025 general election.
Lissu, who leads the opposition Chadema party, has denied the charges, describing the prosecution as politically motivated.
The court said his campaign slogan "No Reforms, No Election" was sufficient for him to be convicted of the charge of incitement.
"By uttering those words with the intention of disseminating them to the public, the accused incited the public to disrupt the 2025 elections," the court ruled.
Lissu said he had only been charged with treason, not incitement.
"The offence of incitement is one that you, honourable judges, have manufactured. You have created an offence that did not exist, and you have done so on political directives," Lissu told the court.
He added that he would like to apply for bail as this was possible for incitement, unlike treason.
He has leave to appeal at the Court of Appeal - the country's highest court.
But if the four-year sentence is upheld, it would rule him out of the next elections, due in 2030.
Treason is among Tanzania's most serious offences and can carry the death penalty.
Human rights group Amnesty International described his conviction as a "travesty of justice".
"Tundu Lissu should never have been arrested, let alone prosecuted and convicted," said its regional director for East and Southern Africa, Tigere Chagutah:
President Samia Suluhu Hassan won the October 2025 election with 98% of the vote - a result the opposition dismissed the result as a "mockery" of democracy as her two main challengers, including Lissu, were excluded.
Her government has repeatedly denied targeting its opponents.
The Chadema leader was arrested six months before the poll, shortly after launching a campaign demanding changes to the electoral system under the slogan "No Reforms, No Election".
Prosecutors accused him of making statements intended to incite the public to disrupt the election and threaten the government.
They argued that his remarks, which were also circulated online, amounted to treason.
But Lissu, a lawyer who represented himself during the trial, maintained that his comments were part of a legitimate political campaign for constitutional and electoral reform.
He argued that prosecutors had taken his statements out of context and failed to prove that he had committed any crime.
Some of the demands raised by Chadema were:
Electoral commissioners should be independently appointed (not by the president)
Police should allow all parties to campaign free of intimidation
Government-appointed district chiefs should no longer act as returning officers
Party agents should be able to observe counting without harassment
It should be possible to challenge presidential election results in court.
Widespread protests and a violent security crackdown after last year's elections left at least 500 people dead, authorities say
During his time in remand custody at Dar es Salaam's Ukonga Prison, Lissu went on hunger strike twice for brief periods when he said he was not allowed access to his lawyers or relatives. He also complained that guards listened to what should have been private consultations his lawyers.
These allegations have been denied by the prison authorities.
His case has attracted international attention, with rights groups expressing concern about the treatment of opposition politicians and the shrinking space for political dissent in Tanzania.
Last year's election was followed by widespread protests and a violent security crackdown that left at least 500 people dead, according to an official inquiry.
Opposition groups have said the death toll was much higher and demanded an independent investigation.
The government has defended its handling of the unrest and rejected accusations of widespread political repression.
Samia, 66, has insisted the election was fair and transparent and blamed foreigners for the unrest, saying it was part of a plot to overthrow her. She has set up another commission to inquiry to identify those behind the violence.
President Samia Suluhu Hassan won 98% of the vote in last year's election
Lissu has long been one of Tanzania's most outspoken critics of the ruling Chama Cha Mapinduzi (CCM) party, which, along with its predecessor Tanu, has dominated the country's politics since independence.
He first became an MP in 2010, representing a constituency near his birth place in Singida, 320km (200 miles) north-west of the capital, Dodoma.
In September 2017, the Chadema politician narrowly survived an assassination attempt when gunmen sprayed his vehicle with bullets outside his home in Dodoma.
He was shot multiple times and underwent extensive medical treatment abroad.
The attack, whose perpetrators have never been brought to justice, forced him to spend years in exile.
He returned to contest the 2020 presidential election against the late President John Magufuli, but lost in a vote that the opposition alleged was marred by widespread irregularities.
Lissu subsequently returned to exile before coming back to Tanzania in 2023, following President Samia's decision to lift a ban on opposition political rallies.
His return was initially seen as a sign of renewed political openness after years of restrictions under Magufuli, who died in office in 2021.
But relations between the government and the opposition deteriorated as the country approached the 2025 election.
Lissu became Chadema's national chairman in January 2025 and intensified his demands for electoral reforms.
His conviction is likely to deepen concerns about the state of democracy in Tanzania.
Last week, Amnesty accused the government of continuing its crackdown following the election and "weaponising counterterrorism laws to silence critics and instil fear".
The authorities did not respond to a request for comment.
Correction: An initial version of this story said Lissu had been convicted of inciting treason. We have corrected this to incitement.

content:
（德国之声中文网）《世界报》评论写道，中国当局再度判处香港民主派人士黄之锋十年监禁。而这一肆意专横的判决说明了一个问题：当今世界的各类冲突都同 争取自由的斗争 密切相关。这篇题为《他在捍卫西方，西方却在走向怯弱和堕落》的评论写道:
“2024年11月，黄之锋在香港被判处 四年半监禁 。这一判决无疑是法治的丑闻。它显示出， 中国专制政权 是多么的腐朽，也显示出，那些及时指出对华依赖危害性的人，又是多么有先见之明。同时，这一判决也在提醒我们，只有提升经济实力和完善市场框架，我们才能摆脱这样的依赖。
现如今， 黄之锋 又一次被判重刑，刑期又增加了十年。但这一次，西方世界却表现出了异乎寻常的沉默，就连左翼职业活动家们也没有高调地给中国当局发出抗议信。
而黄之锋和我们并没有什么区别：他也想像我们一样自由地生活。他要捍卫西方，而西方却面临着日渐怯弱和堕落的风险：为旁支末节的小事争执不休，面对原则问题却沉默不语。黄之锋再度提醒我们，当今世界争执的焦点究竟是什么：自由、个人的自由以及反抗专制和独裁的勇气。”
《世界报》的评论指出，黄之锋曾同另一位香港民主派人士邝颂晴为《世界报》撰写专栏文章，向德国读者介绍香港的局势。黄之锋被捕后，邝颂晴曾在一篇文章中写道：争取香港自由的斗争正变得越来越危险，而西方却任由中国为所欲为：
“为自由而战的人们正在被西方所抛弃，乌克兰局势最具有代表性，委内瑞拉、土耳其、伊朗、尤其是中国也同样如此。无论在任何领域，中国都不可能成为西方的伙伴。无论是个人自由和人权标准，还是民主宪政的层面上，中国都是西方的敌人。
我们能从中得到的唯一教训就是，在经济、外交和国防层面上，西方必须变得更加强大，文化层面上也同样如此。像黄之锋这样的人，对西方自由往往有着更加深刻的理解，远远胜过西方体制内那些安于现状、衣食无忧、而又思想懒惰的大多数人。
当年黄之锋接受我采访时曾说过这样的话：‘如果我们的政治家不愿为我们的未来付出努力，那我就必须站在最前线，为自己的未来而奋斗。’黄之锋的事例清楚地表明，公民的身份早已不再取决于社会地位，而是取决于他为获取更多自由而奋斗的意愿，以及他是否愿意为制止社会各层面上自由的丧失而付出努力。这也正是当前德国社会所需要的。
黄之锋，坚持住，你是国家的未来。自由终究会取得胜利。”
”特朗普在中期选举中的失败，意味着什么？“
对于美国中期选举的结果，德国《明镜周刊》发表评论写道，民主党确实取得了胜利，但不应忘记特朗普的执政期还有八百多天，这位现年八十岁的总统仍有能力让世界与他同归于尽：
“那怎么办呢？我们欧洲人应为 特朗普 统治的晚期准备好求生手册。如果一厢情愿地认为，最糟糕的时期已经成为过去，显然是一种不负责任的态度。当今世界的流氓们会发现特朗普已经变成‘跛脚鸭’，会认为放手一搏的机会到了，而首当其冲的就是普京。欧洲，尤其是德国，必须要义正词严地告诫这位俄罗斯当权者，乌克兰仍将获得该国自卫所需的一切。
普京最擅长读懂权力的语言。只要普京意识到， 特朗普 的影响力正在逐渐消失，他主动邀请欧洲人重返谈判桌的意愿就会骤然上升。过去多年以来，欧洲人实际上被排除在谈判席之外。由此看来，特朗普在中期选举中的失败，或许也能为外交努力创造机会。
中国的情形也大同小异，或许习近平主席会得出这样的结论：现在正是吞并 台湾 的最佳历史窗口。一方面，伊朗战争已经削弱了美国的军事实力。另一方面，特朗普又对习近平这类独裁者表现出了异乎寻常的偏爱。有鉴于此，欧洲必须尽快向北京表明立场：武装侵台需要付出惨痛的代价，欧盟将会大幅限制对华经贸关系。同美国不同的是，欧洲无法以军事手段威慑中国。但我们却有能力让中国经济陷入危机。仅去年一年，中国对欧出口额就高达5590亿欧元。”

Paul Mackenzie's followers believed he was "Jesus's mouthpiece", the judge said last month
Published
A Kenyan court has sentenced the leader of a doomsday cult, Paul Mackenzie, to 200 years in prison for murdering 191 people, all but one of them children.
Alongside 28 others, Mackenzie was found guilty of the murders for instructing members of his cult to starve their children to death so they could "meet Jesus".
Justice Diana Mochache said Mackenzie bore the "primary criminal culpability" for ordering his followers to fast to death, in one of the world's deadliest episodes of cult activity.
"The sentence is appropriate and just, to send an unmistakable message that such atrocities warrant the maximum penalties allowed by law," the judge added.
The self-styled pastor was arrested in 2023 after the discovery of more than 400 bodies in shallow graves in Shakahola forest near the Kenyan coast. The sprawling investigation into the cases shocked Kenya and drew international attention.
The court sentenced Mackenzie to 100 years in prison for homicide and another 100 years for offences related to starvation.
The sentences within each category will run concurrently, but the two sets will run consecutively, bringing his total prison term to 200 years.
Mackenzie also faces separate manslaughter and terrorism charges, which he denies.
Prosecutors had sought the death penalty, arguing that the scale and circumstances of the killings warranted the harshest punishment.
However, Justice Mochache declined to impose the death penalty, despite ruling that the case met the threshold for its consideration.
"Nevertheless, the court declines the invitation to impose the death penalty on any of the victims," she said, adding that capital punishment would eliminate any prospect of rehabilitation and disengagement. The death sentence has not been carried out in Kenya since 1987.
Mackenzie was tried alongside 28 accomplices, including guards who enforced his fasting orders and gravediggers who helped conceal the victims' bodies in mass graves.
They received varying prison sentences of up to 160 years.
Justice Mochache described the killings as "cold and calculated", saying the perpetrators had shown no remorse and had even declared their willingness to fast to death themselves.
Before the hearing began on Friday morning, Francis Wanje, who lost eight relatives including two grandchildren in Shakahola forest, told the BBC's Newsday programme that he was "hoping for... a sentence which will match his [Mackenzie's] deeds in the forest".
Mackenzie and the co-accused had asked for leniency from the court.
Before their conviction on 19 October, they had all pleaded not guilty and repeatedly insisted that nobody was forced to die.
More than 400 bodies were dug up in Shakahola forest
Mackenzie's followers believed he was "Jesus's mouthpiece", Justice Mochache said as she delivered her eight-hour judgement last month.
Those who opposed Mackenzie's teachings were beaten to death.
One of his co-accused said he had told his followers that anyone who "resisted the directive to fast must be forced to go to heaven through kicks and blows".
Burials inside the forest where the cult was based were called "weddings" and those who died "were celebrated as having wedded with Jesus" the judge said.
The judge found that the deaths arose from an organised system, including religious teachings and directives that compelled followers to follow the deadly fasting.
Post-mortem results showed the cause of deaths to be starvation for most victims, while others died from suffocation, strangulation or head injuries.
The cause of death could not be determined for some, with their bodies having decomposed, while others died soon after their rescue as they were so emaciated.
The Shakahola deaths have shone a spotlight on the lack of oversight of rogue religious activities and how they could have carried on for so long.
The gravity of the case prompted President William Ruto to set up a commission of inquiry, although this was later declared unconstitutional.
Investigations by the state-funded Kenya National Commission on Human Rights (KNCHR) revealed that local administration and law enforcement officials had repeatedly turned a blind eye to the cult's activities.
"We expected at that time the police would take action immediately to go and rescue the other members there, but it didn't happen," said Wanje, who reported the case to the police in March 2023.
Wanje said a relative of his in the police force and a former cult participant had managed to save his grandson at the time. The child told the police what had happened and showed them the grave of his siblings.
"It was [supposed to be] his last day.. they [would have killed] my grandson."
The cult leader had previously been arrested and later released for lack of evidence.
Mackenzie established Good News International Ministries in 2003.
Over the next 16 years, the church grew in popularity, drawing thousands of followers in its branches across Kenya.
The church ran a television station called Times TV which would broadcast his sermons from his church in Malindi.
His End Days sermons included conspiracy theories that described education as "evil", healthcare as "against the doctrine" and digital identity cards as "the mark of the devil".
The main church shut down in 2019 and Mackenzie moved to Shakahola forest, encouraging his devotees to follow him.
While the conclusion of the murder cases may bring a sense of justice for the victims and their families, the convictions only account for 191 victims, while more than 400 bodies were exhumed from the forest.

WASHINGTON - Production of Cybertrucks — the pickups hailed by enthusiasts as a symbol of Elon Musk’s futuristic ambitions and equally hated as ugly reminders of the Donald Trump era — will wind down, the Tesla CEO said Friday.
Tesla will stop building the truck at its Texas factory around the middle of 2027 to free up space for its Cybercab robotaxi, the world’s richest man said.
“Tesla will be winding down production of the Cybertruck at Gigafactory Texas around the middle of next year to make room for increased Cybercab production,” Musk wrote on X.
Musk did not say whether the truck would be built elsewhere or discontinued altogether, nor what would happen to outstanding orders.
Wes Morrill, the Cybertruck’s lead engineer, wrote in a separate post that the truck “was an incredible technology development platform and lives on through Cybercab”.
“Thanks to everyone who contributed to making the future (look) like the future,” he added.
Tesla fans lamented the departure of the Cybertruck on X, the social media platform Musk owns, but Musk reassured them that the Cybertruck fleet “will be around for a long time”.
The truck came to be seen as an extension of Musk himself, and its image became entangled with his politics as he took on a high-profile role leading the Trump administration’s cost-cutting Department of Government Efficiency. Some owners reported vandalism and harassment.
The angular stainless-steel behemoth was unveiled in November 2019, and Musk said at the time it had drawn 250,000 preorders within days.
Production was originally slated for 2021 but was repeatedly delayed, with customer deliveries starting in late 2023.
Tesla built its Texas lines with planned capacity of 250,000 trucks a year, but sales have come nowhere near that figure.
As US demand slumped, Tesla began selling the truck abroad, starting deliveries in South Korea in November 2025 and in the United Arab Emirates in January. (Story continues below)
A Tesla Cybertruck is parked at a dealership in Paramus, New Jersey. (Photo: Reuters)
Multiple recalls
Tesla does not break out Cybertruck revenue, but its “other models” category, which includes the pickup, accounts for just a small percentage of sales.
The truck has also been subject to multiple recalls and complaints over build quality.
The Cybercab, a two-seat vehicle with no steering wheel or pedals, was unveiled in October 2024.
Tesla began production at the Texas plant in April and started offering paid Cybercab rides in Austin in September through its existing Robotaxi service.
The robotaxi is central to Musk’s effort to recast Tesla as an artificial intelligence and robotics company rather than a carmaker, though its success depends on the company delivering fully driverless technology, which it has yet to demonstrate at scale.

El Stuttgart parece vivir dos temporadas al mismo tiempo. En la Liga de Campeones mantiene opciones de alcanzar las eliminatorias, mientras que en la Bundesliga todavía busca la regularidad necesaria para acercarse a los puestos europeos. Los goles de Ermedin Demirovic, la aparición de nuevos talentos y dos recientes victorias en las competiciones nacionales ofrecen motivos para el optimismo. Sin embargo, la derrota ante el Galatasaray ha vuelto a recordar que al equipo de Sebastian Hoeness todavía le cuesta mantener su mejor versión.
Altibajos en liga
Después de ocho jornadas, los suabos ocupan la undécima posición liguera, con nueve puntos, tres victorias y cinco derrotas. En la Champions son decimocuartos, con siete puntos en cuatro encuentros. Aunque ambas competiciones tienen formatos diferentes, los promedios reflejan un contraste evidente.
"En la Bundesliga no estamos ahora donde queremos estar", reconoció Hoeness tras la derrota por 2-3 ante el Borussia Mönchengladbach, en declaraciones recogidas por la web oficial del club. Una frase que resume las luces y sombras de un equipo capaz de imponerse al Bayer Leverkusen con una actuación eficaz y colectiva, de avanzar a octavos de final de la Copa de Alemania -aunque tuviera que esperar hasta el último minuto para superar al recién ascendido Paderborn- y de caer frente al colista en poco más de una semana.
Lo que todavía no ha conseguido el Stuttgart es sumar puntos en dos jornadas consecutivas de Bundesliga, una asignatura pendiente que intentará superar frente al equipo del momento, el Werder Bremen.
Demirovic, certeza ofensiva no exenta de críticas
Entre tantos altibajos, el delantero bosnio Ermedin Demirovic continúa siendo una de las grandes referencias del Stuttgart. Suma cinco goles en Bundesliga y cuatro en Champions, nueve de los 21 tantos anotados por su equipo entre ambas competiciones. El atacante, además, disputó su partido oficial número cien con la camiseta suaba precisamente el día en que consiguió su segundo doblete consecutivo, en la victoria frente al Leverkusen. El bosnio reconoció después del encuentro que ni siquiera sabía que estaba alcanzando ese registro.
Desde su llegada en 2024, acumula 41 goles y once asistencias en 101 encuentros oficiales con la camiseta suaba, unas cifras que reflejan su peso en el ataque del Stuttgart y que han despertado el interés de otros clubes.
Entre ellos destaca el Galatasaray, su último rival en la Liga de Campeones, que ya intentó ficharlo durante el pasado verano. Sin embargo, Demirovic decidió permanecer en tierras alemanas. Por ahora no hay negociaciones abiertas ni una salida acordada, aunque el interés del conjunto de Estambul evidencia el atractivo de un futbolista que se ha convertido en una de las principales referencias ofensivas del equipo .
Por otro lado, ni siquiera sus cifras han evitado las críticas. Después de desperdiciar varias ocasiones claras frente al Paderborn, Demirovic recibió numerosos reproches en redes sociales. Una situación que Johann Schicklinski, periodista del medio alemán Sportschau, considera injusta.
"Demirovic aporta un enorme valor añadido al VfB Stuttgart. Es cierto que no es un virtuoso de la técnica, pero sí un delantero incansable. Un futbolista que se deja la piel por su equipo, que busca los duelos individuales, genera espacios y trabaja sin descanso", escribió el periodista en un artículo de opinión publicado el pasado 3 de noviembre.
Schicklinski recuperó además unas palabras pronunciadas por Hoeness hace aproximadamente medio año, cuando el entrenador comparó la entrega del delantero con la de un "jabalí".
"Me parece muy acertada esa comparación con un jabalí. Demirovic es un luchador intrépido, un jugador incansable que pelea cada balón, que tiene olfato para detectar situaciones prometedoras y que se gana sus oportunidades a base de esfuerzo", añadió el redactor.
Como ejemplo de esa intensidad, Schicklinski recordó lo ocurrido en Leverkusen. Apenas un segundo después del pitido inicial, el bosnio cometió una falta sobre el futbolista argentino Facundo Medina, marcando así el tono de un encuentro que se caracterizaría por su intensidad. "Todos los equipos necesitan futbolistas así", sentenció Schicklinski.
Ante su próximo rival liguero, el Werder Bremen, Demirovic tendrá además la oportunidad de disipar las críticas e igualar un registro histórico. Si vuelve a marcar al menos dos goles, alcanzará la hazaña de Serhou Guirassy , quien en septiembre de 2023 consiguió marcar dos dobletes y un hat-trick en tres jornadas consecutivas con el Stuttgart.
Una fábrica de talentos que no se detiene
La irregularidad del equipo de Hoeness resulta todavía más llamativa por la calidad de una plantilla que continúa desarrollando futbolistas de proyección internacional . El jueves 5 de noviembre, el seleccionador alemán Jürgen Klopp convocó a Maximilian Mittelstädt y Finn Jeltsch para los próximos encuentros de la Nations League frente a Serbia y Países Bajos.
Aunque ninguno de los dos defensores se formó en la cantera del Stuttgart -Mittelstädt llegó procedente del Hertha Berlín en 2023 y Jeltsch, del Núremberg en 2025-, ambos representan la capacidad del club para captar y potenciar talento. Mittelstädt se ha consolidado como una pieza importante del equipo, mientras que Jeltsch continúa progresando y aspira a debutar con la selección absoluta.
A ellos se suma ahora Yanik Spalt, una de las grandes promesas del conjunto suabo. Según informaciones de varios medios alemanes, la directiva del Stuttgat planea iniciar conversaciones para ampliar su contrato más allá de junio de 2028.
El centrocampista austríaco, de apenas 19 años, sorprendió con su actuación frente al Galatasaray, pese a la derrota por 2-0 en Estambul, y sus compañeros no tardaron en elogiarlo. Desde Sky Sport, Deniz Undav destacó la seguridad mostrada por el joven en un escenario de máxima exigencia.
Con estos ingredientes, el equipo de Hoeness tiene una máxima clara: trasladar sus buenas actuaciones a la Bundesliga, pues los suabos han perdido los tres encuentros ligueros disputados inmediatamente después de jugar la Champions. La "tendencia" podría romperse este sábado frente al Werder Bremen.

summary: Capaz de vencer al Leverkusen y perder ante el colista, el Stuttgart vive entre dos extremos. Demirovic aporta los goles, pero la regularidad sigue siendo una asignatura pendiente para el equipo de Sebastian Hoeness.

content:
Deeply indebted, politically trapped in a standoff between extremes and led by a government without a parliamentary majority: These are the defining features of France's current predicament.
If, in response to nationwide protests , the government plans to provide €4 billion ($4.48 billion) in low-interest loans to renovate schools by 2030 and allocate a further €1 billion to universities by 2029, it is promising money the state simply does not have.
France's public debt stands at around 120% of gross domestic product (GDP). By comparison, Germany's debt-to-GDP ratio is roughly 65%, despite its €600 billion  investment package for infrastructure and defense.
Germany still enjoys the highest possible AAA credit rating . France, by contrast, is rated AA, A+ or Aa3, depending on the credit agency. While Germany's outlook is consistently rated as stable, several agencies have assigned France a negative outlook.
As a result, the French government must pay higher interest rates on its borrowing than Berlin. The risk premium over German government bonds, known as the spread, is now at its highest level since the financial crisis. France pays nearly 1.6 percentage points more in interest than Germany on 10-year bonds.
A barometer of France's public finances
The spread acts as a kind of "fever gauge" for bond markets, explained Friedrich Heinemann, an economist at the Leibniz Center for European Economic Research (ZEW) in Mannheim.
"This fever gauge then forces a change of course. If the spread rises too sharply, France's financing conditions come under pressure, and anyone in France who needs a loan has to pay higher interest rates. Banks then get into trouble, and the crisis escalates further," Heinemann told DW.
"This could then slide toward a financial crisis, which would finally send a clear signal to everyone: Things cannot continue like this unless you are prepared to risk a genuine economic collapse," he said.
Landry Charrier, a researcher at the University of Bonn's Center for Advanced Security, Strategic and Integration Studies, however, does not expect France's debt-fueled spending spree to end anytime soon.
"French people are aware of the country's high public debt. But debt remains an abstract concept if its consequences are barely felt in everyday life. According to INSEE [the French national statistics agency — Editor's note], 56% of the population receive more in government benefits and services than they pay in taxes and social contributions. The majority therefore have a tangible interest in maintaining the status quo," Charrier told DW.
For more than half a century, France has regularly spent more than it collects in tax revenue. The last time it balanced its national budget was in 1974.
Echoes of eurozone crisis
France last paid a similarly high-risk premium at the end of 2011, during the eurozone debt crisis. What is particularly striking is how quickly it has risen: Since June 2026, the spread over German government bonds has more than doubled.
The main driver is not so much the general level of interest rates. Rather, it's the growing risk premium investors demand in response to high debt levels, political instability, large budget deficits and the  recent unrest .
The higher the interest rates, the larger the share of the national budget that must be devoted to debt servicing alone. France is expected to pay more than €79 billion in interest on its total public debt in 2026. That figure is projected to exceed €91 billion in 2027 and could reach between €125 billion and €132 billion by 2030.
These figures include the costs incurred by social security funds and local authorities. The central government's interest bill alone is currently estimated at €62.6 billion by the Agence France Tresor, a French Treasury agency.
In the coming years, France will have to refinance large amounts of outstanding bonds that were issued when interest rates were at historic lows. At the same time, the country's substantial budget deficit means it must take on additional debt.
Warning shot for Germany
The trend of rising interest costs is also affecting Germany. The ZEW's Heinemann has calculated that German interest payments are likely to increase sharply by the early 2030s.
"For the federal government alone, which has so far paid around €30 billion, the figure will triple within a few years as both debt and interest rates rise. And it won't stop there — it will exceed €90 billion. Reaching €100 billion in annual interest payments in the federal budget is then no longer far off," warned the economist.
Could France's debt crisis become a problem for Europe?

In France, however, economic realities seem to have little impact on political debate. Both the far-right National Rally (RN) and the far-left France Unbowed (LFI) are campaigning on costly promises.
RN leader Marine Le Pen , for example, wants to reinstate the retirement age of 62 while promising €140 billion in savings. Jean-Luc Melenchon, LFI's leader, has even suggested that government bonds held by the French central bank should be "thrown into the fire."
"Nobody will ever notice they've disappeared," he has claimed.
'Fairy tales from the left and the right'
For Heinemann, this is "a good example of radical parties on both the right and the left simply telling economic fairy tales."
Their common message, he said, is that "there is a way out of this mess that requires neither fiscal consolidation nor painful cuts."
Charrier is convinced that many French people have yet to grasp the seriousness of the situation.
"The euro has made it easier for France to access cheap financing and has long softened the pressure to adjust," he pointed out.
"In the past, currency devaluations [of the French franc — Editor's note] made economic imbalances immediately felt through declining purchasing power and rising prices. Today, that warning signal is missing. This has created the illusion that necessary adjustments can be postponed indefinitely," Charrier said.
This article was originally written in German.

KUALA LUMPUR - Malaysia has temporarily postponed a plan to transfer jailed former prime minister Najib Razak to house arrest, the attorney-general’s office said on Friday, saying it needed time to review a pardon issued by the king and a court order allowing the move.
Najib, prime minister from 2009 to 2018, was found guilty of corruption in relation to the embezzlement of billions of dollars tied to 1Malaysia Development Berhad (1MDB), a state investment fund he co-founded while in power. He has consistently denied wrongdoing.
Malaysia’s King Sultan Ibrahim agreed in September to allow Najib to serve the remainder of his sentence under house arrest, in a second royal pardon over his conviction.
Najib’s party, the United Malays National Organisation, said on Friday it had paid a fine of 50 million ringgit ($12.3 million) to fulfill the conditions of the pardon on the ex-premier’s behalf.
A Malaysian court then issued an order allowing Najib’s transfer home, his lawyer said earlier, adding the plan was for that to take place on Friday.
Questions have arisen over the legal interpretation of the pardon and the subsequent court order, the Attorney-General’s Chambers said in a statement.
“In this regard, the implementation of house arrest … should be temporarily suspended until further investigation and clarification… are completed,” it said.
Police stand guard outside the residence of jailed former Malaysian prime minister Najib Razak in anticipation of his arrival, which was later put on hold, on Nov 6, 2026. (Photo: Reuters)

Más de una decena de vuelos en Europa fueron nuevamente objeto el viernes (06.11.2026) de amenazas de bomba, informaron las autoridades de República Checa, Bulgaria y Portugal, así como Irlanda, tras una jornada de perturbación del tráfico aéreo debido a estas alarmas. En la víspera, al menos una veintena de trayectos, la mayoría operados por aerolíneas de bajo costo, recibieron amenazas de explosiones a bordo .
Una portavoz del aeropuerto de Praga reportó amenazas en nueve vuelos, tres con destino a la capital checa y otros seis que partían de ella. Otro portavoz de la infraestructura añadió que se habían recibido "nuevas amenazas", "en las que se señalaba la colocación de artefactos explosivos en un mayor número de aviones". No obstante, explicó que "el funcionamiento" de la plataforma sigue siendo "normal y fluido".
Una portavoz del Ministerio búlgaro de Transportes indicó a la AFP que se habían recibido alertas para dos vuelos con destino a Sofía el viernes, que aterrizaron sin incidentes. Además, la policía portuguesa reportó una amenaza similar para un vuelo entre Lisboa y Roma, que debía partir el viernes. Los agentes "llevaron a cabo una inspección de seguridad de la aeronave, sin encontrar ningún dispositivo explosivo", agregó en un comunicado.
Una "campaña coordinada" que afecta también a medios en Irlanda
El gobierno de Irlanda aseguró hoy que la serie de alertas falsas de bomba de esta semana en varios países europeos son "probablemente" parte de una "campaña coordinada". "Estas amenazas se producen tras las continuas perturbaciones en el sector de la aviación en toda Europa provocadas por amenazas similares, y parece probable que se trate de una campaña coordinada de perturbaciones", dijo el gobierno irlandés en un comunicado.
En un incidente aparte, han sido evacuadas las instalaciones de la radiotelevisión pública irlandesa RTÉ tras recibir una amenaza de bomba por correo electrónico, que también ha sido enviado a otros medios de comunicación de Irlanda y Reino Unido, según informaron fuentes oficiales
La policía acudió a la sede de RTÉ en Dublín, donde se desplegaron agentes armados. La presentadora de Newstalk, Claire Byrne, explicó, tras regresar a antena, que se había aconsejado al personal de la emisora que abandonara el edificio después de recibir "un mensaje". "Nos han comunicado que podíamos regresar al edificio y que la alerta había sido una falsa alarma", añadió.
lgc (afp, efe)
summary: Irlanda apunta a una "campaña coordinada" tras falsos avisos de bomba en Europa que se han extendido también a algunos medios de comunicación en Irlanda y Reino Unido.

Sonia Patricelli et Thomas Baurez évoquent les sorties cinéma de la semaine. Ils débutent avec le film événement "L'Affaire Marie-Claire", inspiré du procès dit de Bobigny. En 1972, l'avocate féministe Gisèle Halimi avait défendu une jeune fille, victime d'un viol, qui avait avorté. Un "crime" dans la France de 1972. Charlotte Gainsbourg campe la célèbre pénaliste, décédée en 2020.
Parmi les autres sorties : "L'Arabe" de Malek Bensmaïl, adapté du roman de Kamel Daoud, "Meursault, contre-enquête", réponse au classique d'Albert Camus, "L'Étranger". Également au programme : "Wild Horse Nine", qui pourrait valoir à John Malkovich un Oscar dans quelques mois, et "Club Kid", qui offre une plongée dans la nuit branchée new-yorkaise de et avec Jordan Firstman, véritable révélation.

content:
The Queensland leader of a group opposing the eradication of fire ants in Australia has been convicted of obstructing government officers, after a magistrate threw out his argument that the commonwealth-funded program is illegal.
Trevor Hold was fined $1,500 but a conviction was not recorded. Hold has described himself as an “ultrapreneur”, a mental health counsellor, an organic cattle farmer and the chief executive officer of the anti-program group the Australian Advocacy Group – and as self-employed.
He was convicted last month of two counts of obstruction for attempting to prevent fire ant treatment at his property, in what is believed to be a Queensland first.
His organisation and others held a series of well-attended meetings last year across south-east Queensland to advise residents on what the group called their legal rights to refuse or prevent access to their properties to the program.
Under Queensland’s Biosecurity Act, landholders must permit program officers to access their property to treat fire ants, which are a declared priority pest.
But the organisations advised landholders to use a provision in the act allowing them to obstruct an officer if they had a “reasonable excuse” to refuse access, a provision in the Biosecurity Act.
On 16 April at about 9.20am, Hold prevented officers from entering his property in Adare in the Lockyer Valley, west of Brisbane. The property was in the treatment zone and due for its annual treatment.
The eradication program had informed Hold in advance that it would treat his property that day. A small group of supporters gathered to film and yell at them while they did so, according to court documents.
The scene was later described as “an increasingly rowdy and crowded and dynamic situation” in the Ipswich magistrates court, which heard Hold’s charges last month.
He was arrested by Queensland police after about 40 minutes for obstructing them by not allowing a gate to be opened. He was then un-arrested. Despite being warned again, he was again arrested after another interaction with program officers.
Hold made three arguments to the magistrate, Leanne Scoines, in his defence.
He argued that he was intimidated by the police and the program officers and “withdrew his consent for their attendance”, describing himself as “frazzled”.
“It was put to Mr Hold that he was not frazzled, and that he had said on three occasions, as heard in the body-worn camera footage, that ‘this is the Trevor Hold show’,” Scoines said.
Through his lawyer, solicitor Beatrice Ludwig, Hold argued that the police had failed to take into account his “reasonable excuse” and were therefore acting outside their powers.
Hold based part of his argument on emails he sent to the Department of Primary Industries in December 2024 and January 2025, notices the magistrate described as “unilateral”, “quasi-legal documents … seeking tacit approval by non-response”. The magistrate found they were of no legal effect.
Finally, he challenged the validity of the program, arguing that the prosecution had not proven it was properly authorised under the Biosecurity Act, Scoines said.
All three arguments were dismissed and the magistrate found that the officers were entitled to proceed on the basis that the DPI officers were exercising powers conferred on them by the Biosecurity Act.
“I am not satisfied that Mr Hold was a credible or liable witness on the critical issues in dispute,” she said.
A police prosecutor told the court “In my respectful submission it was clear he was actually enjoying this incident”.
Hold has appealed against the judgment to the district court.
On his website, Hold advertises fundraising efforts for his defence, and also a mooted class action lawsuit against the program.
Hold would not comment on the case.
David Heilpern, a Southern Cross University law professor, compared some of the arguments used by Hold to sovereign citizen cases he used to judge as a magistrate in the NSW Northern Rivers region, particularly his claim that he hadn’t consented to fire ant treatment.
“That is a tried and tested argument in terms of many of those who are on the fringe of or deep into the sovereign citizen movement; that you have a right to remove consent from the operations of various laws,” Heilpern said.
“Whether you consent or don’t consent is completely immaterial under the biosecurity legislation.”
summary: Legal expert compares Trevor Hold’s failed defence to ‘tried and tested argument’ used by sovereign citizen movement Get our breaking news email , free app or daily news podcast The Queensland leader of a group opposing the eradication of fire ants in Australia has been convicted of obstructing government officers, after a magistrate threw out his argument that the commonwealth-funded program is illegal. Trevor Hold was fined $1,500 but a conviction was not recorded. Hold has described himself as an “ultrapreneur”, a mental health counsellor, an organic cattle farmer and the chief executive officer of the anti-program group the Australian Advocacy Group – and as self-employed. content:
Jess Wilson has barely put a foot wrong since becoming Victorian Liberal leader a little under a year ago. That was until this week, which ended with her campaign bus reversing into a small business.
The bus was launched on Friday, a few days earlier than planned, in what appeared to be an effort to reset Wilson’s relationship with the Spring Street press pack.
A day earlier, journalists had been left waiting for an hour as Wilson announced a $100m investment in medical research to an enthusiastic room of researchers at the Burnet Institute. But when it came to questions she stayed for just four minutes and 39 seconds – answering a single question from each of the nine journalists present before cutting the press conference short.
The pack had been keen to press Wilson on Labor’s claim that the Coalition’s election policies would cost $6.35bn more than they had disclosed.
The treasurer, Colin Brooks, had earlier spent 20 minutes taking journalists through a glossy booklet Labor titled “Jess Wilson’s Dodgy Costings”, which detailed 30 Coalition promises it claimed had not been costed and dozens it said the opposition had underquoted.
It was an interesting stunt given Labor has its own cost blowouts and financial problems – including net debt that is forecast to reach $199bn within four years. But they are not the only ones questioning how the Coalition plans to deliver a surplus by 2032 while making $8bn worth of election promises, offering tax cuts and vowing not to cut frontline services.
The Liberals have made much of their credentials as better economic managers than Labor and Wilson, as shadow treasurer, should have been prepared to stay and defend her own numbers.
The moment played into Brooks’s suggestion earlier in the day that the Liberals “don’t want to be subject to the scrutiny of having journalists … asking questions during the day”.
“They’re thinking they’re going to coast home to this election result, and that’s treating the Victorian people with contempt,” he said.
A similar thing happened last week, when Wilson’s team cancelled a press conference amid confusion over the Coalition’s plan to “pause and review” the multibillion-dollar Suburban Rail Loop project.
Then there is the debate brouhaha. Both News24 and Nine had requested a debate involving Wilson, the Labor premier, Ben Carroll, and the One Nation leader, Warren Pickering – given the latter is now commanding about 20% of primary votes in most polls.
Wilson has refused, instead insisting on a traditional one-on-one format with Labor, arguing that only the two major parties could form government. Carroll wants Pickering to be included – seemingly keen to keep alive the idea of a Liberal-One Nation coalition, despite polling suggesting the Liberal-National Coalition should be able to win government in its own right.
Last week, News24 seemed to resolve the impasse by also inviting the Greens leader, Ellen Sandell.
But no agreement has been reached on Nine’s proposal. Wilson issued a statement on Thursday saying she had agreed to debate Carroll next week. This time Labor refused, claiming Nine has offered Pickering the opportunity to appear in a separate 10-minute segment during the same broadcast.
The Liberals reset on Friday, unveiling the “Jess Express” campaign bus.
Wilson was joined by her team and recruits from Canberra – including her close friend and federal Liberal senator James Paterson, and Kane Silom, who has taken leave from his role as communications director for the federal Liberal leader, Angus Taylor, to work on the Victorian campaign.
She chatted with journalists on the bus before it arrived at a Bentleigh cafe, where she made coffees and served brunch before a press conference, this time clocking in at more than 20 minutes.
Pressed again on her party’s costings, she said voters would have to wait until after early voting begins to see them.
“We cannot release our costings until the government has released its pre-election budget update,” Wilson said.
She batted off questions about the Liberals’ latest election commitment – to sell $1.3bn worth of government-owned land. Labor says this is more “dodgy costings” as it includes land earmarked for first home buyers, and a plot where radioactive cow carcasses were buried that would cost millions to clean up.
“Those costs have been factored in as part of the independent costings by the Parliamentary Budget Office,” Wilson said.
Then it was back on the bus and to the Centre Road shops – one of which became the victim of the Jess Express.
But perhaps there’s a glimmer of hope. Despite the damage, the store owner wasn’t too fussed, provided his awning is repaired.
Nor was it enough for him to rule out voting Liberal – he said he was still undecided.
It will take a little more to stop the Coalition momentum at this stage of the campaign.
Benita Kolovos is Guardian Australia’s Victorian state correspondent

That was until this week, which ended with her campaign bus reversing into a small business . content:
In the tense final hours before his dramatic election as senator for Michigan in this week’s midterms, Abdul El-Sayed had a heated encounter with a British TV journalist that rapidly went viral.
As James Matthews, of Sky News, tried to ask him a question, El-Sayed bit back. “Why would I care to have a conversation with you?” he demanded of Matthews, placing both hands on the reporter’s shoulders in a gesture of emphasis.
“You know how many votes I want to get in the UK? Zero. I am never running for office in the UK. So I actually do not care what you think or the questions you ask.”
The clip has been viewed more than 13m times on X. But the pugnacious senator-elect has not always been so dismissive of British politics and voters. Guardian readers with longer memories may recall a young Rhodes scholar who in April 2010 wrote an article for this newspaper that declared – somewhat boldly for a future US senator – that “UK democracy has the upper hand on the US”.
He also wrote: “As an Arab-American, the likelihood of ever having the opportunity to vote for an Arab-American candidate for national office during my lifetime is minimal.” As it turned out, he was wrong about that: this week, he had the chance to vote for himself.
El-Sayed was then a 25-year-old doctoral student at Oxford University and had just attended a Labour party hustings in Bethnal Green and Bow, east London, to choose a parliamentary candidate. That meeting, he wrote, had persuaded him that the UK’s electoral system was, in some respects, superior to that of the US, leaving him “envious” of the British way of doing things.
“As an American, born, bred, and taught in school that American democracy was the greatest in the world, I was initially sceptical of this foreign brand,” he wrote. “But what I experienced that evening was a ceremony in communal self-determination that I have yet to see in any federal American electoral institution.”
El-Sayed’s election in Michigan was one of the standout headlines of Tuesday’s poll after facing a barrage of racism and Islamophobia during the campaign. Donald Trump mocked his name, called him a “jihadist lunatic” and said the Senate would have to “get a special metal detector for Abdul” if he were elected. He was also denounced at the last minute by Haley Stevens, the Democrat congresswoman he had narrowly defeated for the nomination. She sensationally endorsed his Republican rival.
El-Sayed cut a dash, too, in his campaign appearances, choosing to dress in a uniform of tight black T-shirts to show off a physique described by the BBC’s North America editor, Sarah Smith, as “jacked”.
It’s all a long way from Bethnal Green where, El-Sayed noted in his Guardian article, the smaller size of British constituencies compared with US electoral districts meant minority groups could more easily make their voices heard.
after newsletter promotion
The larger number of parties competing for seats, too, meant elections became “a community exercise in cohesiveness and solidarity, antithetical to the American electoral climate”. And El-Sayed praised the fact that voters were focused on local concerns rather than being distracted by electing a head of state.
“As an American observer, I thought I knew a thing or two about how a democratic debate is supposed to run …” he wrote. “While there are, undoubtedly, some excellent qualities in American democracy, my first hustings in Bethnal Green and Bow left me just a tad envious – what are the odds they’ll allow an American cast his vote on 6 May?”
They didn’t – and nor did El-Sayed’s British sojourn last. The future senator returned to the US in 2011 after completing his doctorate in public health (and captaining the Oxford lacrosse team against Cambridge, a match in which he got a yellow card).
In the the last of his pieces for the Guardian in January 2011, El-Sayed, who is the son of Egyptian immigrants to the US, challenged Barack Obama over his response to the Arab spring, writing: “When I helped elect you into office as the 44th president of the United States of America, I believed I was doing a service by my country”, and challenging him to support the “freedom fighters” who had risen up against Egypt’s Hosni Mubarak.
After his election on Tuesday, El-Sayed had a message for Trump. In an oft-repeated quip from the campaign trail, he said: “Donald, look, I know you struggled with my name. So after JD [Vance] swears me in in January, you can just go on and call me senator.”

content:
The Czechoslovak Group (CSG) arms maker announced in mid-October that it has acquired a stake in Canadian space technology manufacturer MDA Space.
This space mission is part of the company's bid to continue riding the boom that has transformed its fortunes in recent years.
When it listed on the Amsterdam Stock Exchange earlier this year, CSG soared to become the most valuable company in Central and Eastern Europe, with a market capitalization of €14.6 billion ($16.4 billion), propelling its owner, Michal Strnad, to the top of the region's rich list.
From 90s startup to major European player
CSG began life as a 1990s startup , selling military surplus amid the collapse of the Warsaw Pact, the military alliance between the Soviet Union and Europe's socialist Eastern Bloc nations, which was founded in 1955 and disbanded in 1991.
It has since grown to become the second-largest producer of ammunition in Europe after Germany's Rheinmetall and now produces across Europe and in the US .
The impact of the war in Ukraine
The main driver of the company's rising fortunes has been Russia's war in Ukraine , which has driven a dramatic boom across the Czech defense industry as a whole.
In 2021, the sector's exports totaled €600 million. In 2025, these exports had expanded to €4.7 billion, powered by orders placed by Kyiv and its European allies.
By the end of that year, European states had procured approximately €11 billion worth of military support for Ukraine from Czech defense firms.
Orders to the value of roughly €4 billion have arrived via the Czech Ammunition Initiative, a program that coordinates the transfer of artillery shells to Ukraine.
Amid the avalanche of orders sparked by Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022, CSG and Czech peers such as STV, Colt CZ and PBS have been busy expanding production to pump out military vehicles and planes, guns, grenades, shells and bullets.
Historical link
"The war in Ukraine, particularly in its early stages, was especially well suited to Czech firms," Krzysytof Debiec of the Centre for Eastern Studies (OSW) told DW.
Debiec says that this was largely due to the major role that the former Czechoslovakia played in supplying Warsaw Pact countries.
"Specialization in the production of ammunition — including Soviet calibers — the repair of Soviet-era equipment and the manufacture of relatively unsophisticated systems that could be rapidly introduced and were compatible with the Ukrainian army's existing stocks," have all been key, he explained.
At the same time, European states eyeing the threat from the east and broader geopolitical instability are boosting their own defense budgets.
"The shift in US policies vis-a-vis NATO is forcing European nations to increase their defense spending dramatically, and that's another factor" in the Czech defense industry boom, Jan Jires, a former deputy defense minister and now a senior advisor at the International Institute for Strategic Studies, told DW.
Export dependence
However, since launching on the stock exchange, CSG's share price has performed erratically, illustrating the shifting sands on which Czechia 's booming defense industry now stands.
The government in Prague has responded to the sector's surge by transferring the defense industry portfolio from the Ministry of Defense to the Ministry of Industry and Trade to align its growing role in exports with national economic and trade policy.
At the same time, the populist ruling coalition that took power a year ago is made up of parties that have either promised to lower support for Ukraine or — in the case of the far-right Freedom and Direct Democracy party (SPD) — are openly pro-Russian.
As a result, the coalition has halted contributions to the Czech Ammunition Initiative and is dragging its feet on raising defense spending to meet NATO targets .
This only limits an already small domestic market, leaving the industry dependent on exports for about 90% of its revenue — the vast bulk of which is still linked to Ukraine — and lacking a stable base for expansion.
"The Czech industry has outgrown the country's financial means," said Jires. "Unlike German, French or British companies, Czech manufacturers cannot rely on domestic demand to make them globally relevant."
What the future holds
Increased global defense spending looks set to continue, but an end to Russia's war in Ukraine, a change in US foreign policy or a calmer geopolitical environment would hit Czech arms manufacturers hard. For this reason, they must ponder what the future of war, and its funding, might look like.
The conflict in Ukraine offers some indicators, having become increasingly focused on swarms of drones and a technological race between Kyiv and Moscow to improve the performance of the unmanned aircraft.
Major questions must now be asked regarding "the size and role of the military, how it is equipped, what should be purchased and when new weaponry can arrive" Andor Sandor, a defense analyst and former commander of Czechia's Military Intelligence Service, told DW.
For a company like CSG, for which bullets and shells currently account for around 60% of sales, these are vital questions.
"Czech companies — many of which still focus on relatively unsophisticated military production — must invest more in innovative manufacturing," said Debiec, who notes that most are well aware of the challenge. "They have reinvested their extraordinary profits and are already more technologically advanced and diversified in their production than they were in 2022."
Space mission
CSG's acquisition of MDA Space is part of such efforts.
The company, which already held interests in British and German space technology companies, pointed to the close link between the space and defense industries when it announced the deal.
Noting that global government spending on space defense accelerated to €65.83 billion last year, CSG estimates that the overall space economy will triple in size to €1.6 trillion over the next decade.
Developing capabilities in space is "a natural extension" of its activities, the company stated, noting plans for further development in the segment, including a "dedicated space team."
To power such missions, Czech defense companies must make sure they're in a position to tap into funds for defense and space under the next EU budget, which could rise as high as €130 billion, said Jires.
"If they fail to do so, and all this money is grabbed by German, French and Italian companies," he warned, "Czech manufacturers may miss the opportunity to truly scale-up."

content:
As the United States midterm election results landed late on Tuesday night, United States President Donald Trump took a phone call from the news outlet Politico.
A wave for the Democratic Party had sunk Trump’s Republican Party. For the first time in his two stints as president, Trump’s Republican Party no longer controlled either chamber of Congress.
But in the phone interview, Trump put on a brave face — and offered an olive branch: He said that he would be willing to work with Democrats.
“They’ve already called, and they want to work with me. I have the right to veto everything, but I don’t want to be just sitting there for two years just vetoing everything,” he said.
While a handful of seats remain to be counted, the Democrats have won comfortable majorities in both the House of Representatives, where they have secured at least 253 seats out of 435, and in the Senate, where they have won at least 54 out of 100.
Trump has since posted a picture on his Truth Social account using the Make America Great Again red baseball hat to read “VETO”. Despite the Democrats’ success, as president, Trump holds broad executive authority, with Article 1, Section 7 of the US Constitution stipulating that the president has the power to reject legislation passed by Congress through a veto.
Congress can override the veto, but would need to have a two-thirds majority, something that the Democrats do not have in either chamber.
But Trump’s comments to Politico underscore an alternate possibility — the president may pick and choose when to veto, and when to work with Democrats.
Bipartisan negotiations
As it stands, Trump has three options: veto legislation, enforce executive orders or make deals.
Since Trump was inaugurated in January 2025, he has passed 292 executive orders: 67 this year and 225 last year, according to the Federal Register.
But now, according to Andrew Proctor, a lecturer in US politics at University College London, Trump has even less leverage than before with Congress.
“I think the biggest thing is we’re probably going to see a decent amount of gridlock. The Democrats are going to try to pass policies, but he’s got the power to veto them, and Democrats don’t have enough seats in either chamber to overcome any vetoes that he has,” Proctor said.
“So that raises questions about, will he try to work with the Democrats at all on passing legislation? I think recent history says that’s unlikely.”
Still, some Democrats have said that they would work with the president to advance programmes central to their campaign promises.
Michigan’s Abdul El-Sayed, the first Muslim elected to the US Senate, has already said he could work with Trump — even though the US president had used racist and Islamophobic rhetoric to target El-Sayed during the campaign.
El-Sayed told MSNOW on Thursday that if Trump was interested in “getting money out of politics, putting money in pockets and passing Medicare for All, that’s what I ran to do, and I’m looking forward to working with anyone who is willing to do that”.
“He is the president of the United States,” he said. “I’m going to be one United States senator, and if he’s interested in working on issues that I want to work on – getting more people healthcare, ending the Medicare cuts, ending the stupid war, stopping these stupid tariffs with Canada – then let’s talk about doing that and go and deliver for the public.”
Progressive Senator Bernie Sanders has also said, in recent interviews, that he would not rule out Trump signing onto a Medicare for All bill if Democrats pass it in both chambers of Congress. He described Trump as a “politician” who was not “too ideological”.
Proctor argued that Trump could indeed make a deal with the Democrats based on how good it could make him look, but that getting Medicare for All passed in the next two years appeared unlikely.
“I do think that a place where common ground could emerge on healthcare is rolling back, specifically the sort of subsidies that were cut” under Trump’s earlier legislation, he said. “So that would make healthcare more affordable for millions of Americans.”
Proctor pointed out that some Republicans in 2025 had said they were willing to negotiate with Democrats on healthcare reforms.
“That didn’t end up happening, but I could imagine that might be a place for healthcare-specific policy where we could see something emerge,” he said. “I don’t think that a broader healthcare debate on passing Medicare for All, though, is really in the cards.”
Veto or filibuster
Though Trump has said he would be willing to use veto, he has historically not been among the most avid proponents of the practice.
He has so far used the veto twice in this term, and used it 10 times during his first term. Joe Biden used it 12 times in his single term, while Barack Obama used the veto a dozen times over two terms.
Overall, the presidential use of the veto has declined with time: Bill Clinton vetoed legislation 37 times between 1993 and 2001. His predecessor, George HW Bush, used it 44 times in his single term — almost once a month. Ronald Reagan used it 78 times over his two terms.
But Proctor said that Republicans also have a different tool to try and block legislation. That is the filibuster, a tactic that delays a vote on a specific piece of legislation by using an extended debate, which would impact the Democrats’ ability to get something passed.
“This is what they did to [former President Barack] Obama,” Proctor told Al Jazeera. “Senate Republicans will probably try to do the same thing, and it also means that we don’t even get to the point of Trump having the power to veto because the legislation never reaches him in the first place.”
Impeachment
Since the Democrats swept the midterms on Tuesday, calls for investigations against the administration have already emerged.
In his first term, Trump was impeached twice — first for the abuse of power and obstruction of Congress, and the second time for “inciting” the US Capitol riots.
On Tuesday night, US Representative Robert Garcia, who is set to become chairman of the House Oversight Committee, wrote on X: “LAWYER UP.” Senator Ron Wyden, who is expected to lead the Senate Finance Committee, wrote in a post on X: “Subpoenas.”
However, the Trump administration has already denied any wrongdoing.
“If Democrats choose to pursue sham investigations and radical left policies, they are choosing to work against the American people,” said White House spokesperson Lauren Bis on Wednesday.
Reports also suggest that impeachment proceedings against Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth might be imminent, over the Iran war that Trump and other Republicans have blamed for the party’s losses.
summary: Trump has three options to affect legislation, say analysts: veto legislation, enforce executive orders or make deals.

content:
On the sidelines of this month’s Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit in Shenzhen, China, an unprecedented three-way meeting between United States President Donald Trump, Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin could take place.
“China is in communication with relevant parties regarding a meeting between the three heads of state,” Chinese Foreign Ministry spokesperson Mao Ning told reporters in Beijing on Wednesday.
“Work is under way to coordinate such a meeting,” Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said on Tuesday, adding: “We hope that it will be finalised in the coming days.”
Trump has said he is open to three-way talks focused on nuclear weapons. “If President Xi wants to have it, I’d have it,” he told reporters last month.
The three leaders have met separately but have never held formal talks together.
So could the meeting, pencilled in for November 18-19, actually happen, and what would it mean for the rest of the world? Here’s what we know:
What would Russia get out of a three-way meeting with the US and China?
At the very least, a photo opportunity.
“It is a big event,” Alexander Bratersky, a Moscow-based journalist and political analyst, told Al Jazeera.
He pointed to Pyotr Tolstoy, chairman of the Russian parliament’s foreign affairs committee, who he said has described the meeting as a path towards a new Yalta – the 1945 conference where the leaders of the Soviet Union, the US and the United Kingdom shaped the post-war order in Europe.
That allows Moscow to “talk big”, Bratersky said, while putting Ukraine on the sidelines.
Simply being at the table would make Putin “first among equals”, he added, giving him a photo opportunity to show the world that he will be among those deciding the future of Europe’s security architecture after the war in Ukraine.
If the meeting produced results, he said, it would reflect China’s influence on Russia.
“We should take into account that we are dealing with a much weaker US leader after elections,” Bratersky said.
Trump remains in charge of foreign policy, he explained, but will have less leverage if Democrats, who won control of both chambers of Congress in this week’s midterm elections, start sending money to Kyiv.
“A meeting by itself will be a success,” he said. “Putin will be able to sell it at home”.
Whether anything comes of it should become clear within a month or so, Bratersky said, and the meeting could lead to another during the Group of 20 (G20) summit in Miami in December.
If nothing is produced before Christmas, he added, “it will be just a photo op.”
What does Trump want?
Optics and leverage.
Trump wants “a personal, high-drama encounter” that lets him claim he is “dealing with” the other two great powers on his own terms, Inderjeet Parmar, a professor of international politics at City St George’s, University of London, told Al Jazeera.
A three-way meeting would allow Trump to present himself as “the indispensable deal-maker”, Parmar said, talking up potential deals on Ukraine, trade, energy or arms control.
“After the midterms the domestic political need for a foreign policy ‘win’ is real,” he said.
Any image of Trump sitting with Xi and Putin could be spun as evidence that American power still commands the table, he said, “even if the substance is limited or largely symbolic”.
“The domestic audience, and his eroding MAGA base, matters at least as much as the diplomatic one,” Parmar said.
What does China want?
Not a summit on Ukraine.
German President Frank-Walter Steinmeier said he raised the idea of discussing Ukraine with Xi when they met in Beijing on October 30, and could see the “surprise” on his face, Germany’s DPA news agency reported.
Steinmeier told public broadcaster ARD that Xi said the three presidents would probably meet in Shenzhen, but not to discuss Ukraine.
He said Xi explicitly pointed out that the Russia-Ukraine war is a European conflict in which the “Europeans must sit at the table”.
Beijing is also likely to swat away Trump’s push for nuclear talks.
Last month, China’s Foreign Ministry said it would be “neither fair, reasonable nor realistic to ask China to join the so-called trilateral nuclear disarmament negotiations at this stage”.
What would a meeting mean for the rest of the world?
Allies could be sidelined.
Parmar said a three-way meeting would mark “a clear break from the post-1945 pattern”, in which Washington coordinated closely with its European and Asian allies before engaging with Moscow or Beijing.
“A free-standing trilateral [meeting] risks treating those allies as secondary players whose interests can be managed after the fact,” he said, adding that those interests could even be traded.
That would be a shift towards “personalised great-power diplomacy”, he said. But the Trump administration still has hopes to drive a wedge between Russia and China, Parmar added.
Fears of a “G3” are “understandable but overstated in institutional terms”, he said, because the three capitals’ interests diverge sharply on Ukraine, Taiwan, technology and the rules of the international economy.
“The real risk is not a formal G3 secretariat, but the normalisation of great-power deals struck with little consultation of those most affected,” he said.
“History offers many examples of such moments. They rarely produce stable order and often leave the excluded feeling the costs,” Parmar said.

Ireland’s government said on Friday that hoax bomb claims sent to Irish media outlets amid a spate of threats against Europe-wide flights were “likely” part of a “co-ordinated campaign of disruption”.
The hoaxes in Dublin came as more European flights were also hit by bomb threats, forcing authorities to reroute some planes or escort civilian aircraft with fighter jets.
The Irish government confirmed police responded after the national broadcaster RTE, Virgin Media, Newstalk radio and The Irish Independent newspaper all received what turned out to be hoax bomb claims.
“It is not known yet who is responsible for these threats, whether it is individuals or a centralised or co-ordinated effort,” it said in a statement.
“However, these threats come on the heels of the ongoing disruption to aviation around Europe caused by similar threats, and it seems likely that this is a co-ordinated campaign of disruption.”
It added that “the threats made this morning against media organisations here are very serious”.
“Hoax threats such as these cause fear, distress and disruption to people going about their daily lives and activities; they achieve no positive purpose whatsoever,” the statement said.
It noted that police were working alongside Ireland’s military, cyber and aviation authorities, as well as European counterparts, to find the culprits.
“Every effort will be made to identify those responsible and to hold them to account,” the government vowed. (Story continues below)
Passengers from an Aer Lingus flight from Dublin to Rome leave in a bus at the Evreux-Fauville Air Base in France after their plane had been rerouted and escorted by military aircraft following a suspected bomb threat, on Nov 5, 2026. (Photo: AFP)
Searching for the source
Authorities are scrambling to identify the sources of the threats. Some of the messages have come in emails signed by “fighters of the Male State”, which matches the name of a far-right movement in Russia — though AFP has not confirmed any link to the messages.
No explosives have been found in any of the incidents so far.
“We don’t yet know whether it’s an individual behind this effort or some form of a co-ordinated effort,” Irish Deputy Prime Minister Simon Harris told Cork 96FM radio.
He said it was a “serious and evolving situation”.
Ireland is scheduled to host two days of high-profile European Union meetings in Dublin next week.
New threats, meanwhile, targeted multiple flights to and from Lisbon, Rome, Prague and Sofia on Friday, authorities said.
A Ryanair flight scheduled to depart from Lisbon for Rome was targeted with a threat while the plane scheduled to fly the route was still approaching the Portuguese capital on its way over from Italy.
And at least 11 flights were targeted in the Czech Republic and Bulgaria: Four flights arriving at Prague airport and five flights leaving Prague were threatened, as well as two flights to Sofia.
Nearly 30 passenger flights were targeted across Europe on Thursday, including planes bound for London, Madrid and Copenhagen.
Many of the airliner threats have targeted low-cost carriers.
Portuguese police said in a statement that following the threat to the Ryanair flight on Friday, “the Special Police Unit (UEP) carried out a security inspection of the aircraft, without any explosive device or suspicious object being detected”.
Misogynistic messages
Some previous hoax messages seen by AFP have contained misogynistic messages.
“We, fighters of the Male State, with our actions today will leave a mark in history. Your feminist regime will remember it forever. The explosion will occur in 60 minutes. Today your skies will turn red,” said one sent to multiple email addresses for Sofia airport in Bulgaria.
Birmingham Airport in central England confirmed receiving a similar message from a group identified as “Men’s State”.
The Russian group Male State was designated an “extremist” organisation by the country’s courts in 2021.
But it then supported Russia’s invasion of Ukraine in 2022. Experts say it is unclear whether it is connected to Russian authorities.

content:
MADRID - The European Union is investigating the possible misuse of EU funds earmarked for the renovation of a Spanish railway line where a train crash killed 69 people, prosecutors said Friday.
The October accident on the Madrid-Seville high-speed line was one of the worst railway disasters in Europe this century, overshadowing Spain’s upcoming general election in November.
A similar investigation into the same stretch of track had already been opened in March in the wake of another accident that claimed 46 lives in the southern province of Andalusia in January, European prosecutors said.
“Today, the European Public Prosecutor’s Office (EPPO) in Madrid (Spain) is conducting investigative measures at the Administrator of Railway Infrastructure (ADIF), the State Railway Safety Agency (AESF) and the Court of Auditors in Spain,” a statement from the prosecutors said.
“This comes after the opening of an investigation into possible fraud affecting EU funds allocated to the renovation and upgrading of safety, signalling and communications systems on the Madrid-Seville high-speed railway line,” the EPPO added.
“This exceptional confirmation comes following high public interest and no further details will be made public at this stage.”
Spain’s Court of Audit confirmed that Spanish police officers were present at ADIF’s offices to carry out searches at European prosecutors’ request.
The fraud investigation comes on top of another probe launched by a Spanish court to establish how the crash happened.
Transport minister resigns
The accident took place when a train operated by the state-owned Renfe ploughed into the back of a stationary train belonging to the private Spanish company Iryo outside the village of Urda, around 130 kilometres south of Madrid.
The failure of an automatic safety system halted all trains on a 63-kilometre stretch of track, but a control centre authorised the Renfe train to resume its journey, according to the authorities.
Transport minister Oscar Puente, who was also in post during the January crash in Andalusia, submitted his resignation on Tuesday.
Spain’s Socialist Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez named economy minister Carlos Cuerpo as Puente’s temporary replacement.
He added that Cuerpo would take interim charge of the transport portfolio through to the November election, which polls suggest his ruling Socialist party could lose.
The right-wing opposition, which had demanded Puente’s resignation, and unions had criticised the ex-minister for appearing to blame the disaster on one control centre operator.
The train drivers’ union Semaf, which has called strikes for Nov 10 and 12, has denounced a worsening of working conditions and the use of “degraded systems”.
Critics say investment in maintenance has not kept up with the increase in passenger numbers since the 2021 liberalisation of Spain’s rail network, which allowed private companies to break the decades-long monopoly by the national operator Renfe.

media.alt: Cranes deployed to remove wrecked carriages are seen at the site of last week’s deadly train crash near Urda, Spain. (Photo: AFP)
