content:
Nearly 200 nations will gather for the COP31 summit in Turkey on Monday but tensions over geopolitics, finance and fossil fuels are tempering expectations of a major breakthrough in tackling the climate crisis.
More than 100,000 people are expected at the UN’s two-week climate negotiations in the Mediterranean resort city of Antalya.
Tougher action on fossil fuels, the main driver of climate change, appears unlikely and budget-strapped developed countries are reluctant to commit more money to help developing nations cope with climate impacts.
An energy crisis and cost-of-living pressures, fuelled by the war in the Middle East, are also looming over the gathering.
“This is not going to be the COP that changes the world,” said Paul Watkinson, France’s former chief negotiator at climate summits.
“It’s an intermediate COP in many ways. But it is an important conference and it does need to make sure it makes progress,” he said.
A senior EU official, speaking on condition of anonymity, also tempered expectations, saying: “We cannot expect a revolution in terms of climate action from the Antalya COP.”
The talks follow deadly floods in Nepal, searing heatwaves in Europe and major wildfires in Indonesia.
An exceptionally strong El Nino climate phenomenon is forecast to peak later this year, adding to extreme weather and possibly helping to make 2026 or 2027 the hottest year on record.
The outlook is increasingly bleak: the United Nations warned in September that global temperatures were on course to exceed 1.5C above preindustrial levels, breaching the most ambitious threshold set by the Paris Agreement.
‘Implementation COP’
Turkey is presiding over COP31, with Australia leading negotiations under an unusual arrangement that settled a dispute over who would host the conference.
“COP31 comes at a difficult time for the world,” said Australian climate minister Chris Bowen. “Reaching consensus among nearly 200 countries will not be easy but cooperation remains essential.”
COP31 president Murat Kurum, Turkey’s environment minister, said the conference would strive “to turn the commitments of past COPs into real results”.
Turkey is promoting an “action agenda” alongside the formal negotiations that encourages countries to support non-binding pledges on issues from artificial intelligence to waste management.
Its centrepiece is an “electrification” drive to raise the share of global energy demand met by electricity from around 20 percent today to 35 percent by 2035.
“This year’s energy crisis has shocked us out of our complacency,” Kurum said. “Electrification is the answer. It protects communities from volatile global markets and cuts emissions.”
Turkey and Australia also want electrification to appear in a “cover decision” — an overarching political statement negotiated by consensus.
The European Union has called for “clean” electrification — a term that could spark debate over the role of fossil fuels in the Turkish initiative.
The EU official suggested the bloc might be willing to find a compromise.
“The word ‘clean’ may be difficult for some. There may be other ways of formulating this without having it so explicit,” the official said.
Cosima Cassel, a climate diplomacy expert at think tank E3G, said the Turkish COP31 presidency’s proposal was “carefully worded”.
It is “quite an open pledge that I think is going to enable quite a few countries to come on board”, Cassel said.
Money fight
Countries committed to transition away from fossil fuels in a landmark pact at COP28 in 2023 but have struggled to agree on how to turn that pledge into action.
COP30 ended with a deal that made no explicit mention of fossil fuels after oil-producing countries opposed the language.
Instead, Brazil produced a voluntary “roadmap” with proposals for phasing out fossil fuels that each country can tailor to their circumstances.
Observers say Turkey and Australia are keen to avoid a repeat of last year’s fossil fuel fight.
But a feud looms over wealthy nations’ unfulfilled financial commitments to help developing countries deal with climate change.
The group of African negotiators is demanding that a pledge to triple adaptation finance — money to cope with the worsening impacts of climate change — be added to the negotiation agenda.
Recent elections, meanwhile, have given climate campaigners a boost, with Democrats seizing control of the US Congress in a setback to President Donald Trump, who calls global warming a hoax.
A US congressional delegation will attend COP31, but the Trump administration is not taking part in the negotiations.
Fresh from his re-election win over conservative challenger Flavio Bolsonaro, Brazilian President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva will travel to Antalya next week.

media.alt: More than 100,000 people are expected at the COP31 climate summit in Turkey, but no major breakthroughs. (Photo: AFP)

summary: Nearly 200 nations will gather for the COP31 summit in Turkey on Monday but tensions over geopolitics, finance and fossil fuels are tempering expectations of a major breakthrough in tackling the climate crisis.

content:
Trump’s stillborn diesel deal: Why Russian oil tankers are not heading to the US
The first oil tankers scheduled to deliver Russian diesel to the US under a deal between President Donald Trump and his Russian counterpart Vladimir Putin have changed course and are no longer heading toward the US coast. It spells the end of an agreement announced with great fanfare before the midterms.
The Agioi Fanendes, an oil tanker loaded with 40,000 metric tons of diesel, represents US President Donald Trump’s last chance to see his controversial diesel deal with Russian President Vladimir Putin come to fruition.
The deal was reached last month, ahead of the November 3 midterm elections, amid soaring fuel prices and a cost of living crisis in the US. It failed to prevent a thumping in the polls for the Republicans, with a “blue wave” carrying Democrats to a landslide victory across the country.
Now the deal designed to throw Trump a political lifeline is unravelling on the high seas.
The Maltese-flagged Agioi Fanendes is the first of three oil tankers to leave Russia – officially to deliver their precious cargo to the US – that is still heading toward the American coast, the Financial Times reported in an article published a day after the midterm elections.
The Talisman, a Russian oil tanker on international sanctions lists, departed from the St. Petersburg area on October 22. But after sailing through the English Channel, it turned south, skirted the Bay of Biscay and the Portuguese coast before entering the Mediterranean Sea through the Strait of Gibraltar.
The Leruo, also sanctioned by the EU, UK and US, continues its journey across the Atlantic but now has Brazil as its official destination as it sails southwest through the Atlantic.
Moscow has slammed the FT report as “fake” news. Kirill Dmitriev, a Kremlin envoy and negotiator, maintained Thursday that “Tankers destined for the US continue on course," in a post on X.
But when asked about the details of the shipments, Putin's spokesman Dmitry Peskov said it was a "commercial" matter that could not be made public. "All diesel will find its buyers," he added.
Trump met with Dmitriev at the White House on Thursday, while the senior Kremlin envoy was in the US for an event with first lady Melania Trump ahead of next week’s talks between Russian and Ukrainian delegations in Abu Dhabi. The US president, however, declined to give reporters details of his meeting with Dmitriev.
A ‘dead from the start’ deal
For the Agioi Fanendes, anything is still possible. Ship tracking data as of Friday listed its destination as awaiting “orders”. The tanker’s last position was received on October 28.
Just a few days ago, “it was expected in New York over the [November 7 - 8] weekend,” Matt Smith, an analyst at Kpler – a global provider of maritime data and analytics – told the FT. Smith believes there’s little doubt that the Agioi Fanendes, Trump’s last hope of seeing Russian diesel pour into US ports, will end up selling its diesel elsewhere – like the Talisman and the Leruo.
If this prediction holds true, “the diesel deal, for all practical purposes, is dead,” said Kevin Rowlands, a maritime security specialist at the Royal United Services Institute, a UK-based defence think tank. “It may theoretically remain in place. But in practice, I don't believe that any, or much, Russian oil or diesel will be channelled through the United States in the immediate future.” The route taken by these three oil tankers was “very shaky from the start”, he added.
Watch moreTrump’s use of Russian diesel fuel, at Ukraine’s expense, sparks controversy in the US
The diesel deal was announced with great fanfare on October 9 as a response to rising gas prices, with Trump declaring it would “Lower prices for Americans, especially our Great Farmers, Ranchers, and Truckers,” on Truth Social.
Shortly after Trump promised that Moscow would export “millions” of metric tons of Russian diesel to the US, the Treasury Department issued a regulation authorising US companies to purchase, deliver, offload and import Russian diesel despite existing US sanctions.
Following this presidential exemption, Moscow, for its part, lifted the ban on diesel exports, which had been imposed a few months earlier to address the fuel shortage in Russia caused by Ukrainian airstrikes on oil facilities.
And so the Agioi Fanendes, Leruo and Talisman were able to set sail … on the sly. It took the vigilance of NGOs such as Greenpeace and companies like Kpler to track and monitor these shipments.
A ‘victory for European policy-making’
Trump’s compromise on the diesel deal sparked an outcry in the US from both sides of the political spectrum. The economic logic behind an agreement set to bring in millions for Moscow failed to convince analysts. What’s more, the hundreds of thousands of metric tons of diesel promised “rapidly” by Russia were not enough to cover US needs for even a single day.
The arrival of the three tankers would, at the very least, have enabled Trump to declare that he was keeping his promises. The rationale for the decision to change course has stumped several analysts. “It’s hard to know the exact reason for this reversal,” admitted Maximilian Hess, founder of the consulting firm Enmetena Advisory and author of the critically acclaimed book, “Economic War: Ukraine and the Global Conflict Between Russia and the West”.
There may, in fact, be several explanations. The first relates to the risks for buyers of Russian diesel, despite Trump’s signed exemption. “The US president can sign an international agreement, but in enforcing it, the federal government may face resistance from certain governors,” noted Rowlands.
Mikie Sherrill, the Democratic governor of New Jersey, for instance, has threatened ports that accept Russian diesel with legal action and “millions of dollars” in fines. The Agioi Fanendes was originally scheduled to arrive at a port that falls partly under her jurisdiction. The Port of New York and New Jersey is in the New York-Newark metropolitan area and falls under the Port Authority of New York and New Jersey's bi-state jurisdiction.
Underscoring this seeming discrepancy between presidential reach and gubernatorial power is the diversity of sanctions regimes against Russia currently in effect in the US. Opponents of the agreement maintain that the order signed by Trump does not apply to the 2022 Ending Importation of Russian Oil Act, which requires the president to obtain congressional approval before granting an exemption from sanctions on Russian oil.
"Then there is the UK and EU sanctions issue. It appears likely that the diesel on the initial two ships could not find an off-taker in the US who was willing to risk running afoul of these sanctions,” said Hess. The sanctions are triggered as soon as a European entity – an insurer, bank or any other intermediary – is involved in a transaction involving sanctioned oil. If that’s the case, Hess says the tanker diversions are a “victory for European policy-making and anti-circumvention measures”.
No reason to maintain the ‘illusion’
The shifting political climate in the US may have also played a role. “Moscow realised that Donald Trump had lost authority, and the midterm election results only confirmed that the risk of oil tankers being seized in US ports had risen sharply – something that would be unacceptable to the Kremlin,” said Rowlands. Governors like Mikie Sherrill would now be more inclined to override the wishes of a weakened president.
Finally, “it’s possible that these oil tankers never actually intended to go all the way to the US,” suggested Dirk Siebels, a maritime security specialist at Risk Intelligence. The purpose of Trump’s manoeuvre was “purely political – to try to drive down prices ahead of the midterm elections”, he noted. Images of oil tankers actually en route to the US served to send a concrete signal to the financial markets. In this scenario, the political benefit of aligning with Trump was well worth Moscow paying a little more for the detour to the US before diverting to the diesel’s actual destinations, such as Brazil.
“Once the election was over, and this effort had had no effect, there was no longer any reason to maintain this illusion,” said Rowlands.
Regardless of the reason, the oil tankers’ change of course represents the best possible outcome for everyone, according to Rowlands. The US avoids a new source of conflict between the president and the Democrats, the Russians will be able to sell their diesel elsewhere, and Europeans can rejoice at seeing the Trump diesel deal fizzle out.
(This is a translation of the original in French.)

It spells the end of an agreement announced with great fanfare before the midterms.

content:
MOMBASA - A self-proclaimed Kenyan preacher was sentenced to 200 years in prison on Friday for the murder of 190 children and one adult in an infamous starvation cult.
Hundreds of bodies have been discovered since 2023 at the sect’s base near the coastal resort of Malindi, in what became known as the “Shakahola Forest Massacre”.
Self-proclaimed pastor Paul Mackenzie was accused of inciting his followers to starve themselves to death to “meet Jesus”.
Last month, he was convicted of murdering 190 children and one adult between January 2021 and September 2023, alongside 28 co-accused. His lawyer said he would appeal.
On Friday, the court sentenced him to 100 years for the homicide charges and 100 years for the starvation charges.
Twenty-eight accomplices were also sentenced to a variety of lengthy prison terms.
Mackenzie also faces manslaughter and terrorism charges in other trials, which he denies.
The former taxi driver appeared indifferent as he arrived in court on Friday, wearing a polo shirt and sporting a faint smile.
Francis Wanje, a 62-year-old teacher who lost two grandchildren, told AFP he had hoped Mackenzie would be sentenced to death to prevent further tragedies.
“Nothing can ease the pain,” said Wanje, who blamed authorities for failing to act swiftly.
“I really have great (anger) towards the authorities. If they had taken action, we would not be here today,” he added.
Death penalty
Prosecutors had called for the death penalty, citing the scale of the loss of life and the danger posed by his actions.
Although Kenya’s law provides for the death penalty, the country has not carried out an execution since 1987.
Prosecutors also asked the court to sentence Mackenzie’s co-accused to life imprisonment, arguing they had “been deeply indoctrinated by Mackenzie and were at risk of reoffending”.
Around 120 prosecution witnesses testified during the trial.
According to witnesses, the movement denounced formal education as “satanic”, viewed modern medicine and hospitals as instruments of the devil and required followers to cut themselves off from the outside world.
Mackenzie was arrested in April 2023 after a rights group alerted authorities and some followers were rescued from the 325-hectare ranch in the Shakahola forest on Kenya’s coast.
The Kenya National Commission on Human Rights put the death toll at 429 in 2024. Some victims remain unidentified.
The case has fuelled calls for tighter regulation of religious organisations, after it emerged that Mackenzie had previously been arrested twice but released.

content:
Many people living in Zambia  seek careers in the civil service because of the stability and security traditionally associated with government employment. But recent retirements, dismissals and restructuring exercises across several public institutions have unsettled that perception and sparked a national debate about the government's use of "national interest" provisions.
Among those affected is former public relations officer Godfrey Chilabi, whose departure from the Zambia Police Service was announced in October. Choosing not to publicly discuss the circumstances surrounding his exit, Chilabi simply told media that he had been retired in the national interest.
"Yes, I have been retired in national interest," Chilabi said. "I can't give any reason, but know I'm in retirement."
Chilabi's departure came amid a series of changes affecting public institutions in Zambia .
Charity Munganga, a Zambia Police Service deputy inspector general, was dismissed, and all staff members at the Zambia Medicines and Medical Supplies Agency were let go as part of a "reset" following a government audit.
Additionally, all directors in senior management at the Zambia Environmental Management Agency (ZEMA) were put on administrative leave to facilitate an institutional realignment exercise.
The affected ZEMA directors will be assessed for their competence, performance and suitability for their positions before a final decision is made on whether they will be reinstated or separated from the institution, according to an October 20 statement by the Green Economy and Environment Ministry cited by the news portal Mwebantu .
Zambia's public servants on edge
The issue moved to the center of public debate in October, when opposition lawmakers questioned the government in parliament over retirements and dismissals taking place across public institutions following Zambia's general election in August .

Governance and political commentator Andrew Nguvu told DW that retirements carried out in the national interest raise important questions about transparency, fairness and the protection of a professional public service.
"If at all, there are legitimate reasons for retiring any particular civil servant, then obviously the government should clearly explain," Nguvu said.
He said public institutions should operate according to established procedures and the law rather than political considerations that could undermine institutional independence.
Zambian law allows service commissions to retire established officers in the national interest under provisions governing public service employment. Previous governments have also used the measure. However, the current exercise has generated significant scrutiny because it is occurring alongside broader restructuring efforts affecting multiple institutions.
Opposition cries hypocrisy
Critics argue that the issue is particularly sensitive because Zambia's ruling United Party for National Development (UPND) previously opposed the use of retirements in the national interest while in opposition.
As a result, opposition lawmakers, led by Stephen Kampyongo, have criticized the measures, which they view as inconsistent with the ruling party's earlier position.
Kampyongo, speaking during Vice President's Question Time in the National Assembly on October 17, asked what assurances the government was giving public servants, who are "working in fear," and what measures were being taken to ensure that government workers retired in the national interest did not become destitute.
Government pushes back
Responding on behalf of the government, Vice President Mutale Nalumango rejected suggestions that the exercise amounted to a political purge and described it as part of a lawful process of institutional realignment.
Nalumango acknowledged the concerns surrounding the changes but defended the government's authority to make personnel adjustments within the public service framework.
"As provided for in section 39 of the Public Service Pensions Act, there are situations that arise and people fall by the way side," Nalumango told the parliament. "[It is] unfortunate that a life was lost, but maybe it is an issue that public servants/public service workers must brace themselves for."
Nalumango's comments have been cited by critics as evidence that additional changes could occur as the government continues to restructure public institutions.
The debate has been amplified by comments from UPND National Youth Chairperson Gilbert Liswaniso, who said governments naturally sought to work with people aligned with their vision.
"Every political party [that] comes to power has to flush out!" Liswaniso said. "[It] has to work with the people aligned with the vision of that political party!"

Critics say such statements reinforce concerns that political considerations may be influencing decisions within the public service.
The civil rights activist David Chishimba has rejected the notion that perceived political affiliation should determine a person's future in government employment.
"The constitution, however, is very clear on this," Chishimba told DW. "It restricts public officers from participating in partisan politics while in office. This safeguards an impartial civil service. However, it does not prohibit private political belief or otherwise."
Chishimba said civil servants served the country rather than any political organization. "Civil servants serve Zambia," he said, "not a party, the president or a campaign."
Workers face uncertainty
Nguvu said the shift was deeply unsettling for public workers caught in the middle of the administrative realignments.
The measures come as the cost of living and household debt burdens increase in Zambia.
Nguvu said abrupt personnel changes could affect morale throughout the public service and leave workers uncertain about their professional future.
"This can weaken morale and help to destroy institutional memory," Nguvu said. "Most of these decisions lack clear explanations."
Nguvu said such concerns had become more acute when explanations for personnel decisions were not communicated clearly.
The reported dismissals have also raised concerns among civil society groups about due process and accountability.
Chishimba, who is also the president of the Zambia Council of Activists (ZACA), called for greater transparency from the authorities.
"ZACA respectfully calls on the government to publish the names and evidence of those facing dismissal, submit every case to due process, and allow the Civil Service Commission to assert its constitutional independence," he said.

content:
Why is the tournament being held in November?
Since its inception in 1990, the Women's Ice Hockey World Championship has almost always been held in the spring — apart from 2021 and 2022, when the COVID-19 pandemic saw it moved to the summer. This year, though, the tournament, being hosted by Denmark from November 6 to November 16, is being held in November for the first time. The idea is make it easier for all of the world's best players to participate. Since its inception in 2023, the North America-based Professional Women's Hockey League (PWHL) , widely considered the world's best, has had to pause its season to allow players to take part in the Worlds. This is no longer necessary, as the PWHL's regular season doesn't open until December.
"This gives the women's game a unique selling point," International Ice Hockey Federation (IIHF) President Franz Reindl recently told the SID news agency. "Because the PWHL season begins after this, we can be certain that the very best players are participating."
How has the tournament format changed?
Previously, the teams were divided into a stronger group and a weaker group, with the idea being to avoid, as much as possible, lopsided scores. This is because women's hockey is not as balanced as the men's game, with Canada or the United States having won every tournament since its inception. Under the old system, all five teams in the stronger Group A advanced to the quarterfinals. Under the new format, four of the five teams advance from both groups. This also sees the two powerhouses, the USA and Canada in separate groups, meaning the marquee matchup can't occur early in the tournament.
Group A: USA, Czechia, Switzerland, Germany, Austria
Group B: Canada, Finland, Sweden, Japan, Denmark
Will Russia be competing at this tournament?
No. While the Court of Arbitration for Sport (CAS) ruled on October 30, 2026 — a week before the opening faceoff of the Women's Ice Hockey World Championship — that the IIHF must allow Russia back into its tournaments during the 2026-2027 season, it made no mention of this tournament. Under the CAS ruling though, the IIHF will be required to include Russia at the 2027 tournament in Quebec City.
Who are the contenders?
As noted above, either Canada or the United States has won every edition of this tournament – and indeed the two countries have split Olympic gold medals between them (Canada 5, USA 3) since the sport was introduced to the Winter Games in 1998. There is nothing to suggest that this is about to change in Herning and Esbjerg, although Canada enters the tournament with a vastly different roster from the one that won Olympic silver in Milano in February. Among those looking to break this North American domination are Finland , the only other team ever to have made it to a World Championship final and Switzerland , who took bronze in Milano.
Why are the USA and Canada not wearing their traditional uniforms?
The United States and Canada are having to play in generic kits provided by the International Ice Hockey Federation's official supplier due to an ongoing commercial rights dispute. The Canadian federation, Hockey Canada, said in a statement on Wednesday that its players would be wearing jerseys designed by True Hockey instead of their Bauer jerseys featuring the national team logo. USA Hockey has confirmed that its players too will be wearing jerseys without its national emblem.
"While we have yet to see the jersey Canada will be playing in on Friday, our team remains focused on the tournament and representing our country proudly on and off the ice,” Hockey Canada said.
summary: As ice hockey's governing body continues to wrangle over how to respond to a CAS order to reinstate Russia to international play, the top women's tournament gets underway in Denmark without Russia.

content:
Global stock markets have tumbled after investors sold tech shares on fears that the US midterm elections would slow the development of artificial intelligence (AI).
The sell-off, which started in the US and then spread to Asia and Europe, has seen trillions of dollars wiped off the stock value of major tech firms.
In the US, the tech-heavy Nasdaq share index sank 5.5% on Thursday. Asian markets also saw hefty falls on Friday and European markets opened lower.
Investors are worried about tougher regulation of AI, after Democrat candidates opposed the data centres needed by the technology. The share falls also come on top of concerns about whether the huge amounts being spent on AI will pay off.
The sell-off in US stocks meant the so-called magnificent seven tech companies, including Apple, Nvidia and Tesla, shed a trillion dollars in value in a single trading day, with Nvidia shares sliding more than 9%.
Shares in Elon Musk's companies SpaceX and Tesla also plunged, falling 8% and nearly 11% respectively and shaving more than $300bn off the firms' market value.
Musk had spent nearly $450m backing Republican campaigns, including at least $45m in support of Ken Paxton for the Texas senate seat, but Texas turned blue in the Democratic tsunami on Tuesday.
The sharp fall in the Nasdaq meant it lost an estimated $2.5tn (£1.9tn) in market value. The index is now in what market watchers call correction territory, which is where an index or company value falls at least 10% below its recent high.
However, the huge gains seen by tech stocks in recent times - driven by the enthusiasm for AI - mean that even after Thursday's fall, the Nasdaq is still higher than it was a year ago, and up about 4.6% from where it was at the start of this year.
The US sell-off spread into Asia on Friday. The Nikkei share index in Japan closed down 6% as shares in memory chip makers Kioxia and Tokyo Electron saw big falls.
In South Korea, the Kospi index plunged more than 8% at one point, triggering a so-called circuit breaker, a mechanism that temporarily halts trading to curb panic selling.
The Kospi eventually closed down 6%, with shares in chipmaker SK Hynix falling more than 10%.
European markets fell on Friday, although the declines were not as severe as the indexes contain fewer tech stocks. The UK's FTSE 100 index fell nearly 2% while Germany's Dax index was down 2.4%.
Dan Coatsworth, head of markets at AJ Bell, said investors were worried about the huge amounts of money being spent on AI with "no clear idea of when, or whether, there will be payback".
"The midterm election result muddied the waters as the Democrats now have more influence and could slow down the pace of data centre roll-outs and look at new ways to regulate the sector," he added.
"The AI story has all been about speed, and now there is a danger of it moving to a lower gear, and some of the wheels falling off."
Pressure on data centres
Democrats in races across the US campaigned to slow the growth of data centres and AI, and there were dozens of measures on ballots around the country aimed at restricting the development of the hubs crucial for powering the technology.
They won both the US Senate and House of Representatives in the midterms, taking control of Congress for the rest of President Donald Trump's presidency.
"Americans don't want Big Tech oligarchs wrecking the environment, gutting jobs and threatening humanity's future. NATIONAL DATA CENTER MORATORIUM NOW," Democrat Senator Bernie Sanders said in a post on X on Thursday.
Trump blamed the stock slide on his political opponents.
"The Stock Market suffered one of the Worst Days in History based on the results of the Election," he said in a social media post on Thursday.
"Remember, it wasn't Republicans, it was Dumocrats."
He also appeared to take aim at voters too.
"The Stock Market crashed today because the Dumocrats had a big Tuesday — So sad to see, you only have yourselves to blame!" he wrote on Truth Social.
On Friday, Trump restated his support for the AI sector, saying only "foolish leadership" would "say no to the riches they bring".
Some tech leaders have said they were caught off guard by the backlash against data centres in the midterms.
OpenAI president and co-founder Greg Brockman said he believed everyone had been surprised by the reaction to data centres, and more work needed to be done to ensure communities were on board.
"A lot of our shift over the course of this year has really been to realise that from San Francisco trying to build infrastructure in Texas, Georgia, and other places, you can't just tweet and say: 'This is going to be good.' You need to be in those communities," Brockman said at the WSJ Tech conference in Napa, California.
With additional reporting from Lily Jamali
summary: Investors have reacted to possible tougher scrutiny of data centre construction and the AI industry.

content:
Israel and the US have been staunch allies for decades
Published
As the US midterm election results rolled in, long-held Israeli assumptions about the transatlantic alliance began to shatter.
"For us in Israel, this will be a generational sea change," wrote one prominent journalist in Israel's biggest-selling newspaper, right-leaning Yedioth Ahronoth. "The [prime minister, Benjamin] Netanyahu government sowed the wind and reaped the tsunami."
Israel's opposition leaders have lined up to blame their prime minister, with one saying the US results showed "just how toxic Netanyahu has become" among both Democrats and Republicans.
The prime minister himself has so far remained silent.
"Israel's political establishment understood intellectually that things have been shifting. They have not understood how much and how quickly," one US official with knowledge of the situation told me.
Israel's relationship with the US was a campaign issue in races across America.
Many Democratic candidates were sharply critical of Israel's actions in Gaza and the occupied West Bank, and the costs of the joint US-Israeli war on Iran was a key issue for many voters.
The US president himself blamed the Iran War for the Republican rout – a war that Israel's leader is widely seen as having promoted to him.
And US Vice-President JD Vance cited the US relationship to Israel as one of four key reasons voters had deserted the party, hammering home the message that the relationship is now seen as a political problem by its key ally.
"That might be even worse than what happened in the midterms," Israeli political and security analyst Yaakov Katz told me. "Because the Democrats we knew about, now [Vance] is pointing the finger and saying: 'Our voters want us to change our position on Israel' – and Israelis don't fully understand where this is going."
The question plaguing Israelis now is what this means for Israel's security and influence.
The sense of staunch US military and diplomatic support had remained unshaken in Israel despite growing anger among US voters, President Donald Trump's public insults to Netanyahu, and differences over Israel's actions in Iran and Lebanon.
Israel's prime minister continually boasted of his closeness to Trump, describing his "true friendship" and "unwavering support".
And just nine months ago, Israelis watched their armed forces wage war on Iran hand in hand with the US military, as the "unprecedented" coordination of the two allies became a daily mantra among military spokespeople and politicians.
So Trump's unexpected statement during a Fox News interview this week that he would stop $3.8bn (3.4bn euros; £2.8bn) in US military aid to Israel two years earlier than planned, caused shock here – not so much for the loss of aid as for what the move said about Israel's status as a diplomatic partner.
Israel's president said the announcement came as "a bolt from the blue".
"Nobody knows anything," was the headline in a report by Yedioth Ahronoth, adding that officials were still struggling to understand whether Trump's remark was serious, two days on.
The Israeli prime minister's office responded to the news several days later, saying that the shift from US aid to partnership showed "the strength and sophistication" of the bilateral relationship.
US military aid is less than 10% of Israel's annual military budget. But Yaakov Katz, author of several books about Israel's defence and security, said Trump's announcement was the tip of a much larger question around future funding, arms sales and joint military projects with Israel. All of this could be slowed or stalled by a Democrat-controlled Congress, even without the two-thirds majority it would need to overrule Trump.
"Everything that Israel used to get in a simpler, easier process will now potentially be much more complicated, and Israel has to be prepared that this is a new reality," he told me.
"Our entire Air Force is American-made military planes, we're dependent on American spare parts and American weapons. The last three years have shown us how dependent we are on American missile-defence systems. [If] those don't show up at the same pace, that's a real difference – that changes your calculation of what you're able to withstand if you go to war."
Katz believes the midterms could also translate into tougher demands on Israel over its actions in Gaza and Lebanon, and a requirement not to undermine an agreement with Iran.
"Something will change in the US-Israeli relationship, but it's a question of scale," said the US official I spoke to, who was not authorized to speak on the record. "It means shifting to [being] willing to criticise Israel when it's warranted, but the bedrock fundamental relationship will still be there."
In an interview on Israeli television, the US ambassador to Israel Mike Huckabee signalled little shift so far in core American positions, including on Israel's occupation of the West Bank, describing the sanctions imposed by other countries as "irrational" and counterproductive.
Israel's ambassador to the UN, Danny Danon, told another Israeli channel that Trump would be in the White House for the next two years, and that Israel could "feel good" about the US veto in the UN Security Council – something Washington has repeatedly used in the past to block resolutions that target Israel.
"But we have to pay attention to the voices – not only in the Democratic Party but also the Republican Party – criticising Israel," he said. "It will be harder for us."
Trump endorsed Netanyahu in Israel's elections
Questions over its key alliance have come at a particularly sensitive time for Israel, less than two weeks after its own parliamentary elections left neither government nor opposition with a clear majority. Discussions are now taking place with the country's president, who will decide whether Netanyahu or his centrist rival, Gadi Eisenkot, will get the first chance to form a governing coalition.
"Under my leadership, we will renew and deepen that [US] partnership, strengthen the bipartisan foundations that have long sustained it," Eisenkot said in a social media post.
Another member of his opposition bloc, Yair Lapid, said: "What do we do?"
"We go back to the rule that worked for us for seventy years, and which broke in 2015 when Netanyahu went to speak against [US president] Obama in Congress. Israel doesn't choose sides in America. We work with everyone."
Netanyahu's speech to the US Congress in 2015 is seen as a defining moment in Israel's relationship with the US, when the Israeli leader appealed over the head of America's Democratic president to urge Republicans in Congress not to back a nuclear agreement with Iran.
Since then, Netanyahu has increasingly anchored the alliance in Trump's Republican party, even as alienation among Democrats has grown.
The US official I spoke to said that, before the midterms, Netanyahu could have improved the relationship with Washington by getting rid of his two far-right ministers.
"I think everyone understands now it's bigger than [that]," he said.
How much the new tone in transatlantic relations will play into the task of building a new government in Israel is being closely watched.
Some government supporters argue it has increased the need for political stability, and that Netanyahu provides much-needed continuity and a deep knowledge of the US and its leaders.
"We cannot afford to be dragged into endless political disputes and election campaigns," said one opinion writer in Israel's largest-circulation daily, the right-wing Israel Hayom.
Whoever heads Israel's next government, its American ally may demand more than rhetoric.
In the noisy debate around what this will mean for Israel, the silence of its prime minister – once the whisperer of Washington's elite – is perhaps the most telling voice of all.

content:
Global temperatures will almost certainly average over 1.5 degrees Celsius (2.7 F) above preindustrial levels in 2026, the European Union's Copernicus Climate Change Service reported on Friday.
That would make 2026 the second calendar year, after 2024, above the threshold set as part of the Paris Agreement .
What does the 1.5-degree target mean?
The Paris treaty was aimed at preventing global temperatures from rising above 1.5 degrees Celsius in the long term. The 2015 deal was seen as a major step forward in tackling climate change.
Most of the world's nations agreed to hold global temperature rise to well below 2 degrees Celsius compared to pre-industrial levels and "pursue efforts" to keep it below  1.5 degrees .
The target concerns long-term warming, so a single year above 1.5 degrees does not in itself mean it has been breached.
Could 2026 become the warmest year on record?
Copernicus estimates that 2026 will most likely be the second-warmest year after 2024 since records began. However, there is a 20% chance that it could surpass 2024 levels.

The climate service also expects the four-year average for 2023 to 2026 to be above the 1.5 degree threshold.
October 2026 was the warmest October on record globally, with an average global surface temperature of 1.75 degrees above pre-industrial levels for the month. It marked the third consecutive month above the 1.5 degrees threshold.
"An exceptionally strong El Nino is adding further heat to a climate already warmed by human activities, while 2026 is on track to become the second calendar year above 1.5 degrees," said Samantha Burgess of the European Centre for Medium-Range Weather Forecasts.
That goal is no longer within reach
The UN Environment Programme now expects warming to overshoot the Paris Agreement's 1.5-degree target.
Because this threatens drastic climate extremes and dangerous tipping points, the overshoot should be kept as small and short as possible, it said.
According to a September report by the UN Environment Programme (UNEP), every additional fraction of a degree makes the risks and impacts worse.
Climate scientist Johan Rockström, director of the Potsdam Institute for Climate Impact Research, c alled for temperatures to be lowered quickly again by removing CO2 from the atmosphere.
UNEP lays out a scenario in which the world sees warming peak at 1.7 to 1.8 degrees Celsius around mid-century, before falling back to 1.5 degrees Celsius by 2100. Getting there would require steep emissions cuts of 69% by 2040, relative to 2025 levels.
It was now unavoidable that global warming would exceed 1.5 degrees Celsius above pre-industrial levels within the next five years,  Rockström said at a briefing.
He said that humanity was currently on "a path to an unmanageable future."

content:
Европа должна играть "центральную роль" в поисках мирного решения для войны в Украине , заявил в пятницу, 6 ноября, министр иностранных дел Германии Йоханн Вадефуль (Johann Wadephul). Комментарии, которые политик дал перед вылетом в Варшаву для участия в Совете государств Балтийского моря, опубликованы на сайте МИД.
По словам Вадефуля, федеральное правительство придерживается "незыблемого принципа: будущее Украины нельзя определять без участия самой Украины, а вопросы безопасности Европы - без Европы". "Это главный критерий для всех наших усилий, направленных на прекращение российской агрессивной войны, и причина, по которой Европа должна играть здесь центральную роль", - сказал министр.
Вадефуль отметил, что "будущее нашего сосуществования в Европе решается в Украине". Он также подчеркнул важность того, чтобы европейцы и американцы применяли меры в отношении России "сообща и сплоченно".
Правительство ФРГ: Переговоры без Европы не принесут результата
С аналогичным комментарием по важности участия Европы в обсуждениях выступил Штефан Корнелиус (Stefan Kornelius), официальный представитель правительства ФРГ. 6 ноября он заявил, что переговоры по вопросам безопасности в регионе и мирного урегулирования в Украине, "по нашему (правительства ФРГ. - Ред. ) мнению, не принесут результата без участия европейских стран".
Корнелиус также рассказал о прошедшем ночью телефонном разговоре федерального канцлера Фридриха Мерца (Friedrich Merz) и президента США Дональда Трампа . Лидеры поговорили после того, как глава Белого дома встретился со спецпредставителем президента России Кириллом Дмитриевым и анонсировал "масштабное соглашение", которое может затронуть не только Украину, но и "всю Европу"  и от которого "все будут в восторге".
"Правительство Германии осведомлено о переговорах, которые ведет американская администрация. Федеральный канцлер вовлечен в обсуждение планов американского президента", - добавил Корнелиус, отвечая на вопрос о контактах между Россией и США.
Переговоры России, США и Украины пройдут на следующей неделе
Комментарии главы МИД Германии  и представителя правительства страны прозвучали за несколько дней до трехсторонних переговоров России, США и Украины в Абу-Даби, запланированных на 10-11 ноября . Украинская сторона на встрече сосредоточится на вопросах безопасности , "мерах по укреплению доверия" и возможной встрече президента страны Владимира Зеленского с главой РФ Владимиром Путиным , сообщал глава МИД Андрей Сибига .
По словам Корнелиуса, Германия находится "в тесном взаимодействии" с европейскими партнерами по теме переговоров в Абу-Даби.

content:
Will Democratic Party introduce a new 'New Deal'? Key narrative must be 'focused on economic issues'
Issued on: Modified:
Share
With Democrats poised to control both chambers of Congress, the party faces a defining challenge: how to constrain Donald Trump's presidency while carving out a path to the White House in 2028. For Ian Reifowitz, Distinguished Professor of History at SUNY Empire State University, the answer lies in drawing on the historical legacy of Franklin D. Roosevelt's New Deal coalition. Republicans, he argues, have progressively shifted electoral competition towards questions of identity, immigration and cultural conflict. Democrats, by contrast, must recover their traditional strength on economic security, affordability and everyday living standards. "These Democrats across the country ran on affordability." And that's how they must govern, explains Reifowitz.

content:
Flávio Bolsonaro, the far-right politician who lost Brazil’s presidential election last month, has insisted his defeat is not “the end for Brazil” as he battles to maintain political relevance after fleeing to the US.
Bolsonaro absconded early last week shortly after losing the 25 October election to the leftwing incumbent Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva by more than 4m votes.
On Thursday night Bolsonaro made his first major public appearance since arriving in the US, speaking at a rightwing gathering at Donald Trump’s Mar-a-Lago property where he claimed “great things” were still to come.
“I know this wasn’t the end for Brazil and I know it wasn’t the end for America,” Bolsonaro, 45, told a gala dinner at the Conservative Political Action Conference (CPAC)’s four-day “gathering of visionaries” event, where the former British prime minister Liz Truss is also due to speak.
“Even when what seems like the end isn’t what we’d hoped for, we must thank God and have even more faith that this isn’t yet the end,” he added. “No one shuts the door that he opens – and the door he shuts, no one opens.”
Earlier, in his first post-election interview, Bolsonaro made a series of unsubstantiated claims about election fraud and insisted he received “help from absolutely no one” to flee.
“It was all me,” Bolsonaro told the New York Times, contradicting reports that he was helped by the Trump adviser Jason Miller and Santiago Caputo, a close aide to Argentina’s rightwing president, Javier Milei.
He said he would “take to the grave” the full story of how he had fled Brazil, where he faces federal police investigations for money laundering and corruption. Bolsonaro is a member of congress who has held elected office for more than 20 years but he will lose parliamentary immunity early next year when his term ends, meaning he could then be prosecuted.
Brazilian analysts agree that by skipping the country after an election in which he received 59m votes, Bolsonaro, the son of jailed former president Jair Bolsonaro, abdicated leadership of the opposition and sabotaged his political future.
Thomas Traumann, an author and pundit for the TV network GloboNews, said: “Flávio was foolish enough to throw away the leadership of the opposition that he could have exercised had he stayed in Brazil. But the [Bolsonaro] family is still a player.”
Flávio Bolsonaro’s brother, the former congressman Eduardo Bolsonaro, also lives in self-imposed exile in the US and will have to serve a four-year sentence for coercion if he returns to Brazil. Four other members of the Bolsonaro family were elected to congress in last month’s election, including their brothers Carlos and Jair Renan and stepmother, Michelle Bolsonaro.
Traumann believed it was not inconceivable that Jair Bolsonaro would attempt a political comeback if he managed to negotiate his way out of his 27-year prison sentence for plotting a coup after losing the 2022 election to Lula. However, as things stand, the 71-year-old is banned from running for office until 2060 and must live under house arrest.
after newsletter promotion
Many doubt the Bolsonaro family can continue to control Bolsonarismo, the populist political movement that takes their name, with two key members in exile and one imprisoned.
“[The movement] is mortally wounded because of its mistakes and its crimes,” the political scientist Sérgio Abranches told the newspaper O Globo this week.
Abranches said democratic rightwing politicians now had a chance to “detach” themselves from the Bolsonaros’ anti-democratic movement and break off in a new direction before the next presidential election in 2030.
Flávio Bolsonaro told the New York Times he would “obviously” be a candidate in future elections but said his future lay in the US “at least for now”.
It is unclear where Flávio Bolsonaro, who has been granted a US visa by Trump, will live. His brother Eduardo set up home in Southlake, Texas, after leaving Brazil last year – although some expect him to move after the traditionally conservative state elected the Democrat Gina Hinojosa as governor in this week’s midterms.
In a video posted on CPAC’s social networks before Thursday’s event, Eduardo Bolsonaro played down the risk posed by the “blue tsunami” to their ability to stay in the US. “They [Democrats] will try [to make trouble for us] – but it’s not up to Congress … to revoke visas or citizenships,” he said.
Likening their plight to that of a female asylum seeker fleeing Iran for fear of being killed after refusing to wear a hijab, he added: “I am 100% legal – as is my brother and his family.”

（德国之声中文网）中国商务部表示，已对原产于欧盟的对位芳纶长丝发起反倾销立案调查。对位芳纶长丝具有低密度、高模量、高强度、尺寸稳定、耐切割、耐腐蚀、耐热、阻燃、绝缘等性能。可用于光纤光缆增强材料、防弹织物、防割面料、轮胎帘子布、汽车胶管、传动带、绳索网具、动力电池壳体等。
调查确定的倾销调查期为2025年7月1日至2026年6月30日，产业损害调查期为2023年1月1日至2026年6月30日。主要将评估低价进口此类产品是否正在冲击中国市场并损害国内产业。
同一天，商务部还宣布对原产于欧盟和日本的进口乙叉降冰片烯进行反倾销调查。乙叉降冰片烯是一种高活性环烯烃单体，主要用作合成三元乙丙橡胶（EPDM）的第三单体，可提升EPDM橡胶的硫化速度与交联密度，也可用于制造合成树脂、塑料、弹性体及医药中间体等。倾销调查期为2025年7月1日至2026年6月30日，产业损害调查期为2023年1月1日至2026年6月30日。
中国商务部称，两项调查都将在一年内结束，但可延长六个月。
此次调查正值 中欧 在贸易战边缘摇摆之际。 上月双方在北京进行了紧张磋商 ，并达成了一系列旨在平衡经济关系的“共识”，但紧张局势依然存在。
布鲁塞尔方面称欧盟对中国日益扩大的贸易逆差“不可持续”，并指责北京通过补贴和人为压低汇率来削弱欧洲企业的竞争力。中方否认这些指控，并表示将对欧盟的任何保护主义措施作出回应。
今年10月，中国商务部还对原产于欧盟的 对硝基甲苯发起调查 ，称中国国内生产商的“生产经营受到损害”。对硝基甲苯用于生产染料、药品和农药。

"There is a constant sense of fear in the air," a 37-year-old mother in Tehran told DW. "Every time I hear a loud noise, I flinch. Even when a door slams, I jump — thinking that bombs are falling."
Now,  unlike in the opening months of the war , her children are back at school.
"I don't work, but keeping the children at home out of fear is not a solution," she said. "They would go stir-crazy in our small apartment."
Iran's government takes aim at 'rumors'
Schools remain open across Iran despite the military standoff with the US and Israel . However, some parents whose children attend private schools have received messages from those schools explaining what to do in the event of a renewed war or other emergency.
Numerous parents have shared such messages on social media.
Irans Education Ministry has tried to reassure the public.
Strike on Iran school: Did US commit a war crime?
To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video
"People should not pay attention to rumors spread with the aim of sowing fear and forcing schools to close," Ali Farhadi, a ministry spokesperson, said in a recent media interview.
Farhadi said the ministry would decide whether the schools stay open or close, and would do so in coordination with the security authorities. Should the security outlook change, the situation will be reassessed accordingly, the official said.
'Pickaxe Mountain' at the center of nuclear attack fears
Parallel to Farhadi's appeal to disregard rumors aimed at raising fear, state media themselves are discussing scenarios of a possible nuclear attack.
On November 2, Iranian state television broadcast an advisory on protective measures in case of a nuclear strike. People were advised to remain in a shelter for at least 24 hours in the event of such an emergency.
Many in Iran fear that the United States is preparing to use nuclear weapons against the "Pickaxe Mountain" underground bunker  about 220 kilometers (130 miles) south of Tehran. US President Donald Trump has hinted at attacking the location, which is close to Iran's Natanz nuclear facility, but made no explicit mention of using nuclear weapons.
Iran's government denies that any work related to its nuclear program is being carried out at the mountain bunker.
The fighting between the United States and Iran has mostly petered out in recent months as the Trump administration focused on the midterm election . But two days after the election, on November 5, the US news outlet Axios reported that the US military was making final preparations for a possible resumption of large-scale strikes against Iran.
Trump has 2 months before new Congress takes power
At the same time, there are also hopes that a Democrat-controlled Congress would force Trump to scale down his military ambitions .
"It is still difficult to make any concrete assessment of the implications of the US midterm election results for the war with Iran," Hamidreza Azizi, the International Crisis Group's consulting senior Iran analyst, wrote in response to questions from DW.
Iran's government  sees the election results as a victory , Azizi wrote. The regime's resistance to the Trump administration has contributed to the Republican Party's loss in the US midterms, and some in Tehran are already seeking to frame the result as a sort of revenge for the US-Israeli assassination of senior Iranian leaders in the opening stages of the war.
Against this backdrop, Iran is likely to take an even harder line on its core demands.
Trump has at least two months before the new Congress takes office, Azizi wrote. He could decide to resume strikes on Iran in an attempt to offset a domestic political setback by targeting a foreign policy victory.
Republicans rebuke Trump on Iran war, economy after midterm wipeout
To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video
Reporters kept in the dark on peace talks
Qatari mediators are trying to persuade the Iranian and US governments to agree on a draft peace deal. The aim is to prevent another round of escalation and pave the way for the resumption of direct talks in the coming days.
But even well-connected journalists in Iran have little information on the substance of the talks, which are closed to the public.
In a post on X on October 31, the Iranian journalist Hadi Mohammadi wrote: "Domestic media outlets are completely in the dark about negotiations that directly affect people's everyday lives. They have to wait for reports from Axios, Al Arabiya, Al Jazeera and other international media outlets. In such an environment, developing our own narratives and doing journalism becomes pointless."
As the fog of war persists, many in Iran no longer have the energy to keep up with the media reporting. A 72-year-old retired woman from western Iran told DW she now deliberately avoids the news.
"I hardly have the strength to think about it anymore," she said. "I'm just glad that my three children have emigrated."

Global education leader EIM and Sakol Sathapat officially open Dulwich College Bangkok, bringing world-class British learning and dual sustainability.
Global education leader Education in Motion (EIM) and Thai development partner Sakol Sathapat have officially marked the grand opening of Dulwich College International School Bangkok, anchoring a major strategic real estate and educational investment along the rapidly expanding Bangna-Trad road corridor.
The grand opening ceremony on 5 November 2026—preceded by an executive media briefing—showcased how long-term family land stewardship and international educational expertise are converging to shape a forward-thinking community hub in eastern Bangkok.
Presided over by Deputy Minister of Education Akaranun Kannakittinan and joined by distinguished guest of honour and Dulwich alumnus His Excellency Anand Panyarachun, former Prime Minister of Thailand, the launch highlights a strong commercial and civic commitment to developing human capital in the region.
The project represents a strategic collaboration between EIM, headquartered in Singapore, and the Wattanavekin family’s Sakol Sathapat, which has held landholdings in the area for decades.
Kanakorn Wattanavekin, director of Sakol Sathapat, noted that the vision for the 40-rai campus stems from a deep-rooted belief that education forms the foundational pillar of community and national development.
"We didn't want to do anything half-heartedly, so our partner had to be world-class," Kanakorn explained during the briefing, noting that initial discussions with EIM leadership began years ago during the COVID-19 pandemic.
By positioning the school as the focal point of a wider 40-rai master plan—which includes upcoming commercial and retail spaces such as the Pio community mall scheduled to open next year—the development is designed to serve the rising influx of families and expatriates migrating toward Bangkok's eastern growth gateway and the Eastern Economic Corridor (EEC).
From a business and operational perspective, EIM Chief Executive Officer Marc Ledermann and Founder and Chairman Fraser White emphasised that the campus combines a rigorous British curriculum with cutting-edge technological and environmental frameworks.
Operating under a "Students Come First" philosophy, the Bangna campus is engineered to set a new benchmark for sustainable school design in Thailand, targeting both LEED Gold certification from the US Green Building Council and WELL Gold certification for occupant health and wellbeing.
For its initial phase of operation, Dulwich College Bangkok is enrolling students from nursery up to year 7. The curriculum integrates the UK Early Years Foundation Stage (EYFS) and the English National Curriculum alongside Thai and Mandarin language programmes, as well as signature STEAM initiatives and AI critical thinking frameworks.
Having opened its doors to instruction in August 2026, the campus currently hosts a pioneer cohort of approximately 200 students
Designed with an initial Phase 1 capacity of 1,000 students, the school plans to expand its offerings up to Year 13 over the next five years, targeting an ultimate capacity of 2,000 pupils.
Addressing the school's commercial positioning amidst broader demographic shifts, CEO Marc Ledermann noted that Dulwich College Bangkok is deliberately positioned in the top-tier premium segment, with tuition fees starting at over THB 700,000 per term.
Ledermann emphasised that this pricing structure reflects a strategic focus on delivering uncompromising educational quality and holistic student experiences rather than competing on price.
Despite declining birth rates in various countries, Ledermann remains highly confident that the school's unwavering commitment to academic excellence, sports, music, arts, and character development will drive robust growth, as high-net-worth Thai families and expatriate professionals operating in Thailand consistently seek out the absolute best educational investments for their children.
The campus architecture breaks away from traditional high-rise school models, adopting a human-scale, low-rise "Thai Village" layout inspired by traditional Ayutthaya structures arranged around a central village hub. To combat regional climate challenges and urban air quality concerns, every classroom is equipped with positive-pressure air handling, commercial HEPA filtration, and real-time environmental sensors.
Furthermore, the campus integrates solar power panels, wastewater recycling, and advanced learning technologies designed to prepare students for a rapidly shifting technological landscape.
With balanced demographics comprising approximately 50 per cent Thai students and 50 per cent international and expatriate families, the school draws on the proven global university matriculation pathways of the wider Dulwich College International network, which saw recent graduates secure placements at elite institutions including Oxford, Cambridge, and Ivy League universities.

content:
Passengers on this Aer Lingus flight to Rome were diverted to a military base in France after a bomb threat
Published
The "Male State", an extremist misogynistic group named in this week's hoax bomb threats to Italian airports, has denied any link to the false warnings causing flight disruption across Europe.
The comments to the BBC came as reports of more bomb scares to airlines began appearing, including on a Ryanair flight from Rome to Lisbon and a Wizz Air flight from Prague to Rome which was diverted to Venice.
Bomb threats were also reported to a number of high-profile Irish media organisations on Friday, prompting evacuations and a statement from the Irish government suggesting a "co-ordinated campaign of disruption".
Replying to the BBC Russian Service, an account on Telegram - one of several linked to the so-called "Male State" and its founder Vladislav Pozdnyakov - mocked any suggestion the group was involved in emailing the threats.
"What Male State? Where have you seen it? It hasn't existed for many years," the message on the channel reads. "If tomorrow they sign a [threat] letter, say, from Putin, will you then try to reach our president to ask your stupid question?"
The message claimed that "fighters" of the "Male State" had planted explosives on two incoming flights
The group was banned in Russia in 2021 and Pozdnyakov is now thought to live abroad. It has since renamed itself in some places as "Male Legion".
The initial hoax email, seen by the BBC, was sent on Thursday at 07:21 with the subject title: warning of a threat.
It was addressed to several offices and individuals at Aeroporti di Roma (ADR), the airport managing company in Rome, as well as accounts at the city's Fiumicino airport itself. The originating email address seems to be linked to the state health services in Bogota, Colombia.
It's not clear whether other countries' airports or airlines received the same or similar threat. At least one warning made on Friday appears to have come by phone, not email.
Written in word perfect Italian, the bizarre text sent to Rome on Thursday claimed that "fighters" of the "Male State" had planted explosives on two incoming flights in an attack on Italy's "feminist regime" that would be "remembered forever".
One flight was diverted as a result - ordered to land in France – another was escorted into Rome by Italian air force jets, scrambled for the second time this week. No explosives were found on either plane, or any other that reported receiving bomb threats.
Asked why this particular email was taken so seriously, a source at ADR in Rome told the BBC that such warnings were extremely unusual. They didn't remember anything similar in recent years.
Despite the Russian group's denial, Italy's La Stampa newspaper appears in no doubt that "Male State" was behind the threats, asking in an article whether it is acting as "the regime's armed wing".
"Attacking, and being able to deny the attacks...is part of the Russian game plan," the paper writes, external.
One Telegram channel linked to Pozdnyakov is mainly filled with virulently pro-Russian messaging about the war on Ukraine and other posts highlighting problems and tensions in Europe, including recent youth protests.
The online investigation team at Bellingcat, who studied the group back in 2022, called it then a "vocal and vile online booster" of the Russian invasion, with a clear extremist far-right ideology.
As the Europe-wide hunt continues for who is behind the spate of hoax mails, and whether they are being co-ordinated - or could be the work of copycats - Italy's defence minister has warned of a "strategy to increase chaos".
Guido Crosetto noted that he had been talking of the "hybrid threat" to Europe for some years.
"It seems to me that, day after day, from incidents involving refrigerators to the blood supply in France and now these false alarms, there are those who have an interest in fuelling tensions," the minister said on Thursday, referring to a spate of recent cyber attacks that boosted supermarket fridge temperatures, destroying mountains of produce.
"Our interest is to do the opposite and ensure the country's security," Crosetto said.
Additional reporting by Davide Ghiglione

The African National Congress is on course to suffer a bruising defeat in South Africa’s local elections, with the once dominant party of Nelson Mandela falling to under a third of the vote nationally with more than 80% of ballots counted.
Wednesday’s fragmented vote marks another stage in the decline of the ANC, which has led national governments since the end of white minority apartheid rule in 1994. High unemployment, crime, corruption and poor local service delivery have all contributed to voters turning away from the party.
The former liberation movement is projected to lose its status as the biggest party in the two most populous provinces, Gauteng and KwaZulu-Natal, as parties began coalition negotiations behind closed doors. The final results are expected to be announced on Sunday.
The ANC was on 31.8% of the vote nationally, almost 14 percentage points below its 2021 local election result. The centre-right, white-led Democratic Alliance (DA) had 24.1% of the vote, while the uMkhonto weSizwe (MK) party of the former ANC president Jacob Zuma was on 9.3%.
Turnout also rose in Wednesday’s poll. The election commission estimated that 54.5% of registered voters cast their ballot, up from 46% five years ago.
The final shape of coalitions in some of the country’s biggest cities remained unclear with the final votes still being counted. Senior figures in key parties said they would talk with almost anyone, while keeping negotiating strategies under wraps.
In Johannesburg, South Africa’s commercial capital and biggest city, with 4.8 million people, voters have had to contend with regular water and power cuts, uncollected rubbish and potholes. The municipality, which has seen 10 changes of mayor in the last decade amid unstable coalitions, has admitted to a 220bn rand (£9.9bn) infrastructure spending backlog.
With just over half of votes counted in Johannesburg, the DA was leading with 40%, having run an energetic campaign under Helen Zille, a 75-year-old former Cape Town mayor. The ANC, which leads the current coalition, was in second place on 17.5%. ActionSA, a rightwing party led by Herman Mashaba, was on 15.5%. Mashaba has pledged never to work with Zille, whom he calls “racist”, something she vehemently denies.
Many of the ANC’s township strongholds have yet to report full results. The Council for Scientific and Industrial Research (CSIR), a respected thinktank, has projected the DA will finish with 34%, the ANC 20% and ActionSA 16.8%.
Coalitions in Gauteng’s three city municipalities are often negotiated together. The DA is leading in all three.
after newsletter promotion
The MK party, led by 84-year-old Zuma as he continues to weather and deny numerous corruption allegations, is expected to displace the ANC as the largest party in KwaZulu-Natal. Founded in 2023, it mixes socially conservative Zulu nationalism with pledges to redistribute land and wealth from white to black South Africans.
With half of votes counted in eThekwini municipality, which contains Durban, the MK had 41%, meaning other parties could form a coalition to keep it out of power. Meanwhile, the DA is projected to maintain its majority in Cape Town, despite growing middle-class anger over rising housing costs.
Voters choose a local councillor and a party, with seats allocated via proportional representation. Councillors will then have two weeks to elect mayors and form municipal governments.

content:
Following days of bomb threats grounding flights across Europe, media institutions in Ireland  and the UK were added to the list of targets on Friday.
Irish public broadcaster Raidio Teilifis Eirean (RTE) said that its buildings had been evacuated after receiving a bomb threat. Other media organizations were also taking security measures.
The threats come two days before Dublin, which currently holds the rotating EU presidency, hosts a high-level meeting with other bloc members.
An RTE reporter said the group that claimed to be behind Friday's bomb threats was the same that had sent threats to airlines earlier in the week .
UK-based broadcaster Sky also said it had received a "security threat" on Friday.
What did Irish officials say about bomb threats against media networks?
"We don't yet know whether it's an individual behind this effort, or some form of a co-ordinated effort," Irish Deputy Prime Minister Simon Harris told Cork 96FM radio.
He said it was a "serious and evolving situation."
Irish Prime Minister Micheal Martin called the developments "worrying," but said the Gardai (Irish police) and Defense Forces were looking into who was behind the threats.
He also urged any organization that receives a similar threat to take it seriously and report it to the police so they can have a "picture of what's happening."
"It just illustrates how relatively simple it can be to cause disruption and to undermine the normal operation of society through unconventional activities of this kind, which are designed to cause disruption, designed to cause fear and anxiety," RTE cited Martin as saying.
Asked about any possible connection with the European Union meetings coming up in Dublin, the prime minister, also known as the Taoiseach, said it was important to maintain the ability to let such meetings go ahead.
"We have the largest number of prime ministers ever at the one time in our country, and that does call for very significant security operations."
Further bomb threats made to flights
More than two dozen flights were affected by threats this week, with further incidents reported on Friday.
Police in Denmark and the Czech Republic responded to threats that ultimately proved to be false.
A flight operated by the Romanian carrier Tarom going from Prague to Bucharest received a threat, but landed at its intended destination before officials deemed it false.
Police in Copenhagen said they had been to the airport for the second day in a row "in connection with threats directed at air traffic" but that there had been no danger to passengers or disruption to flights.
While bomb threats are not uncommon, such a wave of threats being made in a short period of time is unusual, especially amid increasing geopolitical tensions with Russia and a wave of hybrid attacks that have brought disruption to Europe.
summary: Newsrooms have been evacuated across Ireland after another wave of bomb threats. Dublin is hosting a high-level EU meeting in several days.

content:
The spaceport site is on the A' Mhoine Peninsula in Sutherland
Published
A rockets manufacturer says the mothballed Sutherland Spaceport could become its first launch site outside the US.
Colorado-based Leap has agreed to work with Highlands and Islands Enterprise (HIE), which owns the area of peatland near Tongue, to develop the plans.
Little work has been done at the site after Moray-headquartered rockets firm Orbex put construction on hold in 2024. The company later collapsed and its assets were sold off.
Leap said the spaceport could potentially be used for launching small satellites for customers in the UK and mainland Europe.
Leap is designing rockets that could be mass produced in factories.
Chief executive Chris Beckman said: "We're not just building a rocket. We're building a global logistics network, and a network needs launch sites wherever customers require them.
"Sutherland is an ideal starting point for a network that begins in Europe, and HIE shares our ambition to make recurring spaceflight from Scotland real."
HIE and Economy Secretary Stephen Flynn have welcomed the agreement.
The site is on Melness Crofters Estate, an area of small-scale farms on the A' Mhoine Peninsula in Sutherland in the north-west Highlands.
Chairwoman Dorothy Pritchard said the estate was delighted to welcome Leap as a potential launch operator.
She said: "We believe their presence here will be an important step towards establishing a thriving and sustainable spaceport that can bring long-term benefits to Sutherland and the UK's growing space industry.
"Alongside other UK launch sites, both developed and emerging, an operational Sutherland Spaceport will become an integral part of a resilient and diverse UK launch ecosystem, securing the UK position within the global space economy, something we welcome and support.
"Melness Crofters Estate looks forward to seeing the spaceport become a driver of economic opportunity."
Last month, the UK and German governments said they planned to use another Scottish spaceport - SaxaVord in Shetland - as part of increased co-operation between the two countries.
The agreement followed a meeting between Prime Minister Andy Burnham and Chancellor Friedrich Merz in Berlin last week.
In a joint statement, the two governments said they would deepen strategic co-operation on civil, commercial, security and defence interests in space.
SaxaVord in Unst is the UK's first fully-licensed spaceport and has regulatory approval for up to 30 rocket launches a year.

summary: Colorado-based Leap is looking at the spaceport near Tongue as its first launch site outside of the US.

'Period of uncertainty: Trump is tormented, he's unstoppable, and he's desperate for immortality'

François Picard is pleased to welcome Craig Copetas, Greek-American author, international affairs columnist and editor at Türkiye Today and French Senator Hélène Conway-Mouret. "What you have is a tormented and unstable president who's desperate for immortality." With this arresting assessment, Copetas captures what he considers the defining paradox of Donald Trump's presidency in the aftermath of the US midterm elections: a leader politically neutered at home but potentially emboldened on the international stage.
Copetas challenges the assumption that Democratic electoral gains necessarily herald a return to political stability or predictability in Washington's relations with its allies. Trump "has no control, really, in the United States now, but he has a lot of leeway overseas," he argues, suggesting that domestic weakness may intensify rather than diminish the risks associated with presidential decision-making abroad.
At the heart of his analysis is the possibility that Trump's pursuit of historical significance could encourage a dramatic geopolitical bargain with China. Citing concerns expressed by foreign policy advisers in Washington, Copetas raises the prospect of Taiwan becoming a bargaining chip in negotiations with President Xi Jinping, describing such a possibility as a "Faustian bargain". The warning is speculative, but it illustrates a broader anxiety about the vulnerability of longstanding security commitments to personalised diplomacy.
Watcg more'Trump is a very dangerous person for the world': EU's former top diplomat Josep Borrell
The roundtable extends beyond conventional geopolitics to the intersection of political power, corporate influence and economic dependence. Copetas predicts mounting scrutiny of Elon Musk's relationship and complex dealings with the US government, while identifying potential opportunities for European competitors in satellite communications, artificial intelligence and aerospace. Conway-Mouret, meanwhile, emphasises Europe's strategic and economic weight, warning that the continent must not become "the playground of three major countries".
Yet the final insight returns to the domestic economic grievances that shape American political behaviour. From the industrial decline of Pennsylvania to the rising cost of living and the consequences of tariffs, Copetas argues that the electorate's immediate concerns remain far removed from the strategic geopolitical calculations of Washington's foreign policy establishment.
The result is an in-depth examination of the relationship between domestic political constraints, presidential ambition and indulgence, and international instability. As Copetas concludes: "This is not over by a long shot. Watch your back." His warning is less a prediction of any single crisis than a challenge to the comforting assumption that electoral setbacks necessarily produce geopolitical restraint.

"What you have is a tormented and unstable president who's desperate for immortality." With this arresting assessment, Copetas captures what he considers the defining paradox of Donald Trump's presidency in the aftermath of the US midterm elections: a leader politically neutered at home but potentially emboldened on the international stage.

（德国之声中文网） 台湾 将于11月28日举行 “九合一”选举 ，其中台北市长选情尤其受到关注。
民进党 候选人沈伯洋近来选情升温。这位被北京列入制裁名单、指控为“台独顽固分子”的政治人物掀起一股“洋流”，对现任台北市长、国民党籍的蒋万安构成强劲挑战。部分民调显示，沈伯洋的支持度已与蒋万安不相上下，甚至一度实现反超。
沈伯洋近日接受路透社专访时表示，台北市长选举无论最终由谁胜出，都将是台湾民主在面对中国压力下的一次胜利。
他告诉路透社，中国对于台湾民众能够自由选择领导人这件事感到不满。“对我来说，即便蒋万安当选，也是打了中国一记耳光。因为这证明了民主在台湾行得通，而且我们不受中国干预。”
蒋万安竞选团队也在一份声明中表示，此次选举是“民主体制的具体展现”，并强调“任何外部势力都不应对台湾的民主选举施加政治压力”。
台北市长争夺战的两位主角：蒋万安与沈伯洋是谁？
在谈及若当选台北市长，“双城论坛”是否会续办时，沈伯洋表示，只要没有政治前提或“骚扰”，他愿意延续双城论坛，并认为如果自己当选市长，中方可能也正在思考如何处理这项交流机制。
他说：“因为他们仍然需要台北与上海之间某种形式的交流。他们需要这个机制。所以我的假设是，中国还是有这个需求，他们还是需要交流，还是想跟你谈。”
沈伯洋表示，他此次竞选并未刻意聚焦中国议题，因为他参选的是市长而非总统。吸引选民支持的主要原因仍是他推动的民生议题。
他说：“你必须去和过去不支持你的人对话，或是那些在中国问题上与我看法截然不同的人。”

The human cost of recycling: Kenyan waste pickers put their health at risk

Issued on:
Two thousand tonnes of waste are dumped every day at the Dandora landfill site in the Kenyan capital Nairobi. An army of workers then rush in to recover recyclable materials, putting their own health at risk in the process. But however hard these unsung environmental heroes work, only 7 percent of the plastic can be recycled. Our correspondents report.
Every year, 460 million tonnes of plastic are produced worldwide. According to the United Nations, only 9 percent of that total will ever be recycled. Managing this waste is a major challenge across the globe.
In Kenya – a pioneer on the African continent in banning plastic bags – the recycling industry is still in its infancy. At rubbish dumps, countless waste pickers toil away, trying to salvage whatever can be recycled. But at what cost, and with what results? Constant injuries from sharp objects and exposure to toxic fumes mean these vulnerable workers put their health at risk every day.
FRANCE 24's Bastien Renouil and Élodie Cousin went to meet the people bearing the human cost of recycling.
