content:
A bill to give shoppers temporary relief from soaring prices by cutting the consumption tax on food and drink cleared Japan’s lower house on Friday (November 6).
Every opposition party voted against the bill, which the House of Representatives sent to the Senate, the upper chamber of Japan’s parliament, the Diet.
The ruling Liberal Democratic Party and its coalition partner, the Japan Innovation Party, secured a majority in the lower house’s plenary vote.
The coalition is short of a majority in the Senate and is expected to seek support from two opposition parties, the Democratic Party for the People and Komeito, to get the bill through.
The government and ruling parties aim to make the bill law by 12 December, the final day of the current extraordinary session.
The Liberal Democratic Party and the opposition Constitutional Democratic Party of Japan agreed on Friday that the Senate would begin debating the bill at Wednesday’s plenary sitting.
If enacted, the measure would mark the first reduction since Japan introduced the tax in 1989.
Food and drink now taxed at 8% would be subject to a 1% rate for two years starting in April 2027.
The bill pairs the tax cut with income-linked payments to ease the burden on low- and middle-income earners.
Over the first two years, the payments would be made on a scale equivalent to the 1% consumption tax on food and drink.
The full programme would follow in the 2029 financial year.
Opposition parties criticised the lack of clarity over how the tax cut would be funded and how the new benefit scheme would be designed.
“Details of the bill have not been clarified, so this amounts to disregard for the legislature,” Yuichi Goto of the Democratic Reform Party said.
Yuichiro Tamaki, who leads the Democratic Party for the People, expressed concern that middle-income earners would face a heavier burden once the tax cut expired.
“The lack of an adequate explanation from the ruling side about how to address the problem was the biggest reason for our opposition to the bill,” he said.
The government had previously put the number of eligible workers at about 20 million, based on an annual income range of 1 million yen to 3.5 million yen.
That group represented 30% of the workforce.
Answering questions from opposition lawmakers at the lower house’s Committee on Financial Affairs before the plenary sitting, Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi said 30% or more of Japan’s workers would qualify.
Her reference to broader eligibility appeared intended to make the proposal more acceptable to opposition parties.
After the committee finished its deliberations, the ruling and opposition parties agreed to a committee vote followed by referral of the bill to the full house.
“The prime minister gave detailed answers,” Shinichi Isa of Komeito, who led the opposition side on the committee’s board, told reporters.
“We have decided to put the bill to votes in order to allow deliberations to proceed in the Senate.”

content:
Europeans believe human-made climate change is real, a survey has shown, with most feeling action must be taken soon – as long as they do not have to sacrifice too much to achieve it.
The YouGov poll of six European countries showed between 69% (Germany) and 80% (France) of respondents believed the climate was changing, with few (1%-4%) denying it and 14-20% believing it was changing, but not as a result of human activity.
Europe is the world’s fastest-warming continent and scientists say human-driven climate breakdown through the burning of fossil fuels is increasing the frequency and intensity of heatwaves, droughts, wildfires and destructive storms.
Days before the Cop31 climate conference in Turkey, the polling showed vast majorities (79-89%) in Denmark, France, Germany, Italy, Spain and the UK thought countries would combat the crisis more effectively by working internationally.
Those in the EU were more likely to say that climate action decisions should be made at EU rather than national level, a feeling shared by 50-54% of respondents in France, Italy and Germany as well as 61% in Denmark and 64% in Spain.
Majorities of between 65% and 83% in each country surveyed said they were worried about the climate crisis, including 23%-42% who were “very worried”. YouGov noted an uptick in concern during this summer’s heatwaves.
In April, 74% of respondents in France said they were worried about the climate crisis but that figure was up to 83% by mid-August and still at that level last month.
The number of French people who were “very worried” about climate change also rose, from 28% in April to a record high of 42% in August, a level it held last month. Concern in other countries spiked in August but has since dipped.
In Germany, for example, the number very concerned rose from 27% in April to 40% in August but has now fallen back to 31%. Concern remained relatively stable in Denmark, at 66%-69% “worried” and 20%-23% “very worried”.
Across the six countries surveyed, respondents mostly (45%-63%) thought it was not too late to avert the worst impacts of the climate crisis but that it would require a drastic change in approach. Only 11%-24% believed it was already too late.
after newsletter promotion
Between 9% and 20% said they thought current measures would be enough to prevent the most serious impacts. But in terms of what climate actions had support, those not directly affecting people’s lives were the most popular.
Measures such as planting more trees, subsidising energy efficiency, banning single-use plastics and taxing big emitters were all favoured, while increasing fuel duty, limiting meat and dairy, taxing air fares and banning new petrol and diesel cars were opposed.
A similar pattern emerged when respondents were asked what steps they would be prepared to take: cheap and easy actions such as creating green space at home and eating only seasonal fruit and vegetables were popular, but not shopping exclusively secondhand or paying more for flights.

The YouGov poll of six European countries showed between 69% (Germany) and 80% (France) of respondents believed the climate was changing, with few (1%-4%) denying it and 14-20% believing it was changing, but not as a result of human activity. （德国之声中文网）一段时间以来，世界各地的年轻人频繁走上街头，表达对生活现状和未来前景的不满。
10月底， 德国 首次 爆发全国性的“Z世代”抗议游行 ，希望引起社会对教育体系投入不足、生活成本高企以及房租持续上涨等问题的关注。抗议活动总体以和平方式进行，但期间也发生了个别暴力事件。
“Z世代”抗议活动引发暴力事件：“我们还必须审视根本原因”
根据德国电视一台最新发布的“德国趋势”民调，73%的受访者表示理解年轻人的诉求，理解他们为此走上街头抗议。
不过，示威活动中的暴力行为几乎遭到一致反对。即便是在35岁以下受访者中，也有93%的人对此持反对态度。
此外，82%的受访者认为，德国政界对年轻人的诉求关注不足，甚至显得漠不关心。

对于兵役新规，不同年龄层的看法则存在明显分歧。受访者的年龄越小，对新规的支持度越低。
根据年初生效的新规，所有2008年及以后出生的男性都将再次接受兵役体检，并需填写一份关于服役意愿和适任性的问卷。不过，目前是否服兵役仍由个人自愿决定。

German automaker anchors Southeast Asian growth in Thailand with locally produced S-Class and Maybach, defying import tariffs via local assembly investments.
German luxury automaker Mercedes-Benz has strongly reaffirmed its long-term strategic commitment to using Thailand as a key regional production hub and pillar for its Southeast Asian business, using the domestic launch of its newest top-end luxury sedans to highlight the critical role local manufacturing plays in its global operations.
At an exclusive press preview on the evening of 5 November, preceding the official market release on 6 November, senior global and regional executives outlined how local production capabilities shield the brand from shifting tax landscapes while serving as an engine for electrified transformation across the region.
The event was attended by Industry Minister Varawut Silpa-archa, who voiced strong government backing for Mercedes-Benz's manufacturing presence in the Kingdom.
Speaking from a global operational perspective, Mathias Geisen, Member of the Board of Management of Mercedes-Benz Group AG overseeing Sales & Customer Experience, emphasised that Southeast Asia remains central to the company’s worldwide strategy.
"If you want to run the business worldwide, you have to ensure growth across all markets. This region has always been crucial, with sales established for decades," Geisen noted, adding that Mercedes-Benz is currently navigating the largest product rollout in its history, introducing over 40 new models within two and a half years to give global consumers a flexible choice of advanced powertrains.
Reinforcing the regional focus, Martin Schulz, CEO and President of Mercedes-Benz Malaysia and Head of Region for Mercedes-Benz Cars Southeast Asia, offered a highly optimistic outlook for the regional luxury market.
Schulz, who now oversees a consolidated Southeast Asian cluster spanning Thailand, Malaysia, Vietnam, Singapore, and general distribution markets, emphasised that local assembly remains the brand's primary competitive advantage.
Addressing recent regulatory adjustments in Thailand—including a proposed 35 per cent excise duty structure on imported electric vehicles—Schulz stated that Mercedes-Benz remains largely insulated due to its extensive local assembly strategy in partnership with Thonburi Automotive Assembly Plant Co., Ltd.
"It reaffirms that our commitment to local production is the right strategy," Schulz said.
He noted that while Singapore leads the region in electric vehicle adoption rate, Thailand is following closely behind with battery electric vehicles (BEVs) comprising 25 to 30 per cent of local manufacturing output, whereas Malaysia is experiencing rapid acceleration from a lower base.
Schulz also welcomed growing industry competition across Southeast Asia, noting that market pressure "keeps us on our tracks and active."
He reassured Thai buyers that adequate allocation has been secured for popular imported and locally built models to meet sustained high demand despite global capacity constraints.
The commitment to Thailand’s industrial base was showcased through the official launch of two locally assembled flagship models: the new S-Class and the ultra-luxury Mercedes-Maybach S-Class.
The locally produced S-Class is offered at an identical starting price of THB 7.19 million for both the S 350 d 4MATIC turbocharged diesel and the S 580 e 4MATIC plug-in hybrid (PHEV).
The plug-in hybrid variant features a 21.96 kWh battery offering up to 100 kilometres of pure electric range under WLTP testing.
At the absolute peak of automotive luxury, the locally assembled Mercedes-Maybach S 580 e plug-in hybrid starts at THB 9.9 million, reaching THB 10.9 million for the optional two-tone exterior finish.
The model integrates the proprietary Mercedes-Benz Operating System (MB.OS) alongside an AI-driven MBUX Virtual Assistant.
Christian Schell, president and CEO of Mercedes-Benz (Thailand) Limited, stated that offering both traditional combustion and advanced plug-in powertrains at identical price points provides Thai customers with complete freedom of choice without compromising on luxury.
Both flagship vehicles are now available through the brand's nationwide agent network across Thailand.

Tundu Lissu, the leader of Tanzania's main opposition party , was sentenced to four years in prison on Friday for incitement to unrest after being cleared of treason.
While the verdict removed the threat of a death sentence, judges convicted Lissu of an offense that was not among the charges he faced.
What did the court decide?
Judges found that Chadema leader Lissu's statements about blocking the election were intended to disrupt the vote and encourage violence.
"We are satisfied that through his statements, the accused intended to disrupt elections and instigate violence," the judge said.
Lissu disputed his conviction on a charge different from the treason accusation he had faced.
"I was not charged with incitement but you judges are convicting me with it just to impress the person who gives you the titles," he said, apparently referring to President Samia Suluhu Hassan.
Lissu was arrested in April 2025 over a speech in which prosecutors said he told supporters the opposition would "block the election" and "mobilize rebellion." He pleaded not guilty, arguing that his speech broke no law and that the prosecution was politically motivated . Lissu has already spent 19 months in jail.
The Tanzania voter boycott over opposition party exclusion
To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video
"All this was political persecution. Excuses were created to imprison me," he told the court after the verdict.
How did the case fuel Tanzania's unrest?
Lissu's arrest, alleged abductions of government critics, and Chadema's exclusion from the October 2025 election helped drive protests across the country.
Hundreds died as police opened fire on protesters in several cities. Opposition figures and rights groups put the toll in the thousands.
A commission appointed by President Samia Suluhu Hassan reported in April that at least 518 people had been killed and blamed protesters for the violence. The government denied allegations that security forces used excessive force.
Security was tightened in the commercial capital, Dar es Salaam, and around the courthouse ahead of Friday's verdict.
Why has the trial drawn international criticism?
British and European Union lawmakers described the case as politically motivated and called for Lissu's immediate release.
"The use of capital punishment against a political opponent risks turning the justice system into an instrument of political repression," they wrote to Hassan.

Lissu, 58, has been repeatedly arrested for opposing the government. In 2017, he survived an assassination attempt in which he was shot 16 times. He believes the attack was politically motivated.

An encounter during the 2025 World Exposition in Osaka has driven Canadian indigenous tenor singer Jeremy Dutcher to return to Japan to share a stage with Ainu indigenous musicians from the Asian country's northern region.
A concert was held at the official residence of Canadian Ambassador to Japan Ian McKay in Tokyo on Oct. 26, bringing together Dutcher, Ainu musician OKI, who plays the "tonkori" stringed instrument, and the Marewrew female vocal group, who sing in the traditional Ainu style.
"As Canada and Japan look toward the 100th anniversary of diplomatic relations in 2028, tonight reminds us that relationships grow through encounters, shared experiences and a willingness to listen," said Laurie Peters, minister and deputy head of mission at the embassy.
The bouncing sounds of tonkori strings and energetic singing voices brought the spirit of indigenous cultures into the room. "Music is a means of communication that does not rely on language," OKI said, confident about the unique power of music.
Dutcher said that his first encounter with the Ainu culture at an Osaka Expo indigenous performance event last year led him back to Japan. The encounter with "the beauty of their songs and the strength of their culture" inspired him, he said.
During the concert at the official residence, he also shared an episode of him talking about the experience passionately to his friend and world-renowned cellist Yo-Yo Ma.
"Every time I get to share a stage with (Ainu musicians), I understand a little more deeply how we are connected as indigenous people but also just as humans."
Dutcher is part of the Wolastoqiyik indigenous people, who live in areas in the eastern Canadian provinces of New Brunswick and Quebec and the U.S. state of Maine.
Wolastoqiyik, which means "people of the beautiful river," face challenges from the decreasing number of fluent speakers of their language from birth, which is said to be less than 100, according to Dutcher. This problem is shared by Ainu people, whose language is listed by UNESCO as a language in danger.
His works revive Wolastoqiyik ancestors' voices by incorporating elements from recordings of their voices from over 110 years ago that are kept at the Canadian Museum of History.
Stressing the importance of understanding "the land we stand on," he said, "It's a great honor and privilege for me to come and bring the songs of my people and my ancestors to this beautiful country of Japan."

La Comisión Europea ( CE ) concluyó este viernes (06.11.2026), de forma preliminar, que TikTok incumple la Ley de Servicios Digitales (DSA) porque el algoritmo de su 'feed' "Para ti" (reglas internas que determinan el orden de lo que aparece en la pantalla) encierra a los usuarios en "madrigueras" ('rabbit holes') de contenido dañino para su salud mental, y le exige rediseñarlo.
"Cada vez que un usuario se desplaza o da un 'me gusta' a un vídeo, el algoritmo le sirve más de lo mismo y lo lleva por 'madrigueras' de las que no puede salir fácilmente", afirmó la vicepresidenta ejecutiva de la Comisión, Henna Virkkunen. "En esta fase de la investigación, la Comisión considera que TikTok debe cambiar el diseño" de "Para ti", con más peso de las preferencias explícitas de los usuarios, sin el tiempo de visionado como indicador, con controles más accesibles y con pruebas periódicas del algoritmo, informó el Ejecutivo comunitario en un comunicado.
Posible multa de hasta el 6 % de la facturación anual
Las conclusiones se suman a las ya adoptadas en el procedimiento formal abierto contra la red social en febrero de 2024 centrado en el acceso a datos para investigadores, el diseño adictivo y la protección de menores. Si confirma su postura tras oír a la plataforma, la Comisión podrá imponer multas de hasta el 6 % de la facturación anual mundial de la compañía. TikTok podrá ejercer ahora su derecho de defensa, examinar el expediente y responder por escrito, en consulta con la Junta Europea de Servicios Digitales. La compañía no respondió de inmediato a la solicitud de comentarios por parte de AP.
Este año la Comisión ya ha emitido otros dos conjuntos de conclusiones preliminares, acusando a la plataforma de infringir las normas con características de "diseño adictivo" que conducen al uso compulsivo por parte de los menores y acusándola de no proteger adecuadamente los derechos de privacidad de los menores.
Efectos para la salud
Ese efecto "madriguera", similar al de "caja de resonancia" que replica las propias opiniones, puede tener graves consecuencias para el bienestar, como "tristeza o ansiedad", "insatisfacción corporal", "menor autoestima" o el "empeoramiento de trastornos alimentarios y afecciones mentales ya existentes", según Bruselas. La Comisión también considera ineficaces las medidas que la plataforma aplica actualmente, como las destinadas a diversificar el contenido, que "no reducen lo suficiente la frecuencia" con que se recomiendan vídeos similares.
Además, los controles disponibles no permiten a los usuarios gestionar eficazmente lo que ven: el botón 'No me interesa' "puede no bastar para cambiar el 'feed'" y el algoritmo da prioridad al tiempo de visionado frente a la opción de ver menos contenido de ese tipo. Las conclusiones de hoy "demuestran de nuevo que TikTok debe redoblar sus esfuerzos para proteger el bienestar de los usuarios", incluidos los menores, añadió Virkkunen. Las conclusiones son preliminares y no prejuzgan el resultado final de la investigación.

On a slightly chilly and distinctly smoggy morning in New Delhi, Khushboo Arora was looking for another air purifier for her mother, who has underlying health complications, before the city's air quality deteriorated further.
"Already, I am starting to get a recurring headache," she said. "These days when I wake up, I don't feel fresh. As the day progresses, I feel a heaviness in my head, itching in my eye and a constantly parched throat."
Not long ago, the unpacking of woolens announced the advent of winter in Delhi. Now, it's the light hum of an air purifier in the corner.
Arora said she has already stopped doing yoga in the park and taking her morning walks. She has also filled her house with air-purifying plants and started spraying water mist inside the house to bring down the level of  pollution .
"My parents look at me like I have gone mad. But I feel people are not realizing the gravity of the situation," she said.
A recurring crisis
Winters in Delhi increasingly follow a familiar pattern: Air quality deteriorates, residents struggle to breathe, emergency restrictions kick in and governments exchange blame. Then the season changes, only for the cycle to repeat the following year.
On Thursday, Delhi's air fell into the "Very unhealthy" category, according to Swiss air quality monitor IQAir, with an average PM2.5 concentration of 157.9 micrograms per cubic meter of air. The World Health Organization (WHO) recommends an annual safe limit of no more than 5 micrograms.
Studies have shown that exposure to PM2.5 — air particles with a diameter smaller than 2.5 micrometers that can penetrate deep into the lungs and enter the bloodstream — is associated with an increased incidence of head and neck cancer (HNC), like oral, nasal and throat cancers.
But despite years of attempted interventions,   India 's capital continues to struggle with the same pollution crisis.
What is causing the air pollution?
Delhi is not dealing with an unknown problem. There is considerable scientific understanding of its causes.
A 2026 assessment by an expert panel reviewed by the Delhi government identified the major winter contributors of PM2.5 as vehicular emissions, industrial activity, road and construction dust, biomass and waste burning, and pollution from neighboring regions.
Sunil Dahiya, founder of the environmental group EnviroCatalysts, said Delhi is part of a larger airshed. On most winter days, more pollution comes into Delhi than is generated inside it, according to the environmentalist.
"Analysis of the government's Decision Support System (DSS) data for winter 2025 found that around 65% of Delhi's PM2.5 came from outside the city and about 35% from sources within it," he told DW, adding that neighboring Noida and Gurugram, which comprise the National Capital Region (NCR), are some of the biggest contributors.
Coordinating action across the NCR, which spans Delhi and parts of three neighboring states, remains a major obstacle.
"This is a shared problem, and no single city can solve it alone," Dahiya said.
Why aren't anti-pollution policies working?
To understand why existing policies have not delivered sustained improvements , Dahiya highlighted the gap between scientific recommendations and state action.
"Scientists have said for over a decade that we need airshed-wide, year-round, source-specific action. What we mostly get is seasonal and reactive," he said.
According to the environmentalist, emergency restrictions kick in only after pollution has reached dangerous levels. Short-term measures such as water sprinklers and smog towers provide little relief, while bigger structural changes are slow to materialize. These include stricter enforcement of industrial emissions, cleaner fuels, expanded public transport, vehicle electrification and viable alternatives to crop burning for farmers.
"The science is not the bottleneck. Implementation, regional coordination and political will are," said Dahiya. "Until targets are tied to emission reductions at each source, and someone is held accountable for meeting them, we will keep having the same conversation every November."
Bhavreen Kandhari, co-founder of Warrior Moms, agrees that official responses focus on reacting rather than preventing.
"They allow pollution to occur and then try to clean it up — producing nice photo opportunities of water sprinklers and smog guns, or talking about cloud seeding," Kandhari told DW. "Creating pollution only to clean it up later is a waste of public funds, time, and health."
Kandhari also added that incinerating waste instead of proper waste management has only exacerbated the situation .
The politics of pollution
Another obstacle to a lasting solution has been the political blame game that starts as soon as the air quality worsens.
On Thursday, Delhi Environment Minister Manjinder Singh Sirsa said stubble-burning in the neighboring state of Punjab is contributing to the capital's rising pollution, according to public broadcaster All India Radio. He insisted that in Delhi, construction, vehicle and industrial sources were controlled.
Dahiya agreed that seasonal crop-burning fires in neighboring states of Punjab and Haryana "is an episodic but sharp contributor" which "can tip 'very poor' air into 'severe'" for a few weeks. But it is not the lone contributor.
"Among sources within Delhi, vehicles alone contribute roughly 51-53% of local PM2.5. A large share of winter PM2.5 is also secondary particulate formed from gases like sulfur dioxide, nitrogen oxides and ammonia," Dahiya said. "That points straight back to combustion in power plants, industry and transport."
"If stubble burning ended tomorrow, Delhi would still breathe unhealthy air for most of the year," he added.
DW reached out to several Delhi government officials for a response, but received no reply.
What needs to change?
Delhi is also home to millions of people who cannot afford air purifiers and have no escape from the toxic air.
Among them is Deepika, who works as domestic help in an affluent South Delhi neighborhood. She has been coughing for a week.
It is the same every year, she said.
"I have no choice but to bear it for the next few months."
The people DW spoke to point to a common set of priorities: Addressing Delhi's pollution crisis requires year-round pollution control rather than seasonal restrictions, better coordination between governments and stronger enforcement of existing regulations and measurable targets. They say the city needs a sustained clean-air strategy more than another winter emergency plan.
Namrata Yadav is a Delhi resident and the mother of an eight-year-old boy. They both joined protests against air pollution in November . A year later, the problems persist.
"It is exhausting to repeat the same things year after year, only to be dismissed as paranoid or alarmist for demanding something as basic as clean air," she said.
Calling for lasting solutions driven by science, policy and accountability, Yadav said: "We have spent years learning how to live with pollution. It is time we demanded that those responsible learn how to end it."

content:
Kenyan religious sect leader Paul Mackenzie was sentenced to 200 years in prison on Friday, at the culmination of a trial following the discovery of hundreds of corpses in the woods .
A self-proclaimed pastor and longstanding leader of a new age Christian apocalyptic cult called the Good News International Church, Mackenzie was convicted in October of 191 counts of murder in the deaths of one adult and 190 children.
Justice Diana Kavedza said the sentence was comprised of 100 years for 183 counts of murder by starvation and another 100 years for eight counts of murder by direct homicide.
He could have faced the death penalty, which is still technically on the books in Kenya.
However, like several countries that have kept capital punishment in their legal code but stopped actually using it, Kenya has not executed anybody since 1987.
What was the case about?
While the charges against Mackenzie pertained to 191 deaths, some 400 people were found dead in what became known as the "Shakahola Forest Massacre." Mackenzie's so-called church had been operating since 2003, based in the coastal town of Malindi.
Mackenzie had denied the charges, saying that he did not force the cult followers to starve.
A total of 28 accomplices were given various prison sentences for their roles in the deaths.
They included guards who enforced his fasting directives and gravediggers who helped conceal the dead in shallow graves. They all denied the charges, except for one who pleaded guilty and asked for leniency.
Among them was Mackenzie's assistant "pastor," Smart Mwakalama, who was sentenced to 160 years.
Judge Kavedza dismissed the argument from some of the accused that the fact they had lost their own children altered the nature of their involvement in the deaths of others.
More than 60 of the bodies were positively identified and reburied by their relatives, but many of the remains were so decomposed that they could not be identified or claimed.

content:
Посольство Кыргызстана в Москве направило ноту в министерство иностранных дел РФ  "по вопросу скорейшего возвращения" гражданина республики с инициалами Э.Т. который в "результате мошеннических действий со стороны неустановленных лиц" оказался в одной из российских воинских частей . Об этом сообщается в четверг, 5 ноября, на сайте МИД Кыргызстана.
Диппредставительство страны также направило "официальные письма в компетентные органы" России о "необходимости проведения всесторонней проверки", установления виновных и привлечения их к ответственности. В ведомстве отметили, что поддерживают постоянную связь с родственниками гражданина страны.
"Азаттык": Речь идет о 21-летнем Элистане Токтогулове
Речь в ноте идет о 21-летнем Элистане Токтогулове из города Манас, сообщает онлайн-издание "Азаттык Азия" - кыргызская служба медиакомпании "Радио Свобода". Его родственники 3 ноября собрались на одной из улиц города и записали видеообращение к властям Кыргызстана.
По словам брата Элистана Баястана Куштарбек уулу, молодой человек уехал из страны две недели назад, после того как нашел в соцсети Instagram объявление о работе в России. Он связался с гражданином Кыргызстана, который находился в РФ, ему предложили несколько вакансий - от водителя грузовика до сотрудника службы безопасности - и зарплату до 110 тысяч рублей.
Сейчас Элистан, по данным родственников, находится на полигоне в Воронежской области . Его готовят к отправке на войну в Украину .
Ранее власти Казахстана вернули 12 завербованных граждан
В конце сентября ноту в МИД России направили представители внешнеполитического ведомства Казахстана, передавала местная служба "Радио Свобода". Казахстанский МИД просил оказать содействие в возвращении граждан , которые также подписали военные контракты в РФ.
В частности, ведомство упомянуло 25-летнего Мираса Ташарганова, который в конце августа сказал матери, что уезжает на вахту в Россию. Затем, по его словам, его вынудили подписать контракт на службу в армии. Мать Мираса заявляет, что ее сын успел пройти двухнедельную военную подготовку и находится в Воронеже.
В начале октября МИД Казахстана сообщал, что на горячую линию ведомства продолжают поступать обращения по аналогичным проблемам. В конце месяца местные СМИ со ссылкой на юриста Мейрмана Шекеева писали, что в страну вернулись 12 казахстанцев , которые уехали на заработки в Россию, но оказались завербованы в армию. В их числе -  19-летний Айнабек Келдибек .
ООН: Вербуя иностранцев, РФ занималась торговлей людьми
26 октября независимая международная комиссия по расследованию нарушений по Украине представила Генассамблее ООН доклад, в котором обвинила власти РФ в торговле людьми путем вербовки мужчин-иностранцев в вооруженные силы.
"Комиссия обнаружила убедительные доказательства того, что российские власти занимались торговлей людьми из 29 стран. Для этого использовались обман и принуждение, а также помощь агентов и агентств, действовавших в разных странах", - говорится в докменте.

content:
The Kanagawa Prefectural Museum of Cultural History in the eastern Japan city of Yokohama, south of Tokyo, attracted some 6,800 visitors, including locals, on its reopening day on Oct. 17, after a 21-month closure for improvements.
Located at the center of Yokohama's Bashamichi, a historic street, the museum houses and exhibits archeological artifacts, "ukiyo-e" traditional woodblock prints, historical materials and artworks related to Kanagawa. The current temporary exhibition will run until December.
Thanks to its majestic Western-style exterior, which was completed in 1904 and inherited from former Yokohama Specie Bank's main branch building, the state-designated important cultural property remained a popular sight even during the closure.
The improvement work mainly covered exhibition rooms, adding fixtures such as fine-tunable light-emitting diodes and antireflection film on glass cases.
Chief curator Yuta Jinno emphasized that the viewing environment has dramatically improved for visitors, particularly through soft spotlights that show off museum pieces better and antireflection film, both of which make it easier to view the exhibits and take photographs of them.
Jinno also noted that captions for each exhibit have been revised, with advice from school teachers included. "Clarity must be the top priority," he said, emphasizing efforts to ensure that even people with little knowledge of history can enjoy the museum.
"I hope many people, including first-time visitors, will 'discover' our extensive collections," he said.
Visitors have expressed satisfaction with the results.
A public servant in her 20s from Sagamihara, also Kanagawa, visited the museum with a friend. "I'm glad to see exhibits about my hometown's folk culture," she said with a smile. "I was able to take good pictures of them because the glass cases didn't reflect me."
Kiki Sui, 10, came to the museum with her mother. Sui said that she was fascinated by ukiyo-e prints and other historical materials that she had seen in history textbooks. Although she has just started learning history at school, "there was nothing I couldn't understand in the captions," she said. "An hour flew by before I knew it."
While the renovation has proved successful, museum officials pointed to major challenges, such as how to preserve the historic building and how to deal with persisting inflation.
The renovation work was carefully carried out so as not to damage the building's historic value.
"We've been in contact with the Cultural Affairs Agency for years to discuss what could be changed," Jinno said.
The museum is also designated under the cultural property protection law as a facility that can exhibit state-designated important cultural properties without prior approval of the agency.
The designation has enabled the museum to display choice items from its collection selected by curators for the ongoing temporary exhibition.
While carrying out administrative work needed for the renovation, curators held numerous lectures and educational events across the prefecture to keep the museum in the public eye and maintain relations with other museums and Kanagawa locals, according to Donna Kuwayama, a senior planning and outreach official of the museum.
Another issue is the increasingly severe financial environment surrounding museum management due to recent inflation.
The museum has had to reduce the size and number of pages of its catalogs due to soaring paper and ink costs. However, the museum hopes not to have to raise the entrance fee.
"At a time when admission fees at national museums can exceed 2,000 yen, we believe it's important to continue collecting and exhibiting items related to Kanagawa while keeping admission prices affordable so the public can visit easily," Kuwayama said.
Before the reopening, more than 100 people were lined up, eager to enter the renovated museum as early as possible. Kuwayama said it was "the proof that many people are interested in history and culture."
Expectations are running high that more people will visit not only Yokohama but also the museum, as the city will host the International Horticultural Expo 2027 next spring.
"We are eager to pursue new initiatives, including stronger social media outreach, while continuing to fulfill the museum's core function of preservation, research and public education," she said.
By Sakurako Nakagawa

Europe's crisis of discontent: Student and cost-of-living protests spread across EU
To display this content from YouTube, you must enable advertisement tracking and audience measurement.
One of your browser extensions seems to be blocking the video player from loading. To watch this content, you may need to disable it on this site.
Issued on:
A growing wave of discontent is sweeping across Europe. What began in France as student protests over deteriorating school conditions, teacher shortages and an education system under pressure has quickly grown into something much bigger: a groundswell of discontent over the rising cost of living, unaffordable housing and struggling public services.
The unrest has spread beyond France, with demonstrations in Belgium, Germany, Italy, Spain and Portugal. While many marches have remained peaceful, some have descended into violence, with clashes, looting and destruction. The response from authorities has also come under scrutiny for excessive use of force and mass arrests.
This discontent comes against a backdrop of mounting economic pressure. France, the EU's second-largest economy, is facing sluggish growth and rising public debt, projected to reach 120 percent of GDP by 2027. Meanwhile, inflation across both the European Union and the eurozone hit 3.8 percent in September, up from 2.1 percent in 2024.
Is Europe facing a wider crisis of public discontent and could this be a tipping point for governments already struggling to maintain public trust?
Programme prepared by Perrine Desplats, Oihana Almandoz, Isabelle Romero, Florine Hausfater and Charlotte Prudhomme

（德国之声中文网）美国国务院周四宣布的这轮新制裁，目标涵盖了 古巴 的石油和电子行业。
制裁名单中首次包括了两家 中国 企业，美方指控它们向古巴军方提供了电子产品及其他安全设备。
中国外交部对此表示强烈反对，称这些制裁是非法的，属于典型的“长臂管辖”。
中国外交部发言人郭嘉昆在新闻发布会上表示：“中方坚决反对美方干涉和破坏中古合作。”
他警告称，北京将采取“一切必要措施”来维护本国企业的权益。
更多内容： 特朗普威胁要“解放或接管”古巴
自1月以来，华盛顿对古巴实施了破坏力极强的新制裁及石油封锁，导致古巴经济陷入瘫痪，并引发了大范围停电和生活必需品短缺。
美国总统特朗普曾暗示可能采取军事干预，以推翻古巴执政的共产党。上个月，美国国务卿还敦促古巴民众与美国情报机构开展合作。
周四被列入制裁名单的中国企业包括国有企业中国电子进出口总公司（CEIEC），以及民营企业北京华成昊普科技有限公司（Beijing H&C Technologies）。
制裁名单还涵盖了安妮·罗德里格斯·拉斯特雷斯（Any Rodriguez Lastres），她是古巴最大军方控股商业集团古巴企业管理集团（GAESA）负责人之女。

JOHANNESBURG - South Africa’s once-dominant African National Congress (ANC) was headed for its worst-ever election performance on Friday with about a third of support after 80% of the votes from local government polls had been counted.
Wednesday’s municipal elections were dominated by concerns over failing water and power supplies in one of Africa’s wealthiest nations which became a democracy in 1994 when the ANC took power.
With final results expected by Sunday, the election authority dashboard showed the ANC was still the largest party with 31.8% of votes after 80% had been counted.
Projections released on Thursday by the Council for Scientific and Industrial Research (CSIR), a state-funded research body, put its support at nearly 32%.
This was its lowest score yet for the party after it secured just over 40% at the 2024 national polls and 46% at the previous municipal elections in 2021.
At the heart of South Africa’s anti-apartheid struggle, the ANC — the party of jailed liberation hero-turned-president Nelson Mandela — took nearly 70% of the national vote in 2004.
“This is the most severe result that the ANC would have feared,” political analyst Daniel Silke told AFP. “It’s the ANC’s worst result in history.”
“It will undermine its ability to exert authority across South Africa, not just at a local level, but frankly at a national level as well,” he told AFP.
“And opposition parties will be smelling blood when it comes to the next election in 2029.”
The party now led by President Cyril Ramaphosa has borne the brunt of criticism about years of municipal mismanagement that have left South Africans grappling with failing water supplies, persistent power cuts and crumbling public services.
The pro-business, centre-right Democratic Alliance (DA) was placing second with 24.2% of votes, according to the 80% count. This was up from nearly 22% in the 2021 local government election.

LONDON - Technology shares plunged on Friday after an unnerving rout on Wall Street as fears grew that Democrats would accelerate a backlash against AI after their crushing defeat of President Donald Trump’s Republicans in the US midterm elections.
The Tokyo and Seoul stock markets closed out their weeks with losses of six percent following the Nasdaq’s 5.5% collapse on Thursday, its worst showing since April last year when Trump unveiled his wide-ranging global tariffs.
“The tech sell-off has intensified, with the pain of the brutal sell-off on Wall Street carried straight through to Asia and knocking sentiment in Europe,” said Susannah Streeter, chief investment strategist at Wealth Club.
“Big worries are colliding — the buildout of data centres looks set to slow, which risks shredding the spending spree underpinning the boom, right at the time that investors have become super nervous about returns on this massive investment,” she said.
The London, Paris and Frankfurt stock markets shed around two percent nearing the halfway stage despite featuring few technology firms.
Elsewhere, the dollar firmed before key US jobs data Friday, and oil prices steadied following steep declines this week.
Futures contracts pointed to a rebound on the Nasdaq later this afternoon, but further declines for the broad-based S&P 500.
Data centres have faced broad opposition from US voters across the political spectrum, and many midterm winners have pledged to put the brakes on such projects.
Analysts said investors were also spooked by a call from progressive US Senator Bernie Sanders for a national moratorium on their building.
The results compounded already heightened fears about the hundreds of billions firms had pumped into the sector and when they would see a return, while the recent spike in borrowing costs also fuelled concerns about their financial position.
Bloomberg said the Philadelphia Semiconductor Index had collapsed around 16% this week, putting it on course for its worst run since April last year.
On Seoul’s Kospi stocks index, chip giant SK hynix slumped 10% and its rival Samsung lost 6.4%.
The Kospi more than doubled in value between the end of December and mid-June, when it hit a record, but is down almost 50% over the past four and a half months.
Tokyo dived six percent on Friday as the Japanese tech investor SoftBank gave back more than 10%, while the chipmaker Kioxia collapsed 8.7% and the semiconductor tester Advantest retreated five percent.
A 4.7% drop for the Taiwanese chip giant TSMC dragged down Taipei’s Taiex.
“The blood is in the streets, folks,” wrote Neil Wilson, analyst at Saxo Markets, though he added that the sell-off looked “overdone”.
“The fear is a total momentum unwind as Democrats pace the frontier and kibosh data centre build-out,” he said.

content:
JERUSALEM - Israel’s opposition saw a new path on Friday to oust Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu as one of its leaders backtracked on demands that ultra-Orthodox Jews serve in the military, opening the door to a once improbable alliance with the community.
Neither Netanyahu nor opposition chief Gadi Eisenkot reached a majority in the Oct 27 election, with Israeli society highly polarised over Netanyahu and worn down by three years of war.
Eisenkot, a former military commander whose campaign sought to appeal to secular and liberal Israelis, could form a government with Israeli-Arabs, whose seat count soared on anger over Netanyahu’s far-right government.
But an alliance with Israeli-Arabs faces strong disagreement from opposition partner Avigdor Liberman, a onetime aide to Netanyahu who now sharply criticises the prime minister but shares his hawkish views on the Palestinians.
Liberman said on Friday he would not back down on refusing to work with Israeli-Arabs but called for talks with ultra-Orthodox Jews, even though he has berated the community for years and ran on promises to end its exemption from Israel’s mandatory military service.
Listing the most important goals as removing Netanyahu and avoiding new elections, Liberman said it was time to compromise and “understand that trying to have everything risks getting nothing”.
“This also includes the issue of the conscription law,” he said in a social media statement.
“This pains me, and I know it pains many others as well. But given the full range of challenges we face today, the national interest of the State of Israel and the Jewish people must take precedence over all other considerations.”
President Isaac Herzog plans to announce on Sunday who will have the first chance to form a government — most logically Eisenkot, as he has received the most endorsements thanks to support from Israeli-Arabs.
Yair Golan, Israel’s main left-wing leader and part of the opposition bloc, said “serious work” was under way to form a coalition.
“I’m more optimistic than I was on the Wednesday morning after the election results. There is progress. There is a will,” he said.
Ultra-Orthodox wield power again
Ultra-Orthodox Jews’ exemption from military service has fuelled widespread resentment among other Israelis, with reservists serving multiple tours in the wars Israel has been fighting since the October 7, 2023 attack by Hamas.
Netanyahu, while personally secular, has long relied on the ultra-Orthodox, accepting that the community — which accounts for around 14% of the population and has a much higher birth rate than the Israeli average — can send children to religious schools rather than the army.
But he stopped short of enshrining the military exemption into law, angering the two main ultra-Orthodox parties which left his government, although they did not seek to remove him.
One of the parties, United Torah Judaism, declined Thursday to recommend Netanyahu to form the next government during consultations with Herzog, but without supporting Eisenkot.
Yaakov Asher, a lawmaker from the party, welcomed Liberman’s U-turn and said that its rabbis would assess any formal proposal of an alliance.
“It is encouraging to learn of the flexibility of all political actors on the subject of conscription,” Asher said.
“It is painful to think how much incitement and hatred between brothers could have been avoided had that same flexibility been demonstrated in recent years.”
His party and the other ultra-Orthodox formation, Shas, together have 13 seats, enough to put Eisenkot in power.
Liberman put up posters during the campaign vowing to crack down on the “draft-dodgers”. During an appearance earlier this year, he described ultra-Orthodox Jews as “anti-Jewish” for their demands.
His Yisrael Beiteinu party won seven seats, the fewest among the five core opposition parties. Naftali Bennett, a former prime minister, also ran heavily on promises to end the military exemption, repeatedly vowing “not one shekel” from the government for religious students who do not serve in the army.
Bennett has not commented on Liberman’s about-face.
Only Golan, the left-wing leader, explicitly backed cooperation with lawmakers from the Arab minority, who make up 20% of the population.
Netanyahu campaigned by warning that voting for the opposition would empower Israeli-Arabs, descendants of Palestinians who stayed after Israel’s creation in 1948.

ISTANBUL - A former cabinet minister and senior ruling party official was placed in detention pending trial on Friday as part of an investigation into a multi-billion-dollar investment fund scandal, the Turkish state news agency Anadolu reported.
Fatma Betul Sayan Kaya was remanded in custody by an Istanbul court on charges of “violating the capital markets law” and “membership of an organisation established for the purpose of committing crimes”, it said.
Kaya served as families minister from 2016 to 2018 and until recently was a deputy chair of President Recep Tayyip Erdogan’s ruling AKP.
She stepped down from the party role on Sept 26 after an opposition lawmaker sought clarification over claims she and her husband had made substantial profits through transactions involving shares which they allegedly offloaded before the scandal broke.
According to the prosecutors’ referral document quoted by Anadolu, Kaya is suspected of having access to insider investment information.
It said she knew Erdin Ozel, a manager of the Tera Group, one of the firms at the heart of the investigation, and had been in touch with him “intensively” during the investment process.
Tera Group had invested heavily in shares in shipbuilding firm Ozata Denizcilik, it said.
Suspect share sale
Prosecutors said Kaya had invested in Ozata Denizcilik “in April 2026 and the shares were sold on September 16,” a day before the scandal hit the headlines.
The crisis erupted when several funds were unable to satisfy investor redemption demands, prompting the Capital Markets Board (SPK) to place seven companies into liquidation on Sept 17.
The companies managed 131 investment funds with assets reportedly worth $17 billion.
Prosecutors said proceeds from selling Ozata Denizcilik shares were normally settled within two business days but in Kaya’s case, they were sold through a transfer arrangement and the balance credited to her account the same day.
“It appears the suspect knew the likely price movement range of the stocks and also carried out transactions knowing that the liquidation decision would be taken,” the prosecutors’ document said.
Market manipulation probe
In September, an opposition Yeni Parti MP sought clarification over claims Kaya invested 63 million lira ($26.5 million).
At the time, the MP also raised questions about her husband Ilyas Kaya, who allegedly invested 100 million lira and earned back 826 million lira.
The pair were called in for questioning by investigators on Thursday, with Turkish media saying she was quizzed for over nine hours.
Overnight, a court placed her under arrest but granted her husband conditional release.
It also granted conditional release to former SPK boss Ibrahim Omer Gonul, whose four-year tenure ended in April and who is also under investigation, it said.
Since mid-September, prosecutors have been looking into allegations of widespread market manipulation affecting the savings of nearly half a million investors.
On Tuesday, Justice Minister Akin Gurlek said 112 people had been jailed pending trial in the scandal.
He said investigators had uncovered a “comprehensive criminal network” that infiltrated the highest levels of Turkey’s financial markets.

content:
Sheila Williams has taken on an extra waitress job to help pay for her heating oil
Published
A woman from East Sussex says she is having to take on extra work to pay for the soaring cost of her heating oil.
Sheila Williams, from Golden Cross, has taken on a waitress job for the winter to help her pay her bills.
She said her oil bill had doubled since the start of 2026 and the extra job was needed to help pay for it.
A government spokesperson said: "We have pledged £53m in support for vulnerable households on heating oil and removed the 4% tariff on home heating oil."
Williams, who has lived alone in a park home for seven years, said: "Words cannot express how upset I am about this."
Thousands of homes across Sussex are not connected to the gas mains and rely on oil.
A household wanting to fill a 1,000-litre tank could be facing a bill of more than £970.
Nigel Wanstall, from Sheffield Park, said: "We've no heating at all because I can't afford to fill my oil tank.
"The price of it is so expensive.
"We use an open fire in the lounge and an electric blanket in bed."
Nigel Wanstall said he could not afford to fill his oil tank
Jon Reardon is director at Rye Oil, which supplies 15,000 residents in south-east England.
He said: "On average the oil price has doubled since the war started in the Middle East.
"There are a lot of our customers trying to hold off ordering oil for as long as possible.
"It's had a big impact on our sales."
The issue of rising heating oil prices was debated in Westminster on Wednesday.
Polly Billington, energy minister, said: "Thousands of heating oil customers felt they had nowhere to turn when they paid the price of rising oil and gas costs earlier this year.
"We won't accept that. Energy is an essential good and people should not have to think twice about whether they're protected in the market.
"That's why we will reform the sector, holding heating oil suppliers to account and giving consumers confidence that they will get a fair deal."

（德国之声中文网）现年69岁的澳门前民主派立法会议员区锦新去年7月30日 被澳门警方以涉嫌向“境外反华组织”提供资料等理由拘捕 。区锦新是澳门民主派组织新澳门学社创会成员，曾担任澳门立法会议员20年，至2021年不再参选。离开议会后，区锦新仍持续关注澳门政府的施政、民主发展、劳工权益及社会议题，多年来参与及举办 悼念六四活动 。
本周五，澳门初级法院宣判，区锦新“颠覆国家政权罪”、“与澳门特别行政区以外的组织、团体或个人建立联系作出危害国家安全的行为罪”和一项“违反保密罪”罪成，分别判监11年3个月、3年9个月及9个月。按照澳门《刑法典》数罪并罚规定，法院最后决定判处区锦新入狱12年半。
法院在判决新闻稿中称，区锦新在早前的闭门庭审中，对大部分基础事实没有异议，并称他“承认勾结和串通多个境外组织的事实行为构成犯罪” ，“并认同辩护律师为其辩护的意见”。法院还称，尽管嫌犯为初犯，且承认作出相当部分的犯罪事实，“惟其故意程度极高，有关犯罪的不法性程度及可能造成的后果均十分严重。“
判决新闻稿中称，“区锦新长期亲身协助和配合境外敌对组织收集、预备及公然散布诸多明显充斥属于颠覆国家政权的政治主张以及属于虚假且明显有所歪曲的图片及资讯，借此勾连境外敌对组织的非法手段共谋煽动本澳居民对中央人民政府的仇恨，以图推翻、破坏《中华人民共和国宪法》所确立的国家根本制度，相关颠覆行为即使在《维护国家安全法》于2023年修订生效后仍然持续。” 此外，判决新闻稿指区锦新在2021年担任立法会议员期间，将涉及澳门赌牌续期的闭门会议秘密内容泄露予境外组织，符合“违反保密罪”。
澳门特区政府在法院宣判后发表声明，表示尊重及支持法院裁决，呼吁社会各界尊重法院裁决。
区锦新的妻子：一场毫无根据的迫害
区锦新的妻子郑妙珊（Virginia Cheang）表示裁决不可接受并在一封公开信中谴责该案是政治审判。信中写道：“从闭门审判到公开宣判，这到底算什么？这是一场政治审判，是一场旨在羞辱人格、毫无根据的迫害。”
现居伦敦的区锦新的女儿区汉儿（Au Hon I）此前曾向美联社透露，家属聘请的律师无法在狱中会见区锦新，且家人已近一年无法与他进行任何交流。但法院表示，在法律程序进行期间，已指派一名经区锦新本人认可的律师为其提供代理，且他已行使了辩护权。法院还称准许其家属定期探视。
区锦新的国际法律顾问迈克尔·波拉克（Michael Polak）指出，作为葡萄牙公民的区锦新本不应因其非暴力的信念而遭到拘留；他敦促葡萄牙和欧盟要求允许区锦新离开澳门。
波拉克表示：“针对区先生的这些捏造指控所引发的一系列事件，根本称不上是真正意义上的审判或定罪；这让澳门无异于世界上那些最压迫的国家。”
人权观察：造成寒蝉效应
人权观察（Human Rights Watch）在裁决后发表声明，指“澳门政府对民主派领袖区锦新的不公正检控和严厉判刑，对澳门所有和平批评政府的人士造成寒蝉效应。澳门打压民主派声音，是中国政府更广泛打压异议及基本自由的一环。”现任人权观察亚洲区副主任王松莲表示，区锦新遭受长时间审前羁押丶闭门审讯，以及选择代表律师的权利受到限制，显示案件的司法程序存在违反正当法律程序及公平审讯权利的问题。
由于区锦新拥有 葡萄牙 国籍（欧盟公民），欧盟对外行动署及欧洲议会去年8月发表决议谴责澳门当局的逮捕行动，称此举加剧了对中国澳门地区“政治多元化持续遭到侵蚀”的担忧。欧盟还重申，尊重人权和基本自由是《澳门基本法》和前葡萄牙殖民地所建立的“ 一国两制 ”原则的核心要素。
澳门曾是葡萄牙殖民地，1999年回归中国成为特别行政区。澳门拥有独立的政治和法律体系，也是中国境内唯一博彩业合法的城市。澳门当局于2009年为澳门基本法第23条完成立法，并于2023年完成修订。该法律条文规定，“澳门特别行政区应自行立法禁止任何叛国、分裂国家、煽动叛乱、颠覆中央人民政府及窃取国家机密的行为，禁止外国的政治性组织或团体在澳门特别行政区进行政治活动，禁止澳门特别行政区的政治性组织或团体与外国的政治性组织或团体建立联系。”

Dos jóvenes, entre ellos un menor, murieron y 16 personas resultaron heridas en un accidente de autobús en el este de Francia , según un balance provisional de las autoridades. El accidente se produjo este viernes (06.11.2026) hacia las 07:30, hora local, en la carretera departamental D22, a la altura del municipio de Lent, e implica un autobús de una línea de transporte interurbano, según la prefectura de Ain.
El vehículo, que circulaba entre Lyon y Bourg-en-Bresse, transportaba a 43 personas, entre ellas 15 menores que iban a sus centros escolares, según la fiscalía de esta última localidad, que abrió una investigación por homicidio vial. "El conductor, que se encuentra hospitalizado, aún no ha podido ser interrogado hasta el momento", precisó el ministerio público, que habla de tres heridos en estado crítico.
Chocó contra un árbol
Según Yves Cristin, el alcalde de Lent, el autobús "se salió de la carretera y chocó contra un árbol en la cuneta" por causas aún desconocidas. El sitio del impacto, tras una curva a la derecha, no presentaba dificultades especiales meteorológicas a primera hora de la mañana.
Según un comunicado del Ministerio de Transportes, se han movilizado 102 bomberos, 58 vehículos y 50 gendarmes. También se han desplegado cuatro helicópteros y ocho equipos del SMUR (servicio móvil de emergencias y reanimación). El balance de víctimas es provisional, según las autoridades.
Los accidentes en el transporte público son poco comunes en Francia. En enero de 2025, una estudiante de liceo murió y 20 alumnos resultaron heridos cuando un autobús escolar, cuyo conductor había consumido estupefacientes, volcó sobre una calzada cerca de Châteaudun. En 2019, un accidente de Flixbus dejó 33 heridos .
lgc (afp, efe)

In 2025, an international trial found that people treated for colon cancer were more likely to be alive eight years later if they had received long-term exercise coaching.
The question facing doctors now is less whether people with cancer should exercise, and rather how they should build it into routine care. In the US, that shift is reaching hospital standards. From January 2027, breast cancer centers must screen patients' physical function and recommend exercise or physical therapy where needed.
Yet experts caution that the trial's findings may not apply to every cancer or every patient.
Does exercise improve colon cancer survival?
The 2025 trial, called CHALLENGE , was led by the Canadian Cancer Trials Group. It began enrolling patients in 2009 and published its results in 2025.
The trial's 889 participants came from six countries, most from Canada and Australia. All had finished surgery and chemotherapy for stage 2 or 3 colon cancer, which had not spread to distant organs.
Half received only health education materials on exercise and healthy eating. The other half additionally met a physical activity consultant for three years.
In the exercise group, the target was similar to adding 45 to 60 minutes of brisk walking, three to four times a week. The amount and type of activity varied from person to person, said Tormod Skogstad Nilsen, a cancer exercise researcher in Norway. But he said participants achieved lasting increases in their physical activity.
Exercise helped. People in the exercise group were less likely to see their cancer come back, to develop a new cancer or to die. In all, 93 had at least one of these setbacks, compared with 131 in the health education group.
What does 'living longer' mean for cancer patients?
In cancer research, living longer usually means a larger share of people is still alive at a given point. It does not promise anyone a set number of extra years.
Eight years after joining CHALLENGE, about 90 of every 100 people in the exercise group were alive, compared with about 83 of every 100 in the health education group. That is about 7% more people alive in the group who had guided exercise.

Can exercise prevent cancer?
For people without cancer, the evidence comes from studies that follow people's habits and health over many years. These can show a link, but not prove cause and effect. Active people may also eat better or smoke less.
In  another 2025 study , more than 85,000 adults in the United Kingdom wore a wrist tracker for a week. Over about six years, those who moved most had a 26% lower risk of 13 cancers, including breast and colorectal cancer, than those who moved least.
Even light activity, such as household chores, was linked to lower risk. The link held after researchers accounted for lifestyle, weight and other health conditions.
Earlier research, based on people's self-reporting, has led to similar conclusions. A 2016 analysis of 1.44 million adults in the US and Europe linked free-time activity to a lower risk of many cancers, largely regardless of weight or smoking.
A trial to prove prevention is unlikely: Many cancers take years to develop, so it would need huge numbers of people followed for a long time.
Could exercise help people with breast, prostate or other cancers?
CHALLENGE included only people with colon cancer. But how it picked participants offers a clue: Before joining, they had to pass a fitness test.
Anna Campbell, a professor of clinical exercise science at Edinburgh Napier University in Scotland, sees that as a guide.
"I think patients with any other cancer stage II and III who have a reasonable baseline level of fitness and no major comorbidities that would prevent them from undertaking moderate to vigorous activity could be considered for similar interventions," she said. Comorbidities are other health conditions.
Nilsen noted some people decline to join exercise trials because they feel too unwell or tired, or do not want to exercise. "Hence, study populations are typically younger, 'healthier', and most times slightly more motivated compared to a clinical population," he said.
Why does long-term support matter for cancer patients who exercise?
The coaching aimed to make activity a lasting habit, and Campbell said that is where the trial's value lies.
"The main success of the study is that it enabled the participants to become independent exercisers staying active in a safe and effective and individualized way," she said.
Nilsen agreed. Helping people become more active "in their own environment," without depending on a well-equipped training center, "would likely lead to more sustainable activity behavioral changes," he said.
He is wary of fixed targets, however. "Exercise should be tailored to each individual and the challenges they face, rather than striving to reach a given minimum of exercise required," though health care resources may not always allow it, he added.
Do cancer patients get exercise support?
In  a 2024 survey  of 549 people with cancer, only one in 10 had been referred to an exercise service. Yet almost three in four thought their oncologist should raise the subject.
"There are some excellent examples of effective pathways but these are few and far between," said Campbell. Good services bring everyone on board, from surgeons to community fitness instructors.
"Ideally, one person in the clinical setting needs to champion the program to link all the team together."
What could exercise support look like in routine cancer care?
Campbell expects CHALLENGE's regular coaching will be cut back in everyday care. Apps and live online group sessions could still work, she said, if run by properly trained staff.
One recent study of live online exercise engaged patients from poorer backgrounds, in rural areas and with advanced cancer. "It answered some of the barriers, such as cost, travel and lack of confidence," she said.
Patients can ask their care team what exercise is safe for them and what support exists.
According to Nilsen, a training session can bring structure and company. "You made it here, despite your feeling unwell or fatigued this morning, so you feel mastery based on that," he said.

summary: A major trial found more colon cancer patients were alive eight years after treatment with long-term exercise coaching. But what does "living longer" mean, and who does it apply to?

Their Majesties King Maha Vajiralongkorn and Queen Suthida travelled along Bangkok's Chao Phraya River in the Royal Barge Procession on November 6, 2026, to perform the royal Kathin robe-offering ceremony at Wat Arun Ratchawararam Ratchawaramahawihan.
Large crowds gathered along both banks of the river to pay their respects and offer their best wishes as the royal procession passed.
The ceremony was held to commemorate the auspicious occasion of Her Majesty Queen Suthida's fourth-cycle, or 48th, birthday anniversary on June 3, 2026.
The procession comprised 52 ceremonial barges arranged in five columns and three lines, following traditional royal practice.
The Royal Thai Navy, Bureau of the Royal Household and Fine Arts Department had worked together to restore and repair the vessels, while naval personnel underwent continuous rowing rehearsals to ensure the procession proceeded smoothly.
Four principal royal barges took part: Suphannahong, Anekkachatphutchong, Narai Song Suban King Rama IX and Anantanakkharat.
The Anantanakkharat carried the royal Kathin robes in an ornate ceremonial pavilion, while animal-figure barges and escort vessels completed the formation.
Their Majesties departed Amphorn Sathan Residential Hall at Dusit Palace by royal motorcade at 3pm, accompanied by Her Royal Highness Princess Sirivannavari Nariratana Rajakanya, His Royal Highness Prince Dipangkorn Rasmijoti and Chaokhun Phra Sineenatha Bilasakalyani.
Upon arriving at Wasukri Pier, they were received by privy councillors, the prime minister, the president of the Supreme Court, the president of Parliament and senior government officials.
The Commander-in-Chief of the Royal Thai Navy, acting as commander of the procession, presented a report on the number of participating vessels and naval personnel.
Their Majesties then boarded the Royal Barge Suphannahong, while Princess Sirivannavari, Prince Dipangkorn and Chaokhun Phra Sineenatha boarded the Royal Barge Anekkachatphutchong.
A military guard of honour paid tribute as the band performed the Royal Anthem.
The captain of Suphannahong subsequently requested royal permission to begin the journey. The secretary-general of the Royal Household conveyed the royal command authorising the procession to depart from Wasukri Pier towards Wat Arun.
As the barges moved along the Chao Phraya River, ceremonial drums, conch shells, traditional horns, trumpets and pipes sounded from vessels throughout the procession.
The guard of honour rendered its salute while the military band played March Thong Chai Chaloemphon, accompanying the ceremonial fleet along the river.
Upon reaching Wat Arun, the Royal Barge Anantanakkharat approached the ceremonial landing near the temple's principal prang.
Royal ceremonial officials carried the Kathin robes from the pavilion aboard the barge to the temple's ordination hall.
The Royal Barge Suphannahong then berthed at the landing in front of the ordination hall, allowing Their Majesties to disembark.
A guard of honour saluted as the band again performed the Royal Anthem.
The Royal Barge Anekkachatphutchong subsequently came alongside Suphannahong, enabling Princess Sirivannavari, Prince Dipangkorn and Chaokhun Phra Sineenatha to disembark and accompany Their Majesties to the ordination hall.
Inside the hall, His Majesty lit incense sticks and candles in homage to Phra Buddha Thammisorarat Lokathatdilok, the temple's principal Buddha image.
The King then presented the royal Kathin robes in accordance with royal Buddhist tradition.
Members of the public continued to follow the ceremony, which formed the central purpose of the royal journey.
Following the Kathin ceremony, Their Majesties, accompanied by the royal family members and Chaokhun Phra Sineenatha, visited an exhibition entitled Wat Arun's Prang: From Rattanakosin Identity towards World Heritage.
The royal party subsequently proceeded to the monument of King Buddha Loetla Nabhalai, or King Rama II.
His Majesty laid a floral tribute and lit incense sticks and candles before paying homage to the royal statue.
Their Majesties then returned to Amphorn Sathan Residential Hall at Dusit Palace, concluding the royal Kathin merit-making ceremony and the Royal Barge Procession.
The occasion highlighted Thailand's traditional craftsmanship, naval skills and boatbuilding heritage, while continuing a longstanding royal tradition closely associated with the country's Buddhist culture.

El juicio contra cuatro presuntos cabecillas de la organización de extrema derecha 'Reino de Alemania' (Königreich Deutschland), entre ellos el autoproclamado monarca Peter Fitzek, comenzó este viernes (06.11.2026) ante la Audiencia Territorial de Düsseldorf, en el oeste del país. Las fechas del juicio están programadas hasta septiembre de 2027.
La Fiscalía General del Estado ha acusado a los cuatro de integración en banda criminal y de diferentes delitos fiscales, financieros y de falsificación de documentos. Según la acusación, fundaron el 'Reino de Alemania' en 2012 con el objetivo de sustituir con sus estructuras pseudoestatales a la República Federal Alemana , a la que no reconocían, en línea con el movimiento extremista de los Reichsbürger ( o 'ciudadanos del reino'), en el que representaba el grupo más numeroso, ya que se atribuía contar con seis mil miembros, aunque las autoridades los cifran en unos pocos miles.
Así, crearon supuestamente un sistema bancario y aseguradoras, un registro civil que expedía documentos de identificación del 'Reino de Alemania' e incluso emitieron su propia divisa, el 'nuevo marco alemán'. Tan sólo entre 2020 y 2025 la organización ingresó aproximadamente diez millones de euros a través de transacciones bancarias y negocios de seguros irregulares, así como a través de donativos y tasas de seminarios, asegura la Fiscalía. El grupo fue prohibido en mayo del año pasado .
Dado que estos ingresos no se declararon y que los empleados del 'Reino' no cotizaban ni pagaban impuestos, se le atribuye al grupo haber defraudado más de dos millones de euros al Estado. A Peter Fitzek, de 61 años, una figura excéntrica que se presentaba a sí misma como 'rey de Alemania', se le acusa de haber tenido el control absoluto de la organización y de haber determinado su orientación ideológica, mientras que los otros acusados tenían también papeles de mando subalternos.
lgc (efe, afp)

PARIS - The world is on track for 2026 to be the second-hottest year on record as an exceptionally strong El Nino weather pattern turbocharges human-driven global warming, the EU’s climate monitor said on Friday.
This year still has a “20% chance of tying or exceeding” 2024 as the warmest ever seen, the Copernicus Climate Change Service said in a monthly bulletin.
Global temperatures are now “virtually certain” to exceed 1.5C above pre-industrial levels in 2026, Copernicus said.
The four-year average from 2023 to 2026 is also expected to top 1.5C, the preferred limit set in the Paris Agreement to avert the worst impacts of climate change.
The world experienced its warmest October on record, with average global surface air temperatures 1.75C above pre-industrial times, an era defined as 1850-1900, Copernicus added.
It was the third straight month exceeding 1.5C.
“October has continued the pattern of remarkable global warmth, with record global and surface ocean temperatures,” said Samantha Burgess, strategic lead for climate at the European Centre for Medium-Range Weather Forecasts (ECMWF), which operates Copernicus.
“An exceptionally strong El Nino is adding further heat to a climate already warmed by human activities,” she said.
The latest bulletin comes as nations prepare to meet on Monday for the UN’s two-week COP31 climate summit in Turkey after a year marked by deadly floods in Nepal, searing heatwaves in Europe and major wildfires in Indonesia.
El Nino has yet to peak
Global forecasters have been warning for months that this El Nino, which is expected to peak later this year, would likely become the strongest ever observed.
The intensifying weather phenomenon set an all-time temperature record in a key Pacific zone last month, Copernicus said.
The warming phase of a natural climate cycle, El Nino temporarily raises sea temperatures in the tropical Pacific, triggering changes in weather that can increase the risk of drought and flooding, and exacerbate man-made global warming.
Forecasters say El Nino could help make 2027 the hottest year on record.
Nations agreed at the 2015 UN climate talks in Paris to keep global warming “well below” 2C above pre-industrial levels, while pursuing efforts to limit it to 1.5C.
But the United Nations declared in September that the long-term 1.5C target would be missed in a matter of years.
Scientists say it is crucial to reduce greenhouse gas emissions from fossil fuels to limit the period of “overshoot” above 1.5C and bring temperatures back down as quickly as possible.

WELLINGTON - New Zealand is poised for one of the closest elections in its history on Saturday, as the country votes following a campaign dominated by the cost of living and an economy hammered by the war in the Middle East.
Kiwis are struggling to make ends meet — the price of basic goods remains stubbornly high and unemployment at its highest in over a decade.
Polls suggest that neither the ruling conservative National Party nor the opposition centre-left Labour have offered a programme compelling enough to win the seats needed to govern by themselves.
Prime Minister Christopher Luxon has hoped promises of no new taxes can help his right-wing coalition cling to power after three fractious years in office, two failed bids by his own party to oust him as leader and an economy in the doldrums.
Speaking at a rally in Auckland, he urged voters to “stick to the plan that’s working”.
“Don’t risk a Labour government,” he added.
Pushing to replace him is opposition leader and former premier Chris Hipkins, whose Labour party has proposed a sweeping package of measures to help relieve the economic pressure on New Zealanders. (Story continues below)
Qiulae Wong, leader of the centrist Opportunity Party, has emerged as a potential kingmaker if her party can pass the 5% threshold required to obtain party-list seats without a constituency candidate win. (Photo: AFP)
Opportunity knocks
With the polls so close, attention has turned to New Zealand’s minor parties — in particular the upstart centrist Opportunity Party.
“It’s one of the closest elections, certainly, and one of the hardest elections to predict in my professional life,” David Capie, a professor at Victoria University of Wellington, told AFP.
“I really think it’s really too close to call. There are just so many moving parts.”
On the streets of Wellington, many New Zealanders told AFP they were struggling to get by and thinking twice about paying for things they had once taken for granted.
“The prices are really high,” said Jay Ikaua, a cultural adviser.
“I have to make conscious decisions. Do I buy that? Do I not buy that?”
“And it’s the things we need — public transport, food.”
Rachel Shardlow, a 26-year-old public servant, said the cost of living was “shocking”.
“All I’m doing is paying my rent and my bills, and I’m struggling to put money into savings and save for my future.”
New Zealand has strict election day laws which come into force at midnight, governing media reporting and political campaigning to prevent voters being swayed.
Polls close at 7pm and results are expected to start being released shortly afterwards.
New Zealand’s electoral commission says it expects results from 50% of voting places to be counted by 10pm with the rest are expected by 11.30pm.
Voters want ‘optimism’
New Zealanders have been able to cast their votes since October 26.
As of Thursday, almost 1.7 million people have already cast their ballots, according to the electoral commission — lower than during former prime minister Jacinda Ardern’s landslide victory in 2020 but higher than the last poll.
A final opinion poll released on Friday put Labour at 30% of the vote, just ahead of the National Party.
Under New Zealand’s mixed-member proportional representation (MMP) system, voters must tick two options — a general party list as well as an individual member to represent their electorate.
And the ruling party could still clinch more seats thanks to a so-called “overhang” — in which more lawmakers are returned to parliament than the usual 120.
Polls also put the Opportunity Party on over five percent — the threshold needed to gain seats in parliament without an electorate candidate win. If the poll results translate into votes, it would be the first time since MMP was introduced that a minor party with no links to the two main factions would have done so.
The party is led by former KPMG consultant Qiulae Wong, who has said she could work with either of the two parties if elected.
“I think New Zealanders are really tired of politicians’ name-calling, the bickering, the political point-scoring,” she told AFP last week.
“They want something different, and they really want some hope and optimism for the future.”

content:
El regreso del entrenador Vincent Kompany a entrenamientos y partidos del Bayern Múnich sigue siendo una incógnita. "He mantenido conversaciones telefónicas muy buenas con él en los últimos días. Se muestra muy positivo y parece estar en camino hacia una recuperación completa. No hemos fijado una fecha, pero el parón por partidos internacionales nos brinda una buena oportunidad para reflexionar y evaluar cuándo podrá volver", declaró su asistente, Aaron Danks, antes del partido de la Bundesliga que se disputará este sábado contra el Mainz 05.
Kompany está actualmente de baja debido a una irritación de las meninges (también llamada "signo meníngeo", distinto de la meningitis). El técnico de 40 años recibió el alta hospitalaria la semana pasada.
Larga lista de lesionados
Además de Kompany, el equipo muniqués tampoco podrá contar en Maguncia con los lesionados Luis Díaz , Serge Gnabry, Ismael Saibari y Jamal Musiala . En el caso de Díaz y Musiala, existe la esperanza de que, tras el parón de dos semanas por los compromisos de las selecciones nacionales, puedan "incorporarse de lleno a los entrenamientos con el grupo", señaló Danks. Se trata de un "progreso muy positivo". No obstante, el técnico inglés prefirió no establecer una "fecha límite" para su regreso, ya que "es complicado".
Pavlovic y Neuer son duda
Por otro lado, el entrenador interino del Bayern espera poder contar contra el Mainz con Aleksandar Pavlovic, quien arrastraba molestias. "Ha completado el entrenamiento sin problemas. Solo tenemos que ver cómo responden sus piernas", explicó Danks. También indicó que la situación del portero Manuel Neuer tiene "buena pinta". Por el contrario, sugirió que Alphonso Davies podría descansar: "Hay algunos jugadores a los que vamos a dar un respiro debido a la gran carga de partidos; Alphonso Davies podría ser uno de ellos. Debemos ser prudentes".
summary: Kompany sufrió irritación de las meninges y salió del hospital, pero por el momento no regresa a las canchas.

Unsettled weather is expected to continue in upper Thailand on November 6–7, with thundershowers, gusty winds, hail and isolated heavy rain.
The department urged people to take care in thundershowers and gusty winds, avoid open areas, keep clear of areas beneath large trees and stay away from unsecured billboards.
Rainfall is forecast to increase in the South from November 7–9, with heavy rain in many areas and isolated very heavy rain.
The department urged residents to watch for the effects of accumulated rain, which could trigger flash floods and rapid runoff from forested areas, particularly on slopes near waterways in the foothills and in low-lying areas.
Another high-pressure system, or cold air mass, from China is spreading over upper Thailand and the South China Sea.
This will strengthen easterly winds over Thailand and the Gulf of Thailand.
Waves will exceed 2 metres in areas with thundershowers in the Andaman Sea and the Gulf of Thailand.
The department advised mariners in both waters to check their routes, navigate with caution and avoid areas with thundershowers.
The department urged people to plan daily activities and journeys carefully during the advisory period to stay safe and reduce potential impacts.
It also asked people to keep following its advisories.
Updates are available around the clock on the department’s website or by calling 0-2399-4012-13 or 1182.
The next advisory is due at 5am on November 7.
