Thai children under 18 must show birth certificates to leave Thailand Legacy Thailand’s Immigration Bureau has tightened checks on Thai children under 18 leaving the country , and adults travelling with them must now prove their relationship with a birth certificate and, in most cases, a consent letter.
On November 4, Immigration Bureau Commissioner Police Lieutenant General Nopsin Poonsawat said the screening focuses on whether the adult has a genuine link to the child, and its aim is to prevent human trafficking, cross-border child abduction and children being taken out of Thailand unlawfully.
A valid passport and a birth certificate are required (original, a photocopy or an electronic image), and the rule applies to children of Thai nationality , so it also covers Thai children with a foreign parent.
A foreign or a divorced parent flying out alone with a Thai child will need a consent letter from the other parent.
Photo via AzmanL/Getty Images
A legal guardian must carry a copy of the court order appointing them, and a child travelling with anyone else needs a consent letter from both parents or the legal guardian.
The bureau said every consent letter must be made in front of an official at a district office or an embassy and is valid for no more than 60 days, while pupils on school sports, study or exchange trips can use a school letter instead if the school has gained consent under Education Ministry rules.
The bureau said documents and statements in the 32 refused cases raised suspicion that the children were linked to networks that register Chinese children under fake Thai fathers to obtain Thai nationality. It said these cases led to further investigations, arrests and prosecutions, but gave no figures for them.
The checks build on a notice from Suvarnabhumi Airport’s departure immigration division over the summer, when Thailand began requiring birth certificates for children travelling abroad .

content:
Свыше 21 тысячи жителей Владивостока остались без отопления и горячего водоснабжения. Причиной тому послужило повреждение коммунальных сетей, сообщает прокуратура Приморского края в пятницу, 6 ноября. Отключение коснулось 98 многоквартирных домов и трех социально значимых объектов, добавило ведомство.
Прорыв теплотрассы произошел в районе улицы Посьетской на юго-западе города, уточнило региональное управление МЧС России . Специалисты ведут аварийно-восстановительные работы. В ближайшие дни температура во Владивостоке будет опускаться до минус шести градусов Цельсия.
В конце сентября авария на подстанции "Дальневосточной распределительной сетевой компании" в поселке Штыково привела к масштабному  отключению водоснабжения примерно у 650 тысяч жителей Владивостока, Артема и Надеждинского района Приморья. Часть домохозяйств оставалась без воды более суток.
summary: Отопление из-за повреждения теплотрассы на юго-западе Владивостока отключено в 98 многоквартирных домах, сообщило управление МЧС по Приморскому краю. Затронуты более 21 тысячи человек.

content:
The investigation surrounding television presenter Panadda “Boom” Wongphudee and the Ongkorn Thamdee Foundation has brought renewed attention to Thailand’s laws governing charitable organisations, particularly the management of donations and accountability for public funds.
The controversy has raised questions about several matters, including the use of state-owned land for a trail-running facility, reported transfers of foundation funds linked to pool villa construction and disputes involving family relationships.
While these issues remain subject to scrutiny, the broader concern is how foundations manage donations and ensure that money contributed for charitable purposes is used appropriately. Other foundations associated with public figures have faced similar examinations in the past.
The case has also highlighted the potential legal consequences of misusing donations, particularly where investigators find evidence of deception, misappropriation or other financial offences.
Research cited in the discussion estimates that charitable donations in Thailand amount to approximately THB150 billion a year, covering foundations, associations, non-profit organisations, temples and other religious activities.
The amount is estimated to increase by around 2% annually, with roughly one-third to one-half of donations going towards temples, merit-making and religious ceremonies.
These figures illustrate the substantial financial resources entrusted to charitable and religious organisations, reinforcing the importance of transparent accounting and the ability to trace how donations are collected and spent.
Thailand has an estimated 40,000–50,000 temples, alongside approximately 32,800 foundations, associations and other non-profit organisations.
Although foundations and associations both operate on a non-profit basis, their legal structures differ.
An association is established by people joining together to pursue common activities. A foundation, by contrast, is formed through the allocation of assets for charitable or other public-benefit purposes, without distributing profits to individuals.
Under Thailand’s foundation registration requirements, an organisation generally needs initial capital of THB500,000.
A lower threshold of THB200,000 applies to certain foundations established for purposes including social welfare, education, sport, disaster relief and drug-related prevention or assistance.
Cash funds must be deposited with a commercial bank, with supporting certification provided before registration. A foundation must also have a management committee comprising at least three members.
Foundations are required to operate within their registered objectives and are subject to restrictions concerning partisan political activities and financial or material support for political parties.
A central concern in foundation management is whether money collected from the public can be deposited into an individual's personal bank account.
A legal specialist from the Office of the Attorney-General emphasised that donations intended for a registered foundation should be transferred directly into an account held in the foundation's name.
Where contributions were initially collected through a personal account before a foundation was formally registered, the specialist maintained that the money should be transferred promptly to the foundation's account once registration was completed.
Keeping such funds in a personal account for three or four years, or using them for unrelated expenses, could raise serious legal concerns. Whether an offence has occurred depends on the circumstances and evidence.
Thailand's Fundraising Control Act of 1944 regulates public appeals for donations, including fundraising activities that may require prior authorisation.
Public appeals promoted through online platforms such as Facebook and TikTok can fall within these requirements, depending on the nature and purpose of the fundraising activity.
Organisers operating under a fundraising permit must comply with the relevant conditions and reporting requirements concerning money collected and spent.
Restrictions also apply when donations remain unused or the original charitable objective can no longer be fulfilled.
Funds collected for a specified purpose cannot simply be redirected towards unrelated activities. Where the intended use is no longer possible, organisers must follow the procedures required by the authorities before reallocating the money.
Responsibility for monitoring foundations is divided among several government agencies.
The Ministry of Interior oversees foundation registration and financial reporting, while the Ministry of Finance examines commercial income, taxation and eligibility for public charitable organisation status.
The Anti-Money Laundering Office (AMLO) can investigate financial transactions and trace funds where potential money-laundering concerns arise.
The Department of Special Investigation (DSI) and police may also become involved when suspected criminal offences are identified. Depending on the circumstances, investigations can include possible violations of the Computer Crime Act.
These responsibilities mean that foundation management may be examined from several perspectives, ranging from compliance with registration requirements to financial transactions and potential criminal wrongdoing.
The legal consequences of improperly using charitable donations depend partly on the circumstances in which the money was obtained and the intentions of those involved.
Where investigators establish that funds were solicited through false claims and that there was never a genuine intention to use the money for the stated charitable purpose, the conduct may constitute public fraud.
Public fraud is a criminal offence that cannot be resolved solely through a private settlement between the parties.
A different issue arises when donations were initially collected for genuine charitable purposes but were subsequently diverted to unrelated activities or appropriated for personal benefit.
Such conduct may fall within the offence of misappropriation, depending on the evidence and the legal relationship between those responsible and the funds involved.
Repeated financial irregularities or arrangements involving kickback payments may also prompt investigations into possible money-laundering offences, provided the relevant legal elements are established.
The investigation into the Ongkorn Thamdee Foundation therefore highlights a wider issue for Thailand's charitable sector: ensuring that donations are properly recorded, managed according to their intended purposes and subject to effective oversight.
With an estimated THB150 billion in charitable contributions circulating annually, the ability of foundations and other organisations to demonstrate financial accountability remains central to maintaining public confidence.

content:
Collision running and face-slapping competitions have similar impacts to that of a coward punch or “king-hit”, with death a “distinct possibility”, a concussion expert has told a parliamentary inquiry.
A New South Wales inquiry is examining whether emerging competitions such as Run Nation, in which two players run at each other and collide at high speed, and Power Slap, where players take turns slapping each other across the face, should be considered combat sports to better regulate the safety of participants.
But neurologist Dr Rowena Mobbs, an expert in concussion and chronic traumatic encepalopahty (CTE), told the inquiry she did not think there was “any form of modification” that would make the sports safer.
“Collision running and Power Slap are worse than eye-gouging and should be deemed a king-hit, for death is a distinct possibility,” she said.
A 19-year-old died in New Zealand last year after suffering a critical head injury playing a tackling game believed to have been inspired by the viral “run it straight” challenge, of which Run Nation’s organisers have claimed their competition is a safer version, turning rugby league “hit-ups” into a sport.
The inquiry was established in August. In September, a NSW supreme court judge ruled Run Nation was a combat sport, upholding a cancellation notice for a Sydney event that month from the Combat Sports Authority (CSA) of NSW.
The event has been rescheduled for 28 November after the authority’s medical advisory board approved its permit. Power Slap has yet to host an official event in Australia.
The chair of the CSA, Darren Kane, told the inquiry on Friday he would prefer to see new combat sports regulated, with mandated ambulance and medical support staff.
“If it was a regulated event, there’d be all these systems in place, and the people would have accreditations, they would have done concussion training, there would be doctors mandated at the events,” he said.
“Whereas you have these unregulated things, it’s pot luck.”
Run Nation’s organisers have said their events include on-field doctors and paramedics.
The inquiry did not hear from organisers of either competition, but received submissions from medical experts, bareknuckle boxing and grassroots combat sports groups.
Petero Taremwa, the founder of Get That Guap (GTG) fight club, which hosts mixed martial arts, kickboxing and boxing fights without a promoter’s licence, said the cost of participation was a “serious barrier” to fighters, while organisers faced significant costs from “permits, insurance, venues, and medical services”.
after newsletter promotion
“We’re not here to dispute the importance of regulation. We’re here because we want a realistic pathway to comply,” he said.
Taremwa said there had been no significant injuries at GTG events, which “always had a nurse who is also our DJ, who looks at the fighters right after the fight”.
Under questioning from the inquiry chair, Labor MLC Sarah Kaine, Taremwa said he did not think he knew better than the CSA, but that the cost of on-site ambulances required under regulation was unreasonable for an entry-level organiser.
In her evidence, Mobbs said brain diseases in participants in football codes and traditional combat sports resulted from “subclinical concussions or silent events … when they add up to probably tens of thousands if not hundreds of thousands”.
But she said the stronger impacts experienced in collision running and face-slapping competitions meant a lower number of impacts could “trigger off a neurodegenerative disease, for example, later in life”.
Mobbs said she did not recall treating any patients with injuries from collision running or Power Slap.
She likened the potential impact to that of a coward punch or “king-hit”, because participants could not defend themselves and strikes came “right in the key area where you have most impact”.
The inquiry is expected to report back in December.

content:
President Hassan Sheikh Mohamud's four-year mandate expired in May
Published
Somalia's Supreme Court has ruled that President Hassan Sheikh Mohamud unlawfully extended his term, escalating a political crisis and a standoff between the presidency and judiciary.
Thursday's ruling came a day after Mohamud dismissed Chief Justice Bashe Yusuf Ahmed - a move which the court said the president lacked the authority to take.
The court also ordered political leaders to agree on an electoral plan within 30 days and hold elections within 90 days, potentially disrupting government plans for nationwide polls next year.
Mohamud's four-year mandate expired in May, but his administration extended it by a year through law changes approved by parliament in March.
Opposition groups accuse him of using the constitutional changes to prolong his rule.
But the president insists the reforms are necessary to move Somalia towards fully democratic elections, replacing the clan-based system in which elders pick their representatives which has been used since 2012.
Somalia last held nationwide direct elections in 1969 and has been wracked by civil war for more than 30 years, with Islamist militant group al-Shabab controlling many rural areas.
On Thursday, the Supreme Court ruled that the constitutional changes could not be applied retrospectively to the president's current term.
In a separate decision, the court declared the chief justice's dismissal "null and void", accusing the presidency of interfering with judicial independence.
The president appointed Ibrahim Idle Suleiman, who previously held the position, to replace Ahmed.
The presidency said the dismissal followed complaints about the administration of justice and was intended to achieve a just and transparent judiciary.
But the court rejected that explanation, insisting that the chief justice could only be removed through established constitutional procedures.
Former President Sharif Sheikh Ahmed welcomed the court ruling, saying "the country is facing a grave political crisis", calling on Mohamud to embrace a consensus-based approach.
The confrontation escalated on Thursday when former Prime Minister Hassan Ali Khaire accused the president of deploying security forces to the Supreme Court and attempting to arrest its chief justice.
Khaire accused the president of launching an "assault on the Supreme Court", according to the AFP news agency.
"Somalia stands at a dangerous juncture. The dismantling of our judiciary is a direct threat to the rule of law," he said.
AFP said it could not independently verify the reported security deployment, although photographs circulating in Somali media appeared to show armed personnel inside the court compound.
The rulings have thrown Somalia's electoral timetable into uncertainty.
The electoral commission has scheduled parliamentary elections for 15 April 2027 and a presidential vote a month later, but opposition groups and the regional administrations of Puntland and Jubaland reject the timetable.
Mohamud has called for national talks from 14 to 18 November to resolve the deadlock, but opposition leaders have questioned his legitimacy to convene the discussions.
The political turmoil comes as Somalia continues to battle al-Shabab, which controls large parts of the countryside despite years of military operations.
Uganda, the largest contributor of troops to the African Union mission fighting the militants, announced this week that it planned to withdraw its forces by the end of the year, adding to concerns about Somalia's security.

Kenny G will join Thai and international performers at the free Pattaya International Jazz Festival 2026 on November 6–7, 2026, as the city uses music events to draw tourists and support local businesses.
The festival runs from 4pm to midnight each day at Central Pattaya Beach in Chonburi. Joint organisers Pattaya City and the Chonburi Provincial Administrative Organisation expect 30,000 visitors or more.
Now in its fourth consecutive year, the festival forms part of the “Better Pattaya” policy, which aims to establish the city as a “World Class Event Hub” with international festivals and traditional celebrations throughout the year.
Kenny G’s return is the festival’s principal attraction, with organisers highlighting the award-winning artist’s distinctive sound and international following. The programme also brings together established Thai singers, overseas performers and emerging talent.
The Shang Sisters, a Malaysian female group with experience performing at major events across Asia, will appear alongside Japanese artist TOSH, who has performed at music festivals in Tokyo.
Thai performers include veteran singer Amp Saowaluck, vocalist Ben Chalatit and rising artist WIM.
The Paradise Bangkok Molam International Band will also perform. The band has gained international recognition for bringing Thai instruments to global audiences and has been invited to perform at Britain’s Glastonbury Festival and other major events in Europe and Asia.
The line-up also includes Rattanakosin Breakin Crew and Groovy Doopy featuring Rachael and Adam. Young musicians will have an opportunity to perform through acts such as 808 Band.
Wittaya Khunpluem, president of the Chonburi Provincial Administrative Organisation, described the event as an opportunity to bring international-standard jazz performances to audiences free of charge while supporting residents, communities, businesses and the tourism industry.
“We want audiences to experience a variety of music, with international and Thai artists who each have their own distinctive identity,” Wittaya said.
“One event offers both memorable performances by world-class artists and the colour of Thai music. We are confident it will be a memorable evening for Thai and international visitors.”
The expanded 2026 edition adopts the theme “Eco Jazz Festival”, with the Thai tagline translated as “Earth-friendly rhythms and the beauty of sustainability”. The theme links musical enjoyment with environmental responsibility.
Pattaya mayor Poramet Ngampichet said the organisers wanted visitors to enjoy more than a concert, combining music with relaxation on the beachfront and opportunities to help care for the environment.
“We want this event to be more than simply coming to listen to music. We want people to relax, enjoy a good experience on Pattaya Beach and help look after the environment,” Poramet said.
The festival’s “Eco” and “Go Green” concepts encourage visitors to reduce waste, use less plastic and make efficient use of resources.
“We want everyone to enjoy the music to the full while also helping to reduce waste and plastic use and use resources wisely,” Poramet said.
“We believe enjoyment and caring for the planet can go together.”
The organisers’ stated objectives also cover social and environmental responsibilities, reducing harm to nature, and technology and city management.
Pattaya and Chonburi are using the festival to showcase the city’s coastal setting, culture, food and nightlife, with music serving as a reason for Thai and overseas tourists to visit.
Organisers expect the event to encourage longer stays and generate income for local residents and businesses. The wider aim is to strengthen Pattaya’s tourism image and support the national economy through visitor spending.
The festival is presented as part of a broader tourism strategy supported by improvements in public transport, utilities and other infrastructure in Pattaya and Chonburi.
These developments are intended to accommodate economic growth, investment and tourism under the Eastern Economic Corridor (EEC) development plan.
The approach also emphasises quality, meaningful travel experiences and Thailand’s “5F” soft-power categories: food, film, fashion, fight, meaning martial arts, and festivals. Organisers see the jazz festival as a way to promote these cultural strengths while developing Pattaya as an international events destination.

content:
Thai woman reports missing luxury items after Vienna-Warsaw flight Legacy A Thai woman has reported finding luxury skincare products and perfumes missing from her checked luggage after flying with LOT Polish Airlines from Vienna, Austria, to Warsaw, Poland, on November 2.
The passenger shared her experience on Facebook, alleging that items worth nearly 100,000 baht had been stolen during the journey.
She said she arrived in Warsaw in the evening and noticed that her suitcase was in disarray, with belongings scattered inside. Initially, she assumed the bag had been searched as part of a routine inspection.
However, she said no inspection notice had been left with the luggage.
The passenger did not check everything immediately and only discovered the missing items on November 3, when she searched her luggage for products she wanted to use. Several expensive products were missing, leaving only empty boxes.
Photo via Magnific
The missing items included three unused La Mer skincare products: a 150 millilitre treatment lotion, a 120 millilitre emulsion and a 30 millilitre serum. She also reported that two bottles of Louis Vuitton perfume were missing , with only their boxes left behind.
She appealed to LOT Polish Airlines for assistance, saying she did not know where to begin addressing the situation.
The passenger said she was preparing to file a police report and wanted to share her experience to remind other travellers to be careful about packing valuables in checked luggage.
She later clarified on Facebook that the incident had nothing to do with an airport in Thailand, after some readers misunderstood her original post. The LOT Polish Airlines flight was a journey of less than two hours within Europe’s Schengen Area, she said.
She added that even having priority service had not prevented the loss.

content:
Amnesty International has called for an immediate halt to any plans by the Thai authorities to forcibly return two Uyghur men to China.
It cited reports of possible deportation and said the men could face torture, arbitrary detention and enforced disappearance if sent back.
Agnès Callamard, Amnesty International’s secretary general, said the men had fled persecution in China and could face similar abuses if returned.
Both had told their lawyers they feared for their lives and were unwilling to go back.
Amnesty called for their release so they could live safely and freely, and for access to lawyers of their choice.
It urged Thailand to work urgently with the international community to find a country willing to receive them and other Uyghurs still detained in Thailand so they could leave voluntarily for a place of safety.
Two of the five Uyghurs still in Thailand were released from prison on Wednesday (October 21, 2026) following a royal pardon before being transferred to an immigration detention centre in Bangkok.
Amnesty said the Thai authorities had since denied them access to their lawyers and barred civil society organisations and the National Human Rights Commission of Thailand (NHRCT) from meeting them.
General Chaipruak Doungprapat, secretary-general of the National Security Council (NSC), said at Government House at 12.35pm on Nov 4 that, to his knowledge, the men’s lawyer had already visited them.
He said the matter fell outside the scope of government policy and that the court would decide it through normal judicial procedures.
Chaipruak said all five were from the same group as those previously sent back to China.
Amnesty’s account described their imprisonment as stemming from an attempt to escape from immigration detention.
Chaipruak said they had been prosecuted for escaping from custody and that the three still in prison had a little over a year left to serve.
Chaipruak cited Chinese arrest warrants for all five and the fact that none had been granted refugee status as two differences from the earlier case.
He said China was using its treaty with Thailand to seek their extradition in connection with alleged offences.
Chaipruak said the Ministry of Foreign Affairs would check the warrants on receipt of a formal extradition request from China for the five men.
Prosecutors would take the case forward if the warrants were valid.
The men had appointed lawyers to contest the case, he said.
A move to another country would depend on the outcome of their challenge and whether a country agreed to take them.
He said the treaty would require extradition if the court found they had committed the offences in question.
The two men have been held in Thailand for more than 12 years.
They were among more than 300 Uyghurs detained without charge by the Thai authorities on Mar 13, 2014, after fleeing persecution and discrimination in China’s Xinjiang Uyghur Autonomous Region.
Thailand allowed 173 women and children from the group to travel to Turkey in June 2015.
Amnesty described the return of at least 109 Uyghurs to China as unlawful.
The Chinese embassy in Thailand wrote to the Ministry of Foreign Affairs on Jan 7, 2025, asking it to send the 45 Uyghurs still in the country back to China.
The Thai authorities forcibly returned 40 of them the following month.
Callamard urged Thailand to avoid a repeat, saying those deportations had gone ahead despite the risk of harm and breached international law.
Thai representatives visited Xinjiang twice following the deportations, in February and March 2025, at the Chinese government’s invitation.
The visits were intended to provide reassurance through diplomatic channels.
Non-governmental organisations monitoring the case reported that Thai officials met fewer than 10 of those sent back.
There has been no further information on whether all are alive and safe, and their places of detention have not been disclosed.
Callamard stressed that Thailand was obliged to refrain from returning anyone to a country where they faced a real risk of torture or serious human rights violations, even if China gave diplomatic assurances about their safety.
Amnesty continues to oppose assurances that returnees will be spared torture or cruel treatment.
It considers them unreliable and says they may run counter to the universal prohibition on torture under international law.
Thailand has obligations under the Convention against Torture and the principle of non-refoulement, which bars states from returning people to countries or territories where they face a real risk of persecution or human rights violations.
Section 13 of the Prevention and Suppression of Torture and Enforced Disappearance Act, in force since 2023, also prohibits deportation where there are reasonable grounds to believe a person could face torture, cruel, inhuman or degrading treatment, or enforced disappearance.
Amnesty International published a major report in 2021 documenting evidence of crimes against humanity in Xinjiang, including imprisonment, torture and persecution of Uyghurs, Kazakhs and other predominantly Muslim ethnic groups.
A United Nations assessment in August 2022 reached similar findings.
Amnesty said the Chinese government had yet to implement the recommendations, provide remedies for those affected or investigate to bring those responsible to justice.
It said the government continued to suppress criticism at home and abroad, circulate material denying allegations of human rights abuses and pursue policies of discrimination and forced cultural assimilation.

Trang mother seeks justice for 5 year old son beaten by 2 teenagers Legacy A five year old boy in Trang province was allegedly beaten with a wooden stick and a metal bar by two teenagers , leaving him with multiple injuries and severe distress .
The mother, who identified her son only as A, appealed to news agencies to publicise the incident as she seeks justice for the child. She said a resident brought the boy home at about 8pm on Tuesday, November 3. He had multiple wounds across his back and was crying and visibly frightened.
The boy told his mother that two teenagers, identified as Pond and New, had attacked him using a wooden stick and a metal bar.
The mother said she took him to hospital for treatment. According to her, medical staff said his injuries were consistent with wounds that could have been caused by wooden and metal objects.
Photo via 77 Kaoded
She added that her son’s emotional condition had deteriorated since the incident. He was reportedly frightened of other people and would only allow his mother and another relative to approach him. His physical injuries were also expected to take time to heal.
The mother said the incident was linked to an earlier dispute involving her 12-year-old daughter and Pond, who is 15.
According to her account, Pond had previously shown romantic interest in the girl. He once took her to hospital when she was unwell and kept her identity card.
On the day of the alleged assault, Pond reportedly asked the girl to meet him to collect her ID card. She agreed, retrieved the card and returned home.
Photo via Facebook/ TRANG Todayข่าว
The mother said Pond later asked the five-year-old boy to bring his older sister to meet him. When the boy passed on the request, the girl refused.
The mother alleged that Pond became angry and took the young boy to a school about 500 metres from their home, where he and his 14 year old friend, New, assaulted him.
After the incident, the boy reportedly tried to walk home. Residents noticed his injuries and took him back to his family.
The mother said the families of the two teenagers had contacted her and attempted to arrange a meeting with her and her son. However, she was not ready to meet them.
She confirmed that she had reported the incident to Yan Ta Khao Police Station and wanted legal action to be taken against the alleged attackers.

content:
Thai Airways International Public Company Limited has outlined measures to clear a large backlog of inbound cargo at Suvarnabhumi Airport, including increasing staffing levels, obtaining additional forklifts and working with airport authorities to secure temporary storage space.
The airline acknowledged that a sustained increase in incoming air freight had left numerous unit load devices (ULDs) awaiting cargo sorting and storage, delaying the delivery of some shipments.
Thai Airways apologised to customers, partner airlines and affected businesses, confirming that it was mobilising additional personnel, equipment and resources to clear outstanding cargo and restore normal operations as quickly as possible.
The airline has introduced four measures to address the situation, focusing on operational capacity, additional storage space, cargo management and cooperation with relevant agencies.
To accelerate cargo handling, Thai Airways is increasing staffing levels and procuring more forklifts to speed up the sorting, storage and delivery of goods. Shipments will also be prioritised to help reduce the backlog.
The airline is working with Airports of Thailand Public Company Limited (AOT) to secure additional temporary storage space and ease congestion in the warehouse. Other options for managing available space will also be considered, subject to safety requirements and relevant regulations.
Thai Airways also plans to introduce a warehouse management system covering the entire handling process, from receiving and sorting cargo to identifying storage locations and arranging deliveries.
The system will support continuous monitoring and reporting of inbound and outbound cargo volumes, as well as outstanding shipments. This will allow the airline to assess warehouse conditions, plan staffing and equipment requirements, and adjust operations promptly.
The fourth measure involves closer cooperation with AOT and other relevant agencies to improve overall operational efficiency.
Thai Airways and AOT will jointly promote the AOT Cargo Clearhouse system and encourage businesses to use it to help accelerate cargo deliveries.

content:
Iran appears to be undertaking significant new construction near at least two of its major missile sites and repairing bases damaged by months of US and Israeli air strikes, analysis of satellite images suggests.
Evidence of digging and new buildings are visible in satellite imagery taken in November at the Garmdareh military base in Karaj near the capital Tehran and the Shahroud base in the north, analysts at British intelligence company MAIAR, who reviewed the photos, told BBC Verify.
At least 12 other military sites, including missile complexes and air bases, appear to show signs of repairs. New roofs have been built on destroyed buildings at the Kermanshah missile base in western Iran, near the border with Iraq, while damaged buildings and debris have been cleared at the Parchin military complex - which has been repeatedly repaired despite a succession of air strikes - east of the capital.
The excavations near Shahroud could potentially be related to the production of missiles, said Jim Lamson, a former CIA analyst who focused on Iran. He said that because the nearby air base at Shahroud has been targeted multiple times in recent years, Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guards Corps (IRGC) is probably trying to find ways to move its production facilities underground.
A MAIAR analyst said that Iran has "a pattern of moving infrastructure underground to protect them from further strikes". Mark Mellett, a defence analyst and former head of the Irish military, said the construction of underground facilities had the added benefit of making it "harder for outside observers to assess the extent and operational status".
Speculation has mounted in recent weeks that the US could resume attacks on Iran after the midterm elections held earlier this week. But on Wednesday Vice-President JD Vance cited the war's unpopularity with voters for the Republicans' poor performance in this week's poll, saying that it may have cost his party control of the Senate "for the next 6 years".
At multiple bases across the country, Iranian forces have focused on carrying-out small-scale repairs to complexes which have been heavily damaged by air strikes since the start of the US-Israeli war.
Analysts said that satellite images appear to show that significant construction has been completed at the Taleghan 2 facility at the Parchin military complex, with damaged buildings levelled and the aftermath of attacks on an underground bunker repaired and reinforced with concrete.
At Karaj, external and Shahroud, satellite images appear to show significant excavation. At Karaj, multiple vehicles were visible in satellite images, while improvements appear to have been carried out to the nearby airbase.
The images from Karaj appear to show "a new portal for an underground facility", said Sam Lair, research analyst at the Foreign Policy Research Institute (FPRI), which has looked extensively into recent developments at Iranian sites.
Analysis from Janes also indicates there appears to be a new facility under construction at Karaj, including tunnel entrances and structures which could indicate an expansion of nearby damaged or destroyed missile bases - or could also be for storage or other purposes.
The construction work is unlikely to be part of an effort to deceive foreign intelligence agencies, said Janes analyst Sean O'Connor. He said such a project "would be costly and may achieve little".
The developments come after repeated assurances from the White House that US-Israeli attacks have depleted the Iranian armed forces, which US President Donald Trump dismissed as a "complete and total mess".
A Pentagon spokesperson previously said that the US had "destroyed up to 90% of Iran's drone, ballistic missile, and naval industrial base" and "significantly degraded" the country's ability to launch drone and missile attacks.
But Iran claims it retains large stockpiles of missiles, and footage broadcast on state TV this week claimed to show dozens of missiles at the entrance to an underground facility in southern Iran. Back in August, state TV footage also claimed to show Khordad surface-to-air missiles emerging out of a tunnel near the southern city of Bandar Abbas, external.
A MAIAR analyst also identified new construction and excavations outside tunnel entrances near the city of Qom, close to the Fordo underground uranium enrichment complex, which has been bombed by both the US and Israel multiple times.
Activity related to military assets would show that Tehran is bracing itself for further attacks by the US and Israel, said Mark Cancian, a military analyst with International Security Program at the Center for Strategic and International Studies (CSIS).
"The purpose is to better defend itself against future attacks," he said. "It also indicates a priority on rebuilding military capability rather than rehabilitating the economy."
Additional reporting by Barbara Metzler.

content:
SIAMJNK Group is preparing to strengthen connections between established businesses and a new generation of entrepreneurs through its Chinatown Song Wat project in Bangkok's historic trading district, combining improvements to existing buildings with activities that highlight the neighbourhood's heritage.
The project is situated in Song Wat 1, a lesser-known section of the district near Memorial Bridge. Occupying approximately 0.48 hectares beside the Chao Phraya River, the site offers views from its upper floors towards the river, the Silom–Sathon skyline and the Mahanakhon tower, connecting the atmosphere of Bangkok's old commercial quarter with its modern cityscape.
Thiti Kanthamanond, Chief Executive Officer of SIAMJNK Group, described the initiative as the next step in the company's 25 years of experience developing city warehouses.
Over that period, SIAMJNK has developed projects around the boutique warehouse concept, guided by the belief that well-designed commercial spaces should help businesses grow while supporting quality of life.
The company now aims to build on that experience at SIAMJNK Chinatown Song Wat, creating opportunities for long-established operators and emerging businesses to meet, establish partnerships and grow alongside the neighbourhood.
The project's location is closely connected to the historical development of Song Wat and its surrounding streets.
According to historical information examined by SIAMJNK, Song Wat Road originally formed a continuous route. Following a major fire and the construction of Anuwong Road, its northern section became separated from the original street.
The later construction of Phra Pok Klao Bridge further shaped the area, creating the distinctive enclave now identified on maps as Song Wat 1.
Some academics believe the name may have evolved from "Song Wat Nuea", meaning northern Song Wat, reflecting its geographical relationship with the original road.
SIAMJNK intends to strengthen connections between its existing commercial spaces and the wider Song Wat neighbourhood through building renovations, activities and partnerships among entrepreneurs.
The objective is to make Song Wat 1 another destination where people can discover the area's stories, make use of its spaces and explore business opportunities together.
The first planned activity is SIAMJNK's participation in Bangkok Design Week 2027 through a programme titled "Sen Song Wat Sang Mueang" ( The Lines That Built Bangkok ), loosely translated as "Song Wat Lines Shape the City".
The programme aims to showcase the district's history and potential through design and creativity, inviting visitors, designers, entrepreneurs and business partners to discover Song Wat 1 as another route connecting to the more familiar parts of Song Wat.
A central focus will be the historical development of the neighbourhood, including the origins of its roads and urban layout as recorded in a royal map.
The programme will also revisit the construction of Song Wat Road in 1892, when the road was developed as part of efforts to reorganise the commercial district.
By exploring these historical milestones, SIAMJNK hopes to demonstrate how the area developed over time and the role it once played in the lives of people and businesses within the neighbourhood.
The activities are intended to encourage visitors to rediscover Song Wat 1 while recognising its historical connections with the wider trading district.
Alongside the planned activities, SIAMJNK intends to redesign and renovate a building in Song Wat that is approximately 70 years old, transforming it into a new development while preserving its distinctive architectural features and original charm.
The renovation will seek to balance the building's historical character with practical functions that meet contemporary needs.
This approach reflects what Thiti describes as "Living Infrastructure", a concept based on the belief that urban spaces should evolve alongside the people and businesses that use them.
For SIAMJNK, living infrastructure involves connecting buildings, the stories of a neighbourhood and everyday activities, allowing existing spaces to remain relevant as business requirements and urban lifestyles change.
The renovation of the 70-year-old building is intended to provide a practical example of this philosophy, retaining its original identity while adapting it to support present-day activities.
Through SIAMJNK Chinatown Song Wat, the group hopes to build on the district's existing commercial foundations while creating opportunities for established enterprises and newer businesses to collaborate.
The longer-term vision is to ensure that the area's history continues to be reflected in how its buildings and spaces are used, allowing people and businesses to contribute to Song Wat's future while maintaining its distinctive character.

content:
The Thai Food and Drug Administration (Thai FDA) and the Designated Areas for Sustainable Tourism Administration (Public Organization) (DASTA) signed a memorandum of understanding (MoU) on 5 November 2026 at the Thai FDA’s offices. The agreement, signed by pharmacist Supattra Boonserm, Secretary-General of the Thai FDA, and Siripakorn Cheawsamoot, Director-General of DASTA, aims to raise standards for health products in designated sustainable tourism areas, improve the quality and safety of community products, ensure they meet applicable standards and broaden access to markets.
Supattra noted that Thailand has many products rooted in local knowledge with strong potential, but community entrepreneurs still face difficulties with manufacturing standards, obtaining regulatory approval and finding sales channels. The Thai FDA therefore aims to support entrepreneurs alongside its regulatory work, enabling them to develop products and bring them to market in compliance with the rules.
Discussions on the partnership began in September. DASTA initially identified 37 products from 12 entrepreneurs in nine provinces requiring Thai FDA support. Examples include herbal products from Nan, processed Kluai Khai bananas from Kamphaeng Phet and palmyra palm products from Songkhla. The Thai FDA will work with provincial public health offices to advise entrepreneurs on improving production facilities and products, and on preparing applications for regulatory approval.
“The central goal of this partnership is not simply to produce community goods that meet standards and can be sold. Entrepreneurs must also have the knowledge to build on local wisdom and keep developing their own products. Real success means better living conditions for local people and communities that can grow independently,” Supattra said.
Siripakorn explained that DASTA seeks to develop tourism that benefits local people by turning local resources and knowledge into products reflecting each community’s identity. Working with the Thai FDA will help improve product quality, standards and safety, build confidence among consumers and tourists, and connect entrepreneurs with tourism networks to open up more market opportunities.
“We want local products to be more than souvenirs from tourist destinations. They should be goods that communities take pride in, that meet recognised quality standards and that create opportunities for local people to grow alongside sustainable tourism,” Siripakorn said.

content:
SINGAPORE - Singapore Airlines, long a benchmark for premium travel, is spending more than S$2 billion (US$1.6 billion) to upgrade long-haul seats and provide larger double-bed suites to compete with rivals that are pouring money into high-end cabins.
The airline on Friday unveiled new cabins in all four travel classes in the biggest and most comprehensive overhaul in its history, with the new seats due from the second half of 2027.
In first class, centre seats convert into what Singapore Airlines calls the largest double bed in commercial aviation. Business class gets sliding privacy doors for the first time on the airline, alongside a fully flat bed.
The launch comes as carriers globally such as Air France, British Airways and United Airlines pour billions into premium travel despite industry-wide delays in production and certification of new seats.
Surging fuel costs have squeezed margins and pushed up fares, deterring some more cost-conscious economy passengers, although premium travel has remained relatively resilient.
"We look closely at how our customers work, dine, relax and rest while travelling, and what they value most," Singapore Airlines CEO Goh Choon Phong said at the launch event.
"Their feedback was clear: greater comfort and privacy, intuitive functionality and spaces they can flexibly adapt to their needs, whether they are working, resting or connecting with loved ones from 30,000 feet."
The Singapore Airlines programme covers 72 aircraft, a mix of Airbus A350-900s being retrofitted and Boeing 777-9 jets on order that together will comprise most of its long-haul fleet.
The cabins were originally designed for the 777-9, which is expected to become Singapore Airlines' new long-haul flagship as the A380, which offers smaller double beds, eventually retires.
But the 777-9's entry into service has slipped for years, which Singapore Airlines Chief Commercial Officer Lee Lik Hsin told Reuters had led the carrier to widen the programme to its A350s.
He said the S$2 billion-plus investment included a S$1.1 billion A350 refurbishment plan announced in 2024 and was funded from the airline's strong cash balance, which stood at S$9.1 billion as of end-June.
Most of the investment goes to premium cabins because business and first-class seats cost far more per unit than economy seats, Lee said, with the carrier setting no spending ceiling and planning to keep investing when appropriate to maintain its market leadership.
"Our competitive advantage doesn't derive from aircraft cabin product alone," he said. "It is the hard product, the soft service, the operational excellence. And...it is our people."
David Flynn, editor-in-chief of industry publication Executive Traveller, said the new first class, with a unique curved cabin design that borrowed space from the aisles to add personal space to each suite, ranked among the world's best.
"Business class represent a solid and much-needed catch up to the competition, rather than a mighty leap ahead," he said. "It's hard to top Qatar's business class Qsuite, let alone the next-gen version coming in 2027, but in features and usability, Singapore Airlines looks to have Emirates and arguably Cathay beat here."
Delays and certification
The unveiling arrives against a backdrop of persistent delays. Boeing first targeted 777-9 deliveries around 2020 but repeated certification setbacks, engine issues, the pandemic and tighter oversight by the US Federal Aviation Administration have pushed that to 2027, with Lufthansa expected to be the launch operator.
Lee said slippage on its A350 refurbishment plan and the 777-9 seating were both driven by certification issues.
"The seats are certified on the 777-9, but the 777-9 airplane itself is not certified, and the seats have not yet been certified on the A350," he said.
The A350 certification delay had pushed back their introduction by about half a year, he added.
As airlines design more premium offerings with bespoke features that regulators need to ensure meet stringent crash-safety standards, seat certification has become a bottleneck across the industry.
Boeing CEO Kelly Ortberg last week told investors that deliveries of its 787 Dreamliners had been affected by seat certification challenges.
summary: SINGAPORE - Singapore Airlines, long a benchmark for premium travel, is ‌spending more than S$2 billion (US$1.6 billion) to upgrade long-haul seats and provide larger double-bed suites to compete with rivals that are pouring money into high-end cabins.

content:
El papa León XIV emprendió este viernes (06.11.2026) su viaje a Latinoamérica para visitar Uruguay , Argentina y regresar a Perú , un país donde vivió 20 años, en un exigente periplo de 12 días en el que tomará 14 vuelos, pronunciará cerca de 40 discursos y todo menos de un mes después de la operación en la que le extirparon parte de un pulmón por un cáncer . El pontífice se embarca en uno de los viajes internacionales más intensos realizados por un papa en las últimas décadas.
En una mañana lluviosa en el aeropuerto de Fiumicino de Roma, el pontífice saludó sonriente a los espectadores antes de subir al avión papal de la compañía Ita Airways, que despegó a las 7:05 horas (6:05 GMT) con la delegación vaticana y 80 periodistas de medios de todo el mundo, entre ellos Efe y AFP. Está previsto que llegue al aeropuerto internacional de Montevideo a las 16:30 hora local (13:30 GMT), donde será recibido por el presidente uruguayo, Yamandú Orsi .
"Necesidad de superar las profundas polarizaciones sociales"
El miércoles, el líder espiritual de los 1.400 millones de católicos afirmó que esperaba con entusiasmo regresar a unos países que son "tan queridos" para él. León XIV expresó su deseo de que la visita contribuya a "fortalecer la fe, renovar la esperanza y reavivar el fuego de la caridad" en unos países que afrontan desafíos como el aumento de las desigualdades, la violencia, el descenso demográfico y el retroceso del catolicismo.
Pese a haber sido sometido hace poco más de tres semanas a una intervención para extirpar un tumor canceroso, los médicos le dieron el visto bueno para la gira. El Vaticano confirmó que no se han tomado medidas médicas adicionales a pesar de la reciente operación quirúrgica, ya que el Papa tras la extirpación del cáncer "es una persona, de 71 años, con una buena salud", pero el viaje será una prueba para ver su resistencia ante la importante carga de trabajo.
En la víspera del viaje, el cardenal secretario de Estado, Pietro Parolin, explicó a los medios vaticanos el sentido de este viaje: "Incluso en América Latina, existe más que nunca la necesidad de superar las profundas polarizaciones sociales, y la misión primordial de la Iglesia es dar testimonio de la unidad, ser fermento de paz, diálogo y armonía".
Una apretada agenda en Montevideo
Tras aterrizar después de cerca de 13 horas de vuelo, el Papa participará en la ceremonia oficial de bienvenida en la Plaza Independencia y mantendrá un encuentro con las autoridades, representantes de la sociedad civil y el cuerpo diplomático, ante quienes pronunciará su primer discurso en el país.
Por la tarde, el papa se trasladará a la catedral para celebrar las vísperas con obispos, sacerdotes, diáconos, religiosos, religiosas y seminaristas y el sábado comenzará la jornada con un desplazamiento aéreo a Paysandú, donde celebrará la Santa Misa en el Parque París Londres. Para Parolin, la secularización de las sociedades, incluida la uruguaya, en la que más del 40 % de la población se declara sin religión, "es lamentablemente una realidad", pero "esto no altera la misión de la Iglesia: proclamar el Evangelio, en todo tiempo, sigue siendo su tarea, hoy como ayer".
"A la Iglesia en Uruguay, pequeña en número pero vibrante, que conserva la fe en un contexto que no siempre es fácil, el Santo Padre quiere decirles que no están solos y que su testimonio diario, humilde y gozoso es el camino a través del cual el Evangelio puede hablar una vez más al corazón del país", añadió.
Recuerdo a Francisco en Argentina y regreso a Perú
Mientras que respecto a la etapa en Argentina, el secretario de Estado vaticano observó que "León XIV llegará a una tierra que guarda un recuerdo particularmente vívido del papa Francisco , recordado con gratitud no solo en su propio país, sino en toda la Iglesia y en los corazones de tantos hombres y mujeres en todas partes".
"Creo que querrá rendirle homenaje y, de alguna manera, cumplir un anhelo arraigado por los argentinos: dar la bienvenida al Sucesor de Pedro, dado que el Papa Francisco, lamentablemente, no pudo visitarlos durante su pontificado", añadió. Mientras que del regreso a casa, a Perú, señaló que el Papa "regresa al Perú como Obispo de Roma, Sucesor de Pedro y Pastor de la Iglesia universal, y este es un gran regalo para muchos que lo conocieron y amaron".
Según el experto estadounidense Christopher White, autor de un libro sobre León XIV, este viaje a Sudamérica tiene algo de un doble regreso. "Francisco, el primer papa latinoamericano de la historia, nunca volvió a su país. León, que tiene la nacionalidad peruana, recoge ahora ese legado", explicó a la AFP.

The Department of National Parks, Wildlife and Plant Conservation has seized 473 live and dead mud turtles, a protected species, smuggled into Thailand from Mexico in a shipment falsely declared as leather belts.
Natural Resources and Environment Minister Suchart Chomklin said on Friday that officials from the Suvarnabhumi airport wildlife checkpoint and relevant agencies jointly intercepted the shipment on Nov 3.
The turtles, belonging to the Kinosternidae family, were concealed in five international express parcels at the airport's inbound cargo warehouse free zone, said Mr Suchart.
Authorities detected irregularities during X-ray screening of high-risk parcels arriving on flight KE657 from Mexico. The packages, which were addressed to recipients in Thailand, had been falsely declared as containing "leather belts".
Officials seized the containers and opened them for inspection in the presence of representatives from Thai Airways International Plc, discovering a total of 473 turtles both still alive and dead inside, said the minister.
The case involves alleged violations of the Wild Animal Conservation and Protection Act 2019, the Customs Act 2017, the Animal Epidemics Act 2015 and the Royal Ordinance on Fisheries 2015. The case has been forwarded to investigators at Suvarnabhumi airport police station for legal action.
The Department of National Parks, Wildlife and Plant Conservation would hand over the seized turtles to its wildlife health unit for medical treatment and care in accordance with animal welfare standards, according to officials.
The department said it would step up the screening of air cargo from high-risk countries to prevent international wildlife trafficking networks from using Thailand as a transit point.
Mr Suchart said the ministry attached great importance to preventing and suppressing international wildlife trafficking, which threatens biodiversity and violates both domestic and international laws.
The seizure demonstrated the effectiveness of intelligence sharing and risk analysis among relevant agencies, he added.
Officials from relevant agencies jointly inspect mud turtles concealed in five parcels at Suvanabhumi airport's inbound cargo warehouse on Nov 3. (Photo: Department of National Parks, Wildlife and Plant Conservation)

content:
Hong Kong’s High Court sentenced pro-democracy activist Joshua Wong to 10 years in prison on November 5, 2026, after he pleaded guilty to conspiring to collude with foreign entities under the city’s national security law.
Wong, 30, admitted the charge in September. The case concerned a conspiracy with self-exiled activist Nathan Law and others to ask foreign countries, bodies or individuals outside China to impose sanctions or blockades, or take other hostile action against the government.
High Court Judge William Tam told a packed courtroom that the sentence had to reflect the seriousness of Wong’s actions. The offence carried a maximum penalty of life imprisonment.
“The punishment must fit the gravity of the crime,” Tam said.
“It is also necessary for the court to express the community’s abhorrence of the defendant’s scheme and acts with others to collude with foreign forces or external elements to endanger national security.”
The offences covered July 1 to November 23, 2020. Tam described that period as one of “very high risk” to Hong Kong’s national security and rule of law.
Tam took account of Wong’s guilty plea, remorse and educational efforts in prison when determining the sentence.
Wong told the court during mitigation that he had neither advocated independence nor received overseas funding.
“I have never advocated Hong Kong independence, nor have I ever promoted the ‘collapse of China’ or regime change,” Wong said.
“I have also never received foreign funding or spent money to hire foreign political consultants.”
Wong acknowledged that he had subsequently realised his belief that his activities were lawful had been mistaken.
Before sentencing, Wong repeatedly nodded towards the public gallery. Wearing a blue shirt and dark-framed glasses, with his hair cut short at the back and sides, he was flanked by three guards.
Wong has been detained since November 2020, when he pleaded guilty to inciting and organising an unauthorised anti-government assembly during the protests that swept Hong Kong in 2019. Before the latest sentence, his release had been expected in January 2027.
Wong had previously been detained repeatedly for his role in organising pro-democracy rallies and became an internationally recognised figure in the movement.
Prosecutors used a September hearing to set out what they described as an international media and political campaign by Demosisto, the now-disbanded party Wong helped lead, to secure sanctions and other hostile measures against Hong Kong and China in 2019 and 2020.
The campaign included lobbying visits to Washington DC and meetings with Nancy Pelosi, then speaker of the US House of Representatives, and Marco Rubio, now US secretary of state but a senator at the time.
Demosisto also supported a referendum on Hong Kong’s sovereignty at one stage.
Tam said Wong and Law had entered the “international battleground” before the national security law took effect, then continued and “deliberately adapted” their activities to “further the offence”.
Wong’s contacts with politicians in the United States, Europe and elsewhere angered Beijing, which has called him a “black hand” of foreign forces.
Dozens of Wong’s supporters filled public galleries and waited outside the court. Among them was housewife ET Wong, who described widespread anxiety about the consequences of the security legislation.
“These harsh sentences have left many Hong Kong people deeply fearful,” ET Wong said.
“We don’t know what actions might break the law, what we say might break the law, what we write or what we draw. We just don’t know anymore.”
Beijing imposed the national security law on the former British colony in 2020 following demonstrations that sometimes turned violent. The sweeping legislation has effectively outlawed the protest activities of Wong and other young activists.
Beijing maintains that the law was needed to restore stability in the city.
Steve Li, chief superintendent of the police’s national security department, described Wong as not an “enemy”, but said he needed to respect the law and “understand his own country”.
International human rights groups and some Western and Asian countries are closely following Wong’s case and other prosecutions as they monitor the law’s implementation.
In February, media tycoon Jimmy Lai, one of Hong Kong’s most outspoken critics of China, received a 20-year sentence for collusion with foreign forces and sedition. The landmark trial drew international criticism.

content:
Au was sentenced to 12 years and six months' jail for "subversion against the political power of the state"
Published
Macau has sentenced an ex-lawmaker and pro-democracy campaigner to 12 years and six months' jail in the city's first national security case.
Following a closed-door trial, Au Kam San, 69, was convicted on Friday of "subversion against the political power of the state", among other offences.
His wife Virginia Cheang condemned the ruling, calling the case a "groundless persecution designed to humiliate Au".
Macau was handed back to China in 1999, ending over 400 years of Portuguese administration. Its national security law came into effect in 2009, criminalising acts of treason, secession, and subversion against the Chinese Communist Party.
The law was revised in 2023, broadening its scope to include non-violent acts of secession, and again this year, to allow for trials to be held behind closed doors.
Prosecutors had accused Au of assisting and collaborating with "external hostile organisations" by collecting, preparing and disseminating information that was "manifestly filled with political claims of a subversive nature against the state".
These took place "over a long period of time", the prosecutors claim.
Au was arrested in July 2025 and later charged with three counts of subverting the state's power, three counts of endangering national security by establishing contact with foreign organisations, and one count of breach of confidentiality.
He was found guilty of four of the seven charges following a three-day trial which ended in September. A judge had ordered that the trial be held behind closed doors "to ensure that no prejudice is caused to the interests of national security".
Macau's authorities never publicly disclosed the details of the case. Au's family had earlier told the media Au was not allowed to seek his own legal representation and had instead been assigned a lawyer by the court.
Au's wife Cheang said she hoped authorities would grant her and her family permission to regularly write to and visit Au in prison.
"I dare not hope for more as I believe that will only lead to greater disappointment," she said in an open letter on Friday.
Au, who was formerly a primary school teacher, was elected to the Legislative Assembly in September 2001. For 20 years, he served as one of only a handful of pro-democracy lawmakers in the legislature, largely made up of pro-Beijing loyalists.
Au had co-organised annual vigils in Macau to commemorate the 1989 Tiananmen Square crackdown in Beijing.
These vigils were previously tolerated in places like Macau and Hong Kong, but have effectively been banned in both cities since China imposed a sweeping national security law on Hong Kong in 2020.
Au's jailing comes a day after Hong Kong sentenced Joshua Wong, the face of its now-quashed democracy movement, to 10 years in jail. Wong, 30, whose activism started when he was just a teen, has been in custody for the last six years.
summary: Au Kam San was sentenced to 12 years and six months' jail for "subversion against the political power of the state".

The Ministry of Public Health is advancing the Medical Investment Hub by signing a Memorandum of Understanding (MOU) with Bayer, a global leader in life sciences and medical innovation. Bayer has proposed a potential clinical research investment of approximately THB 153 million as an initial phase, while promoting access to innovative medicines and advancing AI-enabled eye disease screening. The target is to expand screening coverage from 2 million to 4 million people, to increase the chances of detecting disease early and reduce the risk of vision loss.
On 6 November 2026 (B.E. 2569), at the Chai Nat Narenthon Meeting Room, 2nd Floor, Building 1, Office of the Permanent Secretary, Ministry of Public Health, Nonthaburi Province, Mr. Pattana Promphat, Minister of Public Health, presided over the signing ceremony of a Memorandum of Understanding (MOU) on Cooperation to Support the Health Ecosystem for the Benefit of Thailand's Health System and Health Economy, between the Ministry of Public Health and Bayer Thai Co., Ltd. (Bayer). Dr. Somruek Chungsaman, Permanent Secretary of the Ministry of Public Health, signed on behalf of the Ministry.
Mr. Pattana Promphat, Minister of Public Health, said that the Ministry of Public Health is advancing the Medical Investment Hub policy to position the medical and healthcare sector as a new engine of economic growth for Thailand, through three pillars: the Service Hub, which enhances the quality and capacity of medical and healthcare services; the Research and Development Hub, which promotes medical research and clinical trials; and the Product and Health Manufacturing Hub, which strengthens pharmaceutical, vaccine and health product manufacturing. The policy aims to attract over THB 68 billion in new investment and generate an economic contribution of at least 0.5% of GDP. The policy is not only about increasing economic value, but also about using technology and innovation to improve the quality of public health services and people's quality of life.
"Our cooperation with Bayer is another important step in linking innovation investment with the development of the health service system. The company has proposed a potential clinical research investment of approximately THB 153 million as an initial phase, and supports the development of AI-enabled eye disease screening, with the goal of expanding screening coverage from 2 million to 4 million people. This will increase the chances of detecting disease early, reduce the risk of vision loss, and give people access to innovative medicine and modern medical technology."
Dr. Somruek Chungsaman, Permanent Secretary of the Ministry of Public Health, said that the Ministry places importance on using technology and innovation to improve the efficiency of the health service system, particularly early screening and diagnosis, the development of the patient referral system, and greater access to quality medical services. The Ministry also promotes clinical research and the use of real-world evidence to support health policy development.
"The Ministry of Public Health is committed to promoting the application of AI technology in retinal disease screening, especially for at-risk diabetic patients. We are also strengthening the capacity of healthcare facilities and the referral system so that screening, diagnosis and treatment are effectively connected, in order to increase access to services, reduce the risk of vision loss, and improve people's quality of life."
The cooperation also covers proposals to promote access to innovative medicines for patients with retinal diseases and prostate cancer, as well as studies on innovations to prevent recurrent stroke, together with investment in clinical research and the development of real-world evidence. These efforts aim to support the development of the health service system and strengthen Thailand's potential to become a hub for medical research and innovation under the Medical Investment Hub policy.
"Thailand has a clear ambition to strengthen its position as a hub for medical innovation, and Bayer is proud to support that ambition. Through our partnership with the Ministry of Public Health, we want to expand clinical research, help bring innovative treatments to patients earlier and further strengthen local research capabilities. By combining Bayer’s global expertise with Thailand’s strong healthcare ecosystem, we can support better outcomes for patients and contribute to the long-term development of the country’s healthcare system," said Sebastian Guth, Global Chief Operating Officer, Bayer Pharmaceuticals and President, Bayer U.S.
Mr. Simon Rosof, Head of Asia Pacific region, Bayer Pharmaceuticals, said: "Early detection can make a critical difference for patients. By using AI-enabled technology in retinal disease screening, we can help identify people at risk, particularly patients with diabetes, support more efficient referrals and connect them with appropriate care sooner.”
“Our ambition is to support patients across the healthcare journey, from earlier screening and opportunities to participate in clinical research to access to innovative treatments. At the same time, we want to contribute to Thailand’s ambition to strengthen health innovation and medical research. This reflects Bayer’s mission of ‘Health for all, Hunger for none’ and our commitment to supporting Thailand’s public health priorities for more than six decades.”
This collaboration marks another important step in supporting the development of the health service system, improve patient access to innovative medicines, and strengthening Thailand's potential to become a hub for medical research and innovation under the Medical Investment Hub policy.

A woman who was shot during the Bondi beach terror attack has died in hospital almost 12 months after the massacre.
Eva Geller, 90, had been in and out of hospital this year for treatment of injuries sustained during the attack on 14 December, a senior Jewish community source said on Friday.
She had recently returned to hospital after developing an infection, where she died after having a stroke, the source said.
Her funeral was scheduled to take place on Monday. A family spokesperson requested “privacy during this difficult time”.
Rabbi Aron Moss from the Nefesh Synagogue in Sydney said Geller was “a mother, a grandmother, a great-grandmother, a positive person” who had escaped the Holocaust as a child with her family.
“She came to Australia, started a new life, a beautiful family and was strong and pretty healthy, right up until the Bondi attack, where she was shot.
“Everyone in the community really loved her, loved being in her presence,” he said.
“It’s just devastating to think that she’s gone. She’ll be sorely missed, very fondly remembered, and we just pray that her family have a lot of strength and comfort at this time.”
The prime minister, Anthony Albanese, said on Friday he was saddened to hear of Geller’s death, saying “her life was changed forever by an act of terror and antisemitism”.
“We are wrapping our arms around Eva’s family, friends and the Jewish community at this very sad time.”
The New South Wales premier, Chris Minns, said the news of Geller’s death was “heartbreaking”.
“My thoughts are with Eva’s family and the Jewish community as they face another painful loss,” he said in a statement.

The NSW opposition leader, Kellie Sloane, whose Vaucluse electorate takes in Bondi beach, said the death was “a heartbreaking reminder of the ongoing pain that remains for many people from last year’s terror attack”.
“We must continue to support the Jewish community, first responders and all victims.”
In a statement on Friday afternoon, New South Wales police said they were aware of the death. A spokesperson said police were “awaiting further advice and are working with the office of the coroner”.
Fifteen people died after Naveed Akram, 24, and his father, 50-year-old Sajid Akram, opened fire at the Hanukkah festival at Bondi beach on 14 December last year. Forty people were injured.
Sajid was shot dead by police at the scene. Naveed has been charged with 78 offences, including 15 counts of murder and one count of committing a terrorist act that investigators allege may have been “inspired by Isis”. He remains before the courts.

content:
Finance Minister Ekniti Nitithanprapas highlighted developments in international politics on Friday (November 6, 2026) and pointed to what he described as a political transition in the United States (US) following a Democratic Party victory that had brought changes to both the Senate and the House of Representatives.
In the minister’s assessment, these developments had clearly affected the direction of money and capital markets worldwide.
Stock markets overseas had begun to fall amid short-term concerns and volatility, particularly over policy uncertainty surrounding artificial intelligence (AI) and data centres.
The US leadership had yet to clarify its position on either area.
Thailand had been preparing for the volatility, taking into account both the potential benefits and the risks that needed close monitoring, Ekniti said.
The Thai government is continuing trade negotiations with the United States to protect Thai businesses from adverse effects and keep them competitive in the large US market for goods.
Prime Minister Anutin Charnvirakul may have an opportunity to hold talks with the US president during the upcoming Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) meeting.
Thailand was benefiting significantly from its role in the AI supply chain, Ekniti said.
Citing recent meetings of the World Bank and the International Monetary Fund (IMF), the minister said Thailand had been identified as one of four key countries in the global supply chain, alongside Malaysia, Vietnam and South Korea.
Ekniti linked Thailand’s position to a sharp increase in demand for investment promotion, as reflected in applications to the Office of the Board of Investment (BOI).
In the minister’s view, the trend would help Thailand continue attracting more foreign investment.
Thailand’s financial stability and fiscal discipline put the country in a particularly strong position to withstand global economic volatility, according to Ekniti.
The country had maintained fiscal discipline, with public debt at more than 60% of gross domestic product (GDP).
By comparison, the minister pointed to US concerns over the debt ceiling and cited a US figure that had risen sharply to more than 100% of GDP.
“As a result, the interest rate on Thailand’s 10-year government bonds is only 2%, while the corresponding US rate is as high as 5%. This shows that Thailand’s borrowing costs remain clearly lower,” Ekniti said.
The government is monitoring the fall in global oil prices amid volatility in commodity markets and taking a cautious approach as it prepares to respond.
The government’s economic policy emphasises “short-term stimulus, long-term gains” as a framework for strengthening Thailand’s long-term competitiveness.
Measures to promote data centres are due to go before the Cabinet for consideration next week under a government plan to support sustainable growth in the country’s technology infrastructure.
