Police arrested television presenter Panadda “Boom” Wongphudee at her home in Bangkok on Friday morning (November 6), acting on a Criminal Court warrant in an investigation involving donations to the Ongkorn Thamdee Foundation, which she founded.
Officers from the Economic Crime Suppression Division (ECD) arrived at her residence in an upscale housing estate on Nawamin Road, Khlong Kum subdistrict, Bueng Kum district, at approximately 6.27am.
Panadda faces three allegations under the arrest warrant: public fraud, money laundering and offences under the Computer Crime Act.
The arrest took place as she was preparing to speak to journalists gathered outside the residential estate.
Earlier, at approximately 6.15am, her lawyer, Ekkasit “Petch” Srisung, had briefly informed reporters that Panadda was awake and ready to cooperate with the legal process.
However, before she could give an interview, ECD officers arrived in a van, presented the arrest warrant and immediately took her into custody.
Police then escorted Panadda back inside the residence to conduct a search for additional evidence connected to the investigation.
The operation involves four locations in Bangkok and neighbouring Pathum Thani province believed to be connected to the investigation.
Panadda's residence on Nawamin Road was the first confirmed search location.
The other three locations identified for searches were:
The searches are intended to gather further evidence as investigators continue examining the foundation-related allegations.
At approximately 7.45am, officers at the Central Investigation Bureau (CIB) headquarters began arranging metal barriers outside the Phithak Santi Building in preparation for the arrival of suspects.
The barriers divided the waiting journalists into two areas, leaving a clear passage through the building's entrance.
The arrangements were made ahead of the expected transfer of Panadda and her husband, Atip, for questioning and further legal proceedings in connection with the foundation investigation.
Police also placed traffic cones around part of the car park outside the building.
The reserved area was believed to be intended for vehicles or other items that might be seized during the searches and subsequently brought to the bureau for examination.
Investigators are continuing legal proceedings against Panadda over the allegations outlined in the arrest warrant.
At 8:15 AM, Atip arrived to surrender himself at the Complaint Center of the Central Investigation Bureau (CIB). Police officers coordinated his arrival to present him to investigators at the Economic Crime Suppression Division (ECD) to proceed with legal steps.

content:
El secretario de Estado Marco Rubio desmintió que planee dejar el cargo tras la derrota de los republicanos en las legislativas de mitad de mandato en Estados Unidos , según dijo en una entrevista a un medio local este jueves (05.11.2026).
Rubio, que también ejerce como asesor de seguridad nacional del presidente Donald Trump, es considerado por muchos como un potencial candidato en las elecciones presidenciales de 2028.
"Siempre ha sido mi intención" trabajar para el presidente Donald Trump hasta el final de su mandato, declaró Rubio al diario The New York Times .
Pocos días antes de las elecciones del pasado martes, el secretario de Estado hizo una inusual aparición junto a Trump en un mitin. Subió brevemente al estrado para dirigirse a una multitud que lo aclamaba.
Este jueves, esquivó preguntas sobre su futuro político: "Literalmente, no voy a hablar más de 2028".
Acerca de los rumores sobre si estaba considerando dejar el gobierno, Rubio respondió: "Para ser sincero, no sé de dónde salen estas cosas".
Departamento de Estado rechaza versiones de prensa
El jueves por la mañana, Bloomberg News informó de que Rubio estaba sopesando dejar la administración.
Según el reporte, Rubio había hablado con funcionarios de la Casa Blanca sobre su dimisión y que le pidieron que se quedara.
El Departamento de Estado rechazó con vehemencia las versiones sobre la salida de Rubio.
Dylan Johnson, secretario de Estado adjunto para Asuntos Públicos Globales, dijo que el artículo de Bloomberg era "totalmente inventado".
También rechazó como "noticia falsa completamente infundada" un informe del medio The Independent, según el cual Rubio planeaba lanzar su candidatura para la nominación presidencial republicana de 2028.
Rubio ha dicho anteriormente que apoyaría al vicepresidente JD Vance si se presenta a la presidencia.
Vance también es considerado ampliamente como un posible candidato en 2028.
La sucesión de Trump en camino
En los comicios del martes, la oposición demócrata logró una victoria arrolladora y arrebató a los republicanos la mayoría en ambas cámaras del Congreso, con triunfos históricos en bastiones conservadores como Texas, Iowa y Kansas.
Los resultados fueron interpretados como un referéndum sobre la gestión de Trump y como un voto de castigo por la impopular guerra de Irán y la inflación.  Las elecciones abren además la carrera por la sucesión de Trump de cara a las presidenciales de 2028, a las que el actual mandatario no puede concurrir por haber cumplido ya dos mandatos.
Según las encuestas, los principales aspirantes a la nominación republicana son Vance y el propio Rubio, aunque ninguno de los dos ha anunciado oficialmente su candidatura.
jc (afp, efe)
summary: El jefe de la diplomacia de EE.UU. aseguró que no tiene previsto dejar el gobierno de Donald Trump para buscar la presidencia en 2028.

content:
At least 27 passenger flights across Europe were affected by hoax bomb threats on Thursday (November 5), forcing some aircraft to divert or make unscheduled landings while fighter jets were deployed to intercept or escort others.
The disruption marked the second major wave of similar incidents this week. At least seven flights and a cruise ship had received bomb threats on Tuesday (November 3).
Authorities have yet to identify those responsible, and no claim of responsibility has been independently verified.
The incidents have raised concerns about possible coordinated disruption at a time when several European governments have accused Russia of conducting sabotage and other hybrid operations.
However, aviation security specialists have cautioned that the threats could also have originated from individuals acting on personal grievances or people copying earlier incidents.
An airport source in Italy told Reuters that an email headed "Threat report" had been distributed to airlines, airport operators and ground-handling companies at Rome's Fiumicino Airport and Milan's Malpensa Airport.
The message claimed to have been sent by "Fighters of the Male State" and alleged that explosives had been placed aboard incoming flights from Helsinki and Dublin, with detonation threatened within 60 minutes.
Reuters was unable to independently establish who sent the email.
In France, Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu's office reported that fighter jets had been dispatched to intercept an Aer Lingus flight travelling from Dublin to Rome.
The aircraft was escorted to the Évreux military airbase after the pilot did not respond to authorities as expected. The prime minister's office did not provide further details about the pilot's actions.
Bulgaria's air force also deployed fighter jets to accompany three passenger aircraft during their landings.
A Ryanair flight from London to Sofia was diverted to Plovdiv, Bulgaria's second-largest city.
Spanish police, meanwhile, received three bomb-threat emails within 20 minutes. The messages concerned two Air Europa flights from Madrid to Paris and four Iberia flights arriving from Rome and Milan.
Several aircraft were stopped or returned to their parking stands while passengers disembarked and security inspections were carried out.
At Warsaw Airport, a LOT Polish Airlines flight bound for Paris was halted while taxiing towards the runway. Passengers were subsequently transferred to another aircraft.
Danish police also searched two aircraft at Copenhagen Airport following security alerts.
Other threatened services operated by EasyJet, Finnair, LOT, Wizz Air, Ryanair and Air Serbia reached their scheduled destinations, including Prague, Sofia, Vienna, Brussels, Bucharest, Rome and Milan. Some received military escorts.
A passenger aboard a Wizz Air flight from Milan to Bucharest described how the aircraft was directed to a parking area away from the terminal after landing.
Fire engines, ambulances and counter-terrorism personnel surrounded the aircraft, although passengers were informed only that an emergency had occurred.
Joji Waites, director of flight safety at the British Airline Pilots' Association, noted that airlines generally act on bomb threats only after specialist assessors determine that they are credible.
The incidents have prompted renewed examination of security threats facing European transport networks.
Denmark, Poland and Romania, all affected by Thursday's disruptions, have previously accused Russia of involvement in hybrid operations.
Germany has also attributed an attack at Leipzig Airport in August to Russia.
Britain has previously made similar allegations against Moscow and linked Iran to a suspected plot targeting a US airbase.
Both Russia and Iran have denied the accusations.
Hybrid operations can involve relatively inexpensive actions that disrupt essential services while making responsibility difficult to establish. Such incidents may also fall below the threshold likely to provoke a military response.
Eric Schouten, head of aviation security group Dyami, observed that most countries affected by the latest flight disruptions support Ukraine in its war against Russia.
Analysts at aviation risk consultancy Osprey Flight Solutions also considered a connection with Russian hybrid operations plausible.
However, they stressed that other explanations remained possible, including personal disputes and copycat threats.
No evidence has yet established that Russia, Iran or any other state was responsible for the latest aviation incidents.
The latest disruption has also drawn attention to cyberattacks targeting essential infrastructure in Europe.
Eliran Almog, chief executive of aviation cybersecurity company Cyviation, suggested that repeated false bomb threats could serve two purposes: interrupting normal operations and observing how airlines, airports and government agencies respond to emergencies.
He noted that the aviation incidents were occurring alongside cyberattacks targeting refrigeration systems at supermarkets in several European countries.
The cyber incidents also affected blood banks in France.
Almog indicated that disruption to essential services could create economic losses while weakening public confidence in systems on which people depend.
Although the aviation threats and cyberattacks occurred during the same period, their possible connection has not been established.
Authorities across Europe continue to investigate the bomb threats and assess the security risks facing commercial aviation.

content:
The Association of Thai Travel Agents (ATTA) has warned that Chinese tourist arrivals to Thailand could fall by 20% year on year in November and December unless the government takes stronger action to restore confidence following a safety advisory issued by the Chinese embassy.
The warning comes after Chinese visitor numbers fell by 13.57% in October 2026 to 308,942, according to the Ministry of Tourism and Sports. The decline occurred despite China's National Day holiday on October 1, traditionally an important period for outbound travel.
October marked the first year-on-year contraction in Chinese arrivals since February 2026, following a gradual recovery from safety concerns linked to the January 2025 abduction of Chinese actor Wang Xing, who was taken across the Thailand–Myanmar border.
The Chinese embassy's latest advisory, issued in October, urged its citizens to exercise caution when travelling to Thailand because of risks associated with fraudulent job recruitment schemes.
ATTA president Thanapol Cheewarattanaporn told Krungthep Turakij that the advisory had affected confidence among Chinese travellers, particularly those booking organised tours.
Although official figures showed an overall decline of more than 13% in Chinese arrivals in October, ATTA estimated that the Chinese group-tour segment had contracted by at least 40%.
Thanapol cautioned that the downturn could continue into early 2027, with Chinese group-tour arrivals potentially falling by more than 50% during the Lunar New Year holiday if confidence was not restored.
He estimated that overall Chinese arrivals in November and December could be 20% below the corresponding period last year if Thai authorities failed to respond more actively.
Thanapol urged the government to work more closely with Chinese authorities to address safety concerns and counter negative reports circulating in China.
He also called on the Tourism Authority of Thailand (TAT) to strengthen its confidence-building campaigns and organise promotional roadshows in China with private tourism operators.
Although the Thai tourism industry believes the country's overall image remains positive, Thanapol argued that negative coverage in China continued to influence travel decisions.
He stressed that private businesses could not restore confidence through marketing alone and needed stronger government support.
Tourism and Sports Minister Surasak Phancharoenworakul was scheduled to meet the Chinese ambassador to Thailand on Thursday (November 5) to discuss the advisory and its implications for tourism.
ATTA also wants Prime Minister and Interior Minister Anutin Charnvirakul to use the upcoming Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) Economic Leaders' Meeting in Shenzhen, China, on November 18–19 to promote a more positive image of Thailand.
Shenzhen is located in Guangdong province, where Anutin's ancestral village is also situated.
Thanapol suggested that the prime minister visit the village during his trip, presenting his Chinese ancestry as a symbol of the longstanding connections between Thailand and China.
ATTA believes such a visit could generate favourable publicity in China and reinforce the close relationship between the two countries.
The difficulties facing Thailand's tourism industry extend beyond China, according to Thanapol.
He reported that European visitor numbers during the final two months of the year were expected to remain broadly unchanged from the corresponding high season in 2025.
Meanwhile, arrivals from the Middle East, a market known for relatively high tourist spending, remained below last year's levels amid geopolitical tensions.
Thanapol also expressed concern that reports of international conflicts and advice from some governments for citizens to stockpile essential supplies were contributing to uncertainty over overseas travel.
With several tourism markets stagnating or contracting, he described Thai tourism operators as increasingly exhausted and financially vulnerable.
He urged the government to provide additional marketing funds and work more closely with the private sector, particularly in restoring confidence among Chinese travellers, who represent Thailand's largest inbound tourism market.
Figures from the Ministry of Tourism and Sports show that Thailand welcomed 25,464,306 international visitors between January 1 and October 31, 2026, a decline of 4.59% from the same period last year.
Tourism revenue totalled THB1.241 trillion, down 2.85% year on year.
Despite the decline in October, China remained Thailand's largest source market during the first 10 months, contributing 4,244,376 visitors, an increase of 12.44% from the corresponding period in 2025.
Malaysia ranked second with 3,226,484 visitors, down 16.34%, followed by India with 1,924,417, down 3.05%.
Russia contributed 1,414,341 visitors, a decline of 0.27%, while South Korea accounted for 932,066, down 26.86%.
Taiwan ranked sixth with 877,729 visitors, up 6.71%, followed by Japan with 838,893, down 4.41%, and the United States with 838,365, up 0.94%.
The United Kingdom contributed 808,214 visitors, a decline of 3.43%, while Germany completed the top 10 with 712,316, down 2.9%.
Looking specifically at October, Thailand received approximately 2.265 million international tourists, representing a 12% decline from the same month in 2025.
China remained the largest source market, despite its 13.57% decline to 308,942 arrivals.
Malaysia followed with 276,157 visitors, down 26.97%, while arrivals from India fell 7.89% to 196,980.
Russia contributed 143,638 visitors, a decrease of 1.46%, and the United States accounted for 83,525, down 0.48%.
The October figures have heightened concerns among tourism operators that the Chinese market's recovery could lose momentum during the final months of 2026 without stronger efforts to address travellers' safety concerns.
Source: Krungthep Turakij

More than 3,000 tarantulas were seized at an airport in Lima on their way to Germany, Peruvian authorities said.
The spiders were hidden inside dirty socks contained in three suitcases carried by two Germans and a Polish citizen, the National Forestry and Wildlife Service (SERFOR) told Agence France-Presse on Thursday.
They were spotted after agents noticed some unusual wriggling inside the luggage during a routine customs inspection at Jorge Chávez international airport. “We noticed that some of them were moving. There were small ones and large ones,” said Cora Suarez, a SERFOR wildlife control technician.
One tarantula can sell for about €500 ($560) in Europe, Suarez said, meaning the wildlife trafficking scheme would be potentially worth €1.5m for just one trip.
The hidden arachnids, which came from several regions of Peru, were found in varying stages of development, from eggs and hatchlings to adults, Suarez said.
The Europeans accused of smuggling the tarantulas were detained by police specialising in environmental crimes and will face criminal proceedings, SERFOR said.
Illegal wildlife trafficking is a highly lucrative criminal activity that generates around $20bn annually worldwide, according to Interpol.
Such trafficking is among the primary causes of the loss of biodiversity on the planet.

content:
High above the Arctic, powerful winds usually circle the North Pole each winter, helping trap some of the coldest air on Earth.
But this circulation, known as the polar vortex, has weakened and shifted position in recent days.
While such disruptions can occur during winter, scientists say an event this early in November is unprecedented in modern observations.
Similar disruptions in past years have sometimes been followed by colder weather affecting parts of Europe and North America.
However, as this is happening so early in the season, there are few historical examples to compare with and it could throw current winter forecasts into even more uncertainty.
What is the polar vortex?
The polar vortex develops every autumn as temperatures fall in the Arctic.
Strong westerly winds form in the stratosphere, roughly 10 to 30 miles (15-50km) above Earth's surface, locking the coldest air near the pole.
Atmospheric disturbances can cause the air high up to start warming which then makes the vortex winds weaken. This sudden stratospheric warming (SSW) can eventually lead to the strong westerlies reversing into easterly winds.
In the following days and weeks these changes can alter the position of the jet stream, increasing the chance of a blocked weather pattern where it can become drier with a colder northerly or easterly wind bringing Arctic air in.
It can also boost the possibility of snow, especially in eastern UK.
Unknown territory
Most SSW events tend to occur from mid-winter but we are currently witnessing a dramatic weakening of the strong winds with some forecasts even showing a reversal of the polar vortex winds by mid-November.
Due to this weakening, the vortex has stretched and briefly split into two smaller circulations around the Arctic.
Sudden stratospheric warming can lead to a weakening of the polar vortex, resulting it in becoming disrupted, even split, high above the Arctic region
If the winds continue to weaken and end up reversing as forecast, this will be known as a major SSW event.
Jeff Knight, lead climate scientist from the Met Office, told the BBC: "It would appear to be the earliest on record looking back over the 75 years we've been observing…with most experts agreeing this is a very unusual event."
The current earliest major SSW event occurred on 28 November in 1969 and 2025.
Reasons for why we're seeing such an early event is not clear. It could be just part of the variability of our weather patterns.
But we also know in a "normal" El Niño year, this can typically bring a weakening of the polar vortex towards the end of winter.
While the warmer waters of the Pacific in an El Niño directly disrupt the weather around tropical areas, pulses of energy in the atmosphere, known as planetary waves, can cause disturbances even at polar regions.
These waves can push the polar vortex out of position and break the circulation up.
With the current record El Niño taking us into uncharted territory in terms of disruption to worldwide weather patterns, Knight suggested it could have "helped load the dice for this SSW event. However, because this is so rare, there's not enough evidence".
A link between a strong El Niño and early onset of a SSW event is unclear and will need further research.
Will the UK see snow?
Long-range forecasts issued by the Met Office show that the UK was more likely to see a stormy start to winter, followed by a colder spell to end winter. This is consistent with expectations from an El Niño pattern.
However, this unusually early SSW event was not widely expected.
Professor Andrew Charlton-Perez, meteorologist at the University of Reading, said: "The typical response to a SSW is for colder and drier conditions over Europe and the UK."
"Because we haven't seen a SSW event quite like this before, it is harder to anticipate a cold spell at the moment."
One reason is the timing.
The Arctic is not yet as cold as it becomes later in winter, with the polar vortex itself having only recently developed.
Any influence it may have on weather patterns could be weaker than during a mid-winter disruption.
And because the air isn't at mid-winter temperatures yet it means cold and snowy weather for the UK is far from guaranteed.
While snow is not likely in the coming weeks, a possible continuation of drier than average conditions will be concerning for replenishment of our reservoirs
Continuation of drought conditions "more concerning"
Long-term forecasts are based on large-scale climate signals and how they have affected weather patterns in previous years.
Much of the forecast for this autumn and winter has been focused around the influence of the exceptionally strong El Niño, pointing to a stormier start to winter, with the potential to be followed by colder and drier conditions from January.
But this unusually early disruption of the polar vortex and SSW presents meteorologists with a situation for which there are few modern comparisons.
For Charlton-Perez, the "concerning thing would be if this event ends up bringing the typical drier weather pattern and lack of rain" associated with a sudden stratospheric warming over the coming months.
With most of England and Wales still in drought, we need to rely on a wetter winter to fill up extremely low reservoirs.
For now, experts stress that it is too early to know whether recent changes in the polar vortex will change the winter outlook.

content:
Prime Minister Anutin Charnvirakul heard investment plans and proposals from 33 US companies across seven business groups at Government House on November 5, 2026, as Thailand worked to attract further investment and complete a reciprocal trade agreement with Washington.
Brian McFeeters, president and chief executive of the US-ASEAN Business Council (USABC), led the delegation, whose priorities included regulatory reform, trade agreements, energy costs and logistics capacity.
US Ambassador to Thailand Sean O’Neill and McFeeters highlighted more than 200 years of bilateral relations. US businesses valued regular discussions with the government as a way to understand Thai policy and economic opportunities, with some planning further investment. USABC also backed the reciprocal trade negotiations.
Automotive companies reaffirmed their commitment to investment and Thailand’s role as a global vehicle manufacturing and export base, with factory upgrades to accommodate both combustion-engine and electric vehicles. The group requested investment support, development of domestic parts suppliers, excise tax reform and faster free trade negotiations.
Consumer goods businesses praised Thailand’s enforcement of intellectual property laws and action against counterfeit products. The group also supported eliminating malaria by 2030 through cooperation on technology and disease-prevention products.
Transport, logistics and energy representatives offered support for improvements to Thailand’s transport and logistics systems. Their proposals included expanding capacity for cargo flights and developing the aviation and defence industries.
Digital economy and innovation companies reaffirmed their commitment to investment and Thailand’s digital transition, covering artificial intelligence (AI), digital infrastructure, satellite internet and public safety technology.
Manufacturing, food and agriculture businesses called for attention to energy costs and stronger food and animal-feed supply chains. The group also proposed using free trade agreements to expand market opportunities, alongside support for technology, workforce skills and advanced manufacturing innovation.
Tourism and financial services companies backed Thailand’s strategy for high-value tourism. Their recommendations covered better international flight connections, easier travel arrangements, promotion of secondary destinations, improved digital payments and regulatory changes to support business and investment.
Healthcare and life sciences businesses supported Thailand’s development as a regional medical hub. Proposed cooperation covered health promotion, disease prevention, wider access to adult vaccines, preparations for an ageing society, and maternal and child health, with the aim of improving quality of life and the healthcare system.
Deputy Prime Minister and Finance Minister Ekniti Nitithanprapas and Deputy Prime Minister and Commerce Minister Suphajee Suthumpun outlined investment support, including the Board of Investment’s fast-track process and imported-vehicle excise tax measures intended to benefit automotive manufacturers.
Government spokesperson Ekkapob Pianpises reported that Anutin had set out targets for Thailand to rank among the world’s 20 most competitive countries by 2030 and become a high-income country by 2037.
Thailand FastPass aims to shorten approval times for qualifying investments by up to 50%, while Thailand Skill Bridge is intended to align workforce development with industry and labour-market needs.
The government also plans to modernise energy infrastructure and widen access to clean electricity through direct power purchase agreements. Improvements in governance and transparency form part of preparations for membership of the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development.
Anutin described continued US investment across sectors, including new manufacturing bases, expansion of existing operations and participation in Thailand’s capital market. US businesses expressed confidence in the country’s stability, readiness and potential, while requesting changes to outdated laws and regulations to reduce barriers.
Anutin pledged support for major technology companies and the automotive industry, citing the latter’s large production scale and employment of Thai workers.
For data centres and AI, Anutin emphasised investment stability alongside balanced and fair energy management. Data centres’ consumption of domestically produced electricity and other energy must not undermine national energy security or burden the public.
Thailand also welcomed US investment in semiconductors, advanced electronics, AI and the digital economy, alongside cooperation in agriculture, food, biotechnology, healthcare and creative industries. Food security was a particular priority across transport, storage and distribution.
The government intends to negotiate new free trade agreements to broaden market access for Thai and foreign businesses.
Thailand’s investment discussions took place as reciprocal trade negotiations approached their final stages, with signing anticipated in November. The main agreement remains subject to legal review, while a joint statement is being prepared separately.
Anutin maintained that the US midterm election outcome would not affect the negotiations or the tariff arrangement. Talks with the Office of the United States Trade Representative had settled the substantive issues and principal conditions, leaving lawyers from both countries to examine the draft agreement.
Anutin expected the US tariff rate to remain close to 19%. Existing rates would continue until the main agreement was formally signed.
Anutin also maintained that Thailand had fulfilled commitments agreed with the US president concerning military measures, peace efforts and mine clearance, supporting its request for special consideration for a lower tariff.
Thailand’s Foreign Ministry and the US government were drafting a joint statement, with signing anticipated around the Association of Southeast Asian Nations and Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summits in the one to two weeks after November 5. Anutin intended to use those meetings to discuss the matter with US President Donald Trump.
Suphajee stressed the importance of completing the Agreement on Reciprocal Trade (ART), arguing that the US president retained executive powers and could continue using trade measures under provisions including Sections 301 and 232.
Suphajee expected US tariff measures to continue, making the agreement important for Thai competitiveness in the American market and greater certainty for trade and investment. Over the longer term, US legislation, budget decisions and industry support policies would require monitoring for their effects on the economy, international trade and investment.

content:
Iran reported that three more tankers had been damaged in the Strait of Hormuz on November 5, 2026, as shipping remained under threat despite growing political pressure in Washington over the Gulf war.
The reported incidents followed a US election defeat that cost President Donald Trump’s Republicans control of Congress. Vice President JD Vance blamed the war for the party’s losses, prompting renewed scrutiny of the conflict’s political and economic consequences.
Iran’s Revolutionary Guards reported that two tankers struck naval mines and another caught fire on November 5. The Guards generally do not acknowledge firing on merchant vessels, but maintain that passage through the strait is unsafe without Tehran’s permission.
The United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations (UKMTO) reported incidents involving five or more vessels in the Gulf since November 1. The frequency remained close to October’s pace, when 35 vessels were hit, the highest monthly total recorded during the war.
UKMTO also reported that two unidentified projectiles struck a vessel late on November 4.
Vance attributed the Republican defeat to the Iran war in a lengthy social media post on November 4. A White House adviser described some officials and staff as viewing the statement as a departure from Trump’s foreign policy and a public acknowledgement of the war’s economic impact.
Trump defended his decision to launch the conflict when asked about Vance’s comments that day. The president repeated his argument that military action was important to prevent Iran from acquiring a nuclear weapon.
Iranian Parliament Speaker Mohammad Baqer Qalibaf, Vance’s counterpart at earlier peace talks, responded on November 5 by accusing the vice president of allowing Trump to double down like a “losing gambler” through plans for further US strikes.
Qalibaf argued that Vance should persuade Trump to end the conflict if he considered it a mistake. “Skip the TED talk. Why not say this to your boss?” Qalibaf asked.
Oil prices fell sharply in recent days as traders judged that the electoral setback could make Trump less inclined to resume attacks. Trump launched the military campaign alongside Israel in February under the name Operation Epic Fury.
Oil recovered slightly on November 5, but prices remained more than US$20 a barrel below the previous week’s levels.
Two sources nevertheless told Reuters they believed Trump remained likely to order a resumption of hostilities.
“He is planning to bomb Iran. Don’t listen to what he’s saying. He held off because of the midterms. We asked him to hold off until the midterms,” one source told Reuters.
The other source argued that Trump had nothing left to lose politically now that the midterm elections were over.
Iranian officials have been discussing proposals to end the fighting with Qatari mediators since the previous week. Neither Washington nor Tehran has announced a breakthrough on the disputes preventing an agreement.
Negotiations have centred on the future status of the Strait of Hormuz, the US blockade of Iranian ports, sanctions on Iran and restarting talks over Tehran’s nuclear programme.
Qatar reported on November 3 that both countries remained committed to mediation and were examining proposals intended to narrow their differences. Qatar also noted developments in discussions with both sides, although a senior Iranian official described their positions as still far apart that week.
Iranian Supreme Leader Ayatollah Mojtaba Khamenei maintained a firm stance on November 4, rejecting “even the slightest inclination towards submission” to the United States. Khamenei argued that Washington would remain hostile towards Iran regardless of which party held power.

content:
La jornada de movilizaciones y de huelga en defensa del poder adquisitivo y de los servicios públicos en Francia se saldó, de momento, con 448 detenciones, 53 policías heridos y una ligera revisión a la baja de la participación, de los 600.000 hasta los 575.000 manifestantes , informó el Ministerio del Interior la noche del jueves (05.11.2026).
Asimismo, las protestas de este jueves, las más concurridas de este otoño pues, según los sindicatos, reunieron a 1,6 millones de personas en todo el país, requirieron 86 intervenciones por incendio, indicó el Ministerio de Interior, en su balance provisional a las 18 hora local.
La jornada de manifestaciones a escala nacional transcurrió, en su mayor parte, de forma pacífica —a pesar de algunos enfrentamientos con la policía en París y Lyon—, en el marco de una huelga de un día convocada por trabajadores del sector público.
El Gobierno francés consideró que las marchas "transcurrieron en líneas generales con normalidad", aunque señaló que "en numerosas ciudades (Rennes, Marsella, Nantes, Lyon, Burdeos, Estrasburgo) se formaron grupos de riesgo, integrados en cada ocasión por varios centenares de militantes radicales y de extrema izquierda".
Enfrentamientos en Lyon
En Lyon, la policía antidisturbios utilizó gases lacrimógenos y cargó contra un grupo de manifestantes, algunos de los cuales coreaban consignas contra las fuerzas de seguridad. Entre los manifestantes había personas vestidas de negro y con el rostro cubierto. El Ministerio del Interior señaló que, en esa ciudad, la policía se enfrentó a varios cientos de manifestantes; la violencia fue contenida, aunque la tensión se mantuvo elevada.
"Se impidió de manera sistemática que estos grupos pasaran a la acción, si bien mostraron una gran violencia contra los policías y gendarmes desplegados (en particular mediante el lanzamiento de proyectiles y morteros pirotécnicos)", expuso el Ministerio.
Las autoridades también informaron que, el jueves por la mañana, varias personas utilizaron fuegos artificiales para provocar un incendio en un instituto de secundaria en Toulouse, en el suroeste del país. En el lugar, algunos individuos lanzaron objetos contra los bomberos.
"Este comportamiento delictivo es un escándalo absoluto", declaró el ministro de Educación, Edouard Geffray, a través de la red social X.
Incendios en varios institutos de secundaria
Según las autoridades regionales, varios institutos de secundaria en la zona de París sufrieron daños, y uno de ellos, situado en el centro de la ciudad, fue objeto de un incendio provocado.
Mientras las manifestaciones en Lyon y otras ciudades, incluidas Marsella y Nantes, comenzaban por la mañana, la principal marcha de protesta en París partió por la tarde desde la plaza de la República.
Entre los incidentes destacó la quema en Estrasburgo de un gigante de cartón que representaba a un agente antidisturbios (CRS) con la inscripción 'CRS SS' -supuestamente diseñado por alumnos de la Escuela Superior de Arte de la ciudad-, lo que llevó al prefecto a denunciar los hechos ante la justicia a petición del ministro.
En La Courneuve (afueras de París), un individuo se enfrentó a varias personas que bloqueaban un centro escolar y apuñaló a una de ellas. El presunto agresor fue detenido y la víctima fue atendida por los servicios de emergencias sin que su vida corra peligro.
En Toulouse y en Lille se produjeron incendios parciales en instalaciones educativas.
Gran despliegue policial
Las autoridades desplegaron este jueves 70.000 efectivos policiales para evitar un nuevo 17 de octubre, una jornada de extrema violencia urbana ocurrida al margen de manifestaciones sociales en la que resultaron saqueados al menos 3.000 comercios en Francia y quemados edificios como la sede del Ayuntamiento de Limoges.
Los disturbios del 17 de octubre tomaron por sorpresa a las fuerzas de seguridad, dejando comercios y edificios públicos dañados en todo el país y avivando las críticas sobre la gestión de la crisis por parte de Macron. Desde entonces, las autoridades francesas han impuesto toques de queda, prohibido las grandes concentraciones y exigido a los manifestantes que sigan rutas alternativas, alejadas de las avenidas principales. Los sindicatos han denunciado estas medidas.
"El gobierno intentó bloquear las manifestaciones. Las manifestaciones son más grandes que nunca", declaró a los periodistas Sophie Binet, líder del sindicato CGT.
"Estudiantes de secundaria, pensionistas, universitarios, trabajadores: todos juntos. La unidad vence", se leía en una pancarta durante la protesta en Lyon.
jc (afp, reuters)

content:
Renewed attacks on tankers pushed Brent crude futures US$3.67 a barrel higher on November 5, 2026, as concerns about secure oil deliveries tempered optimism over a possible diplomatic resolution to the US-Israeli war with Iran.
Closing prices were: - Brent crude: US$98.29 a barrel, up US$3.67, or 3.88%. - US West Texas Intermediate crude: US$90.52 a barrel, up US$2.40, or 2.72%. Both benchmarks recovered from a sharp sell-off on November 4, when losses of more than 8% took their settlements to the lowest levels since August 31.
The United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations (UKMTO) reported incidents involving five or more vessels in the Gulf since November 1. Attacks remained close to a record pace, comparable with October, when 35 vessels were hit, the highest monthly total of the war.
Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps reported that two oil tankers and a tugboat caught fire in separate incidents after attempting to travel through the Strait of Hormuz on routes it described as unauthorised.
Andy Lipow, president of Lipow Oil Associates, identified reports of tankers striking mines or being targeted by drones in the Middle East as a continuing concern for oil traders. Lipow also pointed to unease over Iran’s unchanged negotiating position towards the United States.
“Today’s rebound reflects caution about pricing in a rapid normalization of oil flows before diplomatic progress translates into dependable shipping and deliveries,” Gelber & Associates wrote in a November 5 note.
A UBS analyst also attributed the modest price recovery to unresolved tensions in the Middle East.
Eurasia Group reduced its estimated probability of renewed US strikes on Iran from 65% to 60%, while doubling the likelihood of a prolonged standoff from 15% to 30%.
Eurasia also cut the probability of an agreement from 20% to 10%, citing Iran’s insistence on demands that Trump was considered unlikely to accept. Despite the recent decline in oil prices, the group estimated that an escalation could lift Brent into a range of US$110–US$125 a barrel.
Citi highlighted a different concern: with the US midterm elections over, the White House could turn its attention to executive powers over foreign policy and potentially intensify the conflict.
US President Donald Trump launched the war alongside Israel in February. The resulting surge in fuel prices became a major grievance for voters, and Democrats defeated Trump’s Republican Party to take control of both chambers of Congress in the November 3 elections.
The incoming Democratic-controlled Congress takes office in January.
Saudi Arabia, the world’s largest oil exporter, issued alerts on November 5 over potential danger in Yanbu, its Red Sea oil export hub. The alerts came as Yemen’s Iran-aligned Houthis continued attacks on the kingdom, extending another front of the Iran war.
The Houthis subsequently claimed an attack on King Fahd airport in Dammam. Saudi authorities had not immediately confirmed the claim.
Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araqchi, meanwhile, held separate telephone discussions with his Saudi and Qatari counterparts. Iran’s foreign ministry described the conversations as covering the “latest progress” in diplomatic efforts to support regional stability.
Ukraine’s renewed attacks on Russian refineries added to concerns about Moscow’s ability to export diesel under an agreement with Trump.
The Ryazan refinery, one of Russia’s largest, appeared to have been targeted during a substantial overnight drone attack on industrial sites southeast of Moscow, according to Reuters video analysis.
If the apparent attack on Ryazan were confirmed, it would make the facility the second Russian refinery hit that week, following the attack on the Yaroslavl plant on the night of November 2.

content:
Culture Minister Sabida Thaised expects Chud Thai, Thailand’s national dress, to receive UNESCO intangible cultural heritage recognition, with an official announcement anticipated on December 2–3, 2026, in Xiamen, China.
Sabida invited Thai people to follow the outcome and share in the pride associated with the country’s national costume, which encompasses traditional dress for both women and men.
Thailand submitted “Chud Thai: knowledge, craftsmanship and practices of the Thai national costume” for inscription on the Representative List of the Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity following a Cabinet resolution in 2024.
The United Nations Educational, Scientific and Cultural Organization (UNESCO) will hold the 21st session of its Intergovernmental Committee for the Safeguarding of the Intangible Cultural Heritage in Xiamen from November 30 to December 5. Sabida’s expected announcement window falls within that meeting.
Her Majesty Queen Sirikit The Queen Mother laid the foundations for women’s national dress through design work and a systematic study of clothing worn in the Thai royal court. She subsequently commissioned specialists to develop styles that preserved their elegance while remaining suitable for contemporary use.
The resulting collection, known as Chud Thai Phra Rajaniyom, or royally favoured Thai dress, became internationally recognised. Its eight styles are Ruean Ton, Chitralada, Amarin, Boromphiman, Dusit, Chakri, Siwalai and Chakraphat.
Men’s national attire is known as Chud Phra Ratchathan, with the shirt referred to as Suea Phra Ratchathan. The clothing comes in three principal forms, distinguished by sleeve length and the use of a waist sash.
Short-sleeved men’s national dress is worn for general occasions, work and ceremonies. The long-sleeved version is intended for ceremonial occasions, while long sleeves combined with a waist sash are reserved for important ceremonies requiring full formal dress.
Chud Thai represents a distinctive part of Thailand’s cultural heritage and soft power. National dress also remains popular among younger people, many of whom wear it for photographs at tourist attractions.

content:
The Bank of Thailand expects a revision to the Manufacturing Production Index (MPI) to add 0.1-0.5 percentage points to the country's GDP growth this year.
Speaking at "Economic Forum 2026: Reinvent Thailand" hosted by The Standard on Thursday, central bank governor Vitai Ratanakorn said the revised MPI, which incorporates additional industrial sectors, could contribute 0.1-0.5 percentage points to Thai economic growth this year.
However, the additional contribution depends on the calculation methodology and the official announcement of third-quarter GDP growth by the National Economic and Social Development Council, he noted.
The Office of Industrial Economics recently introduced a revised MPI series with broader coverage for factory integrated circuits and other electronic components, as well as notebooks and laptops, optical transceivers, and uninterruptible power supplies for data processing equipment.
Excluding the MPI revision, Mr Vitai said the central bank upgraded its GDP growth forecast for 2026 to 2.4%, rising from 2.3%, driven by strong exports, particularly those linked to the artificial intelligence (AI) investment cycle.
In addition, the changing political landscape in the US after the Democratic Party won control of both the Senate and House of Representatives is likely to have far-reaching implications for Thailand in several areas, including trade and investment, he noted.
Financial markets reacted swiftly to changing expectations, as oil prices dipped by 9% amid market expectations of easing conflicts in the Middle East.
Meanwhile, US equities have at times moved in the opposite direction to initial market expectations following political shifts, as investors reassess the prospects for policy changes and economic stability.
Technology stocks have benefited from the AI investment cycle, although changing financing conditions and potentially tighter constraints on data centre investment could affect leverage, capital spending and global financial flows.
"With Thailand's economic resilience and strong fundamentals, the country is expected to have sufficient buffers to navigate the changing global landscape. However, the central bank will continue to closely monitor developments," said Mr Vitai.
Amid the AI boom, the central bank raised its export growth forecast for Thailand this year to 22%, up from 14%.
Rising oil and food prices have placed a disproportionate burden on lower-income households, reinforcing the K-shaped recovery, in which some businesses and households benefit from economic growth while others continue to struggle, he said.
"Thailand needs to balance economic stability with sufficient growth momentum to support household incomes and SMEs. Growth of around 2% could be inadequate to ensure that businesses and households generate sufficient income to meet their expenses," said Mr Vitai.
summary: The Bank of Thailand expects a revision to the Manufacturing Production Index (MPI) to add 0.1-0.5 percentage points to the country's GDP growth this year.

content:
Global spot gold reached US$4,146.63 an ounce on November 5, 2026, its highest level since October 20, as a weaker US dollar and lower Treasury yields supported the metal. Falling oil prices also eased inflation concerns ahead of a closely watched US employment report.
Spot gold subsequently traded 1% higher at US$4,100.27 an ounce at 2.05pm US Eastern Time, or 7.05pm GMT, on November 5. US gold futures for December delivery settled 1% higher at US$4,113.50 an ounce.
Gold’s advance followed a jump of nearly 3.4% on November 4, its biggest daily gain since August 19. At its November 5 intraday peak, gold had recovered more than US$250 an ounce from the one-year low of US$3,869.85 recorded on October 30.
The US dollar index hovered near its lowest level since September 30 on November 5, making gold cheaper for buyers using other currencies. The benchmark US 10-year Treasury yield was also near its lowest level in almost two months.
Brent crude remained below US$100 a barrel after falling nearly 9% on November 4. The oil sell-off reflected hopes that strong Democratic gains in the US elections could reduce the risk of further escalation in the Iran war.
David Meger, director of metals trading at High Ridge Futures, said: “It's not that at this point rate hike expectation has completely disappeared.” Meger added that weaker energy prices could ease inflation fears and reduce the need for further interest-rate increases.
Traders assigned a 66% probability to a December interest-rate increase by the US Federal Reserve on November 5, according to CME Group’s FedWatch tool. Higher interest rates increase the opportunity cost of holding gold, which pays no interest.
Investors were awaiting the US non-farm payrolls report, scheduled for November 6, to assess the Federal Reserve’s likely policy direction.
Independent metals trader Tai Wong said recent payrolls figures had been volatile and that “gold could be vulnerable to a stronger-than-expected print”. Wong added that a strong employment reading would probably reinforce the December rate rise already widely anticipated by the market.
Poland’s central bank has achieved its previously announced target of holding 700 tonnes of gold in its reserves. The central bank has left open the possibility of further purchases.
Silver holds steady as platinum and palladium rise
Other precious metals recorded the following spot prices on November 5: - Silver was unchanged at US$52.23 an ounce. - Platinum rose 1.6% to US$1,520.75 an ounce. - Palladium gained 3.8% to US$1,042.24 an ounce.
summary: Global spot gold reached US$4,146.63 an ounce on November 5, 2026, its highest level since October 20, as a weaker US dollar and lower Treasury yields supported the metal. Falling oil prices also eased inflation concerns ahead of a closely watched US employment report.

content:
A jet engine will have hundreds of turbine blades
Published
Every time you fly, an extraordinary feat of endurance occurs inside the aircraft's engines.
Hidden from view inside the sleek outer nacelle are hundreds of little turbine blades that can shrug off enormous mechanical stresses and temperatures exceeding 1,500C.
It is a true engineering marvel. And these hardy blades are not sculpted or cut from their material – they are grown.
During the 1960s, engineers worked out how to take a molten metal alloy, cast it into the shape of a turbine blade, and then cool it very carefully from one end to the other over a matter of hours. A single crystal or grain of metal alloy forms during this process of gradual, delicate solidification.
Like turning a cup of water into one big snowflake, of your own design, rather than a mini blizzard of many smaller snowflakes.
"It's about as complicated as manufacturing gets," says Ben Fifoot, manufacturing engineer at Rolls-Royce, which makes turbine blades in the UK. "It's a real motivator to get out of bed in the morning."
Only a handful of companies around the world can produce these single crystal turbine blades, and the process has been perfected end-to-end in just five countries, including the US and UK. Engine-makers continually vie for access to the technology.
Rolls-Royce, GE and France's Safran are among the few firms that have perfected the process.
In September, GE Aerospace announced, external it would acquire its turbine blade supplier for $11.75bn (£8.78bn). Neither company responded to BBC News' requests for comment but the move has been described as an effort to ensure supply of these critical components.
Separately, in March, Rolls-Royce said it would invest more than £19m in its Rotherham blade casting facility.
Turbine blade specialists continue to work on improving the capabilities of this little-known technology. All the while, China is desperate to prove that its engineers can produce turbine blades of the same quality as those in the West. Who will come out on top?
"Demand for [turbine blades] is huge. So few companies have managed to do it, which does give it this kind of magical aura," says Bill Sweetman, an aviation industry writer and consultant.
He suspects GE Aerospace's recent move is about securing reliability and predictability in the notoriously volatile aircraft manufacturing supply chain.
The casts play a crucial part in the cooling process
But why is the single crystal casting process, which has been around for decades now, still so specialist?
To grow one of these blades, asserts Fifoot, is to "fight the laws of the universe".
This is because each molten blade would naturally cool into a solid object consisting of many small grains of metal alloy, all jumbled together. But you don't want a crumbly sugar cube, you want a perfect diamond.
Getting a single crystal to grow into the shape of the blade instead isn't just a matter of cooling the molten version down slowly, the process also uses a bizarre trick called a pigtail.
The pigtail is a small spiral at one end of the blade. Fifoot says that, at the beginning of the cooling process, this spiral "chokes" the flow of solidifying crystals so that just one takes over. A bit like a hairpin corner in an F1 race right before the finish line – one driver can take the lead here and go on to win.
"Sometimes we need to play around with the number of turns or the angles on [the pigtail] to try and get more favourable grain," adds Fifoot. Once the blade is formed, this crucial but sacrificial spiral is cut off.
France's Safran is among the few companies that can make single crystal blades
Blades made by Rolls-Royce are used in aircraft engines including the Trent XWB-84, which powers the Airbus A350-900, and the Trent 1000 XE, for the Boeing 787.
The single crystal is essential to ensure each blade's performance. Sometimes a blade doesn't cool quite as planned, for example two crystals form within it instead of just one, and the metal alloy must be reprocessed so that the manufacturer may re-use the material.
Special ceramic coatings also protect blades from extreme temperatures inside engines. And another important feature is that blades are cast with tiny channels that allow a flow of cooler air to coat them in a kind of film while the aircraft engine is working.
"The drive at the moment [across the industry] is currently to make those cooling passages really intricate," says Paul Withey, at the University of Birmingham, who formerly worked for Rolls-Royce. The more turbulent those little flows of cool air are, he explains, the more they will knock heat out of the surrounding, much hotter air.
And blade-makers also seek to reduce the mass of these components as much as possible.
"If we can take any weight out of it, you can run that engine more efficiently using less fuel – you can spin it faster and hotter," says Fifoot.
The turbine blades are used in the Trent 1000 engine among others
Meanwhile, China hopes to become only the sixth country to master the whole technology chain for single crystal blade casting.
A report in May, external quoted one engineer at the AECC Beijing Institute of Aeronautical Materials claiming that China now had a single crystal alloy "superior to or equivalent to the second-generation single-crystal superalloys widely used in Europe and the US". It costs less to make, too, apparently.
But the West has a "huge advantage" over China given that the majority of commercial airliner production happens there, says Sweetman. Supply chains and the latest innovations are generally clustered in the West. Plus, Western manufacturers also have lengthy safety records under their belts.
China must compete on practically every aspect of aircraft manufacturing, external – by no means just on turbine blades – in order to make serious in-roads. "You can definitely see that happening but it's a long, uphill struggle," adds Sweetman.
Demand for aircraft is currently high, which is already straining various supply chains in the industry. That demand could grow higher still, suggests Withey.
During the next few years, one of the two main aircraft manufacturers, Airbus and Boeing, could launch a new short-haul plane, external, he says. Then, the other would have to follow suit in order to remain competitive.
"There'll be a bun fight," says Withey, over who gets to supply the engines and, by extension, those all-important single crystal turbine blades.

summary: Investment has surged into the making of jet turbine blades - an extremely difficult component to make.

content:
Pope Leo is travelling to Uruguay, Argentina and Peru
Published
Pope Leo XIV is beginning a lengthy trip to Latin America just three weeks after surgery for lung cancer - a tour that includes a much-anticipated "homecoming" to Peru where he was a priest for many years.
The Vatican says no extraordinary measures are being taken in relation to the Pope's health, describing him as a "71-year-old who has undergone an operation" not someone with a "permanent medical condition".
It was Leo himself who revealed last month that doctors had discovered a tumour during a routine scan. The growth was removed along with the lower lobe of his right lung and his medical team then confirmed the cancer had not spread.
At a briefing in Rome ahead of the trip, which takes in Uruguay and Argentina as well as Peru, a spokeswoman stressed that Pope Leo had "fantastic stamina" and was "extremely enthusiastic" about the schedule which he had "personally confirmed... with no changes".
Back on track
"The Vatican's message with this trip is, 'that was a short episode and now we're back on track'," Professor Massimo Faggioli of Villanova University told the BBC, pointing out that the Pope has had a busy return to work since his surgery.
"We have seen him in these last few days making speeches, audiences and so on. He seems in great shape. That was important."
On Friday Pope Leo presided over the annual memorial Mass for cardinals and bishops who have died
The 12-day tour would be demanding for anyone, though. It incorporates multiple long-haul and local flights and covers thousands of miles from the Amazon to the Andes.
The starting point will be Uruguay, where the number of Catholics has fallen away steeply in recent years and which is getting its first Papal visit in four decades.
Leo then heads for Argentina, homeland of Pope Francis, his predecessor.
Father Fernando Laguna said his heart was filled with joy when the Pope's visit to Argentina was announced
"This visit is also a homage to Francis, who didn't make it to Argentina [as pope]," says Father Fernando Laguna, the rector of Santa Maria Addolorata, Argentina's national church in Rome.
"When this visit by Pope Leo was announced, it filled all of our hearts with joy," he told the BBC. "I always thought he would go, despite his illness. I don't think he ever thought of calling it off!"
The priest is installing a big screen inside the church in Rome to allow parishioners to follow all the key moments of the trip from afar. The building is already decked out with posters declaring Pope Leo is welcome in Argentina. "We're waiting for you!", one proclaims.
'Welcome Pope Leo' reads this poster in the Argentinian church in Rome
This leg of the Pope's journey - which includes meetings with heads of state as well as religious events - could be the most politically sensitive. President Javier Milei once called Pope Francis "evil on earth" and a "communist" for promoting a doctrine of social justice to help the poor. In turn, Argentina's bishops have criticised Milei's harsh austerity measures, making sweeping cuts to social spending.
But Milei has already welcomed Pope Leo, writing in a post on X that Argentina awaits "with immense joy". Millions are expected to turn out to greet him.
'Homecoming' to Peru
The highlight of the trip is undoubtedly saved for last, when Pope Leo reaches Peru - described by the Vatican as a return to his roots.
"He knows these streets," is how a spokeswoman put it.
Worshippers at Chiclayo cathedral in Peru were delighted when their former bishop became Pope in 2025
Born in the US, the then Robert Prevost spent almost 20 years in Peru, on and off, and even has Peruvian citizenship. That time is seen as fundamental to shaping his papacy.
His schedule includes a return to the diocese of Chiclayo where he was ordained bishop in 2014 and remained until Francis moved him to the Vatican almost a decade later.
He will also travel to Cusco, former capital of the Inca Empire, to say Mass more than 3,000m above sea level before heading to Pucallpa in the Amazon.
In all three countries, the Vatican says the Pope will have meetings with survivors of clerical sexual abuse - an issue which clouded a 2018 visit to Chile and Peru by his predecessor.
"This is how the papacy reconnects with Latin America after Francis, whose visits to the region were not always seamless," is how Professor Faggioli sees it.
He believes Pope Leo has a strong sense of the unity of the Americas as one continent. "Democracies are in trouble there, so there are so many things he can address," he suggests.
"The big question then is the United States. There's no question he wants to go. So will he travel when [President Donald] Trump is still in office? I'm sure they're thinking about this."

content:
Watch: What was your worst ever job interview?
Published
Tiara Allen arrived on time to interview for a retail job. Her interviewer didn't.
She waited for around 40 minutes in a shopping centre while the interviewer's co-worker called them "two or three times".
When they finally showed up, Tiara says she was told it was because the meeting wasn't in the schedule.
She needed work at the time, so took the job when she was offered it, but says she would handle the situation differently now.
"I would not take a job if they took that long," she says, adding that she believed her treatment during the interview was a sign of how the firm tended to treat staff.
Tiara Allen says she took the job despite being made to wait 40 minutes before the interview because she needed work
Tiara is far from alone. She is one of many people who spoke to the BBC about their worst job interview experiences after we wrote about the one interview question that leaves you feeling uncomfortable.
While those situations can be hard to deal with in the moment, they can also teach us a lot about the world of work.
'Are you a crier?'
During an interview for an assistant at a book publisher in New York, Chas Edwards was asked a question he wasn't expecting.
"I was asked for my first job if I was a crier," he recalls.
Thinking the interviewer was being funny, Chas replied that he didn't cry. He was later told that this was why he got the job.
"Her last assistant had cried – too often, I guess? – and she wanted someone who didn't cry. So she was being serious and I thought it was a joke," he says.
It was a bad sign. Chas says it was "a terrible, terrible job with a miserable boss" and while he managed to make it through 13 months there without crying he was "crying inside".
"I set the world record for working for this person. No-one had ever lasted three months with her before," he recalls.
Despite all this, Chas says he is in some ways grateful the experience was so awful.
"Because every job since then, even the bad ones, are not that bad," he says, adding that he can "cry anywhere now".
Chas Edwards says he thought the interviewer's question for his first job was a joke
Corinne Card also found herself floored when the first question she was asked in an interview for an administrative job was if she liked working with people.
When she replied yes, she was told that the job wouldn't be for her and the interview ended there.
"I don't know if it was a deliberate trap. Because who would answer 'I don't like working with people'?"
Corinne Mills, joint managing director of Personal Career Management, says that it can be worth asking an interviewer to clarify any weird questions, perhaps by repeating the question back to them.
However, if a line of questioning is really off-putting, she says it can also be a sign of what it's like to work there, saying that interviews are also about candidates judging the company.
Meanwhile, other questions are not just annoying – they are illegal.
Discrimination against a protected characteristic is against the law, external, meaning an employer cannot treat you less favourably based on your age, disability, gender reassignment, marriage, pregnancy, race, religion, sex, or sexual orientation.
Employment lawyer Roy Magara says that women being asked if they intend on having children in an interview is a "quite common" kind of bias. He says he has also seen a case where an older candidate was told he didn't get the job after an interview because he didn't fit the "vibe" of a younger team.
If you think these sorts of biases took place in your interview, Roy says you can send the company a subject access request, external to see how they discussed your application internally.
Worst-case scenarios like these can make interviews feel very difficult, especially considering the control employers have over candidates.
Euan Cameron, co-founder of hiring software Willo, says that even with this power imbalance it's important not to overthink what an interview is.
"An interview is just a conversation between two people," he says.
Of course, as in Tiara's case, it helps when both of those people show up.

content:
The Transport Ministry will open the entire 196-kilometre Bang Pa-in–Nakhon Ratchasima motorway (M6) free of charge from Dec 25 to ease congestion during the New Year holiday, said Transport Minister Phiphat Ratchakitprakarn.
Mr Phiphat said on Thursday that the motorway would operate around the clock during its trial period, helping divert traffic from Phahon Yothin and Mittraphap roads, the main routes to the Northeast.
Civil works on the M6 are 99.81% complete, while installation of operating systems has reached 96.42%. Full operations and toll collection are scheduled to begin in April 2027.
The ministry is also accelerating two other major road projects to improve traffic flow during the holiday period.
The 24.7-kilometre M82 motorway between Rama II Road and Ban Phaeo is already open for free trial use around the clock.
However, congestion persists at the Ban Phaeo exit, where three elevated lanes merge into one. Mr Phiphat has instructed the Department of Highways (DoH) to expedite plans to widen the exit to two lanes.
Meanwhile, the 18.7-kilometre Rama III–Dao Khanong–Outer Ring Road Expressway is 97.28% complete, with its elevated section above Rama II Road scheduled for trial opening in December.
The outbound connection linking Thotsamarachan Bridge, M82 and Ban Phaeo is targeted for opening by mid-2027.
Separately, deputy government spokeswoman Ploythalay Laksameesaengjan said the M6 exit connecting to the western section of M9 towards Bang Bua Thong, near Bang Pa-in 2 Interchange, would close from Nov 6 until March 31, 2027, for construction of connecting ramps and access roads.
Motorists travelling from Nakhon Ratchasima towards Bang Bua Thong must instead use Phahon Yothin Road or connect via eastern M9.
Traffic in the opposite direction, from western M9 onto M6, will remain unaffected.
During construction, M9 traffic will be diverted onto parallel Highways 3901 and 3902, each expanded to three lanes per direction.
The DoH will confirm the closure arrangements and diversion details before implementation.
Mr Phiphat instructed agencies to inspect road conditions, safety systems and signage ahead of the holiday travel period, while urging motorists to plan their journeys and follow traffic instructions.
summary: The Transport Ministry will open the entire 196-kilometre Bang Pa-in–Nakhon Ratchasima motorway (M6) free of charge from Dec 25 to ease congestion during the New Year holiday,  said Transport Minister Phiphat Ratchakitprakarn.

content:
Chinese electric vehicle (EV) manufacturer Changan Automobile has marked its three-year presence in Thailand with the announcement of a new business strategy aimed at strengthening its operations and expanding its role in the country's automotive industry.
Under the strategy spanning 2027-2029, Changan plans to launch new vehicle models and increase the use of locally sourced EV components, reinforcing Thailand's position as a key production and export hub for the company.
NEW STRATEGIC PLAN
Changan executives said the company intends to expand its product lineup and increase sales as it enters the next phase of growth in Thailand.
"We plan to launch 12 new car models here," said Chris Wu, vice-president of Changan Auto Sales Thailand.
The company is targeting sales of 30,000 vehicles in 2026, supported by marketing campaigns and stronger partnerships to drive demand.
"This is the second stage of our investment in Thailand, while also supporting the government's 30@30 policy," Mr Wu said.
Under the 30@30 policy, the aim is for electric vehicles to account for 30% of total automotive production by 2030, including 725,000 zero-emission cars, 675,000 electric motorcycles and 34,000 electric buses and trucks.
As part of its operational plan, Changan will increase production of high-value components at its Rayong manufacturing plant, expand its workforce to more than 3,000 employees by 2030 and provide training for more than 300 Thai technicians.
The company also plans to expand its service network to more than 150 locations nationwide, establish additional regional body-and-paint repair centres and technical repair facilities, and enhance battery maintenance capabilities down to the cell level.
LOCAL SUPPLY CHAIN
Changan aims to raise the proportion of locally sourced components in its vehicles from 50% to more than 60%, in line with government efforts to strengthen Thailand's domestic supply chain.
"Changan is committed to fostering the growth of local suppliers, enabling them to expand not only in Thailand but also globally," Mr Wu said.
The initiative includes sourcing parts and components from Thai suppliers for both Changan's Rayong facility and the company's manufacturing operations worldwide, including in China.
"This ensures our suppliers grow together with us sustainably and strongly," he said.
The Rayong plant currently produces two models, the Deepal S05 and Nevo Q05, and supports around 300 local suppliers.
Under the new strategy, Changan plans to increase the number of local suppliers in its network to 413, according to Mr Wu.
The company also plans to export battery EVs from Thailand to 18 countries this year, supporting Changan's "Vast Ocean Plan 2.0", which targets overseas sales of 1.5 million vehicles by 2030.
Vast Ocean Plan 2.0 represents the latest phase of the company's global expansion strategy and underscores its long-term commitment to international markets.
THREE-YEAR JOURNEY
Cai Hongwei, president of Changan Auto Southeast Asia, said the company has invested more than 10 billion baht in the construction of its Rayong manufacturing complex, which is being developed in two phases.
The facility, which began commercial operations in May 2025, has a total planned production capacity of 200,000 vehicles a year.
The first phase provides capacity for 100,000 units and includes battery module production as well as a dedicated battery repair centre designed to reduce maintenance costs and shorten repair times for customers.
The second phase will add a further 100,000 units of annual production capacity.
"This was the first stage of Changan's investment in Thailand from 2023 to 2026, focused on introducing our brand and vehicle models and demonstrating our long-term commitment to the Thai market," Mr Cai said.
The company employs 2,143 people in Thailand, more than 90% of whom are Thai nationals, and has generated more than 30,000 jobs across its supply chain.
Since operations began, the Rayong plant has produced more than 40,000 vehicles.
Changan also plans to introduce additional models from China, including the Avatr premium sports utility vehicle, a seven-seat passenger vehicle and a commercial vehicle.
The company is evaluating which future models should be produced locally in Thailand, taking into account market demand in the country and the wider region, as well as prevailing industry conditions.
Wu Xiaokang, vice-president of Changan Auto Southeast Asia, said the company has built a customer base of around 35,000 vehicle owners in Thailand.
During severe flooding in late September, Changan worked with dealers and business partners to assist affected customers.
The company's support measures included sending alerts and flood-response guidance, providing free towing services in heavily affected areas and launching a relief programme offering a 30% discount on spare parts to help customers cope with repair costs and broader cost-of-living pressures.
Mr Wu said since entering the Thai market, including during the recent flooding, the company has not recorded any battery-fire incidents involving vehicles owned by its customers.
summary: Chinese electric vehicle (EV) manufacturer Changan Automobile has marked its three-year presence in Thailand with the announcement of a new business strategy aimed at strengthening its operations and expanding its role in the country's automotive industry.
