content:
People exercise in a park in Delhi on Thursday, breathing in hazy, polluted air
Published
There are two cardboard boxes in Meenu Rana's living room in Delhi. One is filled with Diwali decorations and twinkling lights. The other holds air purifiers.
"The mornings have already started feeling stuffy. It will get worse in the coming days, so it's better to be prepared," says the 43-year-old teacher.
She is not alone. Every year, as winter and the festive season approach, residents of India's capital begin preparing for something far less celebratory: months of breathing polluted air.
Delhi and its satellite cities record some of the world's highest pollution levels through the year. But as winter sets in, the air often becomes unbearable.
Falling temperatures and slower winds trap pollutants close to the ground instead of allowing them to disperse. Smoke from crop residue burning in neighbouring states adds to emissions from vehicles and factories, as well as construction dust. Firecrackers used during festivals often worsen air quality.
The result is noxious air and a familiar question: why does pollution return year after year, and why hasn't more been done to tackle it?
This year, however, the Delhi government announced its Winter Action Plan months before the worst of the smog arrived. The plan is in place from 1 November to 28 February, covering the months when pollution usually spikes.
Experts have called this a step in the right direction, noting that in previous years measures were often rolled out only after the air quality got too bad to ignore. However, they say this by itself won't be enough, calling for more holistic, long-lasting measures.
Just days after the plan came into effect, the city is slipping back into a depressingly familiar pattern.
This week, a grey haze hangs over Delhi, along with a distinct smoky smell that residents unwillingly recognise. People complain of irritation in their eyes and difficulty breathing, and coughs and sneezes are heard everywhere.
For those who can afford them, air purifiers have become a household necessity. Outdoors, people wear masks or cover their faces with cloth, trying to protect themselves from the worst of the pollution.
Anti-smog guns sprinkle water to settle atmospheric dust in Delhi
Tackling pollution was among the promises made by the governing Bharatiya Janata Party during its election campaign last year. Its winter action plan is now a major test of that pledge.
The plan restricts the entry of older, more polluting vehicles registered outside Delhi and denies fuel to vehicles without a certificate which shows they meet emission standards. Demolitions and outdoor construction work that generate dust have been temporarily banned.
Private vehicle use is being discouraged - the government has asked offices to allow half of their employees to work from home, introduced staggered office timings for its staff and doubled parking charges. It says it will also strengthen pollution monitoring and enforcement and promote public transport and electric vehicles.
These measures are separate from the Graded Response Action Plan (Grap), which is overseen by the federal Commission for Air Quality Management.
Grap introduces restrictions in stages, with stricter measures kicking in as pollution levels rise. This week, its second stage is in force, restricting the use of diesel generators and burning of coal and firewood.
Experts say on paper, these actions collectively provide a roadmap for responding to rising pollution levels but their success ultimately depends on enforcement.
"There are a lot of positive changes as far as planning is concerned, but when it comes to execution, we probably still stand at the same level," says Parthaa Bosu, strategic adviser at the Environmental Defense Fund, a non-profit group focused on delivering climate solutions.
Others argue that the problem goes much deeper.
Vehicle entry restrictions have led to huge jams at Delhi's borders
"If we want to reduce pollution, we need to set targets for every sector - including power generation, industry and transport - not just vehicle entry, construction and stubble burning," says Manoj Kumar, an analyst at the Centre for Research on Energy and Clean Air.
"We know how much each sector and each state contributes to pollution. We can set targets to reduce emissions from each of them over the next five years."
Bosu points out that an issue which does not get enough attention is secondary pollutants - when gases in the air react with sunlight, water vapour and other substances to form harmful particles that contribute to pollution.
"Pollution is not just caused by biomass burning or vehicles," he says. "Dust being stirred up from the ground, coal and fly ash, materials burned at brick kilns and the large-scale burning of urban waste are also contributing to the problem. And much of this is still not being stopped."
Delhi's pollution problem is also affected by what happens outside the city. Pollutants travel into Delhi from neighbouring states and other parts of northern India, worsening the situation, Bosu explains.
This means that measures taken by Delhi can achieve only so much. Tackling the problem requires neighbouring states and the wider northern region to work together, he adds.
In the meantime, pollution is harming people's health every day.
During winter, government monitoring stations in Delhi frequently record Air Quality Index (AQI) readings above 300, classified as "very poor".
On particularly bad days, readings can reach 500, the highest point on India's scale. That does not mean pollution cannot rise further, only that domestic trackers do not record it. International trackers such as Swiss-based IQAir have recorded readings close to 1,000 on some days.
The World Health Organization recommends average PM2.5 levels over 24 hours should not exceed 15 micrograms per cubic metre. In Delhi, levels are often at more than 25 times that limit during pollution season.
Dr Manoj Goel, pulmonology unit head at Fortis Memorial Research Institute near Delhi, says these tiny particles "can penetrate deep into the lungs and enter the bloodstream, triggering inflammation and affecting multiple organs".
Even short-term exposure can cause throat irritation, coughing, wheezing and breathlessness. It can also worsen existing heart and lung conditions.
A 2025 report, external by the Energy Policy Institute at the University of Chicago estimated that air pollution could reduce life expectancy in Delhi by up to 8.2 years.
Burning of crop residue in neighbouring states is among the contributors to Delhi's pollution
For residents, the challenge is not just limited to breathing. The restrictions also disrupt everyday life.
Delhi is closely connected to its satellite towns, Noida and Gurugram, with thousands of people travelling between them every day for work. Long queues form at the city's borders as vehicles are stopped and checked, leaving commuters stuck in traffic for hours.
While the new rules offer some hope, frustration is growing.
Protests, political arguments and court interventions have become part of the annual cycle. But despite public pressure and government measures, the pollution returns every winter.
Rana keeps her windows closed and curtains drawn, and has added more indoor plants.
The arrival of another winter fills her family with dread, but unlike many others, they are not planning to move out of Delhi.
"I would have left the city long ago had there been an option, but my son has his school, my husband and I have our jobs as well, which makes it practically impossible," she says.
"What option do we have? It is unfair but we will have to live with it."

content:
California Governor Gavin Newsom's term in office comes to an end in January
Published
California Governor Gavin Newsom has commuted the death sentences of all 548 people on death row in the state, changing them instead to life in prison.
"We can now let these offenders die in obscurity while we forever remember and honour the victims," he said in a letter.
The decision to spare death row inmates is largely symbolic in a state that has not executed an inmate since 2006, though experts say it could save millions of dollars in court costs each year. Only 13 inmates have been executed since voters reinstated the death penalty in 1978.
The decision comes as Newsom, the Democratic leader of the most populous US state, has been discussed as a possible 2028 contender for president.
Newsom, who is term limited, is winding down his final months in office. Fellow Democrat Xavier Becerra is projected to take over after the midterm elections on Tuesday.
Newsom explained in his letter that he is exercising his constitutional clemency authority to commute the sentences to life without the possibility of parole.
"After nearly 30 years in public office, I have come to understand the limits of what government can justly accomplish," Newsom said. "I take this action because I firmly believe that state-sanctioned killing is incompatible with California's values, undermines the foundations of our legal system and diminishes each of us".
California has historically had the largest population of death row inmates. Newsom had previously ordered a halt to the death penalty in the state in 2019.
Americans' views on death penalty after failed execution in Tennessee
Describing his decision as a difficult but "righteous action", Newsom said that although many Californians feel that those who commit brutal crimes deserve to die, he has concluded that "the state cannot morally kill them".
He said that by every measure, California's system for administering the death penalty "is a failure", and that it has not and cannot be fairly applied, resulting in the conviction of innocent people.
Life without the possibility of parole is the most severe punishment he can lawfully impose and that the state can ethically enforce, he said.
He acknowledged that his clemency action will anger and hurt some Californians and said that it will "always weigh heavily on me".
"As governor, I alone bear responsibility for this decision and its impact, just as I alone would bear responsibility for each execution," he wrote.
"For this reason, I am compelled to follow my conscience and, as authorised by our Constitution, take this action for the welfare of the State of California."
Because individual states have the power to prosecute crimes and order executions, much of the power lies with state governors.
Bernard E Harcourt, a law and civil liberties professor at Columbia University, told the BBC that it is not unprecedented for a potential presidential candidate to come out as an abolitionist in the run up to elections - despite the overall popularity of the death penalty in the US.
He noted that François Mitterrand did precisely that in his presidential campaign in France in 1981, taking "the higher ethical ground and was rewarded by the public for that".
"I detect a very similar ethical positioning in Governor Newsom's statements about the commutations. And here too, it may well be something that the voters respect," he said.
San Quentin State Prison's used to house California's death row adjustment centre
Newsom's decision comes after the high-profile botched execution of a woman in Tennessee in late September and while executions have been on the rise in the US. There are three executions scheduled for Thursday in Indiana, Florida and Alabama.
At least four of seven judges on the California Supreme Court will have to sign off on the commutations, CalMatters reported.
It is unclear how Newsom's decision will affect condemned inmates like Keith Doolin, 53, who was sentenced to death in 1996 for murdering two sex workers, Inez Espinoza and Peggy Tucker, and shooting four others. He maintains his innocence.
Doolin lived on death row at San Quentin for decades, until he was moved to another prison in 2025 when the governor announced the state would reform the prison for all but those on death row.
Doolin's mother, Donna Larsen, told the BBC that the news of Newsom's commutations - which includes Doolin - brought mixed emotions.
"At least the execution chamber will not be reconstructed, and no more killing by the people of the state of California," she said.
Anthony D Romero, the executive director of the American Civil Liberties Union, applauded Newsom's action.
"These commutations reflect what justice demands: an end to a racist, error-prone, and inhumane punishment that has burdened California for far too long," Romero said.
"By taking this step, Gov. Newsom has affirmed that the death penalty has no place in California and he showed real courage by confronting racialised injustice head-on."
Nathan Hochman, the top prosecutor in Los Angeles County, said that while Newsom has the power to commute sentences, only state legislature or voters can eliminate the death penalty.
"Californians have been asked on two separate ballot initiatives to abolish the death penalty and both times they have chosen to keep it for the most serious crimes," Hochman said in a statement.
How widely used is the death penalty in the US?
On the federal level, President Donald Trump, a long-time supporter of the death penalty, has described capital punishment as "an essential tool for deterring and punishing those who would commit the most heinous crimes and acts of lethal violence against American citizens".
In 2020, during his first term, he ended a nearly two-decade moratorium on the federal death penalty, by ordering 13 executions over a six-month period.
While the moratorium returned under President Biden, on the first day of Trump's second term in 2025, he signed an executive order that re-instated the death penalty.
No federal executions have been carried out since he signed it, however. In the US, both the federal government and local states authorities can order executions.
The death penalty is legal in 27 states, but has been abolished in 23 states and Washington DC, according to the Death Penalty Information Center, a national non-profit.
California, which primarily uses lethal injection for executions, used to house male death row prisoners in San Quentin State Prison north of San Francisco, and female inmates in the Central California Women's Facility in the Central Valley.
But a 2016 ballot measure allowed for their transfer to other facilities that provide a necessary level of security, according to the California Department of Corrections and Rehabilitation.

content:
Amnesty International has urged Thailand to offer two Uyghur men sanctuary in a safe third country, warning that deporting them to China would endanger their lives and violate international law.
Secretary-General Agnes Callamard called on the Thai government to halt any plans to return the men, provide access to lawyers of their choice and find a safe third-country solution, saying their forced return would breach international law.
"Thai authorities must immediately halt any plans to forcibly return these two Uyghur men to China, where they face a real risk of torture, arbitrary detention and enforced disappearance," Ms Callamard said.
She warned Thailand against repeating its February 2025 deportation of 40 Uyghur men, whose whereabouts and well-being remain unknown despite subsequent visits by Thai representatives to China's Xinjiang region.
The two men are among five Uyghurs remaining in Thailand from a group of more than 300 detained without charge on March 13, 2014, after fleeing persecution and discrimination in Xinjiang.
On Oct 21, the two were released from prison under a royal pardon and transferred to Bangkok's Immigration Detention Centre. Amnesty said they had since been denied access to their lawyers, civil society organisations and the National Human Rights Commission of Thailand.
Both men have told their legal representatives that they fear for their lives if returned to China and do not consent to deportation. They have spent more than 12 years in Thai detention.
Ms Callamard said diplomatic assurances from Beijing could not override Thailand's obligation not to return anyone to a country where they face a real risk of torture or other serious human rights violations.
Amnesty also cited Thailand's obligations under the Convention against Torture and Article 13 of the Prevention and Suppression of Torture and Enforced Disappearance Act, which prohibits deportation where there are substantial grounds to believe a person would face torture, ill-treatment or enforced disappearance.
The organisation said its 2021 report documented crimes against humanity against Uyghurs and other Muslim ethnic groups in Xinjiang.
summary: Amnesty International has urged Thailand to offer two Uyghur men sanctuary in a safe third country, warning that deporting them to China would endanger their lives and violate international law.

content:
AI glasses could shape the global wearable technology market, but concerns over comfort, battery life, privacy and practical usefulness must be addressed before they become widely adopted everyday products, according to Wong Ming Yin, general manager of OBE (H.K.) Ltd.
He made the assessment during the “AI Eyewear Sharpening the Vision” session at the 34th Hong Kong International Optical Fair, held at the Hong Kong Convention and Exhibition Centre (HKCEC) on Wednesday (November 4). Wong described the shift towards intelligent eyewear as irreversible, despite the challenges facing manufacturers.
“I believe smart glasses will continue to define tomorrow’s eyewear. But success depends on four things: understanding what people need, conducting the research, finding manufacturers who can produce specialised components such as hinges, and identifying the right market,” Wong explained.
Industry figures point to rapid expansion. International Data Corporation (IDC) reported that global smart eyewear shipments reached 3.566 million units in the first quarter of 2026, up 130.1% year-on-year.
Separately, Omdia estimated that worldwide AI glasses shipments totalled 8.7 million units in 2025, an increase of 322% from the previous year.
Despite this growth, the industry's challenge is whether rising interest in smart glasses can translate into sustained everyday use, particularly as manufacturers seek to balance increasingly sophisticated functions with comfort and convenience.
By combining digital functions with conventional eyewear, developers hope to make information more accessible without requiring users to repeatedly reach for their smartphones. This potential for hands-free computing is central to the industry's vision of AI glasses becoming a more important part of the wearable market.
Jasper Wu, assistant to the president at INMO, the smart eyewear brand developed by Sichuan Yingmu Technology, highlighted real-time translation and navigation as practical uses for the lightweight Go series.
She described the Air range as wearable computers capable of running applications, while the newly introduced INMO Future extends the concept to spatial computing, including interactive, life-sized 3D models that could support training and education.
Dillion Ho, product designer and co-founder of NIMO, described a similar aim: presenting digital information without disrupting a person's awareness of the physical world.
“The fundamental idea behind smart glasses is to seamlessly present digital information in front of our eyes while keeping us connected to the world around us,” Ho explained.
Ho identified three persistent barriers to daily adoption: physical comfort, appearance and fit, and the ease of retrieving information. Weight and pressure on the nose and neck can make extended use uncomfortable, while differences in face shape and personal style complicate design.
“After decades of development, three primary challenges remain: how the glasses feel, how easy they are to use, and how people find the right fit,” he noted.
He argued that information must be easier and quicker to access through the glasses than by taking out a smartphone. Otherwise, new technology could offer too little advantage to change established habits.
Wong also stressed the practical demands of everyday wear. Hinges must withstand repeated use, batteries must last long enough and frames must appeal to consumers who may prefer ordinary-looking spectacles. He questioned the industry's pursuit of ever-lighter designs if it left too little room for durable components.
Beyond engineering, Wong raised public acceptance and privacy concerns surrounding cameras built into glasses. He also questioned whether specialist uses, such as fishing or golf, could reach large enough markets to justify development costs.
Wu framed the challenge more simply: “As we add more technology to glasses, one question stays with us: will people still want to wear them every day?”
How manufacturers hope to overcome the barriers
Wu proposed an all-in-one approach that incorporates the display, processing chip and controls into the glasses, reducing the need for cables or separate computing devices.
“We aim to bring the display, computing, and controls directly into the glasses, reducing the extra equipment we have to carry with us,” she explained.
She described a magnetic battery design for INMO Go3 intended to make all-day use more convenient, as well as plans for additional frame styles. Her broader point was that technical capability must be weighed against comfort, battery performance and appearance.
For Wong, the solution also requires manufacturers to know which consumers they are serving. A product aimed at a specialist activity may need different functions, styling and price positioning from one designed for everyday use.
Their views suggest that manufacturers must look beyond adding advanced features and focus on whether smart glasses offer enough practical benefits to justify wearing them throughout the day.
AI also changes conventional optical lenses
While the other speakers focused mainly on smart eyewear and its everyday applications, Chris Toh, professional affairs manager for Asia-Pacific at Rodenstock Asia Distributor Partners, described a different use of AI, focused on lens design rather than electronic functions built into frames.
Rodenstock's Biometric Intelligent Glasses (B.I.G.) approach uses AI to help tailor prescription lenses to the characteristics of each eye. Toh cited the company's finding that standard eye models match only about 2% of eyes.
“Standard eye models only match two per cent of the population, but by leveraging AI technology, we fuse your prescription with biometric data to make your vision even sharper,” he explained.
The system draws on relationships identified in a database of more than 500,000 biometric eye scans to estimate individual eye parameters from prescription information, with the aim of improving central and peripheral vision.
“Instead of merely smart, we call them Biometric Intelligent Glasses, where our lenses are optimised based on the unique biometric parameters of your eyes,” Toh added.
These are not connected devices that run AI functions while worn. They illustrate how AI can also influence the design and manufacture of conventional prescription lenses.
Taken together, the presentations suggest that AI could reshape the global eyewear and wearable markets through both hands-free computing and advances in vision correction.
However, the ability of AI glasses to secure a lasting place in everyday life will depend on whether manufacturers can overcome the practical barriers of comfort, durability, battery life, privacy and usability.

The Agriculture and Cooperatives Ministry has given organisers of the Udon Thani International Horticultural Expo 2026 seven days to address visitor complaints about transport, ticketing and facilities following its opening on Nov 1.
Deputy Agriculture and Cooperatives Minister Watcharaphon Khaokham said the ministry had received complaints from visitors and on social media and instructed relevant agencies to fix problems that could be resolved immediately. Issues requiring further coordination would be referred to the provincial event subcommittee.
Parking and transport are among the priorities. Additional parking spaces have been opened near the ticket office, while the province has been asked to arrange shuttle buses, seating and timetable signs. The ministry is also seeking to hire buses from Nakhon Ratchasima Zoo and expand transport services within the venue.
Other improvements include more signs and leaflets to help visitors navigate the six exhibition zones, additional mobile toilets, rubbish bins and better solar-powered lighting. The ministry has also called for more drinking-water points, vending machines, food stalls and souvenir shops.
The ticketing process is also being reviewed. Visitors who buy tickets online currently have to register again at the entrance. Mr Watcharaphon said organisers had explained that the additional step was intended to collect data for an event assessment.
The ministry plans to collect the information after visitors leave instead, eliminating the need for repeat registration before entry.
Mr Watcharaphon also called for shuttle routes connecting the venue with nearby communities and tourist attractions to spread tourism revenue beyond the expo grounds.
The ministry is considering turning the site into a permanent exhibition centre, public park and conservation tourism destination after the event.
The expo runs until March 14 and has a total budget of 2.75 billion baht.
summary: The Agriculture and Cooperatives Ministry has given organisers of the Udon Thani International Horticultural Expo 2026 seven days to address visitor complaints about transport, ticketing and facilities following its opening on Nov 1.

The Thai Meteorological Department (TMD) forecasts thundershowers across 70% of Bangkok and surrounding areas, accompanied by gusty winds and isolated heavy rain. The forecast covers the period from 6am on November 6, 2026, to 6am on November 7, local time.
Bangkok and surrounding areas can expect minimum temperatures of 24–26°C and maximum temperatures of 32–34°C over the forecast period, with southeasterly winds of 10–20 km/h.
A high-pressure system, or cold air mass, from China has spread over upper Thailand and the South China Sea, bringing easterly winds across the Gulf of Thailand, the country and the Andaman Sea, according to TMD.
TMD advised people in upper Thailand to take precautions against heavy rain, thundershowers and gusty winds by avoiding open areas, sheltering under large trees, and standing near unsecured structures or billboards.
Mariners in the Andaman Sea and Gulf of Thailand should navigate cautiously and avoid areas with thundershowers, where waves may exceed two metres, TMD advised.
The Central region faces thundershowers across 70% of its area on November 6–7, with gusty winds, hail and isolated heavy rain in Nakhon Sawan, Uthai Thani, Chai Nat, Lop Buri, Saraburi, Phra Nakhon Si Ayutthaya, Suphan Buri, Kanchanaburi, Ratchaburi, Nakhon Pathom, Samut Sakhon and Samut Songkhram. Minimum temperatures are forecast at 21–26°C and maximum temperatures at 32–35°C, with easterly winds of 10–20 km/h.
In the North, thundershowers are expected across 60% of the region on November 6–7, accompanied by gusty winds, hail and isolated heavy rain in Mae Hong Son, Chiang Mai, Chiang Rai, Lamphun, Lampang, Phayao, Nan, Phrae, Uttaradit, Sukhothai, Tak, Kamphaeng Phet, Phitsanulok, Phichit and Phetchabun. Temperatures will range from minimums of 22–24°C to maximums of 32–35°C, with southeasterly winds of 10–20 km/h.
Thundershowers are forecast across 40% of the Northeast on November 6–7, with gusty winds and isolated heavy rain in Loei and Chaiyaphum. Minimum temperatures will be 22–24°C and maximum temperatures 32–35°C, with easterly winds of 10–20 km/h.
The East can expect thundershowers across 60% of the region on November 6–7, with gusty winds and isolated heavy rain in Nakhon Nayok, Chachoengsao, Chon Buri and Rayong. Minimum temperatures are forecast at 23–25°C and maximum temperatures at 32–34°C, with southeasterly winds of 10–30 km/h. Waves off the eastern coast will remain below one metre but exceed two metres in areas with thundershowers.
Southern Thailand is expected to receive increasing rainfall from November 7–13, with heavy rain in many areas and isolated very heavy rain. TMD attributed the wetter conditions to strengthening easterly winds over the Gulf of Thailand, the South and the Andaman Sea.
For November 6–7, thundershowers are forecast across 60% of the South’s east coast, with isolated heavy rain in Phetchaburi, Prachuap Khiri Khan, Chumphon, Surat Thani, Nakhon Si Thammarat, Songkhla, Pattani and Narathiwat. Minimum temperatures will be 22–25°C and maximum temperatures 32–34°C.
Along the southern Gulf coast on November 6–7, winds will be easterly at 15–30 km/h from Surat Thani northwards and southeasterly at the same speed from Nakhon Si Thammarat southwards. Waves in both areas will be about one metre high, rising above two metres in thundershowers.
The South’s west coast is forecast to have thundershowers across 60% of its area on November 6–7, mainly in Phang Nga, Phuket, Krabi, Trang and Satun. Minimum temperatures will be 24–26°C and maximum temperatures 32–34°C, with easterly winds of 15–30 km/h. Waves will be about one metre high, exceeding one metre offshore and two metres in areas with thundershowers.

Automotive firms represented by the US-Asean Business Council (USABC) reaffirmed plans to maintain and expand investment in Thailand, retaining the country as a key global vehicle manufacturing and export base.
They pledged factory upgrades for combustion-engine and electric vehicles. They urged the government to promote investment, strengthen local parts makers, review excise taxes and speed up free trade talks.
The proposals were among seven sets of recommendations presented by a delegation led by Brian McFeeters, USABC president and chief executive officer, during a meeting with Prime Minister Anutin Charnvirakul on Thursday.
The delegation comprised representatives from 33 US companies across seven business sectors.
Government spokesman Ekkapob Pianpises said on Thursday that the meeting provided an opportunity to exchange views on industry developments, business priorities and ways to strengthen cooperation with Thailand.
Mr Anutin described US businesses as longstanding partners in Thailand's economic development.
"The government aimed to make Thailand one of the world's 20 most competitive economies by 2030 and achieve high-income country status by 2037," Mr Anutin said.
To support these goals, the government is implementing the Thailand FastPass initiative to reduce approval times for qualifying investment projects by up to 50%, alongside the Thailand Skill Bridge programme to align workforce skills with industrial requirements.
It is also modernising energy infrastructure, expanding access to clean energy through Direct Power Purchase Agreements, and strengthening governance and transparency in preparation for Thailand's accession to the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD).
On trade and investment, the prime minister said negotiations with the Office of the United States Trade Representative had reached agreement on key substantive elements.
He said he hoped both sides would have an opportunity to reaffirm their commitment to proceeding with an agreement on reciprocal trade.
Thailand also welcomed further US investment in semiconductors, advanced electronics, artificial intelligence (AI) and the digital economy, as well as cooperation in agriculture, biotechnology, healthcare and creative industries.
"The United States remained an important and enduring economic partner," said Mr Anutin, adding that relevant ministries and agencies would follow up on the delegation's recommendations in coordination with USABC and the Board of Investment (BOI) to support investment and business expansion.
Mr McFeeters said USABC had brought representatives of leading American manufacturers, investors and businesses operating in Thailand to strengthen cooperation.
Previous discussions in New York and during the IMF-World Bank Annual Meetings had helped US companies understand Thailand's policy direction and investment opportunities, with some considering further investment.
USABC also expressed support for the reciprocal trade negotiations.
Beyond the automotive sector, other business groups outlined their priorities and recommendations.
The consumer goods sector commended Thailand's enforcement of intellectual property laws and efforts to combat counterfeit products, while supporting malaria elimination by 2030 through technology and disease-prevention products.
The transport, logistics and energy sector proposed increasing air cargo capacity and developing the aviation and defence industries.
summary: Automotive firms represented by the US-Asean Business Council (USABC) reaffirmed plans to maintain and expand investment in Thailand, retaining the country as a key global vehicle manufacturing and export base.

Prime Minister Anutin Charnvirakul has denied that his Bhumjaithai-led government is seeking to extend its influence over parliament, amid criticism of proposed changes to House regulations governing parliamentary committees.
Speaking at Government House on Thursday, Mr Anutin said the government was acting within the constitution and its mandate from voters.
He was responding to criticism of new parliamentary regulations issued by House Speaker Sophon Zarum, requiring committees to approve by majority vote invitations for individuals to provide information.
Asked whether ministers and officials would attend committee hearings if invited, Mr Anutin said they would comply with the law and constitution, adding that committee procedures were already governed by constitutional laws.
He also denied that the new rules were linked to a request by People's Party MP Rangsiman Rome, chairman of the House Committee on State Security, Border Affairs, National Strategy and National Reform, for him to testify about alleged irregularities in local government recruitment examinations.
Mr Anutin also rejected allegations of a "blue takeover", a reference to Bhumjaithai's political colour and claims that the party was seeking to dominate state institutions.
"We are serving as a government under the constitution," he said.
He also denied describing Thai politics as negative in a speech at the Nov 4 "Reinvent Thailand" event, saying he had merely called for improvements to the political system.
Meanwhile, Bhumjaithai has proposed further amendments to House regulations that would significantly change how parliamentary committees operate.
Under the proposals, invitations for individuals and requests for documents would require approval from at least half of all committee members. Requests involving state officials would also have to be communicated to the prime minister or the minister overseeing the relevant agency.
The amendments would replace the existing allocation of committee chairmanships based on parties' representation in the House with a voting system.
They would also require majority approval for live broadcasts of committee meetings and allow the prime minister or ministers, in certain circumstances, to delegate answers to parliamentary questions to other cabinet members.
summary: Prime Minister Anutin Charnvirakul has denied that his Bhumjaithai-led government is seeking to extend its influence over parliament, amid criticism of proposed changes to House regulations governing parliamentary committees.

Police have arrested three alleged organisers of a network supplying corporate mule accounts to online scammers, bringing the number of suspects detained to 56.
The investigation is linked to at least 130 other fraud cases involving losses of more than 250 million baht.
Pol Col Pakkapol Suchon, superintendent of Highway Police Sub-Division 2, announced the arrests on Thursday at the Central Investigation Bureau (CIB).
The suspects, identified as May, Tum and Yok, allegedly recruited account holders, controlled transactions and arranged cash withdrawals. Another 53 people linked to corporate mule accounts had previously been arrested.
The investigation began after a victim was lured by a Facebook advertisement for stock trading and contacted via LINE by people posing as investment experts. After being promised attractive returns, the victim transferred more than 111.69 million baht in 122 transactions.
When the victim tried to withdraw the money, they were repeatedly told to pay additional fees, guarantees and taxes.
Police traced the payments to company accounts and examined financial records, chat messages, photographs and identity verification data to identify the alleged controllers.
Investigators said May recruited account holders and controlled withdrawals, while Tum helped open accounts and withdraw cash. Yok allegedly advised account holders to contact her when accounts were frozen, claiming she had contacts who could help prepare documents and facilitate the unfreezing process.
The network reportedly obtained accounts by registering companies under recruits' names, taking over troubled businesses or renting existing corporate accounts. Some recruits were offered up to 30,000 baht to serve as company directors.
Although the companies had no genuine business operations, their accounts were used to receive money from fraud victims before the funds were transferred or withdrawn in cash.
Account holders allegedly faced legal consequences when problems arose.
Investigators also found corporate documents used to register 40 mobile numbers. One was allegedly used by a caller impersonating a HomePro employee to defraud a victim of tens of thousands of baht. All 40 numbers were suspended.
The suspects face charges including fraud by impersonation, computer crime, money laundering, unlawful association and criminal conspiracy.
summary: Police have arrested three alleged organisers of a network supplying corporate mule accounts to online scammers, bringing the number of suspects detained to 56.

The Finance Ministry is considering introducing a third phase of policies to promote the electric vehicle (EV) industry, which would enforce new local content requirements.
According to finance permanent secretary Lavaron Sangsnit, after Thailand introduced its EV 3.0 and EV 3.5 incentive schemes, which provided subsidies to EV buyers, eight Chinese EV manufacturers invested in establishing production facilities in Thailand.
The second step, which was recently approved by the cabinet, involves increasing the excise tax on imported EVs to 35% from 2027, up from the current rates of 10% for battery EVs and 15% for range-extended EVs.
The move increases the tax burden on importers of completely built-up (CBU) EVs.
According to Mr Lavaron, the Excise Department's tax calculation system applies the "tax-inclusive" method, meaning the actual tax burden for imported CBU EVs will be much higher than 35%.
Under the tax-inclusive method, the excise tax is calculated based on the vehicle's value including import duties and value-added tax. Importers would face an effective excise tax burden of 49%, he said.
"A higher excise tax burden would significantly raise the cost of imported EVs, making them less competitive with domestically manufactured vehicles," said Mr Lavaron.
"The move is expected to attract more manufacturers to establish production facilities in Thailand. A ninth EV factory in Thailand is already in discussions, with a 10th expected to follow."
For Thailand to become an EV hub, he said Tier 1, Tier 2 and Tier 3 parts manufacturers must benefit. A potential third phase would involve enforcing new local content requirements, said Mr Lavaron.
The Customs Department applies the World Trade Organization local content criteria, which includes financial costs such as profits and water and electricity expenses in the local content calculation.
Under the new criteria, which will apply to both new and existing automotive factories, only locally sourced auto parts counted towards local content.
Factories that meet the prescribed local content requirements or the Made in Thailand criteria can continue to enjoy the existing excise tax rate of 10%, while those that fail to comply with the new criteria or do not use any locally sourced parts are subject to an excise tax of 35%, he said.
Factories that use local content but fail to meet the required threshold may face excise tax rates of 15-20%, said Mr Lavaron.
Pickup Trade-in Scheme
Regarding a vehicle trade-in scheme, he said the Excise Department already submitted the proposal to the committee overseeing the use of the 400-billion-baht emergency loan decree, which he chairs.
The scheme aims to replace old pickups with new ones capable of running on B20 biodiesel, which would help reduce oil imports.
According to a Finance Ministry source who requested anonymity, the pickup trade-in scheme would be funded with 6 billion baht from the loan decree.
The proposal is being submitted to the subcommittee responsible for screening projects under the energy-related loan decree, chaired by Kulit Sombatsiri, a former energy permanent secretary, for consideration.
If approved, the proposal heads to the main screening committee and then the cabinet for approval. The scheme is expected to begin by the end of this year.
Eligible old vehicles can be passenger cars, vans or pickups, provided they were registered before 2012 and are not wrecked, remain operational, have fully paid taxes and are free of outstanding obligations.
The vehicles can be exchanged for domestically manufactured pickups or passenger pickups, as well as multi-purpose vehicles that use either electric technology or B20 biodiesel.
"The objective of this scheme is to reduce environmental pollution and revive Thailand's auto industry. Thailand has an accumulated 8.17 million vehicles aged 10-20 years or older, many of which are older diesel pickups that emit high levels of pollutants," said Mr Lavaron.
"The pickup market is also experiencing a severe downturn as many buyers are unable to obtain financing. The Finance Ministry is accelerating efforts to formulate a policy, while coordinating with the Government Savings Bank to provide low-interest loans at no more than 5% per year."
The ministry is also coordinating with vehicle dismantling facilities capable of handling up to 50,000 scrapped vehicles annually, he noted.
summary: The Finance Ministry is considering introducing a third phase of policies to promote the electric vehicle (EV) industry, which would enforce new local content requirements.

content:
Energy and climate specialists have proposed an alternative version of Thailand's power development plan (PDP) dubbed the "Resilient PDP", aimed at ensuring a smooth transition to a low-carbon economy without relying heavily on natural gas as a bridging fuel.
The proposal was developed by Chalie Charoenlarpnopparut, a scholar at the Sirindhorn International Institute of Technology, in collaboration with SDG Move, a research centre at Thammasat University that supports the UN Sustainable Development Goals, and Agora Energiewende, a non-profit think tank that promotes climate neutrality strategies in Germany, Europe and worldwide.
Under the Resilient PDP, Thailand would install up to 60 gigawatts of rooftop solar capacity, almost three times the 24.3GW target set out in the government's latest PDP. The increased solar deployment would significantly reduce the country's dependence on imported liquefied natural gas (LNG), according to Mr Chalie.
The new government PDP, which covers 2026-2050 and is expected to take effect this month, has been praised for increasing the share of renewable energy.
However, he said the plan still contains several weaknesses that could undermine Thailand's climate goals. Although the PDP sets a target of 24.3GW of solar power generation, the actual output would be constrained by the intermittent nature of solar energy and weather-dependent operating hours, said Mr Chalie.
As a result, gas-fired electricity generation would remain largely unchanged until 2050 despite the higher renewable energy targets.
He also expressed concern over the plan's continued reliance on fossil fuels during the transition period. While coal-fired generation is set to be phased out with no new coal plants planned, the PDP proposes the construction of 9,100 megawatts of new combined-cycle gas turbine (CCGT) power plants between 2026 and 2037.
CCGT technology generates electricity using natural gas while capturing waste heat from the primary turbine to power a secondary steam turbine, improving efficiency. Yet gas-fired power plants remain a significant source of carbon dioxide emissions, noted Mr Chalie.
He warned such heavy dependence on fossil fuels could jeopardise Thailand's ability to meet its near-term climate commitments under the 2035 Nationally Determined Contributions (NDCs), which are countries' official climate action plans submitted under the global climate framework.
Under Thailand's NDC 3.0, greenhouse gas emissions must be reduced to 152 million tonnes of carbon dioxide equivalent by 2035, down from a baseline level of 379 million tonnes recorded in 2019.
Mr Chalie said the country's growing reliance on imported LNG also raises concerns over electricity costs, as fuel prices remain vulnerable to geopolitical conflicts and global market volatility.
He further criticised the PDP's dependence on what he described as expensive or unproven technologies, such as an ambitious carbon capture and storage target of 19 million tonnes a year, which he estimated could increase electricity tariffs by around 1.20 baht per unit, as well as early-stage investments in small modular nuclear reactors, which could produce power at costs of up to 13 baht per unit.
"These are unrealistic technologies at this stage," said Mr Chalie.
Meanwhile, the Resilient PDP is designed to strengthen Thailand's economic competitiveness while honouring its international climate commitments, aligning with the country's NDC 3.0 targets and its long-term ambition to achieve net-zero emissions by 2050, he noted. The alternative plan calls for an accelerated expansion of renewable energy, the cancellation of all new natural gas-fired power plants, and large-scale deployment of advanced battery energy storage systems, including six-hour and eight-hour storage technologies, to ensure a reliable supply.
summary: Energy and climate specialists have proposed an alternative version of Thailand's power development plan (PDP) dubbed the "Resilient PDP", aimed at ensuring a smooth transition to a low-carbon economy without relying heavily on natural gas as a bridging fuel.

content:
Prime Minister Anutin Charnvirakul has pledged to strengthen Thailand's position as a major global food supplier, describing food security as an essential part of national security.
Speaking on Thursday at the opening of the 69th National Defence Course at the National Defence College, Mr Anutin said national security extended beyond military concerns to include economic, social, food, public health, environmental, technological and energy issues.
He said Thailand had considerable potential to supply global food markets, particularly as other countries faced growing challenges in maintaining food security.
"Other countries sell oil, and we place great importance on them. But, with all due respect, oil cannot be eaten or drunk. Without food, we cannot survive," he said.
The government aims to expand the country's capacity to produce, process and export agricultural products, including rice, fruit, vegetables and livestock products, he said.
Mr Anutin also criticised reliance on agricultural subsidies, saying farmers needed opportunities to improve their livelihoods and earn sustainable incomes.
"Giving them 1,000 baht per rai and various forms of compensation all the time is not sustainable," he said.
Turning to economic security, Mr Anutin said improving confidence in Thailand was encouraging foreign investment and technology transfers. He cited Moody's Ratings and S&P Global Ratings maintaining the country's sovereign ratings while revising their outlooks from negative to positive.
He said Thailand's appeal to foreign investors increasingly rested on its strategic location and transport infrastructure rather than cheap labour and production costs.
Describing Thailand as the "yolk of Asean", he said its transport links provided access to regional markets, southern China and South Asia.
Multinational companies increasingly regarded Thailand as an essential base for regional expansion, he said.
"They may not love Thailand, but they have to use Thailand as a base for expanding their businesses," he said.
summary: Prime Minister Anutin Charnvirakul has pledged to strengthen Thailand's position as a major global food supplier, describing food security as an essential part of national security.

content:
Waste dumped at the landfill site on the outskirts of Finningley
Published
More than 1,000 tonnes of "sewage sludge" have been seen at a landfill site near Doncaster, according to an MP for the town.
Lee Pitcher said in a Facebook post he had been told the waste was being stored in "an uncovered stockpile" at the site in Finningley.
The Labour MP said he had been in contact with the Environment Agency (EA), which confirmed on Thursday that it had "set out a series of actions" for the site's operator following an inspection.
The landfill, located in a former quarry, is operated by Tetron Finningley Ltd, which has not previously responded when contacted for comment by the BBC.
Pitcher, who is the MP for Doncaster East and the Isle of Axholme, said EA officers visited the landfill on 9 October and, after he "chased" them for their findings, they responded on Tuesday.
He said the EA had told him that during the visit "approximately 1,000 tonnes of sewage sludge were observed being stored externally in an uncovered stockpile" and had "identified concerns regarding whether site activities were being undertaken in accordance with the operating techniques and management arrangements described within the approved documents".
Pitcher said the EA had given the landfill operator until 10 November to resolve the issue.
The MP said he had subsequently contacted the EA again about "potential asbestos disposal at the site, along with the air quality and environmental ramifications this could bring".
A nearby motocross track closed after riders complained of headaches and dizziness they blamed on the smell coming from the site
Last month, Ed Bradley, a director of the neighbouring Doncaster Moto Parc, said he had been forced to close the venue after people attending the motocross track were suffering from "headaches, nausea and generally feeling unwell" from the smells.
He said he was concerned that the business may no longer be viable if it continues to remain closed.
In a statement on Facebook, he said: "For months, we have raised concerns about the terrible odours coming from the neighbouring site, the effects on our staff and customers, and our inability to operate safely.
"Despite those reports, the situation has continued.
"Unfortunately, while the authorities have been investigating, the financial consequences for Doncaster Moto Parc have been devastating.
"We are now facing the very real possibility of losing the business altogether."
An Environment Agency spokesperson said: "We expect site operators to manage odour effectively and have identified issues around odour management at this site.
"Following an inspection, we have set out a series of actions that we expect the operator to comply with and will not hesitate to take further enforcement action should that be required."

summary: The Environment Agency says it has issued the operator with a series of actions after an inspection.

content:
El caso Ueno Bank es uno de los mayores escándalos financieros y políticos recientes de Paraguay . Combina posibles irregularidades bancarias, cientos de millones de dólares en fondos públicos, sospechas de conflictos de intereses y vínculos empresariales con Santiago Peña , quien renunció el jueves 5 de noviembre de 2026 a la presidencia del país.
La crisis estalló el 3 de noviembre, cuando el Banco Central inició el procedimiento de resolución de Ueno Bank por graves problemas de solvencia. La Fiscalía abrió una investigación penal por presuntas irregularidades financieras y ya imputó a 27 personas.
El escándalo precipitó la renuncia de Peña. Poco después, la Cámara de Diputados aprobó por unanimidad la acusación para someterlo a juicio político, pese a su dimisión. La decisión sobre la continuidad del procedimiento quedó en manos del Senado.
1. ¿Qué es Ueno Bank y qué ocurrió?
Ueno Bank es un banco digital paraguayo perteneciente al Grupo Vázquez, un conglomerado empresarial local. Creció extraordinariamente rápido y llegó a tener alrededor de tres millones de clientes, una cifra enorme en relación con la población de  Paraguay . El problema es que, mientras crecía, comenzaron a aparecer indicios de que había concedido préstamos excesivos a empresas relacionadas con sus propios propietarios.
El 3 de noviembre de 2026, el Banco Central del Paraguay (BCP) decidió intervenirlo porque su índice de solvencia había caído por debajo del mínimo legal. Es decir, el banco no contaba con el respaldo patrimonial suficiente para afrontar los riesgos que había asumido. Se suspendieron sus operaciones y millones de clientes quedaron sin acceso a sus cuentas.
2. ¿Por qué se produjo la crisis?
Las investigaciones apuntan principalmente a tres problemas:
Préstamos a empresas vinculadas: Ueno habría concedido créditos a compañías del mismo grupo económico, presuntamente superando los límites legales.
Posibles maniobras financieras: determinadas operaciones pudieron servir para ocultar problemas patrimoniales y presentar una situación financiera mejor que la real.
Supervisión cuestionada: existen dudas sobre por qué el Banco Central no actuó antes pese a las advertencias.
3. ¿Cuánto dinero público manejaba Ueno Bank y por qué genera preocupación?
Ueno Bank recibió enormes depósitos de instituciones estatales, particularmente del Instituto de Previsión Social (IPS), que administra fondos jubilatorios y prestaciones sociales. Según informaciones publicadas por distintos medios, Ueno Bank llegó a administrar entre 800 y 850 millones de dólares en fondos públicos.
El problema no es solamente el volumen de dinero, sino también su concentración en una entidad financiera que terminó intervenida. Además, surgieron cuestionamientos porque el IPS habría superado los límites legales de inversión en Ueno Bank, mientras otras instituciones públicas continuaban depositando recursos en la entidad. Esto genera interrogantes sobre las decisiones de los organismos estatales y los riesgos a los que quedaron expuestos los fondos públicos, incluidos los destinados a jubilaciones.
4. ¿Cuál es la relación con Santiago Peña?
Hay dos vínculos fundamentales. Primero: su relación empresarial con el Grupo Vázquez. Peña mantuvo una relación empresarial con Grupo Vázquez, propietario de Ueno Bank, hasta marzo de 2025, cuando ya ocupaba la presidencia de Paraguay. El expresidente negó haber tenido participación directa en el banco.
Segundo: el nombramiento del presidente del Banco Central. En 2023, Peña designó a Carlos Carvallo como presidente del BCP. ¿El problema? Carvallo había dirigido anteriormente la financiera Ueno, lo que ha generado cuestionamientos sobre posibles conflictos de intereses y la independencia de la supervisión bancaria. El 3 de noviembre presentó su renuncia a pedido de Peña.
5. ¿Cuál es la situación judicial de los responsables del banco?
El 4 de noviembre, la Fiscalía imputó a 27 personas, entre ellas ocho directivos de Ueno Bank y otras 19 personas vinculadas a empresas del mismo grupo económico. Se investigan presuntos delitos de lesión de confianza, tentativa de estafa, conducta indebida en situaciones de crisis y violación de la obligación de llevar libros de comercio.
La Fiscalía solicitó prisión preventiva para Federico Miguel Vázquez Villasanti y medidas cautelares para los demás imputados. El 5 de noviembre, un juez ordenó prisión preventiva para varios exdirectivos, incluido Vázquez, y arresto domiciliario para dos de las imputadas.
6. ¿Qué puede pasar ahora?
En el plano financiero: el Banco Central inició el procedimiento de resolución de Ueno Bank. Los depósitos cuentan con una garantía legal de hasta 228,3 millones de guaraníes por depositante, aproximadamente 37.600 dólares. Además, se promulgó una ley que permite adelantar la devolución de hasta 121,76 millones de guaraníes por ahorrista, alrededor de 20.000 dólares. Sin embargo, persiste la incertidumbre sobre cuándo podrán recuperar su dinero los ahorristas y qué ocurrirá con los depósitos que superan el límite garantizado.
En el plano político, la sucesión de Santiago Peña tras su renuncia corresponde constitucionalmente al vicepresidente Pedro Alliana. El Congreso deberá elegir a un nuevo vicepresidente para completar el mandato, que concluye en agosto de 2028. El alcance total de las consecuencias del escándalo aún está por determinarse.
(ms)

content:
Gadi Eisenkot, the main rival to Benjamin Netanyahu, secured endorsements on Thursday from a majority of lawmakers to try to form a government but Israel’s president, Isaac Herzog, said it was still unclear who could break the deadlock and that he would decide on Sunday which of the two men should try first.
Of the Knesset’s 120 elected lawmakers, 67 had endorsed Eisenkot through several days of talks with Herzog, while 46 endorsed Netanyahu. Herzog said on Thursday that while the “results of the consultations may appear clear”, there were “mutual vetoes between the blocs and within the blocs themselves” that make it difficult to say who has the best shot to form a government.
He said he would make a pick on Sunday, and that he would hold “personal talks with some of the party leaders” over the Israeli weekend, which runs Friday-Saturday.
A bitterly contested election last month, seen by many observers as one of the most consequential for Israel in many decades, ended with neither Netanyahu nor Eisenkot, a former military general and chief of staff, securing a clear pathway to power.
Netanyahu’s coalition lost its majority, dropping from 68 to 53 seats in the 120-seat Knesset. The Change bloc of Zionist parties led by Eisenkot has 48 seats, leaving parties representing Israeli Palestinians as potential kingmakers with a record 19 seats. The Joint List has 11, while the more conservative, Islamist Ra’am has eight.
In Israel’s political system, the otherwise largely ceremonial president decides which candidate has the best initial chance of building a stable coalition to rule.
Both Arab-majority parties reported backing Eisenkot, according to Haaretz. United Torah Judaism, though often aligned with Netanyahu, did not endorse either man.
Turnout among Arab Israelis – Palestinians with Israeli citizenship, who constitute 20% of the population – more than doubled to about 80%, transforming the political landscape. Palestinians in the occupied West Bank and Gaza had no vote.
The leader of Israel’s main Palestinian coalition has admitted to “disagreements with Eisenkot on many issues” but said on Thursday that Palestinian voters wanted change after facing intensified racism, discrimination, crime and exclusion under the current coalition.
“We are not choosing between good and better but between what we see as bad and even worse,” Yousef Jabareen said, according to Israeli media.
Last month, Jabareen told the Guardian that the first demand of Arab Israeli voters was to get rid of the Netanyahu government, and in particular its most extreme members, Itamar Ben-Gvir, the national security minister, and Bezalel Smotrich, the finance minister.
Eisenkot has also put conditions on any potential coalition with Arab parties: they have to recognise that Israel is a Jewish state, accept compulsory national service – either civil or military – and denounce Hamas as a terrorist organisation.
Jabareen and the Joint List have suggested they would support an opposition from the outside with tactical voting in the Knesset. Ra’am has said it would join a new government led by Eisenkot.
Herzog, who met delegations from the Palestinian Israeli parties and other small parties, has called on all to help avert another round of elections.
“Any reasonable person need only look at the security and diplomatic challenges before us, at the changing region around us, and remember the issues tearing us apart from within, to understand that an immense responsibility rests upon us,” Herzog said.
Netanyahu remains prime minister in a caretaker government until a new coalition is formed or there is another election, which must be held if no candidate succeeds.
Though the 77-year-old political veteran did better than expected in the vote and his Likud party won the most seats, his nationalist-religious coalition, the most rightwing government in Israel’s history, lost its governing majority.
Netanyahu, at risk of losing power, has seized on an investigation by election officials into possible vote tampering to cast doubt on the results, accusing Israeli Palestinian-led parties of stealing the vote. Critics accuse Netanyahu and his partners of trying to undermine the results, which he denies.
Israel’s Central Election Committee said on Wednesday that the election’s integrity had not been compromised. The head of the committee, the supreme court justice Noam Sohlberg, has called on the country’s elected officials to protect public trust.
“This is a real danger. One of the foundations of democracy is the peaceful transfer of power,” Sohlberg told Herzog at his residence on Wednesday. He said high voter turnout, including among the Arab minority, was a blessing.
Netanyahu’s allies on the far right, including Ben-Gvir, have called for the immediate arrest and interrogation of Arab party leaders.

content:
Thailand has made an ambitious bet on putting artificial intelligence (AI) to work. In October, the government outlined three priorities: building an AI industry, applying AI across existing businesses, and extending the benefits to workers and households. The Board of Investment's (BoI) Skill Bridge is reported to have 42 projects approved worth a total of 2.03 billion baht, with a target of training 76,728 people.
The headline number is impressive. The harder question is what those trainees will be able to do when an AI system gives them a persuasive answer that is wrong.
Thai employers need a practical verification test built into the country's AI skills push. A trained employee should be able to check a machine's output against a reliable source, recognise an unusual case, explain a correction and know when to ask a supervisor. Those abilities deserve a place beside technical knowledge on every course completion record.
Thailand already has evidence that buying or adopting a tool comes before building the habits needed to use it well. The National Electronics and Computer Technology Center's 2026 survey covered 574 organisations. It found that 53.7% had started using AI. Among the 308 adopters, average readiness was 40.0%, and governance scored just 28.9%. This is a snapshot of surveyed organisations, rather than a census of every Thai employer, but it identifies the operational gap clearly.
Picture a new hire at a food exporter. An AI assistant drafts a customer quotation, drawing on last month's freight prices and an outdated packaging specification. The language sounds professional. A worker who only learned to prompt the tool might forward it immediately. A worker trained to verify the price, check the current specification and escalate the discrepancy has a skill that protects the customer relationship.
That example can become a structured assessment. Give a trainee a realistic quotation, service request or inventory forecast containing one subtle error and one case that falls outside the standard procedure. Ask the trainee to use AI, locate the mistake, document the correction and make an independent judgement. Evaluate the quality of the final work and the reasoning, not the number of prompts.
Employers should help design these exercises. A hotel can use a disputed reservation. A manufacturer can use a supplier delay. A community clinic can test how administrative staff respond to an incorrect appointment instruction without exposing patient information. Each case teaches the same underlying discipline through work employees actually recognise.
The government can make that discipline central to Skill Bridge. It can require training providers to show an employer-approved work sample, record how trainees performed on verification tasks and check if supervisors observe those habits 30 or 90 days later. It can publish results by training pathway, with appropriate aggregation, so employers and learners can see which programmes build reliable competence.
Small businesses deserve particular attention. Thailand's AI-for-productivity agenda includes tools to help merchants analyse costs, sales and stock. A shop owner needs to know what assumptions an automated recommendation uses before ordering inventory. A short, supervised drill on detecting a bad forecast might deliver more lasting value than another general demonstration of an AI chatbot.
Middle managers must give workers time to test AI on ordinary tasks, correct mistakes kindly, and share cases where human judgement improved the result. If the only target is faster output, employees will learn to hide the review that makes the output dependable.
Thailand's new investment creates an opportunity to lead on useful AI skills. The country should count jobs reached and tasks completed well, while recognising the workers who can challenge the machine when necessary. The most valuable AI certificate will show that its holder knows when to trust an answer, when to test it and how to put a mistake right.
Gleb Tsipursky, PhD, is a behavioural scientist, CEO of Disaster Avoidance Experts, and author of 'The Psychology of AI Adoption at Work: From Resistance to Results' (Georgetown University Press, 2026).

content:
Re: "Democrats seize control of Congress, Senate", (World, Nov 5).
Karma is wonderful. President Trump said to vote as though he was on the ballot, and they did!
Will the Republicans learn the lesson and unshackle themselves from the Trumps? Other countries' political parties should look at this with interest.
Dennis Fitzgerald
Voters prevail
Re: "Trump congratulates Democrats on midterms", (World, Nov 5).
A few days ago, one could hardly imagine such a headline when President Donald Trump was so civil in defeat -- truly trounced by Democrats, especially in the Senate and in the state of Texas, led by a Democrat.
This brought to mind the US Constitution, following the belief of the French philosopher Baron de Montesquieu in the concept of separation of powers with checks and balances on each power, to the extent that power cannot be supreme or "dictatorial" and not challengeable.
The surprising result proves that no power can be forever supreme in life, and even President Trump admitted that within 24 hours. But true to himself, he said he would use his veto power against any future legislatures he dislikes from the Democratic majority in Congress.
One wonders whether the Gulf of America will return to its original name, the Gulf of Mexico, or whether Lake America will return to Lake Ontario.
Songdej Praditsmanont
Artificial minds
Re: "Setting it right", (PostBag, Nov 1) & "China's robot makers shift focus to AI brains", (Business, Nov 3).
The Bangkok Post has a number of recurring items of general interest; Jacques Fortier's letter in PostBag on Sunday tried to set things right regarding the Palestine-West Bank disputes, by intimating that Israelis were not "settlers".
The vast majority of Israel's population arrived en masse after Europe's violent geopolitical settling of age-old disputes early in the 20th century. These displaced peoples were mostly of European origin and were settled, rightly or wrongly, in Palestine by the United Nations. Historically, then, they are settlers.
The Post Business section of Nov 3 gave us insight into China's progression with their humanoid robots; this involves the development of robot brains to give them a human-like intelligence.
This is to speed up robotic skills development and essentially bring in more profit. The main idea is to have robots not driven by computer code, but by common sense. Common sense is a rare attribute; a prime example of its absence would be Donald Trump embarking on a war mission without considering the inevitable consequences.
In every debate about AI, it seems we measure its superior intelligence against our own human sensibilities. We all marvel and wonder at just what is being achieved by computer science, far outstripping our own skills. But it must be realised that there is no comparison between machines and any biological existence on this planet. Super intelligent machines, no matter how super, are different entities that have been created by an Earth-bound biological life form that evolved naturally over so many, many millions of years.
AI machines cannot themselves morph or develop any of the attributes acquired naturally by this planet's biological life, human or otherwise. AI is essentially an entity built on fictional numbers and, as such, has no conscience; it can be logical but devoid of common sense, compassion, and the other human sensibilities we use.
Nick Nicholson

content:
As elections in the United States are more globally consequential than those of any other country, the "midterms" congressional poll results this week bear far-reaching ramifications. That the Democratic Party has convincingly routed the opposing Republican Party and captured both the Senate and the House of Representatives renders Donald J Trump a "lame duck" president in the remainder of his second term, but it does not spell the end of what is known as "Trumpism".
The organic political movement bent on nativism and economic nationalism behind Mr Trump's political ascent and zenith is still alive and well, with popular support on both sides of the party divide. A growing majority of Americans still oppose open and unrestrained immigration, and they remain aggrieved and resentful that the rest of the world has moved ahead at their expense, as Washington has largely underwritten and guaranteed the international system's relative peace and prosperity over the past 80 years.
The call for America to come home and to focus on the home front in view of a ballooning US$40 trillion debt --123% of GDP, trade deficits with myriad partners, loss of economic competitiveness, broken welfare and shoddy health and basic education systems will not suddenly go away. As the electoral focus shifts to the presidential and congressional elections in November 2028, what happens to this Trumpist agenda, which was betrayed and strayed off course by the war with Iran, will determine the next occupant of the White House.
As a first takeaway, these record-setting midterm elections, to me, are a welcome reprieve and a restoration of faith in democratic course-correction. Although final tallies are yet to be declared, the Democrats have already secured at least 54 Senate seats in the 100-member chamber and at least 239 seats in the House of Representatives. The firm majority in both chambers will enable Democrats to closely scrutinise and constrain the Trump administration's policy impulses and hold it more accountable. The American democratic system that relies on institutional checks and balances and separation of powers has been vindicated.
Above all, unlike certain places in the world, the American people have spoken loud and clear about their disenchantment with rising costs of living and the unpopular Iran war, and their voices and preferences are being heard and heeded. Even President Trump acknowledged the Democratic victory and conceded that the Iran war undermined Republican chances.
Not long ago, it looked like the sitting president was on top of America, dictating his terms to the world. There was even speculation that he would not accept unfavourable midterm results and might thwart them by force if necessary. The Trump runaway power and abuses got to a point where a third presidential term was discussed and feared. All that has come to nought. Mr Trump has been reduced and cut down in aura from his presidential perch to political ordinariness.
The second takeaway is: How did all this happen so dramatically? The answer is Mr Trump received so long a rope from his big win in November 2024 that he ended up politically hanging himself with hubris and megalomania. It will remain a mystery as to how and why Mr Trump aborted and sabotaged his "America First" and "Make America Great Again" paradigm. It was outlined and codified as the US National Security Strategy and National Defence Strategy nearly a year ago.
Both the NSS and NDS made it clear that the US would no longer shoulder the burdens and costs of global leadership, that partners and allies are to look after and fund their own security, and that the US would put a stop to foreign "forever wars". Among the five regions laid out in the NSS were the Western Hemisphere, Asia with a focus on the Indo-Pacific, Europe, the Middle East, and Africa -- in that order.
When Mr Trump declared the "liberation day" tariffs in April last year, it fit squarely within the America First campaign. Even though its protectionist consequences ultimately raised consumer prices in the US, no Republican faulted Mr Trump for not keeping his word.
When he ordered the daring raid to capture Venezuelan President Nicolas Maduro and his wife from a military base inside the country, Mr Trump got away with it and was able to boast and gloat about American military prowess.
Had he stuck to US dominance of the Western Hemisphere and focused on the homeland while keeping immigrants out and imports down, President Trump could have stamped a legacy of the nativism and economic nationalism that populist Republicans in US politics espoused in the past, particularly Pat Buchanan in the 1980s and early 90s. But, together with Israel and its Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, Mr Trump got off track into a costly distraction with an attack and a protracted war against Iran.
Herein lies my third, twofold takeaway. The Iran war may get worse before it winds down, and it may never reach a completely peaceful settlement. At issue is the open navigation of the Strait of Hormuz to global shipping, commerce, and access to Persian Gulf oil and other resources.
The Iranian position is essentially a given and can be gleaned from the 14-point memorandum of understanding Tehran and Washington signed on June 17, which the Trump White House unilaterally violated. Iran continues to have the upper hand even if the US renews aerial attacks in the short term. The US post-midterms is likely geared up for some kind of deal that can preserve superpower prestige and credibility.
The corollary is Israel's weakened position in US domestic politics. This is the time for a blame game in the US, and Israel is unlikely to come out of it better off. Notwithstanding entrenched Israeli presence and Jewish representation in American society and politics, Mr Netanyahu will likely be seen as complicit, if not outright instigator, in leading Mr Trump astray at huge costs to US taxpayers and geostrategic interests. The US, in turn, may end up with a more diminished role in the inevitable reshaping of Middle East geopolitics after the Iran war in the medium term.
Thitinan Pongsudhirak, PhD, is a professor of comparative and international politics at Chulalongkorn University's Faculty of Political Science and a non-resident associate with the Southeast Asia Centre at the London School of Economics.
