content:
If the question is: "Is America Back?", then the answer must be: "No". At least not in ways that are meaningful to non-Americans, who make up 96% of the world's population.
For Americans, it's a bit more nuanced. Nothing at all will change until Jan 3, 2027, when all the new and old members of Congress are sworn in. What will happen after that remains to be seen, but it won't include much legislation because Donald Trump is promising to use his right of veto to thwart any measures he dislikes.
So for all the hyperbole about "electoral earthquakes", this is not the dawn of a new and better era in the United States. If the Democrats can stay cool and forensic in their approach they might lay the foundations for another electoral victory and a real reckoning in 2028, but it is not within reach now.
Where Mr Trump remains unconstrained is in his dealings with the rest of the world: his tariffs, his wars, his whims and hates and boundless greed. He is not one whit less powerful in that domain than he was last week, and the damage he can do is both unpredictable and incalculable. Just one example: Iran.
Since Mr Trump was beguiled into making a surprise attack on Iran eight months ago by Israel's Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, he has oscillated endlessly between believing he can bomb the Iranians into submission -- and imagining that he can "negotiate" a better outcome than Barack Obama's nuclear deal with Iran (which Mr Trump tore up eight years ago).
As I write, we have no idea whether or not Mr Trump will resume bombing Iran now that the mid-terms are out of the way. He probably has no idea himself. Of course, Iran still has no nuclear weapon or anything near that -- but senior regime members are now openly debating whether Iran should get the bomb just to deter this kind of nonsense.
And so it goes, from threats to annex the "51st state" (Canada) to rambling monologues about how Mr Trump already controls Greenland to boasts about how the United States now owns most of Venezuela's oil. Most of it is empty threats but bits of it actually come to pass, and you can't really be sure which is which.
Never mind. Only two more years and it will be over -- but will it?
There is no reason to believe that the United States is only dabbling in the business of being a rogue state, and will revert to being the guarantor of global stability once the madman has been removed or retired.
In all the vox pop voter interviews and the politicians' thank-you speeches, did you hear a single American saying that they were worried about their country going rogue? Did anybody say that kidnapping Venezuela's president and stealing the country's oil was illegal, or that conniving in Russia's war against Ukraine was both evil and counter-productive?
No. The most you heard even about Mr Trump's on-again-off-again war on Iran was the complaint that it had driven up the cost of living and especially the cost of diesel fuel. This is not a country that can commit to a serious military alliance on the far side of a large ocean.
There's no good reason it should. Its oceans are sufficient defence against any conventional threat of invasion, and the threat of nuclear weapons is a matter for deterrence, never for fighting.
Once upon a time, a large number of Americans were persuaded to belong to a major overseas alliance by broad ideology and a specific geopolitical concept (The Russians Are Coming!), but those days are long gone. The Russians still need to be deterred, but it doesn't require Americans.
It still makes sense for Europeans to have a sort of post-Nato alliance, because Russia really is aggressive in seeking to regain its old imperial frontiers. It even makes sense for Canada to belong to that post-Nato organisation, because it helps defend Canadian sovereignty from American challenge.
But it's foolish to depend on Americans for support, because they don't have skin in this game.
Gwynne Dyer is an independent journalist whose articles are published in 45 countries. He is the author of 'The Shortest History of War' and more recently 'Intervention Earth: Life-Saving Ideas from the World's Climate Engineers'.

content:
The scandals surrounding celebrity-led foundations should serve as a red flag. When money is placed in the hands of popular personalities without proper public scrutiny, who watches over it?
Allegations surrounding Panadda "Boom" Wongphudee and her Goodness Foundation have raised serious concerns about fund management. Police are investigating possible fraud and money laundering. Allegations against her husband for forest encroachment add personal drama, but the key issue remains the potential abuse of public trust when donations are not properly accounted for.
This is not an isolated case. A foundation run by another social media personality, Kanphat Phongpaiboonvej, aka Gun Jompalang, has also come under scrutiny over its finances.
Organisations like these gained popularity by providing justice when the system fails and by offering relief during natural disasters. Additionally, border tensions with Cambodia have given them a nationalistic platform to enhance their visibility.
Indeed, their success stems from the state's failure to deliver help. Red tape and a lack of understanding of local needs often delay government help. Over-centralisation also leaves local communities with too little money and authority to respond to emergencies themselves.
Celebrity foundations step into this vacuum, mobilising donations and delivering relief more quickly. Their founders become familiar faces whom people trust. Overwhelming donations pour in.
Yet popularity is not accountability. Helping people doesn't give anyone the right to handle donated money without proper scrutiny. Political use of such popularity is another risk, particularly when humanitarian work becomes a vehicle for promoting political figures or reinforcing nationalist narratives that divert attention from underlying policy failures.
How, then, can donation abuse be prevented? Foundations are already required to keep financial records, submit annual reports and undergo audits. Yet these requirements have failed to prevent abuse. The government is now talking about tighter rules and greater public disclosure.
But more regulations alone will not solve the problem. Thailand has no shortage of rules designed to prevent corruption, yet corruption persists even within government agencies.
Temple donations offer a similar lesson. Despite rules governing temples, corruption is rife. Greater external scrutiny and stronger local participation in temple management are often proposed as ways forward.
The same principle should apply to charitable foundations. Independent audits matter, but so do public participation and oversight of their operations. Major decisions should not rest in the hands of one powerful founder.
More importantly, decentralisation must be a part of the answer. Local communities need the funds and authority to manage their affairs with proper community participation and independent oversight. They know their needs. With enough support, they can act without waiting for instructions from Bangkok.
Charities should complement public services, not become substitutes for state responsibility. The challenge is not only how to make celebrity foundations more transparent but also how to empower local communities to help themselves when emergencies arise.
summary: The scandals surrounding celebrity-led foundations should serve as a red flag. When money is placed in the hands of popular personalities without proper public scrutiny, who watches over it?

content:
Paraguay's President Santiago Peña has announced his resignation following a political crisis sparked by the collapse of a bank linked to him.
"I want to apologise to the people if at any point I failed," he said in a video message on social media. "It was never my intention to betray the trust you placed in me."
The crisis erupted after Ueno Bank entered an insolvency process, which froze all operations. Lawmakers accused Peña, who was a shareholder until last year in the company that owned the bank, of conflicts of interest and misconduct.
Peña rejected suggestions of impropriety. His resignation came as Paraguay's lower house of congress voted in favour of pursuing an impeachment trial.
Photos taken near Paraguay's Congress building on Thursday show police officers clashing with protesters demanding Peña be removed from office.
Paraguay's congress must approve the resignation of a president. But a special session convened on Thursday to address his resignation was adjourned in favour of continuing with the impeachment process.
Congress has scheduled a special session for Friday, when Peña is expected to present his defence, according to Reuters news agency.
In a post on X, Peña confirmed he would appear for Senate impeachment proceedings, adding that he would do so to "exercise my right to a defence".
He wrote: "I will provide the information requested of me. Citizens deserve to know the truth, without cover-ups and without anyone being above the law."
Peña earlier said his resignation was to protect stability, social peace and democratic institutions.
Ueno Bank has said it has about three million customers, equivalent to about 60% of Paraguay's adult population.
It held pensions and some other public funds and, after its collapse earlier this week, millions could not access their accounts.
The central bank seized the digital lender, and people took to the streets protesting and demanding Peña's resignation.
A new president of the Central Bank of Paraguay has been appointed and Congress has approved a process to pay depositors.
Protesters gathered near the Paraguayan Congress on Thursday
Peña won election in 2023 representing Paraguay's ruling conservative Colorado Party, beating a centre-left challenger.
The Colorado party dropped impeachment proceedings against Vice President Pedro Alliana, who is next in line for the presidency after Peña.

summary: The move follows a bank collapse and after the lower house of congress voted in favour of pursuing an impeachment trial against him.

The Duchess of Sussex’s estranged half-brother, Thomas Markle Jr, has been named as a “person of interest” in the Philippine authorities’ inquiry into child sexual abuse image allegations made against her father, Thomas Markle Sr.
The country’s interior and local government secretary, Jonvic Remulla, told a press conference in Manila there were “signs that point that the son is involved in the crime as well”.
He added that Markle Jr, 60, who alerted local police and the FBI to images he found in his father’s belongings, was not yet being treated as a suspect. His alleged involvement is not thought to be directly linked to the material he handed to the police.
More than 7,000 photos and one video – all of under-age males and females of Asian, Latin and European descent, with some as young as 10 and 11 – were uncovered, Remulla said.
He described the images as “the most deplorable displays of impunity towards sexual activity that I have ever seen”.
Markle Sr, 82, who is estranged from Meghan, has reportedly been moved into a care home for dementia patients in the US where he is now living.
Remulla said: “We’re determining if [the] son is involved … There are signs that point that the son is involved in the crime as well but only as a person of interest so far.”
He added: “We will know in the next few days.”
Markle Sr, who returned to the US from the Philippines in May, has admitted paying for sex in the Philippines but he has strongly denied possessing child abuse imagery, and suggested he had been “set up”. His son remains in Cebu City in the Philippines.
Remulla has previously described Markle Sr as “a possible sex offender of the grossest kind”.
Markle Jr reported his father after claiming to have found four storage boxes at his father’s home in the Philippines containing “hundreds, if not thousands” of child sex abuse images.
after newsletter promotion
Police and FBI agents have since been investigating whether Markle Sr was in possession of any illegal images while living in the Philippines and in Mexico, where he previously lived, and where other illegal images were reportedly found in one of his storage units.
Markle Jr was recently interviewed at his home in Cordova, Cebu, as part of an international, multi-agency meeting via Microsoft Teams, according to the Sun, which first published the claims. He gave his statement to an FBI agent based in Florida, who specialises in child sex abuse cases.
In a statement issued when the allegations against her father were first published, Meghan said she was “deeply distressed” by the claims. She said she had been informed of disturbing allegations against her father in 2018 and had kept him from having contact with her children, Prince Archie, seven, and Princess Lilibet, five, to protect them.

content:
Interest rates have risen for the first time in more than three years and the Bank of England has signalled a further increase is likely unless the US-Iran war is resolved.
Rates rose to 4% from 3.75% in a bid to curb inflation mainly driven by the conflict's impact on global oil prices.
Andrew Bailey, the Bank's governor, said the decision "shouldn't be seen as the first in an inevitable long sequence of hikes", but warned "unless the conflict in the Middle East is resolved, neither does it seem likely to be the last increase".
The higher level will increase the cost of borrowing for things such as mortgages, loans and credit cards, but will also lead to higher returns on savings.
The Bank's rate-setting committee all backed increasing interest rates, with eight out of nine voting in favour of the rise to 4%. One member wanted an even bigger increase to 4.25%.
Bailey said the hike was warranted due to higher energy prices and pointed to what happens in the Middle East as the main factor in future decisions.
"Put simply, it requires real progress towards settling the conflict in the Middle East," the governor said.
Bailey said he could "see the argument" for a further rate hike, before taking a "more conditional approach" dependent on the path of energy prices and inflation in the coming months.
However, the views of members on the rate-setting committee differed on the path forward.
Clare Lombardelli agreed there was "likely to be a case for a further increase in rates in the near term", while Megan Greene went further, suggesting "additional hikes" might be likely depending on how inflation impacted wages, prices and the jobs market.
However, Alan Taylor said the rate rise was a "a risk-management 'one-for-now' insurance hike".
Inflation, which measures the pace of price rises over time, is well below its peak of a few years ago but remains above the Bank of England's 2% target and is expected to increase further next year.
Prices rose 3.5% in the year to September 2026, largely due to higher fuel prices. Millions of households are also set to be hit by energy bill increases in January.
Higher fuel prices can lead to prices rising for a host of goods and staples as businesses pass on higher costs to customers.
But the Bank said there was "limited evidence" this had happened so far for goods, such as food, with some firms absorbing cost increases and accepting lower margins.
In an interview with the BBC, Bailey defended the decision to raise rates despite the Bank's assessment that inflation was yet to spread to other parts of the economy.
He said further increases in energy prices are putting upward pressure on inflation and "that's what we have to seek to lean against".
Patrick Bryson, from Brighton, is set to see his five-year mortgage term with a 3.51% interest rate end soon.
The best deal the 51-year-old can find is a 5.17% loan with HSBC, which means his repayments will jump from £1,420 to £1,680 a month from February.
"The only thing that bugs me about the mortgage is that after five years of paying it off we are now paying more than we were before," said the father-of-three. "That's a bit of a slap in the face."
The guitar teacher, who has a combined income of around £68,000 a year with his wife, who manages a care home, said the couple is feeling pressure on their finances and so have changed their shopping habits and are looking to reduce their subcription outgoings.
"Over the last year I have stopped buying wine, we don't go out to eat much anymore, we have knocked takeaways on the head. The prices are ridiculous," he said.
The Bank now expects inflation to peak at 4.9% in the middle of next year, higher than it originally estimated, and not return to 2% until 2028.
But in an "adverse scenario", where the US-Iran war could escalate further and send oil prices higher, inflation could reach 6.2% in 2027, it suggested.
While the UK cannot control global energy prices, the Bank raised rates, for the first time since August 2023, in order to limit the knock-on effects of high energy prices resulting in inflation going up across the board.
Its base rate is what it charges other banks and building societies to borrow money, which influences what customers for mortgages, loans, credit cards get charged, as well as savings rates.
The rate rise will see 510,000 tracker mortgage-holders see a £31 monthly jump in repayments, according to banking trade body UK Finance.
Homeowners on fixed deals will see no change, though future products may be affected.
However, people on variable deals will be impacted depending on how their lender reacts to the rate rise. Typically a 0.25pp rise means a £14 increase per month in repayments.

content:
The superstar K-pop group NewJeans signed restrictive record label contracts that waived their right to “sleep, rest and free choice”.
A new report from the New York Times found that the contracts were signed when the members of the record-breaking girl group were aged 14 to 17.
The contracts banned the performers from having an “insincere attitude” and engaging in “inappropriate romantic relationships”. They also struck standard child protection language which protected “basic human rights” including the group members’ right to education.
The contracts from record label Ador (a subsidiary of Hybe, home of the popular groups BTS and Katseye) additionally excluded portions of the Korean government’s K-pop contract template stipulating that the label “shall not demand that a performer who is a minor engage in excessive physical exposure or overly sexually suggestive expression”.
In a statement to the New York Times, Hybe representatives said the company adheres to child-protection laws and works hard to make sure its artists work and train in safe conditions.
NewJeans are one of the decade’s most popular K-pop acts. In 2023, the five-member group followed Blackpink to become the second Korean girl-group to score a number one album on the Billboard charts. In November 2024, the band made global headlines when they announced their decision to leave the label amid contract disputes and claims that Ador had deliberately undermined their careers.
Band member Hanni alleged that NewJeans were mistreated by the label and accused Ador of “deliberate miscommunications and manipulation” in a statement to South Korea’s parliament last year.
Ador has consistently maintained that they did not violate their duty. “A unilateral claim that trust has been broken does not constitute valid grounds for termination of a contract,” the label said in a statement.
The label sued band member Danielle, a member of her family and the band’s producer in December 2025 for a total of nearly $30m for damages and a contract break penalty.
Hybe representatives told the New York Times that its exit penalty fees do not exceed industry standards.
In July, the group promised that 2026 would be the “summer of NewJeans”, with a teaser showing the group as a four-piece sans Danielle. New music has yet to emerge.
The new reports expose the shadowy world of K-pop contracts and shine a light on the restrictive conditions that the genre’s biggest stars can be subject to.
By the time they signed their contracts, the NewJeans members – Minji, Hanni, Haerin, Hyein and Danielle – had already clocked in years of training in K-pop “boot camps” which taught vocal training, choreography and foreign language education.
Schedules were strict, one source told the New York Times, and it was not unusual for rehearsals to stretch as late as 2am. NewJeans’s youngest member, Hyein, was 12 at the time.
After the band members received their exclusive contracts with Ador in January 2022, the parents of one member requested multiple changes. They were told that if they did not sign the contract in its current form, “the contract itself” could be reconsidered.
In a statement to the New York Times, Hybe said its contracts were legal and negotiated in good faith, with protections in place for the artist as well as the label’s investment in them.
That contract struck government language that forbade performers working for “excessive periods of time”. It also stipulated that the band would have to repay a significant percentage of the plastic surgery costs that are common in K-pop.
“We do not even recommend cosmetic surgery or procedures against an individual’s wishes,” Hybe said in a statement.
The NewJeans contract also granted Ador rights to use the band members’ “name, photographs, likeness, handwriting, voice and any other elements” in perpetuity, in a level of ownership that goes further than government recommendations for such rights to end at the point of contract termination.
The clause also grants Ador the right to use the NewJeans members as AI chatbots or clones.
The Guardian has reached out to Hybe for comment.

content:
Air Serbia flight JU134 from Belgrade to Moscow on November 3 was already deep in Lithuanian airspace when the crew received instructions to return to the Serbian capital.
Among the passengers were three senior figures from the regime of former President Aleksandar Vucic : Aleksandar Vulin, former defense and interior minister and former head of Serbia's Security Intelligence Agency (BIA); Dusan Bajatovic, long-serving director of state-owned gas company Srbijagas; and Nenad Popovic, a minister without portfolio.
All three are well known in Serbia for their close ties to Russia and for controversies — including reports of corruption and abuse of public office.
According to unofficial reports published by several media outlets, the plane was ordered back because of a security breach: Vulin had allegedly boarded without undergoing the mandatory security screening.
Since 2023, Vulin has been under US sanctions over what Washington described as "engaging in corrupt and destabilizing activities that undermine the rule of law in the Western Balkans."
Unusual episode
Vulin told the media that he was travelling to Moscow to discuss extending a gas agreement with Russia .
Bajatovic, however, said he did not know why Vulin and Popovic were travelling to Moscow and denied that the two would attend the scheduled meetings on gas supplies.
The incident might have remained nothing more than an unusual news item had it not occurred at a time when Serbia is undergoing a major political transformation .
Judicial developments unfold at remarkable speed
Just nine days earlier, on October 25, the student-backed list won a landslide victory over the Serbian Progressive Party (SNS) in the parliamentary election , ending 14 years of political dominance by Aleksandar Vucic and the SNS, who maintained close relations with Moscow.
Although the new majority has yet to take control of any levers of power, the days after the election brought a series of developments that would have seemed unimaginable just a few weeks ago.
Arrests, new criminal proceedings and the reopening of previously unresolved cases began to unfold at remarkable speed. Some of these cases strike at the very foundations of the system built during the SNS years in power.
"This paints a sad picture of the Serbian prosecution service," prosecutor Bojana Savovic told DW.
Savovic sees the sudden action on the part of prosecutors as an attempt to ingratiate themselves with the new authorities.
"With these actions, they are showing what they could have done but were unwilling to do until just ten days ago," she told DW. "I hope this speed of action will not come at the expense of the quality of indictments and that these are not personal vendettas within the old regime."
Allegations of vote-buying and high-level corruption
Prosecutors have also launched a series of investigations into suspected electoral manipulation, corruption and abuse of public office .
Four people were arrested on suspicion of vote-buying in Novi Sad. Six others were detained in Mali Zvornik on suspicion of helping citizens from Bosnia and Herzegovina register their residence in Serbia so they could vote.
One of the most high-profile cases is the arrest of Davor Macura, the owner of Alta Bank, who is suspected of illegally accessing the bank's vault and removing the equivalent of about €383 million ($430 million).
His arrest came just days after the National Bank of Serbia revoked Alta Bank's license and initiated bankruptcy proceedings. Macura has been publicly associated with the SNS, while his bank had significant business dealings with the state and a large number of Russian clients.
Senior police officials, the head of the Republic Hydrometeorological Institute and several managers of public companies have also been arrested over suspected abuses of office and rigged public procurement procedures.
Alleged destruction of documents
Students and representatives of the new political majority are demanding investigations into corruption cases that have remained unresolved for years.
Their message is that no one should be above the law and that prosecutors and courts must do their jobs — or be held accountable for failing to act.
"When you want the rule of law and when you want something to be done, it is possible. Our regulations allow for it. But it was obvious that there were people obstructing the entire system, putting cases in drawers and leaving them unresolved," Tanja Arsic, an incoming MP from the Students' List, told DW.
In the days after the election, however, reports and video footage emerged that suggested official documents may have been removed or destroyed in state institutions and public companies.
On October 29, Prosecutor General Zagorka Dolovac responded by issuing a binding instruction to all chief public prosecutors to prevent the destruction of official and other records.
The Students' List also called on employees in state institutions and the media to report any destruction of documents to prevent what they called abuse by the outgoing authorities during the transition of power.
Savovic points out that even an attempt to destroy official records is punishable by law.
How high up will investigations reach?
But will the institutions really investigate those who were once at the very top of Serbia's political power structures?
Former President Aleksandar Vucic said he is not afraid of being arrested and that no evidence of financial wrongdoing will be found against him.
"I don't sign or do anything when it comes to money, and nothing can be found in that regard," he said.
But accountability is not just about who signed a document. It is also about establishing who made the decisions, who gave the orders and who wielded the real power to influence the deals now under investigation.
"It would be tragic if the biggest players, whose arrests are expected, were prosecuted without sufficient evidence. Or if they were charged with something far less serious than what they actually did," said Tanja Arsic.
The real test is yet to come
Bojana Savovic makes a point of saying that ultimately, the success of the prosecution service won't be measured by the number of politically popular or populist arrests that are made, but by final convictions and the permanent confiscation of assets acquired through crime.
Arsic agrees and warns that conducting high-quality investigations and gathering robust evidence must take precedence over speed.
"The prosecution must not bring indictments if there is not enough evidence. That would be disastrous," she said. "If things are rushed just to achieve a result, only for the cases to end in acquittals because the prosecution failed to prove the charges against people who were at the top of the government — that would be even more disastrous."
But will that be possible within the existing structures? Savovic is not convinced that it will.
"For decades, people whose only qualification was blind obedience, reading the political climate and self-censorship were promoted in the prosecution service and the courts. Without fundamental changes in the judiciary , the police and the security structures, I see no possibility of a substantial and lasting transformation of society," she said.
The real test will come in the courtroom. The verdicts in these cases will show whether Serbia is finally breaking with its old system of power or merely replacing one set of power brokers with another.

content:
El Como del español Cesc Fàbregas entró este miércoles (05.11.2026) en la historia de la Liga de Campeones tras golear por 1-9 al Lens francés e igualar la mayor diferencia de tantos en una victoria de la competición, además de convertirse en el primer equipo que marca nueve goles fuera de casa.
El conjunto italiano alcanzó los ocho goles de diferencia que establecieron anteriormente el Liverpool y el Real Madrid , ambos con sendas victorias por 8-0.
El equipo inglés lo consiguió ante el Besiktas el 6 de noviembre de 2007, mientras que el club blanco repitió el registro frente al Malmo sueco el 8 de diciembre de 2015.
Récord como visitante
El Como se convirtió también en el segundo equipo capaz de marcar nueve tantos en un partido de la Liga de Campeones, después del Bayern de Múnich, que derrotó por 9-2 al Dinamo de Zagreb el 17 de septiembre de 2024.
Aunque los italianos establecieron un nuevo récord al conseguirlo como visitantes, según los datos difundidos por la organización.
El triunfo ante el Lens figura, además, entre los encuentros con mayor número de goles de la historia del torneo, con diez tantos en total.
Solo cuatro partidos habían alcanzado o superado esa cifra, entre ellos el 8-4 del Borussia Dortmund al Legia de Varsovia en noviembre de 2016, que sigue siendo el encuentro más goleador de la competición, con doce tantos.
O el 2-8 que le endosó el Bayern de Múnich al Barcelona el 14 de agosto de 2020.

content:
Responses to the violent scenes that followed recent Gen Z demonstrations in Germany have revealed differences in opinion within the federal government over who is responsible.
Though there is general agreement that people who committed acts of violence must be held accountable, some conservative lawmakers have largely blamed migrant groups — raising questions about whether they are  reinforcing prejudice .
Leading Social Democrats have warned against generalizations, and at least one Cabinet minister from the Christian Democrats (CDU) would prefer to examine the causes of the violence. Gen Z's fears for the future are at threat of being overshadowed by the discussions in the government and the press's focus on scattered rioting.
In Frankfurt , more than 100 police officers were injured, one severely, in the street battles that erupted after the protest on October 31. Shops were damaged and looted, too. The situation in Cologne, Hamburg and Berlin also escalated.
That Saturday, tens of thousands of young people had taken to the streets across Germany for predominantly peaceful rallies. The initiative Gen Z regelt — which roughly means Gen Z takes charge — had urged young people to highlight their fears for the future and to call for better educational opportunities, affordable housing and more climate action.
CDU initially set tone of debate
German Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt and Roman Poseck, the interior minister of Hesse, the state in which Frankfurt is located, quickly set the tone of the response. Most of those arrested were German citizens, said Poseck ( CDU ), but added: "This group of offenders was predominantly from a migrant background."
Dobrindt, who is from Bavaria's Christian Social Union , a party closely allied with Chancellor Friedrich Merz's CDU, said: "There were peaceful demonstrations, which into the evening were hijacked by violent left-wing groups and migrant hooligans."
Merz backed the statements made by Dobrindt. His assessment of the background of the offenders was based on "the observations of the investigating authorities and the emergency personnel on the ground," his spokesperson Stefan Kornelius said. It also matched "the images that many have seen."
Merz announced a tough approach toward the rioters. "Violence does not belong on our streets, and my government will show no tolerance here," Merz said, according to the script for a speech he was due to give at a closed-door CDU party event in Berlin on Monday (November 2). "Whoever attacks police and emergency services officers and loots shops attacks our freedom, ridicules society and the legitimate interests of young people."
Warnings against generalizations, focus on causes
The center-left Social Democrats ( SPD ), who are in a coalition government with the conservative CDU and CSU bloc, are in agreement on the point that criminals were involved. "It is criminals who attack and injure police officers and commit serious property damage," Defense Minister Boris Pistorius (SPD) told German public broadcaster ZDF on Sunday (November 1).
This is, however, where the similarities end. "What then are ‘migrant groups'?" said Pistorius, challenging the Interior Minister's choice of words. "Does that include people in the third generation living in Germany and who are German citizens? When do we stop drawing this distinction?" he countered. "I think that leads in the wrong direction."
The German federal government's integration commissioner, SPD politician Natalie Pawlik, followed up on Monday (November 2). "Always attributing such violent riots to migrant milieus is too simplistic," Pawlik told the German newspaper, the Frankfurter Allgemeine Zeitung . "Because blanket generalizations about groups also affect those with migrant backgrounds who demonstrated peacefully or who were themselves on duty with the police or emergency services."
She said nothing justified the outbreak of violence and that such crimes had to be punished. However, Pawlik added that if investigations showed that certain groups, in particular, were involved, then the root causes also had to be named. "We cannot ignore difficult questions about the lack of prospects, experiences of marginalization or possible integration problems," the integration commissioner said.

German Family and Education Minister Karin Prien (CDU) also wants to examine the causes of the violent behavior. She told German public radio broadcaster Deutschlandfunk that stirring resentment "would also be politically wrong." It is much more about reflecting upon reality. "If the (perpetrators) come from migrant backgrounds then that should cause us concern," Prien said.
According to Germany's Federal Statistical Office (Destatis), some 31% of the German population have a migration background. The proportion is higher in many big cities. The figure is over 50% in Frankfurt. Prien says it is necessary to examine why integration has been less successful in some groups of immigrants than others. The real challenge lies in facilitating societal participation and preventing parallel societies.
Risk of ban on Gen Z protests?
The political discussion was intensified by the Hesse interior minister suggesting a ban on further Gen Z protests. In respect of demonstrations planned for November 20, Poseck said that the right of assembly was very valuable, but social peace just as crucial. He said there had also been "massive attacks" against the police even during the demonstrations. "The organizers do not have these gatherings under control," he added.
The organizers of the demonstrations reject those accusations. They immediately distanced themselves from the violence. Germany's Family Affairs Ministry has announced that Karin Prien is due to meet with representatives from the Federal School Students Council (BSK) as well as the German Education Union (GEW) this week.
Prien herself called for younger people's interests to be taken into account more. "These are exactly the debates we need to be having, which young people are also very rightfully demanding," she told German public regional broadcaster RBB.
This article was originally written in German

content:
Toyota Motor Corporation earned 2,236.4 billion yen in consolidated net profit in the six months to September, even as its worldwide retail vehicle sales fell.
The Japanese carmaker’s results, released on Thursday, 5 November 2026, showed net profit was up 26.1% year on year, the first increase for the April-to-September period in three years.
Toyota excluded Hino Motors, Ltd. from its consolidated results for the period, a change that accounted for part of the 4.6% decline in global retail sales to 5,381,000 vehicles.
The retail total includes sales by Toyota subsidiary Daihatsu Motor Co., Ltd.
Consolidated vehicle sales rose on a comparable basis once Hino was also removed from the previous year’s figures.
Revenue reached 26,962.4 billion yen, up 9.5% and marking its sixth consecutive increase for the April-to-September period.
An intensive drive to cut costs, along with other measures, offset a 465 billion yen hit from higher raw material prices, which were partly driven by worsening conditions in the Middle East.
Group operating profit rose 9.2% to 2,191.1 billion yen.
Changes to vehicle prices and a smaller hit from US tariffs helped Toyota’s North American operations return to profit.
In Japan, hybrids led strong sales of new vehicles.
A weaker yen and higher revenue from repairs and maintenance also bolstered earnings.
“We were able to limit the impact of changes in the external environment, including developments in the Middle East, through swift responses,” Takanori Azuma, chief officer of Toyota’s Accounting Group, told an online press briefing.
Toyota lowered its revenue forecast from 54 trillion yen to 53.5 trillion yen for the financial year ending in March 2027.
It raised its operating profit forecast from 3.4 trillion yen to 3.9 trillion yen and its consolidated net profit forecast from 3.25 trillion yen to 3.57 trillion yen.
Toyota intends to “accelerate growth again” in China, executive vice-president Yoichi Miyazaki told the briefing.
The company has struggled in the market and plans to buy more from local suppliers to strengthen its competitiveness.
Miyazaki said Toyota was looking to electric vehicles for growth beyond the roughly 10 million vehicles it aims to sell each year, with hybrids underpinning that sales base.
Toyota plans to put robots to work in its own plants before commercialising the technology.
As part of its restructuring, the company will bring its robotics staff and functions together in a new division in January 2027, with the aim of making robotics, including factory automation, a core business.
Miyazaki linked the robotics plan to Toyota’s approach to eliminating waste in manufacturing.
“The initiative represents the digitalization and automation of the Toyota Production System,” he told the briefing.
summary: Toyota Motor Corporation earned 2,236.4 billion yen in consolidated net profit in the six months to September, even as its worldwide retail vehicle sales fell.

content:
The Bank of Japan (BOJ) raised its benchmark short-term interbank rate to around 1.25% in a 7–2 vote at its 17–18 September 2026 meeting, according to minutes released on Thursday, 5 November 2026.
Most Policy Board members backed a quarter-point rise in the uncollateralised overnight call rate.
They saw a risk that underlying consumer price index (CPI) inflation could climb “above the price stability target” of 2%.
One member favoured keeping rates steady, arguing that another rise after the June 2026 increase could hurt “production, employment, and real income” in Japan.
Another argued that the bank would need to raise rates more quickly if there were signs of “an upward deviation in prices”.
Share prices and the yen also figured in the assessment.
A few members said financial conditions could look “more accommodative” once higher share prices and a weaker yen were taken into account.
One board member described the changing task facing the central bank as a “shift in the phase of monetary policy”.
The member noted that policy had previously aimed to lift underlying inflation while it was below 2%.
As inflation approached that level, keeping it close to 2% had become important, the member said.

Strength in gaming, film and music prompted Sony Group Corporation to raise its full-year forecasts on Thursday (November 5, 2026).
The Japanese electronics and entertainment group is now on course for a record year.
Higher revenue from gaming helped Sony post its best half-year results for sales, operating profit and net profit in the first six months of its 2026 financial year.
For the year to March 2027, Sony now puts sales at 13 trillion yen and operating profit at 1.87 trillion yen, against earlier estimates of 12.5 trillion yen and 1.72 trillion yen, respectively.
It also lifted its forecast for consolidated net profit from 1.21 trillion yen to 1.33 trillion yen.
If met, all three forecasts would represent full-year records.
Years of investment in entertainment have brought Sony to the point where it is now releasing a hit film each year, chief financial officer Lin Tao told an online news conference.
She also expects the group’s intellectual property business to diversify.
The hit Spider-Man: Brand New Day is expected to contribute to group earnings through its film business.
The new forecasts include about 16 billion yen in equipment repair and other costs arising from the powerful earthquake that struck Kumamoto Prefecture in south-western Japan in July.
Lin Tao said Sony’s image sensor factory there had recovered from the damage and was operating at the same level as before the quake.
[Copyright The Jiji Press, Ltd.]

content:
Vietnam had reached about 78 per cent of its 2026 target of 25 million international visitors by the end of October.
The Viet Nam National Authority of Tourism (VNAT) recorded 19.5 million arrivals from January to October, up 13.8 per cent on the same period in 2025.
For every four international arrivals, nearly three came from Asia.
The region’s total rose 7.3 per cent to 14.6 million, about 992,000 more than a year earlier.
Europe ranked second by volume, with 3.22 million arrivals, or 16.5 per cent of the total.
Its 51.5 per cent rise was the fastest of any region, and its gain of about 1.09 million visitors was the largest.
Russia was Vietnam’s biggest European market and third overall.
Arrivals from Russia rose 150 per cent to 1.25 million, making it one of only four markets to exceed one million.
China retained first place with nearly 4.4 million arrivals.
The Republic of Korea ranked second with 3.4 million, and Taiwan (China) was fourth with 1.07 million.
The 6.3 per cent decline in arrivals from the Republic of Korea underlined the need for continued policy support, tourism promotion and the development of new products to keep Vietnam competitive in this established market.
Among Vietnam’s other leading Asian markets, Japan accounted for 757,500 arrivals and India for 744,600.
Cambodia brought in 787,100 visitors, a rise of 43.2 per cent.
Arrivals from the Philippines grew faster, rising 52.4 per cent to 579,200.
Vietnam also drew 28.9 per cent more visitors from Singapore and 27.1 per cent more from Indonesia.
Beyond Russia, arrivals from Poland increased by 45.8 per cent, Switzerland by 23.1 per cent, the Czech Republic by 21.9 per cent and Sweden by 21.4 per cent.
Large markets and those growing rapidly both contributed to the overall rise.
Growth in nearby Asian markets is helping broaden Vietnam’s visitor base, while reaching more travellers in long-haul markets, particularly in Europe, is becoming increasingly important to the sector’s growth.
The United States accounted for 808,700 of the 1.04 million arrivals from the Americas.
The region supplied about 5.3 per cent of all visitors, with arrivals up 18.1 per cent.
Africa’s tally rose 30.7 per cent to 59,900, equivalent to 0.3 per cent of the total.
Australia supplied 543,000 of Oceania’s 602,700 arrivals, with its own tally up 21.3 per cent.
Visitor numbers from New Zealand rose 22.9 per cent.
Oceania as a whole recorded growth of 21.5 per cent and accounted for 3.1 per cent of all arrivals.
A safe, stable environment, favourable visa policies and more direct flights linking Vietnam with international tourism hubs helped make the country more accessible.
Vietnam’s rich natural resources and range of tourism products also helped sustain double-digit growth in arrivals.
VNAT said reaching the annual target would take substantial effort in the final two months of 2026, a period it sees as crucial to sustaining growth into the following year.
Local authorities and tourism businesses will need to work together to attract visitors, stage more cultural and tourism events, update their offerings and improve service quality.
The authority plans to continue promoting Vietnam through the end of 2026 in key markets including China, the Republic of Korea, India and Russia.
It expects the programmes to lift arrivals in the closing months of the year, strengthen those markets and build momentum for growth in 2027.
Source: Vietnam News

content:
People riding drunk or dangerously on e-bikes – and those who jump red lights - could face on-the-spot fines under plans to curb anti-social behaviour.
Firms which run shared e-bike schemes will also be expected to manage their fleets better and provide designated parking areas to keep pavements safe.
They could also be required to take out insurance so people can claim compensation if they are hit by someone on a shared bike.
It's part of a crackdown on what ministers called the "wild west" of e-biking – with a patchwork of rules across the country often leaving the streets unsafe for pedestrians.
A consultation launched on Thursday sets out proposed national standards to make journeys safer for everyone and keep pavements clear, particularly for wheelchair users and families with prams.
The first e-bikes were launched in Exeter in 2016 and arrived in London a year later, growing to become a popular commuter option.
According to the Greater London Authority, 37 million trips were taken on dockless e-bikes last year – a third more than the previous year.
Shared e-bikes - such as Lime, Voi, Beryl, Dott, Forest and Bolt - make short journeys quick and convenient.
While some areas enforce rules that mean shared bikes can only be left in specific areas, others have looser rules.
Under the government's proposals, local leaders will be able to license schemes in their area, allowing them to enforce minimum standards and better integrate e-bikes into existing transport networks.
Measures could include requiring operators to have a parking plan and to manage fleet sizes and operating areas, so bikes aren't overcrowding streets.
The consultation will also consider ways to tackle antisocial and illegal behaviour, to prevent users from riding shared cycles drunk, underage, or on pavements. There will also be clear consequences set out – such as fines - for this type of behaviour.
The government is also consulting on whether local leaders should have extra powers, including setting fees and requirements for operators to share data to improve enforcement and journey planning.
The consultation will last for eight weeks after which the government will draw up legislation to implement the changes.
Prime Minister Andy Burnham said the e-bike clampdown was a "small but important everyday fix" which would make streets safer.
Transport Secretary Heidi Alexander said the government wanted e-bike schemes to "grow in popularity" but acknowledged they were "causing a little bit of nuisance at the moment".
Asked how punishments for dangerous cycling could be enforced, Alexander said licensing rules could allow for fines but added: "What you can't do is legislate for every eventuality, you can't legislate for idiots."
"The police enforce the rules of the road to stop cyclists when they are behaving recklessly but police have got a lot on their plate so individuals have to take some responsibility," she added.
Bosses at Lime, Voi and Bolt all welcomed the proposals, adding that consistent standards being applied across the country would provide clarity and certainty for operators, riders and the general public.
Mike Wordingham from the Royal National Institute for the Blind said 92% of blind and partially sighted people had been forced to walk into roads due to e-bikes blocking pavements.
He welcomed the government's announced but warned that tackling rider behaviour would be "difficult" and said a locally-led approach shouldn't lead to "a patchwork of regulations and inconsistency in implementing them".

（德国之声中文网）《商报》注意到，中国社交媒体上，很多人在交流着各种保暖的窍门，也有人在小红书上抱怨北京要到11月15日才开始统一供暖。这篇题为《为了北京的蓝天而挨冻》的评论写道：
“国家提供补贴的集中供暖制度，只适用于中国北方省份的城镇。南方除个别试点项目之外，则没有集中 供暖 ，尽管南方部分地区冬季的温度也会降至零下。是否供暖是以秦岭淮河为界而划分的，这是上世纪50年代为了应对当时的能源短缺而出台的规定。当时确定是否集中供暖的标准是，每年至少有90天的平均温度低于摄氏五度。
不过，即便是在北方，供暖制度也一直是个争议话题：国家是否应当为居民提供价格合理的暖气保障？去年，媒体就曾报道过北京邻省河北农民们冬天挨冻的事件。2010年代，由于北京 空气污染 严重，中国领导层要求首都周边省市放弃烧煤取暖的传统方式，而改用更为‘洁净’的能源，比如天然气或电力。但是，燃气和电力供暖要比烧煤供暖昂贵得多。
当局最开始提供的补贴，早已变得越来越少。由于财政紧张，有些地区甚至已经完全取消了 补贴 。与此同时，由于燃气市场实现了自由化，燃气价格过去几年一路猛涨，很多农村老年人早已负担不起取暖费。也就是说，为了北京的 蓝天白云 ，这些人正在挨冻。中国首都的空气质量倒是确实有了明显的改善。”
《商报》评论援引“策纬咨询”的一份报告写道，北京的“蓝天”形象地反映了中国自上而下的施政方式。如果未能完成上级部署的“蓝天”任务，地方官员很可能会丢掉乌纱帽，但只要空气质量能达标，老百姓挨冻，倒不会影响他们的仕途。
“而在德国，2008年，时任柏林局长的社民党政治家萨拉钦（Thilo Sarrazin）曾引发一场激烈的讨论。当时，他反对为低收入阶层提供电力和暖气福利，他说，穿上一件厚毛衣，15、16度的室温下，人们完全可以正常生活。
上届绿党籍环境部长哈贝克拟议的 暖气法 ，主张将燃油和燃气型暖气转化成有利于环境的热力泵技术。但这一建议遭到激烈抵制，后续的黑红联合政府不得不对相关法律做了大规模弱化处理。凡此种种，也充分说明了民主与专制的不同。不过，即使在中国，由于伊朗战争抬高了天然气价格，有关取暖问题的讨论想必很快也会升温。”
宝马能走出危机吗？
受中国市场销售业绩大幅下滑的影响，德国传统车企宝马也陷入危机。《法兰克福汇报》发表评论写道：
“同斯图加特的奔驰和英格尔施塔特的奥迪公司一样， 宝马 董事长内德利科维奇（Milan Nedeljkovic）也宣布了大规模裁员计划，这说明，位于慕尼黑的宝马也开始面对汽车工业的现实了。尽管裁员计划令‘四缸大厦’里士气低落，但这位懂事长在所不惜。
不过，这场危机并不只涉及成本，更是德国汽车工业商业模式整体所遭遇的危机。内德利科维奇坚信，其前任齐普策（Oliver Zipse）开启的‘新世代’计划、新型高压电池项目，将能够使宝马重返成功轨道。此外，他还计划在中国扩大本土研发的规模。这也是大众以其合肥研发中心以及奥迪推出 中国 本土品牌所追随的战略，但这一战略迄今为止却是失败的。
上任短短几个月内，内德利科维奇所宣布的几项举措，其实听起来并无新意。这也是他和前任的区别：齐普策上台伊始，就营造出了一种令人鼓舞的新气氛。但内德利科维奇却必须接受一个令人不快的事实：治标不治本的举措，是无法化解危机的。”
摘编自其他媒体的内容，不代表德国之声的立场或观点。

content:
The angling club said that the pollution incident killed brown and migratory sea trout
Published
A investigation is underway after "a major fish kill" in a County Down river, the Department for Agriculture, Environment and Rural Affairs (Daera) has confirmed.
The pollution caused the death of brown and migratory sea trout in the Gransha, Ballystockart and Inler (also known as Enler) Rivers.
Glenn McKibbin, the secretary of Inler Angling Club, said about 1,000 fish were killed in the incident and it "could not have happened in a worse location on the river or at a worse time".
The Northern Ireland Environment Agency (NIEA) and Daera Inland Fisheries are working to "identify the source of the pollution and to finalise the numbers of fish killed".
The Department said the incident was reported by a member of the public on Tuesday at 09:30 GMT.
Fish stocks 'obliterated'
The club said that the fish killing impacts resident kingfishers, herons and otters
McKibbin said that "current and future fish stocks obliterated for years to come".
He added that resident and non-resident migratory fish, which only return at this of year to spawn, have been impacted.
"Knock-on effects for other wildlife such as resident kingfishers, herons & otters unavoidable.
"For our members and volunteers who work tirelessly in a bid to improve the river this is soul-destroying, particularly as the river was still in recovery from major pollution incidents / fish kills in 2013 and 2015," McKibbin said.
"Waterways up and down the country continue to be treated like sewers.
"The paltry fines that usually follow incidents of this nature are not a deterrent and the current 'system' is broken."
The Inler River at Comber, County Down
Many migratory fish, such as trout and salmon, swim up smaller tributaries to lay their eggs in cleaner, gravel-bottomed, or cooler waters away from larger predators in the main river.
A tributary is a smaller river that flows into a larger mainstem river where many migratory fish, such as trout and salmon, swim up to lay their eggs away from larger predators in the main river.
Inler Angling Club Chairperson David Pyper said: "For those who dedicate so much time and effort to caring for the river, witnessing the sheer loss of fish in circumstances such as these is particularly disappointing.
"The club hopes that the forthcoming investigations will establish the cause of this latest incident and help ensure appropriate steps are taken to protect the river and its wildlife."
The club has encouraged local representatives and authorities to continue to prioritise rivers and direct resources towards improving water quality and preventing further incidents.

Fresh questions have emerged over Russia 's return to world sport after figures reviewed by DW showed that only four of the 16 Russian weightlifters competing at this year's world championships underwent out-of-competition testing by the International Testing Agency (ITA).
Two-time European champion Anastasiia Romanova, who previously served a two-year doping ban, was among those not tested by the ITA during the first nine months of 2026, according to its quarterly anti-doping reports.
By comparison, all 13 members of the North Korean team underwent at least one ITA test during the same period. North Korea , like Russia, has a history of doping violations in weightlifting.
Men, muscles, and the pursuit of the ‘perfect body’
To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video
The ITA, which runs weightlifting's anti-doping program, told DW that it tested all 16 Russian weightlifters "ahead of their participation in the event." DW understands those tests were conducted in Ningbo, China , where the championships are being held.
In a power sport like weightlifting, performance-enhancing drugs are most beneficial during training, when athletes build strength and muscle mass in the months before competition. Some drugs, such as anabolic steroids, may be harder to detect by the time the competition comes around.
Rob Koehler, head of the athlete-led movement Global Athlete, called the lack of out-of-competition testing "absurd."
"Out-of-competition testing is the backbone of anti-doping," Koehler told DW. "Everybody knows there's going to be testing at the event. But not everybody knows when they're going to be tested 365 days a year outside events. It's concerning that the ITA doesn't see this as a red flag."
ITA: Russians among top 10 tested nationalities
Marta Nawrocka, the ITA's spokesperson, said that Russian athletes were among the 10 most-tested nationalities in weightlifting this year. She also defended the fact that only two Russian weightlifters feature in the sport's highest-priority testing pool, saying inclusion is based on performance and risk profiles.
"Russia's history of doping in weightlifting remains an important factor in the ITA's risk assessment and testing priorities," Nawrocka said. "Russian weightlifters remain subject to substantial testing activity."
Koehler, though, is unconvinced.
"You simply can't treat Russia like any other country," he said. "It has to have more scrutiny. It has to have more testing. If you don't do that, you're undermining athlete confidence in the system."
The International Weightlifting Federation did not respond to a request for comment.
Sochi's enduring legacy
Weightlifting was one of the sports most implicated in Russia's state-sponsored doping scandal, which came to light after the 2014 Sochi Winter Olympics. It ranked second only to athletics for the number of positive cases identified by Canadian lawyer Richard McLaren in his 2016 report commissioned by WADA , the global anti-doping watchdog.
The scandal led to dozens of Russian athletes being banned across numerous sports. RUSADA, Russia's anti-doping agency, has remained suspended for most of the past decade.
As a result, its Moscow laboratory cannot analyze urine and blood samples, meaning samples collected by the agency must be sent abroad for analysis under what WADA described as a "strict chain of custody."
WADA said it continued to monitor RUSADA but had been unable to gain access to the country to review the agency's suspension because of the "ongoing geopolitical situation."
It added that RUSADA had "collected thousands of samples … including hundreds from weightlifters" so far this year.
"Given the history, WADA remains vigilant when it comes to Russia," James Fitzgerald, WADA's spokesperson, told DW. "We must ensure that no stone is left unturned when it comes to verifying that all the proper testing and other anti-doping activities are taking place."
Despite being suspended, RUSADA still has the power to investigate and prosecute anti-doping cases involving Russian athletes, which critics find difficult to reconcile.
"It's a compounding problem that WADA is still giving them a free pass when it can't even get into Russia to see what they're doing," said Koehler, WADA's former deputy director general.
"There's simply no oversight and no accountability. And quite frankly, I don't think there ever really has been."
RUSADA's independence under scrutiny
Critics also argue that ongoing questions over RUSADA's leadership and independence suggest that little has been fixed in the decade since the McLaren report.
Even the International Olympic Committee (IOC), whose president, Kirsty Coventry, supports the full return of Russian athletes, has acknowledged a "lack of confidence" over RUSADA's governance.
Nawrocka said the IOC had "recently entrusted" the ITA with an expanded role within Russia in the run-up to the Los Angeles Olympics in 2028, but did not explain what the role would involve or when it might begin.
In April, investigative outlet The Insider reported that Veronika Loginova, the agency's head, was in a long-term relationship with an alleged FSB officer. The FSB, Russia's domestic security service, played a central role in covering up positive drug tests at the Sochi Games.
Loginova did not respond to questions for this article but dismissed the allegations at the time as "all this nonsense," writing in an email that she believed "sport exists separate from politics."
WADA confirmed to DW only that its investigations unit was examining the allegations against Loginova and that the inquiry was ongoing.

（德国之声中文网）德国联邦总理、基民盟主席默茨主张，国家应尽可能减少对经济事务的干预。周四（11月5日），在柏林由弗里德里希·奥古斯特·冯·哈耶克基金会（Friedrich August von Hayek Foundation）举办的一场活动上，默茨表示：“国家不应亲自做出经济决策——因为它根本没有能力这样做。”“因此，我们需要开放德市场、企业自由和竞争，让最优解决方案能够以去中心化的方式涌现出来。”
在此背景下，默茨为削减屋顶 太阳能 装置补贴的举措进行了辩护，并重申他坚持尽可能降低欧盟贸易壁垒的立场。针对法国提出的 “欧洲制造” （Made in Europe）议题——即通过对非欧洲商品征收更高关税来保护欧盟内部生产，默茨表达了反对意见，认为不应实施过于严格的监管。
默茨主张，国家应专注于构建一个能够让自由蓬勃发展的秩序框架。这包括保障财产权、促进竞争、提供基础设施和有效的金融工具，并执行现有规则。
“国家战略可以提供推动力，但无法取代开放市场中固有的‘探索过程’（即通过市场竞争发现最优方案的过程）。”他指出，特别是在能源政策领域，一些行业长期以来一直受到保护，免受竞争冲击。他主张，现在必须削减补贴。他强调，这绝不是能源转型的终结。恰恰相反，这是实现能源转型的必要步骤。默茨警告称：“这是在一个民主多数因无力负担而干脆扫除这些目标之前，实现经济目标和生态目标的唯一可能方式。”
中国商务部长到访 欧洲在对华贸易问题上会走多远？

不过，他也提出了一个例外情况，并呼吁国家支持建立 欧盟 关键原材料储备。“我们目前正面临重大风险，因为原材料的开采和加工高度集中在极少数国家。国家必须协助降低这些风险，国家必须助力实现供应来源的多样化。”
他表示将在布鲁塞尔提出“非常具体地”建议，在欧洲层面建立这些关键原材料储备。若没有这些原材料，将无法制造电池、高性能电机、半导体以及未来至关重要的各类高科技产品。
中国目前掌控着许多关键原材料的出口与加工环节。中国领导层曾两次实施出口管制，导致供应链出现严重问题。上周， 默茨访问了日本 。日本早在数年前就开始为特定原材料建立储备，并通过其他供应来源替代从中国进口原材料。在欧盟内部，仍需回答的问题是：谁来为储备买单。

（德国之声中文网）在美国， 共和党在中期选举中惨败 ，被视为给 特朗普 总统的一记耳光。在巴西，右翼总统候选人 弗拉维奥·博索纳罗竞选失败 逃往美国。在欧洲， 匈牙利的欧尔班 和 塞尔维亚的武契奇 等独裁政客纷纷下台。“特朗普的败选打破了国际右翼民粹主义势不可挡的论调，”波鸿大学政治学家奥利弗·伦贝克（Oliver Lembcke）表示。
欧洲许多左翼政治家甚至认为正在出现逆转。西班牙首相桑切斯本周三也谈到了其他国家“极右浪潮”的终结。他在X平台上写道，美国民众投票反对那些使民众陷入贫困的政策，反对仇恨、反对大男子主义、反对气候变化否认者和精英特权。作为工人社会党领袖，桑切斯本人也面临选举，并将矛头指向国内的保守派和极右翼。
美国普通家庭 为何越活越累？
To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video
在德国，左翼党联合主席伊内斯·施韦特纳（Ines Schwerdtner）对路透社表示：“这对全球右翼来说是一次惨痛的失败。”社民党议会党团主席德克·维泽（Dirk Wiese）表示，选举结果表明“这股右翼民粹主义浪潮也是可以被遏制的”。他认为，这为与加拿大等伙伴建立更紧密的联盟带来了希望。
在国际上，一股反对特朗普反复无常的民族主义路线的势力正在崛起。德国总理默茨近期在日本、韩国和新加坡积极游说，呼吁建立一个新的全球自由贸易联盟。由 加拿大总理马克·卡尼 牵头的“同盟国联盟”正在全球范围内缓慢形成，其目标不仅是对抗中国，也是为了对抗特朗普。
德国选择党受打击
美国中期选举的结果对德国选择党来说也是一个打击，该党此前一直严重依赖特朗普、他的“让美国再次伟大”（MAGA）运动以及 马斯克 的支持。政治学家伦贝克表示，“美国中期选举表明，民粹主义政党一旦执政，就可能无法兑现自己的承诺。这对德国选择党来说无疑也是一个令人不安的信号。”
德国选择党主席之一的 魏德尔 已经迅速与特朗普划清界限，并亲自将败选归咎于他。她向新闻门户网站t-online表示： “特朗普曾向选民承诺，他不会奉行干涉主义的外交政策，”。“如今，他对这一承诺的违背反噬了共和党。”德国选择党在联邦议院的党团主席贝恩德·鲍曼（Bernd Baumann）在接受《商报》采访时批评了美国的进口关税，并表示选择党现在将把希望寄托在特朗普的继任者身上。
政治学家伦贝克认为，美国中期选举结果并不必然意味德国选择党的支持率会降低，因为两国的政治环境截然不同。他指出，“在匈牙利、美国、巴西和塞尔维亚，都有一些特定的国内议题影响了选举结果。”
究竟哪种趋势会占上风，要到明年才能见分晓。法国几个月后将举行总统和议会选举，目前右翼民粹主义政党国民联盟（RN）在民调中领先。而在波兰，亲欧派总理图斯克将面临一场艰难的连任之战。
(路透社）

The UN-recognised government of Yemen has shaken up its political and military leadership in an attempt to regain territory lost to the Houthis in September and lift the four-week siege of Taiz, the country’s third largest city.
A counteroffensive launched on 5 October and aimed at liberating the entire country from Houthi control has failed amid fighting that has left thousands dead on both sides. The air superiority of the government’s ally Saudi Arabia – which has had to fend off near-daily Houthi attacks on its airports and military bases – has not translated into progress on the ground.
Reuters reported on Monday that Houthi forces were only about 37 miles (60km) from Aden, the nominal seat of the UN-recognised government.
A burst of government dismissals and appointments reflects military reverses and possibly a perceived need to be more sensitive to the demands of southern Yemenis.
Between 1967 and 1990, the country was divided in two, and there is a strong movement built around the banned Southern Transitional Council (STC) seeking to revert to that division, or create a more federated country.
The government has become dependent on southern troops to fend off Houthi advances, but these forces insist they will fight only to defend land inside former South Yemen.
Fresh claims were also aired this week that STC leaders were coerced by the Saudis into dissolving the organisation against their will. The growing criticism of Saudi Arabia from STC officials in the media reflects their confidence that if the north is lost to the Houthis, the Saudis will have to let the STC operate openly. Not all southern separatists support the STC, an organisation that overreached itself in January, making it easier for the Saudi leadership to defer decisions on the southern question.
Some of the most senior figures in the UN-backed government are largely based in hotels in Riyadh rather than operating permanently from inside Yemen and the government is dependent on Saudi money to pay salaries. Critics say the administration has become a “hotel government”.
Earlier this week, its ruling executive – the presidential leadership council – met for the first time in months in Riyadh, where it addressed the loss of swathes of territory to the Houthis along Yemen’s west coast. Since then, the fighting has moved into the mountains around Taiz.
In an attempt to rebalance the north-south divide in his government, President Rashad al-Alimi sacked the long-serving information minister, Muammar al-Eryani, replacing him with Prof Salem al-Awlaki, previously a minister for the civil service and a spokesperson for the STC from 2017 to 2019. Alimi chose two other southerners as ministers for local administration and the civil service and appointed new leaders for the civil aviation authority, the ports of Aden and the ministry of transport.
He also sacked Yusuf al-Sharaji, the military figure responsible for the Taiz front and Abu Bakr al-Jabouli, a brigadier responsible for the Tor al-Baha axis. Widespread accusations had been made about al-Sharaji’s failure to manage operations, resulting in the fall of several areas and districts to the Houthis.
The task of lifting the siege of Taiz and coordinating forces has been handed to Maj Gen Rashad al-Yousfi, a career officer.
Part of the difficulty is the tension between the different forces fighting on the government’s side. It has been claimed that Abu Zara’a, the leader of the Southern Giants, has fallen out with the Homeland Shield Forces, which are funded by Saudi Arabia and affiliated with Abdulrahman al-Lahji.
The Homeland Shield experienced heavy losses, leading al-Lahji to file an official report accusing Abu Zara’a of treason, and warning that the situation in Dhubab, close to the strategic Bab al-Mandab strait, had become extremely dangerous for the government. Repeated claims that control of the strait had been wrested back from the Houthis were contradicted by the evidence.

（德国之声中文网）路透社引述两位知情人士的消息称，约60万块英伟达先进 人工智能 芯片目前存放在香港，等待运往中国内地。尽管中国科技企业存在需求，但北京方面尚未批准这些芯片的大规模进口。
这批H200芯片的库存规模此前未被报道过。它反映出北京不愿进一步加深对美国技术的依赖的同时，中国企业又需要英伟达先进算力，以满足全球第二大经济体对人工智能激增的需求。
三位知情人士表示，近几个月来，中国已允许其中部分芯片进入境内。
其中一位知情人士称，过去几个月里，几家中国大型互联网企业各自获得了约1万枚H200芯片。
知情人士表示，已有少量芯片通过中间商和间接渠道运抵中国，但未明确具体数量。
不过，这些知情人士指出， 北京方面尚未批准向中国内地进行大规模进口 。
中国工业和信息化部以及国家发改委未回应置评请求。英伟达以及中国的科技公司阿里巴巴、字节跳动、深度求索（DeepSeek）和 腾讯 也均未作出回应。.
更多阅读： 黄仁勋：中国终将开放AI芯片市场
H200并非最先进，但极具实用价值
H200虽然不是英伟达最新的AI处理器，但其性能仍是中国替代产品尚未达到的，在训练AI模型时非常有用——尤其是在结合英伟达的软件使用时。
自2022年以来，美国出口管制一直试图限制中国获取先进英伟达芯片以及制造这些芯片所需设备。
由于授权供应受限，中国买家转而寻求中间商或通过间接渠道采购，这推高了非官方市场上的价格。
据一位知情人士透露，截至10月底，在中国大陆，一台搭载8张H200芯片的服务器售价超过600万元人民币（约合90万美元），约为一年前价格的三倍。该知情人士补充称，搭载英伟达更新一代Blackwell芯片（同样受到美国出口管制）的服务器，单台售价则超过了2000万元人民币。
“四兆男”黄仁勋在中国都讲了些什么？

贸易与技术领域的紧张局势
H200芯片正处于华盛顿与北京之间更广泛的贸易与技术紧张局势之中。
美国曾一度禁止向中国出口H200芯片。去年， 特朗普政府允许英伟达向获批的中国客户出售该芯片 。这一政策转变发生在中美贸易谈判之后。
与此同时，北京方面也针对H200的进口实施了限制，这反映出中国对于过度依赖美国技术的担忧。
科技媒体《The Information》在7月份报道称，中国相关部门已告知包括阿里巴巴、字节跳动和深度求索（DeepSeek）在内的企业，它们或许能获准购买数量有限的H200芯片，用于训练AI模型。据报道，获批芯片的总量可能不到20万块。此外，北京方面希望企业在推理环节优先使用中国国产处理器。推理是指运行人工智能模型的任务。
路透社上个月报道称，字节跳动、阿里巴巴和腾讯订购了超过300万张英伟达RTX Pro 5500显卡。这是一款性能较弱、符合出口合规要求的产品，其总标价超过350亿美元。

content:
Interest rates have risen to 4% and the Bank of England has indicated there are more rises to come. The question is how many? There is a split on the rate-setting committee here.
Three of the nine voting members referred to "rises" plural. One member voted for a bigger increase, to 4.25%. Three referred to just one more including governor Andrew Bailey.
My read on this is that the expectation is for one more rise in February. Two and done, but it depends.
It is painful for those on variable mortgages, but should not be seen as the start of a cycle of hikes.
Predicting where interest rates will go is like throwing darts at a board that constantly moves around the wall, with expectations of how long the Iran War will last and its impact on the economy and prices lurching from day to day.
At least there is no blindfold.
The Bank's forecasts indicate inflation is heading to just under 5% next spring as a typical household energy bill surges by 27% in January to £2,150 a year.
Why now?
Why have they raised now? High and rising inflation risks a further cycle of self fulfilling expectations of rising prices. It hasn't been seen so far, however. The war has lasted for 9 months, and led to oil prices used in the forecast averaging $108 a barrel.
And yet on the day they have announced the rate rise, the oil price is actually 13% lower than that having fallen in the run up and after the US mid term elections, reflecting expectations or guesses that President Trump will now retreat or deescalate from the Iran war.
The other notable factor is that the UK economy is performing much better than forecasts and expectations. This is underlined by the Bank of England's latest forecasts.
Growth has been 0.6%, and 0.5% in the first two quarters of the year. It is heading for 0.7%, the Bank said, between July and September, before slowing in the three months to the end of the year. Unemployment has stabilised, actually falling a little.
Some of this has fed through into a better performing currency, with sterling at its highest level since the Brexit referendum, when measured against a basket of currencies. This can help rein in inflation by making imports cheaper.
So, this is an unusual type of uncertainty. Even the expected further rise, probably in February next year is conditional on the war continuing.
The Bank of England stopped waiting for President Trump's war to end today, but perhaps the Democrats' resounding victory in the US midterm elections will stop the inflationary wave? The Bank has thrown a tentative first dart, and there is probably another to come.

Thailand’s Oil Fuel Fund Committee has agreed to cut retail B7 diesel prices by 0.75 baht a litre and petrol and gasohol prices by 1 baht a litre from November 6, 2026, as falling international prices create room to lower motorists’ costs while reducing diesel subsidies.
The committee’s decision on November 5 combines pump-price reductions with changes to the levies and subsidies applied to individual fuel grades. B20 diesel is the retail-price exception, remaining unchanged despite a reduction in its subsidy.
The latest adjustment follows earlier petrol and gasohol price cuts introduced on November 5.
B7 diesel will retail at 41.79 baht a litre under the new schedule, while petrol will fall to 49.33 baht. The Oil Fuel Fund will reduce support for both diesel grades and collect higher levies on most petrol-based fuels, although the subsidy for E85 will increase.
The revised fund rates take effect on November 6, according to the Oil Fuel Fund Office’s published notice.
The following prices and Oil Fuel Fund adjustments take effect on November 6, 2026:
The Oil Fuel Fund Committee attributed the decline in international prices partly to easing geopolitical tensions in the Middle East, which had reduced concerns about supply disruptions. Increased crude oil exports from the Persian Gulf also contributed to the downward pressure.
The committee additionally cited investor profit-taking following the US midterm election results and concerns that a slowing global economy could weaken demand for crude oil.
International diesel prices closed at approximately US$155 a barrel on November 5, down from around US$166 on November 4, according to the committee. Petrol prices fell to approximately US$105 from around US$112 a barrel over the same period.
The Oil Fuel Fund Committee described the adjustments as a way to reduce living costs while improving the fund’s liquidity. Lower subsidy expenditure would ease a burden that had previously reached 69 million baht a day.
Despite the downward trend in international and domestic fuel prices, the committee stressed that conservation and efficient fuel use remained important for Thailand’s energy security and longer-term household savings.

content:
Interest rates have been raised for the first time in more than three years - and it could be good and bad news for you.
Here are three ways the increase to 4% from 3.75% could affect you.
1. Jobs and pay
Rate-setters at the Bank make changes to interest rates to fulfil their role of keeping price rises at a steady level.
Higher rates are meant to encourage people to spend less, reducing demand for goods and services and limiting price rises.
This impacts businesses in two ways - less money to spend among their customers may mean they sell less, but also the cost of borrowing to invest as a company goes up.
Many businesses, particularly small ones, have variable rate loans which are influenced by the Bank rate.
Firms say higher rates limit their ability to offer new jobs and wage rises.
Mitchell Barnes, founder and chief executive of Ryse 3D, which manufactures 3D parts for the defence and automotive sectors, said the "reality" of rising interest rates was to look at the cost of employees and people.
That could include greater use of robots rather than workers.
"It's going to cause issues with, I suppose, employment across all sectors for people," he said.
"You're going to see reduced employment, more automation, more robotics being put into facilities, just in order to increase efficiency and make that money go further."
2. Boost to savings
The Bank rate - and where it is expected to go in future - has a significant impact on the interest rates customers are offered on savings products.
So, if you're saving up for something quite expensive, like a holiday, or very expensive, like a home, then a rate rise could be good news.
When interest rates were low throughout the 2010s, the returns for savers were poor, but borrowing costs were low too.
The answer then and now, according to experts, is to make sure you move your savings to benefit from the best possible rates.
Leaving your savings in an old account (a product not offered to new customers), rather than shopping around, can mean you are penalised for your loyalty.
"Savers have endured years of unrewarded loyalty, with those leaving [a £20,000 cash pot] in closed accounts losing out on an extra £139 over the past three years compared to on-sale easy access accounts," said Rachel Springall, from financial information service Moneyfacts.
She also said locking away your money for longer, with a fixed-term deal, is usually more lucrative.
The other flipside is that renting while you save could get more expensive, because a rising Bank rate may well increase costs for landlords.
3. Mortgages and loans
The big losers from a rate rise are those who borrow money, and specifically those on variable rate mortgages.
About 500,000 homeowners have a mortgage that "tracks" the Bank of England's rate.
Any rise in the Bank rate means an increase in the monthly repayments on their outstanding loan. For a typical loan, the cost is going up by about £31 a month now the Bank has raised the base rate, but it depends on the size of people's loans.
An additional 500,000 homeowners on standard variable rates (SVRs) must wait to see if their lender chooses to pass on any Bank rate rise. Typically, this would mean a £14 increase per month in repayments for a 0.25 percentage points rates rise.
If you, like 87% of mortgage-holders, have a fixed-rate deal, then the payments will stay the same until the end of your current deal, which is usually two or five years.
While monthly payments are not immediately affected by a rate change, future deals are. Lenders had already "priced in" the latest rate rise when quoting new deals. Expectations for the Bank rate into next year are crucial on what they offer next.
The average rate on fixed deals are much higher now than was predicted at the start of the year. It means those remortgaging, possibly after the post-Covid boom in the housing market, are facing the prospect of higher mortgage payments.
Some people have been choosing to move onto tracker deals instead, taking a view - including some risk - of the Bank rate not moving towards a series of further hikes.

content:
"Llegó el día de devolver la camiseta siete a la selección de todos nosotros. Nunca la sentí como exclusivamente mía, pero durante 23 años tuve el privilegio y la responsabilidad de vestirla", dice el astro del fútbol portugués, Cristiano Ronaldo , al comienzo de un video publicado este jueves (5.11.2026) en su perfil en Instagram .
"No fue una decisión fácil", asegura la estrella internacional de 41 años en su mensaje, dirigido "a los portugueses".
"Hoy mi viaje con la selección nacional llega a su fin", añadió el internacionalmente conocido como CR7 .
Retirada tras disputa con el seleccionador
Su retirada queda empañada por la disputa con el seleccionador portugués, Jorge Jesus, pública desde el 27 de septiembre en Oslo: el DT lo dejó en el banquillo y sin minutos en el partido de la Nations League contra Noruega, a pesar de haber calentado en banda más de media hora. Y, antes del siguiente encuentro ante Dinamarca, informó que Ronaldo no sería titular y el jugador abandonó la concentración.
El madeirense realizó este anuncio tras disculparse días después por el desplante, y recibir una sanción simbólica por parte del Consejo de Disciplina de la Federación Portuguesa de Fútbol (FPF): 30 días de suspensión y una multa de 255 euros (286 dólares), el mínimo previsto en el reglamento, por haber abandonado la concentración de Portugal el 30 de septiembre.
Alegato contra Jorge Jesus
La Federación Portuguesa de Fútbol había allanado el camino para su regreso al anunciar la semana pasada que figuraba entre la cincuentena de jugadores preconvocados para enfrentarse a Dinamarca el 14 de noviembre en Braga (norte) y luego a Gales, tres días después, en Cardiff.
Pero aunque Ronaldo lamentó su actitud hacia los aficionados y sus compañeros, arremetió contra el seleccionador Jorge Jesus con un largo alegato en el que lo acusa de haber traicionado su confianza.
Adelantándose 24 horas al anuncio por parte del entrenador de su lista definitiva para los dos próximos partidos de la Liga de las Naciones, el capitán portugués anunció que no volverá.
En su último gran torneo , el Mundial 2026 en Norteamérica, el jugador nacido en la isla de Madeira se convirtió en el primero de la historia en marcar en seis Copas del Mundo, pero la competición concluyó con una actuación discreta, con la eliminación de Portugal en octavos de final ante España (1-0), la futura campeona.
Reconocimiento de la Federación y la selección
La Federación Portuguesa de Fútbol (FPF) reaccionó con "profunda gratitud" a Cristiano Ronaldo. En un comunicado , la entidad presidida por Pedro Proença agradeció la carrera "absolutamente extraordinaria" del delantero, al que calificó de "líder inspirador", "ejemplo de dedicación" y "máximo símbolo del alma" de la selección portuguesa. El sentido del mensaje se reprodujo también en video en las cuentas de redes sociales de la selección portuguesa.
La Federación destacó sus 234 internacionalidades y 146 goles, dos récords mundiales del fútbol masculino, así como su contribución a los tres títulos conquistados por Portugal durante su carrera: la Eurocopa de 2016 y las Ligas de Naciones de 2019 y 2025.
"Cada gota de sudor, cada gol decisivo y cada brazalete honrado en el campo fueron el reflejo de su amor incondicional por nuestra camiseta", señaló la FPF en su comunicado, que subrayó que el legado del futbolista "trasciende las cuatro líneas" del terreno de juego.
El organismo aseguró que Ronaldo elevó el nombre de Portugal en todo el mundo e inspiró a generaciones de jóvenes futbolistas, y sostuvo que "se niega a dejar que este adiós se produzca sin el debido tributo", afirmó en su comunicado.
Por ello, expresó su voluntad de "organizar, planificar, participar y colaborar activamente" en un homenaje en el que los aficionados y el país puedan aplaudir y celebrar nuevamente la carrera del jugador. Aunque la FPF no precisó cuándo ni dónde podría celebrarse ese acto.
"¡Gracias por todo, CAPITÁN! ¡Esta será siempre tu casa! ¡Vamos a por el gol 1.000!", concluyó el comunicado, en referencia al objetivo del delantero de alcanzar el millar de tantos en su carrera profesional.
