（德国之声中文网）在 共和党输掉中期选举 之后，副总统万斯表示：“如果你想争辩说这一切是值得的——即为了这场战争而失去参议院六年的控制权是值得的——那你就尽管去做……”
“但人人都知道我们为什么输了。任何关于我们未来走向的坦诚讨论，都必须从这一点出发，”这位美国副总统周三在社交媒体平台X上写道。“我们失败的原因就是这场（伊朗）战争。总统本人昨晚也这么说了。”
共和党在11月3日的中期选举惨败，将众议院和参议院的控制权拱手让给民主党；此次选举也被视为对特朗普各项政策的一次“全民公投”。
特朗普与以色列在2月份共同发动的对伊战争在美国民众中极不受欢迎，因为战争推高了燃油价格，而且这场冲突目前看来还远未结束。
当被问及万斯的分析时，特朗普表示：“我认为这在很大程度上是对的，因为它在短期内确实推高了汽油价格。”但这位美国总统也坚称对伊开战的决定是正确的。特朗普表示，如果再次面临同样的选择，他仍会做出同样的决定，并继续称这场战争是“值得的”。
万斯和美国国务卿卢比奥都被视为2028年共和党总统候选人提名的有力竞争者。
根据美国法律，美国总统无法竞选第三个任期，因此特朗普无法再次参加竞选。此前对于谁可能成为共和党领袖的继任者，特朗普一直未予明确表态。
周三在白宫宴会厅施工现场面对摄像机时谈及此事时，特朗普说，“也许他（万斯）不会参选。我不知道谁会参选”。

content:
The western city of Frankfurt was a very conscious choice of location for the new academy, which is the first of its kind in Germany. Frankfurt has traditionally been a hub of Jewish intellectual life — still one of the most important centers of Jewish life in Germany today alongside Berlin, Munich and Düsseldorf.
Less than a 10-minute walk from the city's biggest synagogue, the Jewish Academy is also within sight of the historic festival hall building on Frankfurt Trade Fair grounds where the Nazis herded Jewish men in 1938 and deported them to concentration camps .
It was also here that the Central Council of Jews in Germany was founded in 1950; Berlin serves as its headquarters today. Frankfurt is also home to the Central Welfare Board of Jews in Germany (ZWST) and a Jewish museum that opened in 1988.
Jewish thinkers have played a key  role in Frankfurt's intellectual and academic history. The city's Jewish community contributed to the establishment of Goethe University in 1914.
Another important legacy is the Jewish Lehrhaus (house of study). Founded in 1920, it quickly gained prominence and is today associated with the philosopher Franz Rosenzweig (1886–1929). It was closed by the Nazis in 1938. The new academy sees itself in the tradition of Rosenzweig's Lehrhaus .
A place of education and dialogue
Speaking at the opening ceremony on Monday, Josef Schuster, president of the Central Council of Jews in Germany, stressed: "We must combat hatred with education, education and more education."
Schuster said the institute was a "milestone” that represented the "Jewish community's determination to call Germany home." At the same time, he emphasized: "Jewish life in Germany is under greater threat than it has been since the crime against humanity that was the Shoah."
German President Frank-Walter Steinmeier also underlined the need to reject antisemitism "outright and without reservation." He added that it must also be combated politically.
The federal president said the murder of six million Jews in the Holocaust had also targeted the Jewish world of learning and knowledge. He specifically honored Rosenzweig's legacy: "This place of knowledge and dialogue was a source of hope, something exciting and something new."
A bridge between tradition and modernity, as well as academia and the general public
The Jewish Academy combines traditional features of a 110-year-old turn-of-the-century German villa with a four-story modern structure, bringing together old and new, history and modernity.
"We see ourselves as a place where the past, present and future are all explored in equal measure," Sabena Donath, the institution's director, told DW.
Donath and her co-director, Doron Kiesel, view the academy as "a bridge between academia and the general public" and as "a home for scholars and a home for those who ask questions."
Donath said the aim was to put the focus on topics related to the philosophy of religion and ethics as well as on topical debates concerning contemporary Jewish life.
The program aims to reflect the many facets of Jewish life and the diverse forms of Judaism .
Kiesel told DW: "We want to show how Jews live today and how heterogeneous Jewish life is. And that it is completely wrong to speak of 'the' Jews or 'the' Jewish way of thinking."
Ahead of the opening, the president of the Central Council of Jews also named interfaith dialogue as one of the institution's topics, and, in an interview with the German newspaper, the Frankfurter Allgemeine , Schuster expressed the hope that the academy would bring into the public sphere "Jewish themes besides the topic of antisemitism and Jewish persecution.”
But these issues will also be on the agenda. "We have,” said Kiesel, "a problem in this country that antisemitism is concealed behind numerous topics, but keeps on resurfacing, sometimes more evidently, sometimes more subtly.”

The project grew out of an initiative from the former head of the Central Council Dieter Graumann, who encouraged the setting up of an educational department in 2012. Its work was shaped by the directors of the new institution.
Security measures push up price tab
A mezuzah — a small capsule containing verses from the Torah intended to serve as a reminder of God's commandments — is affixed to the entrance of the academy. Security measures are also an integral part of this new building.
"It is a bitter reality that Jewish institutions must be guarded," said Donath. The academy is being protected just as Jewish schools and synagogues must be protected . "For us, this is a sad reality of everyday life."
The construction costs of around €40 million ($45 million) — about half of which was covered by the Central Council of Jews and half by the federal and state governments — ended up being significantly higher than calculated at the groundbreaking in 2021, partly due to the structural security measures.

Cristiano Ronaldo took to social media on Thursday to announce that he had played his last game for Portugal .
"To the Portuguese people, the day has come for me to hand back the No. 7 shirt of our national team," the 41-year-old Ronaldo said in a video on his Instagram account.
"I never felt it belonged to me alone, but for 23 years I had the privilege and the responsibility of wearing it, defending it and carrying it with me into stadiums all around the world," Ronaldo said.
The former Manchester United, Real Madrid and Juventus forward represented his country 234 times, scoring 146 goals — making him the men's record-holder for international appearances and for international goals.
Decision made with 'head and heart'
He captained Portugal to their first major trophy at Euro 2016 and led them to the 2019 and 2025 Nations League titles.
"It was not an easy decision, there are decisions that are not only with the head. They are also made with the heart," Ronaldo continued in the Instagram post.
"If I ever made you happy, if one of my goals ever made you hug someone, forget a worry or feel proud of our country, then it was all worth it."
He also thanked his family, the Portuguese people and the teammates, coaches and staff he worked with over his national team career.
'The greatest of all time'
The Portuguese Football Association (FPF) released a statement expressing its gratitude and respect for the player also known as "CR7."
"Cristiano Ronaldo has raised Portugal's profile and inspired generations of young people who dream of following in his footsteps; for many of us, he is the greatest player of all time!" it read.
The FPF intends to organize a tribute "in which the fans and the country can one more time applaud and celebrate a player who has given us so much."
Training camp walkout
While his long-rival Lionel Messi ended his Argentina career with a much anticipated farewell match last month, Ronaldo's final appearance may go down as Portugal's 1-0 win over Wales on September 24, depending on the nature of the tribute. Portugal coach Jorge Jesus left him on the bench for the following match and said he wouldn't start the next one.
Ronaldo responded by walking out of the Portugal training camp . He was subsequently suspended and fined by the FPF, but he had been expected to return to Portugal for the November international break.
Like Messi , Ronaldo intends to continue his club career with Al-Nassr in Saudi Arabia.

The Bangkok Mass Transit Authority (BMTA) will run free shuttle buses on a loop from Payap Pier on Friday (November 6, 2026) for people going to watch the Royal Barge Procession or catch a ferry across the Chao Phraya River from the pier.
The service is being provided for the 2026 royal kathin ceremony.
Their Majesties the King and Queen will travel in the procession to Wat Arun Ratchawararam Ratchawaramahawihan, where they will make merit by presenting kathin robes as part of the annual ceremony.
The BMTA will run the free service from 11am to 6pm on Friday, or until everyone has left the area.
Passengers can board at regular bus stops along the route.
They should look for a sign on the front of the bus reading “Shuttle Bus” or “Payap Pier loop”.
Payap Pier loop links both banks of the Chao Phraya River
The buses will start and finish at Payap Pier, travelling through areas on the Phra Nakhon and Thon Buri sides of the river.
The BMTA has set out the route below.
Payap Pier → Nakhon Chai Si Road → Samsen Road → Sukhothai Road → Nakhon Ratchasima Road → Ratchawithi Road → Samsen Road → Phra Sumen Road → Dinso Road → Ratchadamnoen Klang Road → Na Phra That Road → Phra Chan Road → Maha Rat Road → Rajinee Pier
Rajinee Pier → Sanam Chai Road → Phra Phiphit Road → Phahurat Road → Tri Phet Road → Memorial Bridge → Prachathipok Road → Ban Khaek Intersection → Itsaraphap Road → Wang Doem Road → Arun Amarin Road → Arun Amarin Bridge
Arun Amarin Bridge → Somdet Phra Pinklao Road → Charan Sanit Wong Road → Bang Phlat Intersection → Ratchawithi Road → Krung Thon Bridge (Sang Hi Bridge) → Khao Road → Sukhothai Road → Samsen Road → Nakhon Chai Si Road → Payap Pier
The free shuttle gives spectators another way to reach the viewing areas and takes passengers to Payap Pier for ferries across the Chao Phraya River.

（德国之声中文网）台湾国防部长顾立雄本周四在被问及美国中期选举后的对台军售问题时表示，“美国国会跨党派一向支持台湾增强防卫力量，我们会持续跟这些国会议员进行沟通，同时跟美国战争部保持密切联系，以确保我们的相关军售都能够如计划进行。”
尽管美国与 台湾 之间没有正式外交关系，但美国仍是台湾最重要的国际支持者和武器供应方。
美国总统特朗普去年12月批准了有史以来规模最大的一笔对台军售案，总额110亿美元，但另一项总价值约140亿美元的军售计划目前处于搁置状态。自今年年初以来，特朗普一直推迟这笔约140亿美元的对台军售计划。在5月份与中国国家主席习近平会晤后，特朗普表示 搁置这笔军售 ，并称这是很好的“谈判筹码”。
中国一贯将台湾问题视为其最敏感、最重要的外交议题，并多次要求停止对台军售。台湾民选政府拒绝接受北京的主权主张，强调只有台湾人民才能决定自己的未来。

军售方案可能会被推迟至2027年？
台北东吴大学副教授陈方隅表示，美国民主党和共和党在台湾问题上存在高度共识。
他补充道：“ 国务卿卢比奥 及其团队依然是核心人物，他们针对印太地区、亚洲乃至全球局势的整体战略，不太可能发生重大改变。”
今年9月，在习近平访问美国首都华盛顿之前，四位共和党人曾敦促特朗普政府发放超过150亿美元、此前处于搁置状态的对台国家安全援助，其中就包括140亿美元的军售方案。
预计在今年年底前，特朗普与习近平至少还会再会晤两次——分别是在本月于中国举行的亚太经合组织（APEC）峰会上，以及12月在佛罗里达州举行的二十国集团（G20）峰会上。
2026年10月20日，现任“美国印太安全研究所”主席、美国国防部印太安全事务前助理国防部长薛瑞福（Randall G.Schriver）在台北出席由陆委会、国防院等机构举办的学术研讨会时表示，由于特朗普和习近平今年年底还会见面，预计相关的重大军售案可能要到2027年才会出现实质进展。
台湾最高学术研究机构“中央研究院”的助理研究员傅泽民（Ronan Fu）指出，当军售恢复时（或许是在明年），可能会被拆分为若干个独立的部分。他补充说：“但如果把所有部分加总起来，我认为总金额大致还是会维持不变。”
（路透社）

The company said it was beginning a "new chapter"
Published
A Newport aviation company, that has grown into a global supplier of aircraft engines, parts and maintenance services, has been bought in a deal worth about £475m.
Japanese firm ORIX Aviation has agreed to acquire AerFin, which employs more than 230 people and operates from sites in the UK and around the world.
Founded by Bob James, AerFin has developed from a south Wales business into a global aviation aftermarket specialist.
Announcing the takeover, AerFin described it as the start of a new chapter for the company.
The firm - which was majority owned by a private equity company prior to the sale - buys, sells, leases and repairs aircraft, engines and components.
In 2025, the company moved into a new purpose-built, 116,000 sq ft facility, external at Indurent Park in Newport.
There are no plans to move its headquarters from Newport.
ORIX Aviation is the aircraft leasing arm of Japanese financial services giant the ORIX Group.
Simon Goodson, AerFin's chief executive, said the deal would help grow the business
Chief executive Simon Goodson called the acquisition a "defining moment" in the company's history.
"I am delighted that AerFin is joining the ORIX Group, a business that shares our values and belief in trusted partnerships, flexible solutions and finding the way ahead for our customers," he said.
He said support from the wider ORIX Group would provide "the confidence and platform" to grow the aviation business.
"This is a defining moment in AerFin's story and the beginning of an exciting new chapter," said Goodson.
Aerfin helps airlines and aviation companies source parts and manage assets
AerFin has built its existing business around extending the life of aircraft and engines through trading, leasing, repair and reuse.
It helps airlines and aviation companies source parts and manage assets. The company claims to serve more than 600 organisations.
AerFin moved into a new purpose-built facility in Newport last year
For ORIX Aviation, the acquisition expands its activities beyond aircraft ownership and leasing, into aftermarket services and end-of-life aircraft management.
The company said the combination would strengthen its capabilities across the entire lifecycle of an aircraft.
James Meyler, chief executive of ORIX Aviation, said AerFin had built "a leading aviation aftermarket platform" supported by extensive technical expertise and an international customer base.
The sale also marks the exit of Danish private equity investor CataCap, which had been the majority shareholder in AerFin.
Founder Bob James said he was pleased to see the business move to what he described as "a long-term home", capable of supporting AerFin's next phase of expansion.
"I recognise a strong leadership team and a long-term home when I see one," James said.

content:
It had been nearly a decade since Celia de Oliveira Soares last voted, and months since the 101-year-old great-grandmother last left her home.
But on 25 October, when Brazil held what many considered its most important presidential election in decades, relatives helped Soares into a wheelchair and drove her to a nearby school to make sure the far-right candidate, Flávio Bolsonaro, did not prevail.
Soares clung to the banister as, step by step, she climbed two flights of stairs to the polling booth under the watchful eye of her granddaughter’s husband, Marcio Marques.
Inside, the frail but jaunty centenarian keyed the number “13” – representing Bolsonaro’s leftwing rival, President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva – into an electronic voting machine and pressed confirm.
“I like Lula. I really do!” enthused Soares, a retired bank employee who has lived in Rio de Janeiro most of her life.
“I don’t like Bolsonaro or his father. So the efficient thing to do was go out and vote,” Soares added, as her grandsons, Tito and Ravi, played on the balcony around her surrounded by pot plants and books.
Soares is one of more than 1 million elderly people who, having missed the election’s 4 October first round – which Lula lost – decided to vote in the second.
Never since the return of democracy in the 1980s had the first-round loser bounced back, but Lula did just that. And after Lula’s shock revival, elderly voters have been hailed as the election’s unsung heroes – including by Lula himself.
At his 81st birthday party last week, the leftist veteran shed tears while describing his gratitude to the elderly people who helped him clinch a historic fourth term while clutching walking frames and sticks.
“I honestly think it was the most powerful and human image I’ve ever seen during an election,” Lula said of viral pictures showing voters in their 80s, 90s and 100s being carried into polling centres by relatives or carers, some in stretchers or wheelchairs.
In north-east Brazil, where Lula was born into rural poverty in the 1940s, a 114-year-old retiree called Josefa Pereira da Conceição went to vote wearing a red T-shirt emblazoned with Lula’s face and the slogan “Strength of the people”.
Election experts are still crunching the numbers to fully understand how Lula pulled off his unprecedented fightback, finding 10.3m extra votes between the first and second rounds.
Explanations include a sharp increase in welfare benefits on the eve of the vote; an extraordinary digital mobilisation involving a pro-Lula WhatsApp group that grew from 50,000 to nearly 11m members in less than a month; and a student-led street rebellion in which millions of citizens protested across Brazil.
Some believe elderly people were also crucial, noting how 1.4 million of the 3 million extra voters who took part in the second round after skipping the first were over 70. Pre-election polls suggested such voters were more inclined to vote for Lula.
Speaking at Lula’s victory celebration, the former minister Simone Tebet called the result a cross-generational triumph which sent a message to the democratic world. “It is possible to resist fascism – all you need to do is mobilise society,” Tebet declared, claiming: “Young people hit the streets and golden-agers saved our democracy.”
The political journalist José Roberto de Toledo said there was concrete evidence of higher turnout among older voters in the runoff, particularly those aged 60 to 79. Voting is only mandatory in Brazil for those aged 18 to 69.
“The images [of elderly people voting] aren’t misleading: they reveal a phenomenon that isn’t just an isolated case. It’s not some made-up story or a staged example. It really happened – and it was a movement you can measure statistically,” Toledo said of the images suggesting an unusually large number of older voters.
That said, Toledo believed the swing to Lula was explained mostly by fear, not age. Voting data suggested many people who backed Lula in the runoff had previously voted for Bolsonaro’s rightwing adversaries, hoping to protest against Lula’s Worker’s party (PT), which has governed for nearly 18 of the last 24 years.
In the runoff, faced with a straight choice between Lula, a familiar and predictable figure even for detractors, and Bolsonaro, who represented a leap into the unknown, many preferred the former.
“A protest vote in the first round [became] a safety vote or a lower-risk vote in the second – even if it wasn’t a happy vote,” said Toledo, who believed Bolsonaro alienated many voters with his “arrogant” behaviour after winning the first round.
Particularly damaging was the rightwinger’s authoritarian-sounding vow to “re-democratise” the already democratic country – something Toledo suspected stoked fears that Bolsonaro aspired to be “the emperor of Brazil”.
Even before those remarks, Soares fretted over the direction Brazil might take under Flávio Bolsonaro, whose father, the former president Jair Bolsonaro, is serving a 27-year sentence for plotting to seize power after losing the 2022 election to Lula.
“His father wanted to stage a coup … and stay on as president, just like Getúlio [Vargas did in 1937],” recalled the great-grandmother, who was 12 at the time and lived through the subsequent eight years of dictatorial rule.
Marques, a 51-year-old food entrepreneur, said his grandmother-in-law was also critical of how Jair Bolsonaro undermined vaccination efforts during the Covid pandemic, when 700,000 Brazilians died.
“She’s got three great-grandchildren … and she understands she’s nearing the end of her life. But she’s worried about the country, about her family and about future generations,” said Marques, becoming visibly emotional as he recalled watching Soares exercise her democratic right, perhaps for the last time.
“It was so moving to see her strength and desire [to vote] … We felt she had an intuition, or something telling her she needed to be part of this … She doesn’t know if she’ll get another chance,” added Marques, whose 85-year-old father, Helço Muniz, also voted Lula – in his case for the first time.
Sitting in her armchair overlooking Rio’s Guanabara Bay, five days after the election, Soares voiced excitement that Lula would soon start his fourth and final term. “I’ve been fond of him ever since he was poor,” she said of the lathe operator turned president, who first took office as president in 2003. “He was poor and he became rich, but he carried on being a simple man.”
Occasionally, Soares’s memory betrayed her and she needed reminding that Lula had pulled off one of modern history’s greatest democratic comebacks. “But that’s wonderful!” she beamed.
Reminded of Lula’s feat, Soares predicted Bolsonaro would flee abroad.
“He’s already gone!” her granddaughter, Poliana Soares Jordão, 46, told her. “His dad’s in prison and he’s fled.”
Soares, who has lived through four coups, 16 presidential elections and four Lula wins, was not surprised. “He must have gone to the US, then,” the centenarian guessed, correctly. “He’d been getting ready for that for a while, hadn’t he?”

content:
Asian nations that have borne the brunt of the US-Israeli war on Iran and US President Donald Trump’s trade tariffs are hopeful that Democrats will be able to temper his most harmful policies.
Democrats have claimed the House of Representatives and the Senate in US midterm elections, with early results from Tuesday’s voting showing strong gains against Republicans.
While Mr Trump will remain in office, his ability to get his way might be constrained by Democrats, who can use congressional powers to control government spending and launch investigations into Mr Trump, his family and his allies.
The Iran conflict is the most pressing issue for Asian countries, especially importers of fossil fuels like crude oil, refined products and liquefied natural gas (LNG).
The war launched by the US and Israel on Feb 28 has seen energy prices surge across Asia, especially for refined fuels, with Singapore gasoil — the building block for diesel — closing at a record high of US$199.89 (6,726 baht) a barrel on March 30.
It has since eased to end at $164.18 a barrel on Tuesday, but this is still 80% higher than the $91.42 from the day before the Iran war started.
Spot LNG prices for delivery to North Asia <LNG-AS> have tripled since the start of the conflict to $32.50 per million British thermal units, while Australian thermal coal at Newcastle Port <CO-FOBNWC-AU>, a grade popular with utilities in Japan and South Korea, has jumped 30% to $151.15 a metric tonne.
It’s not just the price increases that have spooked Asian economies; there have also been issues with securing supply, given the continent was the destination for about 80% of crude oil and refined fuels from the Middle East.
Australia, the world’s largest importer of diesel and a close US ally, had to scramble to ensure sufficient supplies in the early months of the conflict, effectively leveraging its exports of coal and LNG to ensure buyers of these products were able to supply liquid fuels in return.
Asian energy importers will be hoping that Democrats can limit Mr Trump’s ability to continue the war against Iran, while at the same time encouraging a diplomatic end to the conflict.
If Asian economies are to lower the risk of recession, then limiting energy-led inflation is seen as vital.
Asian countries, particularly US allies such as Japan, South Korea and India, will also be hoping that Democrats in Congress will be able to moderate the worst impacts of Mr Trump’s trade policies, which have seen unilateral tariffs imposed and unrealistic promises made in order to seal deals offering some relief.
There is a Trump policy that many Asian countries will be hoping continues: his administration’s efforts to build supply chains outside China for critical minerals.
This has seen US investment into mines and processing facilities and an increase in capital available for new projects.
Given that there is bipartisan support for many of these efforts, it’s likely that Democrats would be broadly supportive of continuing to invest in minerals like rare earths, tungsten and lithium, with the caveat that they may want to launch investigations into companies with ties to Mr Trump that have benefited from funding.
Overall, what Asian nations that are traditional friends of the US want most out of Democrats is a brake on Mr Trump’s impulsive decision-making, an end to the conflict in the Middle East, a rolling back of trade tariffs and more consistency in how allies are treated.
For countries that are less friendly to the United States, or are seen as rivals, such as China, a return to a more predictable foreign and trade policy would be welcome.
The main risks are doubts as to whether Democrats will be able to rein in Trump, given his cavalier attitude to obeying legislation and previously followed rules.
There is also wariness over the risks presented in the next two months until the new Congress first sits on Jan 3, with fears Mr Trump may be tempted to use the window of a lame-duck but still Republican Congress to revive the Iran war and enact more trade tariffs. Reuters
Clyde Russell is a columnist for Reuters.
summary: Asian nations that have borne the brunt of the US-Israeli war on Iran and US President Donald Trump’s trade tariffs are hopeful that Democrats will be able to temper his most harmful policies.

The Thai Meteorological Department issued a weather advisory at 5pm on Thursday (November 5, 2026), forecasting unsettled weather in upper Thailand and heavy to very heavy rain in the South from November 5 to 9.
Upper Thailand is expected to see thundershowers, gusty winds, hail and isolated heavy rain from November 5 to 7.
The Northeast will be affected first, followed by the North, the Central region, including Bangkok and its surrounding areas, and the East.
The department advised people to take precautions during storms and avoid open ground, areas beneath large trees and places near unsecured billboards.
Rainfall in the South is forecast to increase from November 7 to 9, with heavy rain in many areas and isolated very heavy rain.
The department advised residents to watch for flash floods and rapid run-off from the hills as rainfall accumulates, particularly on foothill slopes near waterways and in low-lying areas.
Another high-pressure system or cold air mass from China will spread over upper Thailand and the South China Sea, strengthening the easterly winds blowing across Thailand and the Gulf of Thailand.
Waves are expected to exceed 2 metres in areas with thundershowers in the Andaman Sea and the Gulf of Thailand.
Mariners in both waters were advised to navigate with caution and avoid those areas.
The department urged people to plan their daily activities and travel carefully to stay safe and minimise potential impacts, and to keep following its advisories.
Updates are available around the clock on 0-2399-4012-13 and 1182 and at www.tmd.go.th. The next advisory is due at 5am on November 6.

Was an Italian chef really fired over refusal to put pineapple on pizza?
Italian chef Davide Tamburella was fired from a Brisbane restaurant in May after the establishment's management expressed concerns about a string of complaints about the chef's behaviour.
Among them were Tamburella's refusal to provide ham and pineapple pizza for guests at a function.
It was the third time Tamburella had refused to use the fruit on pizzas in the past four years.
At the time, the chef had stated that putting pineapple on pizza was "offensive to his culture".
Australia correspondent Katy Watson explains what led to Tamburella's dismissal.
summary: The chef had stated that putting pineapple on pizza was "offensive to his culture".

Thailand’s Criminal Court issued arrest warrants for actress Panadda “Bum” Wongphudee and her husband, Atip “Got” Anantawan, on November 5, 2026, in an investigation into alleged donation irregularities involving the Ongkorn Thamdee Foundation. Police are examining donations reportedly totalling 900 million baht.
Panadda, a television presenter and chair of the foundation, was named alongside Atip in an application submitted by the Economic Crime Suppression Division. The court granted the application after reviewing the evidence and case documents presented by investigators.
The Economic Crime Suppression Division confirmed in an update reported at 4.55pm that the court approved the arrest warrants against the couple. Economic crime police said Panadda’s arrest warrant covered three charges: public fraud, money laundering and offences under the Computer Crime Act.
Economic crime police also confirmed that Atip’s arrest warrant concerned a charge of jointly laundering money.
Officers from the Economic Crime Suppression Division and Crime Suppression Division subsequently deployed teams to locate and arrest Panadda and Atip.
Economic crime investigators allege that only 20% of the 900 million baht donated for the Ongkorn Thamdee Foundation had reached the foundation.
Police examining the financial trail reportedly traced more than 300 million baht into Panadda’s personal bank account and another 200 million baht into Atip’s account.
The investigation had already led police to seize or freeze assets belonging to Panadda and people close to her, including her husband, children and parents.
Family assets reportedly frozen in the Panadda investigation were valued at more than 100 million baht. They included three or four houses, several plots of land, 22 cars, six firearms and numerous designer goods.
Panadda’s lawyer, Ekkasit “Petch” Srisung, told reporters by telephone that his client had returned home and that he was with her.
According to Ekkasit, Panadda had been listening to a programme and was uncertain whether an arrest warrant had been issued or what was happening. She therefore decided to return home to collect herself.
“If the police want her or intend to arrest her, they can come to the house,” Panadda’s lawyer Ekkasit said.
Ekkasit described Panadda’s home as being in a housing estate in the Ram Inthra area, close to his law office.
Pol Lt Gen Nattasak Chaowanasai, commissioner of the Central Investigation Bureau, had earlier outlined efforts to build a case against people suspected of using money withdrawn from the foundation’s accounts for purposes other than those intended.
Nattasak emphasised that police were examining forensic evidence and the circumstances surrounding financial transfers. Investigators had consulted judicial officials and prosecutors to ensure that proceedings followed legal requirements.
Before the court’s decision, Nattasak had indicated that police expected to apply for arrest warrants by Friday.
Panadda’s letter requesting assistance would not influence consideration of bail, Nattasak stressed. Decisions would be based on the law and the circumstances of the case, with all parties treated equally.
Police are separately investigating a fraud complaint Panadda filed against Atip and a construction contractor known as "Ae”.
The Interior Ministry’s Department of Provincial Administration announced on November 5 that it had filed a separate police complaint over the Ongkorn Thamdee Foundation’s flood-relief fundraising.
The department reported finding Facebook appeals directing donors to a Kasikornbank account in the foundation’s name. Its examination of fundraising records found no application or permit issued to the foundation or its board.
According to the Department of Provincial Administration, public-benefit fundraising requires prior authorisation under the Fundraising Control Act of 1944. The department considered the appeal a potential breach of the first paragraph of Section 6, with penalties prescribed under Section 17.
Metropolitan Police Station for investigation into the foundation and any individuals involved. That complaint concerns fundraising authorisation, distinct from the investigation into the alleged misuse of donations.

content:
At least a dozen commercial flights made either unscheduled or high-alert landings in Austria, France, Italy, Belgium, Czechia, Spain, Serbia and Bulgaria, according to authorities in the various countries.
Planes made unscheduled landings in Evreux, France; in Vienna, Austria; and in Bulgaria. A flight from Finland landed in Rome as scheduled but with a military escort, and various others touched down at their scheduled destinations across the continent but amid security alerts.
The incident in France became public knowledge first, but the other similar reports soon followed.
No initial signs of a genuine threat, EU says still 'too early' to say if cases linked
This comes after a series of  bomb threats leveled against several European flights earlier this week , prompting similar unscheduled landings.
Tuesday's incidents turned out to be hoaxes, and preliminary information shows no sign of dangerous materials reported in Thursday's threats as yet.
The European Union Commissioner for Transport and Tourism, Apostolos Tzitzikostas, wrote online that any threats against civilians were unacceptable.
"It is too early to draw conclusions on whether the reported incidents are linked," Tzitzikostas said. "National investigations remain ongoing."
What happened in the subsequent alerts across Europe?
News of a series of diversions and bomb scares trickled out during the course of the day, particularly late in the morning:
Finland's Finnair carrier reported that two planes landed at their scheduled destinations but amid security scares.
One Finnair flight from Helsinki to Rome landed with a military escort. Another plane from the Finnish capital, operated by Jettime, also landed in Vienna as scheduled.
A Wizz Air flight from Milan to Warsaw made an unscheduled landing in Vienna.
Bulgaria reported three aircraft making emergency landings because of bomb threats.
Three Ryanair flights to Sofia — from Copenhagen, Madrid and London Stansted — also all landed under high alert.
Two of them touched down in Sofia as scheduled and one diverted to Plovdiv, the airport's CEO said.
Italian news outlets and the Reuters news agency reported, citing airport sources, that two planes — an Aegean Airlines flight from Thessaloniki and a Ryanair flight from Porto — landed at the Malpensa airport in Milan as scheduled after receiving bomb alerts on Thursday morning.
Police in Madrid said that three flights at the Spanish capital's airport were affected by what they called hoax threats, saying that security forces searched the area and ruled out any risk.
Police in the Czech Republic later said that they were preparing officials at Prague airport for four landings after threats of improvised explosive devices being on board.
"We assess the relevance of the threats as low," Czech police said. "Nevertheless, we do not underestimate the threat, which is why all necessary security measures have been activated with the least possible impact on passengers and airport operations."
On Thursday afternoon, Air Serbia issued a statement saying a flight from Belgrade to Bucharest landed safely at its destination after receiving a bomb threat.
What do we know about the first incident outside Paris?
An Airbus A320 plane has been diverted to the Evreux airbase to the west of Paris following a bomb threat.
The office of French Prime Minister Sebastien Lecornu announced the incident on Thursday, saying it was monitoring the situation "in real time."
The flight was headed from Dublin, Ireland, to the Italian capital of Rome.
Tracking websites showed the plane, part of the Aer Lingus fleet, sharply deviating its course as it was around Paris' airspace and heading towards the more isolated airfield in Evreux.
France's air force said that it dispatched planes "as soon as the incident was reported."
"The aircraft has been diverted and is being escorted to Evreux airfield," it said.
Lecornu's office subsequently confirmed that the plane, part of the Aer Lingus fleet, had landed safely at the airfield.
What happened during the earlier disruptions?
The prior threats to commercial flights this week turned out to be hoaxes that nevertheless caused diversions and major security mobilizations.
In one case, the Italian air force escorted a plane to its emergency landing.
The threats targeted airlines including Poland's LOT, Scandinavian Airlines, Wizz Air and Ryanair.
While it's not yet clear if there is a link, these disruptions to commercial aviation also coincided with a series of apparent cyberattacks targeting freezer units in major supermarkets and even French blood banks .
All the cases remain nascent, but have the potential hallmarks of so-called hybrid attacks designed to cause maximum disruption with minimal effort and resources.

summary: At least a dozen flights were either diverted or landed with a military escort after bomb or security threats. The first reported case involved a flight from Dublin to Rome landing outside Paris and more soon followed.

（德国之声中文网）美国总统特朗普领导的共和党在 中期选举 中遭遇重挫，这或许会增强中国在对美贸易谈判中的筹码。不过，北京不太可能为这位美国总统的失利而幸灾乐祸，因为他的继任者 对华态度 可能会更加强硬。
美国选民因生活成本上升而感到愤怒，特朗普对中国及其他国家发起的贸易战加剧了这一问题，他们在周二的投票中转而反对特朗普所在的共和党，使民主党获得了对国会的控制权。
一些政治分析人士指出，这次政治挫折可能会让特朗普在处理与北京之间脆弱的贸易休战协议时更加谨慎，从而使中国在定于本月晚些时候恢复的谈判中获得潜在优势。
一些中西方分析人士还表示，美国国内政治的分裂局面也为北京提供了空间，使其能够在未来可能出现对华更不友好的美国政府上台之前，加强自身实力并实现贸易伙伴多元化。
曾在中国外交部任职的前官员沈伟中在接受路透社采访时表示：“中国人非常现实，清楚新任总统可能会与特朗普截然不同。”
“但如果能再有两年的稳定期，这对中国来说就是件好事……我们拥有的时间越多，就越可能为最终在台湾问题上的摊牌或另一场贸易战中，做好更充分的准备。”沈伟中说道。他目前担任北京智库经士智库的副总裁。
不过，其他分析人士认为，对北京而言，未来两年未必会一帆风顺。
风险在于，特朗普在国内受到掣肘后，可能会更加积极地寻求外交政策上的胜利。与此同时，由民主党控制的国会可能会更强硬地推动他解冻 对台军售 ，而这触及北京的红线。
“特朗普可以采取更多非常规且前所未闻的外交政策行动，”经济学人智库高级中国分析师李子谦（Chim Lee）表示。
“美中政策的总体方向未必会改变，但我认为，人们担忧的是一些非常规的外交政策问题，这些问题可能会对中国产生意想不到的影响，”他说道。
其中最令人担忧的是伊朗战争升级为更广泛的地区冲突。这可能引发全球油价持续飙升，威胁中国的能源安全，并破坏北京在中东的关系。
更多阅读： 专访：民主党赢得中期选举如何影响美国的对华政策？
察觉到弱点
短期来看，外界关注的焦点转向即将举行的贸易谈判。特朗普将于本月晚些时候在深圳举行的亚太经合组织（APEC）峰会期间与中国国家主席习近平会晤，随后将于12月在迈阿密举行的二十国集团（G20）峰会上再次会晤。
谈判的关键在于一项贸易战休战协议——该协议将于明年1月到期。该协议避免了去年全球经济遭受重大冲击。
美国智库捍卫民主基金会高级研究员克雷格·辛格尔顿（Craig Singleton）表示，北京可能会认为特朗普的政治困境意味着他比中国更需要达成协议，从而鼓励中国谈判代表更强硬地要求削减关税以及美国做出其他让步。
然而，辛格尔顿补充说，这也可能导致“误判，进而动摇习近平正试图维护的稳定”。
特朗普曾多次抨击他眼中中国对美贸易的不公平行为，并在去年重返白宫后不久，对中国商品加征三位数关税，以解决他所称“正在扼杀”美国的贸易失衡问题。
然而，此后他的语气明显缓和，在北京和华盛顿举行的两次盛大峰会上对习近平表示欢迎，但这些峰会几乎没有取得任何实质性的经济成果。
特朗普与习近平的友好关系与他的民主党前任拜登形成鲜明对比。拜登曾多次就人权问题发表评论，并承诺如果北京攻击台湾，美国将予以保卫，这些言论都激怒了中国。分析人士认为，特朗普的一些潜在共和党继任者，例如国务卿卢比奥，对华立场也更为强硬。
上海复旦大学教授、中国外交部顾问吴心伯表示，中期选举后，特朗普可能更不愿意破坏他与中国建立起来的稳定关系。
微妙的中美经贸关系
To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video
除了贸易问题外，随着特朗普任期进入倒计时，他或许还会寻求北京的协助来取得其他外交政策胜利，例如促成俄乌冲突的结束，或是安排与朝鲜领导人金正恩的再次会晤。
分析人士指出，鉴于北京与俄罗斯及朝鲜之间保持着深厚的贸易往来，中国可以利用这一筹码，换取特朗普在某些问题上的让步。
然而，在与特朗普打交道多年后，北京如今面对的是一个更有意在人权问题上施压、审查中国投资，并推动向台湾交付140亿美元军售计划的国会。而特朗普此前曾表示，他正将这项军售作为与习近平谈判的“筹码”而暂时搁置。
中国声称对实行民主治理的台湾拥有主权，并一直要求美方停止对台军售。
“中方对此定会做出强烈反应，”曾任中国外交部官员沈伟中表示。他认为，这是中期选举后中方面临的“头号风险”。

El departamento neozelandés de Conservación indicó que las ballenas piloto ( Globicephala melas ) quedaron varadas en la costa de Ngawi, cerca del cabo Palliser, el punto más meridional de la Isla Norte.
"Cuatro de ellas aún están vivas y nos estamos preparando para intentar devolverlas al mar durante la marea alta", apuntó el organismo en Facebook, sin precisar el número de animales muertos.
En los trabajos participan voluntarios de la comunidad local maori y miembros de la organización ecologista Project Jonah, que ha movilizado uno de sus veterinarios para "evaluar el estado de salud" de los supervivientes.
Incidentes recurrentes
Muchos mamíferos marinos, entre ellos ballenas y delfines, suelen quedarse varados con frecuencia en las costas del sur de Australia y de Nueva Zelanda , sin que los expertos hayan logrado esclarecer los motivos.
Se cree que estos incidentes se producen por enfermedades, errores de navegación, cambios repentinos en las mareas, la persecución de depredadores o a condiciones meteorológicas extremas.
En octubre de 2022, casi 500 ballenas piloto fallecieron tras quedarse varadas en una playa en las remotas islas Chatham, a unos 840 kilómetros de la Isla Sur de Nueva Zelanda.

A second buyer has made a rescue bid for Poundland as the discount retailer teeters on the brink of collapse, with thousands of jobs at risk.
London-based Xyra Group has offered to pay off half of Poundland's outstanding debts - a key sticking point in takeover talks so far - immediately. The rest would be deferred.
With Poundland close to collapse, US-based owners Gordon Brothers have already rejected a rival bid from an Irish property group which would have saved its 12,000 staff.
Gordon Brothers said the business has faced years of instability and "remains challenged and vulnerable".
Sources familiar with the offer said Xyra is offering to immediately pay off £12.5m of an outstanding £30m loan on Poundland's books.
The offer came as Business Secretary Jonathan Reynolds held crunch talks with Gordon Brothers about the future of the business, urging the investment firm to protect staff however possible.
Gordon Brothers, which bought Poundland for £1 last June, committed at the meeting to prioritise offers which protect its shops and workers.
The company said: "We are pursuing all avenues through the sale process to find a solution which protects as many jobs as possible and preserves value. Work continues at pace, engaging in active discussions on offers with interested parties."
Xyra is offering to pay off a higher proportion of Poundland's outstanding debts than Martin Property Group, which previously submitted a bid that Gordon Brothers rejected.
But doubts remain about the credibility of Xyra's offer, as there is little evidence they meet Gordon Brothers' tests, including whether they have the money and whether they would be good long-term owners of Poundland.
Sources pointed to the appointment of Andrew Brode to Xyra's board as a sign of its credibility. Brode works for RWS - a company that provides AI solutions for businesses.
Judith MacKenzie, head of Downing Fund Managers, told the BBC Brode is "well known and very credible" among small businesses in the UK.
But she said there is "hardly any information" publicly available about Xyra. "So, although some of the people look good, I can't find any evidence to say that they've got the money to back it up yet," MacKenzie added.
Gordon Brothers said: "Our intent throughout the comprehensive sale process has been to protect as many jobs as possible and preserve value in order to deliver the best available outcome for all the people, creditors and local communities who care about this business as much as we do."
Both Reynolds and Prime Minister Andy Burnham have questioned why a deal for the future of Poundland has not yet been made.
Though Xyra made an offer to take over the whole business, it is unclear whether it would keep Poundland together as its owner or break the company up.
Several Poundland suppliers have said they would also go bust if the retailer collapses. Its founder Steve Smith said two or three thousand suppliers to the firm, those who solely work for Poundland, would be caught up in the collapse.
He added that not only would Poundland's 12,000 staff be affected in that case, but potentially up to 30,000 overall.
summary: A little-known investment group has made a bid to buy the business.

El flamante Balón de Oro 2026, Harry Kane , permanecerá en el FC Bayern hasta 2029. Tras meses de intensas negociaciones, el máximo goleador amplió este jueves (5.11.2026) su contrato —que expiraba al final de la temporada— por dos años más. Así, el club muniqués envía un mensaje contundente a sus poderosos rivales europeos.
"Como en casa en el FC Bayern"
"Me siento como en casa en el FC Bayern: adoro el club, a los aficionados y la ciudad de Múnich. Tenemos un equipo fantástico y un entrenador extraordinario, Vincent Kompany . Me llena de orgullo formar parte de este club. Toda mi familia es muy feliz aquí; quería quedarme, afronto el futuro con ilusión y deseo ganar muchos más títulos con este gran club", declaró el capitán de la selección inglesa.
Kane llegó al club más laureado de Alemania procedente del Tottenham Hotspur en el verano de 2023, por una cifra cercana a los 100 millones de euros, y es considerado ya uno de los mejores fichajes en la historia del Bayern Múnich.
Futbolista del 2026 en Alemania
En los 161 partidos oficiales que ha disputado hasta la fecha con el Bayern, este delantero excepcional ha marcado la increíble cifra de 156 goles (además de repartir 42 asistencias).
Además, Kane —quien no logró conquistar ningún título durante su etapa en los Spurs— ha ganado dos veces la Bundesliga, una la Copa de Alemania (DFB-Pokal) y dos veces la Supercopa.
En 2026 fue elegido Futbolista del Año en Alemania y, durante su estancia en Múnich, ha obtenido en dos ocasiones la Bota de Oro como máximo goleador de Europa.
Balón de Oro 2026, a la caza de la Champions League
El jugador, de 33 años, fue galardonado recientemente con el Balón de Oro . Y, ahora, el objetivo prioritario de Kane con el Bayern es conquistar la Champions League .
Recibir el Balón de Oro fue "una de las mejores sensaciones" que ha tenido "en su vida, en su carrera, sin lugar a dudas", declaró recientemente Kane. "Pero creo que vivir estos momentos con el equipo, tener la oportunidad de ganar la Liga de Campeones con el Bayern de Múnich y levantar el trofeo, sería una sensación sencillamente increíble".
"Lo que comenzó como un gran fichaje se ha convertido, con el tiempo, en un capítulo especial de la historia del FC Bayern. Harry Kane cumple con todas las expectativas que se pueden tener en el fútbol y se ha ganado un lugar en el corazón de los aficionados como una de las figuras más destacadas del deporte en nuestra época", subrayó el presidente Herbert Hainer.
rml (dpa, afp, sid)
summary: El capitán de la selección inglesa y ganador del Balón de Oro, Harry Kane, firmó un nuevo contrato con el Bayern de Múnich, según anunció el club alemán.

The Hong Kong activist Joshua Wong has been sentenced to 10 years in prison after earlier pleading guilty to “foreign collusion”, his second conviction under a national security law critics say has been used to silence political opposition in the city.
Wong, who rose to prominence as the teenage face of Hong Kong’s 2014 pro-democracy demonstrations, submitted his guilty plea in September. He had been accused of working with the exiled Hong Kong activist Nathan Law to urge foreign powers to impose sanctions, blockades or other hostile measures against China.
In his ruling on Thursday, the high court judge William Tam described Wong’s actions as “grave in nature”.
He said Wong had visited the US to seek foreign interference before the national security law’s introduction in 2020, and continued to share posts on social media by Law calling for sanctions after it was enacted.
Wong’s role was to “supply his underground support” and “arouse the attention of foreign countries to bolster the cause”, the judge said. He described Wong’s actions as part of a “scheme” to collude with foreign governments.
Tam said Wong’s sentence would run concurrently with the remaining term of his previous national security offence.
After the ruling, Law said in a statement: “It’s incredibly sad to see my friend Joshua Wong suffer another sentencing over his peaceful advocacy work for Hong Kong’s democracy. The signal the sentencing sent to the world is that [China] is determined to quash any hopes for freedom and democracy on its soil.”
Amnesty International’s deputy regional director, Sarah Brooks, said: “Today’s sentence is another grim reminder of how Hong Kong’s national security law has become a tool to punish dissent rather than to genuinely protect national security.”
Wong wore a dark blue shirt and thick rimmed spectacles in court, and nodded and bowed as supporters waved. Dozens of people had waited in line outside the court building for the hearing, amid a heavy police presence. A group of international diplomats was also present for the sentencing.
The former student leader is already serving a prison term of four years and eight months, imposed in November 2024, for conspiracy to commit subversion for his role in an unofficial primary election. He has spent nearly six years in detention and had been due to be released in January 2027.
The US consulate in Hong Kong said in a statement that it “strongly condemns” the additional sentence and called for Wong’s immediate release. “Wong has been unjustly imprisoned since December 2020, demonstrating that Beijing will go to extraordinary lengths to silence those who advocate for fundamental freedoms in Hong Kong,” a consular spokesperson said.
Shortly afterwards, China warned against “irresponsible” remarks on Hong Kong’s judicial affairs. “Relevant parties should earnestly respect China’s sovereignty, respect Hong Kong’s legal system, stop making irresponsible remarks regarding the trial of … judicial cases,” the foreign ministry spokesperson, Guo Jiakun, told reporters.
Wong, 30, gained international attention during the 2014 Umbrella protests, which paralysed the city’s financial centre and galvanised a generation of young people. In October 2014, he appeared on the cover of Time magazine under the headline: “The face of protest.”
When protests erupted in 2019 over a proposed extradition bill, Wong was serving a prison sentence for his role in the 2014 demonstrations. He was released at the height of the protests and immediately took to the streets.
The following year, Beijing introduced a sweeping national security law it said was needed to restore stability to the former British colony, but critics say has been used to target political opposition, dissolve civil society groups and silence independent media.
Wong is the only activist in Hong Kong prosecuted twice under the law.

content:
For the millions who cast their ballots in the US midterm elections , one issue ranked above all others: the economy.
So what does the Democrats' stunning capture of both the US Senate and House of Representatives mean for the economy and economic policy, given that President Donald Trump still has two years of his term to go?
Market reaction: Is it all about AI and data centers?
Markets have rebounded after initially trending negatively. Global stocks rallied as investors appeared to take heart from the Democrats' victory.
With Democrats now holding comfortable majorities in both houses of Congress and Trump still in the White House, it could lead to gridlock in Washington. Trump has already said he would become "Mr Veto," meaning he would block any legislation the Democrats advance.
"The magnitude of the gains for the Democrats in the midterms does not change too much for the near-term policy outlook, given the party still lacks a filibuster-proof majority in the Senate and President Trump has veto power to block legislation," Stephen Brown, chief North America economist with Capital Economics, said in a note.
"I think we are looking at two years of complete 100% gridlock," Jacob Funk Kirkegaard, nonresident senior fellow with the Peterson Institute for International Economics, told DW after the results came in. "Nothing will get done of any kind."
Some investors appear worried that the Democrats could force through AI regulation, especially if they also win the White House in 2028. Rising opposition among large majorities of the US population to data centers — the key infrastructure behind AI — helped secure victories for many Democratic candidates.
Kirkegaard, who is also a senior fellow at Bruegel, a European economics think tank, said the vote showed the extent of that opposition .  Even if the Democrats can't force regulation, he thinks local opposition will make it harder for data centers to be built, which could hit the valuation of big tech firms that have benefitted from the AI boom.
"This election shows that the political underpinning of the rapid, aggressive AI growth story is shaky," he said. "It doesn't mean it's going to stop or be made illegal, but the dynamic of the growth story has shifted."
If the Democrats were to win the presidency in 2028, Brown said, they would be perfectly placed to make major policy changes. "That includes the potential for tax hikes on corporations and high-income individuals as well as regulation that could delay the AI rollout," he said.
What about Trump's tariff policies?
According to polling conducted in early October by the  Pew Research Center , 56% of Americans say Trump's tariff policies will have mostly negative impacts on the country, with only 20% saying mostly positive.
That sentiment clearly drove many Democrats to victory in the midterms — particularly in states where tariffs have had a particularly negative impact. That includes those with sectors reliant on exports, such as Texas, Michigan, Iowa and Illinois, where counter-tariffs have hit and those that have high trade volumes with Canada.
Yet, barring an unprecedented climbdown from Trump — who has been ideologically wedded to tariffs since he first became a public figure almost 50 years ago — it's not clear how the Democrats could force substantial change to the president's signature economic policy.
"Trump will not be moderated," Deborah Elms, head of trade policy at the Hinrich Foundation in Singapore, told DW earlier this year. "Expect him to continue his trade disruption and tariff policies for as long as he remains in the Oval Office."
Though the US Constitution gives Congress the power to collect and organize tariffs, various laws passed over the years have given presidents power to implement tariffs when they cite certain conditions, such as national security or economic emergencies.
Trump has already used such avenues for his tariffs and can continue to do so, despite some legal rebukes. However, while Congress can't necessarily force an end to Trump's existing tariffs, it can now take further legal action against them to prevent greater escalation.
What about the war in Iran and surging oil prices?
Though Trump and the Democrats are clearly not going to make common cause, Kirkegaard said, the scale of the Republicans ' defeat might force Trump to be less erratic in his policymaking, from escalating his trade war with Canada to his Iran policy.
Trump said in the aftermath of Tuesday's defeats that he would "work with" the Democrats and told the Financial Times in the run-up to the vote that he was unlikely to escalate the war in Iran.
Were a deal to be struck with Iran , soaring energy prices — a pivotal election issue — could finally fall, helping voters with their cost-of-living concerns.
"You've got to get a deal with Iran, and you've got to bring down gas prices," Kirkegaard said. "From a political point of view, that's the most important thing now."
George Saravelos, an analyst with Deutsche Bank FX Research, thinks the markets are beginning to become more optimistic in that area. "With oil flows through the Middle East having materially recovered, the market is pricing a large imminent risk premium of re-escalation and energy supply disruption," he said in a note.
Could Democrats force Trump to table on the economy?
Despite the scale of the Democrats' victory, the fact that Trump remains in the Oval Office will complicate all efforts to force a change to signature economic policies and issues.
Yet Congress can now exert considerable pressure. Another issue vital to voters was corruption and the belief that the Trump administration has engaged in corruption and personal enrichment while in office.
That raises the prospect of the new Democratic-controlled Congress launching legal investigations and potentially pursuing another impeachment of Trump, which could force the president to negotiate on some economic issues to secure his political survival.
"Can you find 10 or 12 Republican senators who, in the face of overwhelming corruption, would be willing to vote for articles of impeachment? I wouldn't rule it out," Kirkegaard said. "And that's a scenario in which Trump might suddenly be much more accommodating to, for instance, abandoning most of his tariffs."
Despite voters' clear rejection of Trump's economic policies, the Democratic Party's newly minted senators, congressmen and congresswomen face an uphill battle in trying to reverse them.

content:
Business Secretary Jonathan Reynolds has met the US-based owners of Poundland as the government hopes to save the retailer from collapse.
The discount chain is on the brink of insolvency and Gordon Brothers, which bought it for £1 last June, has rejected a takeover bid which could have saved the 12,000 jobs currently at risk.
A meeting was due to be held on Thursday but was brought forward as the scramble to secure a rescue deal for the firm intensifies.
Gordon Brothers said it is "pursuing all avenues through the sales process" but that Poundland has faced several years of instability and "remains challenged and vulnerable".
The firm said it is "engaging in active discussions on offers with interested parties".
It added: "When Gordon Brothers acquired the business, it was in distress and required a radical restructure, urgent operational change and significant funding, which we provided to support the company's ability to trade."
Both Reynolds and Prime Minister Andy Burnham have questioned why a deal for the future of the business has not been made.
On Wednesday, a source close to business secretary said Reynolds "has been firm that Gordon Brothers must do everything in their power to protect jobs and provide certainty for workers".
"He is pleased to have secured this commitment from Gordon Brothers in the meeting and will continue to hold the company to account and closely monitor developments," the source added.
It is understood that Gordon Brothers made a commitment in the meeting to prioritise bids that will protect workers and units.
However, it is still unclear whether the US investment firm will keep the business together or break it up.
Meanwhile, MPs say they have called in Poundland's owners for questioning on Wednesday 11 November to explain their role in the discount retailer's looming insolvency.
Liam Byrne, chair of Parliament's business committee, said: "Every report suggests Poundland is a viable, profitable business with a future ahead of it and without good reason to let it crash and burn - and then to break it up and sell it off piece by piece.
"We are asking Gordon Brothers to appear before Parliament to explain themselves and tell us just what it is that's preventing them from accepting the fully-funded deal on the table to save more than 12,000 jobs."
Business Minister Kate Dearden and union representatives met Poundland's managing director Barry Williams on Wednesday.
Mr Williams told the BBC that Poundland is profitable and sales were growing.
"We're back in profit and it has a bright future ahead of it if it's allowed to deliver that," he said.
Poundland has filed a notice of intention to appoint administrators, which protects it from its creditors until next Thursday.
Adam Turner: We would lose "a few million" if Poundland went under
Asked what his message for Poundland's owner was, Burnham said Gordon Brothers should "focus on the people in your employment" and "come up with a practical solution that saves jobs and saves those stores".
"There is a solution to be found here, sit down with us and let's find it," he added.
The meeting comes after a major Poundland supplier has said it will lose millions of pounds if the retailer goes bust.
Adam Turner, sales director at Bradford-based Highcrest Retail Brands, said Poundland was one of its biggest customers and its collapse would cost it "a few million" in lost sales.
The family owned business mainly sells confectionery to Poundland and turns over about £50m.
Turner said the firm becoming insolvent would leave a substantial gap in its balance sheet next year.
Highcrest was a "longstanding business that can stomach this", Turner said. But he warned other medium and small suppliers to the retailer have told him that "if Poundland goes under, so do they".
This echoes a warning from Poundland founder Steve Smith on Monday that two or three thousand suppliers to the firm, which only work for Poundland, would be directly affected by its collapse.
Not only would Poundland's 12,000 staff be affected in that case, but potentially up to 30,000 overall, he told the BBC on Wednesday.
He said he was "amazed" Poundland was being put into administration, pointing to the profitability of the company.
"Also, there's two offers on the table from some really good people," he added.
"All I'm asking is for Gordon Brothers to see if they can put a deal together."
Gordon Brothers said Walsall-based Poundland is "still not cash generative at a sustainable level" because of the economic issues it faces.
If Poundland's stores are sold to new buyers, some of the employees may get new jobs on the same premises.
However, it is understood that buyers are only interested in about half the stores at present – meaning roughly 6,000 employees would not be re-employed.
High stock levels
If Poundland goes under, suppliers will be getting "pennies in the pound" back from the administration, he said, which is "very upsetting" – although he still hopes a deal can be done so Poundland can remain solvent.
Poundland owners Gordon Brothers will be a secured creditor, which means they are first in line to get their money back, and suppliers "who have done nothing wrong" will take the financial hit.
"It's sad. It's a nightmare for us all to be honest with you. It's not just the suppliers, it's the staff at Poundland, some of these guys have been there for many years.
"It's from the warehouse staff all the way to the shop staff to everybody within head office. It's a massive ripple effect through the supply chain," he added.
Turner said he had no knowledge of whether Gordon Brothers had deliberately timed the process of Poundland going into administration so it could take advantage of having high stock levels, which it can then sell.
One of the ways Gordon Brothers makes money is through stock liquidations – selling off stock from collapsed businesses.
One insider familiar with the situation told the BBC that the timing of Poundland facing collapse was "odd" – most retailers don't fall over in the run-up to Christmas.
Ministers' questions
Dearden has said the government doesn't want to interfere with "current ongoing commercial negotiations", but that ministers want "clarity" on the plans for the retailer.
"It's absolutely legitimate for this government to ask the business if they're doing everything they can to protect employees and suppliers up and down the country," she added.
Dearden told MPs that the government would be ready to help the company's employees if Poundland collapses.
The head of Gordon Brothers' European operations reportedly told the government that the firm stood by its stewardship and had given Poundland £85m in additional financing since its purchase in 2025.

content:
'Hopefully things get done': Americans react to historic political shift
Published
Two business owners, half a country apart, want the same thing for different reasons.
In Texas, Kim Hanks, who owns Tillies, a hotel, restaurant and spa business near Austin, says rising grocery and fuel costs are forcing her to raise wages for her 300 staff.
"It's been such a moving target for us on affordability," she told the BBC World Service.
In Indiana, Danny Reynolds, who runs Stephenson's of Elkhart, a clothing and bridalwear store, simply wants Washington to get its act together.
"My hope is that we can just find some consistency, some working together," he said.
Democrats say they heard both messages.
"We ran on affordability, we won on affordability, and now it's our job to govern on affordability," said House Democratic leader Hakeem Jeffries on MS Now's Morning Joe.
But here comes the difficult part. Democrats will hold Congress. Donald Trump still has the power to block their plans.
House Democrat leader Hakeem Jeffries said "now it's our job to govern on affordability"
A message that cut through
The scale of the win was bigger than most forecasters expected, with at least seven Republican-held Senate seats changing hands.
Behind the result was a striking mood: just 21% of Americans are satisfied with the direction of the country, even though the economy looks healthy on paper.
Voters weren't looking at the statistics. They were looking at their grocery bills, electricity bills and the price at the petrol pump.
In rural Texas, rising costs were even hurting Republicans in their own backyard. Sid Miller, the outgoing Republican agriculture commissioner, told me ranchers are getting $300 to $500 less for each head of cattle, while also facing record fertiliser costs.
"They felt betrayed," he said.
This was more than a blue wave. It was a vote about the cost of living. So what can Democrats actually do about it?
The outgoing Republican agriculture commissioner for Texas Sid Miller says ranchers 'feel betrayed'
The affordability plan
Under the banner "Fighting for an Affordable America," Democrats say healthcare is their first priority.
They want to bring back the extra financial help that made health insurance cheaper under the Affordable Care Act and reverse the cuts to Medicaid signed by President Trump in 2025.
Next come tariffs and energy. Democrats want to scrap the president's import taxes, which they say add thousands of dollars a year to the cost of groceries, fertiliser and building materials.
They also want to end the war in Iran, which they link to petrol prices averaging $4.18 a gallon, marking an increase of nearly 40%.
Housing is next. Some Democrats want to build four million new homes over the next decade.
On tax, they want to make billionaires pay more and increase tax credits for families with children.
It's a long list. But how much of it can they actually deliver?
What can they actually pass?
Investor Ken Fisher, founder of Fisher Investments, puts it bluntly:
"Congress can't get anything past a presidential veto. President Trump can't get anything he wants."
The result, he says, is likely to be two years of relative quiet on the legislative and regulatory front.
In other words, winning in Congress does not give Democrats a free hand. President Trump can still block legislation, and getting around a presidential veto requires a two-thirds majority in both the House and Senate.
Import taxes now account for more than 5% of federal revenue
For voters hoping for lower bills, that may be a disappointing result. They didn't vote for political deadlock.
Take tariffs. Trump is unlikely to abandon a trade policy that is central to his agenda. Democrats will need Republican support if they want to change it.
Bernard Yaros, deputy chief US economist at Oxford Economics, expects the average tariff rate on imports to stay around 10% for the rest of Trump's term.
And there's another complication.
Tariffs are bringing in more money for the government. Import taxes accounted for just over 1% of federal revenue in 2024. This year, they account for more than 5%.
That growing contribution to government income, Yaros argues, will make tariffs "tough for a future administration to fully dismantle."
Still, there are bargains to be struck.
Where the deals might be
President Trump told CNBC he could work with Democrats on "many more things than people understand".
Healthcare might be one of them.
Yaros sees the possibility of a big political trade-off: Democrats agree to extend Republican tax cuts in return for restoring health insurance subsidies. But he doesn't expect a deal until late 2027, with the economic benefits arriving in 2028. That's a long time to wait for anyone struggling with bills today.
Oregon Democrat Ron Wyden, who is set to chair the Finance Committee, says he will seek to "reassert congressional authority" over trade policy
Democrats could also turn up the pressure on businesses.
Henrietta Treyz of consultants Veda Partners says Democrats will question companies that passed on the cost of tariffs to customers.
After the Supreme Court ruling in February, she says, the question will be: "Did you turn around, take that tariff rebate, and then lower prices for consumers?"
Companies will also be asked: "What did you get in exchange?"
Democrats, she adds, will "pick and choose very carefully."
In the Senate, Ron Wyden, the Oregon Democrat set to chair the Finance Committee, has summed up his approach in six words: "affordability for us, accountability for them."
He says he will use the committee to "reassert congressional authority" over trade policy. Insurers, drugmakers and banks should expect to be called to explain themselves.
And some of the biggest changes may happen closer to home. State governors and regulators have a say in electricity prices, while local authorities decide where new homes can be built.
Democrats have won governorships in Texas, Ohio and Georgia, where the rising cost of electricity for data centres is already a concern.
The part they can't control
The hardest test may be something Democrats cannot fix with a new law.
The price of petrol, diesel and fertiliser will depend heavily on what happens in the war with Iran. And forecasters disagree about what comes next.
Oxford Economics warns that with the election over, further escalation "appears more likely," because petrol prices will no longer be as much of a political concern for the president.
And here's the awkward part. If prices come down, Democrats may struggle to claim the credit. If they go up, they may share the blame.
There is an immediate test, too. Government funding runs out after 11 December, and the chances of another shutdown look uncomfortably high.
Democrats won the argument. Now they have to show they can make life cheaper.
You can listen to an in-depth discussion about all these issues on a special edition of Business Daily's Power Players out soon.

（德国之声中文网） 香港 民主运动代表人物、前香港众志秘书长 黄之锋 ，週四（11月5日）被香港高等法院宣判，因违反香港《国家安全法》下的“串谋勾结外国势力”罪，判处10年监禁；目前因“47人案”正在服刑的黄之锋须服刑至2036年11月，出狱时或已40岁。
黄之锋上月在狱中度过30岁生日。自2020年11月起，他已因不同案件在狱中还押超过2100天。他去年6月被指控，与流亡海外的香港社运人士罗冠聪等人“串谋勾结外国势力危害国家安全”，在狱中被捕，并于 今年9月承认该项控罪 。但他表示，自己从未主张香港独立，也未曾寻求推翻中国政权。
“我也从未接受外国资金，或花钱聘请外国政治顾问。”黄之锋说。
港媒《法庭线》报道，黄之锋今日上午身穿蓝色深裇衫、咖啡色裤子、戴黑框眼镜，拿著书和一叠绿色簿子，走入法庭。该报记者表示，“法官宣判期间，黄之锋一度望向法庭的时钟，神情看似紧张，似是咬紧了牙。”《集志社》报道，黄之锋听闻判刑时表情平静，一直低头抄写。
主审法官谭耀豪指，被告黄之锋“罪行重大”。本案涉及的犯罪行为发生于2020年7月1日至11月23日之间，案发时香港正受社会动荡的严重影响，国家安全承受极高风险，被告与罗冠聪等人串谋，持续接触外国官员或机构，呼吁制裁中国及香港官员；在国安法实施后依然执行该计划，只是调整了两人的角色。法庭另外裁定，黄与罗为此案主谋。
“你的罪名是因为你叫黄之锋”
To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video
港警国安处“欢迎重判” 人权组织吁“立即释放”
警方国安处总警司李桂华在宣判后向媒体表示，欢迎法庭重判，并指黄之锋从未成年时已开始参与社运，成年后“犯案累累”，不愿守法、不将法庭放在眼内。李桂华称，黄之锋案件有严重影响，尤其当时正值香港动荡时期，希望他“好好反省”。
人权组织“人权观察”发布声明，呼吁港府应立即无条件释放黄之锋、外国政府应谴责不当拘禁民运人士的判刑，并对负责官员实施制裁。
该组织亚洲部主任艾莲・皮尔逊（Elaine Pearson）表示：“以毫无根据的罪名对黄之锋判处如此严厉的刑罚，既残酷又不公正。”
今年2月，香港传媒大亨黎智英因勾结外国势力及煽动罪，被判处20年监禁。皮尔逊表示：“北京对香港日益加剧的打压，至今并未付出任何实质代价。”
台湾方面，陆委会声明批评中共及港府持续利用“港版国安法”等威权工具，对香港民主人士罗织罪名，进行无止尽的政治追诉。陆委会呼吁，即刻释放无辜遭拘押人士，保障港人应有的基本人权与言论自由。

content:
The UK is “dangerously” dependent on China for critical raw materials needed for the military, renewable energy infrastructure and AI, a parliamentary investigation has found.
MPs on the business select committee called for an urgent centralised policy and the creation of a “critical minerals finance facility” to help fund rare earth and other critical mineral mines, and deploy grants, equity and debt to accelerate a diversification programme.
“Critical minerals are the alpha of the new economy,” said the committee’s chair, Liam Byrne. “We cannot rearm Britain, build AI or deliver net zero unless we secure the minerals these technologies depend on.
“Yet 16 years after China first weaponised its chokehold over rare earths, Britain remains dangerously exposed.”
It is the second time in a week that the government’s policy on China has been criticised by Byrne’s committee.
China has a stranglehold on the world’s supply of rare earths and other critical minerals, as well as their refined byproducts that are used in everything from military jets to car-locking systems and consumer products such as fridges and washing machines.
The committee heard that “the processing stage” was where the bottlenecks were, with China dominating the refining of seven categories of minerals, including refined lithium needed for electric vehicles and rare earths used in the fuselage and wings of military aircraft to help withstand temperature extremes.
MPs were told that demand for lithium alone would increase 45-fold between 2024 and 2030, leaving the UK in a high-risk dependency relationship with China.
The demand for rare earths needed for permanent magnets used in military jets and other applications would rise 16-fold in the same period as Britain was seeking to rebuild its military capabilities.
But with China capable of suddenly turning off rare earth supplies, as it did in 2025, a dependency on Beijing was a strategic vulnerability for the UK economy and national security, the committee found.
Separate restrictions on legacy chips after a row over a Dutch intervention in the China-owned Nexperia left the European car industry “days away” from stoppages last October.
The EU, the US and other countries faced the same risk of supplies of rare earths being cut off by China, and the committee said the UK was not putting enough effort into finding alternative supplies.
Donald Trump secured a one-year reprieve on global export restrictions on rare earths from Xi Jinping in October last year. This was extended to January 2027 after the Chinese president’s recent visit to Washington.
However, the reprieve means the UK is at the mercy of US-China relations, the report suggests.
after newsletter promotion
The most “realistic” solution was for the UK to work closely with G7 partners, the rest of Europe and Indo-Pacific countries, to “aggregate demand” and bring in new suppliers.
The committee said its investigation was frustrated by lack of transparency by the government.
“Parliament has no visibility of the capabilities the government is seeking to protect, the vulnerabilities it has identified, or the projects it is backing to reduce risk,” it said.
The committee has drawn up a 10-point plan that includes: working to identify domestic mining; refining and recycling opportunities and their costs; a strategy to encourage business to reduce procurement from China; a plan to unlock investment; and assess planning and permitting processes that may prove a barrier to mining.
As it stood, the committee said it could not be confident the government could satisfy any of its 10 tests.
“The UK requires new institutional and financial muscle,” it concluded.
A government spokesperson denied it did not have a critical minerals strategy saying it was delivering £400m “to ramp up domestic production and recycling” and forge new international partnerships. “Our strategy also sets clear goals for 2035, including meeting 10% of demand through domestic production and 20% through recycling, with no more than 60% of any critical minerals coming from any single country,” they added.
summary: Delivering net zero also at risk, say MPs as they call for centralised policy and funding for mines and diversification The UK is “dangerously” dependent on China for critical raw materials needed for the military, renewable energy infrastructure and AI, a parliamentary investigation has found. MPs on the business select committee called for an urgent centralised policy and the creation of a “critical minerals finance facility” to help fund rare earth and other critical mineral mines, and deploy grants, equity and debt to accelerate a diversification programme. The pound has risen to its highest overall level since the Brexit referendum over a decade ago.
Sterling has risen notably in recent weeks against the euro and the dollar, ahead of an expected rise in interest rates.
The most-watched measure of the value of the British currency against a basket of 18 of the world's main currencies this week reached its joint highest level since the June 2016 referendum, according to Bank of England figures.
The value reached 86.4 on an index where 100 equals the value in 2005. The Bank will officially confirm the calculation on Thursday.
The value of sterling fell significantly after the Brexit referendum in June 2016, and reached further lows during the Brexit process, the Covid pandemic and the 2022 mini-Budget.
Some traders said the UK was being seen in a different light given relative political stability, solid growth and the rapprochement with the European Union.
Sterling has responded strongly to Brexit developments and political uncertainty in recent years.
Jim O'Neill, an economist and former Treasury minister, said: "I'm not surprised. People were, and to a lesser extent, are, underestimating the improving momentum in the UK."
A stronger pound can help rein in inflation, and increase buying power for consumers on imports and on holidays.
UK growth so far this year has outperformed all forecasts, but there are signs that higher energy and fuel prices have now hit consumer confidence.
The Bank's nine-member Monetary Policy Committee faces an important decision on interest rates on Thursday, with the first rise in three years widely expected.
The pound was up 0.13% against the dollar at $1.3495 and 0.16% lower against the euro at €1.1979 as of 04:15 GMT on Thursday.
summary: Pound reaches highest level against a basket of currencies since the Brexit referendum a decade ago.
