Australia's oldest department store, David Jones, has gone into voluntary administration
Published
David Jones, Australia's oldest department store chain, has gone into voluntary administration, putting thousands of jobs at risk.
It comes after years of financial struggles for the 188-year-old retailer - known locally as DJs - as customers desert traditional shops for online shopping.
David Jones's physical and online stores will continue to operate while receivers FTI Consulting review the company, said voluntary administrators McGrathNicol.
"David Jones is an iconic company and so many Australians have stories and memories of visiting DJ's stores," said its CEO Erica Berthold, adding the brand has a "well-developed plan" to "reset the business for the future".
Berthold thanked "customers, our team members and our partners for their continued support of David Jones through this period".
David Jones employs about 6,000 staff and has 38 physical stores, with 17 of those in Westfield shopping centres.
Hours before the board voted to go into administration, Scentre - which owns Westfield - said the retailer had not paid its rent for October and was "therefore in breach" of its tenancy agreement.
"We understand the current retail trading environment, rising costs, a significant and outdated retail footprint, and supply chain challenges have led to this point," said Christopher Hill from receivers FTI Consulting.
By appointing administrators and receivers, David Jones will get "breathing space" and a chance to restructure the business, Hill said.
For many Australians, David Jones - and its trademark black-and-white houndstooth design - represented luxury.
But its collapse signalled the "death knell" for the department store format, said Jana Bowden, who teaches marketing at Macquarie University's Business School.
"It was once the epitome of glamour shopping in Australia - the Aussie version of Harrods," she said, "a place you would go to see and be a part of the glitz and glamour, where you could marvel at all the premium luxury labels, and feel like you'd made it."
Visiting the flagship city stores in Sydney and Melbourne was also a ritual for many Australian families, especially to see the festive Christmas window displays.
"People would travel from hours away from the city just to see those windows and experience the magic," Bowden said, but in recent years, the brand had lost its shine.
"The city stores have retained their upper end airs and graces, but the suburban stores leave a lot to be desired – they're mundane, they lack excitement and there's definitely no glitz," she said.
During Queen Elizabeth II's first visit to Sydney in 1954, the then-27-year-old monarch attended a banquet dinner on the seventh floor of the Elizabeth St store, according to the Sydney Morning Herald.
summary: The brand's 38 physical stores and online site will continue to operate while receivers review its operations.

content:
Fishermen return to sea under a crimson sky in August after China's Jiangsu province is hit by Super Typhoon Dolphin
Published
Wild weather is a way of life for people living along the coast in the Philippines, Taiwan, China and Japan. But the last few months have been extraordinary.
A wave of intense and, at times, unpredictable storms exacerbated by the El Niño weather pattern has killed dozens, shuttered major airports and wiped out crops and infrastructure across a swathe of East Asia.
In October, nearly all of Taiwan shut down as a monster storm big enough to engulf the island of 23 million roared towards its north-eastern coast. Equivalent to a category five hurricane, Typhoon Champi's 295km/h (193mph) winds had the power to flatten homes and whip up destructive waves.
Thankfully it did not make landfall in Taiwan, skirting past the island while dousing it in rain. But it had far-reaching impacts: hundreds of flights were cancelled in Hong Kong, Taiwan and Japan. In the Philippines' Batanes archipelago, seaside highways shut as huge waves crashed onto the shore, and in southern Japan's Okinawa islands, power was cut to 15,000 homes.
El Niño is a naturally occurring climate phenomenon in which warm waters pooling in the eastern Pacific and altered wind patterns drive extreme weather events around the world.
It happens around every two to seven years, lasting for around a year. This year's El Niño, which the UK Met Office has forecast to be the "strongest in living memory", is likely to last until February or March.
In June, Japan watched two storms - Typhoon Mekkhala and Severe Tropical Storm Higos - race towards its eastern coast simultaneously, forcing one million people to evacuate. In July, Tropical Storm Narra grazed China's southern coast along Guangxi, submerging villages and displacing tens of thousands.
This riverside park in the south-eastern Chinese city of Nanning was submerged by Tropical Storm Narra
August brought Super Typhoon Dolphin, which churned across the Pacific for 16 days - before slamming into eastern China, triggering heavy floods and dozens of casualties.
Later that month Typhoon Saudel made landfall in three south-eastern Chinese cities over one week, shutting transport networks and forcing thousands to evacuate.
'Burning with fever'
The Pacific Ocean, heated to record levels by El Niño, is now brimming with typhoon energy, according to the Accumulated Cyclone Energy (ACE) metric which measures the total intensity of a season's storms. This year, the ACE reading for South East and East Asia is forecast to be nearly double the 30-year average.
El Niño also affects wind patterns and in this case, that means typhoons are tending to form further east than usual. They are also becoming stronger as they remain over warm waters for longer.
The Pacific can be likened to someone "burning with fever", says Ana Liza Solis, head of climatology at the Philippines' national weather bureau. "It can go into convulsions soon," she said at a press briefing in Manila in September.
Forecasts suggest the worst may not be over. Last month, sea surface temperatures in the equatorial Pacific - the area monitored by the Japan Meteorological Agency for its El Niño predictions - soared to 4C above normal, the highest since records began in 1949. The previous record - 3.6C - was set in December 1997.
China's climate agency has warned of sea surface temperatures continuing to rise over the next three months because of the El Niño.
Despite typhoon season usually peaking around September to October, this is likely to raise concerns across a region that has already been battered by back-to-back storms.
China has seen back-to-back typhoons as the 2026 El Niño intensifies
'Very, very scary' simulations
In August, Typhoon Chan-Hom baffled storm watchers in Japan by crossing the country from east to west, as opposed to the usual south-to-north trajectory. Japan's well-resourced and prepared authorities were able to evacuate people swiftly, but this would be far more challenging in some neighbouring countries.
To get a better picture of how rising temperatures could amplify the risks, Manila-based climatologist Rafaela Jane Delfino and colleagues simulated the effects of warmer conditions on the Philippines' most recent monster storms, including 2013's Super Typhoon Haiyan (Yolanda) which killed more than 6,000 people.
They arrived at what she describes as "very, very scary findings": higher temperatures increased total accumulated rainfall by 26%. It's a devastating prospect in a country where flooding from monsoon rains and some 20 tropical storms per year has emerged as one of the main disaster risks.
In recent years, floods have paralysed entire cities for days, and tired of the annual ordeal, Filipinos have taken to the streets to protest against corruption which they say is gnawing away at millions of dollars from flood-control projects.
Delfino, in an article on the University of the Philippines website, insists leaders and officials must gain a better understanding of climate hazards if communities are to be better prepared.
Tide of rubbish blankets Philippines river in August after weeks of monsoon rains
Preparing for the onslaught
Countries are bracing for the immediate impact. Japan has urged citizens to stockpile food and essentials for the typhoon season, and to secure outdoor furniture that could become deadly projectiles when typhoon winds hit. China has asked local officials to identify vulnerable areas and is upgrading its warning and monitoring systems.
The Philippines and its South East Asian neighbours are preparing for disruptions to food production, especially rice, and have increased support for famers, including the provision of fertilisers.
But what happens in the long term is less clear. The window for governments to act on El Niño is "closing", the United Nations Development Programme in Asia and the Pacific said recently.
"How severely a community experiences an El Niño is decided years in advance, by where roads and settlements are built, how water is managed, who is covered by social protection and whether public budgets have room to absorb a shock.
"Every El Niño tests the resilience we have built; this one should also drive us to build more," it added.

content:
Watch: Key moments from the US midterm election results
Published
Elon Musk spent almost $450m (£334m) – more than anyone ever has in an election cycle – to back Republican political candidates in the US midterm races. It was not enough to keep Democrats from a resounding victory.
Among the most striking wins went to Democrat James Talarico, who beat Republican Ken Paxton for a US Senate seat in Texas. Musk spent at least $45m in support of Paxton, according to a BBC analysis of campaign finance data.
Other races where Musk spent millions included Arizona, Michigan, Wisconsin and Minnesota. His spending continued into Monday, records show.
By Tuesday night, Musk seemed to admit defeat, joking on X that his "election-interfering space lasers didn't work."
LIVE UPDATES: All the latest developments
BOWEN: Trump's loss limits powers at home, but it will likely be different abroad
RESULTS: How America voted in maps and charts
EXPLAINER: Five reasons why Trump did so badly
ZURCHER: Midterm carnage weakens Trump but he still wields power for now
REACTION: Angry Republicans blame Trump for midterms 'disaster'
NEWSLETTER: Sign up for Anthony Zurcher's analysis in your inbox
The loss this week of so many Republican seats may have significant implications for Musk and his businesses.
SpaceX has gained an estimated, external $10bn in new government contracts since Trump was elected to his second non-consecutive term. Several Democratic lawmakers have said the company's extensive and growing role in government and national security should be investigated, external.
SpaceX's future development of massive data centres is also facing new potential difficulties - as are the data centre developments of other tech companies.
In Georgia for instance, where SpaceX has data centre operations, the just elected Democratic governor ran in-part on limiting the rapid rise of the massive buildings, as well as the huge tax breaks tech companies usually get to build them.
A number of other politicians ran on limiting data centres and dozens of state measures to limit their development passed on Tuesday, external.
Data centres are sprawling buildings that house stacks of computing hardware. Tech and artificial intelligence (AI) companies use them to run online platforms such as ChatGPT, Claude, and Musk's X and his AI company xAI.
Musk posted to X on Tuesday that his previously floated idea to somehow build data centres in space was "looking pretty appealing right now."
Tech companies involved in AI may be in for a tougher government scrutiny and potential regulation with Democrats in power, though any legislation would need Trump's approval.
James Flintoft, head of investment solutions at AJ Bell, pointed to Musk's unsuccessful spending on Republican candidates and the scale of wins by Democrats as bringing in a "period of uncertainty for investors as they assess whether tech companies are set to face greater regulation."
Senator Ed Markey on Wednesday responded on X to a person asking if major tech industry executives would be the target of investigations, saying: "They are going to need to plant new forests for all of the subpoenas we'll be printing."
Tech stocks were broadly up on Wednesday morning. Yet, Musk's Tesla and SpaceX were down by 4.9% and 3.4% respectively.
By Wednesday, Musk had stopped posting to X about politics and was instead posting in praise of GrokBot, an AI chatbot produced by xAI. It was a stark contrast to the 2025 election, when Musk would post to X sometimes hundreds of times in a day about politics.
He also unpinned a post that had been saved to the top of his X profile since last week that explained his "concern" with Democratic politicians winning more midterm races.
Those concerns included the idea that the US could welcome more immigrants, make Washington DC and Puerto Rico individual states, and expand the number of justices on the Supreme Court.
Another post telling his 241 million X followers to "Vote red today!" appeared on Wednesday to have been deleted from Musk's profile.
The BBC has contacted SpaceX for comment about Musk's spending and posts.
While Musk spent millions of dollars backing Republican candidates in multiple US states, a lot of his political focus seemed to be on Texas.
In recent years, Musk made the state the corporate headquarters of Tesla and SpaceX, both of which still have large operations in California where they were founded.
"There is something deeply wrong with Talarico", Musk posted to X in October.
Talarico posted in response: "There is something deeply wrong with a political system that allows one trillionaire to buy his own personal US Senator."
Not all billionaires in the US shared Musk's preference for Republicans.
Reid Hoffman, a tech billionaire and the founder of LinkedIn who is a major donor to Democrats, hailed the results of Tuesday's elections as an event that "blew the doors off our expectations."
"These elections were an overwhelming wave against Trump and his cronies," Hoffman wrote on X and on LinkedIn. "While people like Elon are spending outrageous amounts to keep authoritarian clowns in power, those of us who believe in the ideals of America cannot yield."

summary: Musk spent nearly $500m in the 2026 US midterm elections, an individual election spending record.

content:
Millions of dollars of food grown in illegal Israeli settlements in the occupied West Bank has been shipped to Australia labelled as “produce of Israel”, a new analysis of trade data has shown.
The human rights legal organisation Global Echo has analysed commercial documents and official trade data from the Israeli government and the Australian Bureau of Statistics, showing at least US$5m (A$7.2m) of organic dates grown in illegal settlements across the West Bank have been shipped to Australia over the past eight years.
Global Echo analysed 132 agricultural shipments from Israel to Australia between August 2018 and August 2026. Of those, 85 – or 64% – contained settlement products.
The proportion of settlement goods is higher in more recent years. Between January 2025 and August 2026, 20 of 24 shipments of dates to Australia analysed by Global Echo were sourced from settlements.
Israel’s settlements in the West Bank are illegal under international law.
The settlements where dates bound for Australia are grown – including Netiv Hagdud, Beit Haarava, Arvot Jericho, Hamra, Tomer, Mechora, and Naaran – are occupied parts of the West Bank, recognised as part of the state of Palestine by Australia.
Israeli law obliges exports to label the origin of products from settlements as being from Israel, unless they are being exported to a country with laws that prohibit such labelling.
There is no law in Australia banning the import of goods from settlement areas, and no requirement that those goods be labelled as originating from occupied land.
The executive director of Global Echo, Emily Schaeffer Omer-Man, said Australian consumers would likely find it “startling” that settlement goods were on the Australian market, and that they formed the majority of agricultural products labelled as being imported from Israel in the shipments that were analysed.
“This means that Australian consumers of Israeli dates and other Israeli agricultural products are quite likely contributing to the ongoing occupation and settlement of Palestinian land.”
The foreign minister, Penny Wong, told the Senate in September that Israel’s settlements in Palestine’s West Bank were illegal, and said the Australian government called on Israel “to stop settlers from destroying properties, displacing families and beating, torturing, sexually assaulting and killing Palestinians”.
But she said Australia was not pursuing a blanket import ban on settlement goods, as other countries such as the UK, Spain, Belgium, Ireland and the Netherlands have either announced or imposed.
“We have concerns about the implementation of a blanket ban and unintended consequences for Australian businesses,” Wong said.
In June Global Echo released a report, Importing Occupation, which detailed the practice of Israeli exporters to Europe hiding the origin of produce grown in occupied Palestine to qualify for tax breaks and bolster the settler economy.
Schaeffer Omer-Man said the mislabelling of produce was neither aberration nor accident.
“Agriculture has been used since the start of the settlement enterprise as a means of large-scale land grab and creeping annexation. This is not a secret; it has been declared openly by Israeli government officials and politicians over decades.”
Schaeffer Omer-Man said import bans on settlement goods in Europe – Israel’s largest market – would lead exporters looking to other markets, potentially including Australia.
“One of the other markets where settlement goods currently fly under the radar is Australia. So it’s going to places like Australia, like Russia, like the US, places that are not demanding that settlement goods are treated any differently.”
after newsletter promotion
Sarah Sanbar, a researcher at Human Rights Watch, said international trade was “one of the lifelines” of illegal settlements.
“These settlements are not simply residential communities – they are illegal, and they are inextricably linked to human rights abuses.”
The settlements fragmented and undermined the Palestinian economy, Sanbar said. Israeli authorities restrict Palestinian access to land and natural resources, in particular water, restrict movement and access to land, and limit Palestinian development.
“A Palestinian farmer who can no longer access his agricultural land because of settlement expansion may lose his livelihood, only to see a settlement-based agricultural business then profit off that very same land,” Sanbar said.
“The result is an economic environment that is increasingly unequal by design, and a hallmark of apartheid.”
Wong was contacted for comment.
A spokesperson for the Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade said: “Australia is pursuing further targeted measures, in coordination with international partners, to deter illegal settlements and settler violence.”
The Israeli embassy in Canberra did not respond to a request for comment.
In announcing the UK’s trade ban on settlement goods in September, its foreign secretary, Ed Miliband, said “settler terrorists” were committing ethnic cleansing in the West Bank.
Israel’s ambassador to Australia, Hillel Newman, told The Australian newspaper at the time that the issue of settlements had been “blown out of proportion” and that Australia should not follow the UK’s example.
“It would be a deep mistake to take steps in such a direction,” Newman said.
summary: Analysis by human rights organisation Global Echo shows 85 of 132 shipments over eight years contained more than US$5m of organic dates grown in settlements Get our breaking news email , free app or daily news podcast Millions of dollars of food grown in illegal Israeli settlements in the occupied West Bank has been shipped to Australia labelled as “produce of Israel”, a new analysis of trade data has shown. The human rights legal organisation Global Echo has analysed commercial documents and official trade data from the Israeli government and the Australian Bureau of Statistics, showing at least US$5m (A$7.2m) of organic dates grown in illegal settlements across the West Bank have been shipped to Australia over the past eight years. content:
Kellogg's has told the BBC the "snap, crackle and pop" sound made by its Rice Krispies may be noticeably quieter after an uproar over the cereal giant's recipe change.
Rice Krispies and Coco Pops are no longer being made with whole rice grains, with the tiny toasted puffs being made using corn flour and rice flour instead.
A Kellogg's spokesperson said retaining the iconic sound had been a "huge focus" when designing the new recipe, but that customers "might notice that the sound may be quieter and not as instant as before".
The firm was responding to complaints online that the taste of the breakfast staples had changed, with some fans adding they missed the "pop" sound.
Kellogg's said it had adapted the recipes due to "changing weather conditions" that have disrupted supplies of some grains and cereals.
The cereal giant said the new versions had been "carefully assessed for taste, appearance and texture", but some shoppers said their children would no longer eat them.
Some expressed dismay that the taste and texture were "totally different" and dubbed the change "grim" and "disgusting".
"There's no snap, crackle and pop in these," a parent named Dani wrote on TikTok. "My toddler won't eat them."
Lauren, also posting on TikTok, added that she had been eating Rice Krispies every day for breakfast "for years and years".
"I had a bowl of the new recipe and you can immediately tell the difference," she said. "They don't have the snapping sound when you put in the milk."
Jessicake meanwhile said they tasted "weird and stale".
The "Snap, Crackle and Pop" - made when milk is added to the puffed rice - has been a centrepiece of the brand's marketing since the 1950s.
Kellogg's insisted the snap, crackle and pop is "still there, but consumers might notice that the sound may be quieter and not as instant as before".
Recipe changes are notoriously difficult for big brands. Chocolate makers are constantly accused of reducing cocoa content in their products and debates rage online over whether ketchup ingredients have changed.
When Scottish fizzy drink Irn Bru cut its sugar content in 2018, fans famously stockpiled crates of the old version.
No changes are being made to Rice Krispies products in the US and Canada, which are owned by a separate company.
Kellogg's said the recipe change in the UK would help "maintain consistent quality" as extreme weather takes a toll on crops and pushes up ingredient prices.
Extreme weather in Spain in 2022 and 2023 in particular had reduced availability of the types of rice the company uses for its breakfast cereals, the company said.
Rice Krispies, launched nearly a century ago, are sold around the world and come in variations such as vanilla and strawberry flavours in some markets alongside the widespread chocolate-flavoured Coco Pops version.
"We appreciate that even small changes to a much-loved product can feel noticeable and that's why we have approached this with a lot of care and consideration," Kellogg's said.
The firm said it appreciated the customer feedback and would "continue to look at ways to make [its] products even better in the future".
The cereals have already undergone some change, with reductions in salt content in the 1990s and lowered sugar in 2018. The company said Rice Krispies and Coco Pops will continue to meet UK food standards on levels of fat, salt and sugar in food.
A backlash against processed foods in recent years, especially those low in fibre and high in sugar, has put breakfast cereals generally under the spotlight from healthy eating advocates.
Kellogg's stressed the cereals contain no artificial colours, flavours or sweeteners and the nutritional benefits in each bowl, such as fibre, Vitamin D and iron are staying the same.
However, the new recipes mean packaging will now include a "contains wheat gluten" warning. It also continues to contain barley-malt extract.
Kellogg's said it has not changed the recipe for any of its other cereals.
Many parts of the world have been affected by droughts, floods and heatwaves this year due to the El Niño weather phenomenon. The weather event is expected to severely affect crop production from South East Asia in particular. The region produces more than a quarter of the world's rice.
The World Meteorological Agency expects the record-breaking El Niño will last until at least 2027.
That will intensify pressure on food manufacturing companies, already looking at ways to source reliable and affordable ingredients.
The original Kellogg company separated into two distinct firms in 2023.
The largest is Kellanova, which focuses on snacks, cereals, noodles and other food products like Eggo, Pringles and Pop-Tarts sold globally. It is now owned by Mars, which makes confectionery and pet food.
The other business, WK Kellogg's, operates in North America and has since been taken over by Italian chocolate giant Ferrero.

content:
On November 4, 1956, tens of thousands of Soviet soldiers and tanks swept into Hungary , brutally suppressing the country's anti-Communist uprising. Decades of dictatorship followed, relying on Hungary's brutal secret police to keep the system in place.
Events on Nov. 4 this year represent something of a reckoning with this dark chapter of Hungarian history.
Prime Minister Peter Magyar's government is ordering the full release of the country's secret police "agent files," which contain the names of Hungarian state security informants, some of whom cooperated out of their own volition even as others passed on information unwittingly.
Magyar and his Tisza party had previously promised to make the "agent files" public if elected. Their release is an historic event, as it comes after over three decades of heated debate over how to handle such sensitive files. The decision to publish is also sure to spark further debate on Communist-era guilt and responsibility.
Release opposed for years
Hungarians have been calling for the release of the files for years. After the fall of the Berlin Wall in 1989 and the end of Soviet rule, civil rights activists and smaller Hungarian political parties said the files should be released. Demands for their publication were expressed repeatedly over following decades.
Yet Hungary's first post-Communist prime minister Jozsef Antall, a conservative, rejected the idea as did Viktor Orban 's long-ruling Fidesz party. The latter blocked efforts to open the files, voting more than 30 times against such plans since 2010, according to Hungarian news platform Telex.
A partial release of state security files did occur in the 1990s, when the Hungarian parliament passed the so-called "agents law" in 1994. This required members of the government, members of parliament and certain public servants to undergo background checks to determine whether they had ever worked for the former state security services.
From 1997, Hungarian citizens have been able to view their own files and in 2003, permissions were expanded. But they have never been able to find out the names of informants.
The law relevant to the files contained provisions that were open to broad interpretation, which allowed government agencies such as the Ministry of Interior to prevent the transfer of files from the secret police to the Historical Archives of the Hungarian State Security, or ABTL, if they believed it would compromise  national security.
Such a selective release of files not only prevented Hungarian society from learning the truth about its state security service, it also made it possible for files to be exploited in political power struggles, for example, by leaking compromising information about politicians to the public.
One such case involved former Hungarian Prime Minister Peter Medgyessy, who was exposed by the Fidesz-affiliated daily Magyar Nemzet  in 2002 for having worked as a Communist-era secret agent.
Political fallout expected
Magyar's government is putting an end to this. From Nov. 4, databases containing all the names of, and key information about, informants will be made available online.
Additional databases will be released as well. They include one of the most extensive databases on individuals recruited to work for the Hungarian state security agency. Confidentiality provisions set out in the old "agent law" have also been scaled back, meaning significantly more files will likely be accessible in the future.
The upcoming release of data on up to 60,000 out of an estimated 150,000 secret police informants could have major political consequences. Even so, ABTL director Bendeguz Gergo Cseh recently cautioned that, "you can't believe everything the state security agencies and their files claim." Many documents were incomplete and not fully reliable and many files had been destroyed, he said.
Others are also skeptical about the release. Historian Janos M. Rainer, an expert on Hungary's dictatorship, told Telex that the publication would have made sense right after the fall of the regime. Releasing the files after all these years is more of a symbolic gesture, he argued.
Meanwhile historian Krisztian Ungvary, who has researched the state security files extensively, welcomes the upcoming publication. It will allow historians to pursue new research and society to engage in fresh debates, Ungvary told DW. He believes Hungary will benefit from such reflection, as "societal lies inevitably lead to a strained relationship with politics and the price we paid for that was 16 years of Fidesz rule."
Political reckoning
For Magyar, making this information public carries great significance. The idea of coming to terms with the past, especially the years of the Orban regime, is one of his favorite topics.
When the Hungarian parliament amended the law about the files in mid-September, Magyar wrote on Facebook that, "after a 36-year delay, the Hungarian parliament today decided, at the initiative of Tisza, to make the 'agent files' public. Fidesz did not support the motion. I wonder why?"
It was an allusion to the fact that many prominent figures in Fidesz' ranks and in Orban's inner circle were members of the Hungarian Communist party or secret police.
The most well-known of the latter is likely Jozsef Horvath, a former full-time employee of the department of Hungarian state security that was responsible for suppressing the domestic opposition.
Under Orban, Horvath worked as an intelligence officer and security advisor, and in 2024, he became the research director of Orban's Sovereignty Protection Office. This was an agency that exposed supposed enemies of the Orban regime, branding them " foreign agents ."
This article was originally published in German.

content:
On the eve of a midterm election that ended in an unequivocal rejection of his brand of politics, even Donald Trump seemed to recognize that the US-Israel relationship had become a political liability.
Trump’s 11th-hour suggestion, on election morning, that he would cut military aid to Israel at the end of the year because, as he put it, “they don’t need it”, was condemned across the board – with pro-Palestinian advocates dismissing it as “desperate” and pro-Israel ones as “unserious”.
Trump’s suggestion that he would replace nearly $4bn in annual military aid with arms sales signaled little would change in practice – the funding would continue and it would be harder to track. But it was still a notable recognition by the president of just how much support for Israel has tanked against the backdrop of the latest war in Gaza, which has killed more than 70,000 Palestinians, been widely described as a genocide, and reshaped US politics in ways unthinkable just three years ago.
Indeed, come January, the US House will include an army doctor who went on a medical mission in Gaza, a lawyer who was fired by her firm over a blogpost criticizing Israel’s war, a Jewish lawmaker who was recently detained by Israeli forces while helping Palestinians harvest olives in the occupied West Bank, and a community organizer who participated in a pro-Palestine student encampment and scored one of the primary season’s most stunning upsets under the banner “babies, not bombs”.
Pro-Palestinian candidates – including Palestinian-American ones – have won downballot races. And in Michigan, Abdul El-Sayed became the first Muslim to be elected to the US Senate, following a campaign that saw more than $40m spent by Aipac in an effort to defeat him, last-minute drama, and unprecedented levels of Islamophobic rhetoric and bigotry.
“The old bipartisan consensus on Israel is over,” Beth Miller, political director of Jewish Voice for Peace Action, said. Without that consensus in place, the next Congress could push a number of measures, from an arms embargo on Israel to sanctions against violent settlers and officials – though Trump would retain veto power to block them.
The vote was also a rejection of Trump’s war in Iran – something even JD Vance said on Wednesday was “obvious to almost everyone”. Foreign policy issues rarely determine US elections – that is, until those issues have a direct effect on Americans’ lives at home.
“Americans were reminded of the failures of the Iran war with every visit to the gas station and grocery store,” said Yousef Munayyer, head of the Palestine/Israel Program at the Arab Center Washington DC. “Israel is a central piece of that story.”
Across the country, and up and down the ballot, unabashedly pro-Palestinian candidates defeated pro-Israel ones despite groups like Aipac pouring tens of millions of dollars into a failed attempt to reverse Israel’s collapsing standing among US voters. Last month, Aipac acknowledged its open support was hurting pro-Israel candidates more than it helped them, and announced it would stop making direct endorsements and contributions – a remarkable admission even if one with little practical consequence.
The victories of El-Sayed and several other candidates whom the right sought to cast as antisemitic over their support for Palestinians also marked a significant rejection of the narrative that pro-Israel voices and the Trump administration have relentlessly advanced over the last three years – that criticism of Israel is, by default, antisemitic.
“They try to call you hateful if you believe that Palestinian kids should get to grow up in the land of their forefathers without being murdered by our tax dollars,” El-Sayed, who has continued to speak plainly about his support for Palestinians despite coming under enormous pressure over it, said during his acceptance speech. “If you believe in equal rights to peace, dignity, and self determination, that’s not hate, it’s love.”
In Michigan, El-Sayed won a majority of Jewish voters, according to exit polls. Despite warnings that Jews would leave the Democratic party en masse over its shifts on Israel, J Street said its polling found that 72% of Jews voted for Democrats on Tuesday, even though the Republican party increased its share of the Jewish vote since 2024.
This does not mean that the Democratic party is unified on Israel and Palestine and or in opposition to foreign wars.
For decades, the party has “excluded or marginalized anyone whose progressive values extend to support for Palestine”, Lara Friedman, the president of the Foundation for Middle East Peace, said. “American voters, organizers, and a cohort of enormously talented candidates came together and kicked the door down.”
Matt Duss, executive vice-president of the Center for International Policy and a former foreign policy aide to Senator Bernie Sanders, said that the Democrats now must seize the opportunity to become the party opposed to war.
“Trump ran and won as an anti-war candidate in 2024, because unfortunately Democrats left that lane wide open for him,” he said. “The question is: will Democrats finally get it? Will they finally realize that Americans are tired of war and want a new foreign policy?”

A British healthcare worker with Ebola is being evacuated from the Democratic Republic of the Congo to the UK for medical treatment, it has been confirmed.
“A British citizen currently in the DR Congo has tested positive for Ebola,” a spokesperson for the UK government said in a statement on Wednesday. “The UK has well-established procedures for dealing with cases like this, and those processes have been activated … The risk to the UK public from Ebola remains low.”
The patient, whose identity is unknown, is in a stable condition and is expected to arrive in the UK on Wednesday or Thursday before being transferred in a specialist ambulance to a “high consequence” infectious disease unit, according to an official document seen by Reuters.
A humanitarian organisation sent the worker to DR Congo to help in the response to the outbreak, which is the second largest on record. It is the first case involving a British national contracting Ebola in the current outbreak.
The Royal Free hospital in London has a high-level isolation unit for infectious diseases such as Ebola; other centres are in Newcastle and Liverpool.
Ebola is a highly contagious, severe and often fatal illness. It is spread through direct contact with body fluids such as the blood or vomit of infected people, or dead bodies.
The current outbreak, declared on 15 May by DR Congo’s health ministry, has surpassed 10,000 cases, and 5,000 deaths. It is the 17th in DR Congo since Ebola was identified, was caused by the Bundibugyo virus, and has become the largest and deadliest in the country’s history. The Bundibugyo virus has no approved treatment, though vaccine trials are under way.
Since the outbreak started, it has spread to Kenya and Uganda in east Africa, while last month Nigeria confirmed a case in the capital, Abuja, after a woman who arrived from Uganda tested positive for the virus. She, along with a close contact, were evacuated to Switzerland for treatment.
In an interview with the Guardian last month, Dr Jean Kaseya, the director general of the Africa Centres for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC), said the “unprecedented” spread of the Ebola outbreak meant it could reach the UK and other countries.
“We want all countries to know that they are not safe if they don’t take appropriate measures,” he said. “Each country, not only in the African region, but all continents, must now increase the preparedness level and the possibility for treatment.
“It is the first time three African regions have been affected [by Ebola]. The geographic extension of this outbreak is unprecedented.”
Other patients who have been medically evacuated for specialised care since the start of the outbreak include two sent to Germany and one to the Netherlands. Another case was reported in France in July.
British health authorities say the risk to the wider public from imported Ebola cases remains low and the NHS has procedures in place to manage suspected and confirmed infections.
There have only been four confirmed cases recorded in Britain since 1976, according to the UK Health Security Agency.

content:
The Anutin Charnvirakul government and the opposition bloc are heading for another showdown over proposed changes to House committee rules that could weaken parliament's role in holding the government to account.
Under the proposed rules, committee chairs would lose the power to independently call individuals or agencies to provide information. Instead, they would have to seek approval from their panels before issuing invitations. Chairs would also be barred from changing agendas approved by committee resolutions, while committees would be prohibited from holding overlapping meetings on the same issue, even when examining it from different angles.
The changes, which appear to dilute legislative oversight, are the latest initiative of Bhumjaithai MP Supachai Jaisamut. Citing duplication among House committees, he submitted a letter to House Speaker Sophon Zarum on Sept 17 seeking a ruling. Mr Sophon, also a Bhumjaithai MP, has agreed to the proposed changes.
Under the current rules, opposition MPs have used House committees to scrutinise contentious state projects and scandals involving cabinet ministers and government MPs. These include the controversial TH-AI passport project, an attempted murder of a southern MP that raised questions about links between the hitmen and security officials, and the alleged involvement of a Bhumjaithai MP's husband in an online gambling website.
The existing rules give committees the flexibility to summon individuals and officials and obtain information. The public benefits from this kind of effective legislative scrutiny.
Young lawmakers, including opposition MPs Rangsiman Rome and Rukchanok Srinork, have brought public concerns into parliament and used committee investigations to put information into the public domain.
Mr Supachai's claim the changes would reduce duplication is difficult to understand. More concerning is the prospect that the revamp, if adopted, would weaken parliamentary scrutiny. In political terms, government MPs outnumber the opposition in all House committees. This gives coalition MPs considerable influence over which issues panels prioritise, whom they invite and which matters are left at the bottom of the agenda.
The opposition has vowed to challenge the proposed changes, which it says are unprecedented and lack a clear basis in parliamentary rules and procedures.
Parit Wacharasindhu, a People's Party MP, said the party would seek support from other opposition members for a letter to the House speaker opposing the changes and requesting discussions before they take effect.
House committees' work should be streamlined, but any reform must strengthen legislative oversight, not undermine it. The proposed changes would do the opposite.
Bhumjaithai and its coalition partners must reject Mr Supachai's unproductive initiative, which would weaken parliament's ability to hold the government to account. Mr Anutin must remember that his responsibilities as prime minister extend beyond maintaining the government's stability. As an elected leader, he has a duty to ensure transparent governance. Good governance depends on effective checks and balances.
Scrutiny can alert the government to irregularities that might otherwise go unnoticed, allowing problems to be addressed before the damage becomes so serious that it threatens the government itself.
summary: The Anutin Charnvirakul government and the opposition bloc are heading for another showdown over proposed changes to House committee rules that could weaken parliament's role in holding the government to account.

content:
In the nearly two years since he returned to the White House, US President Donald Trump has picked up where he left off in his first term, shredding the open multilateral trading system that has served the world so well since the end of World War II.
He has imposed sweeping tariffs on dozens of countries, repeatedly raising and lowering them and changing rates on individual goods and countries, seemingly on a whim. As a result, US tariff rates are now higher than at any time since the Great Depression's Smoot-Hawley tariffs.
Mr Trump's tariffs have provided domestic industries with some protection, but at the expense of others that depend on them. His 50% tariff on steel imports, for example, has contributed to a 52% rise in the average US price of hot-rolled coil steel over the past year. This has boosted steel producers' production and profits while harming manufacturers of automobiles, farm equipment, and household appliances.
Mr Trump's objectives, at least as he initially presented them, were to increase employment (especially in manufacturing industries), reduce America's current-account and trade deficits, and strengthen the US industrial base. None of these objectives has been achieved, and inflation has accelerated.
Federal Reserve Bank of New York researchers have found that without Mr Trump's tariffs, US prices would actually have fallen slightly in 2026. Instead, prices have skyrocketed, with gasoline prices rising 34%, fuel oil up 74%, and significant increases for computer software (28%) and airfares (22%).
Soaring prices have walloped Mr Trump's popularity, while the chaotic and erratic way in which his tariffs have been imposed and amended has created enormous uncertainty worldwide. A Brookings Institution study found that his tariff regime "is more administratively complex and less predictable than the system that preceded it," with little clarity about the tariffs' duration and scope. A framework intended to promote domestic manufacturing capacity and bargaining leverage may thus "introduce costs and instability that undermine those objectives."
And despite the higher costs, the US merchandise trade deficit has not declined, rising to $114.7 billion (3.862 trillion baht) by August. Although the goods deficit with China shrank by 32%, the trade deficit increased to $1.2 trillion in 2025 as imports from other countries offset that decrease.
Nor has there been much job creation. Manufacturing employment fell by 1.2% in 2025, following a 0.7% decline in 2024. Other sectors of the US economy, most notably agriculture, have been hit hard as countries responded to Mr Trump's tariffs by turning to alternative suppliers.
In addition to damaging the US economy, Mr Trump's tariff shenanigans have hurt most of America's trading partners. The damage has extended well beyond China to countries previously regarded as strong allies and supporters of the multilateral trading system. Canada and Mexico's experience under the North American Free Trade Agreement, which Mr Trump renegotiated during his first term and is now renegotiating again, is illustrative.
Bizarrely, Mr Trump also raised tariffs on Australia and the United Kingdom because they were allegedly not doing enough to crack down on forced labour.
When Mr Trump resumed his war on the multilateral trading system, critics were virtually unanimous in predicting that his tariffs would do nothing to reduce America's trade and current-account deficits while undermining the system itself. They forecast that trade volumes would fall as countries retaliated with tariff hikes of their own.
They were certainly right about the deficit. A country that spends more than it earns must, by definition, run a current-account deficit, with the trade deficit the largest component. Tariffs did not address that imbalance, which has remained relatively constant.
Still, there is cause for hope. Most countries have resisted the urge to retaliate against Mr Trump's tariff hikes, limiting the harm that might otherwise have been done, both to themselves and to the US. As a result, global trade and economic growth have held up better than expected.
In April, the International Monetary Fund forecast that global growth would slow from 3.5% in 2025 to 3% this year. It later revised its forecast to 3.1%, despite the war in Iran and the surge in fuel prices. The World Trade Organization, for its part, more than doubled its growth forecast for global trade in 2026, from 1.9% to 3.9%.
These developments offer hope that trade relations will improve after Mr Trump leaves the White House, especially given how unpopular his tariffs are with American voters. If Republicans take a beating in the Nov 4 midterm elections, US politicians will be reluctant to endorse further tariff hikes. The resilience of international trade, combined with public pressure, may even lead to tariff reductions.
If that happens, it could mark the beginning of a virtuous circle in which lower tariffs help reduce inflation and economic uncertainty. Undoing Mr Trump's errors might be just the stimulus the US and world economy need. ©2026 Project Syndicate
Anne O. Krueger, a former World Bank chief economist and former first deputy managing director of the International Monetary Fund, is Senior Research Professor of International Economics at the Johns Hopkins University School of Advanced International Studies and Senior Fellow at the Center for International Development at Stanford University.
summary: In the nearly two years since he returned to the White House, US President Donald Trump has picked up where he left off in his first term, shredding the open multilateral trading system that has served the world so well since the end of World War II.

content:
For the past few years, the Sai River in Chiang Rai, a tributary of the Mekong, has remained thick and muddy throughout the year.
The murky water is unprecedented. In the past, its waters ran clear during the cool and dry seasons. The change has been linked to rapid expansion of mining activities to extract gold, rare earth and other mineral mining upstream in Shan State, Myanmar.
The mining areas are controlled by the United Wa State Army (UWSA), the Myanmar military and local militias. Investment money comes from Chinese businesses operating many of the mines.
Mining activities, mostly conducted through rudimentary open-pit methods, have severely affected the Sai River.
The tributary is just 30 kilometres long, originates in Shan State, and forms part of the border between Mae Sai district in Chiang Rai and Tachileik in Myanmar. Yet this short river now carries a pollution crisis that communities downstream have little power to stop.
For more than a year, Thailand's Pollution Control Department (PCD) has repeatedly detected arsenic and other contaminants above water-quality standards in the river. Similar contamination has been found in the Kok, Ruak and Mekong rivers.
Tests of samples collected in August found arsenic in the Sai River at up to 28 times the standard and lead at more than five times the permissive levels set by the Pollution Control Department (PCD).
The findings prompted Chiang Rai's governor to issue a public health warning covering five subdistricts in Mae Sai district.
For several months, residents and businesses were urged to avoid using untreated river water for drinking, cooking and food preparation, and to avoid consuming aquatic animals from affected areas, particularly fish organs and bottom-dwelling species. Water suppliers were instructed to strengthen treatment and test water before distribution.
The warning is necessary, but it exposes how little the government can do to solve the problem and protect the health of affected villagers.
Residents are being told to change how they obtain water and food, while water suppliers must work harder to make contaminated water safe. These measures may reduce exposure. They cannot stop pollution while upstream mining continues unchecked.
Of course, villagers need to be informed and warned. But more than anything, they need the river to be clear, clean and safe to use.
Thai security agencies say there are 14 gold and rare-earth mining sites in the upper Sai River basin.
More than half operate in or directly beside the river and its tributaries. Needless to say, during heavy rainfall, mine waste and contaminated sediment can be washed downstream.
Without effective controls on mining and waste disposal, downstream communities face recurring contamination. Monitoring can tell us how serious the problem has become. It cannot remove its source.
The alarming test results have coincided with the rapid expansion of large mines around Mong Hsat in Shan State. During field investigations by Transborder News, we observed extensive clearing of new land. Several mining sites are visible from the Thai side of the border in Mae Fah Luang district, Chiang Rai.
Our observations indicate that mining is expanding rapidly despite growing evidence of harm downstream.
The central problem is a lack of accountability.
Unlike responsible mining activities that are conducted with reliable environmental safeguards and punitive laws, in Myanmar, armed groups control access to mining areas, businesses extract the minerals, and communities bear the consequences. There is little visible evidence of effective environmental regulation or any mechanism through which affected people can demand remedies.
Both countries' governments have acknowledged the pollution problem. The broader question is what they have done.
In August, the Thai and Myanmar governments signed terms of reference on managing transboundary pollution during Myanmar military leader Gen Min Aung Hlaing's visit to Thailand.
Yet the agreement has offered downstream communities little reassurance that the mines will be brought under control. As of now, nothing has been done, and what villagers get is a warning to avoid using the water.
Diplomatic engagement should be judged by what changes at the source: whether mining operations are inspected, waste discharges are controlled, and findings are made public. An agreement alone cannot protect a river.
Accounts from villagers living near the mines offer little hope.
"Mining trucks run day and night," one villager told Transborder News. "The Wa troops have now expanded the mining area into farmland belonging to people in the village. Some received very little compensation. If a family refused to sell, their land was simply seized.
"We could no longer stay there. We crossed into Thailand to live with relatives and find work. We do not plan to return."
Villagers describe communities around Mong Hsat as having wasted land after mining damages forests, farmland and waterways. The destruction is driving people from the land and livelihoods.
What will they do? For generations, these folks have depended on farming for income.
Downstream in Thailand, residents of Mae Sai district live in fear every time they use tap water. Local tap water comes from the Sai River. Many families have to dig deep into their pockets to buy bottled water or water supplied from elsewhere.
These folks are middle class in cities. Having to buy bottled water for daily use means less money to spend on other essentials.
Their fear does not establish that treated tap water is unsafe. It does show why authorities must ensure that the tap water is safe to use. Authorities should publish clear, regular results on treated water, alongside information about river contamination.
People need to know whether the water reaching their homes meets the relevant standards.
A dependable alternative water source also remains unresolved. An earlier proposal sought funding to pump water from the Mekong. But contamination detected there raises further questions about source selection, treatment and long-term safety.
The implications extend to agriculture. Irrigation systems draw directly from the Sai River, creating concerns about contamination of farmland and possible movement through the food chain.
These concerns require systematic testing of soil, crops and irrigation water, with results disclosed to farmers and consumers.
The burden of uncertainty should not fall on households deciding what water to drink, farmers deciding whether to irrigate, or families deciding whether local fish are safe to eat.
Thailand's response must therefore go beyond warnings.
It must provide reliable access to safe water, transparent monitoring and sustained health surveillance, while making control of upstream pollution a concrete priority in dealings with Myanmar and the businesses involved.
Questions about sampling and laboratory methods should be resolved through reliable, transparent verification and monitoring. They must not become a reason to delay protective action while evidence of contamination continues to mount.
Meanwhile, the mines continue to expand.
The costs are being passed downstream -- to households buying water, farmers worried about their land and communities losing confidence in the river that sustains them.
People in the Sai River basin and downstream along the Mekong are being left increasingly isolated in a disaster they did not create.
Paskorn Jumlongrach is the founding editor of a non-profit independent news outlet based in Thailand, www.transbordernews.in.th.
summary: For the past few years, the Sai River in Chiang Rai, a tributary of the Mekong, has remained thick and muddy throughout the year.

content:
Re: "Trump says in interview that he will accept election results", (Online, Nov 4).
While the midterm elections in the United States are yielding fruit from an election fought with vitriol, anger and frustration among the voters, President Donald Trump has come to the moment of truth that his presidency for the next two years will be painful, and at his age, the fire and rage of his greener years will morph into lame duck passivity.
The larger lessons that need to be learned can be summarised in the following points:
The America as we have known it for the past 50 years will look very different in the near future. The agenda of resentment and rejection of the blacks, Hispanics, and minority faiths will turn into tolerance, acceptance and hopefully coexistence in America. The fabled melting pots of cultures that America has been known to call itself will have to be the accepted reality if democracy is to survive, albeit with more nuanced tones of the liberal, leftists and inclusivism as the new norms.
The egalitarian vision of democracy, which the French Revolution of 1789 and the American Independence of 1776 will now have to be reexamined under the iconoclastic lens of the Jan 6, 2021 putsch on the Capitol, the re-election of Trump as a felon to the presidency of the United States and the cover-ups of the Epstein files, the cryptocurrency conspiracies, the brazen exoneration of the billionaires and the super-rich oligarchs through tax exemptions.
Democracy is now wounded; the middle class and poor in America are the new poverty-stricken classes, and the senseless attacks against Iran and through Iranian counterattacks on the neighbouring Islamic countries under the pretext of securing oil markets and containing the demonic tendencies of Iran will be written indelibly in history books as deteriorative blows to democracy itself.
Added to the sin-lists of democratic America is the irrational support of the Trump administration for Israel's onslaughts on Iran in a futile attempt to change its regime and the shameless support of America for Russia in its aggression against Ukraine and the resultant alienation of Nato allies. The "wild west" vision of Trump's designs to attach Greenland, Canada and the Gulf of Mexico and the reprehensible capture of Nicolás Maduro and the strangulation of Cuba's energy, subjecting it to blackouts and social pain, are unpardonable in the ideals of democracy and religious edicts themselves.
Western Democracy, as typified by America, is dying, and if it is to rise again, will its rise betoken a Halloween rainbow or the unquenchable fires of Hades?
Glen Chatelier
Echoes of 1997
Re: "Strict rules in place", (PostBag, Nov 3), "Watching brief", (PostBag, Nov 2) & "Foreign investment in Thai stocks set to rebound", (Business, Oct 27).
Delta stock, a solid company, has been the most actively traded stock here for a long time.
But it is now down about 50% compared to just 3 months ago.
Yet there are no reports of any forced-margin selling.
Forced margin-selling levels are determined by the stock exchange, not the brokers, and its failure to enforce them was a key reason for the 1997 Asian financial crisis.
The worst ever, I know I was there.
Back then, 56 finance and finance-and-securities companies were permanently closed by December 1997, and about 22 of them held brokerage licences.
I presume that we just have to take Mr James Debenture's word that it's being properly followed now, as he so claims.
Paul Renaud
summary: Re: "Trump says in interview that he will accept election results", (Online, Nov 4).

content:
Halit Yozgat was killed at point-blank range on April 6, 2006, in Kassel, in the German state of Hesse . Before him, eight other men with immigrant backgrounds had also been shot point-blank since September 2000 . The 10th and final person killed by the group Germany would come to know as the National Socialist Underground did not fit this pattern: She was a woman. Police officer Michèle Kiesewetter was killed by the NSU on April 25, 2007, in Heilbronn, in the German state of Baden-Württemberg .
Four and a half years after Kiesewetter's death, the identities of the people behind the murders came to light. On November 4, 2011, Beate Zschäpe, who is now imprisoned with little likelihood of release before 2035, revealed the existence of the NSU . The group also included Uwe Böhnhardt and Uwe Mundlos, who were found dead in a burned-out RV on the same day.
The two men are believed to have died in a murder-suicided following a failed bank robbery in the eastern German city of Eisenach, under circumstances that have never been fully clarified. In a macabre confession video that Zschäpe sent to the media, they boasted that they had shot and killed nine men on racist grounds.
Second NSU trial ends with suspended sentence
One of the many unanswered questions is why Kiesewetter was also killed. No definitive answers were provided either in the first NSU trial before a Munich court, which lasted from 2013 to 2018 , or in numerous parliamentary investigative committees.
Fifteen years after the neo-Nazi terrorist group was exposed, the families of the murder victims are increasingly losing hope that any new information will come to light. One such opportunity was the trial of Susann Eminger — who was sentenced in July by a court in Dresden, in the state of Saxony, to two years of probation for supporting the terrorist group.
Eminger helped Zschäpe assume a different identity during doctor's visits and when dealing with the police by letting Zschäpe use her health insurance card and ID card. However, the court was unable to prove that she was aware of the series of murders committed by the NSU.
Relatives of the murder victims and the survivors of a nail-bombing carried out by the NSU in the western city of Cologne say the verdict beggars belief. "Ten people were executed in cold blood, and countless others were injured in bombings," said Michalina Boulgarides, whose father, Theodoros, was shot dead in Munich on June 15, 2005.
"When will the victims get justice?" Boulgarides asked in response to the suspended sentence handed down to Eminger in the second — and likely final — NSU trial. Eminger's husband, André, had received a two-and-a-half-year prison sentence in 2018 in the first criminal trial against the terrorist group, but he was required to serve only two-thirds of it. That, too, has outraged the victims' families.
Neo-Nazi Ralf Wohlleben completed his 10-year prison sentence for aiding and abetting murder in the first NSU trial in May. This means that Beate Zschäpe remains the only person convicted in connection to the NSU who is still incarcerated; she is likely to remain behind bars until 2035. All other investigations by the Federal Prosecutor's Office against suspected NSU supporters have been dropped.
NSU documentation center planned for Nuremberg
Though legal proceedings appear to be largely concluded, the broader societal debate surrounding the unprecedented series of murders and attacks carried out by the nationalist terrorists continues. Two key projects, however, are making slow progress: the national memorial center planned for Nuremberg (Bavaria) and the memorial on Keupstraße in Cologne.
Nuremberg is an obvious choice for a national documentation center for the victims of racism and right-wing extremism. It was here where the NSU murdered its first victim, Enver Şimşek, a florist, followed by two others. Another man was badly injured here in what is believed to be the first NSU bombing.
What's more, Nuremberg also played a major role during the Nazi era. Adolf Hitler held Nazi Party rallies featuring mass marches and speeches.
The German Bundestag has been considering the idea of an NSU Documentation Center since 2024. However, plans for a swift implementation fell by the wayside because the governing coalition at the time, led by Chancellor Olaf Scholz (SPD), collapsed prematurely. The project is now set to be completed by 2030.
A response from the federal government to a parliamentary inquiry from the Greens provides initial details: Just under €9 million ($10 million) has been earmarked to create the central memorial site under the leadership of the Federal Agency for Civic Education (BpB).
Mehmet Daimagüler: "The German state protected leading neo-Nazis"
To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video
How far has Germany come in 15 years?
In Chemnitz, in the eastern German state of Saxony, a documentation center on the NSU complex has been in operation since 2025, the year in which the city was European Capital of Culture. The title of the exhibition, "Open Trial," speaks to its broad, ambitious approach as a space for education, research and events.
Gamze Kubaşık gave a speech at the opening. Her father, Mehmet, was shot and killed by the NSU in Dortmund on April 4, 2006. In fact, Chemnitz was where the terrorists Zschäpe, Mundlos and Böhnhardt had been in hiding for years. "This is also where they planned my father's murder," said Gamze Kubaşık, highlighting the significance of the location. "The support they received from the local neo-Nazi scene enabled them to carry out their schemes and reinforced their ideology."
The executive directors of the Chemnitz-based organization, Nora Krzywinski and Esther Gerstenberg, believe a national memorial and documentation center dedicated to the NSU complex is necessary. "However, it cannot replace the work being done at the actual sites of terror and to address the social conditions that gave rise to it," they emphasized in their response to a written inquiry from DW.
The guiding concept for the exhibition, Krzywinski and Gerstenberg said, is to highlight the perspectives of those affected and to link remembrance with an examination of the persistence of racism and the responsibility of the state and society. "That is why we do not view our work as a substitute for a national memorial site but rather as part of an integrated system that connects sustained local, regional and national efforts to remember and come to terms with the past in a lasting way."
Though efforts to address the multifaceted NSU complex in Chemnitz have already taken concrete form, the residents of Keupstrasse in Cologne are still waiting for the promised memorial to the 22 people injured in the June 9, 2004, nail-bomb attack. According to media reports, however, construction cannot begin until 2030 at the earliest, because old buildings around the planned site must first be demolished and new ones erected.
This means that it will take more than a quarter century until a memorial honoring the victims of the NSU bombing on Keupstrasse can be erected where it took place. Now, 15 years after the NSU was revealed, the German Bundestag has agreed to hold a debate on Thursday.
It is titled: "Commemorating the Victims, Living Up to Our Responsibilities and Taking Today's Threats Seriously."
This text was originally written in German.

content:
French authorities say that fridges used in medical facilities to store blood for donations were impacted by recent cyber-attacks by unknown hackers.
The French Blood Establishment (EFS) said cold rooms storing blood were impacted by hackers, with temperatures set to rise - but staff intervened to protect blood supplies.
"No health impact has been identified and no loss of blood products is to be reported," the EFS said.
Up until now, only supermarkets were known to have been impacted by the hacks.
Meanwhile rumours have been circulating online about Russian hacktivist groups claiming they worked together to hack one of the systems that was used in the attacks which have affected European supermarkets.
Noname057(16) and Z-Pentest Alliance posted that they successfully hacked Danfoss which led to speculation that they were the culprits behind the freezer hacks.
But analysts now question whether or not that meant they were behind the supermarket cyber-attacks.
While Russian groups are not being ruled out, experts say Iranian hacktivists or nation state hackers - or even teenagers pulling pranks - could also be the culprits.
Cyber-security researchers at multiple firms are poring over evidence gathered from so-called "honeypots" to provide clues as to who is behind the waves of freezer hacks.
Three separate cyber-security firms have deployed fake freezer software traps to monitor how hackers attempt to use them for attacks.
In cyber-security, a "honeypot" is a digital decoy - such as a fake computer network or file - deliberately set up to look like a vulnerable target to lure and trap hackers.
By monitoring these traps, security experts can safely study an attacker's methods without putting real systems at risk.
According to activity gathered after the first wave of cyber-attacks, the second wave which hit several European countries was highly targeted.
"The fact that all these fridge freezers were hit simultaneously suggests planning and coordination," says Ryan Dewhurst from Spanish cyber-security company Previdian.
The entry point to the affected freezer software products was not difficult to exploit as they were poorly protected, with known attack methods already floating around online.
But experts like Dewhurst say the hacker or hackers had to gather the information about the devices' public IP addresses to create a target list then take time to plan which methods to use and when to execute them.
"Given the reported timing of when the devices had their temperatures increased, which seems to have been overnight for maximum damage - this is further evidence that the attack was planned and co-ordinated," he said.
Another cyber firm which has deployed similar honeypot tech to lure the hackers into revealing their tactics is Strathclyde-based Lupovis.
It had honeypots which appeared to be located around the world, and started seeing activity 10 days before the second wave of cyber-attacks.
Intriguingly, the team saw hackers scanning and probing their fake freezer sites only in Europe.
"We saw none of our honeypots in places like Africa or South America targeted at all," said Lupovis founder Dr Xavier Bellekens.
"Even pots in Ukraine were left alone."
'Hybrid warfare' claim
A third company - French cyber-defence firm Sekoia - also noticed scanning activity prior to the second wave of cyber-attacks, but said it could have been automatic scanning without malicious intent.
In a report to its customers, it said evidence suggested the nature of the attack aligned with activity of Russian hacktivists or the Russian government, which is being accused of carrying out so-called "hybrid warfare" cyber-attacks across Europe.
But Sekoia's research also points to Iranian regime hackers or hacktivists too.
"Iranian-aligned actors have an established record of targeting internet-exposed industrial control systems and previous incidents involved the same equipment in Israel and the US - both adversaries of Iran," the report said.
According to Sekoia, about 40 Israeli supermarkets running Danfoss controllers were compromised back in 2022.
Meanwhile in late August, freezers in at least six US military bases were forced into defrost mode, as in France. The controller models remain unconfirmed and investigations are ongoing.
"To date, we have no technical evidence indicating the involvement of Russian-speaking groups," a Sekoia spokesperson told the BBC.
"Furthermore, as NoName057 is not known to effectively conduct operations beyond DDoS attacks and has a history of making false attributions, we remain sceptical of their alleged claim of responsibility."
Distributed denial of service (DDoS) attacks work by flooding a website or online service with internet traffic in an attempt to throw it offline, or otherwise make it inaccessible.
Authorities in several countries are actively investigating the hacks and warning supermarkets about potential future attacks.
But no formal attribution has been made.
None of the three cyber firms which have been gathering honey pot data are ruling out that it could be a teenager.
But with the degree of planning necessary the experts all agree it would have to be a well co-ordinated group - and if so, they would expect online bragging to surface soon.
Sekoia also said the possibility remains that all three waves could have been carried out by different and distinct groups or copycats.
Additional reporting from Chris Vallance

content:
Arlinda Zekaj repeatedly asked the Kosovo police for protection. They said she was exaggerating.
On October 25, the 49-year-old once again reported her husband to the police. This time, he was arrested. But Zekaj also asked the police for additional protection — this time against her husband's family. But to no avail.
The police drove Arlinda Zekaj home. Her killer was waiting. At 8:58 p.m., Zekaj got out of the squad car. A short time later, the police received an emergency call. When officers arrived at Zekaj's house at 9:10 p.m., they found only her body.
The 49-year-old had been brutally murdered in her bedroom with an axe. By that time, the alleged perpetrator — her brother-in-law, Albert Sylaj — had fled.
Protests across Kosovo
The murder, which took place in the village of Vitomirica, near the city of Peja in western Kosovo, has sparked numerous public protests and demonstrations involving thousands of people across the country.
It was the eighth femicide in Kosovo  in 2026 — and apparently the most brutal.
More so than almost any other femicide in the country in recent years, Zekaj's death demonstrated that one of the things that made her killing possible was the fact that police and prosecutors ignored the victim's pleas for help .
Ministers refuse to resign
One of the first protests took place on October 26, when a group of feminists emptied buckets of red paint on steps outside the seat of Kosovo's government in the capital, Pristina.
"The state killed Arlinda" read a banner that the activists hung at the entrance to the building.
In the days that followed and on November 1, public anger brought thousands of people to streets across Kosovo. Many carried photographs of murdered women. One slogan appeared again and again: "The government has blood on its hands."
The protesters are demanding that charges be brought against the police officers and prosecutors responsible for handling Zekaj's case.
They are also calling for the resignation of Interior Minister Xhelal Svecla and Justice Minister Donika Gervalla, whom Kosovo Prime Minister Albin Kurti appointed national coordinator for protection against domestic violence in March.
Both Svecla and Gervalla have rejected calls to step down.
Kurti acknowledged that certain state institutions had "failed."
A murder foretold
In many ways, this was a murder foretold.
In the summer, Zekaj reported her husband to the police for threatening her. A court in Peja subsequently issued a protection order, granted her temporary custody of their son and gave her the right to remain in the family home.
The protection order allowed her husband to continue living in the same house, provided that he did not come within 2 meters (about 6.5 feet) of her. Outside the home, he was required to keep a distance of at least 20 meters.
Zekaj had decided against moving to a shelter because she wanted to continue living in her own home with her son.
After the protection order was issued, she repeatedly made reports to the police, including about threats from her brother-in-law Albert Sylaj.
Three days before the killing, on October 22, Zekaj reported that members of her husband's family, including Sylaj, were in her home against her wishes. According to her account, he threatened her with the words: "Leave or I'll kill you."
Sylaj was questioned only as a witness in the case against Zekaj's husband.
Police arrested him near Peja on October 27. He is now under investigation for murder.
'Collapse of the state and society in relation to women'
Since 2010, 55 women in Kosovo have been killed by partners or family members — often after years of documented abuse and ignored reports to law enforcement.
In recent years, successive Kosovo governments have adopted a number of laws and regulations aimed at better combating violence against women .
These measures include the possibility of life sentences for perpetrators in femicide cases.
Activists say the authorities responsible for enforcing these measures — including police, social services, prosecutors and courts — have failed to implement them consistently and in a coordinated manner.
In an article for the newsportal Nacionale,  the lawyer Njomeza Zejnullahu wrote that "after every murder, we hear the same word: failure. 'The institutions have failed.' I disagree. Failure is when something happens once, when a system that normally works breaks down at one point. When the cases keep repeating themselves, when the victims are almost always women and each of them had previously knocked on the door of an institution, it is no longer a failure. It is a collapse of the state and society in relation to women in general."
What needs to change?
In the aftermath of Zekaj's killing, several senior police officers from Peja and the surrounding area have been suspended. A prosecutor who had handled Zekaj's complaints has also been suspended.
For the protesters in Kosovo, however, this is not nearly enough.
"All those involved within the chain of responsibility must not only be removed from office but also criminally prosecuted for failing to fulfill their official duties," Liridona Sijarina, a political scientist and feminist activist with Kosovo's Kolektivi Feminist (Feminist Collective), told DW.
"That includes not only police officers, prosecutors and judges, but also mayor of Peja Gazmend Muhaxheri and, ultimately, government ministers," she said.
Sijarina said feminist activists were also calling on the Interior Ministry to create a dedicated unit that would treat women's safety as a matter of national security and focus specifically on preventing femicides.
She said the government should make its draft legislation on affordable social housing a top political priority and ensure that women who have experienced domestic violence are eligible for social housing.
"In our view, the behavior of the institutions so far has deepened women's distrust of the state and, as a result, allowed violence against them to escalate," Sijarina said. "The government now has the opportunity to show whether it truly takes women's lives seriously by clearly responding to our demands."
This article was originally published in German.
