德国之声：中国对美国中期选举结果反应谨慎。外交部发言人毛宁在例行记者会上被问及对美国中期选举的看法时表示，中期选举是美国内政。中方愿继续同美方一道，维护好落实好两国元首重要共识。您怎么看这样的表态？
费多丽教授：首先，中国评价美国选举结果态度审慎是非常典型的做法。他们通常不会明确表达倾向，而是往往以“这是内政”作为回应。不过，“中方愿继续同美方一道，维护好落实好两国元首重要共识”这种措辞显示，中方预料到，外界可能会认为中国对选举结果会不那么满意，因为他们刚刚才和特朗普达成了安排。换句话说，他们认为民主党人，或者很多人认为民主党人，现在会采取更进一步的行动。因此中方强调，“我们仍然愿意合作。”
德国之声：中国看来有些担心中期选举的这一结果可能会对中美关系产生一些影响。那么您认为影响会有多大？
费多丽教授：根据近年来的经验，中国政府担心民主党人对华的态度会比特朗普更具批判性。特朗普被指折服于习近平的领导才能，在这一层面上建立了不一样的关系，因此在处理对华关系方面对抗性有所降低。但必须指出的是，美国在特朗普执政期间也对中国实施了制裁措施。虽然他们今年还没有向台湾交付武器，但也并没有真正对中国采取友好，或者和解的态度。情况非常复杂。可以说，过去这些年，无论谁入主白宫，在对华问题上都相对一致。拜登并没有完全推翻特朗普第一任期对华政策，特朗普也没有推翻拜登的做法。当然，他们的优先事项不同，处理方式也截然不同。但从根本上讲，共和党人和民主党人都认为中国是主要挑战，需要采取战略性应对措施。
德国之声：具体而言，中期选举后，美国在外交、贸易和关税政策上可能有不同的做法吗？
费多丽教授：就外交政策，包括贸易政策和关税政策而言，现任总统很明显不怎么遵循国会的建议。因此，我们不知道，民主党主导国会后，是否真的有能力通过国会正常的、合法的、既定的程序来阻止特朗普在这些领域采取独立行动。或许可以提起诉讼，但这需要时间。所以，目前情况很复杂。这不仅关系对华政策。
微妙的中美经贸关系

观察人士认为，民主党可能会试图对白宫施加更大的压力。但实际上——正如有人所说——特朗普现在这个所谓的“跛脚鸭”，在接下来的两年内，也可能变成一只愤怒的鸭子，想要强行推进某些事情。因此，我们对接下来会怎样其实一无所知。我们可以看看月底的APEC峰会上发生什么。我相信习近平和特朗普的会晤仍将按计划举行。或许我们能从中窥见事态的发展方向。我认为我们不会立即看到巨大的变化，短期内美国的对华政策不会有大的变化。
德国之声：您刚才提到台湾，在这方面美国的政策会有什么改变吗？
费多丽教授：我不是台湾问题专家，但如果我理解没错的话，在特朗普执政期间，原计划今年运往台湾的武器已被暂停。理论上讲，可以想象民主党人会更加努力地推动对这批武器的交付。但努力归努力，最终是否能促成此事就完全是另一回事了。
德国之声：您能简单总结一下特朗普执政两年来，中美的地位和力量对比发生什么变化吗？
费多丽教授：中国的确也受了特朗普政府制裁的打击，但我认为，目前最关键的是，世界其他地区，尤其是全球南方国家，认为特朗普政府在各种领域的政策都难以预测，很难知道特朗普政府下一步会做什么，想要什么，以及它的声明有多可靠。这包括贸易战，但也延伸到伊朗战争和类似问题。特朗普政府的这种等级森严且难以预测性，导致了中国形象和实力的普遍提升。但与此同时，也有另外一种趋势。在欧洲，我们也感受到了 在美国蔓延的对中国的恐惧 。这种恐惧正在欧洲日益扩散。
不过，如果我们暂时忽略这些因素，只关注特朗普及其政府在国际政治中的行为，那么中国无疑已经从中受益，中国在世界上的地位似乎得到了加强。
至于特朗普对中国的经济政策，中国现任领导层可以把功劳归于自己，说我们对特朗普的反应是正确的，我们挺身对抗他， 展现了实力 ，事实证明这很有效，正因为如此，特朗普现在才相对放过了我们。有些人从心理层面分析，认为特朗普确实喜欢强人，所以他才会在某种程度上欣赏中国。不过，涉及实际的贸易冲突、安全冲突、信息和虚假信息问题等等，中国也并非完全占据上风。大家都在摸索，试图找到解决这些冲突的方法。
此外，中国经济目前面临着诸多问题，包括一些需求方面的问题。近期股市的疲软也被解读为对人工智能能力缺乏信心。中国经济目前似乎正处于低迷状态，但这种情况我们现在在美国也看到了。但这些问题并非主要由中美双边关系决定，中国目前面临的困境也并非出口市场之类的问题，而是与中国的经济政策、政策的实施方式以及优先事项的设定密切相关。
德国之声：美国对中国商品，比如电动汽车等商品进口有很多限制，这样的趋势还会继续吗？
费多丽教授：我不认为国会会向白宫施压，要求对中国实施更多贸易限制，至少不会以太多商品从中国流入美国为由。如果真有什么动向，那也只会是出于安全方面的考虑。但我认为他们不会把这作为首要任务。民主党首先需要理顺内部事务，弄清楚如何应对这种新局面，如何稳定现在这股浪潮，从而在两年后再次赢得总统大选。而且国会现在是否真的拥有影响力并能带来巨大变革，比如在关税政策方面，我对此表示怀疑。如果主要目的是抑制通货膨胀，他们也许会说，或许我们应该降低关税。但通货膨胀当然也很大程度上受能源价格的影响，而关税对能源价格没有影响。所以情况很复杂。我预计民主党人需要一些时间来站稳脚跟，适应他们的新角色。

"After the referee lifted my hand to show I'm now a two-time world champion, it was a very overwhelming feeling," Mariam Bsharat said. "Making history once is something, but making it twice is really something else. I felt very happy and I felt a big relief. Only I know how many sacrifices I made and how many hardships I needed to overcome."
Themes of relief, joy and sacrifice are commonplace in the reflections of athletes after a big win. In Mariam Bsharat's case, it's about more than just dedication to training and taking care of the body. The 17-year-old won her second under-21 World Karate Championship gold medal competing for the  Palestine  national team in Poland in October.
"It was everyday life, seeing people get killed around me and houses getting bombed," she told DW of her upbringing in the occupied West Bank .
"I faced challenges in transportation," Bsharat said. "I wasn't able to go from one city to another to be able to train with other people, so that I can actually prepare for competitions. I needed to travel to other countries like Jordan or Egypt ... which was very hard for me. And, financially, the support wasn't really the support an elite athlete needed."
Skepticism turns to sporting success
Growing up in Nablus , Bsharat had a narrow path to the top. But initially, it was her own reluctance that threatened to stop a champion career before it started.
"When I was a little kid, I did not really love it," said Bsharat, who competes in the division for fighters who weigh under 66 kilograms (145 pounds).
"I started it because my family was in that sport," Bsharat said. "My father had a dojo, and my mother also did that sport. My siblings and my aunts and my uncles — it's a family thing. I started it because they were all doing it. In time, I started getting into it."
How much power do Israeli settlers have over West Bank policy?

Family has been a constant source of comfort and inspiration for Bsharat. Her father and uncle have acted as manager and coach respectively. While her mother and siblings moved with Mariam to Hamburg, Germany , last year, her father remained in order to take care of his business, the dojo, though he visits and tries to be with his daughter in competitions. Integration has been made easier by her mastery of the language, taught to her by her German mother.
Bsharat has mixed feelings about leaving her homeland.
"I'm thankful to be here because being in Germany opened lot of doors for me, and I think I have a brighter future here," Bsharat said. "But also being in Palestine was just my everyday life, and I loved it there. My family was around me, my friends were around me, and I just felt comfortable, which was a big change coming here to Germany. I think every change comes with hardships."
Pressures from homeland weigh heavy
As well as the obvious difficulties of living in an area occupied by Israel , there are particular challenges for sportspeople living in the West Bank and the Gaza Strip , with access to facilities, travel and constant security fears among them. As such, very few people from the Palestinian territories become successful on the international sporting stage. That, Bsharat said, gives her responsibilities that are unusual and heavy for a person of any age, let alone a 17-year-old.
Hamburg's refugee cricketers
To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video
"Being an elite athlete in Palestine is something very special because not everybody in Palestine has that opportunity. There aren't really a lot of athletes that are elite and who win international medals,” Bsharat said.
"So all that pressure from all the country and all the people, the family, the coaches are on me because I'm representing them, raising their flag,” she said. "I sometimes even forget to fight for myself and actually think about myself."
Olympic dream alive — should karate be an event again
That has not yet proved a barrier to Bsharat, who is is ranked first in the world in her category by the World Karate Federation (WKF) . With Palestine recognized by the International Olympic Committee, Bsharat would likely have been a contender to raise that flag in Los Angeles at the 2028 Olympics. But the sport was dropped from the Games in 2024.
"The global karate community remains steadfast in our belief that the natural place for karate is within the Olympic Games, and we sincerely hope that the incongruence we suffered in Paris 2024 and LA 2028 will be corrected for Brisbane 2032, if not sooner," the WKF wrote in response to the decision in 2024. The sport was also taken off the slate for the recent Youth Games in Senegal.
Should karate return in Brisbane, Bsharat would likely be approaching her prime. In the meantime, she is looking forward to starting her journey as a senior when she turns 18. But she won't be hanging around.
"My goal is it to be a world champion at seniors, which is the hardest and the best thing you can achieve in karate," she said.
"But winning an Olympic medal , being called Olympic champion or just representing my country with that flag [is a thought that] is just full of happiness and pride."
The interview was conducted by Janek Speight.

On November 4, 2001, London's Leicester Square became a world of witches and wizards. The occasion was the world premiere of "Harry Potter and the Philosopher's Stone" (released in the US and India as "Harry Potter and the Sorcerer's Stone").
"Thousands of excited fans, some dressed up in wizard hats and cloaks, gathered to catch a glimpse of arriving celebrities," the BBC reported at the time.
Daniel Radcliffe , who played Harry Potter , was just 12 years old and clearly impressed by the spectacle. The BBC quoted him as saying, "It is so cool. I have never heard my name shouted so much in an hour."
The crowds showed just how far Harry Potter fever had spread in only four years.
The first Harry Potter book was published by Britain's Bloomsbury in June 1997, with an initial print run of just 500 hardcover copies.
About 5,000 paperback copies were also released around the same time.
Today, first editions are prized collectors' items, with hardcover copies commanding high prices at auction . In mid-October, one sold for $400,000 through US auction house Heritage Auctions.
At first, the book's popularity grew largely by word of mouth among schoolchildren. Media attention followed when it won the prestigious Nestle Smarties Book Prize later that year.
With an estimated 120 million-plus copies sold worldwide, it is the best-selling book in the series and ranks among the best-selling novels of all time.
J.K. Rowling, a controversial author
For years, J.K. Rowling 's public image was defined by her extraordinary rise from a single mother on welfare to a billionaire.
But in recent years, debate over her views on gender and transgender identity has increasingly overshadowed that success. It's an issue Rowling herself frequently weighs in on.
In an essay published on her website on October 21, 2026, Rowling reiterated her opposition to what she calls the "current, dominant strain of trans activism." She argues that this movement "holds that a man who declares himself a woman is, literally, a woman, and is therefore entitled to be treated as a woman in all contexts." Rowling argues that allowing trans women into single-sex spaces poses a risk. She describes biological sex as an indisputable biological fact.
Such statements have led critics to accuse Rowling of transphobia, while others regard her stance as a defense of women's rights and safety.
The controversy has also divided her fans. Some stand by Rowling, while others try to draw a distinction between the books and their author.
Others have left Harry Potter behind altogether. One former fan is German YouTuber Coldmirror, known for her Harry Potter parodies. The media artist from the Bremen area, whose real name is Kathrin Fricke, told the Süddeutsche Zeitung newspaper: "I don't have any love left for Harry. I'm still somewhat interested, but I can no longer watch it in good conscience." She cited Rowling's campaigning against transgender people as the reason.
The "Harry Potter" film cast is divided as well. The three main stars — Daniel Radcliffe, Emma Watson and Rupert Grint — have publicly spoken out in support of transgender people. Meanwhile, Ralph Fiennes, who played Lord Voldemort, and Helena Bonham Carter, who portrayed Bellatrix Lestrange, have defended Rowling's right to express her views.
Harry Potter TV series set to premiere at Christmas
Despite the controversy surrounding Rowling, Warner Bros., which holds the Harry Potter film rights, is bringing the books back to the screen — this time as a series for HBO . The premiere is scheduled for December 25.
The eight-episode first season is an an adaption of the first book. Even though the episode lengths haven't been announced, the scope of a TV series gives each book much more room than the original films did. That means more time to explore subplots, character development and everyday life at Hogwarts. While many fans are looking forward to a more detailed adaptation, others remain skeptical. They find it hard to imagine the familiar characters being played by anyone else.
The new trio consists of Dominic McLaughlin as Harry Potter, Arabella Stanton as Hermione Granger and Alastair Stout as Ron Weasley.
J.K. Rowling is an executive producer on the show. HBO says, however, that her views on gender identity won't be reflected in the storyline. Several people involved in the new production have publicly distanced themselves from her views. Paapa Essiedu, who has been cast as Severus Snape, signed an open letter supporting transgender people. Rowling subsequently said she had neither the power nor the desire to have him removed from the show because of it. John Lithgow, who plays Dumbledore, and Nick Frost, who portrays Hagrid, have also spoken out against Rowling's views.
Meanwhile, the Harry Potter merchandising machine is still going strong. On November 4, Britain's largest Harry Potter store to date is set to open in London. According to Warner Bros., the two-story shop covers more than 1,950 square meters.
This article was originally written in German.

（德国之声中文网）特朗普总统放宽芯片对华出口限制，以及搁置对台军售案的做法，一直以来都是国会的争议话题。网络新闻平台China Table在中期选举前发表的一份分析指出，一旦民主党重新赢得国会多数，特朗普对北京做出的种种妥协，就将面临严峻考验。这篇题为《美国中期选举：特朗普的对华交易面临严峻考验》的分析文章写道：
“早在中期选举之前， 美国民主党 人就对特朗普的对华路线提出了质疑。9月，习近平结束访美行程后，就有民主党籍参议员指责特朗普，为了眼前的商业利益，而牺牲了美国的技术霸主地位。白宫批准向中国出售高端芯片和芯片制造设备的决定，尤其引起民主党政治家们的强烈批评。与此同时，民主党人还要求放行一宗对台军售案，这笔价值140亿美元的对台军售案此前本已获得国会的批准，但却一直被白宫搁置一边。民主党人发出的信号很明确: 特朗普不能为了讨好习近平，就把美国的长期利益当作儿戏。
明年1月开始，民主党将可以利用在众议院的多数地位对特朗普的 对华政策 进行监督。届时，他们将有权让政府官员前来听证，并就总统豁免关税的依据等事项展开调查。美国战略与国际关系中心的莱恩什（William Alan Reinsch）在中期选举前撰写的一篇分析文章就指出，民主党的这类提案会令政府陷入被动。
中国和台湾民众如何看待“习特高峰会”
To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video
而一旦民主党也赢得了 参议院 的多数地位，他们还可以通过制定新法律来制约特朗普的对华政策。不过，特朗普总统也同样可以行使否决权来阻止这样的法律。不过，无论如何，国会的各类调查都有可能会让政府疲于应对，以至于政府出台新举措的空间大大缩小。
国会同白宫的相互掣肘在台湾问题上表现得尤为明显。芝加哥全球事务学会的赫尔（Paul Heer）表示，国会内已经形成了一种‘松散的跨党派共识，认为特朗普对习近平做出了过多的让步。不过，赫尔同时也表示，特朗普是否会在意国会压力，则另当别论。今后，特朗普仍完全有可能会不顾一切地向习近平靠拢。”
China Table分析文章援引复旦大学政治学者吴心伯的话写道，中期选举的失利，或许也会激励特朗普总统在中美关系等外交领域拿出政绩的决心。
“特朗普一旦面临民主党掌控的国会调查，就有可能会采取主动出击的策略。例如，他有可能会挑起一场新的关税战。布鲁金斯协会的哈斯（Ryan Hass）认为，在贸易政策领域， 特朗普 很有可能会采取‘不断出击’的策略。他会将自己的总统权限发挥到极致，以挑起争端的形式来回避国会对他本人及政府的调查。新的关税可能会矛头直指北京，从而使刚刚趋于稳定的中美关系再出变数。”
“爱上外国人，就是女叛徒？”
一位美国网红对数名中国女性疑似实施性剥削的消息曝光之后，中国网上舆论的怒火，却逐渐转向了那些拥有外籍伴侣的中国女性，并将这类女性称为“民族败类”。 《南德意志报》写道：
“格罗宁根大学传媒学者Qian Huang认为，这种舆论攻势的背后，就是要为女性制定明确的行为规范：一名‘好的中国女性’既不应当对外国男性产生性冲动，更不应同他们建立婚恋关系。Qian Huang在2003年的一份论文中写道：违背这些期待的女性，就会在网上被贴上“不爱国”的标签，并遭到排斥。
尽管女性在中国的许多领域都享有平等权利，但父权思想仍相当顽固。党的最高领导层一律由男性组成。而女权运动现在也成了中国的政治敏感话题，一些女权活动人士甚至会遭到打压。其幕后原因之一，是政府担心，愈来愈独立的女性，将会进一步拉低中国的结婚率和出生率。
围绕美国留学生网红及其对待中国女性的方式的讨论，还有另外一个原因让中国领导层感到尴尬。就在今年五月，国家媒体还曾将这位美国学生誉为‘新一代外国网红’的代表。他所制作的视频中，将自己塑造成‘亲华人士’，并刻意同那些据说一位抹黑中国的网红和媒体保持距离。这种表态一时让他在中国畅通无阻，不过，现如今，他的账户已经转为私密状态。

The African National Congress is on course for a bruising result in South Africa’s local elections on Wednesday as voters go to the polls amid deep discontent over water outages, power cuts and crumbling infrastructure.
The former liberation movement, which Nelson Mandela led to power in 1994 at the end of apartheid as South Africa’s first black president, is still likely to be the largest party. However, polls showed it getting less than a third of the vote, down from 45.6% at the last municipal elections in 2021 and 40.2% in 2024’s national elections.
In Kensington, a diverse Johannesburg suburb that has sustained repeated water and power outages in recent weeks, voters said they wanted to see change. The city is currently led by Dada Morero, the ANC mayor, in coalition with the far-left Economic Freedom Fighters (EFF) and the rightwing populist Patriotic Alliance (PA).
“Service delivery is bad, it’s horrible,” said Tshepiso Makotse, 26, a call centre worker. “Water, electricity – everything, basically.”
Makotse said she had split her two votes, casting one for the centre-right Democratic Alliance (DA) local councillor and her party vote for the leftwing uMkhonto weSizwe (MK) party of the former ANC president Jacob Zuma. “I just want change,” she said.
Terrence Pieters, a retired boilermaker, said: “The infrastructure in Johannesburg is shot.” He declined to say which party he had voted for, other than it was “one of the offshoots of the DA”.
“I would like to see things get better and great people in charge,” said the 72-year-old. “But … there’s no one party that’s going to take over here. It’s going to be a circus, it’s going to be a coalition.”
Vote fragmentation means the ANC could still end up leading many city coalition governments while losing control of others.
Unstable coalitions are already a feature of many of South Africa’s 257 municipalities, and analysts point to their high turnover as a major reason for poor service delivery.
Johannesburg, a city of 4.8 million people that has faced water shortages for more than a week, has had 10 mayors in as many years. The neighbouring municipality of Ekurhuleni has had three mayors since 2021. To the north, in Tshwane, which contains the capital, Pretoria, the mayoralty has rotated between parties four times since 2020. In October, more than 800 people contracted a gastrointestinal illness from contaminated water in Bronkhorstspruit, in east Tshwane.
The ANC’s national leadership is open to working with the DA in Gauteng, according to South African media, mirroring the government of national unity, where the two parties are the largest in the national coalition. However, local ANC leaders are reportedly not in favour of a DA tie-up. Currently, the ANC governs in various coalitions across the province’s three metros, including under an ActionSA mayor in Tshwane.
In Johannesburg, the DA’s Helen Zille has led a spirited campaign, with viral stunts including the 75-year-old snorkelling in a pothole and kayaking along a flooded street. However, the former Cape Town mayor is still viewed with suspicion by many, especially black voters, due to past comments appearing to excuse colonialism. Some voters also point to soaring housing costs in Cape Town, which has been run by the DA since 2006, as a reason not to vote for Zille.
The former Johannesburg DA mayor Herman Mashaba, who now leads ActionSA, which is polling around 10%, has ruled out working with Zille in Johannesburg. Mashaba has called Zille a “racist”, an allegation she has always fervently denied. The ANC, for its part, has three possible mayoral candidates for the city, amid factional infighting.
In eThekwini metro, which contains the port city of Durban, the MK party was polling above 40%. Zuma, its 84-year-old leader, who has weathered and denied numerous corruption allegations, is set to take many of the votes of his former party, which won 42% in eThekwini in 2021 and is now polling around 10%.
The DA looks set to retain its majority in Cape Town, although probably with less than the 58% of the vote it won in 2021, as unaffordable housing turns more voters against the party.
South Africa’s electoral commission will have a week to announce the final results of Wednesday’s vote, which chooses councillors and parties, with mayors not directly elected. Parties will then have two weeks from the announcement to form councils and elect mayors.

Tinto Brass, fallecido este miércoles (4.11.2026) con 93 años, solía presentarse como el cineasta "más censurado de todos los tiempos". Sus películas eróticas y sexuales siempre sufrieron las mutilaciones de los jueces de la moral mientras pellizcaban a la sociedad de los 70, como su película más recordada y turbulenta, "Calígula".
El director residió sus últimos años de vida junto a su última esposa, Caterina Varzi, en una casa comprada hace medio siglo en la campiña romana para tener más espacio para la que siempre fue auténtica pasión: el montaje cinematográfico.
Nacido en Milán en 1933, en plena era fascista, Giovanni Brass, su verdadero nombre, se consideraba natural de la isla veneciana de la Giudecca y desde niño se interesó por el arte. De hecho su abuelo le apodó "Tinto" en honor a Tintoretto, por su habilidad en el dibujo.
Cine de vanguardia, experimental, provocador
Dio sus primeros pasos profesionales en los círculos de la Cinémathèque de París, en pleno hervor de la 'Nouvelle Vague', y llegó a asistir al maestro del neorrealismo Roberto Rossellini en cintas históricas como "Il generale Della Rovere" (1959).
Comenzó su carrera como cineasta de vanguardia y experimental en la década de 1960. Actores de renombre, como Helen Mirren y Vanessa Redgrave, protagonizaron sus películas.
Con el tiempo, Brass consagró su carrera a una cinematografía de marcado carácter libertario, hedonista y provocador, desafiando durante décadas los límites de la censura oficial y convirtiendo casi la totalidad de sus producciones en sonados debates sociales y judiciales.
"Calígula" (1979), un escándalo
El ejemplo más evidente es su obra más recordada, "Calígula" (1979), con la que sacudió su época por sus orgías y que incluso fue denunciada por necrofilia.
Mirren describió su experiencia en "Calígula" como "extraordinaria" y afirmó que "adoraba" a Brass. "Me encantaba el caos y esa especie de anarquía radical", declaró durante una conferencia de prensa en Berlín en 2020.
Brass también dirigió "Todas lo hacen", una versión provocadora de la ópera Cosi fan tutte, de Mozart.

content:
Iran this week unveiled a huge billboard and banners over Enqelab Square in central Tehran. The billboard pledged in English: “We will kill Trump” – elevating the degree of personal animus with which Donald Trump is viewed in official Iranian circles.
The poster depicts the US president behind bars with his head bowed. And in a sense, given the US midterm election results on Tuesday, Iran has indeed killed Trump, or at least the second term of his presidency. Trump’s reverse is all the more piquant because it comes on the day Iran’s leadership celebrates the anniversary of the seizure of the US embassy in Tehran in 1979, an event that ensnared Jimmy Carter, and a reminder of how Iran has ruined the prospects of more than one US president.
Not surprisingly, the keenly followed election results have led to a good degree of triumphalism inside Iran.
Ehsan Movaheidian, an international relations scholar, claimed: “The Islamic Republic of Iran has succeeded in regime change in America. The same will soon happen in Europe as well. Bow down before the power of Iran.”
Meisam Zohurian, a conservative member of parliament, said: “The joy over the outcome of the US elections has nothing to do with the arrival of this party or the departure of that party. The issue is the aggressor was smeared in the dirt and Iran had an impact on the result.”
Ali Nikzad, the first deputy speaker of the parliament, said: “These electoral defeats are the aftershocks of Trump’s defeat by the Iranian people.”
Iran’s supreme leader said anyone expecting a shift in US policy was “seriously mistaken”, however. “Those who still harbour even the slightest hope that the behaviour of the hegemonic system might change through partisan or factional shifts, or who imagine that making concessions to the United States can dissuade it from hostility towards the Iranian nation, are seriously mistaken,” Mojtaba Khamenei wrote.
Others predicted further electoral defeats for those they considered to be the warmongers in Europe, and the expulsion of US bases from the entire Middle East.
The resistance – or bloody-mindedness – shown by Iran for the past eight gruelling months did allow the strait of Hormuz to become an Iranian-controlled channel through which inflation and high diesel prices were transmitted to the US system. Even Trump himself on Wednesday accepted, and lamented, that the American people had decided the “short-term” pain of inflation was not a price worth paying to prevent Iran becoming a nuclear power.
But the big question now is whether either side will regard these seismic results as a moment to review their diplomatic strategy. Iran’s chief negotiator, Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf, was quick to call on Trump to accept the wisdom of the American people. On social media he urged Trump to bow to the verdict of America: “Whether driven by conscience or the cost of living, America said no to war and we endorse this message.”
Ghalibaf added: “If the US government betrays the public will in order to serve international paymasters and blackmailers, it will learn our ‘no’ comes with a nightmare.”
Yet Iran will also be asked to reflect on the wisdom of war by the Gulf monarchies, and possibly by Russia and China – the latter a country that finally seems to be stirring itself to find a solution to the blockade in the strait of Hormuz which is preventing badly needed Middle East oil exports from reaching its industries.
China tends to knock only on doors it knows are going to open, so it is probably testing the feasibility of a deal in which Iran “downblends” – or dilutes – its stockpile of highly enriched uranium inside Iran under international supervision. A Chinese special envoy is travelling to Oman, Iran and Saudi Arabia almost immediately.
These countries, some sympathetic to Iran’s predicament, can point out that if Tehran ever thought in the run-up to the elections Trump would capitulate and turn his carrier fleet around, it was mistaken. Some Iranian diplomats had indeed hoped that the prospect of defeat in the midterms, and pressure from within the Republican party, would have led Trump to make concessions to Tehran.
after newsletter promotion
In fact, both sides and the chief mediator, Qatar, clearly did try to use polling day as a lever, but in the end neither retreated. Trump, for once, was true to his word and refused to allow the darkening opinion polls to reduce his determination to keep Iran in his vice. Confined to a holding bay of “neither war nor peace”, Trump’s priority was to keep the oil price as low as possible by repeatedly suggesting a settlement might be imminent.
For the next two months before the new Congress convenes in January – so reducing his budgetary options – Trump has greater latitude, and little accountability. The damage to the Republican party has been done and cannot be undone.
Unsurprisingly the Trump influencers who advocated for the war in the first place are piling on pressure to strike again quickly. Laura Loomer wrote on X: “Time for President Trump to deal with Iran once and for all. Just do it, Nothing to lose now. Finish the job.”
But the credibility of Loomer and her like has been severely damaged: in February, she advised Trump that regime change in Iran – “a little excursion” – could be as easy as knocking over the Maduro regime in Venezuela. Similarly, Benjamin Netanyahu is now touting intelligence showing that Iran is preparing to use chemical weapons. The ease with which the Israeli prime minister conjures up intelligence to justify another assault on Iran may by now have struck the White House.
Hillary Clinton, Trump’s old sparring partner, is one who thinks Trump will probably launch the long-delayed attack. She said: “I think he will feel trapped. He will feel angry and resentful and he will react aggressively.”
Having come so far, and paid so high a political price, Trump may in the next two months try to secure a legacy by finishing the job – however he defines that. He is convinced, as he told Fox News this week, that “Iran has very few missiles and drones left, and even less capacity to build any more”. He crowed: “We are dealing with total strength. We can end it any time.”
Unfortunately, such blithe optimism has been heard before.

content:
The International Ice Hockey Federation (IIHF) said in a statement on Wednesday that the impact of last week's Court of Arbitration for Sport (CAS) decision requiring it to reinstate Russia to international play had been "significantly underestimated."
It added that it "maintains" its disagreement with the decision and that it remained "in dialogue with Member National Associations, organizing committees, host authorities and other key stakeholders to determine the best way forward."
Shortly after Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022 , the IIHF barred its teams from competing in international ice hockey tournaments , citing security concerns. In last Friday's ruling, the CAS said that the IIHF's concerns were "not supported by sufficient evidence."
Wednesday's statement comes after two days of talks by the IIHF Council aimed at charting a way forward following Friday's CAS decision, which appears to have caught most of the international ice hockey community off guard.
Two of the organizing committees the statement refers to are those of Canada, which is due to host the IIHF World Junior Championship starting next month, and Germany, which is to host the IIHF Men's World Championship next May. Both countries are strong supporters of Ukraine in its war against Russia, and both have expressed serious reservations about their upcoming tournaments in light of the CAS ruling.
'Russians will not be in Canada'
On Tuesday, Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney ruled out allowing Russians to compete in the World Juniors in Alberta.
"While Russia and Belarus are supporting this illegal, unjustified war in Ukraine , as long as that's going on, there will be none of those athletes competing for their countries in Canada," he told reporters at a press conference in Antigua, where he was attending a Commonwealth meeting.
"So, if you're asking specifically about the World Juniors, the Russians will not be there."
Last weekend, Frank Lutz, chairman of the German Ice Hockey Federation (DEB) conceded in a television interview that following the CAS decision, the DEB would "also have to consider the option of handing back (hosting rights to) this championship."
In a statement to DW on Wednesday, a German government spokesperson reiterated Berlin's position on the matter from the weekend, saying it viewed Friday's CAS ruling "very critically."
The spokesperson also said  the government would "consult with the German Ice Hockey Federation in the near future regarding the potential consequences of this decision, including its impact on the 2027 Ice Hockey World Championship in Germany."
Growing European boycott of Russia
Meanwhile, the ice hockey association of Finland , the defending men's world champions, has been spearheading an effort to boycott upcoming IIHF tournaments should the Russians be allowed to compete.
"We are currently working to bring as many countries as possible into a united front to tell the IIHF that none of us will play against Russia under these circumstances," Finnish Ice Hockey Association boss Heikki Hietanen said in a statement released on the organization's website on Monday.
"Our stance is that we will not play against Russia as long as the war of aggression against Ukraine continues," added Hietanen, who is also a member of the IIHF Council.
Sweden , Norway , Denmark and Czechia have since made similar statements.
"The Three Crowns will not play Russia in coming world championship tournaments," Swedish Ice Hockey Federation boss Anders Larsson said.
This came shortly after Norway said it would not play Russia at the Men's World Championship and the Danish Ice Hockey Federation issued a similar statement on its website.
"Denmark will – based on the current situation and the information available to us today – not play against Russia at the World Championship in Germany in May 2027," it read. Denmark did not qualify for the World Juniors.
Czechia Ice Hockey Association President Alois Hadamczik confirmed on Tuesday that they too would refrain from playing Russian teams.
Latvia's federation said it “reaffirms its longstanding and firm position" not to play against Russia or its ally Belarus.
Alexander Helwig, chairman of the Austrian Ice Hockey Association told public broadcaster ORF that “as of now, we would certainly not play against Russia."
USA Hockey has yet to comment on the CAS ruling.
Pressure from sponsors increasing
At the same time, sponsors of IIHF tournaments are also getting cold feet. Skoda, which has been the main sponsor of the Men's World Championship for more than three decades, told the Associated Press that it would "reassess" its position if Russia takes part.
"We do not support the Court of Arbitration for Sport's decision regarding the participation of Russian national teams in IIHF competitions. With Russia's aggression continuing, we believe the Russian national team's return to the world championship is incompatible with the values we have consistently upheld," the Czech carmaker said.
Skoda isn't alone either, Finnish tire manufacturer Nokian had said it would end its backing if Russia took part and Swedish furniture maker AJ Products, whose logo has been seen on the boards and officials' jerseys at World Championships since 1989, said Monday it would ask for its logo not to be shown.
On Wednesday afternoon, yet another sponsor joined the list, with German workwear company Strauss saying it would "forgo all logo exposure associated with the (men's) tournament" and was considering withdrawing its sponsporship entirely.
With the IIHF Council having failed to agree on how to proceed during its meetings on Monday and Tuesday, President Franz Reindl told Germany's SID news agency on Wednesday, that it would reconvene for further talks on Thursday.
This article was originally published on November 4, 2026. It was updated on November 5, 2026 with the German government statement to DW.

（德国之声中文网）人权组织对这5名男子的处境表示担忧。他们属于穆斯林少数民族群体，活动人士称该群体在中国受到迫害。上个月，其中两人获得泰国赦免。
2014年，泰国拘押了300多名 维吾尔人 ，他们就是其中一部分。此后，大多数人已离开泰国—— 包括去年被送往中国的约40人 ，此举曾引发国际社会强烈谴责。
这5人因2020年试图逃离移民拘留中心而被判入狱。根据泰国法律，他们必须服完刑期后才会被驱逐出境。
其中两人上个月获赦，目前被关押在移民拘留中心，等待命运安排。
泰国国家安全委员会秘书长猜普鲁克·敦普拉帕特（Chaipruak Doungprapat）周三对记者表示：“这5人在中国面临逮捕令，且他们并未获得难民身份。”
他说，如果中国提出引渡请求，泰国外交部将进行评估，随后由法院作出裁决。
猜普鲁克说：“如果法院裁定他们有罪，他们将根据引渡条约被移交给中方。”
“如果他们胜诉，那么最终的结果将取决于是否有其他国家愿意接收他们。”
周三被问及这五人的命运时，中国外交部发言人毛宁没有提供细节。
她表示：“中泰开展打击非法移民等跨境犯罪活动合作，符合两国法律、国际法和国际惯例。”
更多阅读： 泰国遣返维吾尔人细节曝光：一边否认一边准备遣返？
“严重风险”
泰国并非《联合国难民公约》缔约国，但受国际法“不推回原则”（non-refoulement）这一国际法律原则的约束；该原则禁止各国将人员遣返至其生命或自由可能面临危险的地方。
人权观察组织周三警告称，这些维吾尔人在中国面临“遭受酷刑和其他严重虐待的重大风险”，应被允许前往一个安全的第三国。
北京被指自2017年以来拘押了超过100万名维吾尔人和其他穆斯林，联合国此前曾表示，这一行动可能构成“危害人类罪”。
中国坚决否认这些指控，称其政策促进了经济发展，并在多数维吾尔人所在的 新疆 地区铲除了极端主义。
由和平权利基金会（Peace Rights Foundation）向法新社分享的两名获赦男子所写信件中，他们表示不想返回中国。该基金会为他们提供法律代理。
其中一封信写道：“如果我们回到中国，我们和我们的父母一定会被判死刑。”
“维吾尔人没有人权，所受待遇甚至不如动物。”
信中还写道：“中国在诽谤我们。我们不是恐怖分子。”

“宁死不愿回去”
泰国外交部没有立即回复法新社通过电子邮件提出的置评请求。
但根据议会会议记录，一名外交部官员9月16日对议会一个委员会表示，中国和一个西方国家均曾要求将5名被拘留的维吾尔族人移交给他们。
和平权利基金会主席坎纳维·苏布桑（Kannavee Suebsang）表示，自10月21日这两名获赦男子被转至移民拘留所后，辩护律师便无法再与他们会面。
苏布桑告诉法新社，这两人周三对泰国一名人权专员表示，他们希望被安置到第三国。
“他们拒绝返回中国，宁可去死也不愿回去。”

El CD Tenerife, club de la segunda división del fútbol español, despedirá este sábado a su fallecido delantero Jesús de Miguel con un gran acto público de homenaje. Según informó el club, todos los aficionados están invitados a asistir a la ceremonia, que tendrá lugar en el estadio Heliodoro Rodríguez López, en Santa Cruz.
Asimismo, se comunicó que el equipo, junto con el cuerpo técnico y la directiva, se desplazará a Navahermosa, en la provincia de Toledo, para asistir al funeral. El Tenerife ha decretado además seis días de luto oficial y ha suspendido todas las actividades de sus equipos masculinos, femeninos y de las categorías inferiores hasta el final de la semana. El partido contra el FC Granada, previsto para este sábado, fue cancelado el miércoles.
La trágica muerte de De Miguel, de 30 años —quien falleció el martes por la mañana en el hospital a consecuencia de las heridas sufridas tras un fuerte choque durante el partido de liga contra el FC Andorra—, resulta difícil de asimilar, declaró a los medios españoles el accionista mayoritario, Rayco García. "Estamos sufriendo muchísimo. Todo Tenerife está de luto. Son cosas que, por más que uno intente comprenderlas, resultan incomprensibles. Pero somos una gran familia y superaremos esto juntos".
Messi, CR7 y Mbappé se conduelen
En el comunicado emitido por el club, la familia de De Miguel agradeció las numerosas muestras de condolencia y solicitó, al mismo tiempo, el máximo respeto para su privacidad. García valoró positivamente la investigación iniciada por la policía española sobre las circunstancias del fallecimiento. "Necesitamos saber por qué y cómo pudo ocurrir esto", afirmó.
Mientras tanto, las muestras de pesar han trascendido con creces el ámbito del fútbol español. Estrellas mundiales como Lionel Messi, Cristiano Ronaldo y Kylian Mbappé expresaron sus condolencias a través de las redes sociales, al igual que el icono del tenis Rafael Nadal y la exestrella de la NBA Pau Gasol. El presidente de la FIFA, Gianni Infantino , calificó lo sucedido como una "verdadera tragedia".
Los compañeros de equipo de De Miguel también quedaron profundamente consternados. Junto a numerosos aficionados, se reunieron el martes ante la puerta número 9 del estadio —el número que lucía el fallecido en su camiseta— para darle el último adiós. Enric Gallego describió a su compañero de ataque como "una de las mejores personas" que ha conocido jamás: "Me alegra mucho haber compartido vestuario contigo. Te voy a echar mucho de menos". El centrocampista Juanjo Sánchez escribió: "Me dejaste entrar en tu corazón y te ganaste un lugar en el mío, pues compartimos momentos de risas cada día".

content:
German carmaker BMW reported a nearly 15% drop in third-quarter net profit on Wednesday, as competition from China shakes the global car industry.
Net profit for the third quarter fell to 1.45 billion euros ($1.61 billion), while sales fell nearly 6% to 30.45 billion euros, BMW said.
The main cause of the decline was BMW's poor business in China . Although the company sold more cars in the US and Europe compared to the same period last year, this could only partially offset the decline in China.
BMW's car deliveries in China, which were already at their lowest level since 2017 last year, fell 24.8% in the quarter and consequently dragged global deliveries down by 6.3.
CEO Milan Nedeljkovic said his company would "specifically intensify and accelerate structural measures."
Can crisis reinvent the car again?
To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video
BMW on Tuesday also lowered its outlook for the current year, citing the faster-than-planned implementation of restructuring measures that includes 8,000 layoffs in its home market.
Germany's auto industry struggling because of weak demand and competition from China
German carmakers have been struggling to compete with their Chinese counterparts in the electric vehicle market,  resulting in cost-cutting measures.
Volkswagen , the world's second-largest carmaker, is battling mounting competition from falling demand in its core Chinese market.
BMW, and its industry heavyweight peers, Volkswagen and Mercedes-Benz, have announced plans to scale back production and reduce costs.
The legacy car industry is in crisis. How can it move on?
To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video
The Volkswagen Group posted its worst quarterly results in more than a decade earlier this October.
It is looking to cut about 15% of its workforce worldwide, or 100,000 jobs, by the end of the decade. BMW has announced that it will cut up to 8,000 jobs — about 5% of its workforce — by the end of 2027.
On the other hand, German auto parts supplier Schaeffler announced on Tuesday that it planned to cut almost 3,500 jobs and close five sites in Europe, by 2028.
According to the company statement, three-fourths of the 3,460 job cuts and four of the five site closures will be in Germany.
German automotive supplier Bosch, the world's biggest, announced last year that it would cut 13,000 jobs, mostly in its auto division.

content:
El autor e ilustrador de libros infantiles Janosch murió el martes (4.11.2026) a los 95 años, según confirmó este miércoles en Tubinga su agente y editor, Bernhard Feil, citando a la esposa de Janosch.
Con sus  libros ilustrados con infinita ternura , el artista cautivó a niños de todo el mundo desde la década de 1970. Creó historias infantiles que se convirtieron en títulos emblemáticos como "¡Qué bonito es Panamá", "Correo para el tigre", "El tigre y el oso en la ciudad" o "Vamos a buscar un tesoro", y que están disponibles en español (así como en otras lenguas cooficiales de España como el catalán o el gallego).
Historias infantiles como antítesis de su propia infancia
Janosch era el seudónimo del artista Horst Ecker, nacido el 11 de marzo de 1931 en la Alta Silesia, en la actual Polonia , donde pasó gran parte de su infancia, marcada por la pobreza, la violencia y el alcoholismo de su padre. Su madre también bebía y ambos lo golpeaban cuando no se comportaba como esperaban.
Tras la Segunda Guerra Mundial (1939-1945), su familia se instaló cerca de Oldenburgo, en el norte de Alemania . Pero su origen siguió siendo para Janosch lo que describiría más tarde en su novela Polski Blues : "Una tierra de añoranza".
Sus historias infantiles funcionan como una antítesis de aquella época difícil —que él mismo intentó durante mucho tiempo reprimir mediante el alcohol—: son divertidas, anárquicamente descaradas y, a menudo, algo melancólicas. Sus personajes se rebelan contra la opresión y la injusticia; son valientes, pícaros y poseen un gran corazón.
"¡Qué bonito es Panamá!"
Sus personajes, el Tigre, el Oso y el Pato Tigre ( Tigerente ), que han acompañado a generaciones de niños, surgieron como una especie de reacción de rebeldía, cuenta la agencia alemana de noticias dpa.
Janosch estaba enojado: la Academia de Arte de Múnich lo había rechazado y sus primeros libros no habían tenido demasiado éxito. Por eso "quería hacer un libro kitsch", confesó en un documental de la cadena bávara BR . "Tenía que haber un oso de peluche y ese oso debía emprender un viaje y tener un amigo".
Ese "libro kitsch" tuvo un efecto inesperado. "Qué bonito es Panamá!" ( Oh, wie schön ist Panama! ) trajo al artista el éxito que tanto había buscado. Desde su primera publicación en 1978, el libro vendió más de dos millones de ejemplares en todo el mundo, según la editorial Beltz, y fue traducido a innumerables idiomas.
El libro infantil , convertido ya en un clásico y su obra cumbre, es especialmente simbólico y conocido en el país centroamericano. El cuento narra cómo el Pequeño Oso y el Pequeño Tigre viajan buscando "la tierra de sus sueños" guiados por el olor a bananas de una caja flotante.
Aunque es una visión de fantasía, el libro generó por décadas un fuerte vínculo cultural, reseñado con orgullo en medios de comunicación panameños, por el impacto positivo que tiene el nombre del país en niños de todo el mundo.
Hoy en día, sus libros infantiles gozan de gran popularidad en el mundo hispanohablante. Editoriales de distribución internacional como Kalandraka o Loqueleo (Santillana) hacen llegar sus álbumes ilustrados a librerías de América Latina.
Además, plataformas de audiolibros y formatos digitales como Storytel México y Argentina ofrecen sus cuentos en español para el público latinoamericano.
Traducido a casi 40 idiomas
Según su agencia, sus obras han sido traducidas a cerca de 40 idiomas y galardonadas con numerosos premios.  Su tirada total asciende a millones de ejemplares.
Para muchas generaciones latinoamericanas, el primer contacto con el universo de Janosch no fue a través de los libros, sino de la televisión.
Su serie animada Janoschs Traumstunde,  conocida en español como "El oso, el tigre y los demás", fue emitida con éxito en la televisión de varios países de habla hispana.
Se transmitió doblada al español. Y canales de televisión pública, cultural o de cable en países como México, Argentina, Colombia y Chile emitieron sus episodios, dejando una huella de nostalgia en los niños de la década de 1990.
Más de 40 años en Tenerife
Janosch se convirtió en una marca. Sus personajes (el Tigre, el Oso y el Pato Tigre) fueron comercializados con éxito bajo licencia y aparecieron en tazas, bicicletas, chupetes y otros objetos.
Tras el arrollador éxito, en la década de 1980 Janosch se retiró a la isla española de Tenerife, en las Canarias, donde residía junto a su esposa, Ines.
Desde allí, a partir de 2013 y durante varios años, deleitó también a los lectores del semanario Die Zeit  con las sabias ocurrencias de su excéntrico personaje Wondrak, el "alter ego" del artista.
"Un hombre sencillo que no necesita gran cosa"
"Mi marido es un hombre sencillo que no necesita gran cosa", comentó en una ocasión su esposa.
"En la obra de Janosch, se convierten en héroes aquellos a quienes nadie más presta atención", escribió Tillmann Prüfer, redactor del semanario Die Zeit , en el epílogo del libro "¡El señor Wondrak salva el mundo, hurra", que reúne las columnas de Janosch en la revista.
En sus obras para adultos, Janosch ofrece una visión de su dura infancia, como en su aclamada primera novela "Cholonek o el buen Dios de barro" ( Cholonek oder Der liebe Gott aus Lehm ).
En contraste con el universo tierno, alegre e inocente de sus famosos libros infantiles, esta obra muestra el lado más oscuro, crudo y autobiográfico del autor.
"Los primeros años de mi vida supusieron la destrucción total de mi persona", declaró en una ocasión el autor al diario Süddeutsche Zeitung .
Además, el autor y artista escribió obras de teatro e ilustró los relatos picantes del noble francés marqués de Sade.

content:
Janosch, the pen name of  German author and illustrator Horst Eckert, won hearts around the world with his warm and simple sense of humor. He charmed children and adults alike with his iconic Tiger, Bear, Tiger-Duck and other animals.
Janosch created more than 150 books , which have been translated into over 30 languages.
His best-selling children's book, "Oh, wie schön ist Panama," translated into English as "The Trip to Panama," was so lucrative that Janosch was able to settle down on the Canary Island of Tenerife in 1980, where he lived together with his wife Ines. The writer and illustrator died peacefully at the age of 95, his publisher Bernhard Feil announced on Wednesday.
Dismissed from arts school
Janosch was born as Horst Eckert on March 11, 1931, in Hindenburg (now Zabrze, Poland) in what was then Upper Silesia. After World War II, his family had to flee to Germany.
In 1953, Janosch started studying at the Academy of Art in Munich, thinking that it would be easy to become an artist. He was however dismissed after just a few terms for "lack of talent."
But luckily for his later readers, Janosch did not give up. He continued to work as a freelance artist, soon discovering his second great gift, namely writing.
His first children's book about a horse named Valek was published in 1960.
Although Janosch became famous primarily for his children's books, he also wrote books for adults that focused on his own childhood.
The dream of a beautiful childhood
Even though he wrote cheerful books for children, Janosch hardly had any positive memories of his own childhood, as his father was an alcoholic. He was beaten not only by him but also by his mother and grandmother. Raised in a strictly Catholic environment, he was continuously threatened to be punished by God.
Later on, Janosch tried to overcome the burden of his childhood memories by turning to alcohol as well.
He always expressed a great deal of understanding for children, trying to encourage them to stand up for their rights. As a result of his childhood experiences, Janosch did not want to have children himself, and his attitude towards the Catholic Church always remained divided. "As I am a sinner and a heretic, God will let me live a long life so that I can return to the Church," he told his biographer Angela Bajorek.
Janosch's animal figures are endearing but not always well-behaved. They love all kinds of nonsense. But even if they lie to each other or put their own interests first, the true winner at the end of stories is always friendship and solidarity.
Janosch's path towards world fame
Janosch achieved his major breakthrough with "The Trip to Panama," a story about two friends, a little tiger and a bear, who set out to find their paradise in Panama. After touring around in circles, they finally end up where they started out; they realize that their journey was the destination. Janosch received the German Youth Book Prize in 1979 for the work.
Janosch's protagonists have become familiar to generations of children all over the world. They come up over and over again in the various stories carefully illustrated with water colors.
There is the honest lion Hans from the toy chest who fails to catch a nutcracker with his lies. There is Schnuddel and a ridiculous bragger Günter the Box-Frog . And then there is a tiger that collects mushrooms while looking out for his devoted friend, a bear, who always stands up for him even when the tiger temporarily leaves him because of a little pig in one of the stories.
Merchandising with a Tiger-Duck
The "Tigerente," literally "Tiger-Duck," a wooden duck on wheels with yellow-brown stripes, appears on numerous pictures by the illustrator. At times, the animal has been tossed into a corner, at times it is hanging from the ceiling, or the Box-Frog pulls it across the drawing.
His iconic figures, especially the Tiger-Duck, have served as motifs on various items, from cups to stamps to jewelry, and even on airplanes. Film adaptations and TV series based on his stories were produced in German and English.
'He who needs almost nothing, has everything'
Guests who visited Janosch in Tenerife were impressed by his very modest lifestyle. He always said that hanging around in his hammock doing nothing was what he enjoyed most. And yet Janosch remained very active until the end of his life.
From 2013 to 2019, he wrote a column for the German weekly Die Zeit , taking on the role of Mr. Wondrak, who commented on world affairs. Shortly before his 90th birthday in 2021, the complete collection of his Mr. Wondrak columns were published as a book in German.
Like the protagonists in his stories, Janosch always tried to content himself with few things. As he wrote in one of his books: "He who needs almost nothing, has everything."
This article was originally written in German.

content:
Air pollution is an annual problem in Delhi and large parts of northern India
Published
Delhi is once again battling worsening air pollution as the onset of winter brings a familiar deterioration in air quality to India's capital.
The city's air quality index (AQI) - which measures PM2.5, fine particulate matter that can clog lungs - has crossed 300, entering the "very poor" category and raising health concerns for millions of residents.
Breathing such polluted air over prolonged periods can cause respiratory problems and worsen existing illnesses, with children and older people particularly vulnerable.
Authorities have responded by invoking Stage II of the Graded Response Action Plan (GRAP), introducing measures to curb dust, vehicle emissions and other sources of pollution.
GRAP is a set of emergency measures that become progressively stricter as pollution levels rise. The latest restrictions include more intensive road cleaning, higher parking charges to discourage private vehicle use and increased public transport services. Delhi Metro has introduced 20 additional weekday train trips, while authorities have been directed to stagger government office timings to ease traffic congestion.
Officials said the measures were introduced after forecasts suggested air quality would remain very poor over the coming days.
Delhi and neighbouring parts of northern India grapple with hazardous air every winter, particularly around Diwali, one of India's biggest festivals, which is just days away.
The festival is celebrated with lights, lamps and fireworks, which often worsen the city's already poor air quality by releasing fine particles and harmful gases into the atmosphere.
The annual pollution crisis is driven by a combination of factors, including vehicle exhaust, industrial emissions, falling temperatures, low wind speeds and the burning of crop stubble in neighbouring states.
The sharp rise in pollution follows an unusually clean October, when Delhi recorded its lowest average AQI for the month in eight years.
Experts have attributed the sudden deterioration to falling temperatures, slow winds and an increase in crop-residue burning in the neighbouring states of Punjab and Haryana.
A recent storm had brought rain and stronger winds, helping clear the air. But as the weather settled, northwesterly winds returned, carrying smoke from burning fields towards the capital.
India's pollution watchdog classifies AQI readings between 301 and 400 as "very poor", while anything above 400 is considered "severe". On Wednesday morning, Delhi's AQI stood at 377.
The index takes into account eight major pollutants, including PM2.5 - tiny particles about 30 times smaller than the width of a human hair that can penetrate deep into the lungs.
Firecrackers set off during Diwali release particulate matter and gases into the air, adding to the existing pollution
With Diwali just days away, there are concerns that fireworks could push pollution levels even higher.
Last year, Delhi woke up to a toxic haze the morning after the festival, despite a court directive to use less-polluting firecrackers.
Authorities have imposed restrictions on firecrackers over the years, including outright bans on their manufacture, sale and use, but enforcing them has proved difficult.
On Monday, India's Supreme Court allowed the manufacture, sale and use of certified green firecrackers in Delhi and neighbouring areas for a limited period.
It said the crackers could be set off only between 06:00 and 07:00 local time (00:30-01:30 GMT) and between 20:00 and 22:00 (14:30-16:30 GMT) on 7 and 8 November, during the Diwali weekend.
The court also banned fireworks within 300m of hospitals, care homes, schools and other designated silence zones.
Green firecrackers use modified chemical formulations designed to produce fewer emissions than conventional fireworks. They must carry QR codes that allow buyers and authorities to verify details of their manufacturer and certification.
But ensuring that only approved firecrackers are sold remains a major challenge.
In its latest order, the Supreme Court acknowledged that conventional firecrackers had continued to be sold as green alternatives, even when a complete ban was in place.
Even Mumbai, India's financial capital, has recorded very high levels of pollution in recent days
It has directed police to patrol designated sales areas, carry out random QR-code checks and seize illegal firecrackers.
During particularly severe pollution episodes, Delhi authorities have also introduced measures such as hybrid schooling, work-from-home arrangements and restrictions on certain vehicles.
The problem is not confined to the capital. Mumbai, India's financial hub, has also recorded elevated pollution levels over the past month, despite benefiting from coastal winds that typically help disperse pollutants.
On 24 October, Mumbai's AQI had reached 322, placing it in the "very poor" category. The spike was attributed to a combination of low wind speeds, construction dust, garbage burning, firecracker emissions and pollutants carried from neighbouring regions.
The city's air quality has improved in recent days - and it recorded an AQI of 89, classified as "satisfactory", on Wednesday. Neighbouring Navi Mumbai recorded a "moderate" AQI of 118.
The improvement follows nearly two weeks of smoggy conditions, with residents sharing photos and videos of the haze on social media.

content:
Prince William thanked the firefighters, military and volunteers who were instrumental in controlling the fire in Treherbert
Published
There is a "terrifying prospect" of more UK wildfires in future due to climate change and preparation will be "crucial", the Prince of Wales has said.
Visiting Treherbert in Rhondda Cynon Taf, which was threatened by a huge mountain fire in August, Prince William praised a "gargantuan" effort to save homes, land and lives.
"We need to start taking wildfires as seriously as the continent has done," he said, raising issues such as a lack of firefighting aircraft.
He also suggested the community's response to the incident was an example for others to follow, after locals rallied around to support those fighting the flames.
Prince William met firefighters who spent the summer tackling blazes
The hillside, just metres away from the community centre where Prince William met fire crews, military personnel and local volunteers is burnt black.
"You looked up [and] the mountain was alight - it was like lava," explained Kath Edwards, managing director of charity Valleys Kids, which runs the building.
"I genuinely thought we were going to lose the centre - but more importantly people were going to lose their homes.
"You never think this is going to come literally to your door and that's what it was - it was just crazy."
South Wales Fire and Rescue Service (SWFRS) declared a major incident as it was forced to respond to 14 wildfires at the same time in August, including the one above Treherbert.
Support was drafted in from 22 other UK fire services while soldiers were deployed to dig fire breaks and help supply 2.1 million litres of water to douse the flames, including 200 members of the Queen's Own Gurkha Logistic Regiment.
Aled Bound, who is crew manager at Maesteg fire station and a retained - on-call - firefighter at Treorchy told Prince William it was "the hardest wildfire season" he and his colleagues had ever dealt with.
Residents were given the order to evacuate as the fire came closer to the village
Months of record-breaking heat and dry conditions sparked a wave of wildfires across the UK through spring and summer.
He described it was "mentally and physically draining".
"I've never had to take so much water up a mountain to put on a fire and still come back the next day because that fire has relit, because it's so deep-seated," Bound said.
With climate change, he warned it "could well be a sign of what's to come".
Figures from the National Fire Chiefs Council show a new all-time high for recorded significant wildfires - 1,350 across England and Wales, up by more than 300 on 2025 and more than 1,000 on 2024.
Aled Bound would have a break after finishing his day job at Maesteg fire station, before racing to Treorchy to fight more fires as an on-call firefighter
Prince William told firefighters that 2026 was the first summer "where I've felt generally worried about the scale of the wildfires in the country".
He added: "We might go again next season... it's quite a terrifying prospect if we're not... on the ball."
He asked about availability of firefighting aircraft, noting that "the need for aerial assets has been hoisted quite high up in government" as an area "we're lacking".
The prince served a three-year tour flying Sea King helicopters with the Search and Rescue team at RAF Valley on Anglesey between 2010 and 2013, qualifying as a captain.
He recalled flying water bowsers in the Falklands "putting out range fires... and once the Sea King went, we don't have the assets any more".
"I think it's front and centre of many people's minds now, how do we recreate that."
Military helicopters dropped water on fires to ensure they could not return despite the intense heat in the ground - the hillside is still black two months later
Conversation turned to the kit available to fire crews working in unbearable heat, proactive land management practices and whether social media firms could do more to discourage people from setting fires.
Recently, the UK government announced that the RAF's Chinook helicopters and A400M aircraft, external would be equipped to fight fires in future.
A separate Welsh government wildfire summit also led to promises of action to improve preparedness, external.
"It feels like this is something we're going to have to live with as a country or as a world now every summer," Prince William said.
Prince William personally thanked firefighters including Adam Openshaw [centre, in firefighting kit] and Aled Bound [to his left]
"It's fair to say that we've learnt a lot from this season... and there's lots that we'll be putting into place, particularly following the wildfire summits," said Adam Openshaw, deputy chief fire officer for SWFRS.
He described the response of people in Treherbert as "the best demonstration of the community coming together to support the wildfire response".
He said it really helped as fire crews worked "tirelessly" in "challenging circumstances".
The fire at Treherbert was considered small but high risk due to its proximity to properties, the difficult terrain and the likelihood of its spreading
Edwards explained that volunteers kept the community centre open 24 hours a day from the Saturday evening of the fire until the following Thursday "to provide whatever service we could".
Due to the unprecedented nature of the fire, the centre became a control hub for the firefighting operation, a place to rest and regroup and a focal point for people wanting to show their support.
Businesses donated food - "40 pizzas arrived within the first 20 minutes" - and there were regular visits from an ice cream van.
Prince William asked whether volunteers should be used more in future and was told the community's efforts, hand in hand with military support, enabled the fire service to focus on bringing the incident under control.
Staff at the Penyrenglyn community centre including Kath Edwards [left] kept the centre open 24/7 for six successive days
"From something really quite horrific, the valleys did what the valleys do very, very well - we pulled together to make a difference," Edwards said.
Communities in the south Wales valleys were already experiencing the effects of climate change, she warned.
"We've had floods, fires... we've got [coal] tips that move as well.
"I think the message I was keen to get across is... we are motivated as a community to ask how do we solve this?
"How can we work together as a community and voluntary sector to support agencies [like the fire service]?"

content:
Some studies have linked disgust sensitivity to socially conservative attitudes.
But as Americans vote in the US midterm elections , it's time to think about how disgust shapes our politics, or whether our beliefs shape what we find disgusting?
The smell of rotten food can make us recoil. Certain sexual practices can provoke a similar reaction. And in today's polarized political climate , even political opponents can become objects of disgust.
Psychologists have long investigated whether sensitivity to disgust helps explain political beliefs. A review of 24 studies found that people who reported being more easily disgusted tended to hold more socially conservative views.
One explanation begins with evolution.
"We think that it evolved in part to reduce exposure to things that could make you sick," psychologist Yoel Inbar, of the University of British Columbia in Canada , told DW.
What are the three types of disgust?
But disgust is not a single emotion. The Three-Domain Disgust Scale , developed in 2009, distinguishes three types:
Pathogen disgust: Reactions to potential sources of infection, such as rotten food, vomit or bodily waste.
Sexual disgust: Reactions to particular sexual behaviors or situations.
Moral disgust: Reactions to wrongdoing, such as betrayal or cruelty. Researchers debate whether this reflects physical revulsion or moral disapproval.
One theory is that people who are especially wary of germs and disease may also prefer traditional social rules.
Inbar explains that avoiding potential sources of infection can also mean missing out on new experiences.
"Some people are more on the cautious conservative side, and some people are more on the exploring risk-taking side when it comes to pathogen exposure," he said.
Indeed, the language of contamination also appears in political rhetoric. During his 2024 presidential campaign, Donald Trump repeatedly described immigrants as "poisoning the blood of our country." Trump has also described himself as a "germaphobe."
Inbar acknowledges that the evidence linking sensitivity to disgust with conservative political beliefs remains uncertain.
"We have hypotheses. I don't know that we have as strong of evidence as I would like," Inbar said.
Do liberals and conservatives feel disgust differently?
Disgust is not exclusively conservative. And what people find revolting can depend on their values.
A 2020 study titled "Is Disgust a "Conservative" Emotion?" found that liberals and conservatives were disgusted by different things.
Conservatives, generally aligned with the Republicans in  US politics , reported greater disgust at examples involving sexual behaviors and drug use, while liberals, generally aligned with the Democrats , reported greater disgust at animal abuse and environmental pollution.
However, when asked how easily disgusted they were in general, there was no clear difference across the political spectrum.
Can our bodies reveal our politics?
Some early studies suggested conservatives showed stronger physical reactions to frightening or disgusting images, measured partly through changes in sweating.

But subsequent research, including a 2020 study by political psychologist Bert Bakker at the University of Amsterdam , struggled to reproduce those findings.
Studies based on questionnaires, however, have generally found that people with more conservative attitudes report being more easily disgusted.
"If bodily reactions don't differ across political groups, why do feelings?" Manos Tsakiris, of Royal Holloway and the Centre for the Politics of Feelings at the University of London , told DW.
How do gut feelings influence political beliefs?
Tsakiris and colleague Mariana von Mohr wondered whether the answer might lie in how people perceive and interpret signals from their bodies.
Scientists call the perception of internal sensations, such as hunger, breathing or a racing heart, "interoception." It's sometimes called our eighth sense, alongside the familiar five, plus our senses of balance and body position.
"A bodily signal doesn't arrive with a label attached," Tsakiris told DW. "We have to notice it and make sense of it."
The researchers surveyed 632 US adults , asking how much they noticed and trusted signals from their bodies — a measure known as "interoceptive sensibility."
They found that people who were more easily disgusted by sexual behavior tended to be more conservative, regardless of how aware they felt of their bodies.
But for moral disgust, the link to conservatism was found only among people who reported lower bodily awareness.
What particularly surprised Tsakiris was that perceived bodily awareness alone had no link to political views.
"People who are highly attuned to their bodies were neither more liberal nor more conservative," he said.
Can disgust actually be measured?
Inbar questions whether all forms of disgust are equally useful for studying political attitudes.
He and Joshua Tybur, one of the creators of the Three-Domain Disgust Scale, generally prefer measuring pathogen disgust — reactions to potential sources of disease — rather than sexual disgust.
Questions about sexual disgust may already reflect conservative beliefs about sex.
"It's almost asking people the same thing twice," Inbar said.
The new study found no significant link between pathogen disgust and conservative views.
Inbar wants the findings on bodily awareness and disgust tested again, with predictions set out in advance. For now, he considers them "suggestive at best."
How might politicians exploit feelings of disgust?
Tsakiris suggests that people who struggle to understand their bodily feelings may be more vulnerable to political messages telling them what those feelings mean.
"I know what you're feeling. You're feeling angry or you're feeling disgusted about this thing," he said, illustrating how someone might put an emotional label on another person's unease.
Such labels could influence political behavior, he argues, although the study did not directly test this.
What's behind the rising polarization in German politics?
To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video
"This is how disgust can do political work: it can turn moral judgments about individuals into judgments about whole groups," he said.
Does disgust influence how people vote?
The research cannot establish whether disgust shapes political beliefs or existing beliefs shape what people find disgusting. Bakker notes that political beliefs can influence how people describe their own personalities, suggesting the relationship could work both ways.
"Voting behavior is very complex and citizens make up their mind about politics in a complex way," he told DW.
Inbar also cautions against exaggerating disgust's importance. "The thing to emphasize in your story is that the relationship, while it's consistent, is quite small," he said.
"It's one of the many influences on people's politics."
Tsakiris advocates what he calls "critical feeling": questioning our emotional responses to provocative material, including social media posts, just as we question the information itself.
He also emphasizes discussing our feelings with others and listening to different perspectives, even when we disagree.
"Life and politics and democracy is a contact sport," he said. Edited by: Rosalie Delaney

content:
Canva co-founder Melanie Perkins says this year has been "our hardest" yet
Published
Canva, one of Australia's best known start-ups, has announced a shake up of the business that will affect 22% of its workers, including job cuts.
In what was "without doubt the hardest moment in our thirteen-year history" co-founder and CEO Melanie Perkins said 1,271 people would either lose their jobs, be asked to relocate or change roles.
The firm's value has reportedly dropped in the past year over concerns about the impact of artificial intelligence (AI) on its business as well as the cost of incorporating the technology into its platforms.
It had been "our hardest year yet, and as we shared earlier this year, our growth has slowed for the first time in a decade," Perkins wrote to staff.
The "incredibly hard decision" meant "significant changes," Perkins said.
"For some people, this will mean changes to their roles or being asked to relocate to centralised hubs. Sadly, it will also mean saying goodbye to teammates and friends who have helped build Canva into what it is today."
The company, which has staff in 37 countries, said Sydney would become the "primary home" for more of its product teams and that as of next year hybrid workers would be expected to spend two to three days in the office.
Earlier this year two of its backers, Blackbird Ventures and Airtree, reportedly downgraded its valuation from A$60bn ($41.8bn; £31.1bn) at the end of last year to about A$49bn.
Canva also reportedly cut its own internal valuation amid soaring AI expenses related to the roll out of new products.
"New technology is transforming what people can create, how they create it, and what they expect from the products they use," Perkins said in her note on Wednesday.
Perkins, who left university at 19 to found her first venture, launched Canva in 2013.
The company offers a variety of templates and tools to help users without technical skills or a design background to create a range of professional-looking graphics and presentations, from wedding invitations to business pitch decks.
summary: CEO Melanie Perkins says more than 1,000 staff will either lose their jobs or be asked to change roles.

title: Canva announces major job cuts after 'our hardest year yet'

content:
Managing AI agents is a big part of Lotte Underwood's job
Published
Recent university graduate Lotte Underwood is a public relations executive with a twist - she spends more time using AI than actually doing PR.
Underwood, 25, joined London-based PR agency Fight or Flight in November last year, in the new role of "AI associate" after completing a degree and then a masters in marketing.
She's part of a recently established, dedicated AI team that has built around 30 AI agents. Specific tasks include industry research, client reporting, media interview preparation, helping clients create clearer briefs, and image generation.
A big part of Underwood's job is to manage those agents, check their outputs and feed those to the team members who are dealing directly with clients and the media.
Another key responsibility of hers is to monitor how clients appear in the responses from AI tools like ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini and others.
"A huge part is being in client meetings and calls to work out what is actually going to be most helpful from these agents," says Underwood.
AI is seen as one of the main factors behind graduate job cuts, but companies are also creating dedicated AI-specific graduate roles like Underwood's.
Dillan Patel, for example, joined engineering software company Stride 18 months ago as an intern. A business management graduate, he was put to work developing an internal chatbot designed to capture the knowledge of a senior staff member transitioning into retirement.
Patel, 24, is now an AI automation analyst, tasked with developing further internal agents to provide specific information to individual teams, while also identifying which manual or repetitive tasks across the company could be done by AI.
"My role focuses on finding practical ways to use technology, automation, data and AI to improve how we operate," says Coventry-based Patel.
Debra Maxwell is looking for "AI disruptors"
Such AI savvy graduates are also in demand from companies like ArvatoConnect, an outsourced contact centre company.
CEO Debra Maxwell says the company's usual graduate intake is on hold this year, but she plans to resume it next year with a bigger focus on AI.
"We would be looking for more AI-disruptor type roles, where you can challenge us as an organisation to think more holistically about where AI can be applied and where we could grow our business from," says London-based Maxwell.
"We see our graduates as not filling administrative roles, but actually adding value to the organisation in a different way."
Maxwell adds: "For example, one of our recent graduates is using AI to do deep dives on specific markets, and provide more information for when we're bidding [for new contracts]. It's basically giving him a more rounded role."
If AI can make a graduate job bigger and more integral to the organisation, Maxwell argues that companies can create a more loyal, engaged workforce that is able to contribute more meaningfully, much earlier.
Research from consultancy PwC found that some graduate roles are assuming more responsibilities because of AI, as it allows companies to demand more senior abilities from junior hires.
For the consultancy's 2026 AI Jobs Barometer, external, it analysed 2.4 million entry-level jobs in the US. It found that the entry-level roles most influenced by AI are now seven times more likely to require traditionally senior-level skills. These include motivational leadership, strategic decision making and team building.
Those entry-level roles with higher expectations have in fact grown 35% since 2019, PwC found, while other entry-level roles actually shrank by 10%.
Cian Clinton uses around ten AI agents for work tasks
Cian Clinton, who joined consultancy Valliance last September after graduating from a Bachelor of Science in 2024, says the incorporation of AI into his role makes him feel less like a graduate, and more like an equal team member. He uses around 10 AI agents daily for different tasks.
"Your ideas and your creativity are a lot more valued because you actually get to implement those firsthand, and the responsibility you take on is a lot greater because of that," says London-based Clinton, 23.
"I am now taking on responsibilities which would usually take me four or five years to get to."
His career progression, he believes, will now be faster as a result.
"AI is killing the 'pyramid' approach…progression is no longer based on your knowledge bank. Now it's more based on your critical thinking and understanding of the processes," says Clinton.
'Learning the trade'
There's no doubt Underwood, Patel and Clinton are developing valuable AI knowledge which can help them across their careers.
But with their time at work so focused on AI, does it matter how much - or how little - time they're spending learning about the professional field they're supposed to be operating in?
Underwood says she'd like to still pick up the traditional PR skills her role isn't currently focused on, but is confident of her future in the agency's growing AI team.
"There's certain things that I haven't had the chance to do yet, like directly pitching to the media. I absolutely plan to do this," she says.
Graduates becoming too AI-centric is an issue for Simon Pratt, chief operating officer at Portman Finance Group. He says being able to use AI effectively is important, but the company's two-year graduate programme is fully centred on "learning the trade".
"Our graduates rotate across four areas at six-month intervals, working directly alongside senior relationship managers to learn their trade," Northampton-based Pratt explains.
"They'll learn all of our financial products, how to draft credit papers for submission to lenders, and how to build meaningful relationships with our customers. They'll progress to running transactions from start to finish."
Claire Reid, PwC UK's chief technology and innovation officer, believes graduate roles that are too AI heavy won't necessarily provide graduates long-term career progression.
"There will be no graduate job now that doesn't require a baseline of AI literacy," says Glasgow-based Reid.
"But AI skills on their own are not going to help you in your career. You've got to couple that with that sector knowledge of what that client actually wants."
Back in Coventry, Dillan Patel is confident his AI work will continue to be valuable, and he wants to keep building on it.
"I don't think I'd want to explore different positions within the business. Through my involvement in AI-related projects, I already work closely with different areas of the business and I'm gaining valuable knowledge and experience along the way," he says.

summary: Graduates are spending more time managing AI, but are they missing out on other work experience?
