content:
The UK and EU have agreed a draft deal on removing post-Brexit checks from food and agriculture exports, ahead of the UK-EU summit later this month.
The BBC understands the 200-page draft text for this so called "SPS" [sanitary and phytosanitary] agreement has been circulated to EU nations in Brussels for consideration at a meeting on Wednesday.
Similar texts for deals on emissions trading and a youth travel and work scheme have also been circulated alongside a 15-page draft joint statement for UK and EU top leaders.
The food deal is the most significant part of the so-called Brexit reset agreed so far, removing checks and red tape that hit exporters after the UK exited the EU's single market.
As a result of the agreement, the government claims the UK economy will eventually see £5.1bn worth of annual benefits.
Speaking during the Commonwealth Heads of Government Meeting (Chogm) in Antigua and Barbuda, the prime minister said a UK-EU deal could add up to 0.4% extra on GDP.
The deal could have the following impact:
Exports to the EU of fresh sausages, burgers, shellfish from domestic waters and seed potatoes would be able to resume
It should remove the need for £200 Export Health Certificates, which confirm the product meets the health requirements of the country it is heading to
It should also end the need for £25 Phytosanitary certificates, which show that plants or plant products are free from pests and diseases
Inspector fees, organic certificates, some port fees and other checks for exports and imports to and from the EU could be removed
It will bring back passports for British pets being taken into the EU
In return, the UK is expected to commit to observing and adapting to existing EU regulations on plant, animal and food trade standards - a process called "dynamic alignment".
Each of the elements on the table was up for discussion under Sir Keir Starmer, and the summit would have taken place by now had Labour not replaced its leader in July.
Under Andy Burnham, Britain's approach to post-Brexit relations with the EU have shifted significantly. Sir Keir said the UK would not rejoin the bloc in his lifetime, while Burnham has said he would like to see Britain back in the EU in his.
At Chogm on Tuesday, Burnham said: "I think people in Britain would expect me to take that with both hands, given where we've been in recent times, and that's what I'm doing."
Pressed on whether it would be acceptable for the UK to have its rules on food trade made by the EU, he said: "We're not in the EU, therefore we do have to work with them in a different way.
"But if that can get growth, if that can help our farmers, if that can remove red tape from British businesses, I think most people would expect me to go to that summit and negotiate the best deal that I can.
"And that's what I've been doing in recent weeks, leaning in, being positive, having a really constructive relationship with our European partners and hopefully we can land a good deal for Britain in terms of growth but also I hope more collaboration on controlling immigration."
Jon Walsh of Bio&Me said his firm had stopped exporting yoghurt due to vets' fees
Jon Walsh, the chief executive and co-founder of Bio&Me, which makes granolas, mueslis and yoghurts, told BBC 5 Live the draft deal sounded like "really good news".
"We're just a small company but when we were trying to export our yoghurts before, every time we'd send a pallet we had to pay a vet to inspect it and that was £140, and that meant that you'd lose money... so we had to stop."
The company also had problems exporting granola and overnight oats, with some shipments being returned.
"It was so frustrating because it was the same person filling out the same form and yet half would make it through and half wouldn't," Walsh said.
"You just kind of give up because you're losing money."
In an interview with ITV, Burnham said "public opinion has changed nationally" since the 2016 Brexit vote, but added he would "not run ahead of public opinion" on the issue.
"The public need to be the boss when it comes to whatever happens with Brexit," he added.
Burnham also said he had not proposed the return of freedom of movement between the UK and EU.
Asked by the BBC about the UK's relationship with the EU, Tory Leader Kemi Badenoch said that while we should "work closely", "dynamic alignment" with the EU would be a red line and "actually take us backwards".
Liberal Democrat Europe spokesperson Al Pinkerton said the draft deal was a "patch, not a fix".
"The real solution is to rejoin the single market and to establish a customs union with the EU," he added.
Reform UK's business spokesman Richard Tice said: "One of the key benefits of Brexit was that Britain no longer had to adhere to ridiculous EU rules.
"Returning to any form of alignment with Europe would crush Britain's competitiveness and force us to surrender sovereignty over trade policy, putting trade deals worth hundreds of billions of pounds at risk."
European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen with Prime Minister Andy Burnham
While UK rules remain mostly aligned with EU ones, there are some areas where England has diverged from the EU rule book, for example on "precision breeding" of plants, previously known as gene editing. In recent weeks, agreement has been struck on transition arrangements while the EU's new regulations come in to force.
The government has already announced a European Partnerships Bill which will provide a legal mechanism for the application of new EU rules and regulations. This will also allow for the necessary alignments for the linking of the UK emissions trading scheme with the EU's, and save the need for UK exporters to pay the EU's new carbon border tax.
The draft agreements will be discussed at a meeting of EU ambassadors called Coreper on Wednesday, with some key details on the planned numbers in a Youth Experience Scheme to be finalised at a political level in the coming days. A discount on full foreign student fees for EU students is likely to be pushed to next year alongside a plan to reconnect electricity markets.
The BBC understands the draft agreements will also include some references to UK involvement in defence co-operation schemes, access to law enforcement databases and some reassurances over the EU's "Made in Europe" plans.
A food deal will have particular significance for Northern Ireland, radically reducing the impact of the post-Brexit Irish Sea border.
Northern Ireland's Brexit deal kept it inside the EU's single market for goods. That means food products from elsewhere in the UK require paperwork and some physical checks when arriving at NI's ports. A deal will ultimately end those requirements.
While the food trade plans have been backed by supermarkets and farmers representatives, some pro-Brexit campaigners have criticised the reapplication of EU rules. The post-Brexit trade deal signed by Boris Johnson's government prioritised regulatory freedoms for the UK over avoiding new regulatory red tape, checks and delays.
But William Bain, the British Chamber of Commerce's (BCC) head of trade policy, told the BBC's Today programme that business overall thought it was a "price is worth paying" to follow common rules, as companies would benefit from "lower costs, reduced delays [and] increased market access".
At the moment, he said, the requirement for Export Health Certificates can add thousands of pounds of costs to each truck carrying goods, in addition "to the delays that people find at the ports or at the borders".
"So we get lower exports because of the delays and the massive increases in costs that have come into the supply chain."
The BCC has released a new analysis of its members' views suggesting options for a closer relationship.
The business lobby group says the current trade relationship is "failing to deliver", leaving firms "struggling with a thicket of Brexit red tape" nearly six years after the UK's exit from the bloc.

content:
Hackers who stole a record $6.3bn (£4.7bn) from Binance used fake job interviews and a compromised internal AI tool, the firm has revealed.
Initial findings published by the company, which operates the world's largest cryptocurrency exchange, said hackers gained access to its systems through a "sophisticated, multi-stage campaign".
It said they used a range of techniques such as malicious software downloads to compromise the computers of Binance engineers and gain control over tools to drain its wallet of billions of dollars worth of crypto.
Binance called it a "serious and highly sophisticated security incident" and apologised, saying "this should not have happened".
In a post on X, external, Binance said hackers targeted its engineers using social engineering techniques.
These see hackers use approaches such as phishing to trick people into parting with sensitive or personal details, which can then be used to try and access their accounts.
Binance said as part of the hack, one of its engineers was contacted through a legitimate job-hunting platform and invited to bogus job interviews with fake company representatives.
It said the perpetrators used "more advanced and deceptive" methods to build trust with him, such as sharing social media accounts which contained personal images.
The engineer in question was instructed to download malware masquerading as an "assignment" during a second interview, which deployed malicious code with "obfuscation techniques" evading detection.
Binance said hackers then leveraged the engineer's compromised computer and an internal AI tool to gain control over two other engineers' laptops, and execute the next steps of the attack.
The incident led the firm to suspend withdrawals for customers globally, meaning users could not get their cryptocurrency out of the platform until the service was restored on Sunday.
Customers withdrew billions of dollars worth of assets after it reopened.
"We apologise for the concern, disruption and uncertainty it caused our users, partners and the wider industry," it said.
The company added it had taken a range of steps following the incident, including working with law enforcement to trace and freeze affected assets.
It said it had also set aside more than 100% of the funds needed to cover the loss, and said 98% of the token assets impacted had been "replenished" as of Saturday.
It is thought to be the largest crypto hack to date.
What we know about the $6.3bn Binance hack
North Korea involvement
US crime agencies, including the FBI and Secret Service, have been assisting Binance in tracing the crypto taken from the platform's own wallets.
The agencies, along with a range of cyber analysts, said the hack - like similar breaches before it - bore the signs of having been orchestrated by North Korea.
Pyongyang hit back at the claims on Tuesday, denying it was behind the hack.
Kim Yo Jong, a top North Korean official and the sister of leader Kim Jong Un, said the accusations were another "sinister attempt" by the US to damage the counry's public image.
The country has consistently denied being behind a number of major cyber-attacks it has been blamed for in recent years.
The TraderTraitor unit, which is also known as the Lazarus Group, was blamed for a then-record $1.5bn hack of crypto exchange Bybit in 2025.
Binance had previously not responded to the BBC's queries about North Korea's alleged involvement in the hack.
But on Tuesday, the company wrote in its post on X, external: "The latest information released by the Federal Bureau of Investigation indicates that the Democratic People's Republic of Korea is responsible for this incident."
As part of its security efforts following the attack, Binance said it would also increase investment in AI tools which can detect security threats, as well as engage third-party cyber experts to carry out a full-scale review of the incident.
It also said that it would seek to establish a security research fund and work with leading AI and security firms on targeted initiatives.

（德国之声中文网）在 俄罗斯 与 乌克兰 即将就 结束战争 展开新一轮谈判之际，乌克兰总统泽连斯基访问柏林。德国总理默茨在总理府与其举行会见。
泽连斯基在会面时表示，欧洲的参与对于实现和平至关重要，将尽一切努力确保欧洲各国在所有安全挑战上形成共同立场， 包括如何结束这场战争 。他还强调， 和平必须是有尊严的 ，只有这样，和平才能持久。
泽连斯基此前在社交平台X上表示，计划与默茨讨论乌克兰防空问题，以及如何帮助乌克兰修复和保障遭受重创的能源供应系统。出于安全考虑，此次访问事先并未对外公布。
泽连斯基还在会上表示，乌美俄三方会谈将于近期恢复，时间为11月10日至11日。
这与美国总统特使史蒂夫·威特科夫（Steve Witkoff）宣布的消息吻合。威特科夫表示美俄乌将于下周二、周三在阿联酋首都阿布扎比举行新一轮会谈。谈判将由三国政府首脑及国家元首的顾问级代表参加。
威特科夫说：“会谈将围绕战后安全安排、局势降级、人道主义援助措施以及迈向和平的后续行动展开。”
DW专访泽连斯基：愿去美国见普京
To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video
欧洲国家要求参与谈判
威特科夫还表示，美国特使本周将与德国、法国、英国、北约以及欧盟代表举行会晤。此次在布鲁塞尔举行的会谈将讨论乌克兰安全保障、战后欧洲安全秩序以及乌克兰重建等议题。
欧洲国家坚持要求参与与俄罗斯的谈判。德国方面预计，即便目前看来欧洲代表未必能直接坐在谈判桌前，他们也将以某种形式出现在阿布扎比。
年底前还有三场重要峰会
阿布扎比会谈后，今年年底前还将举行三场重要峰会。
亚太经合组织（APEC）峰会。11月18日至19日，在中国深圳举行的APEC峰会期间， 美中俄领导人可能借此机会举行三方峰会 。 中国是俄罗斯 在乌克兰战争中最重要的支持者。西方多国政要表示，如果没有中国的帮助，普京根本无法继续这场战争。
“志愿者联盟”峰会。大约在同一时期，柏林计划举行“志愿者联盟”峰会。该联盟由约35个支持乌克兰的国家组成。峰会将讨论如何进一步援助乌克兰，尤其是帮助乌克兰抵御俄罗斯在冬季发动的攻势。
乌克兰急需爱国者拦截导弹
To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video
G20峰会： 12月13日至15日，二十国集团（G20）峰会将在美国佛罗里达州举行。一个引人关注的问题是：自俄罗斯入侵乌克兰以来，俄罗斯总统是否会首次重返G20峰会？如果普京出席，作为东道主的特朗普是否也会邀请乌克兰总统泽连斯基？
乌克兰需要防空导弹和700亿欧元
默茨与泽连斯基在柏林的会谈，预计也将涉及德国及其他国家对乌克兰进一步的军事和财政援助。
在军事方面， 乌克兰尤其需要防空导弹 ，以拦截俄罗斯弹道导弹。其中最有效的装备是美制“爱国者”（Patriot）防空系统。尽管许多其他国家也拥有这类系统，但很难将其调拨出去，因为这些国家自身也需要防空保护。
德国联邦国防军已经交出了 所有在不危及自身防空能力的前提下能够提供的“爱国者”系统。
泽连斯基表示，乌克兰明年还需要欧洲国家额外提供700亿欧元。这一金额是他在今年10月举行的欧盟峰会上提出的。
如何筹集这笔资金，将成为今年剩余三场欧盟峰会的讨论议题之一。届时，讨论重点将是欧盟的中期财政规划。

content:
It’s easy to run out of words to describe Rabindranath Tagore. The first non-European to win the Nobel prize in literature, Tagore was a Bengali poet, musician, novelist, philosopher, songwriter, painter, humanist and educator.
Born in 1861, Tagore left an indelible mark on the subcontinent’s literature, music, education and art. Among his enduring legacies are the national anthems of India and Bangladesh.
As Nobel laureate economist Amartya Sen once wrote, Tagore was “a towering figure in the millennium-old literature of Bengal”, whose songs resonate across eastern India and Bangladesh, while his ideas on education, nationalism and freedom of the mind remain relevant today.
Yet his work also made a deep impression on the literary world far beyond the shores of India. WB Yeats is said to have described Tagore as “greater than any of us”. Gitanjali, the collection of poems that won Tagore the Nobel prize that same year, was praised by the committee for its “profoundly sensitive, fresh and beautiful verse”. Tagore’s English translation was published in London that March and reprinted 10 times by the time the prize was announced in November.
Tagore’s life and works have, of course, been well documented, but a collection of material preserved in a private family archive is now being brought into public view for the first time at an exhibition by Christie’s, opening in Mumbai this month. The archive draws from Tagore’s visits to the family home of his protege, Maitreyi Devi, in the bucolic village of Mungpoo in Darjeeling between 1938 and 1940. He died in 1941.
The collection on display – artworks, manuscripts, letters, photographs and personal effects – offers an intimate glimpse into Tagore’s creative process and personal world in his final years.
I spoke to the exhibition curator, Nishad Avari, head of south Asian modern and contemporary art at Christie’s, about the stories behind the archive.
One instructive document Avari points to is a manuscript from 1940. It appears to be a draft of Tagore’s memoir Chelebela or My Boyhood Days, in which he reflects on his life – from growing up in a large family in Calcutta (modern-day Kolkata) to the rapidly changing world ushered in by electricity and the motorcar.
For Avari, what stood out was how the ideas in the document echoed the educational philosophy Tagore put into practice in Santiniketan (or Abode of Peace), the experimental school he set up about 100 miles from the state capital.
“He speaks about how education is like being in prison and that it should be open and free … about the idea of wonder and even fear as inspiring creativity,” Avari told me.
“That’s a direct relationship to Santiniketan and the open model of the school where people sat under trees with their gurus and learned in the open. Education didn’t feel like a restriction, prison or imposition,” he added.
Avari points to another detail that makes this particular document valuable. Of the 10 complete manuscripts in the exhibition, it is the only one dictated to Devi, whose father was a close friend of Tagore’s. For Avari, this speaks to their close relationship and the trust he placed in her.
“If you look at the collection as a whole, she has copies of almost every single one of his publications signed to her by him,” he says. The collection includes hundreds of letters, too: first between Tagore and her father, and later between Tagore and Devi herself.
There are doodles among corrections, Avari explains, which show how his literary practice fed into his artistic practice. Alongside the manuscripts and correspondence are vintage photographs and personal effects, including a kurta and a lungi that Tagore left behind at the family home.
Among the artworks in the collection is a portrait of Devi, particularly notable because Tagore’s figure studies were not generally attributed to specific individuals in the way that portraits by his nephews, Abanindranath and Gaganendranath, often were, Avari said. There is also a landscape depicting the forests of Mungpoo, which Tagore embraced as a retreat.
On the international art market, Tagore’s paintings command significant prices. This year, Sotheby’s sold one of his watercolours for £1.02m (Rs 12.97 crore), nearly four times its low estimate.
Institutions such as Visva-Bharati in Santiniketan and the National Gallery of Modern Art hold much of Tagore’s archival materials, making the discovery of a private archive particularly rare.
He hopes that making these materials public will offer historians, scholars and admirers alike additional perspectives on Tagore. “We hope to add to the understanding of the artist, their career, and in this case, of course, our understanding of the man beyond his art as well.”
Rabindranath Tagore and Mungpoo runs between 10 November and 18 December at Christie’s space in south Mumbai.
What else we’re reading about
Politics | India has invited Pakistan to attend the Shanghai Cooperation Organisation’s Civilisational Dialogue Forum in New Delhi later this month, the Indian Express reported. It is the first invitation since the two neighbouring states engaged in a military conflict last year.
Law | Twenty-one media organisations have challenged India’s privacy laws in court, arguing that the controversial provisions threaten press freedom, Reuters reported. The petition warns that the law could expose journalists’ sources and force publishers to remove stories at the direction of authorities.
after newsletter promotion
Academia | Indian academic Mahmood Kooria, a lecturer at the University of Edinburgh, is among this year’s recipients of the Philip Leverhulme prize in Humanities. The £100,000 award recognises his work on the premodern Indian Ocean world.
Guest shelf
A recommendation from someone with great taste
Freddy Birdy, a copywriter whose delightful words have earned him a devoted Instagram following, recommends writer and historian Malvika Singh’s cookbook, Cooking for My Firefly.
“This book isn’t about recipes, though it does include them. It is a voyage through another time and place, tracing the social fabric of India of the 60s, 70s and 80s, trickling down to today. Told in Malvika’s beautiful prose, it takes us to a time when people entertained in homes, not in restaurants; when dishes were cooked in-house and there were no caterers or party planners. An era long before Instagram posts, WhatsApp invitations, celebrity chefs and food delivery apps, when the point of having a party was simply to have fun. It is an archive of photographs, food, culture, gossip, movie stars, politicians, royalty, set against the spectacular backdrop of Malvika’s dining tables through the decades. I like to dip into it every now and then, much as one might do standing in a dark kitchen with the light of the refrigerator enticing you to midnight goodies.”
Count it
A number worth knowing
22,495
Indians lost Rs 22,495 crore (£1.77bn) to cyberfraud in 2025, Times of India reported citing data from the Home Ministry. While the figure is marginally down from the previous year, losses have risen sharply since 2023.
Vibe check
At a time when public anger has spilled into the streets, artist Aamir Aziz’s new track, Dopeher Blues (Afternoon Blues), captures the frustration and angst of a generation that has lived through many crises.
Aziz describes the song as an expression of a period of deep suffocation. Issues such as farmer suicides, unemployment and conflicts in Palestine and Kashmir, he told me, are things he has grown up with even as public attention shifts with the news cycle. It is also a warning, in part, against internet culture, where injustices risk becoming normalised.
Aziz, 35, works in acting, music and writing, and became an internet sensation with his defiant poem Sab Yaad Rakha Jayega (Everything Will Be Remembered) during the citizenship protests. At the heart of his new track is a note of defiance and hope: “We’ll find a way to sing,” he says, as he calls on everyone “to keep speaking up even in a climate of fear, misinformation and oppression.”
Get in touch
Do you have any thoughts or responses to this week’s newsletter? Is there anything you’d like us to cover in the future? Share your feedback by emailing us at thisisindia@theguardian.com and we may include your response in a future issue.

content:
（德国之声中文网）欧盟委员会批准中国电商巨头京东收购欧洲最大的电子产品零售商MediaMarkt/Saturn的计划，但需满足特定条件。京东和Ceconomy在一份联合新闻稿中宣布，所有交割条件均已满足，交易将在未来几天内完成。
京东于去年7月宣布已签署协议 ，收购总部位于德国杜塞尔多夫的Ceconomy。Ceconomy是两大主要零售商MediaMarkt和Saturn的母公司，估值为22亿欧元。MediaMarkt和Saturn拥有1000多家电子产品门店，主要分布在德国，同时也分布在其他几个欧洲国家，并运营着在线销售平台。
由于京东收购Ceconomy的交易触发欧盟2023年7月正式生效的《外国补贴条例》以及传统的反垄断合并审查机制，因此该交易完成前必须由欧盟委员会进行审理及放行。 欧委会于2026年4月正式受理该交易申报。
5月份进行初步调查后，欧盟认为京东在这次收购中“可能获得了扭曲欧盟内部市场的中国政府的直接补贴、税收优惠或低息贷款”，并于5月28日依据欧盟《外国补贴条例》 启动了第二阶段深入调查 。调查重点为这些补贴手段是否使京东能够为收购Ceconomy的交易中出价更高，以及这些援助是否提升了合并后实体的竞争地位。
针对欧盟的调查，中国司法部2026年8月曾公开表态， 这构成“不当域外管辖” 并下令相关方应对。
此次收购也引起了柏林方面的关注，德国政府已就该收购是否会对国家安全构成风险展开独立调查，并于今年6月底 有附带条件地批准了这项交易 。附带条件旨在确保德国客户的个人数据得到充分保护。此外，德国政府还获得了广泛的监督控制权，可以在发生违规行为时撤销此次批准。
附条件批准
欧委会在调查后认定，京东曾以优惠融资、税收减免和拨款的形式从中国获得补贴。欧委会同时也认为，以这种方式获得的产能最终可能也会被提供给Ceconomy，并且可能通过“激进定价”向竞争对手施压。
欧委会因此在11月3日宣布，依据《外国补贴条例》对该交易给予附条件批准，包括要求确保京东与 Ceconomy 合并后的集团内部交易、以及京东向其未来子公司提供的资金支持，必须严格按照市场条件进行，以防止产生交叉补贴及扭曲欧盟单一市场。
此外，京东必须承诺，向欧盟其他第三方零售商提供仓储、物流及技术服务时，所适用的条件和条款不得逊于提供给 Ceconomy 的条件。 上述各项承诺的有效期为10年。
针对欧盟委员会附条件批准京东收购的Ceconomy的决定，京东表示，其商业模式和战略保持不变，并将继续以此为基础实现加速增长。
京东的年销售额接近1590亿美元（2024 年），据EHI零售研究所的数据，它是中国最大的零售集团之一，也是全球十大零售集团之一。该集团拥有约57万名员工，业务还涉及科技、物流和医疗保健等领域。迄今为止，其在德国的业务规模有限。今年3月， 京东推出了线上商城Joybuy 。
（德新社、法新社）

（德国之声中文网）《法兰克福汇报》分析文章指出，一段时间以来，欧洲人一直担心，一场新版“雅尔塔会议”即将上演，即由中美俄三国领导人商讨乌克兰乃至整个欧洲的未来。不过，上周五，中国国家领导人习近平同德国总统施泰因迈尔举行的会谈中，习近平已经亲口否认了这种说法，并强调这是欧洲的冲突，欧洲人必须参与谈判。《法兰克福汇报》以《他不想要新版雅尔塔》为题的分析文章写道：
“这一说法也印证了此前中西方代表的相关会谈内容。 中国 显然既没有兴趣举办这样一个关于乌克兰问题的高峰会晤，也不愿意进一步得罪欧洲，更不希望为促成乌克兰和平去承担任何责任。更重要的是，在重塑世界格局的问题上，中国并不认为俄罗斯是一个可以与其平起平坐的会谈伙伴。
一名观察家认为：‘中国想要的是G2。’被华盛顿视为地位平等的超级大国，才是中国的战略利益所在。中国和 美国 才是同一等级的超级大国，俄罗斯并不属于这一阵营。另一名观察家也表示，中国并不希望主办乌克兰问题峰会。不过，中美俄三国领导人在深圳就其他议题举行峰会，则仍有可能。 在下届APEC峰会期间，举行 中美俄三方会谈 的建议最先是由俄罗斯方面提出的。据《华尔街日报》未经证实的报道，普京本人曾建议在深圳举行谈判，以期在对莫斯科有利的条件下结束俄乌战争。这样的会谈显然会提升普京的国际地位。这也就引发了所谓‘第二次雅尔塔会议’的讨论：世界三大强国就如何划分势力范围展开谈判。相关报道在欧洲引起了极大的担忧，因为欧洲各国以及乌克兰并非太平洋沿岸国家，因此也无缘参与深圳的APEC峰会。乌克兰外长瑟比加就曾明确发出警告说，绝不可以在被入侵国缺席的情况下举办所谓的三方峰会。10月21日，乌克兰外长还同中国驻基辅大使举行了会谈。”
《法兰克福汇报》分析文章认为，鉴于美国中期选举、伊朗战争走向都还不明朗，在深圳APEC峰会期间，即便中美俄领导人会举行三方会谈，其象征意义也会多过实质内容：
“此外，北京显然不希望同欧盟的矛盾进一步升级。 欧盟 强化了其贸易保护工具，并在积极扩展同 亚洲民主国家 的关系。中国需要欧洲市场。观察家们普遍认为，至少在2027年的党代会之前，出于稳定内部政治环境的需要，中国希望保持和谐稳定的对外关系。
为此目的，北京首先会利用深圳峰会的机会，向世界展示中国的强国地位，并赢得国际声誉。中国当然乐见俄罗斯继续活跃在外交舞台上，但北京绝不愿意为乌克兰谈判担负责任，更不愿意为这场战争提供安全保障。显然，对中国来说，战争继续打下去的局面是可以接受的。毕竟这场战争牵制了北约和欧洲，并给他们造成了巨大负担。这也正是北京称乌克兰战争是‘欧洲事务’的原因之一。”
《商报》评论指出，一些德国企业一边在中国扩大投资，一边却在德国本土裁员关厂，这种趋势不仅削弱了德国的产业基础，也与对华“去风险”目标背道而驰：
“凡此种种都充分说明，企业持续推动‘中国本土化’的决策，越来越同德国和欧洲的经济利益背道而驰。过去，在境外建厂能够产生更大的规模效益和利润，进而可以扩大在德国本土的研发投入。而现如今，企业在 中国 获取的利润会再度投入当地，德国本土却在削减工作岗位。
有鉴于此，除了设立新的贸易保护工具以及推动供应链多样化之外， 欧盟 还应采取更多的措施，比如加强对欧洲企业境外投资的监管力度。
2025年初， 欧盟 曾对各成员国提出建议，希望他们从欧洲供应安全的视角，去评估半导体、人工智能和量子技术领域的境外投资。现在，应首先将这一建议转化成具有约束力的规定，并将其适用范围扩大至更多技术领域和供应链范畴。此后，还应采取进一步的措施。例如，获得公共资金支持应与企业的研发和产能是否留在欧洲相互挂钩。”
摘编自其他媒体的内容，不代表德国之声的立场或观点。

Asda headquarters are based in Leeds city centre
Published
Asda has appointed a former Morrisons boss as chief executive to help lead revival efforts at the supermarket chain.
Asda, which is based in Leeds, said David Potts would take on the role with immediate effect, while current boss Allan Leighton would become non-executive chairman, two years after returning to lead the supermarket chain.
Potts led Morrisons from its Bradford headquarters for eight years until 2023, overseeing a turnaround during which the supermarket chain was bought by US private equity firm Clayton, Dubilier & Rice.
Potts said Asda had "made good progress but significant opportunities remain" to reinvigorate sales, with a focus on keeping prices low for shoppers.
"By making improvements to the shopping trip every week, which customers can experience and feel in their pockets, we will revitalise the business and bring benefits for all our stakeholders, including our 116,296 very hard-working colleagues," he said.
Before joining Morrisons, Potts was chief executive of Tesco's Irish business, its UK arm and its Asian operation.
David Potts led Morrisons for eight years until 2023
According to Asda, Leighton had planned to step aside from the day-to-day running of the group, after he returned in 2024, more than two decades after serving as chief executive.
"Over the last two years, we have stabilised the business and returned it to some growth," said Leighton.
"David has an outstanding record in our industry, his experience is exactly what we now require for the next stage of our transformation and beyond and it will be great to work with him."
Last year, issues with an IT upgrade hit product availability at the supermarket and dented sales, impacting its bottom line.
But in August, it reported sales had returned to growth for the current quarter for the first time in two years.

Rio Tinto is ploughing millions of dollars into stopping the poisonous cane toad reaching the Pilbara region of western Australia, where the mining giant has a vast iron ore operation.
The firm, alongside Curtin University in Perth and others, will spend A$28m (£14.5m) building a "toad containment zone" to prevent the pest travelling south.
While the cane toad is not a direct threat to Rio Tinto's business, it produces toxins lethal to native wildlife and poses a threat to Pilbara's ecosystem.
Rio Tinto has previously faced criticism for destroying two sacred Aboriginal rock shelters in Pilbara which sat above tonnes of iron ore.
The decision cost the former chief executive his job, provoked a widespread backlash and saw Rio Tinto commit to rebuilding trust with Indigenous communities.
Commenting on the proposed containment zone, Roberta Hunter, a ranger in Australia's Nyangumarta Warrarn Indigenous Protected Area, said: "Cane toads destroy the water and animals.
"When toads come close to our country, we want to be there to stop them because we don't want the country to be destroyed."
The plan is to cut off the toad's water supply by building a barrier across 7,500 sq km (2,895 sq m) of land between the Great Sandy Desert and the Indian Ocean.
In drier months, the cane toad needs water every few days to survive.
If there are no natural water sources, the toad relies on artificial water points normally used for cattle and irrigation.
The funding will be used to stop the toad accessing dams, storage tanks or other ground-level water sources. The five-year project will begin in 2027.
A number of native species are at risk if the toad gets into Pilbara. These include the northern quoll, whose numbers have been decreasing, the goanna lizard and the ghost bat.
The toads were introduced into Australia in 1935 to control beetles within the sugar cane industry.
The northern quoll is at risk from the cane toad in Australia
Since then, they have been on a slow march west across the country's northern landscape, according to the Australian government, travelling between 40 km and 60 km a year.
There are no predators or diseases that control the toads, which defend themselves using poison.
Ben Phillips, a professor at Curtin University, said the toads would reach Pilbara within two decades without action.
He said: "The toad containment zone is a once in a lifetime opportunity to stop one of the world's worst invasive species in its tracks and protect the region's unique wildlife."

media.alt: A northern quoll sits on the branch of a tree

summary: Rio Tinto is jointly funding a A$28m "toad containment zone" to protect the Pilbara region.

"Adira" is an Arabic slang term used in Levantine queer culture to describe someone with a strong presence — someone powerful and accomplished.
It is also the name of a Berlin-based collective that curates events and club nights celebrating the diversity of queer Arab* culture. The asterisk signals the inclusion of non-Arab ethnic minorities and people with diverse identities and roots in Southwest Asia and North Africa.
Among the collective's events is the ADIRA Drag Festival , which celebrated its third edition in Berlin in late October.
This year's theme, "Who's Your Diva?!," brought together drag performers paying tribute to legendary figures from across the Eastern Mediterranean who have become queer icons — from Egyptian music legend Umm Kulthum to Turkish star Bülent Ersoy and Lebanese pop icon Haifa Wehbe.
Hassandra, co-founder of ADIRA and the ADIRA Drag Festival, was among the performers, taking on the persona of Lebanese pop star Elissa.
Inspired by 'imperfect' divas
"It is very important for me to bring my Lebanese Arab identity and culture into what I do, because I think it's a very beautiful culture. And there's a lot of campy, glamorous, beautiful divas," Hassandra said.
Elissa's "whole discography is very romantic, raw, soft, kind of like very Adele vibes," Hassandra told DW ahead of the October 30 show. "However, her personality is known to be the extreme opposite. She's very feisty. Very blunt, very unfiltered. Not soft at all as a person."
The star is also known for speaking out on political issues in Lebanon. She has publicly voiced support for LGBTQ+ communities in the Middle East, while also frequently sparking controversy across the Arab world with her outspoken positions on other political issues.
Hassandra's ADIRA Drag Festival performance addresses this complexity, ultimately "tapping into her sort of controversial political opinions," the drag artist explained.
This reflects one of the ideas Hassandra hopes to promote with the theme of this year's festival. "As queer people, we tend to idealize a lot of pop divas. But these pop divas are very imperfect in their nature," Hassandra said. The show provides an opportunity to critically revisit these divas' legacy through a more critical lens.
"And this sort of critical lens can be taken into the outside world, as in: never follow anyone in life blindly. No one should follow any politician, any political party, any pop diva, any activist blindly."
Building community through drag
Born in Beirut in 1994, Hassandra studied theater and stage acting at the Lebanese University before moving to Berlin in 2017. "I would say it was it was just a very sort of impulsive decision at the age of 22. I mean, there's no doubt that the economic situation was really bad in Lebanon and continued to become even worse," the artist said.
In Berlin, Hassandra became increasingly involved in the city's independent art scene and queer nightlife. Drag emerged as another form of self-expression for the actor.
Through performances that combine theatrical intensity, political humor, grotesque aesthetics and moments of tenderness, Hassandra challenges conventional understandings of gender and identity.
Their work explores themes of home, nostalgia, displacement and queer Arab culture. These ideas are also central to ADIRA, which Hassandra founded in 2023 with Syrian-German DJ and cultural producer Zuher Jazmati, also known as xanax_attax.
Through panel discussions, performances and music events, ADIRA fosters collective participation and community-building.
As  Islamophobia and homophobia rise alongside  the far right , spaces like ADIRA offer a sense of belonging and support for Arab queer communities.
That sense of community has become even more important following the deadly Islamist terrorist attack during  Berlin's Christopher Street Day pride parade in July.
What does the Berlin Pride attack mean for city's identity?
To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video
In the aftermath, Hassandra felt caught between their different identities. As an Arab queer person, "you fall in this position where then you start receiving a lot of racism," they said.
"And I think this is why it's important, for us queer Arabs, to say we are sad over what happened, but that we also reject any of the racism that comes from that," Hassandra said. "I think we [the Arab community] are being used in a lot of ways as a punching bag for a lot of things that are happening."
Rather than allowing the attack to fuel hatred and racism, Hassandra said, "we should make Germany a safer place for everyone to live in." "There's place for everyone. It's a huge country," they added.
The interview with Hassandra was conducted by Gönna Ketels.

content:
In an interview with the Cyprus News Agency on October 4, the new US ambassador to Cyprus , John Breslow, outlined plans to upgrade the Andreas Papandreou Air Base in Paphos to accommodate large US military transport aircraft.
He also announced plans for more frequent visits by US warships to Cypriot ports and an expansion of joint military activities.
But one statement carried particular political weight: his assurance that "the United States will protect Cyprus in the future."
Although the remark does not constitute a formal US security guarantee, it reflects the growing cooperation between the two countries.
For a country that for decades maintained close ties with Moscow, viewed US foreign policy with suspicion and is not a member of NATO , the prospect of an expanded American military presence marks a significant geopolitical shift.
It is perhaps the clearest indication yet of Cyprus's gradual loosening of ties with Russia and its increasingly close strategic alignment with the United States.
The nonalignment years
The shift is particularly striking given Cyprus's political history.
In the years after it gained independence from the United Kingdom in 1960, the Republic of Cyprus sought to balance its relations between East and West.
Under the leadership of Archbishop Makarios III, the first president of independent Cyprus, the country became a founding member in 1961 of the Non-Aligned Movement , a forum of nations that did not align with either of the two superpowers of the day: the United States and the Soviet Union .
This approach allowed Nicosia to maintain close ties with the Soviet Union without severing its connections to the West.
EU membership
Even after joining the European Union in 2004, Cyprus maintained strong political, economic and military ties with Moscow.
Relations with the United States, by contrast, remained overshadowed by the Turkish invasion of the island in 1974 and the US's failure to take decisive action against Ankara.
The United States prioritized maintaining its strategic relationship with Turkey , a key NATO ally, over taking a tougher stance against the invasion.
The US position fueled widespread anti-American sentiment in Cyprus, culminating in a violent demonstration outside the embassy in Nicosia on August 19, 1974, during which US Ambassador Roger Davies was shot dead.
Mistrust deepened further in 1987, when the United States imposed an arms embargo on the Republic of Cyprus, officially intended to prevent an arms race on the island and avoid undermining efforts to resolve the Cyprus conflict .
Close relations with Moscow
The US arms embargo contributed to the reliance of the Cypriot National Guard (the armed forces of the Republic of Cyprus) on Russia-made weapons systems, strengthening the Kremlin's position as a major military partner.
The response by Cyprus to Russia's annexation of Crimea in 2014 illustrated the strength of these ties.
The Cypriot government expressed serious reservations about imposing tougher EU sanctions on Russia. Then-Foreign Minister Ioannis Kasoulides warned that such measures could have devastating consequences for the Cypriot economy.
Relations with Moscow deepened further in February 2015, when President Nicos Anastasiades visited the Russian capital and signed a series of agreements with President Vladimir Putin .
These included a naval cooperation memorandum facilitating visits by Russian warships to Cypriot ports. Moscow also agreed to more favorable repayment terms for its €2.5 billion loan to Cyprus in 2011.
Cooperation remained close as recently as October 2021, when then Foreign Minister and current President Nikos Christodoulides signed a Strategic Cooperation Framework for 2022–2024 in Moscow alongside his Russian counterpart, Sergey Lavrov.
Turning point in 2022
The decisive turning point came just four months later, in February 2022, with Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine .
Konstantinos Adamides, an associate professor of international relations at the University of Nicosia, told DW that the invasion accelerated a geopolitical shift toward the West that had already begun.
"For the first time, the Republic of Cyprus openly and unequivocally chose to side with the West, despite the economic and political costs of breaking with Moscow," Adamides said.
Nicosia aligned itself with EU sanctions against Russia, despite the Cypriot economy's strong links to Moscow, particularly in services, investment and tourism.
The decision marked a significant departure from Cyprus's traditional foreign policy approach of maintaining a balance between Russia and the West.
Adamides said the government's position on Russia paved the way for closer relations with the United States, particularly in the field of security.
Cyprus, he said, succeeded in convincing Washington that it could serve as a reliable partner in the Eastern Mediterranean.
What form does the rapprochement take?
The rapprochement had already gained an institutional foundation before the war, with a bilateral statement of intent on security cooperation signed in 2018.
Further initiatives followed, including the Cyprus Center for Land, Open-seas and Port Security (CYCLOPS), a US-funded training facility inaugurated in Larnaca in April 2022. The center provides training for security personnel from Cyprus and other countries in the region in areas such as port security, counterterrorism and preventing the trafficking of hazardous materials.
An even more significant development for the Cypriot National Guard came in September 2022, when Washington announced the full suspension of the arms embargo imposed in 1987.
The decision allowed for the export of lethal military equipment to Cyprus, subject to the necessary US approvals. The suspension, which was not permanent and remains subject to periodic renewal, has been renewed until September 30, 2027.
Cyprus and NATO
The strategic security reorientation is also significant because Cyprus is not a member of NATO.
The crash landing of an Iranian done on the British military base at Akrotiri in March reignited a debate in Cyprus about whether the country should join NATO.
At the time, Christodoulides said Cyprus was preparing for potential membership at the military, operational and administrative level and would apply to join NATO "even tomorrow if it were possible."
Christodoulides said, however, that joining the alliance was not possible because "the political conditions are not there, taking into account the well-known position of Turkey."
Phasing out Russian weapons
The country's changing strategic orientation is also reflected in the modernization of its armed forces.
After decades of relying heavily on Russian military equipment, Cyprus is seeking to gradually reduce its dependence on Russian-made T-80 tanks and Tor-M1 and Buk air defense systems.
The process accelerated following Russia's invasion of Ukraine, as sanctions against Moscow made it increasingly difficult to secure spare parts and ammunition for Russian weapons systems.
Another important step came in January 2025, when then President Joe Biden authorized Cyprus to participate in US defense procurement programs, including Foreign Military Sales (FMS) and Excess Defense Articles (EDA).
The decision gave Nicosia access to additional mechanisms for acquiring US military equipment, further strengthening defense cooperation between Cyprus and the United States.

content:
Polish authorities said they carried out inspections of two passenger planes targeted by bomb threats on Tuesday but did not find any explosives, in a string of bomb threats that hit several European airports.
A bomb alert forced a LOT flight from London's Heathrow to make an unscheduled landing at Warsaw -Modlin airport, prompting the airport to shut down. Operations resumed around midday.
"The passengers were evacuated and the plane underwent security checks. Nothing was found," airport spokesman Adam Szablowski told the French AFP news agency. "The airport has been reopened and is operating normally."
A SAS Scandinavian Airlines flight from Copenhagen also received a bomb threat before landing safely at Warsaw's central Chopin airport, where it underwent a security inspection.
No explosives were found on either plane. It was not immediately clear whether the threats were linked.
Flights bound for Spain, Bulgaria also targeted
Also on Tuesday, a Ryanair flight from Manchester, UK, to Murcia, Spain , was hit by a bomb threat. It landed safely and underwent checks after all the passengers had disembarked.
The Spanish government's delegate in the region of Murcia, Francisco Lucas, confirmed on X that police "ruled out the presence of explosives on the plane."
"The International Airport of the Region of Murcia resumes its activity normally. Thanks to the emergency teams that have participated in the operation," he said.
And in the fourth such incident, the Reuters news agency reported that another flight traveling from Israel landed in the Bulgarian capital, Sofia , on Tuesday after a bomb threat was received via email. Counter-terrorism units were checking the plane for possible explosive devices, BTA news agency quoted Interior Minister Secretary General Lyubomir Nikolov as saying.
Later, two more bomb threats also targeted Ryanair flights from Lisbon and Dublin to Rome’s Fiumicino airport, according to Italian media. Air Force jets were deployed as a result. Both threats turned out to be false alarms.
The six threats on Tuesday come after a WizzAir flight from London to Sofia was redirected to the Hungarian capital, Budapest, on Monday after it received a bomb threat mid-air.
Similar such incidents have been reported across different European airports in recent weeks, with alerts later turning out to be false.
summary: The bomb threats involved two passenger planes bound for Warsaw, a Ryanair flight from London to Spain, two flights to Rome and a flight traveling from Israel to the Bulgarian capital, Sofia. No explosives were found.

（德国之声中文网）据《北京商报》《凤凰财经》等中国媒体报道，周一（11月2日）晚，头部主播李佳琦与千问办公CEO陈宇森在直播间带货千问办公会员月卡，原价每份28元的会员月卡以直播价0.01元促销，经过半个小时手速火拼，该月卡售出10万份，对应的 算力 额度约为2万亿个AI Token。
Token，即词元，是 人工智能 模型处理文本时使用的基本单位。
据《北京商报》报道，这款办公会员月卡包含每月通用积分、产物存储云盘、排队并行任务数量等服务，该报评论称商家联手头部主播，赚的是流量，会员转化，以及未来商业变现的想象空间。
这是AI算力套餐首次作为重要消费品类进入“双11”促销活动。“双11”是全球规模最大的购物节，最初定于每年11月11日举行。
科技研究机构Omdia首席分析师苏廉节（Lian Jye Su）对路透社表示：“ 中国消费者现在已经非常习惯使用AI生产力工具 。”
他补充说，频繁使用这些工具的消费者可能会遇到算力额度不足的情况，因此在促销期间大量购买“是非常合理的选择”。
“口红一哥”首次销售AI产品
这场直播是李佳琦首次销售AI产品。他因在网上销售大量口红、积累了庞大的粉丝群体，而获得“口红一哥”的称号。
直播中展示了千问办公算力套餐、搭载AI功能的笔记本电脑以及办公设备如DingtalkA1、QwenNoteA2AI听记卡等AI硬件。
李佳琦询问陈宇森，能否利用AI为自己制作一个数字分身，让它全天候与粉丝聊天互动。
陈雨森回应说，AI虽然无法取代李佳琦，但他希望AI能够帮助用户处理日常事务，让人们有更多时间陪伴家人。
AI算力进入大众消费场景
《北京商报》援引艾媒咨询集团CEO兼首席分析师张毅的话指出“李佳琦卖Token事件，表达的意图可能比卖多少Token还要重要。”卖Token更像是一场大众客户端市场启蒙运动，把面向企业客户端的技术叙事拽进大众消费的语境里。
电商巨头阿里巴巴表示，旗下天猫已为“双11”推出AI Token专区，提供来自阿里云、MiniMax、月之暗面和智谱AI的面向消费者的算力套餐。
京东也设立了AI Token专区，整合了包括DeepSeek、智谱AI以及字节跳动旗下火山引擎在内的多家企业服务。
AI更像“人”了，但我们准备好了吗？
To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video
阿里巴巴 表示，10月1日至20日，AI算力套餐销量较上月同期增长450%。此外，在“双11”促销活动正式开启后的第一个小时内，AI个人电脑笔记本的销量同比增长超过300%。
苏廉节对路透社表示，算力套餐通常设有相对较长的有效期，这可能促使消费者提前囤积。不过，他也提醒，AI产品更新迭代迅速，消费者可能会担心预付费购买的服务很快被新产品取代，甚至停止运营，因此对提前付费有所顾虑。
“双11”购物节自2009年启动，旨在刺激消费。第三方数据机构星图数据（Syntun）统计显示，去年各大电商平台“双11”总销售额达到1.70万亿元人民币（约合2550亿美元）。

content:
Sweden was among countries to report a cyber incident in which some supermarket fridge units had been hiked up in temperature
Published
Businesses in the UK's food supply chain have been impacted by the cyber-attack which hit supermarket fridges and freezers across Europe on Monday.
The National Cyber Security Centre (NCSC) says it is aware of "a couple of instances where vulnerable technology had been exploited in the UK."
The NCSC's chief executive Dr Richard Horne told the Today programme, on BBC Radio Four, that it had "worked through the night" to alert potentially affected organisations in the UK.
The British Association of Independent Meat Suppliers (AIMS) told the BBC some of its more than 300 members had unexpectedly become what it called "collateral" as part of the hacks.
Two members saw their fridges begin to defrost, AIMS said, while another saw their cold units rise up to 100C (212F) in temperature.
AIMS spokesman Tony Goodger said the affected devices were empty at the time so no produce was lost - but urged businesses to be vigilant.
The incident "must act as a reminder to all in the food industry at whatever point in the supply chain they are that their businesses may be seen by some as targets," he said.
On Monday, supermarkets in countries including Ireland, Sweden, Estonia, and Belgium reported fridges and freezers being hiked in temperature.
The events followed attacks targeting supermarkets and food suppliers across France in early October.
Hundreds of stores were targeted by the overnight hack, which spoiled fresh and frozen food estimated to be worth millions of euros.
Those attacks exploited vulnerabilities in some systems used to remotely control and manage cold refrigeration units that had been surfaced by cyber-security researchers months prior.
Horne told the BBC on Tuesday that it was still "too early to say" who was behind the hacks.
But he said it pointed to an urgent need for organisations and businesses to ensure the technology underpinning a whole range of applications we use and need daily was secure and up-to-date.
"That technology base we rely on as a society has not been invested on to the extent it needs to be," Horne said, noting many firms had extended systems beyond their end of life, not upgraded them nor kept them in secure compartments disconnected from the internet.
Such actions can create vulnerabilities that many cyber-security experts say amounts to low-hanging fruit for hackers, and can be easily exploited.
But the UK's cyber chief said that they could be found and exploited more quickly and easily via "AI in the hands of our adversaries".
"We do need all organisations to look at what they rely on, to invest in renewal," he said.
"We intervene where we can. But, at the end of the day, it's your business. It's your charity. It's your life. You need to make the choice and choose wisely."
Thrown away food
Around 40 Delhaize supermarkets in Belgium and Luxembourg were affected in Monday's cyber incident, while a smaller number of shops were hit in Sweden, Ireland, the Netherlands, Estonia and Finland.
Sabcobel, a Belgian company that manufactures some of the affected refrigerators, said the units' evaporators were switched to defrost mode, causing them to warm up.
The same method was thought to have been used in last month's incident that hit hundreds of French supermarkets.
As with that incident, many of the retailers affected on Monday said they had no choice but to throw away spoiled food - some saying this amounted to hundreds of thousands of euro in lost produce.
Mathieu Tilman, who runs a Delhaize supermarket in Belgium, told the BBC he found it "truly distressing".
"There's so many people starving, people who don't have enough to eat. How can we end up throwing away so much food?"
"In moments like these, you just feel like quitting your job."
So far, there have been little to no signs of any such impact in the UK.
But the BBC has approached major UK supermarkets for comment and asked what action, if any, they are taking to safeguard against any similar hacks attempts.
"Retailers invest heavily in their cybersecurity and are currently working with the NCSC to ensure their fridges and freezers are secure as possible against potential attacks," said Graham Wynn, assistant director of regulatory affairs at the British Retail Consortium.
Asda, Lidl, M&S, Sainsbury's and Tesco are among the retail trade association's members.
Paul Chichester, director of operations at the NCSC, said at the launch of its annual report on Tuesday it was continuing to work with and monitor UK organisations affected.
"At the moment, the impact is minimal," he added.
"We're working with organisations identifying existing vulnerabilities in the UK and trying to get those closed before somebody exploits them."

（德国之声中文网）英国《金融时报》报道援引了三位知情人士的消息称，中国证监会过去几天与投资银行举行会议，通过“窗口指导”非正式要求暂缓推进企业上市。报道还称，现有股东的大规模减持已暂时叫停，直至市场回暖。
路透社未能立即核实该报道。中国金融监管机构尚未回复路透社的置评请求。
“微调”收效甚微
中国证监会、中国人民银行和国家金融监督管理总局本周一（11月2日）向外公布，已与证券公司和基金公司举行会议，讨论稳定股市的措施，包括将股票回购增持再贷款工具从阶段性安排转为长期制度性安排，股票回购再贷款款利率从1.25%下调至1%等等。
然而，这些提振 股市 的努力收效甚微。本周二（11月3日），人工智能相关股票领跌，A股主要指数震荡下跌，截至收盘，沪指跌0.82%，深证成指跌1.21%，创业板指跌2.73%，科创综指跌4.84%。全市场超3300只个股下跌。
中国能取代美国 成为头号强国吗？
To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video
投资者认为，目前的金融支持措施力度不足。业内人士指出，当前的问题在于市场缺乏信心。一旦信心丧失，就必须依靠持续的现金买入来支撑股价。但目前政府推出的稳定市场措施仍是敦促市场参与者自行出资，而非由政府直接提供资金。而大股东缺乏足够的动力去借钱买入正在下跌的股票，因为他们必须自行承担相应的风险。
此前，受人工智能相关股票大跌拖累，中国股市基准沪深300指数在10月份暴跌8.5%，创下十多年来最大单月跌幅。今年以来，这一指数已累计下跌约14%，同期美国标普500指数则上涨10%。
“国家队”出马？
2024年9月，中国曾通过降息和下调存款准备金率来刺激经济，从而开启了随后 两年的牛市 。花旗集团（Citi）中国首席经济学家余向荣表示：“鉴于实际增长和名义增长均面临压力，我们认为，规模堪比2024年9月24日的政策支持，或许已为时不远。”
瑞银（UBS）经济学家团队也认为政策支持力度有望进一步增强，但淡化了政策力度能与两年多前相提并论的可能性，因为在其看来，目前中国经济增长仍处于决策者可接受的范围内。
本周一，中国人民银行宣布自11月15日起，将外汇存款准备金率由4%上调至6%。这是中国央行近5年首次出手上调外汇存准率。人民币汇率当天创下五个月来单日最大跌幅。央行此举旨在给人民币近期的涨势“降温”。遏制人民币汇率过快上涨有助于出口，而出口堪称当前中国经济中唯一的亮点。
此外，据China.Table的报道，投资银行高盛估计，10月份短短两周内，约有1700亿元人民币流入指定的交易所交易基金（ETF），并由所谓的“国家队”（由北京支持的投资公司）通过支撑性购买遏制股市下跌。
报道称，稳定股市对北京来说也是一个敏感的社会问题。房地产价格多年下跌后，股市本应提振市场信心，从而达到鼓励民众增加投资收益和消费支出的目的。
然而，过去几个月股市的惨淡表现对于许多散户投资者来说，无疑是巨大的打击。“他们原本希望北京在芯片、人工智能和机器人领域的数十亿美元投资能够带动股价上涨。然而，那些入场较晚的投资者如今却蒙受了巨大损失。”
报道认为，目前的情况可能促使北京对股市进行近一年半以来最强有力的干预。

content:
Drivers may be offered compensation from lenders ahead of the next legal battle in the car finance mis-selling saga.
Regulator the Financial Conduct Authority (FCA) said it would welcome lenders making settlement offers as long as customers were not given a worse deal than under its proposed central scheme.
That scheme is facing a legal challenge, to be heard in February, with resulting compensation unlikely to be paid until late next year.
But Barclays has confirmed it will make early compensation offers from now, with others expected to follow suit.
The FCA said it would still only expect a minority of claimants to be made early offers, with most having to wait for the outcome of next year's court case.
Stephen Braviner Roman, the FCA's general counsel and co-lead on the motor finance project, said: "Fair settlement offers could result in some people getting money sooner. It's clear they want the choice.
"Anyone who wants to wait can, and there's no obligation to agree to the offer. We'll closely monitor firms making offers and expect them to be clear what accepting an offer means."
Why drivers will receive payouts
The vast majority of new cars, and many second-hand ones, are bought with finance agreements. Customers pay an initial deposit to secure the vehicle, then a monthly fee with interest.
But millions of drivers who took out a car loan between April 2007 and November 2024 will be entitled to compensation after the loans were mis-sold.
They mostly related to when car dealers received commission from lenders, based on the interest rate charged to the customer. These were known as discretionary commission arrangements (DCAs) and customers were often not told about them.
Average compensation payouts of about £829 are expected to be made related to about 12 million car loans - about 37% of the total number during the period.
Compensation will cost the industry up to £9.1bn, including administrative costs. Individual payouts will vary, depending on the degree of harm each driver faced.
With huge compensation payouts inevitable, some lenders have already set aside millions of pounds to cover the cost.
Barclays has decided to start making compensation payments early, potentially to start clearing the cost off its balance sheet. It pointed out that claimants had already faced "a considerable wait".
"By making these early settlement offers, we are giving some customers the option of receiving redress sooner, rather than waiting for the legal challenges and any subsequent FCA action to conclude," said a Barclays Partner Finance spokesperson.
"Each offer will be calculated using the FCA's redress scheme methodology. We will clearly explain how it has been calculated and what accepting a full and final settlement means, so customers can decide whether accepting the offer is right for them."
The lender said claimants would start to be contacted directly "in the coming weeks".
But it stressed not all customers whose complaints were acknowledged on or before 1 October 2026 would receive an early settlement offer.
Guidelines on whether to accept an offer
The FCA has published a factsheet to help drivers, external work out whether they should accept early settlements from lenders.
It will include a list of lenders who are making early offers, to ensure claimants with other lenders are not scammed.
The regulator said lenders will need to be clear with people about what accepting any offer means. This includes:
Being able to keep any payment, even if the final settlement under the central scheme after the legal challenges proved to be smaller
Claimants would not be able to claim more later if the outcome of the legal challenge meant they would have been paid more
Accepting an offer takes you out of the scheme and stops any further input from the financial ombudsman
The Finance and Leasing Association, which represents lenders, said: "We want to see consumers receive the fairest outcome in as timely a way as possible and recognise that, in some cases, that may point to early settlement, while in others it may be appropriate to await greater legal certainty."
But Kevin Durkin, solicitor advocate and director at HD Law, who represented Marcus Johnson who won his case in the Supreme Court, said he had "real reservations" that fair compensation would be offered.
"These are only heightened by reports that just a small number of claimants will receive what could be lowball offers. I fear this is crumbs from the table, for some customers who are highly likely to be owed more, while the vast majority will receive no offer at all," he said.
The main proposed FCA scheme remains partially suspended, pending legal challenges in February.
Consumer group Consumer Voice said the proposed compensation scheme left "too many people short-changed". Three lenders - Volkswagen Financial Services, Mercedes Benz Financial Services, and Credit Agricole Auto Finance - are also challenging the scheme.
The UK's Upper Tribunal has agreed to hear legal challenges to the scheme, with a hearing scheduled from 16 February to 3 March.
Anyone who is concerned about their car finance deal and has not yet complained can still complain directly to their lender. There is information on the FCA website on how to complain for free, external.
summary: The regulator says it supports lenders offering early compensation offers, as long as they are fair.

"Heartbroken with pain, with a lump in our throat and unable to believe this is real." Those were the words with which Spanish second division football club Tenerife confirmed the death of 30-year-old Jesus de Miguel on Tuesday.
De Miguel was involved in a clash in the middle of the pitch with FC Andorra's  Equatorial Guinea international goalkeeper Jesus Owono, who had raced out of his goal to try and clear the ball with the score 2-2 late in the game. Owono was sent off and the match was abandoned.
Spanish media reported that De Miguel suffered a cardiac arrest and was resuscitated. The player was taken to hospital and placed in intensive care, with Tenerife later saying that De Miguel's condition had "worsened neurologically" before his death.
After confirming the death on Tuesday morning, the club posted that: "No words can ease the pain, nothing can lessen this great feeling of sadness. Our thoughts are with the family, his close friends and Tenerife fans, who today are grieving over this terrible news."
Andorra also sent their "most sincere condolences" as messages of support began to flood in on Tuesday.
"I am so deeply sorry. Rest in peace, Jesus," former Barcelona defender Gerard Pique, Andorra's majority shareholder, wrote on social media.
Real Madrid , Barcelona, Atletico Madrid and other clubs in Spain also sent messages of condolence, as well as the Spanish FA (RFEF).
"Shattered by this sad news, the Royal Spanish Football Federation wishes to express our deepest sorrow at his passing today," wrote the federation in a statement.
The RFEF postponed Tuesday's matches in the Copa del Rey and Copa de la Reina, "as a gesture of respect and solidarity."
De Miguel had been with Tenerife since joining from from Castellon in 2025. He began his career with Leganes at youth level in the Madrid suburbs, playing for a string of teams, including Unionistas de Salamanca, before signing for Castellon in 2023.

summary: Tenerife forward Jesus de Miguel has died following a collision with the opposing goalkeeper. The Spanish second-division club has said it is "heartbroken" by the loss.

A little over two months before it was set to kick off, the Asian Football Confederation (AFC) has postponed its flagship international football tournament in the wake of recent deadly attacks on host country, Saudi Arabia .
The AFC cited "substantial logistical complexities and travel disruptions" caused by conflicts in the region .
Instead of January 7, 2027, the tournament will now kick off on December 23 and end on January 21, 2028. The postponement follows delays and cancellations of a number of sporting events in the region, including a Formula One race , the men's and women's tennis finals, the 2027 Dakar Rally and disruption to Asia's marquee continental club football tournament, the AFC Champions League Elite.
Saudi Arabia hosted, and won, the Gulf Cup last month , but there had already been much talk about whether the much larger Asian Cup could go ahead.
Houthi attacks make tournament impossible
It was scheduled to feature 24 teams playing matches in eight venues across Riyadh, Jeddah and Khobar. However, the AFC said that "circumstances arising from developments in the region , including substantial logistical complexities and travel disruptions," made the tournament impossible.
"Exceptional circumstances have been created for the organization and delivery of the competition as originally scheduled, making the postponement necessary in the interest of all participating teams, officials, spectators and other stakeholders."
In particular, the postponement was forced by a recent wave of deadly attacks on Saudi Arabia by Iran-backed Houthi rebels as well as other raging conflicts in the region. The Houthis have targeted Saudi infrastructure, including airports. They are fighting a Saudi-led coalition supporting Yemen's internationally recognized government, a civil war that reignited in July following a years-long truce.
More fighting between Yemen's Houthis, Saudi Arabia
To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video
The AFC had been under pressure from several federations to postpone the tournament, with South Korea's players leading the way.
Player and fan safety comes first
"The ongoing military tensions and security instability in the Middle East are issues that cannot be taken lightly," Lee Keun-ho, president of the Korea Professional Footballers Association, said last month, according to the Yonhap News Agency.
Lee added that "no tournament's value can take precedence over the lives and safety of players and football fans."
It seems that the AFC now agrees. However, following the announcement of the postponement, Yasser al-Misehal, chairman of the local organizing committee, promised that Saudi Arabia was "fully ready" whenever the tournament ended up being held.
"The tournament will move to the new dates, and our preparations will continue as planned," he told the Saudi Press Agency.
"We're working closely with the AFC and all our partners to make sure the tournament runs smoothly and meets the high standards expected of Saudi Arabia and the Asian Cup."
Saudi sports investments dwindling with World Cup on horizon
Saudi Arabia has invested hugely in sports over the last decade, from owning Premier League teams to hosting boxing title fights and bidding for a number of major sporting events, most notably World Cup 2034 , which they won the right to host unopposed.
However, the country has recently withdrawn or slashed funding for a number of sporting events including golf , rugby, tennis and winter sports.

content:
The so-called "quiet quitting" trend where workers do the basic requirements of a job but refuse to do anything more might be hitting the economy, analysis has found.
Over the last decade, Britons have become less engaged with the jobs they do and are less willing to put in extra effort, according to a Resolution Foundation report.
The thinktank said this could partly help explain the slump in productivity since the pandemic.
"This is self-evidently bad for workers, but it also doesn't bode well for productivity and labour supply, both of which are vital for lifting living standards in the years ahead," said Hannah Slaughter, principal economist at the Resolution Foundation.
Quiet quitting was popularised on social media shortly after the pandemic.
Frustrated by high demands, low pay, and a squeeze in living standards, many online posts said workers should only do what their bosses asked and nothing more.
So you still show up for work, but no more helping out with additional tasks or checking emails outside work hours, instead focusing on work-life balance and "acting your wage".
Yet, far from being just a talking point on TikTok, the Resolution Foundation said the findings in its report were "consistent" with the idea of quiet quitting.
The percentage of those surveyed willing to go the extra mile to help their employer has sunk from 69% in 2015 to 55% in 2025, according to their survey of 4,656 adults.
Meanwhile, those who were not even "fairly" satisfied with their roles has sunk to one-in-four, the lowest level on record.
In addition, workers are less likely than 10 years ago to say they have an interesting job, with 63% of those surveyed saying so, down from 74%.
"Workers today are indeed a little less committed to their employers, and a little less intrinsically drawn to work in general, than workers were a decade ago," the report added.
This shift over the last decade "may have contributed to weak productivity growth", which has slowed since the financial crisis and weakened again after the pandemic, the Resolution Foundation found.
Workers were also more focused on pay than in the past, which it said was "perhaps unsurprising... given the flatlining living standards of the past decade".
Sir John Curtice, politics professor and co-editor of the report, said the analysis does not mean that young people have "become more 'work-shy', nor have workers in general become more reluctant to change jobs".
"But if workers are to be fully engaged in their work, it has seemingly become more important for employers to provide jobs that are both financially rewarding and have flexible work hours," he added.

media.alt: BBC Your News banner

summary: Britons have become less engaged with the jobs they do and are less willing to put in extra effort, a report has found.

content:
Apple has said it does not know when it will get more of its new foldable iPhones back in stock as the company heads towards the key Christmas trading period.
The iPhone Duo sold out just over a week after its launch, despite being Apple's most expensive smartphone at a cost of nearly $2,000.
The company warned of "constraints" in sourcing key components and admitted it was "really hard to predict when supply and demand will be in balance".
Meanwhile, Apple's new chief executive John Ternus said the firm was seeing an "unprecedented" price rise in memory costs, including chips, as the artificial intelligence (AI) industry continues to invest billions of dollars in building data centres.
Ternus launched the Duo after he took over from previous boss Tim Cook in September.
It is the smartphone's first major design change in almost 20 years but some buyers have reported problems with the Duo's screen.
Last week, the company said it would replace any handsets that were affected by an issue that caused a "small number" to crack along the inside fold.
As it released its latest financial figures on Monday, Apple's executives did not mention any problems with the iPhone Duo.
Ternus said he was "thrilled" by the early reaction to the foldable phone. Chief operating officer Sabih Khan said the company was working hard to get the Duo "into the hands of our customers as quickly as possible".
Apple's results for the three months to 26 September did not include sales of the Duo, which was released at the end of October.
Nevertheless, Apple said it had sold more iPhones globally over the last year than ever before.
iPhone revenue for the quarter rose 17% to $57bn (£42bn).
Sales of Mac computers also grew over the three months by 27% to a record $10.7bn.
Overall, Apple's sales between July and September rose from $102bn to $114bn. Pre-tax profit also increased, from $32.8bn to $36.1bn.
However, sales for both the iPad and Apple's wearable products, including its headphones and watch, fell by 10% and 7%, respectively.
Khan said that most Apple devices were still experiencing supply constraints driven in part by difficulty in getting enough microprocessors with advanced nodes.
Those components are essentially computer chip technology that allow Apple devices to operate more quickly, most of which it has manufactured through TSMC, which is based in Taiwan.
Khan said the problem was expected to continue into next year, particularly impacting iPads and Macs.
The situation has been made worse by what the company has repeatedly insisted is "unexpected demand" for its products.
Ternus noted, too, that Apple is still seeing "unprecedented" cost increases for memory, or the ability of devices to store data like apps, photos and text messages.
Much memory storage runs through data centres, which have experienced a boom in demand for space as AI chatbots and platforms - including those developed by the likes of OpenAI and Anthropic - have become popular.
Watch: Would you buy Apple's $2,000 foldable phone?
Storage prices have gone up for tech companies like Apple.
Earlier this year, Cook referred to a sudden increase in data centre costs as a "thousand year flood".
Apple has lifted prices on nearly all of its hardware products by around 20%.
Sunil Krishnan from Aviva Investors told the BBC's Today programme that Apple posted "a reasonably solid set of results" with a "pretty good performance" from its iPhone business.
While there were concerns over the company's guidance on profit margins and the cost of memory chips, Krishnan added that in the broader context, "margins well north of 45% for a very well-established company, I think, are pretty impressive".
However, Apple's share price fell by 1.8% in after-hours trading.
summary: The tech giant reports strong sales but admits "constraints" are affecting supplies of the iPhone Duo.

content:
With more than $1 trillion (€900 billion) pouring into the artificial intelligence (AI) buildout, US tech giants are now competing with governments and companies in Europe for the same investment capital.
Four of the Big Five hyperscalers —  Amazon , Google  owner Alphabet, Meta and Oracle — have issued about $250 billion in bonds in dollars since the beginning of 2025, according to a tally of filings to US financial regulators by AI Industry Reviews, an independent platform that evaluates AI tools. They have sold a further €37 billion ($41 billion) of bonds in euros.
Recently, Microsoft, the last of the Big Five to hold back, joined the AI borrowing spree with a $25 billion bond sale, all in dollars.
Next year, Goldman Sachs projects that total new  AI hyperscaler bond sales are expected to reach $420 billion. About €60 billion will be issued in euros, according to Dutch bank ING.
Battle for investor capital heats up
That is unwelcome news for European companies and countries like  France , Germany and  Italy , whose sovereign bond yields have risen sharply in recent months and are already straining public finances.
With public debt at 119% of gross domestic product (GDP) and a deficit still running above 5%, France is already paying a sizable risk premium on its debt. Over the past six months, yields on French 10-year bonds have climbed from roughly 3.7% to nearly 5%.
The French government's interest bill is set to rise from €79 billion currently to €91 billion next year and over €100 billion by 2028.
Based on these figures alone, France's Finance Ministry needs to find tens of billions of euros in additional cuts, tax hikes, or more borrowing by the end of the decade.
Could France's debt crisis spread across Europe?
To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video
In August, economists at the European Central Bank said the euro bond market was adapting well to the presence of AI giants but warned they "could make it harder for other companies and other economic sectors to access finance."
Writing in a blog post, they also questioned whether the bloc's financial markets can "smoothly handle such large and concentrated debt inflows and warned of a "potential spillover to the sovereign and supranational segment of the bond market."
That means governments and international lenders such as the European Union and the European Investment Bank could also end up paying more to borrow.
'Bond abundance' helps drive up yields
Viktor Hjort, global head of credit strategy at the French bank BNP Paribas, described the phenomenon as "bond abundance."
Hjort told DW that the presence of the hyperscalers in the euro bond market is "already high enough to create competition" within the corporate sector and "between corporates and governments for available fixed income funds." These are investment funds that mostly buy bonds, which pay regular interest.
Bond yields jumped again last month, driven by rebounding energy prices linked to the Iran war and France’s political crisis, which Hjort said further revealed the growing competition for capital, as government and company borrowing costs rose together.
Normally, nervous investors move into government bonds during uncertain times, which pushes their borrowing costs down.
AI is much hyped, frequently feared, and possibly overrated
To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video
European companies could also feel more pain
Goldman Sachs warned last week that rising interest costs were starting to hurt earnings at European companies. Among firms in the Stoxx 600 — an index of 600 large, mid-sized and small companies across Europe — Goldman found that interest costs as a share of sales have risen by nearly half since 2022.
The bank's analysts said this had cut earnings by more than 5% over the same period.
Factor in the competition from AI bonds, and European firms could now face pressure to cut their investments in new plants, equipment and research, as well as shareholder payouts, to prioritize loan repayments.
Regional governments paying the price for AI
The pressure doesn't stop at national governments. Europe's cities and regions, whose borrowing helps to fund schools, transport and infrastructure, may also feel the effects of the AI boom.
A study for the Organization for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD), published in January, compared local bond markets in Belgium, Germany, Spain, Sweden and Canada. Where AI was spreading fastest, measured by the share of AI-related job vacancies, borrowing costs for cities and regions tended to rise.
"Whereas in the United States, my research has found that AI investments are linked to a lower cost of borrowing for municipalities, the opposite appears to hold in several European countries," the study's co-author, Christos Makridis of Arizona State University's W. P. Carey School of Business, told DW.
While AI bonds are far from the sole cause of Europe's widening fiscal strains, US Big Tech's huge appetite for capital could add further pressure next year, due to the additional billions in new bonds planned.
The irony is that European taxpayers could end up paying more on their own governments' debt, partly to help finance an AI boom across the Atlantic.

Audit Wales has criticised the lack of progress made by organisations in tackling climate change
Published
A spending watchdog has strongly criticised the lack of progress made by public sector organisations in tackling climate change.
Audit Wales says since a Welsh government "climate emergency" was declared, external in 2019, "decarbonisation" has become a lower priority for public bodies.
It says there are many examples of positive changes but the "collective ambition" for a net zero public sector in Wales by 2030 is unlikely to be met.
It has been estimated that it would cost at least £2.3bn to decarbonise Welsh council buildings alone.
The Welsh government said its 2030 ambition had "driven action and leadership, but it's clear that there is more work to do".
Net zero means balancing the amount of planet-warming "greenhouse" gases produced by human activities with the amount being actively removed from the atmosphere.
Effectively this means no longer adding to the total amount of these gases in the atmosphere to limit climate change.
In its new report, the spending watchdog said public bodies in all sectors recognise decarbonisation is important.
But it said: "Since 2022, financial and political pressures have caused decarbonisation to fall down the priority list.
"Public bodies told us their overall financial pressures mean they are struggling to invest in decarbonisation."
It criticised the Welsh government for not defining the "collective ambition" for net zero by 2030 as a "target".
"There are also no penalties or incentives to drive compliance. Some public bodies told us this had added to uncertainty around the level of priority to attach to carbon reduction."
On spending, it added that public bodies had made "limited progress" overall in understanding how much it will cost to decarbonise in the near or longer term.
"Where public bodies have estimated the longer-term cost, some described it as unaffordable."
Ann-Marie Harkin from Audit Wales said: "We can list positive examples, but not enough progress has been made overall, and we owe it to future generations to do better."
In 2017, the then-Labour Welsh government called for a net zero public sector by 2030, saying that public bodies were "uniquely placed" to influence emissions in areas such as buildings and transport.
The thinking was that if government-backed bodies made the switch and invested in infrastructure like electric vehicles and charge points, renewable power and heating systems, it would make it easier and cheaper for the public to follow suit.
The "collective ambition" does not require every public body to reach net zero individually by 2030 but it is meant to provide a shared direction of travel and an expectation that all public bodies contribute towards reducing emissions.
Responding to the report, a spokesperson for the Welsh government said: "A net zero public sector is a priority for Welsh government.
"We want to continue to support the decarbonisation of the public sector to lower emissions, energy bills and strengthen energy security.
"The 2030 ambition has driven action and leadership, but it's clear that there is more work to do on decarbonisation across and beyond the public sector in Wales."
The current Plaid Cymru government's ambition is for Wales, as a whole, to reach net zero by 2040 - which is ten years sooner than the current legally binding target for Wales and UK.
summary: A watchdog has criticised the lack of progress made by organisations in tackling climate change.
