content:
Kim Yo Jong, the sister of North Korea's leader Kim Jong Un
Published
North Korea has denied claims that it was behind the record $6.3bn (£4.7bn) hack of cryptocurrency exchange Binance, calling the allegations "absurd rhetoric".
Kim Yo Jong, a top Democratic People's Republic of Korea official and the sister of leader Kim Jong Un, said on Tuesday that the accusations are another "sinister attempt" by the US to damage Pyongyang's public image.
The US Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI), the Secret Service and cyber analysts have said North Korea orchestrated the hack, which has been described as the largest in history.
This is the latest hack to be linked to North Korea, which has been accused of relying on cyber-crime to help finance its sanctioned economy.
Blockchain analysts and the FBI have said the attack was led by state-backed hacking group TraderTraitor.
The FBI has called on industry partners to help block transactions involving cryptocurrency accounts linked to the group.
"The US has made a trite provocation of linking it with the Democratic People's Republic of Korea again," Kim Yo-jong, the director of North Korea's General Affairs Department, said in a statement.
"It is a grave political provocation against the DPRK that the US misleads the international public opinion as if all the cyber crimes in different parts of the world are our deeds," she said.
But Pyongyang has been blamed for a number of major cyber attacks in recent years - accusations that it has denied.
The TraderTraitor unit, which is also known as the Lazarus Group, was blamed for a then-record $1.5bn hack of crypto exchange Bybit in 2025.
Pyongyang has systematically built its cyber operations, recruiting promising students from universities and sending them to hacker units overseen by North Korea's intelligence agency, research groups like the S Rajaratnam School of International Studies think tank have said.
The country has consistently denied such claims.
Kim Yo Jong said "it is the consistent policy stand of the DPRK government to resolutely oppose all sorts of malicious acts in cyberspace".
Binance did not respond to the BBC's queries about North Korea's alleged involvement in the hack.
Since the incident, the crypto giant has largely focused its public statements on the technical nature of the breach and its response to protect users.
The company's spokesperson said that a net $4.72bn has been withdrawn from the exchange since transactions resumed on Sunday.
The net outflow represents a "relatively limited portion" of Binance's total assets, which stand at approximately $157bn, the spokesperson told the BBC on Tuesday.
That figure reflects the impact of the hack, subsequent withdrawals and market price changes.
"Withdrawal levels are stabilising to what we would consider normal and expected on-chain activity," she added.
The company said last week that initial checks indicated that an engineer's laptop had been compromised, enabling an attacker to make unauthorised withdrawals.
Trading in major cryptocurrencies on Binance has since resumed after the exchange worked with issuers to freeze assets impacted by the hack.
The company has repeatedly said it would cover all of the losses linked to the attack and that it has so far covered around 95% of the assets stolen in the breach.

media.alt: Kim Yo-jong, sister of North Korean leader Kim Jong Un, attends a wreath laying ceremony at the Ho Chi Minh Mausoleum in Hanoi, Vietnam, on Saturday, March 2, 2019.

summary: US government agencies and cyber analysts have blamed Pyongyang for the record-breaking heist.

content:
'I've always looked in bins for clothes'
Published
Darryl Baker was shocked to see piles of clothes dumped beside the recycling bins outside her local supermarket.
On several trips to the dumpsters she has also found a host of other items, such as "a perfectly decent" Ikea picture frame and children's scooters.
Always on the lookout for ways to save money and appalled by the waste, the thrifty mother-of-two from north London asked supermarket staff if she could take some of it.
Permission granted, "I got my children entire new wardrobes," says Darryl, 39, adding that she's stuff put away for years to come.
During a six-month stint this year, "I have probably saved hundreds of pounds," says the freelance journalist.
Darryl reels off the names of brands she has salvaged - Ralph Lauren, Nike and The North Face, among others. "My mind was blown," she says. "This stuff is just strewn all over the floor."
Darryl Baker takes the clothes for herself and her children, and to sell
In addition to finding clothing for her children and her nephews and nieces, she keeps some for herself. Others she donates or sells, including recently getting £30 for a men's Barbour jacket.
Darryl has joined the ranks of so-called dumpster divers – people who rummage through commercial bins for treasures. Motivations include saving money, giving items to charity and disgust at how often perfectly usable items are being consigned to waste - or a combination of all three.
'I'm a bit of a Robin Hood'
Texan Jeff Ferrell has been rooting around in trash for more than 50 years.
"I still dumpster dive every day by bicycle," says the 72-year old, who lives in Fort Worth, and has written books on the topic. "I still enjoy it as much, or more, than ever."
Jeff considers himself a "bit of Robin Hood mixed with anarchist direct action", only scrounging in more affluent neighbourhoods and giving away many of his finds.
"Almost everything in our home is scrounged, and I never buy, for example, soap or toiletries or medical supplies, or shoes and clothes and tools and garden supplies," he says.
Jeff Ferrell sells some of what he finds, and gives away other items
Jeff looks for discarded metal to sell at a scrapyard which, he says, earns him around $150 (£110) every two weeks. His wife sells his other finds, such as "an antique or piece of jewellery", on eBay.
Through savings and selling the more valuable items, he estimates his finds are worth "tens of thousands of dollars a year".
'If something catches my eye, I'll grab it'
While dumpster diving may have been considered taboo in the past, it's now something many people are proud to do and post about online.
Millie Diamond, a London-based stylist, posts videos on Instagram of her rummaging through bins. But she has a very specific aim - to unearth fabrics and clothing that she can salvage and refashion into new items, some of which she then sells.
Millie Diamond turns dumped textiles and clothes into new outfits
She estimates that one dress she found was worth £600.
"I'm a bit of a magpie. I like collecting things off the street or anywhere that there's a freebie. If I see something that catches my eye, then I'll grab it."
Millie, 36, began bin diving after spotting some fabrics discarded by a business that had shut down. "I literally clambered into the bin. It turned out it was loads of vintage clothes."
'I haven't bought shampoo for years'
For Charlotte Bayford in Essex it's all about timing. Her best finds come when students at Essex University head home for the summer and ditch anything they don't want to take with them.
This includes half-filled toiletries. "I haven't bought shampoo for eight years," says the 44-year-old sales assistant. "I'd say that has saved me some money."
Like other dumpster divers, Charlotte gives a lot of her finds to charity. But she has also filled her house with salvaged objects, and sells on some valuable items.
Food, as long as it remains sealed, is fair game too. "I've found tins of Heinz baked beans, perfectly fine. I'm quite happy to eat those," Charlotte says.
Charlotte Bayford gives some of her finds to charity
But is taking things out of bins and keeping them acceptable in the eyes of the law?
Jeff, who is professor emeritus of sociology at Texas Christian University, says many US cities have made the practice illegal, including New York, Cleveland and Wichita.
"Dumpster diving is considered illegal [in such places] because that which is thrown away now belongs to the city... or to the private company that provided trash services," he explains. Any dumpster diver also risks trespass charges.
In Fort Worth, where Jeff lives, items can only be removed from bins if they are on public land, external.
In the UK, Sunjay Versani of Duncan Lewis Solicitors says it depends on the circumstances.
"In many cases involving genuinely discarded goods, prosecution is unlikely," he says.
"But there is no general rule that something is free to take simply because it has been put in a skip or bin. If in doubt, the safest approach is to ask the owner or business for permission."

media.alt: Darryl Baker stands in front of piles of clothes on the floor by recycling bins at her local supermarket
Jeff Ferrell sitting on the ground, leaning against a wall
Millie Diamond sitting on top of a recycling bin
Charlotte Bayford looking at items in a commercial bin

summary: The men and women who rummage through commercial bins to take clothes and other items.

content:
This blog is now closed. It was a roundup of some of the top stories from and about Germany on November 3, 2026:
The 25th Berlin Security Conference is kicking off in the German capital
The conference will focus on the war in Ukraine and ways to counter growing Russian aggression against European countries
Justice Minister Stefanie Hubig has presented a bill that broadens the definition of sexual harassment and envisages higher penalties for sexual offenses
Conservative Bavarian Premier Markus Söder has called for a European-Arab free trade area during a trip to the United Arab Emirates
Another child has been reported injured by a sharp object hidden in Halloween candy
Thank you for reading
We are closing the blog. Thank you for reading!
We'll be back tomorrow again.
Prosecutors report arrest of Turkish man in connection with Starlink attack in Poland
Prosecutors in Germany on Tuesday announced the arrest of a Turkish man in connection with a fire set at a Polish Starlink station in late September.
Tuesday's arrest in the southwestern city of Reutlingen follows the October 12 apprehension of two further Turkish passport holders.
Prosecutors say the man is suspected of having "commissioned the two men arrested on October 12 with carrying out the arson attack in Poland."
Authorities believe he "arranged for the men to be driven to Poland by another female suspect on the night of the 22-23 September, in order to set fire to the terminal of a satellite internet service."
Police discovered eight cellphones as well as munitions at the suspect's home.
Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk has labelled the fire an "act of hybrid warfare" and his country is seeking extradition of those arrested.
The station targeted belongs to Poland's state-owned telecommunications company Exatel and is used by Elon Musk's satellite internet company Starlink, a key component of Ukraine's self-defense against Russian missiles and drones.
Poland, a NATO member state, has joined a growing chorus of European nations in accusing Russia of carrying out "hybrid warfare" on Ukraine's allies.
The station remained operational after the fire.
Merz meets Zelenskyy in Berlin, pledges winter aid for Ukraine
German Chancellor Friedrich Merz hosted Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy in Berlin on Tuesday, vowing continued support for Kyiv, while calling on Russia to take serious steps toward ending the war it launched in February 2022.
"We will continue our support until this war is over," Merz said during a joint press conference with Zelenskyy, emphasizing that the outcome "will shape European security for a long time."
Merz said Germany would provide Ukraine with aid over the winter, during which Russia is expected to heavily strike civilian infrastructure.
Germany's DPA news agency reported the additional winter aid is expected to total €200 million ($223.8 million).
Zelenskyy thanked Germany and Europe for support, saying that Ukraine would "not have survived" without it.
Amid US-organized talks planned in Abu Dhabi for next week including Ukrainian and Russian negotiators, Merz said he is doubtful Russia is serious about pursuing peace.
"It is important that Russia finally and seriously engages in negotiations about a ceasefire and a subsequent peace agreement," the chancellor said. "I do not see that happening so far."
"Our message to Russia is therefore clear: it is time to bring this war to an end," Merz said.
New gas-fired plants to be built as wind and solar energy backup
New gas-fired power stations are to be built across Germany by 2031 to supply electricity to the grid when wind and solar generation is not sufficient, according to plans announced by the Federal Network Agency on Tuesday.
The projects were selected through a tender process in which 41 bids were submitted.
Eleven of those were successful, with 10 going to energy giants RWE and LEAG or their affiliates.
The average contract price was said to be €155,296 ($173,829) per megawatt-hour, which results in annual costs of just over €800 million for the 11 power station projects.
Those costs are to be borne by all electricity consumers via a new levy that will raise prices, though it remains unclear by how much.
Initially, the new plants will be fired by natural gas, but it is planned that they will use climate-neutral hydrogen by 2045 at the latest.
The environmental organization Greenpeace has criticized the plan, saying that the government "continues to chain our country" to fossil fuel.
It said modern, environmentally friendly and increasingly cheap alternatives such as energy storage systems had been excluded from the first tender process.
The conservative Economy and Energy Minister Katherina Reiche has faced much criticism over her ties to the energy sector, her former field of work.
Merz reports progress on bill to stop Berlin Left's expropriation scheme
A bill that aims to prevent the Left Party from putting large private housing companies into public ownership in Berlin if it comes to power is making progress, Chancellor Friedrich Merz said on Tuesday.
"The bill is finished," Merz, the leader of the conservative Christian Democrats (CDU),said at an event organized by the Berlin Chamber of Industry and Commerce.
He said the only open question was whether 100% or 80% of the market value had to be compensated.
"I don't think I need to spell out that we favor 100% market value," he said.
His remarks come as the socialist Left Party, which emerged as strongest force in state elections in Berlin in September, is holding coalition talks with the Greens and center-left Social Democrats (SPD).
Move to reduce cost of rentals
An exploratory paper issued by the three parties includes plan to expropriate private housing companies with holdings of at least 10,000 apartments in Berlin, with some compensation also planned, though critics say it is too little.
The Left Party argues that offering the then state-owned apartments at lower rents would have a knock-on effect, reducing prices across Berlin.
Merz, for his part, said that such an expropriation in the German capital would have negative "repercussions as far as the capital markets in London, Paris and New York," saying that protecting property was a basic principle underpinning the economic order.
He said seizing companies in this way would severely damage the business environment, while failing to create jobs or housing.
However, it is in doubt whether the federal government can legally ban the planned expropriation, with Justice Minister Stefanie Hubig from the SPD among those expressing doubts about a general prohibition.
Another child injured eating Halloween candy
A second child has received slight mouth injuries after eating manipulated candy collected at Halloween, police in the northeastern city of Rostock said on Tuesday.
The child was said to have bitten on a needle hidden in the candy.
This comes after a 9-year-old girl in Bremervörde in the state of Lower Saxony also suffered injuries to her tongue from a 5-cm (2-inch) pin contained in a chocolate bar.
Police in several other states have also reported finds of sharp metal items in Halloween candy, with parents warned to carefully examine treats collected during trick-and-treating on October 31.
It remains unclear how the items came to be in the candy, but police are looking into the possibility that intentional physical harm was in play.
Bavarian Premier Söder calls for European-Arab free trade zone
Markus Söder, the leader of Bavaria's Christian Social Union (CSU) and premier of the southern state, has said Europe should establish a free trade area with Arab countries.
On the sidelines of a visit to the United Arab Emirates, Söder, whose party is allied with Chancellor Friedrich Merz's Christian Democrats (CDU), said, "I believe that further free trade areas are needed to facilitate all the investments that can be made there."
He said other Arab countries other than the Emirates would also be interested.
In September, the Emirati head of state, Mohamed bin Zayed Al Nahyan, announced investments worth up to tens of billions in Germany during a state visit, with €10 billion ($11.1 billion) intended for Bavaria.
Söder is to visit Qatar on Tuesday as part of his trip.
IN DEPTH: Ukraine's Zelenskyy to visit Berlin for talks
German Chancellor Friedrich Merz has announced that Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy will pay a surprise visit to Berlin on Tuesday.
The visit, which was kept secret for security reasons, comes as Zelenskyy is demanding more help from European allies to help defend his country against Russia's invasion as the US proves increasingly unreliable in this regard.
You can read more in this DW article: Ukrainian President Zelenskyy to make surprise Berlin visit this Tuesday, Merz says
First supermarket freezer attacks reported in Germany
Several media outlets are reporting that hacking attacks have targeted freezers in German supermarkets for the first time, causing them to heat up to 50 C (122 F) and thus damaging the food they contain.
One reported attack was at a supermarket in Lower Bavaria in southern Germany, while others were said to have occurred in the western state of North Rhine-Westphalia.
In one case, the attack was reportedly not directly on the supermarket concerned, but on the company that monitored the freezer systems remotely.
The attacks follow similar incidents in several other European countries, including France, Belgium, Estonia, Ireland, Luxembourg and Sweden.
So far, authorities have failed to identify the person or people responsible for the attacks.
Justice Minister Hubig presents bill on sexual offenses
A new bill put forward by Justice Minister Stefanie Hubig envisages tightening law on sexual offenses, among other things by criminalizing verbal sexual harassment and raising penalties for gang rapes.
According to the bill, "anyone harassing another person with a sexually meant utterance or gesture that could intimidate or pressure them" could face criminal charges.
The bill thus seeks to make "catcalling" an offense, although the bill does not use this term, as Hubig's ministry argues that the word is controversial and trivializes the act.
The draft legislation would also make gang rapes punishable by a prison sentence of no fewer than five years, while sexual assaults or sexual coercion carried out by several perpetrators would bring a minimum sentence of three years rather than the current two.
Under the provisions of the bill, limitation periods would also be set uniformly at 20 years for gang rapes and sexual assaults.
Currently, the period can be as short as five years in some cases.
"Sexual harassment and sexualized violence are a massive problem and are part of everyday life for too many woman," Hubig said.
She said "red lines and punishments" were needed to make offenders realize that "sexual offenses are unacceptable," whether physical or verbal in character.
"No matter whether at home, online or on the street and squares — women have to be safe from assault," she said.
Berlin Security Conference kicks off
The two-day Berlin Security Conference is kicking off in the German capital for the 25th time on Tuesday.
This year, the focus will be on what many see as the biggest challenge toRussia's war in Ukraine European peace for decades: the threat of Russian aggression as reflected in its invasion of Ukraine and hybrid attacks on other European countries.
The conference's partner country this year is Lithuania, a country that shares an uncomfortable border with Russia and fears greatly for its own security.
Lithuanian President Gitanas Nauseda is to open the event and later to meet with Chancellor Friedrich Merz, with not just security issues but also Lithuania's upcoming presidency of the Council of the European Union on the agenda.
The program for the conference also includes a speech by a still unnamed "special guest" to be held mid-morning.
The conference has been taking place annually since 2001.
Welcome to our coverage
Guten Tag from DW's newsroom on the banks of the still-languishing Rhine River in Bonn!
Today, we will be looking at what comes out of this year's Berlin Security Conference, where European lawmakers, military figures and security authorities will discuss the threat emanating from Russia as it continues its invasion of Ukraine.
We will also focus on a bill envisaging a wider definition of what constitutes a sexual offense and harsher penalties for those guilty of perpetrating them.
And there has been another report of a child's being injured from eating Halloween candy.
You can read about these stories and more in our updates from the heart of Europe.
summary: A security conference in the German capital is addressing defending Europe against threats from Russia. Meanwhile, Germany's justice minister wants to raise penalties for sexual offenses. DW has more.

content:
The Shetland Isles previously had many army, naval and RAF personnel stationed across the isles
Published
Calls are being made for the defence of the Shetland Isles to be strengthened after increased sightings of Russian trawlers off the coast of Scotland.
Recent analysis by the Daily Telegraph, external also revealed that there have been more than 500 incidents where Russian boats have been stationed above undersea cables linking Britain with Europe and the US.
These cables carry the majority of telecoms data abroad.
The growing importance of undersea infrastructure prompted a parliamentary report, external last year to warn of security vulnerabilities in areas including transport and supply chains, financial services and payment systems.
There are also concerns that the £30m SaxaVord Spaceport in Shetland could be a Russian target.
But do the Shetland Isles really need better protection by the military?
Why are there concerns now?
A Russian vessel was suspected of damaging an undersea telecoms cable running from Helsinki to Estonia
In recent years there have been a number of incidents in the Baltic Sea where underwater cables have been damaged or completely cut.
In December last year, Finnish police detained a vessel sailing from Russia, which was suspected of damaging an undersea telecoms cable running from Helsinki to Estonia, across the Gulf of Finland.
In 2022, Shetland was cut off from the mainland after a nearby subsea cable was damaged.
And last year there were two cable breaks in Shetland, which disrupted internet services and, in one case, took weeks to repair.
There has been no suggestion that there was any Russian involvement in the Shetland incidents but they demonstrate how fragile the cables are and show the devastating effect on the islanders when they are damaged.
In July, Royal Navy warships and helicopters spent 21 days monitoring Russian activity in UK waters and the North Atlantic - this was a 25% increase on previous time spent monitoring.
The recent Telegraph revelation of more than 500 incidents where Russian boats have been stationed above undersea cables has also caused concern.
What is the history of Shetland's defences?
History teacher and tour guide Jon Sandison said military presence in Shetland reduced in the second half of the 20th Century
Jon Sandison, a high school history teacher and Shetland tour guide, said there were real concerns that Shetland could be attacked after Germany invaded Norway in 1940, during World War Two.
"Shetland could have been a stepping stone towards Orkney and mainland Scotland," he said.
There were many army, naval and RAF personnel stationed across the isles and coastal defences were built to defend Lerwick and the rest of the archipelago.
The SaxaVord Spaceport sits on a former RAF base and RAF Skaw played an important role in efforts to detect enemy aircraft from 1941.
RAF Saxa Vord was later involved in Nato's radar network to monitor Soviet activity during the Cold War.
The radar station closed in 2006 but it was revived in 2018 for Arctic surveillance as an automated remote radar head.
Sandison said that while military presence reduced in the second half of the 20th Century, Shetland's geographical position would never change.
"Where we are in the UK is always going to be a pivotal geographical location in relation to the North Sea, the Arctic Circle and wider scope of Britain," he said.
He added that coastal infrastructure was built very quickly during the Second World War.
"Air raid shelters, anti-aircraft defences - it's remarkable how much was built in a short space of time," he added.
"Not much of the infrastructure remains. It's part of our history, and part of our past."
What are the politicians saying?
MP Alistair Carmichael has urged the UK government to step up efforts to protect critical infrastructure
First Minister John Swinney has accused the UK government of leaving "Scotland's vast coastline dangerously exposed".
He pointed to waters off Shetland as an area of significant Russian activity.
"I don't think we've got nearly the presence in those areas that we require today," he told BBC Scotland News.
Liberal Democrat MP Alistair Carmichael, whose constituency covers Shetland, has urged the UK government to step up efforts to protect critical infrastructure.
He told the BBC's Radio Scotland Breakfast programme: "This is something we do need to be taking seriously.
"We're not expecting an imminent problem here but this is a time where the government is already telling us that we should all be keeping baked beans and a wind-up torch in a cupboard."
Carmichael added that if the world had changed so much, some of the decisions made by the UK government to remove military presence from the northern isles may now need to be looked at again.
He said that over the last 20 years, there had been just one local full-time soldier running a reserved unit in Shetland but they were now managed from the Scottish mainland.
Carmichael said there should be restoration of a full-time presence to support the unit and more reserves should be recruited in the northern isles as numbers were low.
But he added: "If the signal that the government is sending the community is that we don't even think its important enough to send one full-time solider to run these units then you can't expect the community themselves to be particularly enthusiastic about it."
What is the significance of the spaceport?
SaxaVord in Unst is the UK's first fully-licensed spaceport
SaxaVord in Unst is the UK's first fully-licensed spaceport with several companies interested in using the site to launch small satellites into orbit.
In September, the UK government announced investment of £30m in the project, as part of a new £7.8bn space strategy.
Alistair Carmichael said the spaceport would draw more attention to Shetland as a significant asset.
The German and UK governments plan to use SaxaVord to deepen their co-operation on space.
In October, Prime Minister Andy Burnham and Chancellor Friedrich Merz met in Berlin and announced plans to work more closely on economic growth, defence and technology.
SaxaVord Spaceport was identified as a focus for immediate work on European launches.
Two German companies are currently in a race to be the first to test a rocket in Shetland.
Chief executive Scott Hammond said: "The space strategy is absolutely critical.
"We're at the heart of the UK government's plans for assured access to space.
"That's also for our economic and Nato partners."
He added that the UK government had joined as one of its majority investors, with a member on the board, but stressed that SaxaVord Spaceport was still a private commercial company.
What has the MoD said?
A Ministry of Defence spokesperson said: "We are clear-eyed about the threat Russia poses.
"Through the UK-led Joint Expeditionary Force, we are leading allied activity across the High North, strengthening Nato's northern flank and increasing our ability to respond rapidly to emerging threats.
"This government is also investing in the capabilities needed to meet those threats, with £1.5bn backing Atlantic Bastion to deliver a next-generation Hybrid Navy and a further £330m to strengthen the protection of critical undersea infrastructure."

content:
The zeptoverse explained by BBC science correspondent Pallab Ghosh
Published
Scientists have picked up signals from the smallest scale of nature ever explored – 100 billion times smaller than an atom.
A world so small that some physicists have nicknamed it the zeptoverse.
The research, led by scientists based in Cambridge, was obtained from an experiment at the Large Hadron Collider (LHC).
This vast machine at the European Laboratory for Particle Physics (Cern) on the Swiss-French border smashes atoms together to break them apart and discover what is inside them.
The result is important because it could help researchers develop a new, more complete theory of how the Universe works.
Many sub-atomic particles are created by smashing the insides of atoms together
'Knocking on the door' of the zeptoverse
Dark matter makes up a large part of our cosmos, and yet researchers have struggled to detect it.
Scientists know it is there because its gravitational force influences normal matter, but in all other respects it has remained completely invisible.
So in this experiment, particles were smashed together at high energy and scientists studied the material that was thrown out - the shrapnel of collisions.
One of these is a sub-atomic particle - smaller than an atom - called a beauty quark.
The particle is unstable and exists for just one and a half trillionths of a second before breaking down into other forms - decaying.
Despite its short lifetime, researchers managed to detect it interacting with other tiny particles at a scale of a billion-trillionth of a metre.
Some theories suggest that at these scales particles are more sensitive to dark matter and it could influence how the quarks interact and break down. So, detecting activity in this tiny world could help scientists detect dark matter.
"We're knocking on the door of this zeptoverse," Dr Harry Cliff, of Cambridge University who led the analysis of the data, told BBC News.
He said this sub-atomic dance provided researchers with a ringside seat to the behaviour of possible new particles.
"And what we want to do now is go in and explore and find what new particles are waiting there. And to do that, what we need is more data," Cliff added.
Dr Harry Cliff is one of a team of British scientists involved in the research
The 28 countries involved in the project have agreed a £150m upgrade to this detector at the Large Hadron Collider (LHCb), which would increase the frequency of these decays tenfold.
"With that we can probe inside the zeptoverse and see what's waiting," Cliff said.
But last year the UK Research and Innovation (UKRI) agency, the government body in charge of research funding, announced that it was withdrawing its share of the money for the planned upgrade.
It later announced cuts to several other particle physics and astronomy projects this Summer, including Jodrell Bank's iconic Lovell telescope.
Although this research was led by scientists based in Cambridge, because of the cuts, Prof Tim Gershon, who leads the LHCb international collaboration, told BBC News that the UK's full involvement in the research would be in doubt.
"The UK is at risk of not being involved and making really major discoveries," he told BBC News.
"But I think the biggest long-term impact comes from the fact that the UK won't get the benefits from training young people who really are our greatest product."
Dr Mary Richardson-Slipper is questioning whether to continue her physics research career in the UK or find work abroad
Among those early-career researchers is Dr Mary Richardson-Slipper, who is part of the team that made the zeptoverse discovery. She is reconsidering her future in light of the physics cuts.
"I love being here in the UK, but I am looking at jobs abroad because that seems to be where there are more opportunities at the moment," said Richardson-Slipper.
She added that "lots" of her fellow researchers working in fundamental physics had already moved.
The cuts are being made despite an overall record increase in the science budget.
Prof Brian Cox, TV presenter and particle researcher at the University of Manchester, who is not part of the research team, described the result as "important".
But he condemned the recent decision to cut UK funding for the Cern project.
"It would be extraordinary to walk away from UK scientific leadership at this moment, damaging the future research programme and seriously damaging our hard-won international reputation," Cox said.
The UKRI told BBC News that it remained a fully engaged member of Cern as its second largest funder at around £175m per year.
A UKRI spokesperson said: "We sought independent advice and have taken forward an exciting portfolio of new infrastructure investments, which include projects in clean energy, medical imaging and cultural heritage.
"However, as usual, there were more exciting applications for funding than we were able to support."
Published28 October

content:
British government ministers were told not to engage formally with Vantara, the controversial mega-zoo run by the Indian billionaire Anant Ambani, after lobbying efforts by the private animal sanctuary in the run-up to a UK-chaired meeting on the trade in endangered species, according to documents.
This week, the UK heads a 32-country committee meeting in Geneva of Cites, the United Nations body that regulates trade in endangered species. The meeting will examine how India has responded to compliance concerns about imports of endangered animals.
Documents obtained by the Guardian and the news outlet Mongabay under the UK’s Freedom of Information Act reveal Vantara’s efforts to lobby British officials and ministers before the meeting.
Ambani, 31, is the heir to the oil and gas fortune of one of India’s richest men, Mukesh Ambani. He set up a 1,400-hectare (3,500-acre) private zoo near his family’s oil-refining facilities in Gujarat, where more than 150,000 animals have reportedly been amassed since 2022. Vantara boasts high welfare standards for animals in its care, including facilities such as an elephant hydrotherapy pool, where more than 260 elephants can also receive oil therapies and Ayurvedic massage.
But conservation groups have repeatedly questioned how such a vast number of species, many of which are endangered, were gathered so quickly. Last year, India’s supreme court cleared the zoo’s operators of any wrongdoing.
A subsequent Cites fact-finding mission looking into the zoo raised concerns about India’s compliance with international rules on animal imports in 2025. It recommended temporary restrictions on India, although the recommendation was later withdrawn.
Its November 2025 report said: “There is a need for caution to ensure that imports of large numbers of animals by these facilities are not inadvertently creating a demand for illegally sourced animals.”
In May, officials from the UK’s Department for Environment, Food and Rural Affairs (Defra) met a representative from Vantara and the US lobbyist firm Checkmate Government Relations, founded by Ches McDowell, a hunting friend of Donald Trump Jr.
Before the meeting, internal briefing documents said Checkmate was “seeking to persuade the UK to take a more sympathetic view of India’s handling of imports to Vantara and of Checkmate’s argument that responsibility for verifying legality sits primarily with exporting or re-exporting parties rather than with India as importer”.
During the meeting, the Vantara representative invited UK officials to visit the zoo – an invitation that was subsequently declined to ensure the impartiality of the UK’s Cites chair role.
After the meeting, a representative from another lobbying firm, Atlas Strategy, working on behalf of Vantara, approached the then secretary of state, Emma Reynolds, and then nature minister, Mary Creagh, also raising the prospect of a visit to the zoo.
When a department official asked for advice, a note was issued recommending that ministers did not engage formally with Vantara.
The government documents also reveal concerns about an application by Vantara to import falcons and falcon hybrids, after an unnamed organisation made a £50,000 “donation” to a breeder in the UK, whose identity was also not disclosed. British Cites officials classified the transaction as commercial, according to the documents. The falcons were not exported to India.
A spokesperson for Vantara said it had not imported falcons from the UK, nor had the zoo hired or paid a lobbying firm. It is understood that Checkmate and Altas Strategy were working pro bono for Vantara and not required to register with the Office of the Registrar of Consultant Lobbyists.
After recent scrutiny, Vantara has sought to “reset” its activities by voluntarily suspending animal imports for a year and hiring John Scanlon, a former Cites chief, to oversee its operations. In an interview with the Sunday Times this year, Ambani said he only brought animals to Vantara legally to ensure their welfare, mentioning a group of hippos he had saved from a hunting lodge in South Africa and jackass penguins saved from a shopping centre in Qatar.
“I think since I was a baby I have been taking care of animals. It’s always been a passion,” he said.
Vantara was used to host Ambani’s lavish pre-wedding celebrations in 2024, which were attended by celebrity guests and politicians. In September, Newcastle University awarded the oil heir a professorship of practice for “his work in conservation, biodiversity protection, animal welfare and environmental stewardship”, sparking a backlash from conservationists.
A Defra spokesperson said: “The UK has strict rules in place to protect endangered species and ensuring international wildlife trade is legal and sustainable, with every application assessed individually against internationally agreed and domestic requirements.”
Find more age of extinction coverage here, and follow the biodiversity reporters Rebecca Ratcliffe, Phoebe Weston and Patrick Greenfield in the Guardian app for more nature coverage.

content:
Supermarkets across Europe have been hit by a suspected cyber-attack affecting their fridges and freezers, and raising concern about the vulnerabilities of internet-connected hardware from industrial machinery to humble domestic appliances.
Smart devices which are connected to the internet can include fridges, central heating, and even washing machines.
And while that makes them easier to control remotely, in theory, any device which goes online can potentially be exploited by malicious actors.
However, that doesn't mean hackers can easily take control of it, and big brands generally go to great lengths to make sure their tech is secure.
Exploits have been found before in some devices. In 2015, researchers demonstrated how a vulnerability in a Samsung smart fridge could allow them to intercept internet traffic.
But there's no evidence domestic appliances are being targeted in the cyber-attacks which targeted supermarkets in November.
Ciaran Martin, former chief executive of the UK's National Cyber Security Centre (NCSC) says manufacturers needed to do more to make connected devices secure.
"There's a lot more that we need to demand of big tech to give us safer devices and products in the first place," he said.
He advised consumers to keep devices updated and enable multi-factor authentication wherever possible.
"I know it's a pain, but it only takes a few seconds," he said.
Since April 2024, UK law has required manufacturers of certain consumer smart devices to meet minimum cyber security standards, including requirements around passwords and security updates.
The NCSC said it was working with international partners and industry to understand the supermarket incidents, but it was unaware of any impact on the UK.
However, researchers from UK Cyber Defence have identified more than 800 refrigeration and building-control interfaces associated with British retailers that can be accessed over the public internet.
That doesn't necessarily mean they can be hacked, but it could leave them exposed to attackers exploiting weak passwords or software vulnerabilities.
The government has already held talks with senior food retailers about cyber resilience, following earlier attacks on supermarkets.
Helen Dickinson, chief executive of the British Retail Consortium, has said cyber incidents are a major concern for retailers, with businesses working alongside the NCSC to share intelligence and strengthen their defences.
It would not be the first time that hacks have raised concern about impact on food supply.
When UK supermarkets M&S and the Co-op were targeted by ransomware hackers in May 2025, the retailers struggled to stock some shop shelves with fresh deliveries.
Customers across the UK complained of empty shelves in the days following the attack.
Tom Hegel, a researcher at cyber-security firm SentinelOne, said retailers must be clearer about responsibility.
"The question retailers need to answer is who owns the security of that equipment, not just who repairs it," he said.
He said internet connectivity can make everyday technology more convenient, but security needed to keep pace.
"Once an attacker can operate those controls, legitimate functions such as defrosting become tools for disruption," he said.
"Changing a setting can destroy physical stock, not just interrupt a computer system."
Could cars, power plants and water supplies be vulnerable?
Outside of the home, connected tech is used to remotely manage industrial machinery and vehicles.
Cyber security expert Ken Munro pointed to a 2015 demonstration in which researchers remotely hacked a Jeep through its internet-connected entertainment system, prompting improvements in vehicle security.
"Fortunately, the vehicle industry woke up to this and fixed the problem," he said.
Mobile connections are also widely used to monitor equipment in power plants and water networks, allowing engineers to manage systems remotely.
Munro said UK utilities were generally good at securing these connections, but standards varied around the world.
His biggest concern was smaller, poorly funded utility companies which may still be relying on older, vulnerable equipment.
Without proper protections, "any factory or equipment" connected to the internet - ranging from carmakers to electricity or transport infrastructure - could face similar risks, said Olivier Daloy, a cybersecurity expert at Zscaler.

content:
The president of the International Ice Hockey Federation (IIHF), Franz Reindl, announced shortly after the decision by the Court of Arbitration for Sport (CAS) on Friday, that he had called a meeting of its main decision-making body for Monday and Tuesday.
The Lausanne-based court had ruled that the IIHF must allow Russian national teams to take part in ice hockey world championships again . They had been barred from doing so since shortly after Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022 .
"Our task now is to implement this ruling responsibly," said Germany's Reindl, who was elected IIHF president just last month.
"Several championships are only weeks away, and changes to participation affect many people; players, teams, organizing committees and host cities," he said. "We will work closely with all of them to find practical solutions."
The first tournament the CAS decision applies to is the World Juniors, to be held beginning on December 26 in Canada. Just how it will affect the tournament is not clear. Hockey Canada said it was in contact with the IIHF and had briefed Prime Minister Mark Carney's government on the decision.
Canada to 'maintain restrictions' on Russian athletes
Foreign Affairs Minister Anita Anand told public broadcaster CBC that she is "not comfortable" with allowing a Russian team to take part in the tournament in Alberta.
"This is a very unwelcome decision given the geopolitical situation, given the actions of Russia," she said. "All options are on the table, and I will say, again, I greet this decision with great disappointment."
Canada 's secretary of state for sport, Adam van Koeverden, appeared to rule out Russian athletes being granted visas for the tournament
"Canada will maintain restrictions on the participation of Russian athletes at events hosted in Canada that receive funding from the Government of Canada and explore further options to ensure that the Russian government is held accountable," he said in a statement.
German hosts mull 'possible consequences' for Worlds
Germany is also considering its options as it prepares to host the Men's Ice Hockey World Championship in Gelsenkirchen, Düsseldorf and Mannheim in May.
"The German government takes a very critical view of the decision by the Court of Arbitration for Sport, a government spokesman said on Sunday, according to the DPA news agency.
"The German government will discuss possible consequences of the ruling, including for the 2027 Ice Hockey World Championship in Germany, with the German Ice Hockey Federation (DEB) promptly."
The DEB's chief executive, Frank Lutz, is to travel to Berlin to discuss the matter with government officials this week. Speaking on broadcaster MagentaSport on the weekend, he conceded that surrendering Germany's hosting rights for the lucrative tournament was a possibility.
"I do not want to paint a black picture. I do not want to call the World Championship into question either. But of course, we at the DEB also have to consider the option of handing back this championship," he said.
Many disappointed, Russia delighted
Several other national ice hockey federations have expressed disappointment at the CAS decision, including those of Ukraine , Sweden , Finland , and  Czechia .
The International Olympic Committee opened the door for Russian athletes to return to international competition when it lifted its ban of the Russian Olympic Committee in July. However, the IIHF had already decided to continue to exclude Russian teams for the 2026-27 season – over security concerns. The CAS decision – handed down after an appeal by Russia – found this reasoning was insufficiently proven.
The Kremlin's reaction to the ruling was, unsurprisingly, positive.
"Russia is returning to world hockey. This place rightfully belongs to us, and discrimination in hockey has been brought to an end," Sports Minister Mikhail Degtyarev told state television channel Vesti.
Finland leading boycott movement
A boycott of the World Juniors, Men's World Championships or other tournaments by individual nations is now emerging as a real possibility.
"We are currently working to bring as many countries as possible into a united front to tell the IIHF that none of us will play against Russia under these circumstances," Finnish Ice Hockey Association boss Heikki Hietanen said in a statement released on the organization's website on Monday evening.
"Our stance is that we will not play against Russia as long as the war of aggression against Ukraine continues," added Hietanen, who is also a member of the IIHF Council.
By Tuesday afternoon, the Finland-led effort was gaining steam, with Sweden, Norway and Denmark making similar statements.
"The Three Crowns will not play Russia in coming world championship tournaments," Swedish Ice Hockey Federation boss Anders Larsson said in a statement.
This came shortly after Norway said it would not play Russia at the Men's World Championship and the Danish Ice Hockey Federation issued a similar statement on its website.
"Denmark will – based on the current situation and the information available to us today – not play against Russia at the World Championship in Germany in May 2027," it read. Denmark did not qualify for the World Juniors tournament.
Further-reaching implications?
There has been the suggestion, that having won this victory at the CAS, Russia's next focus could be on football, where its national and club teams remain excluded from international competitions.
Russian FA general secretary Maxim Mitrofanov told state news agency Tass that there "should be one rule for all."
World football's governing body FIFA allowed a Russia boys' team to play under its national flag in the inaugural Under-15 World Cup and Festival in Azerbaijan, which kicked off last week and ends on Saturday.
This article was originally published on November 2, 2026. It was updated on November 3 with the statement from the Finnish Ice Hockey Association. It was later updated with the statements from the Swedish, Norwegian and Danish federations.

事实上，就任总理之后，形势比人强，默茨的立场已经发生了变化。去年，默茨首次以德国总理身份访问华盛顿时，还曾对同特朗普开展合作充满信心。然而，一年半过后，这份信心几乎荡然无存。而同今年年初访华时的情景相比，现实也已经发生了很大的变化。总而言之，默茨对中美两国的措辞变得越来越强硬。柏林当然不希望发生贸易战，但也同样不能接受不公平的依赖关系。用来自柏林政治圈的话说就是，‘语气’已经变了，在 对华政策 问题上尤为如此。”
《商报》评论指出，敢于对中美两大强国“说不”，是默茨此次亚洲之行所发出的明确信号，而且也获得了盟友们的积极响应：
“不过，私下里也传出一些疑虑的声音。日本和韩国就很担心，德国和欧洲采取更为强硬的对华政策之后，会不会从整体上转向贸易保护主义，从而使日韩也陷入不利境地。 默茨 总理对这种担忧表示惊讶，也进行了必要的解释。但这也恰恰体现了此次亚洲之行的意义所在：只有通过密切的交流和沟通，才能发现彼此的顾虑和担忧，才能最终建立起经得起考验的伙伴关系。也只有这样，中等强国联盟战略才能充满活力。”
”出访亚洲是正确的选择“
内政危机不断加剧的关键时刻，总理默茨选择出访亚洲，因此在德国国内招致了“逃避现实”、“不务正业”的批评。《法兰克福汇报》评论写道：
“无论如何，默茨此次出行都是一个正确的决定。德国每四个工作岗位中，就有一个依赖出口，工业领域这一比例更是接近一半。中国咄咄逼人的贸易政策每个月都会导致德国流失1.5万个就业岗位。而与此同时，美国作为贸易伙伴也已不再靠谱。有鉴于此，德国经济急需同其他国家建立伙伴合作关系。德国总理亲自出马寻求伙伴，无疑是一件好事。
在德国，并不是所有人都意识到了‘ 中国冲击2.0 ’对德国繁荣构成了多么大的威胁。如果德国的经济前景得不到改善，后果将不堪设想。相比之下，工作45年后是否能拿到全额退休金，父母能休几个月的育儿假就都不是紧要问题了。在战争不断、危机四伏的当今世界，德国却仍在就如何捍卫社会福利制度而吵得不可开交，这简直让人感到不可思议。德国很少将对外贸易列为施政重点，而默茨正是通过此次亚洲之行，强调了对外贸易的重要性。
在基民盟内部，一些同经济界关系密切的人士对 默茨 总理的对华政策颇有微词。然而，当 中国 以补贴和压低汇率的方式冲击全球市场，将关键原材料当作地缘政治武器时，欧洲难道要袖手旁观吗？当然，欧洲人也不应矫枉过正，当前拟议中的‘欧洲制造’政策，同样也引起了默茨正在争取的东亚和东南亚国家的不满。除了各类强调友谊的宣言之外，这也是默茨此次带回柏林的重要信息。”

Los Angeles has become the largest city in the US to ban oil drilling, after years of lawsuits and campaigning by residents who raised the alarm over pollution and potential health risks from nearby wells .
"Front-line communities have pushed the city for a solution for this for over a decade," said local resident Wendy Miranda, who has campaigned for years with STAND-LA, a coalition of community groups working to end neighborhood oil drilling.
The ordinance, approved by the LA City Council on October 28, puts an immediate stop to oil extraction and bans the redrilling or deepening of wells. Existing operations must be phased out within city limits over the next 20 years.
Though LA City is only part of greater Los Angeles, the move affects hundreds of active wells and thousands of inactive ones, many located in working class communities of color.
"In South LA, working-class families have had corporations drilling across the street from their homes," said council president Marqueece Harris-Dawson in a statement. "No one should have to live near an oil drilling site."
Rock Zierman, CEO of the California Independent Petroleum Association (CIPA), told DW, "CIPA believes this ordinance constitutes an unlawful taking of private property."
LA follows much smaller Culver City, also in California, in moving against urban oil production, and begins the process of ending its long, complex relationship with fossil fuels.
Why residents campaigned to end city oil drilling
California's oil industry expanded rapidly in the early 20th century, when the state produced roughly a quarter of the world's oil. Lots of that so-called black gold was around LA and as the city grew, homes, schools and businesses were built around existing oil infrastructure.
Today, wells can be found beneath residential areas, close to playgrounds, along the coast and in some of the city's most densely populated and largely working-class neighborhoods. Some have been permanently sealed or plugged for decades, while others remain active or are idle.
Under California law, an idle well is one that has not produced oil for two years. Unlike plugged wells, they can potentially return to production.
How LA is plugging hidden oil wells

Residents living near the active and inactive wells report strong odors, headaches, nausea and breathing difficulties. Another concern is air quality. Oil wells can release toxic pollutants, including benzene and hydrogen sulfide, and research has linked proximity to oil extraction with higher rates of respiratory illness and reduced lung function.
But both active and idle wells can also leak methane — a potent greenhouse gas that contributes to climate change — while residents say occasional accidents or breakages send oil flowing down city streets.
"Frontline communities have been experiencing or have experienced for decades living near these toxic sites and having to pay for that with their health," said Miranda, a policy director with Esperanza Community Housing, a nonprofit providing affordable housing services.
Miranda told DW she and her mother both have asthma. The council vote "definitely represents hope," she added.
Previous attempts to ban oil production
LA City Council initially approved an ordinance to phase out oil extraction back in 2022 after successful lobbying by residents like Wendy Miranda. But oil companies challenged the measure in court, with industry groups successfully arguing that the city lacked the legal authority to impose the ban.
California subsequently passed legislation giving local governments greater power to regulate and restrict oil and gas operations, putting the possibility of a phaseout back on the table.
In an emailed statement to DW, CIPA CEO Rock Zierman said energy companies were prepared to challenge the new ordinance.
Zierman added that it would make city residents more dependent on foreign oil from countries with lower environmental standards when they are "already struggling" with high gas prices.
"It sends the jobs, investment and revenue elsewhere while leaving Californians to pay the bill," said Zierman.
The relationship between local oil production and prices at the pump is not straightforward and is influenced by a number of factors, according to the California Energy Commission, the state's main energy policy agency. Those include the cost of crude oil, refining, transportation, distribution and local taxes.
Even though the US is the world's largest oil producer, it exports and imports crude oil, as well as refined petroleum products. Because oil is traded globally, US residents are exposed to the same price fluctuations as people elsewhere, no matter how much of the fossil fuel is produced domestically.
California's oil industry and the amount of oil it produces have been steadily declining since the 1980s. In the coastal lowlands known as the LA Basin, output is 43% lower than eight years ago, with the amount of oil extracted falling more rapidly than the number of open wells.
Who will foot the bill for the cleanup?
When wells stop producing, it is up to the oil operators to remove equipment and plug them. The state agency that regulates oil and gas, CalGEM, and the LA fire department oversee plugging operations, and also seal wells for which no-one takes responsibility.
But many have not yet been plugged — some 80% of idle wells in LA have been inactive for more than eight years, and about a third for over a century.
The cost of plugging a well also varies widely, with estimates ranging from hundreds of thousands to millions of dollars. California law requires operators to submit plugging plans or face annual fines that increase with the amount of time the well has been idle.
But those fines aren't always paid. According to CalGEM's own data, the agency collected just $1 million out of $36 million (€32 million) in fines in 2025.
A report by Carbon Tracker also found that if all future profits from oil companies operating in California went to decommissioning wells, the state would still face a shortfall of $7 billion. The cost would by default fall to taxpayers, according to Carbon Tracker.
Miranda told DW that the next step for community activists is to reduce the 20-year timeline and have the oil sector "pay for this cleanup."  For now, she is says both she and her mother are hopeful that future generations "can have better health and breathe cleaner air."

British adventurer Karl Bushby, 57, arrived back his hometown in  England on Monday after crossing four continents on foot.
He was met by a cheering crowd of about 500 people in the northeastern city of Hull at the end of his 50,000-kilometer (31,000-mile) journey, which began in the far south of South America in 1998.
"I didn't do this alone. There was a big team, the biggest team, Earth. That's what it took to get me back," Bushby told the crowd.
On his trip, he obeyed two rules: to avoid all forms of motorized transport to advance; and not to return until he had finished what he had set out to do.
A very final leg of his journey was to take him to north Hull, where he was to reunite with his mother, Angela, his 36-year-old son, Adam, and a 12-year-old granddaughter he had never met.
What did Bushby experience on his epic journey?
Bushby, a former paratrooper, began his adventure in Chile aged 29 after a marriage breakup that saw his wife return to Northern Ireland with their son.
During the trip, he crossed an iced-over Bering Strait from Alaska to Russia with French explorer Dimitri Kieffer in 2006 — nearly losing his life in the process — and, returning to Britain early last month, he swam the English Channel from northern France to Dover over four days.
He interrupted, or was forced to pause, his journey several times, including when he was refused a visa by Russia , which caused a journey originally planned to take 12 years to last more than double that time.
He also spent some jail time in Panama for entering the country without a visa.
The COVID-19 pandemic also caused delays, and he spent some time living at a base in Mexico.
But he always resumed the trek at the exact spot where he had left off.
The famous German filmmaker Werner Herzog is making a feature-length documentary about the journey entitled "Walk of Life."
In an interview with the AFP news agency from northern France in September, Bushby expressed apprehension about returning to a more normal life back in Britain.
"I've got to try and get established in the grown-up world again," he said.

"We are choosing between war and peace," Bulgarian Prime Minister Rumen Radev told voters ahead of Sunday's presidential election runoff between incumbent President Iliana Yotova, who opposes military aid to Ukraine and favors dialogue with Russia, and former caretaker Prime Minister Andrey Gyurov, who is regarded as staunchly pro-European and pro-Ukrainian.
With these words, it was clear that Sunday's runoff had turned into a kind of referendum on the country's foreign policy and stance on the war in Ukraine .
Now that the official results are in and it is clear that Iliana Yotova won the election decisively by 57.6% to Gyurov's 39.5%, Radev claims that Bulgarians have chosen peace.
But is it really as simple as all that?
First-round surprise
When the presidential election campaign began in Bulgaria on September 25, there did not seem to be any doubt about the outcome: Iliana Yotova was well ahead in the polls on 44.5%. Gyurov, her main rival, trailed far behind on 26.1%.
Yotova was backed by both the prime minister and his ruling Progressive Bulgaria party, which won an absolute majority in the parliamentary election on April 19.
But the first round turned out to be much tighter than anticipated.
While Yotova got 34.8% of the vote in the first round, Gyurov was close behind on 31.95%, which meant that a runoff between the two was necessary.
Decisive victory, clear divide
While Yotova won the runoff convincingly, both the campaign and the outcome showed that the Bulgarian electorate is divided.
This division is both generational and geographical, explains Dimitar Ganev, sociologist and political scientist at the Trend market and electoral research agency.
"Younger voters — those aged between 18 and 40 — favor Gyurov. Those over 40 tend to prefer Yotova," Ganev told DW. "It also appears that Gyurov dominates in the capital, Sofia. In smaller regional cities, other towns and villages, Yotova dominates decisively," he said.
'President of peace'
This divide was also evident during the campaign.
While Andrey Gyurov relied mainly on social media for his campaign, Yotova chose to speak mostly to supporters of Progressive Bulgaria in closed venues.
At such events, the war in Ukraine was always high on the agenda.
"As long as I am president, and if you place your trust in me, not a single Bulgarian soldier will go to Ukraine," Yotova declared at an election rally on October 6 — even though according to the Bulgarian Constitution, only parliament (not the president) has the authority to send troops abroad or declare war.
Throughout the campaign, she referred to her opponents as "warmongers" and described herself as the "president of peace."
"We won because we talked to people about income and about peace," Yotova said after the election.
Russia's war in Ukraine a major campaign issue
In this, she is similar to Prime Minister Rumen Radev.
When it comes to Ukraine, Radev regularly speaks of the need for peace and avoids calling Russia an "aggressor." Both Radev and Yotova oppose military aid to Ukraine and criticize European leaders for not making sufficient efforts to engage with Russian President Vladimir Putin .
Gyurov, on the other hand, has sharply criticized Russian aggression in Ukraine.
Appointed caretaker prime minister by Yotova in February, Gyurov in March signed a security cooperation agreement with Ukraine, provoking the disapproval of both Yotova and Radev.
The impact of drone attacks in the Black Sea
In the weeks leading up to the election, several ships in the Black Sea were hit by drones off the Bulgarian coast .
The European Council criticized Russia for the escalation, and the European Parliament called on the EU and its member states "to consider deploying an EU naval operation" there.
Prime Minister Radev, however, was not as equivocal, going no further than summoning the Russian ambassador and stating that "logic suggests that the outcome" of the attacks in the Black Sea "is to the advantage of the Russian Federation."
Just days before the runoff, he noted that "two ships were struck and sunk in Romanian territorial waters" after Romania had held Russia responsible for the attacks in the Black Sea .
"Many people think that once the aggressor is identified, the attacks will stop," he said, downplaying the Kremlin's responsibility. His remarks drew criticism from politicians and the media in Romania.
Yotova also did not name Russia as the perpetrator, instead saying during her campaign that she did not want to see "foreign flags in Bulgaria" — a clear reference to the Ukrainian flag, which has been displayed outside several institutions in Bulgaria as a sign of solidarity with the war-torn country.
How other voters voted
Most opposition parties, including the right-wing conservative GERB led by former long-serving Prime Minister Boyko Borisov, refused to field a candidate for the presidency, which is one reason why turnout on Sunday was less than 30%.
In the first round, the pro-Russian candidate Kostadin Kostadinov from the nationalist Vazrazhdane (Revival) party came third with 12.5% of the vote. According to Dimitar Ganev, around 70% of Vazrazhdane voters backed Yotova in the runoff.
To secure their support, Yotova targeted pro-Russian voters.
How Russian aggression is shaping Bulgaria's presidential election

"Russia is by no means an enemy of Bulgaria," she said in a podcast interview just two days before the runoff, adding "Russia is part of our history, and I very much hope that it will be a key factor in the future security architecture across Europe, including for us."
In the days leading up to the vote, some of her supporters began claiming that the opposition was preparing a "Maidan," a reference to the Ukrainian revolution of 2014 that culminated in the ousting of President Viktor Yanukkovych, who had close ties to Moscow .
"All of Gyurov's lackeys are speaking openly about inevitable protests. They're using prime time to stir up a Maidan. Every single one of them," Sonya Momchilova, who was appointed to the media regulator by Radev, wrote on Facebook on Sunday.
Similar claims were made by both  former Hungarian Prime Minister Viktor Orban and former Serbian President Aleksandar Vucic ahead of this year's elections in their countries.
Bulgaria in the EU and NATO
"This claim that Ms. Yotova will be a president of peace is directly linked to the incitement of a fear of war," said former Defense Minister Todor Tagarev, who was part of the committee that nominated Andrey Gyurov for president. "Bulgaria will be in a much worse position within Europe and NATO under her leadership," he said during a TV interview.
Dimitar Ganev, on the other hand, sees no threat to Bulgaria's commitment to the EU and NATO . "Over two-thirds of Bulgarians do not question the country's geopolitical orientation, and around two-thirds have a positive attitude towards the EU," he told DW.
But the positions of Radev and Yotova, which many view as ambivalent , mobilized both the pro-European camp and Eurosceptic voters, who, according to Ganev, make up around a third of the country's population.
According to Prime Minister Rumen Radev and President Iliana Yotova, the Bulgarian people chose peace in the presidential election. Nevertheless, the war continues.
Edited by: Aingeal Flanagan
